en: Homage to him who bears a digit of the moon— a digit that seems as if it has trickled down from the steady radiance of Gaurī’s cheek. (1) The Chapter on Conduct (Ācārādhyāya).

Victorious is he, by whose ascetic heats— which consist of the orb of light of the ever-active *cintya* and others, and which burn with the *sāman* and *yajus* chants— he gathered the white *yajus* mantras from the abode of the Creator.
Victorious is the meaning of the Vedas, which has its roots firmly established in the Vedas, whose branches are purifying, whose trunk is the great sacrifice,
which bears the flowers of the three aims of life, and yields the fruit of liberation.

Through its powers of illusion, it perceives the one Indra as many-formed; it awakens even that which is asleep, and knows that which is far-reaching, luminous among lights—may that mind of mine be of auspicious intent. (4)
Having bowed to the Sun, the Great Naga, and likewise to Tilakasvāmin and Vināyaka together with the excellent cows,
this Smṛti is illuminated by me.

This *Dharmaśāstra* of Yājñavalkya, beginning with the words "Yogīśvaram," is now introduced with the desire to provide a commentary upon it. For the exertion involved in exposition and the like has great purpose when directed toward that which is the cause of prosperity (*abhyudaya*), and this treatise is such a cause. Thus says the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "One's study and teaching of the Veda become dear; one becomes disciplined in mind; day by day one accomplishes one's goals without being dependent on others; one sleeps happily; one becomes the supreme physician for oneself; and there is restraint of the senses, one-pointedness, growth of wisdom, fame, and the ripening of the world [through virtue]" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 11.5.7). Here, the mention of "teaching" (*pravacana*) should be understood as an illustration that includes the composition of a book and other such activities. But how can the treatise be the cause of prosperity? This must be explained at the very outset, because it constitutes the purpose of the treatise; for it is an established principle that the purpose must be stated at the commencement of every treatise. And so he says:
"For indeed, of any treatise whatsoever, or even of any action, as long as the purpose has not been stated, by whom would it be undertaken? (ŚVār 1.12).

Although some consider the statement of the subject matter, the purpose, and the connection to be somewhat superfluous—on account of the meagerness of the purpose and the difficulty of establishing them—nevertheless, out of some friendship, a mere indication is shown. And therein:
The subject matter is indicated by the verse, as is the purpose called "Dharma";
the fourfold aims beginning with that [purpose], and the relationship which consists of necessity.

The subject matter (*viṣaya*) is, first of all, "Tell [me] the dharmas," as indicated by the verse, and it is *dharma* because of its designation (*samākhyā*). The purpose (*prayojana*), however, consists of *dharma*, wealth (*artha*), pleasure (*kāma*), and liberation (*apavarga*). Likewise, because it is characterized by its opposite, *adharma* is also a subject matter; and following from that, *adharma*, non-wealth (*anartha*), suffering (*duḥkha*), and bondage (*bandha*) constitute the purpose. This group of eight, consisting of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, is understood through this very treatise as having the nature of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*); this is the restriction, which constitutes the connection (*saṃbandha*). Even though wealth and pleasure are determined through perception, their attainment does not occur directly for those who do not rely on the scripture, and it is only when attained directly that they function as a purpose. Therefore, there is no fault. But how can both the subject matter and the purpose belong to the same single *dharma*? This is not a flaw, because that which is being understood is the subject matter, while that which has been understood is the purpose. For something does not become a purpose if it fails to attain the status of being the subject matter of the scripture through the process of being understood. [Objection: If this were so, then wealth, pleasure, and liberation would not be the purpose of the scripture, since they are not its subject matter. [Reply: If you say they will also be subject matters, we say no, because they are not explicitly mentioned. [Objection: Since the word *dharma* is used figuratively (*upalakṣaṇa*), they are indeed included. [Reply: No, because that is already established by the literal sense of the word itself. Alternatively, one must either abandon the status of wealth and the others as purposes, or accept that they are not subject matters. To this it is replied: The purpose of actions is twofold—based on a causal factor (*kāraka*) and not based on a causal factor. Among these, that which is based on a causal factor does not become a purpose without attaining the status of being a subject matter. Nor can it be argued that it is not a subject matter due to a difference in form.
Just as rice grains, in the states of being softened and having been softened,
do not undergo differentiation because they are not distinct from the substrate, even though they possess various forms.

Even though the state of being cooked rice does not exist while the grains of rice are still softening, there is no fault, because the status of being an object is established since the nature of the rice-grains has not been lost. Furthermore, that which is not the locus of an action becomes a purpose (*prayojana*) precisely without attaining the status of an object; for example, heaven is the purpose of the sacrifice, and the acquisition of wages is the purpose of cooking and so forth. Thus, just as with cooked rice, dharma possesses both the status of an object and a purpose; and just as with the acquisition of wages, wealth and the like possess the status of a mere purpose. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Alternatively, wealth and the like also possess the status of being objects of the treatise (*śāstra*), for it will be stated thus:
"One should not neglect dharma, artha, and kāma according to one's capacity" (YDh 1.114).
Therefore, women should be enjoyed. "And one should resort to a lord for the sake of accomplishing acquisition and preservation" (YDh 1.99).
Likewise,
one should perceive the self as imperishable.

And so forth. As for the argument that [the word *dharma*] is not explicitly specified, that has been refuted by the fact that the term *dharma* is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). But how can there be an illustrative sense when a literal meaning is possible? For the opening statement does not follow the concluding one. It is said in reply: We do not say that the opening statement follows the conclusion. What then? This is understood from the opening statement itself, because of the qualification "Lord of Yoga" (*yogīśvara*). Indeed, that qualification is for the sake of knowledge regarding the four aims of life (*caturvarga*), since dharma is the primary among them; therefore, it was stated as "dharmas" (in the plural). Thus, it is established that objects such as wealth (*artha*) and the rest also constitute the subject matter and the purpose. By this, the other three of the four aims are also explained.

Furthermore, how is the justification for this restriction—that this group of eight [aims of life] is understood from this very treatise alone—established? For if all of this is understood from the Veda itself, and it is then claimed that it is also understood from this [treatise], even so, the restriction remains untenable. Moreover, pleasure (*kāma*) and wealth (*artha*) are indeed cognizable through other means of knowledge. As for the claim that they are "directly" known from the treatise, that too is incorrect; for it cannot be said that the desire born from approaching another's wife is false. Furthermore, for one who regards liberation—which is of the nature of bliss—as the goal because it is the cause of suffering, even dharma would not be a human aim (*puruṣārtha*), since it consists of bondage.

This is not the core point. We do not deny experience; rather, it was stated that [worldly objects] are not the goals of man (*apuruṣārtha*) because they are causes of suffering. For those of refined intellect do not seek objects that are accompanied by suffering. Nor is conduct performed without prior reflection subject to critical inquiry. Therefore, it is said: "Because of the understanding of bliss derived from the scripture (*śāstra*), wealth (*artha*) and pleasure (*kāma*) are scriptural goals. Furthermore, for one who follows the scripture, dharma, wealth, and pleasure are truly human goals (*puruṣārtha*) because they are sought after and are not accompanied by suffering. And how they do not constitute obstacles to liberation (*apavarga*), we shall explain in the exposition of liberation. Moreover, this being the case, the cognition obtained through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is not contradictory. As for the objection that a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is untenable because of the understanding derived from the Veda, that is not a valid criticism, because this very scripture is itself regulated by its very basis in the Veda. For the exclusion [of worldly objects] is in relation to other means of knowledge, not in relation to the Veda, since the traditional scripture (*smṛti-śāstra*) is dependent upon that [Veda]. And thus says the *Svāyaṃbhuva*:

"For those desiring to know *dharma*, the supreme authority is the *Śruti*" (MDh 2.13). Furthermore, the word *dharma* is intended by the Blessed One as an indicator for the four aims of life (*caturvarga*). This very Veda, according to whether it is directly perceived or not, is denoted by the terms *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. Therefore, it is rightly said that from this very scripture, all prosperity (*abhyudaya*) is attained through the comprehension of these eight categories; enough of this digression.
But why, then, does the Blessed One exert himself in composing this treatise regarding a matter already established by the Veda? Because:
Having honored Yājñavalkya, the Lord of Yoga, the sages said:
"Tell us completely the duties of those belonging to the castes and stages of life, as well as others. (1.1)

Since even the sages who know the true essence of the Veda approached him with full reverence and spoke out of a desire for instruction, it should be understood that this effort of the Blessed One was undertaken in accordance with their request. And this is appropriate, for such persons are worthy of being taught. Thus Manu has said:

"The son of the teacher, one who is obedient, a giver of knowledge, righteous, pure, capable, a giver of wealth, one who seeks [instruction], a kinsman, and a virtuous man—these ten are to be taught according to dharma" (MDh 2.109).

But why did they speak with such effort? Because they considered him a lord of yogis (*yogīśvara*), and because of his lineage as Yājñavalkya, he was worthy of being taught due to his high birth. Thus says Āpastamba: "Therefore, one should seek a teacher who is distinguished by both learning and noble birth" (ĀpDh 1.1.2). And it is appropriate that the sages posed questions to Yājñavalkya, who possessed such excellence of qualities, for even those who have known the true nature of reality may sometimes experience doubt. As Vyāsa has said: "Even by one who has understood the true meaning of the Vedas and practices the duties..."
"To ensure there is no doubt, some degree of proximity to the Guru must be maintained. Thus it is said.

Alternatively, even those who possess knowledge may, being characterized by a lack of confidence, follow someone of great renown in the capacity of disciples in order to establish their own reputation; or they may ask out of a desire to know: "What is the cause of this fame for him as a lord of yogis? In any case, since a question is appropriate and those who have approached must necessarily be taught, there is no ground for reproach. As it has been said: "But one should explain [the truth] to one who has approached. What, then, did he not say? It is replied: Wealth (*artha*), pleasure (*kāma*), and liberation (*apavarga*) would then not be the subject matter of the treatise, because they were not asked about. Furthermore, since *dharma* is a singular entity, the plural form *dharmān* (laws) is indeed improper. Nor is it correct to claim that this plural is intended to include various types of *dharma*, for that would result in the redundancy of the other word *aśeṣataḥ* (without remainder). This is not a fault, because the word *dharma* was stated as an inclusive term (*upalakṣaṇa*). Otherwise, the title "Lord of Yogis" (*yogīśvara*) would not be justified. If it were argued that the title is for the sake of praise (*stuti*), that too is incorrect; for it is not proper that something connected to the action (*kārya*) should be a mere matter of praise. Let us grant that it is connected to the action; nevertheless, it must be explained how it functions as an inclusive term. To this it is said: it would seem inconsistent to say that those who consider him a Lord of Yogis are asking about *dharma*, because yogis are already knowers of *dharma*. Among them, the Lord—the best among the knowers of Brahman—is the teacher. And he should be questioned about Brahman itself, not about *dharma*. But surely, even a knower of *dharma* is in the ultimate sense a Lord of Yogis. Does he not also know wealth and pleasure? We do not say that he does not know them; rather, the designation "Lord of Yogis" is used here with the intention of referring to him as a knower of *dharma*. This is not tenable. The opening term "Lord of Yogis," whose existence depends on the concluding term "laws" (*dharma*), cannot be restricted to a specific meaning when it is contradicted by that term. Nor, this being the case, should it be concluded that the question concerns only liberation, given the omniscience of the Lord of Yogis and the justification of the plural "laws. Moreover, if the question were only about *dharma* or only about liberation, the entire treatise would be inconsistent, as all four aims will be discussed later. Furthermore, such an interpretation favors the majority of the subjects. Moreover, even the primary terms "Lord of Yogis" and "laws" have their capacities obstructed by mutual contradiction and are thus weak. And in this way, the wide scope of the treatise is preserved. Enough of this digression.

Thinking him to be such a lord of yogins, they spoke to Yājñavalkya. According to the Purāṇas, Yājñavalkya is a son of Brahmā; thus he is his offspring. How did they speak? Having honored him. Here, "honoring" (pūjā) should be understood as characterized by approaching him for instruction (*upasadana*) and so forth, because the prefix *sam-* has the sense of "properly" (*samyak*). The sages (*munayaḥ*) are those who know the meaning of the Vedas. The connection is: "Tell us, without omission, the duties (*dharmān*) of those other than the [four] castes and stages of life. The castes (*varṇāḥ*) are the Brāhmaṇas and so forth. The stages of life (*āśramāḥ*) are the student (*brahmacārin*) and so forth. Those other than the castes (*varṇetara*) are those born in between, such as the *anuloma* offspring. Those other than the stages of life (*āśrametara*) are the heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*) and so forth. "Of those other than the castes and stages of life"—the meaning of the verse is: "Tell us the scripture that sets forth the eightfold group consisting of complete worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*). It is expressed in this way because it is impossible to state the duties and so forth exhaustively. Furthermore, "tell" (*brūhi*) is a request, given the venerable one's status as a teacher. "Without omission" (*aśeṣataḥ*) means "in its entirety. The word "from the Veda" (*vedāt*) is to be supplied. Or rather, the Veda itself is called "without omission" (*aśeṣa*) because it has nothing else remaining as a remainder. Therefore, the meaning is: "For the sake of favoring us, tell us the duties without omission. There is another reading: "of the castes together with the stages of life" (*varṇānāṃ sāśramāṇām*). Here too, the meaning is the same. Even those born in between (*antaraja*), such as the *anuloma*, are indeed castes, as Manu says: [Manu 10.4] "The offspring of a Brāhmaṇa from a Śūdra woman is a Pāraśava; from a Vaiśya woman, a Vaiṇa; from a Kṣatriya woman, a Māgadha; these are the three born in the direct order (*anuloma*). [Manu 10.5] "From a Kṣatriya, a Niṣāda is born from a Śūdra woman, and a Sūta from a Vaiśya woman; from a Brāhmaṇa, a Ratha-kāra is born from a Vaiśya woman, and an Āyogava from a Kṣatriya woman. [Manu 10.6] "From a Vaiśya, an Ambaṣṭha is born from a Kṣatriya woman, and a Māhiṣya from a Brāhmaṇa woman; from a Śūdra, an Ugra is born from a Kṣatriya woman, and a Kṣattṛ from a Vaiśya woman. [Manu 10.7] "From a Śūdra, a Pukkasa is born from a Kṣatriya woman, and a Śvapāka from a Brāhmaṇa woman; from a Vaiśya, a Vaidehaka is born from a Kṣatriya woman, and a Māgadha from a Brāhmaṇa woman. [Manu 10.8] "From a Kṣatriya, a Sūta is born from a Vaiśya woman, and a Māgadha from a Śūdra woman; from a Brāhmaṇa, an Āyogava is born from a Śūdra woman, and a Cāṇḍāla from a Vaiśya woman. [Manu 10.9] "These six, the Sūta and others, are known as the 'born in the reverse order' (*pratiloma*); they are outside the pale of the castes and excluded from the sacraments (*saṃskāra*). [Manu 10.10] "But the sons of those born in the reverse order are not even to be mentioned among the castes; they are outside the pale of the castes, excluded from the sacraments, and called 'outcastes' (*vrātya*). [Manu 10.11] "The son of a Brāhmaṇa from a Kṣatriya woman is a Sūta; from a Vaiśya woman, an Āyogava; from a Śūdra woman, a Cāṇḍāla, who is the lowest of men. [Manu 10.12] "The son of a Kṣatriya from a Vaiśya woman is a Māgadha; from a Śūdra woman, a Kṣattṛ; the son of a Vaiśya from a Śūdra woman is a Vaiṇa. [Manu 10.13] "The son of a Śūdra from a Brāhmaṇa woman is a Cāṇḍāla, the lowest of men; from a Kṣatriya woman, a Sūta; from a Vaiśya woman, a Vaidehaka. [Manu 10.14] "The son of a Vaiśya from a Kṣatriya woman is an Ambaṣṭha; from a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Māhiṣya; the son of a Kṣatriya from a Brāhmaṇa woman is a Pāraśava. [Manu 10.15] "The son of a Brāhmaṇa from a Śūdra woman is a Pāraśava; he is not fit for the sacraments; he is declared to be a 'border-dweller' (*mleccha*). [Manu 10.16] "The son of a Kṣatriya from a Śūdra woman is a Niṣāda; some call him a Pukkasa; the son of a Vaiśya from a Śūdra woman is a Vaiṇa. [Manu 10.17] "The son of a Śūdra from a Brāhmaṇa woman is a Cāṇḍāla, the lowest of men; from a Kṣatriya woman, a Sūta; from a Vaiśya woman, a Vaidehaka. [Manu 10.18] "The son of a Vaiśya from a Kṣatriya woman is an Ambaṣṭha; from a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Māhiṣya; the son of a Kṣatriya from a Brāhmaṇa woman is a Pāraśava. [Manu 10.19] "The son of a Brāhmaṇa from a Śūdra woman is a Pāraśava; he is not fit for the sacraments; he is declared to be a 'border-dweller' (*mleccha*). [Manu 10.20] "The son of a Kṣatriya from a Śūdra woman is a Niṣāda; some call him a Pukkasa; the son of a Vaiśya from a Śūdra woman is a Vaiṇa. [Manu 10.21] "The son of a Śūdra from a Brāhmaṇa woman is a Cāṇḍāla, the lowest of men; from a Kṣatriya woman, a Sūta; from a Vaiśya woman, a Vaidehaka. [Manu 10.22] "The son of a Vaiśya from a Kṣatriya woman is an Ambaṣṭha; from a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Māhiṣya; the son of a Kṣatriya from a Brāhmaṇa woman is a Pāraśava. [Manu 10.23] "The son of a Brāhmaṇa from a Śūdra woman is a Pāra

"Those sons of the twice-born who are born of women immediately following [the wife] in order, as previously stated, are designated by the name 'anantara' (immediate) because of the defect of their mothers. Thus it is said.

The mention of "immediate succession" (*anantara*) should also be understood to include those separated by one or two intervening classes. Furthermore, because the sequence is specified as immediate, those born in the reverse order (*pratiloma*) are considered to be outside the caste system (*avarṇa*). Thus Gautama says: "But from the reverse order, one is devoid of *dharma*" (GDh 4.25), stating this with the very intention of excluding them from the caste system. And Jātūkarṇa says: "Those born in the reverse order are outcasts (*antāvasāyinaḥ*). As for whatever incidental description of their duties (*dharmas*) there may be, that refers to secondary matters; the question, however, concerns the primary subject. The term "stages of life" (*āśrama*) includes the heretics (*pāṣaṇḍins*), since their practice of *dharma* is for the purpose of entering a stage of life. In this way, other variant readings are also to be explained. Alternatively, the connection is: "not [the duty] of those who are neither caste nor stage of life. For we ourselves are indeed "neither caste nor stage of life" as long as *dharma* remains undetermined. Therefore, [the request is]: "Speak for our determination! (1)
Was the Lord of Yogins questioned by the sages without even approaching him? No, it is said:
while staying in Mithilā, that Lord of Yogins, having meditated thoroughly, spoke to the sages:
"In whatever region there is a black antelope, there you should learn the duties. (1.2)

Indeed, the sages were not capable of asking questions without first approaching the Lord of Yogins while he was staying in Mithilā. From the mention of his being in Mithilā, it is established that the sages were located in another country; otherwise, the qualification would be meaningless. Furthermore, it is proper to ask questions regarding what is beneficial only after having approached [the teacher]. Thus says the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]: "The great seers, having approached... (MDh 1.1). Jātūkarṇa also said: "One should not question the Guru in a casual assembly. Now, having been questioned by them, what did he do? "Having meditated thoroughly, he spoke to the sages. Or, "thoroughly" (*samyak*) is a qualifier of the question itself. Having meditated—having ascertained the fitness and other qualities of the sages. Others read "having meditated for a moment" (*kṣaṇaṃ dhyātvā*). For them, there is an intention to specify time. [The meaning is: in just a moment, such a profoundly deep scriptural matter was reflected upon. Surely this must be the Lord of Yogins. This is either to demonstrate the excellence of the Teacher, or to establish a rule regarding the method of instruction. What, then, did he say? "In whatever land the black antelope (*kṛṣṇamṛga*) is found, in that land learn the duties (*dharma*). The plural number [of the verb] has already been explained. Those, however, who read "dharma" (singular), intend to show that Dharma is the primary subject. "Learn" (*nibodhata*) is used to ensure the focused attention of the disciples. Although Dharma was already mentioned, it is stated again to connect it with the land characterized by the black antelope. How could anyone else say, "O Lord of Yogins, Yājñavalkya," or "That Lord of Yogins resides in Mithilā"? Nor can it be claimed that someone else is the author, because it will be stated later: "For even these three verses are from him" (YDh 3.334); thus it is understood that the Blessed One himself is the author of the work. We do not say that the *Dharmaśāstra* was composed by another; rather, the Blessed One refers to himself indirectly (*parokṣīkṛtya*), because self-praise is forbidden. For if he had said, "Me, the Lord of Yogins," or "I am the Lord of Yogins," it would result in self-adulation. This must be stated for the purpose of explaining the motive for his own activity. Therefore, because it is something to be spoken, and because self-praise is inappropriate to hear, and because he speaks indirectly, this is not a valid objection. Now, one might object: it is improper to mention a remote region without first stating the primary application, namely, "In whatever land the black antelope is found. Moreover, is it not intended that regions like Brahmāvarta are subordinate (*aṅga*) to this? Or is the intention that beyond this point the land is unfit for sacrifice? That too is incorrect, because by the statement "To the east is the rising of the sun" (BDh 1.2.12), lands devoid of the black antelope are also shown to be praiseworthy. Fool! That is correct. Even though the land is a subordinate factor, it is mentioned at the very beginning because it is primary as the locus of eligibility (*adhikāra*), and because it is useful for all the matters to be discussed. Otherwise, proximity might lead one to suspect that it serves the purpose of only a single ritual act. Nor is the order [of topics] fixed by necessity; such is the intention of the Teacher. The reason Brahmāvarta and other regions are not mentioned here is that they yield specific results (*viśiṣṭaphala*), but they are not the only lands fit for Dharma (*dharmya*). This [land of the black antelope], however, is a constant auxiliary (*nityāṅga*) to rituals, since the restriction of Dharma is based precisely on its being fit for sacrifice (*yajñiya*). Thus says the Vedic tradition: "Sacrifice is indeed the black [antelope]; having become a black antelope, he wandered over the earth. Following him, Dharma moved," and so forth. And the Śvetāśvataras say: "He became a black antelope. Having become a black antelope, he wandered over the earth. Following him, Dharma moved," and so forth. Lands devoid of that [black antelope] are not fit for Dharma. Thus is the verse of the Bhāllavins: "Where behind is the Sindhu [Ocean], and where in front is the rising of the sun" (cf. VaDh 1.14–15). "Viharaṇa" means the time of sunset, for it "cuts off" (*vicchidya*) the life of men. That which contains this is "viharaṇī. "Sindhu" means either the ocean or a mountain, as there is no difference in the sense of "flowing" (*syandana*) in both cases. The rest is straightforward. Thus, on the earth characterized by sunrise and sunset, as far as the black [antelope] wanders, so far is there spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). The meaning is "only so far. Even in the reading "yāvad vā," the word "vā" is for the sake of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), not for the sake of an option. Thus says Śaṅkha: "The land of the Āryas is virtuous, from the setting of the sun to the rising of the sun," starting from there, and concluding: "It is holy as far as the black [antelope] wanders; therein the conduct (*ācāra*) should prevail. Here too, the word "vā" is for the sake of emphasis. And so says Manu: *(Note: The provided text ends mid-sentence regarding Manu's citation.)*
"That region is to be known as fit for sacrifice; beyond that, however, is the land of the Mlecchas. (MDh 2.23)

And there is a traditional teaching (*āmnāya*): "The gods gathered him together; Dharma followed after him, for Dharma is indeed the sacrifice" (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*). By restating that Dharma follows [the land] through the word "indeed" (*hi*), [the text] shows that a region possessing that [Dharma] is itself *dharmya*. Therefore, it is well said: "In whatever land the black antelope [dwells]" (*Manusmṛti* 2.23). The verb "is born" (*utpadyate*) must be supplied, in accordance with other *śruti* and *smṛti* passages. Even the status of Brahmāvarta and other regions as *dharmya* is due to their being characterized by the black antelope, based on the eternal authority of *śruti* and *smṛti*; however, their being the cause of specific results arises from identity [with that land]. Enough of this digression. || 2 ||

Even though the sages were not told, "Speak of the *dharma*s from the Veda alone," nevertheless, the understanding of *dharma* does not arise from the Veda characterized solely by the *mantra*s and *brāhmaṇa*s; what then?
"The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, the Dharmaśāstras, and the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*s)—the Vedas, together with these, are the fourteen sources of knowledge and of *dharma*. (1.3)

The utility of the Purāṇas and other such texts for the sake of Dharma is well known. Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā constitute one field of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*). By "Purāṇa," both Itihāsa and Purāṇa are included. *Dharmaśāstra* refers to the Smṛtis. The six auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*) are Śikṣā and the rest. There are four Vedas. Thus, there are fourteen. Others, however, describe Nyāya as beginning with that of Akṣapāda; according to their view, Itihāsa and Purāṇa are considered a single unit. Furthermore, because of the statement regarding their being a mixture, it is asserted that the Purāṇas and others possess independence from the Vedas by virtue of being instruments of the Veda. The two genitives in the phrase "of the sciences" and "of Dharma" are intended to express the connection of the word "science" with the synonym "Dharma. The term "fourteen" is used to exclude the works of Śākyamuni and others. The particle "tu" (but/however) serves to emphasize; the meaning is that there are exactly fourteen, and no more. [Objection: If this were so, then all Smṛtis taken together would constitute a single *dharmaśāstra*, otherwise the number [fourteen] could not be applied. [Response: This is not a fault, because even though the *dharmaśāstra* is determined by each individual Smṛti, the use of the singular number is justified by taking the collection as a whole, just like the word "forest" (*vana*). || 3 ||
If it is argued that non-difference is indeed established, he says "no":
"The authors of the Dharmaśāstras are Manu, Viṣṇu, Yama, Aṅgiras, Vasiṣṭha, Dakṣa, Saṃvarta, Śātātapa, and Parāśara. (1.4)
Āpastamba, Uśanas, Vyāsa, Kātyāyana, Bṛhaspati, Gautama, Śaṅkha and Likhita, Hārīta, Atri, and likewise I [Yājñavalkya]. (1.5)

The term "speakers" (*vaktāraḥ*) intends that they are preceded by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The meaning is: "Having understood [the law] from the Veda, we are speakers, not direct perceivers. The plural number in "of the Dharmaśāstras" is for the purpose of stating their diversity. The mention of the most renowned names, such as "Manu" and "Viṣṇu," is for the purpose of indicating their authority. The final self-designation "I" is for the purpose of maintaining the tradition of practice (*ācāra*). The word "likewise" (*tathā*) is for the purpose of including those not explicitly mentioned. And thus, after mentioning the proclaimers of Dharma, Vṛddhayājñavalkya says:
"Speakers of the Dharma have arisen in great numbers, and likewise will arise;
yet the Veda alone is the eternal treasury of all dharmas.
Thus he spoke again.

"Nārada, Pulaha, Gārgya, Pulastya, Śaunaka, Kratu, Baudhāyana, Jātūkarṇa, Viśvāmitra, and Pitāmaha. [Thus it is said. He is Manu because he reflects (*mananāt*). Viṣṇu is so called because he has bathed (*snātaḥ*) in various forms of knowledge, being pure or enveloped [by it]. Yama is so called because he restrains (*yamanāt*) dharma or living beings. This and other such etymologies are to be applied everywhere for the sake of expressing the excellence of his praise.

What, then, is the root of this Smṛti? It is not, first of all, the Vedic tradition (Āmnāya), for that establishes the distinctions between the various Dharmaśāstras. Nor is it the Nyāya (reasoning) derived from that [tradition]. Rather, because there is a complete synthesis of what is heard in the Śruti, and because [Smṛti] is preceded by that, the same applies here as well. Furthermore, the comprehension of Dharma occurs through its entirety; for indeed, the acquisition of all Dharmas does not occur through the study of a single Smṛti alone. Moreover, if there were a distinction [between Smṛtis], there would be no study of both, just as with different Vedic branches (Śākhās). Yet that is accepted, based on the statement: "one who recites two Droṇas of Smṛti. This is not so. For the declaration of Dharma by Manu and others does not depend upon a tradition [of other texts], since they declare it in its entirety in every case. Otherwise, there would be a declaration of only certain items in one place, while in another there would be injunctions of subsidiary qualities (guṇavidhi). Furthermore, dependence is observed in some cases due to the specific wording. For example:
"Having correctly extracted [the essence] from the sacred tradition (āmnāya), Śaṅkha and likewise Likhita [did so]. Thus [it is said].

Furthermore, it is not possible to assert identity among the objects to be inferred (anumeya), because the diversity of the possessors of the marks (liṅgin) is understood in accordance with the diversity of the marks (liṅga). And the marks, such as the *aṣṭaka* and others, are distinct in each recension (*śākhā*), as they are observed to be so. Likewise, there is a traditional remembrance (*smaraṇa*) of them as distinct; for otherwise, only a single form of performance would have been remembered. As for the statement that there is a "compilation" (*upasaharaṇa*) as in the case of other recensions, that is appropriate for Vedic rites (*śrauta-karman*) because, being perceptible, they do not differ in their ritual context (*prakaraṇa*). But here, a difference in the primary [rites] is stated due to the difference in the marks; therefore, there is a disparity. However, those injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhāna*) which are given by name are indeed to be combined even here, without distinction. For example, Śātātapa, without explicitly mentioning the *śrāddha*, speaks of its constituent qualities:
He who, without his sacred thread, should apply fragrant unguents;

And so forth. The undertaking of the *Smṛti* on the meaning of the qualities (*guṇa*) is for the sake of how there might be "universality" (*sarvārthatā*). As for the study of the *Droṇa* [portion] of the *Smṛti*, even though there is a multiplicity [of texts], it is for the purpose of obtaining an abundance of results through the performance of many ancillary rites (*aṅga*), and for the purpose of incorporating additional qualities. However, regarding the word *droṇa*, it should be understood that either an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) arises from the restrictive rule (*niyama*), just as in the case of the study of vows (*vrata*), or the word *droṇa* is used with the intention of expressing abundance. As for the statement, "The entirety of Dharma is not in one place," that is not a lack of entirety at all, because it does not exclude the various clusters of *vaitānika* (sacrificial) rituals. If it is argued that "entirety" consists in relying upon all transcendental matters (*parokṣārtha*), that too is unproven, because rites such as the piercing of the ear (*karṇavedha*) are not included. If it is argued that they are included by virtue of the authority of custom (*ācāra*), that is already established by the very statement "the Veda is the root of Dharma," so there is no need for this treatise (*śāstra*). Furthermore, since there is no determination of the number of teachers of Dharma, the completion of the entire *dharmaśāstra* would be contingent upon others; consequently, there would be non-performance [of the rites]. Nor is there a fixed number, because the enumeration is merely illustrative and there is no other reason [for limitation]; such is the direction of the argument.

But surely, even if there is a difference in the performance (*prayoga*), for those who depend on other Smṛtis for the sake of the secondary qualities (*guṇa*), the non-performance remains in that same state. Not so. If, even when the performance is complete, the inclusion of further qualities is for the sake of spiritual excellence (*abhyudaya*), then performance as an obligatory duty (*nitya*) is justified even by those qualities not included; thus there is no contradiction. Or rather, let there be a mandatory inclusion of them. However, when knowledge exists, one does not achieve fulfillment merely by performing the procedure known from a single Smṛti while abandoning other known qualities. The known procedure must be performed, and other qualities must be sought. Furthermore, there is transgression (*pratyavāya*) from not including qualities that have been perceived. But if the Smṛtis were dependent [on each other], then because it would be impossible to perform [the rite] before the performance is determined, and because the means of determination would be unavailable, there would be non-performance; this is the point of difference. When the performance is complete, however, the connection with occasional (*naimittika*) subsidiaries is intended, as in the case of "He offers when [the vessel] is broken. Moreover, the occasional nature of qualities is seen even within the context of knowledge. For example: regarding the taking of the Vaiśvānara cup, [it says] "If he should recite [the mantra] for the Carakas or for those falling [from the chariot]" (ŚB 4.2.4.1). It is the same here as well. If another quality, being sought by those who are not negligent, is perceived, then it should be included. But if it is not perceived, there is no fault. And when there is perception of that which was being sought, then since there is transgression from not including it, the performance is unimpeded. But where the performance is incomplete and there is only an instruction of what ought to be done—as in the case of initiation (*upanayana*) and so forth—there the dependence on another Smṛti is indeed inferred. Just as, when it is understood from the word "with earth-clods" (*mṛdbhiḥ*) that there is a plurality of clods, the number "three or five" is known from another Smṛti. Thus it should be inferred everywhere. The very diversity of remembrance (*smaraṇa*) is the proof (*pramāṇa*) for this assumption; therefore, no other reason need be sought. If, however, there were identity of performance, the aforementioned inconsistency would apply. Therefore, it is well said: "The speakers of the Dharmaśāstras... [referring to] the multiplicity of Smṛtis. (4–5)
It has been stated that dharma and the other [ends] are the subject matter of the treatise; however, their definition must be stated. Therefore, he says:
"That which is given by those endowed with faith, in the proper place, at the proper time, by the proper means, and to a worthy recipient—that is the complete definition of dharma. (1.6)

Place (*deśa*) is twofold, consisting of both the general and the specific. Generally, it is characterized by being black; specifically, it is [places such as] Śuddhā and so forth. Time (*kāla*) likewise consists of the day, the forenoon, and so on. The means (*upāya*), however, is the collection of constituent parts (*aṅgakalāpa*) which serve visible and invisible purposes. For example: "Having approached and sat down, one should give gold. Although place and time are also means, they are mentioned separately because they are connected with the qualification (*adhikāra*) [for the act], whereas substance (*dravya*) is the primary factor. Substance refers to white gold and so forth. Faith (*śraddhā*) is well known. The prefix *sam-* has the sense of "properly" (*samyak*). "Endowed" (*anvita*) means "joined" (*yukta*). A worthy recipient (*pātra*) is one perfected in birth, sacramental rites, learning, conduct, and austerity. Such a gift is faultless and constitutes complete merit (*dharma*). This term "gift" (*dāna*) should be understood as an illustration for all prescribed duties, such as sacrifice (*yāga*) and the like. Conversely, that which is contrary is demerit (*adharma*). As for the fact that only giving was cited as an example, that is for the purpose of demonstrating the qualification of all social classes (*varṇa*). Kurukṣetra, lunar eclipses, and so forth, are to be understood as optional (*kāmya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) acts. Thus says Śaṅkha: "In this regard, the characteristics of merit are: place, time, means, substance, faith, the recipient, and renunciation—this is the rule. When these are present, there is the arising of merit; otherwise, it is the opposite. By stating that it is "contrary" when place and the other factors are absent, he shows that these [acts] are obligatory (*nitya*). Furthermore, it is not possible for Kurukṣetra and the like to be obligatory, because it would follow that one could never reside elsewhere. And this is not reasonable. Therefore, it is well said that such things are purely optional and occasional. (6)

[Objection]: But surely this determination of the characteristics of dharma appears to be without foundation. [Reply]: O you who are ignorant of the sacred tradition, do not say so! "The Veda, the Smṛti, the conduct of the virtuous, and what is pleasing to oneself, as well as desire born of a right resolve—this is remembered as the root of dharma. (1.7)

For if *smṛti* and the other sources were said to be the root of *dharma* independently of the Veda, then they would be rootless. But since even these are inseparable from the Veda, the claim that they are rootless is mere idle chatter. Their authority is derived from their being preceded by the Veda; therefore, it is rightly said: "This is remembered as the root of *dharma*. And as Manu says: "And the *smṛti* and conduct (*śīla*) of those who know that [the Veda]. The Veda and *smṛti* are well known. Those who are free from desire, devoid of hypocrisy and the like, who know the meaning of the Veda, and who are performers [of duty]—their practice for the sake of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) is good conduct (*sadācāra*). Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "The cultured man (*śiṣṭa*), moreover, is one whose nature is free from desire; his conduct is *dharma* when no [other] cause is perceived. Because it is not included in the *smṛti*, it is mentioned separately, like the term "Brāhmaṇas and wandering mendicants" (*brāhmaṇaparivrājaka*). However, its lack of formal composition is like the content of another *smṛti*. That which does not contradict the Veda, is not impulsive, and is pleasing to oneself—for example, renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) when the family is suffering—is [good conduct]. The separate mention of *smṛti* and conduct is due to the suspicion of doubt; we shall explain how this is so in the section defining the stages of life (*āśrama*). Desire born of right resolve (*samyaksaṅkalpa*) is a wish produced by affection in one who does not harm himself, such as the determination between two optional alternatives. The separate mention is made so that there may be no suspicion of human authorship regarding activity prompted by desire. The rest is straightforward.

Alternatively, "samyak" (correctly/properly) qualifies each [term] individually. The correctness of the Veda consists in the determination of the analysis of its statements, since other Smṛtis are restricted by being rooted in it. Or else, "of oneself" refers to family dharma, meaning the conduct of one's father and ancestors; this should also be applied here in the phrase "for the non-harming of the virtuous. Thus they say:
"The path by which his fathers have gone, by which his grandfathers have gone—that path of the virtuous he should follow; going by that, he does not come to harm. (MDh 4.178)

But what is dear to oneself is one's own satisfaction; that too is a root of Dharma. What, then, is dear to oneself? It is the desire born of right resolve (*samyaksaṅkalpa*). For some, the ascertainment of reality may occur merely through the instruction of a trustworthy person; for another, it occurs through the realization of the fundamental means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As long as one’s desire born of right resolve becomes free from doubt, then that which is dear to oneself should be understood as having its root in Dharma. This is faultless because, even among men of diverse intellects, there is a restriction of desire by virtue of its being born of right resolve. The rest is the same.

Alternatively, "one's own dear [goal]" refers to the definition of liberation (*apavarga*); "properly" (*samyak*) and so forth refer to wealth (*artha*) and pleasure (*kāma*); as for dharma (*dharma*), it has already been explained. All of this is established by the *Smṛti* scripture. And because it is rooted in the Veda, it is considered to be the Veda itself; with this intention, it is said: "This is remembered as the root of dharma. Furthermore, because the verse is rooted in logic (*nyāya*), its possession of multiple meanings is not a fault.

Furthermore, from what source is this fact—that *smṛti* is rooted in *śruti*—understood? First of all, there is no perception of Vedic sentences that serve as the source for all *smṛtis*. As for the observation of a few [corresponding] sentences, that is no different even in the case of false traditions (*asadāgama*). Nor is it possible for the Veda itself to establish its own status as a source. Furthermore, the incapacity of inference and other means of knowledge [to prove this] is well known; or rather, they would function [only] in the opposite case, since it is impossible for them to be rooted in a Veda that is the soul of everything. To begin with, it cannot be of the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*), because such is not observed and because [if it were so,] *smṛti* would be rendered purposeless. For instance:
While the Veda exists as direct perception and as a prescriptive form, the Smṛti is useless;
at that time, the authors of the Kalpas would have composed their works for the sake of brevity.
If it is argued that the Smṛti exists for the purpose of collecting scattered statements, that is incorrect;
for if it were so, the Jyotiṣa [Veda] would also have to be considered Smṛti, since it possesses that same character.
Even though there is only one branch due to the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), there is a synthesis of the elements occurring at the beginning, middle, and end,
as well as those belonging to other branches, just as in the case of the *pravargya* rite.
Do not say so; for here, our state of being scattered is not comparable to that of light.
For a procedure (itikartavyatā) similar to that [of light] has not been established in its proximity.
Because each individual [Smṛti] consists of a collection of both subsidiary and principal elements scattered [across various sources],
it is extremely difficult to assert that Smṛtis are equal to the Jyotiṣṭoma and other Vedic sacrifices.
Due to the scattered nature of the branches [of the Veda], due to human negligence,
and because they are situated in various sections, the basis of the Smṛtis is not perceived.
Therefore, a summary [of the teaching] must be made for the sake of favoring individuals;
thus, the fact that it is not seen in the Veda does not constitute a fault in this case.
For there are thousands of injunctions in the Veda that have their root in memory (smṛti);
however, out of fear of the destruction of the tradition, they were not directly compiled [in the Veda].

However, it is ordained that this [offender] shall be known as one who must be excluded from society and not allowed to dwell with a woman in her courses; such is the rule agreed upon as being rooted in the Smṛtis.
Even by killing a woman of the Ātreya clan, one would become sinful;
therefore, one should not deviate from the conduct of one who is beyond reproach.
And this rule—that gold and bullion should not be worn—applies without exception;
furthermore, for the sake of perfect appearance, one should likewise be well-dressed.
But in that case, the diversity of the various Smṛtis would not be tenable,
because the rites such as the Kṛcchra penance, which are to be combined [from different sources], are identical.
This distinctness does not exist at all, even in the study of perception,
for actions are distinguished by means of number, quality, and a change of context.
And because the primary acts are distinct, the distinction of their constituent parts is based upon them;
therefore, the performances of the Smārta rites, such as the adṛṣṭaka and others, are distinct.

For an auxiliary (aṅga) enjoined with reference to a primary (pradhāna) characterized by specific qualities, being intended for that unity alone, does not result in being for the sake of all [the primarys].
For there will indeed be one commonality among the Smṛtis, just like the word "akṣa"; their diversity of form arises from their encompassing different subject matters.
Having performed each of the eightfold rites, men become accomplished;
because the fruits are equal, there is no grasping at all by a single agent.
Whatever duties belong to all men have been compiled by Manu and others; for the most part, the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas) are common to all without distinction.
And thus, this root of tradition (smṛti), which is observed to be supported by various scattered branches and sub-branches, cannot be discarded.
This has not been correctly observed by the Teacher,
because it is untenable for scattered injunctive statements to constitute the root [of the system].
The entitlement to perform the Aṣṭakā and other rites would belong either to one who is alive or to one who desires [the results].
If it belongs to one who is alive, then everything must be performed by all those capable of performing it.

Since there is no difference in their being duties to be performed, they would not all achieve their purpose through a single ritual act; for if one did not perform the *iṣṭi*, then by parity of reasoning, neither the performers of that rite nor the maintainers of the *agnihotra* would be successful.
If one were to say "let it be so," because [the Veda] is subsumed under what lacks that nature, then the authority of Manu and others would be lost, and religious practice would become impossible.
Indeed, a fault arises for the authors [of the Smṛtis] from the inclusion of what ought not to be done;
it does not arise, however, from the failure to include all that ought to be done.

Furthermore, that mutual independence of the recollections which has been described should be understood as applying to the employment of a single action, not to the apprehension of the entire [text].
It is not so; for even in a single performance, the Veda does not prescribe the grasping of all [the Soma cups].
Furthermore, the contradiction regarding the actual performance is equal, even if the ritual acts are distinct.
Whatever effect belongs to a single agent by necessity at one time, that is the object of memory; it is for the sake of independence regarding the whole self within each individual part.
We shall explain all of this in detail in the *Śrāddhasaṃgraha*,
[showing] how there is no authoritative status for the Smṛti when it does not conform to the form stated above.
If it is thought that [the causes] act as one because they are not contradictory due to being simultaneous,
even so, the action belongs to as many [causes] as possess the capacity [to produce it].
If it is argued that there is no application [of the morning time] because it is not mentioned in the context of the morning and because it is a subordinate factor,
then its application is not tenable, as it would subvert the primary element.
Furthermore, because they are purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*), those who have been purified by one [act] would not perform another;
thus, the status of being a purificatory act must be asserted for all rites prescribed in the Smṛtis.
Having performed one *aṣṭakā*, they may perform another, even if it is not prescribed by their own specific *gṛhya-sūtra*;
however, since this pertains to those with desires, there is no fixed rule due to the freedom of choice.
In that case, the constant recollection by those who remember would be without basis;
nor is there any other way for [their] qualification [to exist]. Therefore, this is not a valid conceptualization.
Furthermore:
If the auxiliary and principal rites were combined individually from their scattered state,
then the modified rites (*vaikṛta*), such as the *pauṣṇacarū* sacrifice and others, would become merely Smārta (based on tradition).
If it is argued that there is no scattering [of details] there because of the connection with a pre-established relationship of assistance,
then the Aṣṭakā and other rites would likewise [be included], since they are modifications of the Paurṇamāsī sacrifice.
Furthermore, there is no absence of modification for those [mantras] belonging to the Smṛti when they are being recited;
as for the *darvihoma* offerings, their status as *apūrva* (novel) has been stated because of the loss of similarity.
And this was stated by way of rebuttal, as it is scattered among the injunctive texts;
yet even amidst a thousand branches [of the Veda], not a single one recites [the injunction for] the Aṣṭakā.
Those human laws and injunctions which are seen scattered here and there are the source of the observances (niyamas) and restraints (yamas), not of ritual acts (karmas).
For since the rituals being recited are directly perceived to be scattered [in various sources],
the authors of the Kalpasūtras would be censurable if they failed to compile them due to incapacity.
Since the authors of the Smṛtis proclaim that their work is rooted in Mantras and Arthavādas, how could that which is non-existent— such as Vasiṣṭha plowing with a plow— be so stated?

From the explanatory [passage], as in the mention of Śunaḥśepha, there arise those born of arthavāda; and when there is a contradiction with direct Vedic statement (śruti), there is an option, because they are equal to a mandatory injunction (vidhi).
In that regard, the statement of Śaṅkha is untenable; between those two, the Śruti is superior.
The second [authority] is the Smṛti of Baudhāyana, which is an explanatory commentary upon it.
Following this line of reasoning,
those who argue for the lack of authority of the Smṛtis must thoroughly refute this position through discernment in every respect.

Thus, first of all, the view that [the Smṛti] is based on a scattered injunction (*viprakīrṇavidhi*) is untenable. As for the Mantras and Arthavādas, they cannot serve as its source because they are intended for other purposes. Furthermore, a Mantra must either belong to a specific context (*prakaraṇa*) or not. A Mantra belonging to a context is solely subservient to another purpose. Even the other type [not belonging to a context] lacks a basis, because we do not admit that a Mantra can be applied through indicative power (*liṅga*) when it is devoid of any mention of its application (*upādāna*). As for the injunction regarding the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayanavidhi*), it remains indifferent [toward the Smṛti], because it is satisfied by the utility of the study for recitation-sacrifices (*japayajña*) and so forth. As for the Arthavādas, those which are recited outside of any specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*) are incomplete until an injunction is postulated; once such an injunction is postulated, the Arthavāda serves its purpose and thus ceases to be a cause [for the Smṛti]. Now, if it be argued that the basis for the Smṛti is another inferred injunction consistent with the Mantras and Arthavādas, in order to establish the truth of the objects denoted by them—for example, in the Mantra dedicated to Agni, "I shall sacrifice for you" (*pra te yakṣi*, RV 10.4.1), the illustrative phrase "like a watering-trough in the desert" (*dhanvann iva prapā asi*, RV 10.4.1) is untenable according to worldly common sense; therefore, for its own establishment, it postulates another injunction: "A watering-trough should be made. Similarly, in the Arthavāda regarding a horse following a donkey, "Therefore, a worse person follows behind one who is better" (*tasmāc chreyāṃsaṃ yantaṃ pāpīyān paścād anveti*, TS 5.1.2.3), since a reason is stated, it might be argued that the basis is the meaning of an inferred injunction such as "A better person should be followed," established for the sake of that [statement]. That too is insubstantial. Even a practice produced by delusion (*bhrānti*) can serve as the basis for the apprehension of an object. If one asks, "What is this delusion? it arises precisely from the reversal of the sentence-meaning. Or, if it has a basis [in reality] due to being true, what contradiction is there? One would have to assert the truth even of such passages as "a mass of consciousness" (*vijñānaghana*); and consequently, the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmya*) would follow, making the practical application of the Vedic injunctions (*codanā*) inconsistent. If you say, "Let it be so," then who indeed would invalidate the Veda—which has its authority established without any need for postulation—by superimposing a postulation? Just as the objects of the wrong views of heretics, though born of delusion, serve as bases for the objects of negation, so it is for these [Mantras and Arthavādas]; thus there is no fault. Furthermore, even if a postulation were made, since it would be included within the injunction of the fruitful performance (*phalavatprayoga*), it would serve that purpose and not be a human goal (*puruṣārtha*); thus, it would follow that it is not a subject for Smṛti. As for Names (*nāmadheya*), their utility is limited merely to connecting qualities with results; therefore, their status as a source [of Smṛti] is far removed.

By this, the theory that [the Smṛtis] are rooted in lost branches [of the Veda] is explained. For even those [Vedic texts] that have been lost are of exactly this same nature. Furthermore, one would have to assume a loss [of the Veda] for which there is no evidence. Indeed, the loss of an entire branch [of the Veda] is impossible, because no other branch of such a nature is ever perceived. Some branches of all four Vedas are indeed studied; yet not even in a single one is there found any similarity to the dharma propounded in the Smṛtis. Nor is it logical to treat them as different branches simply because they are entirely distinct in character; for the Maitrāyaṇī branch is not entirely distinct from the Kāṭhaka branch. Alternatively, if [the Smṛtis] were rooted in only a portion of a branch, there would be the assumption of a vast amount of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). As for the theory that they are rooted in a lost Veda, it is not at all convincing, given the established existence of the four Vedas. Moreover, it would follow that the Smṛtis did not exist prior to their supposed loss. Or, if they were remembered out of fear of such a loss, then rites like the *agnihotra* would also have to be classified as merely "Smārta" (based on Smṛti). Therefore, this position is untenable.

However, those who maintain that the Smṛtis possess authority due to their eternity—just like the Vedas—claiming that names such as "Manu" and others are based merely on the act of promulgation (*pravacana*), are indeed beyond reproach in their silence. For even if they do not constitute a contradiction [to the Veda], the Veda remains authoritative precisely because it was not composed by a person; yet here, its non-composition by a person is excluded from the entire world. And if this were so, it would be impossible to avoid the consequence that these texts are of the same nature as false scriptures (*asad-āgama*). If you say, "Let it be so," then enough with the science of Smṛti! Now, it would follow that even wells, groves, and the like—which have ceased to have an author since ancient times—would lack an author. Furthermore, statements such as "all that has been declared in the Veda" regarding Manu and others would result in being false. Alternatively, one would have to laboriously interpret them as mere explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) by somehow casting aside their reputation through strained imagination. Moreover, the various *caraṇas* (schools) such as the Kaṭhas preserve their respective branches of the Veda, but no school of the Mānavas and others is observed. Nor can it be said that, like the *Chāndogya-brāhmaṇa*, these very schools are the preservers of the branches, because they are not included within any of the Vedic branches. As for the preservation of the branches that is observed, that too is by virtue of being Smṛti and not the Veda, just like the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*). In this way, the neglect of observances and study becomes intelligible. And it must be stated that these Smṛtis are non-eternal. If it is argued that they were composed only by certain individuals like Manu, then the consequence follows that Nārada and others would lack authority. If you say, "Let it be so," then a specific reason must be stated. Furthermore, there would be no reverence for Smṛtis composed recently by Baudhāyana and others, comparable to that for Manu and the rest. As for the claim that all [Smṛtis] issued effortlessly from the mouth of Brahmā, that is far more gross than the teaching of Śākyamuni. Moreover, if the Smṛtis were eternal, there would be a break in the tradition due to the absence of an injunction for their study. But surely, there is one? [Reply: No. [The opponent says: There is. [Reply: It is not so. Even if it were so, the Smṛtis would still be non-eternal. If it is argued that the injunction for study exists because they are recited by the learned, then the same applies to the Veda. If it is argued that the Smṛtis are recited by those who know the Veda, then the Veda is likewise recited by those who know the Smṛtis. If it is argued that the Smṛtis are recited by those who know both, then the Veda is likewise recited by those who know both. If it is argued that the Smṛtis are recited by those who know the Veda together with its meaning, then the Veda is likewise recited by those who know it with its meaning. If it is argued that the Smṛtis are recited by those who know the Veda together with its meaning and its application (*prayoga*), then the Veda is likewise recited by those who know it with its meaning and its application. If it is argued that the Smṛtis are recited by those who know the Veda together with its meaning, its application, and its secret doctrine (*rahasya*), then the Veda is likewise recited by those who know it with its meaning, its application, and its secret doctrine. If it is argued that the Smṛtis are recited by those who know the Veda together with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, and its ritual practice (*anuṣṭhāna*), then the Veda is likewise recited by those who know it with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, and its ritual practice. If it is argued that the Smṛtis are recited by those who know the Veda together with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, its ritual practice, and its results (*phala*), then the Veda is likewise recited by those who know it with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, its ritual practice, and its results. If it is argued that the Smṛtis are recited by those who know the Veda together with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, its ritual practice, its results, and its purpose (*prayojana*), then the Veda is likewise recited by those who know it with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, its ritual practice, its results, and its purpose. If it is argued that the Smṛtis are recited by those who know the Veda together with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, its ritual practice, its results, its purpose, and its connection (*sambandha*), then the Veda is likewise recited by those who know it with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, its ritual practice, its results, its purpose, and its connection. If it is argued that the Smṛtis are recited by those who know the Veda together with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, its ritual practice, its results, its purpose, its connection, and its excellence (*viśeṣa*), then the Veda is likewise recited by those who know it with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, its ritual practice, its results, its purpose, its connection, and its excellence. If it is argued that the Smṛtis are recited by those who know the Veda together with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, its ritual practice, its results, its purpose, its connection, its excellence, and its sublation (*bādha*), then the Veda is likewise recited by those who know it with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, its ritual practice, its results, its purpose, its connection, its excellence, and its sublation. If it is argued that the Smṛtis are recited by those who know the Veda together with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, its ritual practice, its results, its purpose, its connection, its excellence, its sublation, and its means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then the Veda is likewise recited by those who know it with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, its ritual practice, its results, its purpose, its connection, its excellence, its sublation, and its means of knowledge. If it is argued that the Smṛtis are recited by those who know the Veda together with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, its ritual practice, its results, its purpose, its connection, its excellence, its sublation, its means of knowledge, and its object (*viṣaya*), then the Veda is likewise recited by those who know it with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, its ritual practice, its results, its purpose, its connection, its excellence, its sublation, its means of knowledge, and its object. If it is argued that the Smṛtis are recited by those who know the Veda together with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, its ritual practice, its results, its purpose, its connection, its excellence, its sublation, its means of knowledge, its object, and its fruit (*phala*), then the Veda is likewise recited by those who know it with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, its ritual practice, its results, its purpose, its connection, its excellence, its sublation, its means of knowledge, its object, and its fruit. If it is argued that the Smṛtis are recited by those who know the Veda together with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, its ritual practice, its results, its purpose, its connection, its excellence, its sublation, its means of knowledge, its object, its fruit, and its ultimate goal (*niḥśreyasa*), then the Veda is likewise recited by those who know it with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, its ritual practice, its results, its purpose, its connection, its excellence, its sublation, its means of knowledge, its object, its fruit, and its ultimate goal. If it is argued that the Smṛtis are recited by those who know the Veda together with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, its ritual practice, its results, its purpose, its connection, its excellence, its sublation, its means of knowledge, its object, its fruit, its ultimate goal, and its method (*upāya*), then the Veda is likewise recited by those who know it with its meaning, its application, its secret doctrine, its ritual practice, its results, its purpose, its connection, its excellence, its sublation, its means of knowledge, its object, its fruit, its ultimate goal, and its method. If it is argued that the
"This should be studied with diligence by a learned Brāhmaṇa. (MDh 1.103)

It is not the case that there is a rule for the study of all *smṛtis* by that [same injunction], because the phrase "this" refers specifically to the subject at hand. And since there is a contradiction regarding the subject at hand, [the injunction] lacks the capacity [to apply]. Furthermore, if it were argued that the meaning of this injunction, "it must be studied," is understood through the purpose [of the Veda], then—given that one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*) is equal to a *śūdra*, and that the initiated person studies the Veda for the sake of its meaning, and given the scriptural statement that he must be instructed in only a few matters such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*)—there would be no study of the *smṛtis*. Moreover, the departure from the teacher’s house after having studied the Veda, and so forth, would have to be elaborated [as consequences]. However, if this [study of *smṛtis*] were to terminate in mere recitation, then since that too would have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), the tradition of the *smṛtis* would be difficult to maintain. But if they are rooted in the Veda, then it might somehow be possible due to the expansion of the injunction to study one's own portion of the Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*). Yet that very thing is difficult to establish, as stated previously. Those whose intellect is aided by a cleverness in turning away from the web of broken alternatives do not grasp [the matter] in this way. Or rather, who would say that the authority of the *smṛtis* is due to their being rooted in the Veda? For the *smṛtis* are independent, just like the Veda, because their tradition is uninterrupted. Nor is there an elaboration of the defects mentioned before, because the eternity of the texts is not admitted. Furthermore, there is no great need for the text itself, because there is no time devoid of the performance of the rites prescribed by the *smṛtis*. Just as agriculture and the like are perceived in the world as means to specific results, so too are the *aṣṭakā* rites and others; for this is the case. But there is this much difference: agriculture and the like have proximate results, whereas the *aṣṭakā* rites have uncertain results. And one cannot say they are worldly merely on this account, precisely because of this determination of distinction. If it is argued that this distinction is known through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) even through error, we say no. Since other means of knowledge have been refuted, and since firmness is apprehended, there is no error. If one were to assume error, one might even suspect that the Veda itself was grasped as being non-Vedic. Just as the cognition "this is the Veda" is said not to be an error—even when [the object] is worldly—because of the remembrance of its denotative power, so too should it be understood that there is a restriction of the nature of the means and results in the case of the *aṣṭakā* rites and others. Nor is the expression "non-worldly" used because the power of the means to produce a result is imperceptible, just as in the case of the power of words. If it is argued that this power exists because the comprehension [of the result] would otherwise be impossible, that is the same here, because the conviction is firm. For just as words are the cause for postulating a power by virtue of their being denoters, so too are objects which are the causes of established comprehension; thus there is no fault. Or rather, what is imperceptible here? The *aṣṭakā* rites and others, being performed by other persons, are perceived directly with all their constituent parts. And therein, the derivation of the word "aṣṭakā" and so forth occurs just like the word "Veda. Furthermore, the performance of those rites is based on a specific purpose, and thus it is understood from the performers themselves, just like the nature [of the rites]. And when the related entity is postulated through the impossibility of explaining the established usage, there is no obstruction to the operation [of the word], just as in the case of a denotative power. Therefore, it has been stated that the *smṛtis* are independent. And so he says:
"The composition of the word *ca* for meanings that are not [otherwise] connected by a compound.

And the traditional teaching (*āmnāya*) begins with "If [the mantra] has been uttered as *bhūr*," and after stating "from the Yajus and from the Sāman," it says, "If it is unknown (*avijñātam*). According to the tradition, "unknown" refers to what is based on the Smṛti. That would be untenable if it were rooted in the Veda, because it is impossible for anything to be entirely unknown. For when the source exists and is being examined, one cannot say it is "unknown. If "unknown" were meant in relation to another person, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). However, under the view of independence (*svātantrya*), there is no contradiction.

"O reckless man, do not speak thus! This is a kingdom-protected land. Indeed, women who are protected by the virtuous do not become independent. For a worldly practice that lacks a basis in authoritative scripture (*pramāṇa*) cannot be sufficient for determining the true nature of the meaning of the *Smṛtis*. Otherwise, the same would apply even to practices such as the worship of *caityas*. If you argue that there is a distinction because those who do not know the Veda perform those [other] practices, then what need have those who advocate independence for people who know the Veda? Surely, the Veda is not authoritative merely because it is accepted by those who know the Veda; nor do worldly activities such as agriculture depend upon those who know the Veda. If you say they are so because their fruits are visible (*sāṃdṛṣṭika*), how else could they be considered dependent on worldly convention? For the world is not capable of understanding an invisible purpose without depending on scripture. Alternatively, if you claim that dependence on worldly usage is like the power of expressive words, that is incorrect. In that case (the theory of words), the impossibility of cognizing the meaning is the root of the hypothesis. But here (in our case), what is impossible? Since worldly usage is observed even in the worship of *caityas* and the like. Nor can a distinction be established based on the recollection of Manu and others who are experts, for if worldly usage were the root, there would be no difference from false traditions (*asadāgama*). But surely it has been said that the Veda is authoritative, and those who perform the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices prescribed therein are experts regarding Dharma. And they are the performers of the *Aṣṭakā* and other rites. Therefore, there is a distinction from other worldly practices. Do not say so, for the opposite is even more easily established. For those who know the Veda, having attained their ends through that alone, have no regard for the Dharma of worldly usage. However, for those who have abandoned worldly practices rooted in the Veda, there is a firm adherence to worldly usage because they have no other recourse. If you say, "Let it be; let them also have a duty," then in that case, their authority is perfectly well-established."

If that is so, then let the cause capable of prompting that activity be inferred simply from the commonality of the worldly practice of those who carry out the meaning of the injunction (*codanā*). But has it not been said that such a thing does not even exist? It is for this very reason that it is inferred. Can something non-existent be inferred? Indeed, when there is an available inferential mark (*liṅga*) that indicates it, one cannot say it is non-existent. What, then, is that mark? The worldly practice of the three twice-born classes, which is not immediately perceptible, is seen to have its root in an injunction; and this [practice under discussion] is of that same kind. Therefore, there too exists an injunction as the underlying root. Nor does it follow that it would be perceived in that same way; thus, there is no contradiction with the qualification [of the inference], because non-perception is not a subverting factor. However, there is a difference [between this case and others] due to the lack of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the case of other types of worldly practice. Does an injunction prompt practice while itself remaining unperceived? What is the use of this useless deliberation? It prompts it in every respect. And non-perception [does not preclude existence] because of inference both generally and specifically. For effects, having specific causes, lead to the understanding of their own causes in that very same way. And in this manner, the performance of the meaning of an injunction is justified. Otherwise, the performance of the action would be independent; and in that case, there would be the consequence of an absence of fruit, since fruits do not arise immediately nor are they connected [to the act]. Nor can it be said that the production of fruit at a later time occurs through the mediation of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), because that would contradict common worldly usage and because there is no basis for such a hypothesis. Therefore, this position alone is superior. Furthermore, the scriptural observations (*darśana*) are indeed consistent with this view as well.

This position cannot be sustained. Indeed, means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) do not become known through their objects (*prameya*). For one who postulates a cause based on the impossibility of performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), how can there be performance? For performance is not established prior to the postulation of a cause; if that [performance] were already established, the postulation of a cause would be futile. If it is argued that there is no fault because, having observed the performance residing in another person, one infers a cause due to the impossibility of that [performance otherwise], and subsequently engages in performance, that is incorrect. For there is no impossibility regarding the performance of another person, since that is already established. Furthermore, as for the inference stated—that [Smṛti is authoritative] because of the commonality of the performers—there too the reason is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*). For the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* and other rites are not considered righteous (*dharmya*) simply because they are performed by the three higher castes, but rather because they are enjoined by the Veda. And these [Smṛtis] do not possess that [Vedic injunction]. If it is argued that their performance is righteous because it is not seen to have a visible purpose (*adṛṣṭika*), that too is fallacious. For even in non-Vedic matters, we observe the performance of defective rites. If it is claimed that this is due to delusion (*bhrānti*), then in this case too there is fallacy due to the influence of delusion. If it is said that it is not a delusion because there is no sublation (*abādha*), that is also unproven; for no lack of sublation is observed in the case of the meaning of Smṛti when it contradicts the Veda. If it is argued that where such [contradiction] is absent, it is authoritative, that too is difficult to ascertain. Moreover, every performance not enjoined by the Veda that is contrary to it is indeed invisible in its result. Therefore, this position is also worthless. Consequently, statements such as "All that has been declared in the Veda" (MDh 2.7) would be incoherent. If one postulates a cause devoid of any means of knowledge, it results in a blind tradition (*andhaparamparā*). However, the very existence of the systems of philosophy (*darśana*) depends upon reasoning (*nyāya*). This is not the scope of the rule "But the statements [are authoritative] because of their novelty" (PMS 3.5.21). In this manner, the objection should be expanded. In every respect, however, the Smṛtis lack authority because their source-cause is not perceived, just like the recollection of the daughter's son of a barren woman, since they are merely Smṛtis.

To this, it is replied: It is not proper to attribute a lack of authority to the Smṛtis by means of webs of conceptual constructions devised by oneself.
