For Manu and others themselves have stated: "All that is declared in the Veda" (MDh 2.7); "The Veda is the root of Dharma" (GDh 1.1); "Custom is authoritative because of the authority of the sacred tradition" (BDh 1.1.1); "The second [source] is the Smṛti which explains that [Veda]" (BDh 1.1.3); and "The Veda, the Smṛti, and the conduct of the virtuous" (MDh 2.12), and so forth. Nor is it proper to seek another basis while transgressing such an accepted principle, since there is no other means of knowledge for this matter; for there is the restrictive rule: "Dharma is characterized solely by Vedic injunction" (PMS 1.1.2). Furthermore, the assumption of error and the like is untenable, as it contradicts the acceptance [of these texts] by those who know the Veda. Nor is their acceptance possible if they were based on something else, as is the case with the worship of Caityas and similar practices. Or, if one assumes error and the like, it would follow that even the Veda itself is not the Veda. Nor is it impossible for them to be rooted in the Veda, since there is the traditional teaching: "Manu and others are indeed knowers of the Veda. This is not due to error, just as the tradition regarding their status as "rememberers" (smartṛtva) is not. Therefore, it is well said that they are rooted in the Veda. And it has been said:

"Because of the experience of error, because of the deceptive speech of men, and because [the goal] is to be accomplished in accordance with what is observed, the Vedic injunction alone is the most parsimonious [means of knowledge]. (TV II: 74)

[Objection: But was it not already stated that this very basis in the Veda (*vedamūlatva*) is difficult to establish? For it has been argued in every way that the status of the Veda as the source is untenable. [Reply: That was not correctly stated, because its status as a source is established through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Indeed, the fact that the Smṛtis are rooted in the Veda is perceived, since they are obtained through the necessity of otherwise explaining the meaning of the injunctions (*vidhi*). To illustrate: when it is said, "One's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) should be studied," and [the injunction] "One should teach the Veda" is mentioned, another injunction is postulated there due to the mutual inconsistency of these two. For the injunction "One should teach the Veda" impels one to study for the sake of accomplishing oneself [as a teacher]. The injunction to study, too, having its performance accomplished by that very impulsion, reaches a state of indifference (*audāsīnya*) without the assumption of a separate qualification (*adhikāra*). Furthermore, a teacher is not able to teach without first initiating the student (*upanīya*). Therefore, for the sake of making both injunctions consistent, another injunction is inferred: "One should initiate Brāhmaṇas and others. Thus, once the two injunctions have fulfilled their purpose following the comprehension of the Vedic meaning, immediately thereafter, upon the requirement of the injunction to procreate offspring, since that is impossible in the absence of a wife and because marriage is the sole means to achieve desire, another injunction arises: "One should marry a woman with auspicious marks" (YDh 1.52). Moreover, since the performance of the Agnihotra and other rites depends on a wife, and because she must be present, the injunction regarding non-transgression arises: "One should sacrifice together with her" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.2.1.1). Likewise, "One should approach her during the season" (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 5.1), and so forth. In each such case, injunctions that bring about the primary acts and possess qualifications (*sādhikāra*) are to be postulated in this very manner. Similarly, the connection with the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) is to be determined through direct and inferential means, such as *śruti* and the rest. We shall demonstrate this more precisely only in the commentary on the text itself. And this being the case, there is no lack of coherence in the authority of the Smṛtis.

But if this were so, it would follow that injunctions are merely implied by the sense (*smārta*). For example, when it is stated, "One should sacrifice with clarified butter (*sarpiṣā*)," and [also] "He cuts [the portion] with a *sruva*-ladle," there arises another injunction: "One should take the clarified butter with the *sruva*. For just as the oblation of clarified butter, characterized by the fourfold cutting (*caturavatta*), requires a specific substance capable of being cut and thus expects an implement such as the *sruva*, so too the injunction regarding the *sruva*—"He cuts with the *sruva*"—being understood through its own capacity to have a liquid substance as its object, and perceiving a tendency toward a specific [substance], brings forth another injunction: "One should take the clarified butter with the *sruva*. Injunctions of this kind would all result in being merely implied by the sense.

It is not so, because this [Vedic text] results merely in an application (*viniyoga*). For that which is either the producer of a thing or its instigator of performance is the cause of instruction; however, there is no contradiction in the fact that it does not even restrict the purpose (*idamarthya*) of what has already arisen. If that were the case, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even those things enjoined by Smṛti would lack the status of being based on Śruti. No, for there is a difference because Smṛti produces the thing itself. What then of the *Aṣṭakā* and other rites? There is no impossibility of any Vedic knowledge (*vid*) existing in their absence, since the injunction to study one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana-vidhi*) and the existence of the mantras are established. It is said: here too, the injunction to study one’s own Veda is not possible if it lacks the mantras designated by names such as *Aṣṭakā*. For the designation is not possible when there is only a connection with recitation (*japa-yajña*), etc. Nor is a more explicit application (*viniyoga*) perceived, by the force of which the name might be set aside. Furthermore, it is possible for the mantras to establish the connection between the substance and the deity, as well as the grounds for eligibility (*adhikāra*). And from the impossibility of the injunction to study being connected with those [mantras], the necessity of performing the rite is understood. The manner of connecting the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) has already been explained. Objection: If this is so, then because of the non-difference of the name, all the mantras would imply only a single *Aṣṭakā* rite. Reply: Not so, because of the difference in capacity (*sāmarthya*). Mantras present the rite according to their own power, and they do not possess the capacity to present a single rite. Therefore, the distinction between the *Aṣṭakā* rites and others is established. Moreover, if this were the case, the performance of the *Aṣṭakā* and other rites obtained from all branches (*śākhā*) would belong to only one person. Indeed, if one performs a rite obtained from only one branch, the sin resulting from the non-performance of it would not be avoided. For if the rites were merely to be inferred, that would be untenable; because the connection with a non-different time, such as the *Aṣṭakā*, implies a non-difference in purpose according to that [time]. A purpose must be postulated in a way that does not contradict the known connection with time and so forth. And that is impossible if multiple rites are performed, for it is not possible to perform multiple rites at one time. Nor is there any distinction regarding the time of the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) and so on in the case of an inferred rite, any more than in the case of one being recited. Furthermore, a rite that is being recited leads to the postulation of a sin in non-performance in order to compel its own performance. But a purely imaginary rite would be postulated only through the impossibility of the recitation otherwise. And that [recitation] is possible even without postulating a fault caused by the non-performance of an imaginary rite; thus, there is no occasion for such a postulation. If it were postulated because the understanding of the performance of a settled rite is otherwise impossible, then the postulation would take this form: "He who does not perform the rite called *Aṣṭakā* at this time shall incur sin. This being the case, one would be satisfied even by performing only one rite bearing that name. Nor can it be argued that because the cause for postulation exists in each individual case, there is the undesirable consequence of postulating many [rites], for that is not contradictory even if only one is postulated. If it is argued that because no distinction is perceived, many are postulated, then that is untenable because it refers to what is recited in a single branch; it is not the case that no distinction is perceived even when [the rites] are obtained from different branches. If it is argued that this is the same even for what is being recited, we say no, because that [recited text] impels performance by its own inherent power. Here, however, there is a difference because the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is understood from another source. Moreover, the postulation is for the sake of making the performance possible. And that possibility is not achieved by assuming that all rites are to be performed by a single agent. For postulations cannot exist in contradiction with their own causes. In the case of direct Vedic study, even if a conflict arises because time is secondary, the contradiction might be resolved, but not in the case of an inferred rite. Therefore, it is well said: "Even by performing one, one would be satisfied. Since no contradiction is seen, the practice of performing four *Aṣṭakās* is faultless. And thus, there is a general understanding of the duty. In some cases, even though there is a general understanding of the duty through direct recitation, the mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) provide specific details. These too have Smṛti as their source. As the Brāhmaṇa says: "This indeed is truly austerity: non-violence, self-restraint, charity, and hospitality. Now, the supreme austerity for beings is the desire to help; therefore, one who knows this should truly benefit all beings. "True benefit" (*addhopakāra*) is a benefit devoid of visible motives. The specific methods required by that [benefit], even if presented by mantras and explanatory passages intended for other purposes, are not improper. For example: "They enclose water on dry land" refers to the construction of tanks and the like; and "like in a desert" (RV 10.4.1) refers to the digging of wells. As for the argument that even a postulated [rite] is for the sake of the fruitful performance because it is included within it—that is not to be questioned, because the context (*prakaraṇa*) is set aside by the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), however, are mostly based on direct perception. Where, however, there is no direct perception, nor an established general rule, and where the mantras and explanatory passages are justified by having another purpose or being figurative, they do not possess the truth of the things connected to them. Thus, there is a difference from false traditions (*asadāgama*). Smṛtis, too, are sublated precisely because they are of that [figurative] nature. One need not go so far as to postulate their falsity despite their having a root; enough of this digression. In every way, the rootedness of Smṛtis in the Veda is established. And this being the case, it is possible to say that Smṛtis are "unrecognized," because they are imaginary. The *Ṛgveda* and so on are the cause of the imagination, not the cause of the designation. Thus Manu, by stating the mantra of naming, "All that is declared in the Veda" (MDh 2.7), shows that there is no designation of "Veda" for an injunction because it is to be imagined. And Āpastamba, saying, "The injunctions are stated in the Brāhmaṇas; their lost readings are inferred from usage" (ĀpDh 1.12.10), indicates the reality of their root. The meaning is that although they are as if lost, they are inferred from usage. In this way, the beginninglessness of the designations "Smārta" is also established. This is the direction. And in case of conflict, sublation is more appropriate. Otherwise, in case of conflict, there would be an option (*vikalpa*). Nor can it be said, "Let it be so," because it is not accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭa*). If it is argued that the acceptance of the learned is the opposite, for they are not seen to respect even what is stated in Śruti if it contradicts Smṛti—for instance: [Here follows a citation of a verse regarding the superiority of Smṛti over Śruti. ...Thus it is said. Therefore, the Smṛtis are authoritative. And the Smṛtis are not sublated by the Śruti, because the Śruti is the source of the Smṛti. Even if there is a conflict, the Smṛti is not sublated, because the Smṛti is the means of knowing the Śruti. If it is argued that the Smṛti is sublated because it is the means of knowing the Śruti, we say no, because the Smṛti is the means of knowing the Śruti only insofar as it is not contradictory to it. If it is argued that it
Those who know the truth do not approve of the killing of a cow, even if it is enjoined by the Śruti,
because its status as the foremost among minor offenses (upapātaka) is proclaimed in the Smṛti.
And the performance of rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma is known from Śruti;
yet even by means of acquiring wealth through theft and the like, that [performance] does not occur, because it would contradict the Smṛti.

Do not say so; for indeed, among the learned, there is never a firm refusal to practice the meaning declared by the Śruti on account of a conflict with Smṛti, even if they are the most insignificant of men.
For those who know the truth do not perform the slaughter of goats even when it is prohibited;
yet if it were not prohibited by the Smṛti, the slaughter of cows would indeed be equal to that.
For all Smārta injunctions are distinct from those declared in the Śruti;
therefore, being in contradiction with the Smṛti is not a reason for non-performance.

Even according to the Smṛti, there is the slaughter of a cow; one should first offer the guest-offering (arghya) with a cow, for that is the cause for the performance of the obligatory rites such as the Aṣṭakā, and it serves as the reason for the fault incurred by their non-performance.
Whether it be based on the strength of the Veda or even a delusion regarding the Vedic tradition,
cultured people (*śiṣṭas*) would not fail to perform Vedic rites merely on the strength of the Smṛtis.
Beginning when the sun is half-set until the stars appear,
the recitation prescribed by the Smṛti has been abandoned by those who maintain the sacred fires (agnihotrin) due to its contradiction [with their ritual duties].
The cause for performing or not performing [an action] lies in its strength or weakness;
let it not be that dharma is something one might even wear as a garment while mounted upon a donkey.
Manu, however, considers the Veda alone to be the authority regarding matters beyond the reach of perception,
because of his statement that "the Śruti is the supreme authority in dharma," and so forth.
And the authors of the Smṛtis consider the Smṛti to be far weaker than Śruti;
for they declare that the Veda is the root of Dharma for those who know it.
Therefore, it is established that Smṛti which contradicts the Veda is sublated,
because its assumption is untenable due to its contradiction with what is directly heard [in the Veda].
Even a perceptual injunction regarding assistance and the like, having for its object a general category,
would yield way to a recollection whose object is a particular, once it has considered the weakness [of the former].

The Smṛtis were composed by sages who, for the most part, were variously divided in their views regarding injunctions, as they sought to establish alternative interpretations of the meaning of those injunctions.

One should effect the completions by means of mantras, explanatory passages (arthavādas), and injunctions— both perceptible and inferable— for that which is correctly established through direct perception and conceptualization as being subject to general rules.
And thus, having thoroughly shaken off the mire of being composed by humans, this golden garland called the Dharma bears the lotuses of the meaning of the Vedas,
which have been blossomed by the rays of the sun that is the sacred tradition (āmnāya).
Having thus considered the authority of the Smṛti on the basis of its being rooted in the Veda, Lord Manu has declared that they are not to be questioned regarding any matters. (7)

But if this is so, then because of the statement, “This is known to be the root of dharma,” it would follow that wealth (*artha*) and the like do not have a root. Not so; for the word *dharma* is intended to be illustrative. Or even if the word *dharma* were restricted to *dharma* alone, nevertheless, wealth and pleasure, as determined by the scriptures, are indeed consistent with *dharma*. If it is argued that liberation (*apavarga*) is something different [from these], that too is incorrect.
“Of the acts of sacrifice, conduct, self-restraint, non-violence, charity, and study of the Vedas—this is the supreme *dharma*: the vision of the Self through yoga. (1.8)

The term *ijyā* (sacrifice) is an elliptical designation for Vedic rites such as sacrifices and the like. *Ācāra* (conduct) refers to Smṛti-based practices, both those that are codified and those that are not. *Dama* is the restraint of the senses. *Ahiṃsā* (non-violence) applies except in cases such as sacrifice or when dealing with an assassin (*ātatāyin*). *Dāna* (charity) is well known. *Svādhyāya* is the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*). Although it is well known that these actions constitute *dharma*, nevertheless this [practice] is a "minor *dharma*" because, due to the limited nature of its retention, the yoga is not perfected. This alone is the supreme *dharma*: the vision of the Self through yoga. Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. That direct vision of the Self which results from it is the supreme *dharma* by virtue of being ultimate retention. Therefore, it is established that objects and so forth are to be understood through the scriptures. But why are self-restraint and the others mentioned separately, even though they are included within the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*? It is for the purpose of showing their basis in the *Smṛti*. Conduct (*ācāra*) is the indicator of Smṛti-based practices, and those include self-restraint and the rest. For this very reason, the sacrifice to Brahman is also cited here; for even if it were recited in the direct *Śruti*, since it is based on *Smṛti*, how could it apply to a *Śūdra* as well? Alternatively, the separate prescription of self-restraint and the rest is for the sake of universal eligibility. By the word *ācāra*, however, the inclusion is of the *Aṣṭakā* and other rites intended for the three higher castes. Thus they say:
"Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, purity, and restraint of the senses—this is proclaimed as the common dharma for the four castes. (MDh 10.63)

And here, by the utterance of the word "truth" (*satya*), the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*) is implied; for truthful speech is obtained precisely through the restraint of the senses. And he will state this later: "One should not omit the five sacrifices" (YDh 1.120). Alternatively, "sacrifice" (*ijyā*) is an indication of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), while "conduct" (*ācāra*) refers to the qualities of the self. Self-restraint and the others are mentioned merely as examples. The rest is the same. This verse is intended to define liberation (*apavarga*). This very point has also been stated in a *ṛc*: "Having known Him thus, one transcends death" (VS 31.18). And the *Smṛti*, introducing the knowledge of the self, says:
"For that is the foremost of all sciences, for immortality is attained from it" (MDh 12.85).
And since all of this is to be understood through the Śruti and Smṛti, their status as the root of Dharma is well-stated. 8.

But surely, even if the Śruti and Smṛti were not inherently expressive of meaning, the determination of that meaning would arise through intuition in dependence upon the capacity of the person; for indeed, we see people understanding one and the same sentence in various different ways. And if this were so, how could there be a definitive determination of Dharma? As it has been said: "The true essence of Dharma is hidden in a cave" (MBh 3. App. 32.67). This is true, provided there were no means of determination. But such a means does exist:
"A council (*parṣad*) consisting of four who know the Dharma of the Vedas, or even three who possess the triple knowledge (*traividya*)."
She said: "That alone would be the Dharma which is held by the one who is most excellent among those who know the inner self. (1.9)

The restriction "four" is intended to exclude five or more, because of the difficulty of reaching a definitive conclusion in a large assembly. Those who know the Vedas and those who know the *dharmaśāstras* are "knowers of the Veda and Dharma. Furthermore, because knowledge is for the sake of another, they do not stop at mere theoretical knowledge. Rather, that assembly consists of those who are both knowers and practitioners, endowed with discernment (*savivekāḥ*). Alternatively, it refers to the "threefold knowledge" (*traividyam*); that in which the threefold knowledge—characterized by the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman*—resides is the "threefold knowledge," meaning three persons who have mastered the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman*. Because of the restriction on the number of persons, the study of the *Arthavāda* (explanatory passages) is not contradictory. And in this view, those who understand the relationship of root and derivative between the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* for every individual statement are included. The particle *eva* (only/alone), however, has the sense of "also" (*api*), and that is used in the sense of possibility. The word "or" (*vā*) is intended to indicate an option based on relative importance. Even if there are three, or if there should be two, or even if there should be only one who is the best among those who know the supreme self (*adhyātmavittamaḥ*), he indeed is a true knower and one who speaks otherwise than the truth. Thus it has been said: [The verse follows: "One who knows the supreme self alone is sufficient; what need is there for many? He alone is the authority, for he is the speaker of the truth. Thus it is stated.

"Even a single best of the twice-born who knows the Vedas, whatever dharma he may determine," so [it is said] (MDh 12.113). This refers to householders who are self-sacrificing, as well as lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika*) who know Brahman, and forest-dwellers. For that reason, the term "one who knows the supreme self" (*adhyātmavittama*) was used with the intention of including all these stages of life (*āśrama*). But is this not improper? For indeed, he is one who "does not undertake acts of injury or favor" (GDh 3.24–5). Who, then, has called him an undertaker of such acts? We have already stated that when approached and questioned regarding a doubt, even he would speak. And so Vyāsa says:
"One who does no harm to the hosts of all living beings may wander about without even speaking;
when questioned by other virtuous men, he should speak, and he may question others regarding his doubts.

As for the statement, "Prior to the highest [stage], there are three types of *āśramins*" (GDh 28.49), that refers to the *vaikhānasa* (forest-dweller), because the prohibition against the gathering of mendicants (*bhikṣu*) should be understood as applying to groups of ten or more. Even in that case, however, if someone should join them by transgressing his own rules, then the assembly remains endowed with its proper qualities. Thus says Aṅgiras:
"Beyond the stage of the student (brahmacāryāśrama), three [other] stages of life are recorded," so he says.

And because of the two occurrences of the word "or" (vā), it is stated that there are "two or" [others]. Furthermore, in comparison with the former, those two should be understood as possessing superior qualities. Thus they have said:
"Whether there be four, or three, or two, or even one who is irreproachable..."
"Even a single one among the ascetics who possess the foremost knowledge may become the presiding member of the assembly. Thus it is said.

That which the assembly, having deliberated among themselves and correctly ascertained, declares—that should be the Dharma; it is to be understood that such Dharma is free from doubt. And so says Gautama: "One should practice that which those who possess self-control, who are aged, properly disciplined, free from hypocrisy, greed, and delusion, and learned in the Vedas, declare" (GDh 9.62). Śaṅkha also says: "In case of conflict with the Śruti, the decision rests with assemblies of those learned in the three Vedas," and "They should speak according to their conviction based on the scriptures. As for the assembly of at least five or ten members mentioned by the expounders of Dharma, that should be understood to apply to the subject of penance for mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*) and the like, because purity and impurity are made manifest therein. However, as for the assembly of twenty-one hundred members mentioned by Aṅgiras, that indeed must be considered as being based on mere faith, thinking "whatever those many Brāhmaṇas say, that shall be so," because even those whose essence is merely the *Gāyatrī* and who have performed their vows are unable to determine the Dharma. Or [the larger number] may be for the purpose of praising the aforementioned assembly, or for the purpose of censuring the ignorant. And so it has been said: "But not others, even by the thousands" (BDh 1.1.9). Or, if it refers to those possessing specific qualities, it is for the purpose of making known the gravity of the matter at hand. As for that which...
For kings, that same [fine] is declared to be double; for Vaiśyas, it is triple.

This [statement] is intended either to emphasize the need for extra effort in bestowing penance upon Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, or to refer to cases of distress (*āpad*), or to make known the mandatory nature of penance, or to establish the rule that the declaration must be made verbally before an assembly (*pariṣad*). As for the point that the authority to grant penance to Kṣatriyas and others belongs to the family priest (*purohita*) and so forth, while others [may grant it] in other cases—that we shall explain in the section on penance. In every respect, the determination of Dharma occurs within an assembly. And the Master’s intention is that even a small assembly is praiseworthy if its members possess excellent qualities. Since the Smṛti rules regarding the purpose of an assembly’s decision are rooted in logic (*nyāya*), it is not contradictory for them to have multiple applications. One should exercise discrimination in this very manner. (9)
Thus ends the section on the introduction.
Now begins the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*).

The nature and the means of knowledge regarding dharma and the other categories have been stated. Now, their instruments must be explained. Since the agent is common to all ritual actions, it is appropriate to mention him first; therefore, he says:
The castes are the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras; however, the first three are the twice-born (dvija).
For them, indeed, the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony and ending with those at the cremation ground are performed with sacred mantras.

The Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra—these four are the social classes (*varṇa*). This is a technical definition for the purpose of conventional usage. The word "but" (*tu*) is to be understood as having been displaced [from its position] for the sake of emphasis. The designation "the first three are twice-born" (*dvija*) is also to be understood as before. Now, one might object: it would suffice to say "the first are twice-born," since the number three is understood from the plural ending. True, this is so; however, the word "three" is used for the purpose of excluding the *Rathakāra*. As for the mention of the initiation (*upanayana*) of the *Rathakāra* in another Smṛti, that should be understood as resulting from a confusion regarding his eligibility for the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), or else let there be an option. The Teacher says: "No. For those twice-born, the rites are performed with mantras, beginning from conception (*niṣeka*) until the collection of the bones after death. The meaning is "according to the scriptures. The ablative case (*pañcamī*) should be seen here in the sense of the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*). The particle "vai" signifies a reason. Since their birth called initiation is worthy of mantras, therefore the rites are accompanied by mantras. (10)
What, then, are those rites, and at what time are they to be performed? To this he says:

The ceremony for entering the womb [is performed] during the fertile season; the rite for ensuring a male child before the movement [of the fetus]; the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair) in the sixth or eighth month; and after that, the *jātakarman* (birth-rite). (1.11)

The first sacrament (*saṃskāra*) is called *garbhādhāna* (conception), characterized by the act of impregnation. It should be performed during the woman’s fertile period (*ṛtu*). By implication, this refers to the period to be described later, not the spring season and so forth. The second sacrament is called *puṃsavana* (the rite for securing a male child), and it is to be performed before the movement of the fetus. Thus Pāraskara says: "Now follows the *puṃsavana*, prior to the movement [of the fetus]" (PārGṛ 1.14.1); this states the primary rule. The third sacrament, called *sīmantonnayana* (parting the hair), takes place in the sixth or eighth month of pregnancy. After this, the *jātakarma* (birth-rite) occurs at the time indicated by its very name; the word "and" (*ca*) implies the *soṣyantī-karma* (the rite for the woman about to give birth). Thus he says: "He sprinkles the woman about to give birth with water," and "And of the newborn boy" (PārGṛ 1.16.1, 3). These sacraments are to be understood in their entirety from the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. Furthermore, they are repeated with each pregnancy, up to but not including the *sīmantonnayana*, because that is a sacrament of the woman. Its status as a sacrament of the woman is established by the statement: "They part the hair upwards" (PārGṛ 1.15.4), and by the wording of the mantra: "Be fruitful throughout your life" (PārGṛ 1.15.6), as well as by the designation *sīmantinī* ("she whose hair is parted"). There is also another Smṛti: "The *sīmantonnayana* is like the *puṃsavana*: in the first pregnancy, in the sixth or eighth month" (PārGṛ 1.15.1–2). Nor should this be interpreted as being for the purpose of restricting the month in the first pregnancy alone, for that would result in a contradiction of the revealed scripture (*śruti*). Nor should one fear to say that there is a repetition even though it is a sacrament of the woman, on the grounds that it is occasioned by the pregnancy; for the occasioning factor is specifically the first pregnancy. Moreover, there is no repetition because there is no further task to be accomplished. The *garbhādhāna* repeats itself by the very nature of the matter. The *puṃsavana* repeats due to an indicative mark (*liṅga*). The *soṣyantī-karma* repeats because its purpose is a comfortable delivery. Therefore, there is no inequality [between the cases]. Hence it is well said: "They proceed, excluding the *sīmantonnayana*. And thus, there is conformity with traditional practice. || 11 ||
Furthermore:
On the eleventh day [after birth], the naming ceremony; in the fourth month, the first outing;
in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food; and the tonsure ceremony should be performed according to family custom.

The naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) should be performed on the eleventh day; the same applies to the rite of going out of the house (*niṣkramaṇa*). Thus it is said: "In the fourth month, he performs the going out" (PārGṛ 1.17.5). As for the statement, "On the tenth day, having raised [the child] and fed the Brahmins, the father gives him a name" (PārGṛ 1.17.1), the meaning there is "when the tenth day has dawned. Likewise, Manu says: "One should cause his naming to be performed on the tenth or the twelfth day" (MDh 2.30).

The particle *ca* has the sense of "immediate succession. It should be understood as meaning "on the tenth or the twelfth day [after birth]. It is not stated that it occurs on the eleventh day because [the child] is born from a portion [of the parents]. Furthermore, by the word *tu*, it is indicated that this alone is the primary rule (*kalpa*). If, however, its meaning is "only on the tenth day," then it should be understood as referring to one whose purification occurs before the ten nights have passed, since that would not contradict the statements regarding the period of impurity (*sūtaka*). On the eleventh day, however, it is the primary rule without distinction. The phrase "according to family custom" refers to the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*). For example: "The Bharadvājas have five tufts of hair. Time, however, is a subordinate factor (*aṅga*). The relative weight of these matters is to be understood from the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. Alternatively, this may be intended to refer to time in general, applying even to the rites such as the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) and others. For instance: the birth-rite is performed on the next day or within ten nights; the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) on the eleventh or twelfth day, or after a hundred nights, or under an auspicious asterism (*nakṣatra*); the first outing (*niṣkramaṇa*) within ten nights or in the fourth month; the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) in the sixth month or in the first year; and the tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*) in the first year or in the third year (or the year and a half). All of these should be performed either according to family custom or at the times specified. The repetition of the word "month" is for the sake of metrical convenience. The rest is straightforward. 12.

But why must these purificatory rites (*saṃskārakarman*) be performed with effort and as a matter of necessity? It is said: because sin arising from seed and womb is thus pacified; and since sin has specific causes and must be removed, they are performed with effort and as a rule. Furthermore, even when performed for the sake of the embryo, if they are not performed, the transgression belongs to the parents alone. Thus Manu says:
"The sin pertaining to seed and the sin pertaining to the womb are wiped away for the twice-born. (MDh 2.27).
But are these rites intended only for males? No, he says:
"These rites for women are performed silently."

The phrase "they should also be performed" is the ellipsis [to be supplied], because there is no difference in their status as objects of refinement (*saṃskāryatva*). Regarding the word "these" (*etāḥ*), it should be understood that the pronoun refers to the subjects of the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) and others, as delimited by the word "then" (*ataḥ*). However, there is no distinction regarding the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*) and the rest. Furthermore, the rite for the woman about to give birth (*soṣyantī-karman*)—which is understood from the conjunction "and" (*ca*)—is also included, since its purpose is to ensure an easy delivery. Now, one might object: "If this is the case, the eligibility (*adhikāra*) of women for rites associated with mantras would be difficult to maintain, due to the absence of mantras for them. This objection is not valid, because eligibility is established through direct scriptural statement (*vacana*). Moreover, there is no absolute absence of mantras for women. Even if the birth-rite and others were indeed performed silently (*tūṣṇīm*), [the eligibility remains].
But the marriage ceremony is accompanied by mantras. || 1.13 ||

It is indeed accompanied by mantras; therefore, there is no contradiction. However, because of the absence of a specific purpose (*kārya*), the performance of sacraments (*saṃskāra*) ceases in the case of a eunuch. But rites characterized by their purpose (*artha-lakṣaṇa*), such as the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) and others, proceed even for a Śūdra. Thus says Manu: "For a Śūdra, [the rites] are joined with service" (MDh 2.32), since they are neither enjoined nor prohibited. Śaṅkha states: "For a Śūdra, [rites are performed] excluding mantras. Some say this is because of the statement regarding his equality with women in all respects. But that should not be relied upon in legal practice (*vyavahāra*), which is defined by verbal testimony (*śabda-lakṣaṇa*), because it is merely an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*). And these sacraments for women of the Brāhmaṇa and other classes also take place at these very same times. || 13 ||
Henceforth: "The initiation (upanayana) of a Brāhmaṇa takes place in the eighth year after conception or in the eighth year [itself];
for Kṣatriyas in the eleventh, and for Vaiśyas in the twelfth, or according to family custom. (1.14)

[Objection: Is it not the case that, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), this initiation (*upanayana*) is stated to belong to the Brāhmaṇa alone, because of the statement, "The first three are the twice-born"? [Response: It is incorrect to mention the Brāhmaṇa specifically. If it is argued that the mention of the Brāhmaṇa is for the purpose of making known that initiation belongs to one who is already a Brāhmaṇa, and that Brāhmaṇahood does not arise from initiation, even that is worthless, since this is already established by the very definition of the social classes (*varṇa*). [Reply: It is said: This is for the sake of providing a reason (*hetvartha*). One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception or from birth. Why? Precisely because he is a Brāhmaṇa. For such is the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "The Brāhmaṇa is indeed the *Gāyatrī*; the *Gāyatrī* has eight syllables; therefore, one should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years of age," and so forth. The same should be applied to the terms *Kṣatriya* and *Vaiśya*. However, the statement of the reason in the verse is for the purpose of establishing the specific times, such as spring (*vasanta*). Thus says the tradition: "For spring is the *Brāhmaṇa*, summer is the *Kṣatriya*, and the rainy season is the *Vaiśya*" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 2.1.3.5). By restating through words the connection of the Brāhmaṇas and others with spring and so on—which is already established elsewhere—it shows that the initiation of a Brāhmaṇa must take place in spring. Although these sentences occur in the context of the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) and other rites, nevertheless, there is no contradiction in their providing the time required for initiation, as this serves to establish the validity of the reason. And the wording of a mantra says: "The *Gāyatrī* is of spring," meaning that the *Gāyatrī* metre was fashioned from the spring season. This is precisely its meaning. The Carakas, however, read these more clearly in the context of initiation itself. Accordingly, Āpastamba follows them: "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in spring," and so forth (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.1.19). Śaṅkha also says: "Spring, summer, and autumn are the seasons. But for the Vaiśya, there is an option. Initiation (*upanayana*) is the leading near to a teacher for the purpose of Vedic study; it is called *upanayana* for the sake of the meter, or it refers to the ritual act performed for that purpose. The phrase "of kings" is for the purpose of making known that the words *Kṣatriya* and *Rājan* have the same meaning. The remainder is that the initiation should be performed in the eleventh year. "In the twelfth for the Vaiśyas" means in the twelfth year. The repetition "some according to family custom" introduces an alternative view. Some desire it according to family custom, not necessarily in spring and so on. We, however, hold that one should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years in spring. These same times apply even to those born of women in the direct order (*anuloma*), because they are designated by the caste of their mother, as seen in the statement of Manu: "Sons are those born of women of the next lower caste" (Manu Smṛti 10.14). Since the gender is intended to be significant, there is no application of these rules to women. Those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), however, are simply not entitled [to these rites]. Thus says Gautama: "But from the inverse order, one is devoid of dharma" (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 4.25). || 14 ||
Now, one might ask: "Should the Veda itself be taught immediately after initiation, since that is the purpose of initiation? Indeed, such would be the case; therefore, he says:
"Having initiated the pupil, the teacher should subsequently teach him the Veda preceded by the Mahāvyāhṛtis, and should also instruct him in the rules of purification and conduct. (1.15)

The word "ca" has the sense of "tu. One should not teach the Veda immediately after the initiation (*upanayana*); rather, [one should do so] afterwards. The intention is that one should instruct [the student] in the rules of purity and conduct immediately thereafter. And so says Manu: "Having initiated the pupil, the teacher should first instruct him in purity, as well as in conduct, the fire-ritual, and the twilight devotions" (MDh 2.69).

But when he should teach [the Veda], then it should be preceded by the *mahāvyāhṛtis*. By the term *mahāvyāhṛti*, one should understand the syllable *oṃ*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī*, according to another *smṛti* source. As Manu says:
"The three imperishable *mahāvyāhṛtis* preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, and the three-footed *gāyatrī*, should be known as the mouth of Brahman" (MDh 2.81).

The rule of Gautama, however, pertains to the Sāmaveda; this should be understood from the statement, “The five *vyāhṛtis* preceded by *oṃ* and ending with *satya*” (GDh 1.51), for therein the five are recited as “*puruṣaḥ satyam*. Alternatively, it may mean that the Veda which has the *mahāvyāhṛtis* first is “preceded by the *mahāvyāhṛtis*”; since a compound cannot be formed with a term requiring an external correlative (*sāpekṣa*), there is no mention of the *Sāvitrī*. However, the *oṃkāra* must certainly be performed at the beginning and end, because of the statement, “That which is not preceded by *oṃ* flows away” (MDh 2.74). The rule of Manu, on the other hand, should be explained as an option: either the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by *oṃ* constitute the mouth of Brahman, or the *Sāvitrī* is preceded by them. Such is the established practice (*samācāra*). The mention of the “preceptor” (*guru*) is primary because the father is the one who performs the initiation (*upanetṛ*). Thus says the Śruti: “Therefore, they say that a son who has been instructed is worthy of the world” (BĀU 1.5.17). The mention of the “pupil” (*śiṣya*), however, is for the purpose of ensuring complete service even when he is a son. Since Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas also act as initiators of sons in times of distress, their status as preceptors is not contradictory. Initiation by an *ācārya*, however, is a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) for a Brāhmaṇa. “Purity and conduct” (*śaucācāra*) refers to purity and proper behavior. Purity is threefold, characterized by mind, speech, and body. Mental purity is the absence of improper intentions, because anything other than the virtuous is opposed to it. Verbal purity consists of the use of correct words and truthful speech. Thus says Bhāradvāja: “One should not learn the language of the Mlecchas; for it is known that he who uses incorrect words is a Mleccha. Therefore, having initiated a pupil, one should teach him correct words, the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), the kindling of the fire (*agnīndhana*), and so forth” (cf. VaDh 6.41). Physical purity, consisting of earth and water, is well known. Others, however, describe five kinds of purity. For instance:
"Truth, purity, purity of mind, purity as the restraint of the senses, compassion toward all beings, and fifthly, purity through water. Thus it is said.

The *ācāras* consist of duties related to the stages of life (*āśrama*), such as maintaining the sacred fires and kindling the fire, as well as those related to the social classes (*varṇa*), such as non-stealing and so forth. Because of the instruction "he should train [him]," there is no application of these rules prior to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). Thus says Gautama: "Prior to initiation, one may act, speak, and eat according to one's desire" (GDh 2.1). Even if some wise person should know for himself, he still lacks the qualification [to perform these rites] before initiation, precisely because of Gautama’s statement. Furthermore, the mention of "initiation" is intended to define the time [for the commencement of duties], not to signify a sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) itself, since the time is what is required. For the duties of the classes (*varṇadharma*), which are obstructed immediately after birth by incapacity—and since that incapacity is indefinite for each individual—require a fixed time until they become capable; thus, with that as their primary concern, they adopt the scriptural injunction regarding initiation. Accordingly, the *Vitānakalpa* of the Atharvaṇas shows this focus on time: "Before the eighth spring, boys act according to their desire, being sinless, following the law of the sovereign, and performing the fivefold sacrifice. Likewise, women have freedom of action until marriage, because that alone is stated to be the Vedic rule. As Manu has said:
"The marriage rite is declared to be the Vedic sacrament for women. (MDh 2.67)

And when the initiation (*upanayana*) or marriage proceeds as determined by Vedic authority, one should understand that other duties of the social classes (*varṇadharma*) likewise apply at that very time due to that commonality. Thus, those learned in the ritual logic (*nyāyavidha*) recite: "Or rather, they should proceed by means of initiation because of its equality with the Vedas" (PMS 6.2.22). As for the Śūdra, however, since there is no instruction regarding the time for his death-rite, his capacity (*sāmarthya*) is the regulating factor; or else, [the period] until the sixteenth year, prior to the traditional limit of childhood, according to the rule: "A child is one who is less than sixteen years of age" (ViDh 54.33). Regarding Brāhmaṇas as well, some hold that before the ultimate time for initiation, those who have not been initiated may act according to their own will (*kāmacāritva*); and for women, [this freedom lasts] until three menstrual periods, for that is the ultimate time for marriage. But that view is not much favored because it lacks authoritative evidence, since initiation is intended precisely to define the primary period [of eligibility]. And thus it has already been stated that [the period of] sinlessness for them ends before the eighth year; so enough of this digression. || 15 ||
Now, with the desire to explain purification, he states the rule for the voiding of urine and feces, since that [purification] is dependent upon it:
"During the day and at the twilights, with the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) placed over the ear, one should void urine and feces facing north; but at night, facing south. (1.16)

During the day and at the two twilights, having placed the sacred thread over the ear, one should void urine and feces facing north. At night, it is likewise; however, the specific difference is that one should face south. From the word *cet* ("if"), it is understood that this procedure applies whenever one performs these acts. The word *tu* ("but") is for the purpose of restriction: one should perform [this] only for urine and feces, and not for other acts such as the emission of semen. Alternatively, the word *ca* (or) is used in the sense of including other Smṛti texts. As Śaṅkha says: "Restraining his speech and covering his head, he should urinate without covering the ground. And he should be seated, because of the mention of rising [later]. 16.
But must purification be performed in that very same place? No, he says:
"Having risen with the penis still held, one should perform purification without sloth, using earth and drawn-up water, until the odor and the residue are removed. (1.17)

By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that one who has already withdrawn his penis may also perform this; having risen from that place, he should perform purification with earth and water drawn up [from a well]. The plural number in the word "with earths" (*mṛdbhiḥ*) is for the purpose of obtaining the specific quantities prescribed in other Smṛtis. As Manu says:
"One application on the penis, three on the anus, and likewise ten on one hand. (MDh 5.136).
As for the statement in another Smṛti, "five on the anus" (DkSm 5.5), that should be understood as referring specifically to the Agnihotrin, according to the declaration of Pulastya:

"Three [purifications] for a *snātaka*, five for one who maintains the *agnihotra* fire; one should apply all these rules of purification to householders. This same rule is doubled for a *naiṣṭhika* student, tripled for a forest-dweller without a wife, and quadrupled for a mendicant of knowledge (*jñānabhikṣu*). According to Manu, however, the rule is doubled and so forth starting from the *upakurvāṇa* student (MDh 5.137). As Vyāsa has said:
Just as a white, washed cloth may become soiled again,
yet becomes stainless once more through cleansing, so it is with the classes of women and men and the stages of life (āśramas) in relation to their afflictions.
"Accordingly, penance, punishment, and purification should be prescribed in due order:
the highest for the highest [offense], the middling for the middling, and the lowest for the lowest.
As for the specific quantity of earth mentioned by Dakṣa:

"The first clay is declared to be the measure of half a handful"—this statement must be understood as being for the purpose of illustration, because it would otherwise contradict the requirement to remove both odor and residue when there are three applications; thus, each preceding application of clay is greater, while each subsequent one is smaller. As for the purification after urination mentioned in that same context: "One application of clay should be given to the penis, and likewise three on one hand."

Thus, this [rule] refers specifically to the purification after voiding urine, because elsewhere the purification of the hands is governed by the Tantric rules. This same purification for urine applies to all stages of life (*āśrama*), since no specific exception has been stated. Furthermore, it does not imply a doubling of the requirement for a householder. Likewise, the characteristics of the clay must also be sought:

"That which comes from an anthill or a mouse-hole, that which is taken from water on a path, or that which remains after another purification has been performed—with these six, purification is not achieved."

And so forth. "With water drawn up" means from a reservoir by hand or other means. "Effecting the removal of odor and stain": the meaning is that clay should be taken in such a way that the destruction of odor and stain occurs with exactly three applications. This should be understood as referring specifically to phlegm and the like; for in other cases, the removal of stains is accomplished simply by removing the odor. "Atandritaḥ" means not indolent. "One should perform purification according to the rule" (*yathāvidhiṃ*) means one should not do it just whenever one pleases (*yadā*). Alternatively, they should perform purification with clay and water as prescribed. One should perform purification according to the specific quantity ordained for each stage of life (*āśrama*). However, for those such as Śūdras for whom no specific quantity is mentioned by name, they should perform purification with clay and water that effects the removal of odor and stain. And thus says Pitāmaha:
"Those who are not initiated among the three [twice-born classes]—Śūdras, the Saudhanvanas, and women—their purification from the removal of odors and stains is by means of earth and water. (17)
Having thus performed the purification characterized by soft water, and having departed from that place and washed his feet,
the twice-born man should always perform the ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) while seated in a clean spot with his knees enclosed, facing either north or east, using the Brāhma-tīrtha. (1.18)

The meaning is "either facing east" (*prāk*) or "facing the east" (*praṅmukha*). Furthermore, from another *Smṛti*: "With his topknot tied and his waistband fastened, having washed his hands up to the wrists, a twice-born man should always perform the ritual sipping (*upaspṛśet*) with the *brāhma* tīrtha. Likewise, Gautama states: "He should begin the purification facing east or north; sitting in a clean place, placing his right arm between his knees, wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavītin*), having washed his hands up to the wrists, and remaining silent," and so forth (GDh 1.36). The mention of the "twice-born" (*dvija*) is for the purpose of excluding women and others. Because of the word "always" (*nitya*), this very rule for ritual sipping applies to all stages of life (*āśrama*). Others hold that there is no cessation of this even during periods of birth or death impurity (*sūtaka*). || 18 ||
It has been stated, "by means of the *brāhma* tīrtha. Since this is not something known through ordinary experience, he provides its definition:
"The base of the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb, as well as the tip of the hand, are respectively the *prājāpatya*, *pitrya*, *brāhma*, and *daiva* tīrthas. (1.19)

In connection with the *brāhma* [tīrtha], other *tīrthas* are also mentioned because they are useful for specific ritual purposes. The term *tīrtha* is a designation for the points of entry on the right hand. In common worldly usage as well, the word *tīrtha* is well known to refer to a landing place for descending into water and so forth. These [other *tīrthas*] are designated by the names of deities for the sake of praise, because they are useful for particular functions. For the sake of conventional usage regarding the four that have been understood through their purpose, specific technical names are stated. At the base of the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*) is the *prājāpatya*; at the base of the index finger (*deśinī*) is the *pitrya*; the *deśinī* is the finger next to the thumb; the meaning is "the space between that [finger] and the thumb. The *brāhma*, however, is at the base of the thumb; at the tip of the hand is the *daiva*. There, the connection with the subject at hand is: "one should touch [water] with the *brāhma*. And thus says the *Śāṭyāyanaka-kalpa*: "In the right hand of a Brāhmaṇa there are five *tīrthas*: if facing east, the *daiva* is in front; to the south, the *pitrya*; behind, the *brāhma*; to the north, the *prājāpatya*; and in the middle, the *pārameṣṭhya*," and so forth. It is the same in the *Vṛddhavāsiṣṭha*, with the distinction that "in the middle is the *saumya*. The Teacher does not mention five *tīrthas* because his [use of them] has little purpose, being employed for touching the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and similar acts. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is for the purpose of illustration, as it refers to others as well. Because of the contradiction [of using both hands], there is an absence of *tīrthas* on the left hand. And therefore, from the very instruction regarding the *brāhma*, it is understood that the sipping of water (*ācamana*) is performed with the right hand. Thus it is said: "The sipping of water is with the right hand."

It has been stated that "one should touch [water]. The term *upaspṛśana* (touching) is used commonly for both touching [the body] and bathing. Its specific determination is made through supplementary statements (*vākyaśeṣa*) that prescribe particular qualities. What, then, are those supplementary statements prescribing qualities? To this he says:
"Having sipped water three times, one should wipe [the mouth] twice and touch the cavities and the upper [parts of the body]."

Having drunk water three times, he should wipe [his mouth] twice. The word *ud-* (up) has the sense of *pari* (around), because its purpose is visible. For this very reason, there is wiping of the mouth, according to the statement: "He should touch the apertures upward. By the word "upward," the apertures of the head, such as the eyes and so forth, are meant. Because of the word *ca* ("and"), there is also [wiping] downward, in accordance with another Smṛti: "He should sprinkle his feet, apply [water] to the head, and touch the navel. First comes the sprinkling of the feet, then the touching of the sense organs. And because of the use of the prefix *upa*, the touching is external, not of the eyes. In this context, since water is the subject under discussion, it is done with water. Furthermore, the rule regarding the fingers as stated by Dakṣa and others should be followed. Due to the lack of distinction and the force of the word *ca*, there is also a difference in the application of the sipping of water (*ācamana*), such as: "First, he should touch the mouth with three fingers joined together," and so forth.
Furthermore, what are the characteristics of water that is fit for sipping? To this he says: "But with water that is in its natural state, free from foam and bubbles... (1.20).

The repetition of the word "with water" (*adbhir*) is for the purpose of specifying a particular quality; the particle *tu* serves to distinguish it. [The rule means] with water alone, not mixed with anything else. Thus says Śaṅkha: "having drawn out and purified them. "Existing in their natural state" (*prakṛtisthāḥ*) means remaining as they are by nature, that is, neither salty nor boiled. Accordingly, Āpastamba states: "Nor with heated water, except for a specific reason" (ĀpDh 1.15.6). However, water heated by the sun or other sources in a reservoir does not become defiled. And the Mānava [Smṛti] says: "with non-hot water" (MDh 2.16). Based on the statement of Śaṅkha, this should be explained as meaning "with unboiled water. Likewise, there is an exception in the case of illness.

"In the absence of an emergency, just as for the twice-born there is purification by water that has not been boiled, so too shall there be purification by [water] that has been boiled for those who drink boiled [water]. This is precisely the meaning of the statement, "And not with heated [water] without cause. The rest is straightforward. || 20 ||
What, then, is their measure? It is said:
"The twice-born are purified by [the waters] reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate, respectively; a woman and a Śūdra are purified by those merely touching the lips once. (1.21)

By the word *tu* ("but"), it is indicated that impurity exists prior to the water reaching the heart, but not after it has gone further. Regarding the rule, "A woman and a Śūdra [are purified] by waters touched once at the end," the preceding *ca* ("and") should be interpreted as having the sense of *eva* ("only"), meaning "by waters touched only once. Consequently, because this is a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*), there is an exclusion of touching the sense organs and so forth. However, wiping (*parimārjana*) proceeds because it serves a visible purpose. Thus Baudhāyana says: "One should not drink with bubbles, nor with foam, nor with turbid water; nor laughing, nor talking, nor standing, nor looking around, nor bent over, nor prostrate, nor with the topknot untied, nor with the girdle unbuckled, nor with the knees outside [the hands], nor making a sound; one should drink water reaching the heart three times and wipe twice. Some say 'three times' [for both]. For a Śūdra and for a woman, both [acts] are done once. This shows that wiping is done once. "At the end" means "with the tongue. The ablative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. 21.
Having thus stated the rule for sipping water (ācamana), he next describes the rules for bathing and so forth:
"Bathing with mantras dedicated to the waters, sprinkling (mārjana), restraint of the breath (prāṇāyāma), worship of the Sun, and the daily recitation of the Gāyatrī. (1.22)
The word "kārya" (should be performed) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. One should perform the bath every day; and its procedure has been stated elsewhere by the Teacher himself:
"Indeed, when abundant [water] is available, one should not perform the bath with a small amount."

For bathing is of a dual nature, consisting of both purification (*śauca*) and proper conduct (*ācāra*). Regarding this, some say it is fivefold, beginning with "that which pertains to Agni and that which pertains to Varuṇa. However, that should be understood as referring to the case of a householder in times of distress. In this context, however, the bathing of the student (*brahmacārin*) consists of immersion in water alone, because of the injunction for him to plunge like a staff. The *saṃdhyopāsana* (twilight worship) and so forth, on the other hand, constitute his proper conduct. In that regard, this is the procedure for *saṃdhyopāsana*: "Sprinkling (*mārjana*) with mantras addressed to the waters," such as "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and others; and the restraint of breath (*prāṇasaṃyama*), which will be described later; and "the worship (*upasthāna*) of the Sun," and by the word "and" (*ca*), [the worship] of the *drupadā* verse as well. Thus says Hārīta in the rule for *saṃdhyopāsana*.
"For by concentrating the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and reciting the *Drupadā* verse three times at the three junctions of the day,
one is liberated from sin and shines like a lamp.
And the worship of the Sun (*sūryopasthāna*) is performed with two solar verses, as has been stated.
"Having purified himself with water using the *āpo hi ṣṭhā* hymn of nine verses, the pure man should then worship the sun with the two verses beginning with *ud u tyam*.
And he should daily mutter the *Sāvitrī*, the *Gāyatrī*, preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and the *vyāhṛtis*, namely "tatsavitur... Thus says Manu.
"By muttering this syllable and this [Gāyatrī] preceded by the *vyāhṛtis* during both twilights, a Brahmin is endowed with the merit of the Veda.

(MDh 2.78). Because of the word "also" (*api*), bathing and so forth are also obligatory. And for a student (*brahmacārin*), bathing by immersing oneself like a staff is not prohibited. However, the rule of Gautama (GDh 1.13) is a prohibition against bathing for the sake of pleasure. Likewise, Āpastamba says, "One should not bathe in water while praising oneself" (ĀpDh 1.2.30), which shows that bathing for the sake of unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is not forbidden. Thus says Manu.
"Having bathed daily and being pure, one should perform the libations for the gods, sages, and ancestors. (MDh 2.176).
The word "api" (also/even) should be explained as intended to include the libations for the gods and others, precisely because of this statement of Manu. || 22 ||
It has been stated that breath control (prāṇāyāma) must be performed. He describes its essential nature:
"One should recite the Gāyatrī together with its head, preceded by the Vyāhṛtis and joined with each Oṃ; this threefold [recitation] is the restraint of breath (prāṇasaṃyama). (1.23)

One should recite the verse: “*mahar janaḥ tapaḥ satyaṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar tat savitur vareṇyam*,” as well as the sacred head of the *Sāvitrī*: “*āpo jyotī raso ’mṛtam*. Furthermore, it should be understood that this restraint of breath (*prāṇasaṃyama*) must be performed three times. Others, however, describe it thus: one should mutter the *Sāvitrī* in its full form three times, and this is the restraint of breath. Moreover, this recitation should be performed with the breath restrained, because of the traditional designation; and so says Manu:
"One should recite [the verse] three times while restraining the breath; that is called *prāṇāyāma*. (An addition to MDh 2.83).
Since the sequence of recitation would suggest that *prāṇāyāma* occurs after the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*), he says:
"Having restrained the vital breaths and being purified, one should [recite] the triplet sacred to the Waters (*ab-daivata*)."
He should sit reciting the Sāvitrī until the appearance of the stars.

Alternatively, this sequence applies specifically to the evening twilight (*sāyaṃsaṃdhyā*). First, having restrained the breaths (*prāṇāyāma*), the purification (*saṃśodhana*) should be performed. Because of the word *sam* (in *saṃśodhana*), there is also the sprinkling (*mārjana*) with water using *darbha* grass. The phrase "with the three verses" (*tṛcena*) is for the purpose of excluding any additional [verses]. The repetition [of the rule] is for this very reason. Consequently, an addition at midday is not contradictory. The particle *tu* has the sense of *ca* (and), meaning "and for the purpose of reaching the *drupadā*" verse. Having restrained the breaths when the sun is half-set, and having sprinkled himself with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and having recited the *drupadā*, he should worship the sun and sit facing west, reciting the *Sāvitrī* preceded by the syllable *Oṃ* and the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*), until the rising of the stars. As for what was said, "until the appearance of light," that too is merely for the purpose of indicating the rising [of the stars], since the actual appearance is not fixed. By this verse, two things are enjoined: the priority of the breath-restraint and the performance of the evening twilight rite, as indicated by the sign "until the appearance of the stars. Or rather, it may be an injunction for the twilight worship characterized by a specific time. In this way, the repetition of the rule "with the three verses addressed to the Waters" is meaningful, as it serves to exclude any additional [verses]. This will be made clear in the section on the rules for bathing (*snāna*). (24)
Is the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) to be performed only in the evening, or also in the morning? And when it is in the morning, is it to be done in exactly the same way? It is said:
"One should perform the twilight worship in the east in the morning in this manner until the sun is seen.
Then one should perform the fire-rite (agnikārya); [this applies] for both twilights. (1.25)

In this very manner, one should perform the morning twilight worship (*prātaḥ-saṃdhyopāsana*). However, there is this distinction: standing and facing the east, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) starting from the appearance of the stars until the appearance of the sun. At midday, however, since no specific direction is mentioned, one should recite the *Sāvitrī* according to one's capacity while seated, facing either the east or the north. Others, however, say that one should stand facing the sun and recite it a thousand times or more, based on the statement of Hārīta: "The Goddess [Sāvitrī] has a thousand heads, a hundred middles, and ten ends; therefore, one should recite her from a thousand down to a hundred, and from a hundred down to ten."

However, that [prohibition] should be understood as referring specifically to the *agnihotrin* due to the obstruction of his ritual duties. Some maintain that there is a postponement because the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) is impossible before sunrise; yet such is not the established practice. The prefix *ā-* should be understood here as signifying inclusion (*abhividhi*), for another Smṛti states: "By virtue of their long *saṃdhyā*, the seers attained long life" (MDh 4.94). Furthermore, *saṃdhyā* is the name of the rite of attendance itself, since the time is already established by other sources. As Gārgya has said:

"One should perform the morning *saṃdhyā* with the stars until the rising of the sun, and the evening *saṃdhyā* with the sun until the appearance of the stars. Thus says [the tradition]. Saṃvarta states: "[The evening *saṃdhyā* is] when the sun has half-set. Now, the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) is for the purpose of purifying oneself and is an ancillary part of the *saṃdhyā*. Others, however, consider the act of recitation (*japa*) to be the primary element. As Manu says:
"One should stand reciting the Sāvitrī during the morning twilight until the sun appears. (MDh 4.93)

The phrase "standing, he should mutter" involves a change of grammatical case; thus, having performed the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), one should perform the fire-rite (*agnikārya*). The procedure for this is to be understood from the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. The term "twilight" (*saṃdhyā*) here indicates the time immediately following [the twilight], because of the contradiction [otherwise]. The mention of "both" (*ubhayoḥ*) is for the sake of emphasis. This emphasis is intended to prevent the doubt that the fire-rite mentioned in the verse "having performed the fire-rite, he should eat" (YDh 1.35) might refer to some other rite; rather, it refers to the very same one. Others, however, believe that the phrase "in both twilights" expresses a relationship of primary and subordinate acts (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*). But that is not particularly sound, because of the statement of sequence with the word "then" (*tataḥ*) and because of the use of the locative case. The word "api" is for the purpose of indicating its obligatory nature, since it is drawn forward from the expression "day after day. (25)
Having thus completed the fire-ritual,
he should then salute his elders, saying, "I am so-and-so," and he should also attend upon his teacher with a concentrated mind for the sake of Vedic study. 1.26.

The word *tataḥ* is used for the sake of sequence. One should "salute the elders" (*abhivādayed vṛddhān*) on account of their learning, lineage, conduct, age, wealth, and so forth. The phrase *asau* indicates the mention of one's own name. The particle *iti* has the sense of "in this manner. As Baudhāyana says: "If permitted by his teacher, he may [salute] another person of good conduct at will, touching the ear with the words *asāv ahaṃ bhoḥ* for the purpose of concentrating the mind, [placing his hands] below the knees down to the feet," and so on (BDh 1.3.26–28). Some hold that the touching of the ear is restricted to specific regions according to established custom. As Āpastamba states: "A Brāhmaṇa should salute, having extended his right arm level with his ear," and so on (ĀpDh 1.5.16). Since that has a visible purpose, it should be understood to apply to cases where the person is at a distance. The distinction between those who should be saluted and those who should not be saluted must be investigated. For example: "Neither when one is impure, nor toward one who is impure," and so on (BDh 1.3.29); likewise: "One should not salute while holding sacrificial fuel, earth, or a water-pot in one's hand" (BDh 1.3.31). Other similar rules include: "There is no salutation in a crowd, nor among the wives of brothers, if one has attained virility," and so on (BDh 1.3.32–33); and "Those who do not know the protracted vowel (*pluti*) at the end of a name," and so forth. In the phrase "and one should attend upon the teacher" (*guruṃ caivopāsīta*), the word *ca* carries the sense of the particle *tu*. The word *eva* ends in the letter *m*. The meaning is: "one should clasp the teacher's feet (*upasaṃgṛhṇīyāt*) in this manner, but one should not [merely] salute him (*nābhivādayet*). As Manu says: [he should clasp the feet].
The clasping of the teacher's feet should be performed with crossed hands:
the left foot is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand. (MDh 2.72)

Because of this statement. As for that which was stated by Āpastamba, "Having wiped his right foot with both hands, he should grasp [the teacher's] hand" (ĀpDh 1.5.21), that is an occasional rite (*naimittika*) because it is intended for a specific mark of favor. First comes the clasping of the teacher's feet, because of the statement, "being permitted by the teacher. He should not merely clasp [his feet], but should also attend upon him for the sake of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), being concentrated and focused in mind. Or rather, the meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that he should attend upon him even without [the specific purpose of] Vedic study. || 26 ||
And this is another duty toward him:
when summoned, he should study; whatever he has obtained, he should offer to him;
and he should always act for his benefit through the actions of mind, speech, and body. (1.27)

When summoned by his teacher, he should go without hesitation; the word *ca* ("and") implies that he should do so even when not summoned. Furthermore: he may also study (*apy adhīyīta*) when permitted by the teacher; the word *api* here indicates inclusion, for those learned in the science of words (*śabdajña*) maintain that the particle *api* has the sense of "also" (*prakāra*), as seen in the statement: "One should constantly examine the meaning" (*arthanityaḥ parīkṣeta*, Nirukta 2.1). Gautama also states this mode of behavior: "Having grasped [the teacher's] left hand with his own," and so forth (GDh 1.46). He should announce the alms he has obtained to him, because there is no other occasion for doing so. Alternatively, anything else that is unasked for and not to be refused—such as what has been brought by a Brāhmaṇa or others—he may accept based on this very injunction. Or, he may beg for the sake of the teacher with his permission. Thus says Āpastamba: "Bringing all gain to the teacher" (ĀpDh 1.3.25); because of the use of the word "all" and because alms are mentioned separately, this very rule makes it known. As for the saying, "Beggars are the masters of cooked food," that should be understood as referring to his own subsistence. "He should always practice what is beneficial for him"—by the word *ca* ("and"), one understands "what is pleasing" as well. Thus says Gautama: "He should be intent upon what is pleasing and beneficial" (GDh 2.30). Even something unpleasant may indeed be beneficial at the time, such as medicine; therefore, they are mentioned separately. From the word *nitya* ("always"), it is understood that this applies even after he has returned home from his studies (*samāvṛtta*). "By acts of mind, speech, and body"—the meaning is "in every way. As the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) says: "Whoever would not harm you in any way... those Brahmins who do not honor their teacher in thought, word, or deed" (cf. VaDh 2.9, 11). The specific types of what is beneficial are to be understood from common worldly experience and from other scriptures. These are the rules for the religious student (*brahmacārin*). 27.

Furthermore, regarding the teacher: those who are grateful, non-malicious, intelligent, pure, of noble birth, free from envy, virtuous, capable, trustworthy, and who provide for his own needs—these, according to dharma, are to be taught. 1.28.

One who is grateful is indeed well-known. One who is non-malicious toward all beings (*adrohī*), because being non-malicious toward one's teacher is already established by the very mention of "beneficial speech. "Pure" (*śuci*) has been explained. "Noble-born" (*kulya*) means of good family (*kulīna*). "Free from envy" (*anasūyakāḥ*) means devoid of malice (*asūyā*); malice is the pointing out of another's secrets through gestures and the like, or it is slander. This [term] qualifies those mentioned and those yet to be mentioned, due to the force of the plural number; even in the reading with the singular, this is an introduction of other persons to be taught. "Virtuous" (*sādhu*) is explained by the virtuous (*sadbhiḥ*). "Capable" (*śakta*) means able to grasp the application [of the rules] or capable of reasoning and refutation (*ūhāpoha*). "Trustworthy" (*āpta*) means a friend. "One's own" (*sva*) refers to a brother or similar relative, excluding a son. "A giver of wealth" (*arthada*) means a giver of material goods or a giver of knowledge; for another *smṛti* states: "Knowledge and men are ordained to be exchanged" (VaDh 2.39). And the giver of wealth is so by way of trade, because of the statement "according to dharma" (*dharmataḥ*) and because of the prohibition against teaching for wages (*bhṛtaka-adhyāpana*). These are to be taught according to dharma. By the word "but" (*tu*), it is implied that there may be others for the sake of livelihood, as Manu says: *Manu 4.31*: "But he who, out of greed, teaches the Veda to those who have not performed the
