"The son of the teacher, one who is obedient, a giver of knowledge, righteous, pure, capable, a provider of wealth, one who seeks [instruction], his own [kinsman], and the virtuous—these ten are to be taught according to the Dharma" (MDh 2.109).

These qualities of a student are prescribed under the guise of the teacher; the meaning is that one possessing such qualities is to be taught, and he must conduct himself accordingly. And these [qualities] apply specifically to the *brahmacārin*. 28.
He should carry a staff, a deerskin, a sacred thread, and a girdle;
he should go about for alms among blameless Brahmins for the sake of his own livelihood. 1.29.

The word *eva* should be understood as ending in the letter *m*, signifying the manner (*prakāra*) mentioned in other Smṛtis. The word *ca* has the sense of including what has not been mentioned. As Gautama says: "Clothes made of hemp, linen, bark, and blankets are for all [students]" (GDh 1.17), and so forth. And the types of staffs: "The staffs of a Brāhmaṇa are made of Bilva or Palāśa wood" (GDh 1.22), and so forth. "The skins of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, and the goat" (GDh 1.16)—this refers to the types of skins; and these are to be worn as upper garments. As Āpastamba says: "They should wear a skin as an upper garment" (ĀpDh 1.3.10). And the sacred thread (*upavīta*). As Baudhāyana says: "The sacrificial thread is made of Kuśa grass or cotton, triple-stranded and threefold. Having placed it under the right arm as far as the navel, one should place it over the head" (BDh 1.8.5–7). But the text of Manu—"when the right hand is raised" (MDh 2.63), etc.—is for the purpose of the specific mode of wearing it. As for the rule regarding specific castes—"the sacrificial thread of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of cotton" (MDh 2.44), etc.—that refers specifically to initiated students (*dīkṣita*), according to the statement of Jātūkarṇi: "If they are a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who have been initiated, they should use threads of hemp and wool. And the types of girdles: "A girdle of Muñja grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth" (MDh 2.42), and so forth. These items, such as the staff and others, must be worn constantly during times that are not prohibited. As for what was said by Manu: "Having taken the desired staff" (MDh 2.48), that should be understood as referring to taking another staff in case of necessity. "He should beg alms from blameless Brāhmaṇas for his own subsistence"—this is not for all purposes. "From families of Brāhmaṇas"—this is the primary rule (*prathama-kalpa*). "From families of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas"—this is the secondary rule (*anukalpa*). "Even from Śūdra families"—this is the rule for times of distress (*āpatkalpa*). Thus Manu has said.
A student, being self-restrained, should daily collect alms from the houses of those who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifices, who are praiseworthy in their own duties.
Or, in the absence of those previously mentioned, he may wander through the entire village. (MDh 2.183, 185)

And Gautama says: "The practice of begging for alms is common to all castes" (GDh 2.35). Even though the word *brāhmaṇa* [is used], the begging of alms is from Brāhmaṇa women. As Āpastamba says: "From those who do not refuse" (ĀpDh 1.3.26). And the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) shows that one should beg from a woman: "They say that she whose conduct is most abundant and who is gentle—she is the one from whom one should beg; that is conducive to the world [of the ancestors]. Now, if he should not find another woman from whom to beg, he may even beg from his own teacher’s wife. This indicates that a woman is the one from whom alms are to be begged. Furthermore, the rule: "Having had a blessing pronounced, the giving of alms is preceded by water" (GDh 5.18), refers specifically to the case of a woman. Or, since this [blessing] pertains to the giver [of the food], there is no fault. || 29 ||

Anticipating the objection that this practice of living on alms applies exclusively to the Brāhmaṇa because the other two [castes] lack the authority to accept gifts, the author states its applicability by way of teaching their respective qualities:
"The practice of wandering for alms belongs, respectively, to the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya, characterized by the word *bhavat* at the beginning, middle, and end. (1.30)
This verse is self-explanatory. || 30 ||
Since [the rule] would otherwise apply even to one who possesses no wealth because it is for the sake of subsistence, he says:
"One established in studentship (brahmacarya) shall not eat food from a single person except in times of distress;
a Brāhmaṇa may, however, eat at a śrāddha feast at will, provided he does not violate his vow. (1.31)

Because of the statement that he is "established" [in his vow], he would cease to be a celibate student (*abrahmacārī*) were he to act otherwise. By stating, "One should not eat in a single house except in times of distress," the author shows—by means of this counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding times of distress—that even for one who possesses wealth, there is a restriction on subsistence through begging. "A Brāhmaṇa may eat at will," provided he has come for the sake of alms and is invited by blameless persons; but not so the Kṣatriya or the Vaiśya. "Without violating his vow" means excluding honey, meat, and the like. And thus says Manu:
"When a rite for the gods or for the ancestors has arrived, one should eat as if observing a vow."
"He may eat at his pleasure when invited; his vow is not thereby violated" (MDh 2.189).

Furthermore, by means of this praise of the Brāhmaṇa, [the author] shows that the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya have no entitlement [to this]. As for the penance prescribed for a student (brahmacārin) who eats at a śrāddha, that should be understood to apply to one who was invited on the previous day. || 31 ||
The observances for the religious student (*brahmacārin*) have been stated; now the restraints (*yama*) are being described:
He should avoid honey, meat, collyrium, food-leavings, fermented acids, women, and the harming of living beings; he should also avoid looking at the sun, vulgar speech, and slander. (1.32)

Although the consumption of honey is permitted in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) by the statement, "He should eat that which makes it sweet," nevertheless, for the teacher, this alone is the intended position: that one who is a religious student (*brahmacārī*) should not eat honey. This is because the permission is restricted to times of distress (*āpad*). The meaning is that a learned man engaged in worldly activities through the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas may, in times of distress, eat honey as something that ought to be done, but not otherwise. Thus the Carakas recite: "Kilāsa seized Śvetaketu, the son of Āruṇi, while he was practicing studentship. The Aśvins said to him: 'Honey and meat are indeed your medicine. He replied: 'Being a student, how may I eat honey? They both said: 'When a person lives by his own self, then I shall perform other meritorious deeds; for one must protect the self above all else. Furthermore, the Vājasaneyins say: "We shall give honey and meat to the teacher, and we shall eat what remains of it. In this way we do not incur sin; it will be for us just like the remnant of the *agnihotra* sacrifice. From this, it is understood that the statement of the Vājasaneyins refers specifically to times of distress. Consequently, there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for eating otherwise when not in distress. The mention of "ointment" (*añjana*) is intended to indicate ornaments in general. And the "remnant" (*ucchiṣṭa*) belongs to anyone other than the teacher. Thus they say: "The remnant of anyone other than the teacher is not to be eaten. "Sour" (*śukta*) refers to stale food, such as cooked grains and the like. And [one should avoid] women even in conversation and so forth, except for necessary duties. Thus Āpastamba says: "One should converse with women only as much as is necessary" (ĀpDh 1.3.16). "Injury to living beings" applies even in thought. Thus Bharadvāja says: "If one injures a living being even in thought, one should repeat the *drupadā* verse three times. "Gazing at the sun" refers to the times of its rising and setting, etc., as they say: [and so forth].
"One should never look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting. (MDh 4.37)

Even improper mental intention (*saṅkalpana*) is forbidden, according to the Vedic revelation: "If he forms an improper intention... As for the statement, "or harsh words" (GDh 2.19), that is intended for the purpose of a specific expiation. One may also engage in slander against those who hate him; the word "and" (*ca*) is used to include the restraints mentioned in other Smṛtis. For example, as stated: "shoes, umbrellas, lust, anger," and so forth (GDh 2.13). Furthermore, collyrium and the like are not prohibited when used for medicinal purposes, since they do not constitute ornamentation. Thus the sacred tradition shows: "One should indeed protect oneself from all sides. In this way, a few restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) have been stated by way of illustration. It should be understood, however, that whatever the Guru or Teacher may prescribe in every respect, those alone are the restraints and observances for the student (*brahmacārin*). And so Śaunaka says: "Whatever the learned Teacher may say, one should perform that without hesitation; for it is known that the duty of the student consists precisely in following the instruction. (32)
Furthermore, what are the characteristics of a *guru*, and what are the characteristics of an *ācārya*? It is said:
He is a *guru* who, having performed the rites, imparts the Veda to him; he who initiates him and gives him the Veda is declared an *ācārya*. (1.33)

He who, having performed the rites beginning with the *niṣeka*, imparts the Veda to him is called a *guru*. Based on another Smṛti text stating, "the rites beginning with the *niṣeka*," the meaning is that he is the father. He who merely performs the initiation (*upanayana*) and gives the Veda is designated an *ācārya* by Manu and others. Thus Manu says:

"But that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) and the secret doctrines (*rahasya*), him they call an *ācārya*" (MDh 2.140). || 33 ||
In order to make known their status as venerable persons, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the teacher (*upādhyāya*) are mentioned here by way of context.

A teacher is one who instructs a portion [of the Veda], while an officiating priest is one who performs a sacrifice. These are to be honored according to their seniority; among them, however, the mother is the most venerable. (1.34)
One who imparts a single portion of the Veda, or all the Vedāṅgas, is called an *upādhyāya*. As Manu has said:
"He who teaches for the sake of his livelihood either a single portion of the Veda or even the Vedāṅgas is called an *upādhyāya*" (MDh 2.141).

In this verse, the phrase "also for the sake of his livelihood" (*vṛttyartham api*) should be construed [with the preceding]. However, one who performs a sacrifice for the sake of another is called an *ṛtvij* (priest). And he is of three kinds. As Nārada has said:

"The *ṛtvij* is declared by the ancients to be of three types: one chosen by the patron himself, one previously engaged [by the patron], and one who performs the priestly office according to the rules out of his own free will. (NSm 3.10)

As for that which is stated in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]: "He who, being chosen, performs the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the *pākayajña* sacrifices, and the *makha* sacrifices such as the *agniṣṭoma*,
is here called an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) in this context" (MDh 2.143).

The use of the word *iha* (here) is for the purpose of making known the superiority of honor, and not for the purpose of excluding others. Among these, each preceding one is more honorable than the next; however, it should be understood that the mother is the most venerable of all. And so says Gautama: “Some say ‘the mother’” (GDh 2.51). Manu also states that the mother is more venerable than such a father:
“But the mother exceeds a thousand fathers in terms of honor” (MDh 2.145).

But a father of a different kind is inferior to the teacher. Thus Āpastamba says: "That is the most excellent birth which the mother and father produce as a physical body" (ĀpDh 1.1.18). Even though he is merely the progenitor, the mother alone is weightier than the father. However, a father who performs or causes to be performed the rites beginning with the *niṣeka* according to rule before the initiation (*upanayana*), and who sustains him with food, is equal to the teacher. As Manu says: "He who performs the rites beginning with the *niṣeka* according to rule..."

"And that Brahmin who honors [him] with food is called a guru. (MDh 2.142) The mention of the "Brahmin" is for the sake of illustration (*upalakṣaṇārtha*), because [the status of guru] does not depend on being initiated. For even a mother is to be honored after due consideration of her qualities—whether she possesses virtues or lacks them—in comparison to the father and others. As for other persons who are to be honored on account of wealth and so forth, they are not mentioned here; for while honoring them brings about prosperity (*abhyudaya*), there is no sin (*pratyavāya*) in failing to do so. From the mention of the "mother," it is understood that other women as well are to be honored. As Manu says: "Toward one's father's sister, one's mother's sister, and also toward an elder sister..."
"One should maintain a conduct toward them like that toward a mother; yet the mother is more venerable than these. (MDh 2.133)

Furthermore, all those connected to one's father and mother are to be honored, according to other Smṛtis and established custom. They become honored only when those related to them are also honored; therefore, those connected to persons worthy of honor are themselves indeed worthy of honor. Among them, there is a distinction in the degree of honor based on wealth and other factors. It has been stated that even for those not connected to persons worthy of honor, honor may be accorded through wealth and so forth at one's own discretion. We shall discuss the statements regarding wealth and the rest in their proper place. In every respect, however, the conclusion reached upon considering the entire body of texts is this: "But sacred learning is weightier than all [other qualities]" (GDh 6.21). Since the reason "because Dharma is rooted therein" (GDh 6.22) is stated, wealth and the other qualities are also causes for honor. || 34 ||
Furthermore, in order to demonstrate the venerability of the teacher, he says:

"Having performed the fire-ritual, restrained in speech, and by the teacher's permission, he should eat, preceded by the ritual of sipping water (apośana), honoring the food and not disparaging it. (1.35)

The connection [of the words] is: "Having been permitted by the teacher, he should eat food with due respect. In this way, the teacher is to be honored, since even for one who has performed the fire-rite (*agnikārya*), eating and the consecration of the food (*annasaṃskāra*) occur only by his permission. The fire-rite, however, is restated as being specifically that of the morning time for the purpose of praising the teacher. Alternatively, the fire-rite—by virtue of the context—is the oblation into the fire from the alms-food (*bhaikṣa*), not the placing of fuel-sticks (*samidādhāna*), because of the rule [stating] "in the evening and in the morning" (ĀpDh 1.4.16). Thus Āpastamba shows that this alone is the fire-rite in the passage beginning, "having performed [the offering] in the fire from the alms-food" (ĀpDh 1.3.42). And so, having offered into the fire from the alms-food and having announced it to the teacher, he should eat—with speech restrained and preceded by the act of honoring—only after the teacher's permission. Furthermore, the announcement of the alms-food to the teacher is a consecration of the alms for the sake of an unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*), because of the statement "for his own livelihood" (*ātmavṛttaye*). "Not disparaging" means not pointing out defects in the food. || 35 ||
But how long is the duration for such practice of the vow? It is said:

"The period of studentship (*brahmacarya*) for each Veda is twelve years or five; some say it lasts until the Veda has been mastered; and the tonsure ceremony (*keśānta*) takes place in the sixteenth year. (1.36)
The commencement of another Veda occurs after one Veda has been completed; and that [commencement] is optional, not mandatory. As Manu says:
"Having studied the Vedas, or two Vedas, or even one Veda, in due order... (MDh 3.2).

"Some say [it lasts] until the end of the period of study. Here, the particle *iti* signifies a reason. Some hold the view that because celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is for the purpose of Vedic study, it is proper that it should last only until the completion of that study. However, in all views, the tonsure (*keśānta*) must be performed in the sixteenth year. The word *ca* (and) has the sense of *tu* (but). The emphatic particle *eva* (only) is displaced [to the end]. Furthermore, the sacrament called *keśānta* is slightly distinct from the *cūḍākaraṇa* (first tonsure); it is to be understood from the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. When, however, one is somehow not initiated before the sixteenth year, then upon the arrival of that time, the initiation of one who was previously uninitiated does not take place; and in that case, even for one who has not returned home, the *keśānta* proceeds. But at that time, the initiation (*upanayana*) should be performed first, because it is the primary rite. Since the *keśānta* is secondary, its timing is set aside. Would initiation then proceed even after the time starting from the eighth month of pregnancy? Certainly it would. Because time is secondary, there is no contradiction in the performance of the primary rite even in the absence of the aforementioned [specific] time. || 36 ||
If that were so, then the initiation would have to take place throughout one's entire life. He says: "No;
for Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, the time for initiation extends until the sixteenth, the twenty-second, and the twenty-fourth year, respectively. (1.37)

In the phrase "until the sixteenth," the particle *āṅ* should be understood as inclusive (*abhividhi*), based on the statement of Jātukarṇi: "A Brāhmaṇa who has exceeded twice the [duration of] the Gāyatrī becomes a Vrātya. Gautama also indicates this very point by using the term "exceeding" in the rule: "For a Vaiśya, [the period is] two years more" (GDh 1.14). In the cases of "until the twenty-second" and "until the twenty-fourth," the particle *āṅ* should likewise be supplied. Thus, although time is a subordinate factor, there is no initiation beyond these limits. || 37 ||
He clarifies this very point by means of a deprecatory explanatory passage (arthavāda):
"From this time forward, these fall [from their caste], excluded from all religious duties;
they are fallen from the Sāvitrī, being Vratyas, except through the Vratyastoma sacrifice. (1.38)

Beyond this—namely, after the sixteenth, twenty-second, and twenty-fourth year respectively—these twice-born men, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, fall from their duties as members of the twice-born. Prior to these times, even in times of distress, though there may be no initiation (*upanayana*), they do not fall provided there is the capacity for study; however, after the primary period has elapsed, there is indeed a fall. As Manu says: "He who, being capable of following the primary rule, conducts himself according to the secondary rule... (MDh 11.30).

And so forth. Consequently, because they have abandoned the duties of the twice-born (*dvijāti*), they are excluded from all religious duties (*dharma*) and become unfit for social intercourse (*asaṃvyavahārya*). Āpastamba demonstrates this state of being unfit for intercourse by stating: "They are declared to be slayers of Brahmins; one should avoid their approach, eating with them, and marriage with them" (ĀpDh 1.1.33–34), and so on. Why, then, are they unfit for intercourse? Because they are *vrātyas* who have fallen away from the *Sāvitrī*. The word *sāvitrī* is used here as an indicator for the time of initiation (*upanayana*). Thus Vasiṣṭha says: "From this point forward, they become those who have fallen from the *Sāvitrī*; one should not initiate them" (VaDh 11.74–75), and so forth. The mention of their specific designation is for the purpose of indicating their censurable status in social dealings. Now, are these people *vrātyas* alone? No. [The text says]: "Except through the *vrātyastoma* sacrifice. The mention of "sacrifice" (*kratu*) is for the sake of emphasis, or to exclude the mere *stoma* chant. Accordingly, the ritualists say: "Having sacrificed with the *vrātyastoma*, they should cease being *vrātyas* and become fit for social intercourse" (KātŚr 22.4.27–28). Or, it may be for the sake of emphasizing the gravity of the task. The statement regarding the penance (*prāyaścitta*) outside of its immediate context is for the purpose of performing it immediately thereafter, or for the sake of brevity. We shall explain the distinctions among the various penances for *vrātyas* mentioned in other Smṛtis at their appropriate occasion. Granted that initiation or Vedic study may not occur due to having fallen from the *Sāvitrī*, but as for the loss of the duties of the twice-born—how can that be? It is said: because they are no longer twice-born (*advijātitvāt*). || 38 ||

But why are they called "twice-born"? Because Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are first born from their mothers, and secondly at the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass; therefore, these are the twice-born. (1.39)

"‘That is the second birth’" (GDh 1.8), according to another Smṛti. And that [second birth] does not exist for those who have not been initiated. For this very reason, even a Śūdra is a non-twice-born (advijāti). Precisely because he is a non-twice-born, he falls from the duties of the twice-born. However, it has been stated that the duties pertaining to the social classes (varṇadharma) do apply to him. Therefore, it is well said: "These fall, excluded from all religious duties. (39)
To further strengthen this very point, there is this other censure of the Vrātyas or praise of the twice-born:
"For the twice-born, the Veda alone is the supreme means for attaining the highest good, whether through sacrifices, austerities, or auspicious ritual acts. (1.40)

The words *ca* and *eva* serve to establish the meter. Among sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and among austerities such as the Cāndrāyaṇa, this [study of the Veda] is the supreme root. It is "supreme" because it brings about the highest good (*naiḥśreyasa*), as it is the root of liberation (*apavarga*). Furthermore, since all ritual acts depend upon their causes, there is no contradiction in designating this as supreme. This is either praise, meaning that it belongs only to the twice-born (*dvijāti*), or it is censure, implying that for those who are not twice-born, this very thing does not exist. Moreover, this serves as an introduction to the "Sacrifice to Brahman" (*brahmayajña*). In this way, the connection to the subject matter must also be stated for the verses to be recited hereafter. Even though the intent is to enjoin the Sacrifice to Brahman, this is censure of the *vrātyas*, because they lack the qualification [for it]; or it is praise of the twice-born, because they possess that qualification. (40)
And so it has been said:
"The twice-born who studies the Rigveda verses every day shall satisfy the gods with honey and milk, and the ancestors with honey and clarified butter. (1.41)

The mention of the "twice-born" (*dvija*) is for the sake of praise. The term "daily" (*anvaham*) is intended to indicate a mandatory obligation (*nityādhikāra*), because there is no specific qualification [restricting it] and because it is not connected with a word denoting desire (*kāma*). The "satiating of the gods and others" (*devāditarpaṇa*) is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*); and from such praise, the formulation of an injunction is inferred. The particle "ca" (and) has the function of bringing down [the preceding term]. The construction is "and the ancestors" (*pitṝṃś ca*). In this manner, the subsequent verses concerning the topics to be described should also be explained. It should be understood—by virtue of the force of the introduction—that words such as "Ṛk" and so forth refer specifically to the *Ṛgveda* and the other Vedas. The rest is straightforward. 41.
He who studies the Yajus formulas daily according to his ability satisfies the gods with clarified butter and nectar, as well as the ancestors with sacrificial ghee and honey. || 1.42 ||

The word "satisfies" (*prīṇāti*) is to be supplied [to each clause]. *Ghṛtāmṛtāni* means clarified butter (*ghṛta*) that is like nectar (*amṛta*). The abundance of clarified butter is due to the variety of oblations (*āhuti*). Alternatively, *amṛta* refers to gold because it possesses the quality of immortality; by means of that, there is satisfaction in rites such as the *śatakṛṣṇala*. Or else, it refers to that which originates from the ocean of milk, which is well known among those who relate historical traditions (*aitihāsika*). || 42 ||
He who recites this daily shall satisfy the gods with Soma and clarified butter;
and he shall bring satisfaction to the ancestors with honey and ghee.
By drawing forward the word "ca" (and), the construction is "of the ancestors as well. || 43 ||
Reciting the Atharva-Angiras hymns, the twice-born man should satisfy the gods with fat, and the ancestors daily with honey and clarified butter, according to his ability. (1.44)

The phrase "again and again, every day" is stated for the sake of emphasizing diligence, or else to express the independence of the *Ṛgveda* and the other Vedas from one another. The mention of the "twice-born" (*dvija*) here is intended to exclude non-twice-born individuals from the study of the *Vākovākya* and other such texts. The rest is straightforward. (44)
He who studies daily according to his ability the dialogues, the Purāṇas, the Nārāśaṃsī verses, the Gāthās, and likewise the Itihāsas and the sciences (vidyā). || 1.45 ||

*Vākovākya* refers to treatises on debate following the three Vedas. *Nārāśaṃsyaḥ* are the *paureṣeyya* sacrificial verses; others maintain that these are hymns to the gods composed by humans. *Gāthā* are verses concerning the doctrine of the Self (*ātmavāda*). Others maintain that sacrificial verses (*yajñagāthā*) are indeed composed by humans. *Vidyā* refers to the Mīmāṃsā and other such sciences. Whatever a twice-born person, or even one who is not twice-born, being qualified, studies daily according to his ability. (45)
He provides the gods with a satiating meal of meat, milk-rice,
and honey, and likewise satisfies the ancestors with honey and clarified butter.

He provides satisfaction with meat-rice, milk-rice, and honey. Those whose dwelling and residence are in heaven are "divaukasaḥ"; the meaning is "gods. Likewise, the construction is that he brings about the gratification of the ancestors (*pitṛs*) with honey and clarified butter. 46.
But what is the purpose of them being satisfied?
When they are satisfied, they satisfy him with the auspicious fruits of all his desires;
whatever sacrifice he studies, he shall obtain the fruit of each one.

Those gods and ancestors, being satisfied, satisfy this student of the Veda (*svādhyāyin*) with the fruits of all desires; that is, they bring him satisfaction through sacrifices (*kratavaḥ*) which have all desires as their fruit. The word "auspicious" (*śubhaiḥ*) is used to exclude [sacrifices] such as the Śyena. This is the same for both the twice-born (*dvijāti*) and the non-twice-born (*advijāti*). Alternatively, when the *Ṛg* and other Vedas have been thus practiced as the *brahmayajña*, the mantras become limbs of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*), and the *Brāhmaṇa* texts become capable of providing injunctions. Consequently, whichever person studies whichever sacrifice, he obtains its fruit by virtue of attaining the qualification (*adhikāra*) therein, and no one else. Furthermore, because the non-twice-born are not entitled to study and are thus ineligible for sacrifices of great fruit, there is a censure [of them]. And since it mentions sacrifices, this verse is a supplement to the study of the *Ṛgveda* and so forth, or rather, it constitutes the second half [of the preceding thought]; it is not a supplement to the study of the *Vākovākya* and other such texts. (47)
This is another supreme praise of the sacrifice to Brahman:

the twice-born who constantly engages in private Vedic study here on earth enjoys the fruit of giving away the earth filled with wealth three times over, as well as the fruit of the highest austerity. 1.48.

And thus says the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "As much as one wins the heavenly world by giving away this earth filled with wealth, three times that amount, and even more—indeed, inexhaustible—one wins. (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 11.5.6.3). And he enjoys the fruit of the highest austerity; the meaning is: for one who has entered the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśrama*). [But] "even here" means while remaining in the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*), being constantly engaged in Vedic study and free from desire. The mention of the "twice-born" (*dvija*) has the meaning already stated. Alternatively, there is another meaning for the word "here": even while established in worldly duty (*grāmya-dharma*), adorned and enjoying pleasures, lying upon a comfortable bed, one may obtain the fruit of the highest austerity. The mention of the "twice-born" is for the purpose of making known that this sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*) lasts for the whole life of the twice-born classes. And so Manu has said:
"Truly, that twice-born man performs the highest austerity even unto his fingertips who, though wearing a garland, studies his own Veda daily to the best of his ability. (MDh 2.167)

And this third mention of the term "twice-born" (dvija) is for the purpose of indication (upalakṣaṇa); that is to say, whether twice-born or not twice-born, whoever possesses the Vedic study (svādhyāya) as prescribed shall obtain this name. Thus, this verse applies as a supplement to all [the preceding rules]. Furthermore, it must be elaborated that the attainment of sacrifices and so forth are explanatory passages concerning rewards (phalārthavāda). And those [attainments], being based upon that [name], may somehow be justified through metaphorical treatment—applying the effect to the cause—or through similarity and other such means. || 48 ||

When the aforementioned period has been completed, one should immediately return from the teacher’s house (*gurukula*) in order to perform the duties of a householder; or else, lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya*) should be undertaken immediately thereafter. As Vasiṣṭha says: “One whose student-life (*brahmacarya*) has ended may dwell with whomever he wishes” (VaDh 7.3). And Gautama shows this very point when he states: “Some declare that for him there is an option regarding the stages of life” (GDh 3.1); the meaning of this is “for him whose vow has ended. Among these, because of the immediate sequence, first another mode for the student himself—namely, lifelong celibacy—is described.
But the lifelong celibate student (naiṣṭhika) shall dwell in the presence of his teacher; in his absence, he may dwell with the teacher’s son, his wife, or even in the sacred fire.

The word "tu" (but) is to be displaced [to the end of the sentence]. However, the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) shall dwell in the presence of his teacher. Because of the mention of "presence," this dwelling is for the sake of spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*). And because of the designation [of the term], he should be intent on serving him and reach his final goal (*niṣṭhā*) right there. In the absence of the teacher, however, he should do so with the teacher’s son who possesses good qualities, or with the wife who possesses good qualities; or—by virtue of the words "vā" (or) and "api"—with a *sapiṇḍa* of the teacher, or with one's own fellow-student (*sabrahmacārin*). Thus Manu says: "But when the teacher has indeed passed away, [he should dwell] with the teacher’s son who possesses good qualities..."

"Or [he may serve] the wife of his guru or a sapinda, desiring the unsurpassed goal" (MDh 2.247). And Gautama says: "In the absence of the guru, service is to be rendered to his offspring; in his absence, to an aged fellow-student," and so forth (GDh 3.7–8). Or else, "even in the Vaiśvānara fire," he should emaciate his body through specific forms of service, such as constant maintenance, begging for alms, offering oblations, tending the sacred fuel, and smearing the ground. There is an option based on preference between the teacher and the fire. When the teacher is at fault, the fire is the alternative. However, among the others, the choice depends on their absence or their qualities, since perfection is lacking in all cases. 49.
And therefore: "One who masters the senses and perfects the body according to this rule attains the world of Brahmā and is not born here again. (1.50)

"Sādhana" means the practice of austerity (*kṣapaṇa*). By this aforementioned method—consisting of the fire, fuel, and so forth—while completing his body in the presence of a teacher or other elders, he attains the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) and is not born here again. Alternatively, "by this method" refers to the method prescribed in another *smṛti*, since that is established by the very context of this section; namely, the method stated in another *smṛti* such as, "eating at the fourth, sixth, and eighth meal-times, [subsisting on] alms" (*VaDh* 7.8–9). Furthermore, mastery over the senses is intended here as the meditation upon the Self (*ātmopāsana*), because of the mention of attaining the world of Brahman and the prohibition of being born again. Thus says Manu:
"But that Brahmin who serves his teacher until the dissolution of the body goes straightway to the eternal abode of Brahman" (MDh 2.244).

"Straightway" means by means of self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*). Gautama states: "He should recite [the Veda] with what remains from the duties for the teacher" (GDh 3.6). Such a person, having conquered his senses, attains the world of Brahman; "such a person" means one who has conquered his senses and is a knower of the Self (*ātmavit*). The conquest of the external senses, however, has already been mentioned.

But surely this Smṛti injunction regarding lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhikatva*) contradicts the Vedic revelation (*āmnāya*). How so? There is direct Vedic revelation such as: "One should perform the *agnihotra* as long as one lives," and "One should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as long as one lives" (cf. Śabara on PMS 2.4.1). If lifelong celibacy were to exist, these would be obstructed. And it has been stated that Smṛtis contradicting such [Veda] are not authoritative. Nor is there any possibility of non-contradiction in this way, [arguing] that the injunctions for the *agnihotra* and so forth apply only to those who have already taken a wife. For even prior to the connection with life [the rites are required], and one who possesses them [the fires] has the entitlement (*adhikāra*). Let it be granted that the taking of a wife belongs only to those who are entitled. But it cannot be said that, this being the case, there would be the contingency [of performing rites] before initiation or immediately upon initiation; for one who lacks knowledge has no entitlement. Nor can there be an entitlement based solely on a scriptural statement (*vācanika*), like that of the Niṣādas, because that would entail the consequence of not studying the Vedas. For if there were entitlement for those lacking knowledge, who would undergo the hardship of study and so forth? Nor can it be said that there is some other fruit from study, since none is heard of. Furthermore, because they serve a purpose by making known the fruitful ritual acts, the mentions of streams of clarified butter and the like are merely explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). Nor can it be said, "Let there be study [only later]," because that would entail the destruction of the traditional lineage (*saṃpradāya*). Therefore, it is proper to maintain the assumption that those lacking knowledge have no entitlement. Nor is it proper to say that those lacking knowledge have no entitlement prior to study, but do have it afterwards when they possess knowledge, because that would entail an inconsistency (*vairūpya*). Thus, those lacking knowledge are excluded. If it is argued that for those possessing knowledge, the absence of a wife is the cause for the entitlement [to lifelong celibacy], then let the taking of a wife simply be performed. Nor can it be said that she is motivated solely by desire, because of the scriptural statement: "In the absence of either, one should take a wife. Moreover, beginning with the passage, "A Brāhmaṇa, at birth, is born with three debts," [the text] shows the rule for procreating offspring through such statements as, "Now he becomes free from debt if he is a sacrificer, a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), and produces offspring" (TS 6.3.10.5). This is not possible if one has not taken a wife. For this reason also, the taking of a wife must be performed as a mandatory duty (*niyoga*). Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the Smṛti, due to the neglect of the obligatory sacraments (*saṃskāra*). And thus says Manu: [Manu 2.27–28]... [text continues]... Thus, the taking of a wife is established by both Veda and Smṛti. Therefore, the Smṛti concerning lifelong celibacy is not authoritative. It is only for those who have taken a wife that the injunctions for the *agnihotra* and so forth are intended. As for the argument that the taking of a wife is prompted solely by desire, that is not so, because of the scriptural statement: "In the absence of either, one should take a wife. "By means of the great sacrifices and the [regular] sacrifices, this body is made fit for Brahman. (MDh 2.28)

Gautama states: "He is consecrated by forty sacraments" (GDh 8.8). This is not possible for one who is not a householder. Nor is it logical to say that this [set of sacraments] belongs only to him who is a householder, because the scriptural injunction is without qualification. Thus, Gautama, having begun with "Some declare an option regarding his stages of life" (GDh 3.1) and having enumerated the stages of life, concludes immediately after: "But the teachers [maintain] there is only one stage of life, because the householder's state is directly enjoined" (GDh 3.36). By thus concluding, he clarifies exactly what we have described. Therefore, the Smṛti concerning the perpetual celibate (naiṣṭhika) is unsubstantial. In this regard, others explain that the Smṛtis concerning the perpetual celibate and other stages apply to those who are ineligible for the Agnihotra and other rites—such as those lacking the three ancestral lineages (atryārṣeya), the blind, the lame, and so forth. For them too, the combination of the stages of life is simply untenable. Furthermore, the postulation of a specific subject based on their own intention—that "he may dwell in whichever [stage] he desires" (VaDh 7.3)—is merely a fabrication of a meaning not found in the scriptures. Hence, rather than such a fabrication of non-scriptural meaning, it is better to admit a lack of authority altogether. And so says Aṅgiras:
"Whatever action is performed according to one's own whims but is devoid of Dharma,
all that is as useless as the play of children."

To this it is replied: This is not a forgotten tradition (*apasmṛti*), because there is no difference in its being rooted in the Veda. If it is argued that it is not rooted in that [Veda] due to contradiction, what indeed is the contradiction here? For if those who have not taken a wife were to act according to their own desire, then the injunctions for the *agnihotra* and other rites would be assumed to be the motivators (*prayojaka*). But when desires themselves are the motivators, there is no occasion for such an assumption. Nor is there any evidence for [the wife] being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). Nor can it be said that the wife is like the acquisition of wealth (*dravya*), because in the absence of wealth, living is impossible. Indeed, everyone seeks wealth, and therefore [the injunction] prevents one from being without property. Thus the ritualists who know the logic say: "It is untenable [to claim] they will live by means of the injunction. And there is no such engagement in taking a wife; hence there is a disparity. For in the absence of a wife, there is no impossibility of living. As for the suspicion that the sacrifice is the motivator based on the statement, "In the event of the failure of either, one should take a wife," that is [addressed by the fact] that one is entitled [only] after having taken a wife, and it is no different from the acquisition of wealth when a wife exists merely for personal utility. Just as one engaged in acquiring wealth for his own sake also acquires it for the sake of the sacrifice because there is no difference in the purpose of "for oneself," and does not think, "I am unentitled because I lack wealth," so too one who has not taken a wife should not despise himself, thinking, "I am one who has not taken a wife while he has. However, for one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*), there is no entitlement because there is no engagement even for his own sake. And thus Vasiṣṭha shows exactly this in the passage: "The householder is one whose anger and joy are subdued" (VaDh 8.1). Householdership belongs only to one whose anger and joy are unsubdued, whereas for one whose anger and joy are subdued, the meaning is given by: "He may dwell wherever he wishes" (VaDh 7.3). As for the Gautama rule, "There is only one stage of life" (GDh 3.36), we shall determine that in the discussion of the forest-dweller’s stage (*vanasthāśrama*). As for the statement, "This body is made Brahmic" (MDh 2.28), its meaning is that sacrifices and the like are purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*), but it does not mean that the body of those devoid of them is non-Brahmic. It has already been stated that the Gautama text is for the purpose of praising the qualities of the self; thus it is faultless. In this way, the verse regarding the debts (*ṛṇavākya*) should also be explained as referring specifically to the householder. Just as for the ignorant man there is no taking of a wife for the purpose of procreation, so too for the learned man who is free from passion.

[Objection: But surely this [charge of being motivated by desire] applies equally even to one who has not returned home, since desire is possible for him as well. [Reply: It is not so. If the student's acquisition of a wife were motivated by desire, it would be refuted by the Smṛti; but if it were motivated by the injunction to procreate offspring, or by the injunctions regarding the Agnihotra and other rites, then because of the weakness of the Smṛti [in comparison to Śruti], by whom could it be prevented? Therefore, there is a difference when the motivation is desire. Furthermore, the sacred text—"And those who in the forest worship faith and truth" (ChU 5.10.1)—shows that the attainment of liberation occurs without dependence on the Agnihotra and other such rites. Likewise, in the Chāndogya, the passage—"There are three branches of duty: sacrifice, study, and charity constitute the first; austerity alone is the second; the third is the student who dwells in the teacher’s family, never returning from the teacher’s house" (ChU 2.23.1)—shows the state of a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika). Thus, it is rightly said: "The lifelong celibate," and so forth. || 50 ||
Thus ends the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*).
Now begins the section on marriage (*vivāha*).
The religious student has been described; next, the householder (*gṛhastha*) must be discussed. To explain that, he says:
But having given a gift to the teacher, he should bathe with his permission,
either after having mastered the Veda, or the vows, or both.

The word *api* ("also") is to be drawn back and applied [to the preceding clause], because it forms a single syntactical unit with another *smṛti* and because it serves a purposeful meaning. Having studied the Veda, one should dwell in a lifelong stage of life (*naiṣṭhika*) and so forth; or else, one should perform the ritual bath (*snāna*) in order to enter the householder stage (*gārhasthya*). "Bathing" (*snāna*) is the name of a sacramental rite (*saṃskārakarman*), and that is to be understood from the *Gṛhyasūtras*. And for one who is actually entering the state of a householder, the sacrament of bathing is prescribed, not for entering another stage of life, because the injunction is directed toward that [householder] alone. As Gautama says: "Having bathed according to the rule... (GDh 9.1). By the word "he" (*saḥ*), the householder is designated. Likewise, Vasiṣṭha also, having introduced the topic with "A householder whose anger and joy are subdued," prescribes the bath with: "Having been permitted by his teacher, he shall bathe... (VaDh 8.1). When he should bathe, then he should give a gift (*vara*) to the teacher. Giving a gift means the giving of excellent items such as a cow and so forth. As Pāraskara says: "A cow is the gift for a Brāhmaṇa, a village for a Kṣatriya, and a horse for a Vaiśya" (PārG 1.8.15–17). And once permitted by the teacher, he should not consider himself finished merely by the giving of the gift. Or rather, he may bathe after giving a gift; or, with the teacher's permission, he may bathe even without giving a gift. Thus says Gautama: "Or, for one who has been permitted, the bath [is performed]" (GDh 2.49). The particle *tu* ("but") is for the sake of emphasis. Only the teacher should receive the gift, not anyone else. Some say that permission may come from someone other than the teacher. However, in that case, there would be an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*) and an inconsistency. Therefore, the particle *tu* is intended to remove the doubt regarding the father’s non-receipt of the gift. "Having brought the Veda or the vows to completion. Bringing the Veda to completion means mastering it both in its meaning and its text, not merely the text. Thus people say: "This man is a student of the Veda (*vedādhyāyin*), not a master of the Veda (*vedapāraga*). Bringing the vows to completion means their diligent performance for twelve years. Or, having brought both—the Veda and the vows—to completion; this is the primary rule (*prathamaḥ kalpaḥ*) because it favors both, and also because of the use of the restrictive particle *eva*. "The Veda" is the secondary rule (*anukalpaḥ*), since even though the Veda is primary, the vows are not omitted. "The vows alone" is the rule for times of distress (*āpatkalpaḥ*), because celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is for the sake of the Veda, and because that [celibacy] cannot be fulfilled [without the vows], and so forth should be elaborated. Furthermore, the singular number in "the Veda" (*vedam*) is for the purpose of excluding the study of multiple recensions (*śākhā*), because in the office of the Brahman priest, the connection with all three Vedas is mentioned. And thus Manu says.

"Having studied the Vedas—either all of them, two of them, or even one—in due order" (MDh 3.2). Even in the alternative reading, the meaning is the same: "or having brought to completion either the Vedic observances (*vedavrata*) alone, or both. The analysis of the compound *vedavratāni* is as follows: "the Vedas and the observances" (*vedaś ca vratāni ca vedavratāni*). The particle *hi* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). The word *yadā* ("when") must be supplied; that is, "when he shall bathe [in the concluding ceremony], then it is thus. The rest is the same. || 51 ||
Since the obligation of celibacy ceases for one who has returned home after completing his student life (*samāvṛtta*) due to the completion of the rules of *brahmacarya*, the author says:
"One whose *brahmacarya* is unbroken should marry a woman endowed with auspicious marks—one who has not belonged to another, who is pleasing, who is not a *sapiṇḍa*, and who is younger. (1.52)

Even after returning home from his teacher, he should marry only if his student life (*brahmacarya*) has remained unbroken. Because of the specific mention of *brahmacarya*, there is a possibility of its violation through such acts as eating honey. But how can there be a suspicion of violation prior to marriage? For approaching the wives of others is indeed strictly forbidden. True; however, the author will say: "one who has been carefully examined for virility" (YDh 1.55). Since there is a need for such examination, the suspicion of violation certainly exists. Others, however, claim that violation occurs in the case of *niyoga* (levirate). [He should marry] one who is *lakṣaṇyā*, endowed with auspicious marks. As Manu says: "of the same caste and endowed with auspicious marks" (MDh 3.4). And so it is.
"One whose limbs are unimpaired, who has an auspicious name, and who walks with the gait of a swan or an elephant" (MDh 3.10).

The mention of "woman" (*strī*) is either a restatement (*anuvāda*) or for the sake of specifying her qualities; the meaning is that she should be modest by nature. Likewise, "one who has had no prior husband" means one who has not been enjoyed by another. And "lovely" (*kāntā*) means desirable. And "not a *sapiṇḍa* on the mother’s or father’s side. "Younger" (*yavīyasī*) means of lower age than oneself. The connection is: "he shall marry her who possesses such aforementioned characteristics. || 52 ||
Furthermore:
"One who is healthy, has brothers, and is not born of the same lineage as the sage (ṛṣi);
she should be the fifth or seventh [generation] from the mother's side, and likewise from the father's side. (1.53)

"Healthy" means free from diseases such as leprosy (*kuṣṭha*). Since the Smṛti has its root in direct perception (*dṛṣṭamūlatva*), there is no fault in the fact that she must be cured of any disease [she may have]. "Having a brother" is for the purpose of removing the suspicion that she might be an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), because of the Śruti of the Bhāllavins: "One should not marry a girl who has no brother, for her offspring becomes his [the father's]. When this statement is taken as a *hetuvannigada* (an explanatory declaration), they understand it thus: "One should not marry a girl who has no brother. "She is born of a different *ṛṣi* and *gotra*" means she originates from a different *ṛṣi*, *gotra*, and *pravara*. This is the meaning of "having different *pravaras*. Thus says Gautama: "Marriage is with those who have different *pravaras*" (GDh 4.2). As for the rule of Manu, "one who is not of the same *gotra*" (MDh 3.5), that too should be explained in exactly this way. Consequently, marriage is not prohibited even among those of the same *gotra* provided they have different *pravaras*, such as the Bharadvājas who have five *ṛṣis* or three *ṛṣis*. Furthermore: "The fifth on the mother’s side, the seventh on the father’s side. The words "mother" and "father" here indicate their agnates (*jñāti*), according to another Smṛti: "from the maternal kinsmen and the paternal kinsmen. Although this is already established by the term "not a *sapiṇḍa*," this new beginning is for the sake of distinction, so that it should not be [confused]...
The sapinda relationship ceases with the seventh person. (MDh 5.60)

Because of this non-specific statement, *sapiṇḍatā* extends to seven generations on the mother’s side as well. Thus Gautama says: “The cessation of the *piṇḍas* occurs at the seventh or the fifth” (GDh 14.13). And this is its meaning: [it means] at the seventh from the father’s side and the fifth from the mother’s side, because the text begins with the phrase “from the fifth [removed] from the mother’s kinsmen. The word *tathā* (‘likewise’) is for the purpose of including the progenitor (*bījī*). Thus Gautama says: “Beyond the seventh from the paternal kinsmen and beyond the fifth from the maternal kinsmen of the progenitor” (GDh 4.3–5). The words *ca* and *eva* are for the sake of metrical completion; or else, the word *ca* has the sense of an option (*vikalpa*). One may marry [a girl] who is fifth or seventh from the mother’s side and fifth or seventh from the father’s side, since that is the limit of *sapiṇḍatā*. In this way, Gautama’s sūtra is justified by its non-specific expression. Consequently, marriage would take place at the fifth degree in both cases. As for the statement, “Beyond the seventh from the paternal kinsmen and beyond the fifth from the maternal kinsmen” (GDh 4.3–5), that is intended as a restrictive rule (*avadhāraṇa*) meaning “only beyond the fifth from the mother’s side”; whereas regarding the father’s side, there is an option between the seventh and the fifth. This mention of the fifth is a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*), as other [options] would otherwise be rendered meaningless. Furthermore, since the primary option shows a deficiency [in the number of degrees], it is considered a secondary alternative. Some say that [marriage] is even permissible in the fourth degree from the mother’s side. That, however, is based on a general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*). Therefore, the secondary alternative is simply equality in both cases. Thus Śaṅkha says: “Or the fifth from both sides. As for the Vedic passage: “Therefore, from the very same person, the eater and the eaten are born. For we two shall unite in the fourth or third generation; thus he sat with his wife, playing at dice” (ŚB 4.1.5.14), some say that this is to be disregarded because it is merely a figurative praise (*stuti*) of a modification of the mantra. Even if it were argued that the injunction must be followed for the sake of making the meaning of words like *jānyā* (wife) logically consistent, they reply that it applies only to those [practices] restricted to specific regions (*deśopasaṃhṛta*). But that contradicts logic and the Smṛtis. As Baudhāyana says, beginning with: “There is a fivefold divergence of practice, southern and northern,” and after stating, “Doing one thing in one region and another in another, one becomes corrupted,” he concludes: “But one should not respect either of them” (BDh 1.2.1–8). And the ritualists who know logic say: “Or rather, it should be a universal duty (*sarvadharma*), because the injunction is logical” (PMS 1.3.16). Therefore, when it is something to be performed, it is a universal duty. And this is the meaning of the sentence here: from one and the same common person, both the eater—the enjoyer—and the eaten—the object of enjoyment—are produced. There, the husband, immediately upon being born, while sporting, resolves: “I shall enjoy this object of enjoyment in the fourth or third generation. From the person of birth, the fifth [generation] arises; in the case of the third-generation option, the fourth. These are the four alternatives according to Śruti and Smṛti: (1) beyond the seventh or the fifth; (2) at the fifth from the mother’s side and the seventh from the father’s side; (3) at the fifth from both sides; and (4) even in the fourth. Each preceding one is better. The last alternative refers specifically to women, because the pronoun *idam* (this) refers to the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*). And thus, there is no marriage with a girl who is the fourth from the groom’s side. The Vedic verse (*mantravarṇa*) should also be explained in this very way: “Like a wife of a maternal uncle” (RV 10.40.2), for the genitive case is appropriate even when there is an intervention, as in “the sacrificial post of the Vājapeya”; and also “like the omentum of a father’s sister” (RVKh 7.55.8), for the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is not contradicted even when referring to the offspring of an offspring. Such is the direction of the construction in accordance with Śruti and Smṛti. And by considering the past state of being (*bhūtapūrvagati*), there is *sapiṇḍatā* from the mother’s side, so there is no contingency of impurity (*sūtaka*) and so forth. Objection: If this is so, then it would follow that [impurity] applies even in the third generation from the woman’s side, because of Vasiṣṭha’s statement: “For unmarried women, *sapiṇḍatā* is known to extend to three generations” (VaDh 4.18). Not so; for that refers only to the subject of impurity (*āśauca*). That definition was stated specifically for unmarried women. Thus, it is established that marriage takes place at the fifth degree. Otherwise, that [rule] would be inconsistent. However, for Kṣatriyas and others born from Brāhmaṇas and so forth, marriage in the fourth degree from both sides is not prohibited. But for those born from Kṣatriyas and others, since there is no specific rule, the previously mentioned alternative alone applies. Thus says Śaṅkha.
"If many [sons] born of one [woman] have separate fields, are commoners, share a single funeral ball (*piṇḍa*), yet have separate purifications—the funeral ball, however, revolves among three.
In this same manner, other statements as well are to be applied according to this very direction. || 53 ||
Furthermore:
[He should be] from a great family of Vedic scholars renowned for ten generations, and though prosperous, free from the defect of hereditary diseases. (1.54)
Renown through being a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) alone is more weighty than honors from kings and the like. Thus Manu said:
"But families that are enriched by the sacred mantras, even if possessing little wealth, enter into the reckoning of noble lineages and attain great fame" (MDh 3.66).

Therefore, one should marry a maiden from a family of *śrotriya*s even if they possess little wealth, but not from one that is affluent in wealth and other assets yet afflicted by contagious diseases or physical defects. For foolishness and the like are indeed contagious through contact with maternal uncles and others, as are diseases such as vitiligo (*śvitra*) and leprosy (*kuṣṭha*). However, headaches and the like, even if they are contagious, are not included here, because the basis for the Smṛti rule is clearly perceived. Thus Manu says:
"Even if they are highly prosperous in cattle, goats, sheep, wealth, and grain, one should avoid these ten families when forming a marriage alliance."

"One who performs low acts, one lacking male progeny, one devoid of Vedic desire, one with excessive body hair, one afflicted with hemorrhoids; and families that suffer from consumption, chronic disease, epilepsy, leucoderma, and leprosy. (MDh 3.6–7).

Since the status of the family is already established by the inclusion of the term "family" (*kula*), the specific mention of "one who is free from disease" (*arogiṇīm*) is for the sake of emphasis. In this manner, other qualities and defects should also be sought from other *smṛtis* and from common worldly practice, because the *smṛti* has its basis in other means of valid knowledge. || 54 ||
The qualities of the bride have been stated. Now those of the groom are described:

A groom who possesses these very same qualities, who is of the same caste, learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), carefully tested for virility, young, wise, and beloved by the people [is recommended]. (1.55)

The groom (*vara*) should also be endowed with these very same qualities; however, this is the distinction: he must be of the same caste (*savarṇa*) and a learned scholar of the Vedas (*śrotriya*). The inclusion of the term "of the same caste" is for the purpose of excluding those of a lower caste. Alternatively, it is intended to indicate that [marrying one who is merely] highly learned in the Vedas is a secondary option (*anukalpa*). This status as a secondary option arises because of the remoteness of the qualification [from the primary rule] and because of conformity with worldly practice. As for men, however, because of the statement "from a great family of Vedic scholars," the primary rule (*kalpa*) is indeed to marry three [wives]. Or, according to another Smṛti, marrying someone other than one of the same caste is the secondary option. Thus Manu has said:
"For the twice-born, a wife of the same caste is recommended for the rite of marriage;
however, for those who proceed out of desire, these [following] women are the preferred options in successive order. (MDh 3.12)

Even though he possesses such qualities, he must be carefully examined with regard to his virility (*puṃstva*) through the preservation of celibacy, by means of excluding those whose seed is spent and so forth. In this same way, women also must be examined regarding their womanhood (*strītva*), because the mention of "virility" is intended as an illustration. Alternatively, this very purpose applies to the inclusion of the word "woman" in the rule "one should marry a woman. Or, it may be for the sake of emphasis. The specific mention of examining the man is to indicate that he is not to be abandoned. The condition of "not having belonged to another" (*ananyapūrvatva*) applies specifically to the woman; even if it were to apply to the man, it would be the primary requirement. He who is such as this should be the groom (*vara*). He is to be chosen. Or, it may be explained thus: one should choose such a person as a bridegroom for the maiden. The rest is straightforward. (55)

Because of the statement, "from a great family of those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*)," marriage with a *śūdra* woman would not be permitted. Yet, since this is desired by some, the Teacher here sets forth his own view:
"That which is said—that for the twice-born there may be the taking of a wife from a *śūdra*—is not my opinion, because in that case, he himself is born [again] therein. (1.56)

"The woman of dark complexion is to be approached solely for the sake of pleasure"—this is the saying of the Brāhmaṇas. Furthermore, it is not fitting for the learned to engage in activity for the sake of desire. Therefore, he clarifies this very point—that the marriage of a Śūdra woman should not be performed—by means of a reason: "Because in her he himself is born. Thus the Bahvṛcas recite: "The husband enters the wife; having become an embryo, he enters the mother.
Having become new once more in her, he is born in the tenth month. (AitB 7.13)
Therefore, this is not my intended position. || 56 ||
This, moreover, is also our own view:
three, two, and likewise one, in due order, are the wives belonging to the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya respectively; for one born of the Śūdra caste, [only] his own [caste]. (1.57)

Although it should have been said "of a Śūdra," the expression "of one born as a Śūdra" is used in order to indicate that even she, having been born from a Brāhmaṇa or other [higher caste], is not to be married by one born as a Śūdra. In this same manner, the rule should be applied accordingly to Kṣatriyas and others, as well as to those of intermediate origin, whether born in the direct (anuloma) or inverse (pratiloma) order. In every respect, a woman of even slightly superior birth must not be married by one of inferior birth; however, even an inferior woman may be married according to the degree of proximity in the sequence. This is the meaning of the verse. The rest is straightforward. || 57 ||

[Objection: But surely this sacrament called marriage cannot be performed as an obligatory duty (*nitya*), because the acquisition of a maiden depends upon another [party]. [Reply: It would indeed be a fault if, due to the absence of a giver, a maiden who has not been requested were not given away, or if there were sin for one who does give her; but nowadays, on the contrary, it is a source of prosperity for the giver. As it is said:
"The *brāhma* marriage consists of giving away a girl, adorned according to one's ability, after having invited [the groom];
the son born of that union purifies twenty-one persons on both sides. (1.58)

Because a Brāhmaṇa alone is worthy of him, it is called *brāhma*. Regarding this, the following is the rule: when one has adorned [the bride] according to one’s ability, invited a groom possessing the aforementioned characteristics, and gives away the girl according to the procedure prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, then the aforementioned fault does not arise. Nor should those who follow the world wonder how a girl can be given away without being requested; for this very thing is the duty (*dharma*) of the virtuous. A son born of such a marriage purifies—meaning he cleanses—twenty-one lineages on both sides, from the father and from the mother. Alternatively, the construction is as follows: ten past, ten future, and himself. Thus says Gautama: "The son of a *brāhma* marriage [purifies] ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself" (GDh 4.33). This is merely a eulogy (*stuti*), because it is impossible for those already born or yet to be born to be purified. Or, if it were possible, it would entail the fallacy of the destruction of what has been done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtāgama*). Alternatively, let it be an injunction regarding the fruit (*phalavidhi*), since a specific form of marriage requires a specific fruit. Nor can it be said that there is no logical consistency in a matter that conforms to scripture; for the Naiyāyikas say: "Indeed, there is no overburdening of a scriptural statement" (Śabara-bhāṣya on PMS 5.3.10). And this is the primary form of marriage for a Brāhmaṇa. (58)
But these are the secondary options:
for a priest officiating at a sacrifice, the gift is according to the *daiva* rite; for one who receives [the bride] according to the *ārṣa* rite, it is a pair of cows.
The son born of the first [marriage] purifies fourteen generations, and the son born of the latter [marriage], six. (1.59)

The mention of "one engaged in a sacrifice" (*yajñastha*) is for the purpose of excluding those who have previously enjoyed [the fruit]. It is called *daiva* (pertaining to the gods) because the gods, acting as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), are worthy of this [gift]. Consequently, this applies only to a Brāhmaṇa, since the other two [castes] lack the qualification for officiating at sacrifices. And [it applies] to the great officiating priests (*mahartvig*). As Vyāsa has said:

"If I were to commit theft of lotus stalks from you, the great officiating priests, while the sacrificial ritual is spread out—I would give my daughter to the Adhvaryu, or to the Udgātṛ, or to the Brahman, or even to the Hotṛ."

And because of the statement of the *udgātṛ*, there is the understanding that the Soma-priest is the recipient. This gift is in addition to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), because its fruit is heard [in scripture]. However, it is called "from the seer" (*ārṣa*) because he takes two cows as a boon; and that is a pair, according to another Smṛti. The Brahmins who are the seers (*ṛṣi*) are the "seers" (*ārṣaḥ*) because they are worthy of him. The word "however" (*tu*) is for the purpose of removing the suspicion that this is a purchase (*parikraya*). Thus Manu says: "Having taken one or two pairs of cattle from the bridegroom in accordance with the law... (MDh 3.29).

Why, then, are these two secondary methods? Because their fruit is inferior to the former. Thus it is said: "The first-born purifies fourteen; the first is the *daiva* [rite], and one born therein is 'first-born. Likewise, the later-born purifies six; the later is the *ārṣa* [rite], and one born therein is 'later-born. This is the application [of the terms] by dividing them according to their sequence. And so Manu says: "The son of a woman wedded by the *daiva* rite purifies seven descendants and seven ancestors; the son of a woman wedded by the *ārṣa* rite purifies three descendants and three ancestors; the son born of a woman wedded by the *kāya* rite purifies six descendants and six ancestors. (MDh 3.38)

Furthermore, because its fruit is inferior, it is lower than the *daiva* [form of marriage]. And because it is mentioned alongside the *daiva*, this too belongs exclusively to the Brāhmaṇa. Although its fruit is inferior to that of the *prājāpatya*, it should be understood that for this very reason it is placed first in the sequence. || 59 ||
But this [gift] belongs to all castes.
That which is given to a seeker after saying, "Let dharma be practiced together," is the first kind of bodily gift; it purifies six ancestors and six descendants, along with oneself. (1.60)

The *prājāpatya* [form of marriage] is that gift of a daughter to one who requests her, after having said only this much: "Let dharma be practiced. Because of the word "having said," it does not follow from mere consent alone. As Gautama says: "In the *prājāpatya*, there is a mantra for the union," and so forth (GDh 4.7). Because of the commonality of the desire to procreate offspring (*prajā*), the *snātaka* is called *prajāpati*. That which is worthy of him is *prājāpatya*. Thus, the mention of "one who requests" is a restatement intended to prescribe the mantra. Even though it applies to all castes, the exclusion of the *śūdra* follows from the employment of the mantra. This *prājāpatya* is the first, meaning it precedes the *ārṣa*. Why is this so? Because of the greater fruitfulness; for a son born here purifies six ancestors on each side and himself, whereas one born of the *ārṣa* form purifies three on each side, including himself. This phrase "including himself" should also be applied to the preceding case. || 60 ||

[Objection: But if this were the case, even if someone, having been invited, did not give his daughter for the sake of officiating at a sacrifice (*ārtvijya*) or other such duties, the householder’s stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*) would still remain untenable. [Reply: True, provided these were the only forms of marriage. However, other marriages are also taught. Therefore, this is not an unfounded assumption. What, then, are they? To this he says:
The Āsura [marriage] arises from the taking of wealth; the Gāndharva from mutual agreement; the Rākṣasa from abduction by force; and the Paiśāca from the deception of the girl. (1.61)
*Samaya* means a convention; it signifies "mutually" or "together. *Āsura* refers to the taking of wealth for one's own sake and for the sake of the bride. As Manu says:
"Having given wealth to the kinsmen and according to one's ability to the girl herself, the giving away of the daughter at one's own will is called the *āsura* rite."
The mutual union of the maiden and the groom through desire is to be known as the Gāndharva rite; it is based on sexual union and arises from passion.
The forcible abduction of a maiden from her home while she is crying out and weeping— after having slain, wounded, or broken through [obstacles]— is called the Rākṣasa rite.
"He who approaches a woman in secret when she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged—this is the most sinful of marriages, known as the eighth, the Paiśāca. (MDh 3.31–34)

Some maintain that the word *upagamana* refers to embracing and so forth; however, that should be disregarded because it is not the literal meaning of the term. Furthermore, in this way, the extreme wickedness [of such an act] becomes more appropriately established, owing to its connection with a minor offense (*upapātaka*). Otherwise, it would be inconsistent. Thus, Vasiṣṭha also makes this very point after stating, "She who has been consecrated solely by mantras," and then saying, "If she should be one whose womb is intact" (VaDh 17.74). Therefore, it is proper to accept the literal meaning. The Asuras are wealthy; the Gandharvas are attached to women. For this reason, these two forms of marriage are available for all castes (*sarvavarṇika*). Because of their commonality of cruelty, the Rākṣasas are Kṣatriyas. He is worthy of them, hence he is called *rākṣasa*; the meaning is "belonging to the Kṣatriya. And so Vasiṣṭha says, beginning with "having broken and having cut," "That is the Kṣātra [form]" (VaDh 1.33). The Piśācas are those whose conduct is deceitful; he is worthy of them, hence he is called *paiśāca*. This alone is the secondary rule (*apatkalpa*) for all castes. As for the Āsura and the others, the attribution of praise or blame is made according to their names and with reference to specific distinctions such as the Kṣatriyas. (61)
Is the marriage between those of the same caste and those of a different caste of one single form? No, it is said:
"The hand should be taken in the case of women of the same caste; a Kṣatriya woman should take hold of an arrow;
a Vaiśya woman should take up a goad, when marrying a man of a higher birth. (1.62)

The Kṣatriya woman should take hold of the bow and arrow held by the hand of the Brāhmaṇa; the Vaiśya woman should take hold of the goad. The goad belongs to the Vājinika [class]. Because the woman is the agent in the act of taking hold, there is an exclusion of the mantra. Others say that there should be an adaptation (*ūha*) of the mantra during its employment. Some maintain that even when marrying a Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya woman should take hold of the goad alone, based on the statement of Manu: "When marrying a superior" (MDh 3.44). However, that is incorrect, because a general rule cannot be restricted to a particular case. || 62 ||

To whom, then, does this instruction regarding the giving away of a daughter apply? If it applies first to the father, then in his absence there would be a total lack of authority. If it applies to another even in his absence, why would he give away someone else’s daughter? Therefore, who should give the girl in marriage? It is said: The father, the maternal grandfather, the brother, a kinsman, and likewise the mother—each subsequent one is the giver of the girl in the absence of each preceding one, provided they are of sound mind. (1.63)

“*Svakulyaḥ*” (one’s own kinsman) is an epithet of the brother, intended to exclude the son of a paternal uncle and others. In the absence of each preceding person, each subsequent one is the giver of the girl. “*Prakṛtisthaḥ*” means being in his natural state; that is to say, not overcome by insanity or other such conditions. From the expression “giver of the girl,” it follows that the giving of an intact maiden is obligatory. However, some maintain that a father may give even a girl who has already lost her virginity. Furthermore, the maternal grandfather is mentioned first for the sake of the meter; but according to the sense, the brother indeed comes first. There is no contradiction because all are entitled to act due to their relationship of ownership, or because they proceed from scriptural injunction. Or there is another reading: “The father, the grandfather, the brother, the kinsman (*sakulya*), and likewise the mother. In that case, the rule is determined precisely by the order of the sequence. And “kinsman” (*sakulya*) is intended to include the maternal uncle and others. Thus, the phrase “others also related by birth” is to be supplied. The rest is the same. (63)
As for the question of why one should give what belongs to another, he says in response: "Because by not giving, he incurs the guilt of killing an embryo at every menstrual cycle.
This is either a deprecatory explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) intended to encourage compliance, or it is a rule prescribing a transgression (*pratyavāya-vidhi*). (63ab)

But has this not also been said? "In the absence of a giver, the householder stage of life is indeed difficult to maintain. In that case, men may still be successful by resorting to other stages of life; but what is the fate of women? It is replied: This would be a fault if the dependence of women were absolute. However, their dependence exists only when a giver is present. What happens in his absence? It is said: "In the absence of givers, a maiden should herself choose a husband. (1.64)

A "suitable" (gamya) man is one who possesses the aforementioned characteristics and is worthy of being approached. If she herself has reached puberty, after three years have passed, she may choose a husband in the absence of a giver. Even if a giver is present, if he does not give her away, then in that state she may discard his ornaments and choose a husband for herself, according to another Smṛti. Even when a man possessing the aforementioned characteristics does not desire her, it is not contradictory for her to resort to someone of the same caste. As Baudhāyana says: "A girl who has reached puberty should wait for three years for the command of her father."
Then, in the fourth year, she shall find a suitable husband.

"If one does not find a suitable [partner], one may resort to one who is deficient in qualities. (BDh 4.1.14). Furthermore, there is a restriction based on caste for those possessing [specific] qualities. In every respect, the wife attains her husband, and the husband attains his wife; thus, the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*) is irreproachable. And so says the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "Indeed, even when begging, one certainly finds a giver; therefore, the husband [finds] the wife," and so forth. (64)

But why, after having given a girl with water and speech, should another not give her to someone else out of independence when the previous giver has died? Because: "A girl is given only once; he who takes her away incurs the punishment of a thief.
Therefore, one should not give her to another; one should have the marriage performed with that very same person. (64ab)
Is this the general rule? No, he says:
"One may take back even what has been given, if a more excellent groom should arrive first. (1.65)

On account of the preceding statement, one may take back even that which has been given by water or by word; however, the intention is that this does not apply to a bride who has been led away by the sacred mantra, even if she has obtained a more excellent groom. || 65 ||

But as for one who gives away a defective maiden thinking, "She is not defective," what can be said of him? It is replied: such a person, giving her away without disclosing the defect, is to be punished with the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*).

Or rather, the construction is as follows: he who, having clearly known of a defect in the previously chosen groom, conceals it and gives her to another out of the conviction that he is superior, is to be punished.
Not only the giver, but the groom as well, shall pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas] if he abandons an unblemished maiden after having falsely defamed her. 1.66.

He who abandons a girl who is free from defects shall likewise be punished. However, one who falsely defames her shall be fined one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*, because of the mention of "falsely" (*mṛṣā*). Furthermore, there is no fault in abandoning a girl who is actually defective on account of a statement that she is not defective. 66.
Why, then, is she who has been defiled by the mere taking of the hand not given again to another man upon the death of her husband? Because:
