"Whether she be *akṣatā* (virgin) or *kṣatā* (deflowered), she is a *punarbhū* (remarried woman) when consecrated again.

Just as one whose womb has been deflowered (*kṣatayoni*) becomes a *punarbhū* through union with a husband, so too does one whose womb is not deflowered (*akṣatayoni*), since there is no distinction between them. Why, then, is there a giving [of her] again? From another *smṛti*; as Manu says:
"If she be one whose virginity is unimpaired... she deserves to undergo the sacramental rite again" (MDh 9.176).
This is a specific rule for when [the act] is undertaken out of desire; it is not an instruction that it ought to be performed as a duty. Thus Manu says:
"The marrying of a widow is nowhere mentioned in the rules for marriage" (MDh 9.65).
"And for virtuous women, a second husband is nowhere prescribed. (MDh 5.162). Therefore, there is no re-consecration; such is the intention of the Teacher.

But when she herself resorts to another man of equal or superior caste, what fault is there? It is said: "A wanton woman who, having abandoned her husband, resorts to a man of equal caste out of lust [is guilty]. (1.67)

The designations *punarbhū* (a remarried woman) and *svairiṇī* (an unchaste woman) are intended to indicate their wickedness. She who, out of independence, abandons her husband—whether he be living or dead—and resorts to a man of her own caste or of a higher caste, she too is a *svairiṇī*. Therefore, even she herself must not resort to another. As for what was stated by Śaṅkha, "Three are *punarbhūs*, four are *svairiṇīs*," that is either for the purpose of elaborating upon the wickedness of these two or for the purpose of distinguishing their penances; it is not particularly useful [in this context]. Likewise, the definition of a *punarbhū* in the *Vasiṣṭha-dharma-sūtra* (VaDh 17.19–20) is to be understood in the same way. In every respect, since these two are determined to be objects of enjoyment [by others], they are to be disregarded; such is the meaning of the verse. And so he will say: "Whether her husband is dead or living... (YDh 1.75). || 67 ||

But if this were so, would it not follow that for one who dies without a son, there would be the consequence of the extinction of the lineage? Let it be so; what harm is there to us? Or rather: "Upon the permission of the elders, a brother-in-law or a sapinda or a sagotra, desiring a son, may approach a childless woman during her season, anointed with ghee. (1.68)

The mention of anointing with ghee is for the purpose of restraining the impulse toward sexual desire; consequently, acts such as embracing are far removed from this because they are provocative. The inclusion of the term "during the fertile period" (ṛtu) is intended to ensure that even looking and so forth do not occur at other times. || 68 ||

Is the approach [to the wife] to be done only once? No, because that would entail the consequence of the act being for an invisible (transcendental) purpose. For this approach is indeed for the sake of offspring. Therefore: "He should approach her until conception occurs; otherwise he would become fallen. This means until the birth of the embryo. The word *tu* has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*.
Or rather, the construction is as follows: "But surely this position of *niyoga* is ill-founded, because it entails the risk of sin. No;
for by this rule, the son born shall belong to the owner of the field. (1.69)

By this rule of appointment (*niyoga*), the son born becomes like a legitimate son (*aurasa*) to the owner of the field (*kṣetrin*), such as the brother and so forth; this is the injunction. The meaning is that no doubt should be entertained in this matter. Nor does one who acts in this manner become fallen (*patita*). How then is it said, "But he would be fallen otherwise"? The intention is that he becomes fallen by approaching [the woman] without being appointed or through a transformation [of intent]. This appointment, moreover, is blameless, as it shares in spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*) because it is undertaken for the sake of helping another. Regarding this, they raise an objection: "This position of *niyoga* is not superior, because it contradicts both the *smṛtis* and established custom (*ācāra*). And thus Manu says:
"A widow must not be appointed to another [man] by the twice-born;
for those who appoint her to another would destroy the eternal Dharma. (MDh 9.64). This was concluded after citing an ancient precedent.
"From that time forward, virtuous men censure him who, out of delusion, employs a woman whose husband has died for the sake of offspring. (MDh 9.68).

Therefore, there is no *niyoga*. Such also is the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭasamācāra*). But is this not also a traditional law (*smṛti*), such as [Yājñavalkya’s] "a sonless woman, with the permission of her elders," and so forth? And likewise in the *Mānava* [Code]:
"By the king, or by a sapinda relative, a woman who is properly authorized...

(MDh 9.59), and so forth. Nor can it be said that this [practice] is rooted in greed or other such motives, because there is an absolute prohibition against any transformation [of the body]. Thus it is said: "Anointed with ghee" (YDh 1.68). And Manu also says:
"But he who is authorized to approach a widow shall do so at night, anointed with ghee and restrained in speech" (MDh 9.60).

Therefore, this is not a lapse of memory. Now, if greed should be suspected on account of the desire for the father-in-law's wealth and so forth, that too has already been refuted by the verse: "When the lineage is about to perish, even what is desired by the subjects may be acquired" (MDh 9.59). And thus it has been said:
"Having gone [to another], they both become outcasts, even if authorized, except in times of distress" (MDh 9.58).

Vasiṣṭha also states: "There is no authorization due to greed for wealth" (VaDh 17.65). Therefore, it is faultless. However, because the scriptural injunctions do not differ, the prohibition serves as an option; thus, there is no contradiction. Others, however, describe the eligibility for *niyoga* when the husband has died prior to marriage, based on the principle of the sublation of a general rule by a specific one. As Manu says: "If the husband of a maiden should die after the verbal betrothal has been made..."
"Her own brother-in-law shall take her according to this procedure. (MDh 9.69)

But that [objection] has already been refuted by the very statement, "one who is appointed to a widow" (*niyuktas tu vidhavāyām*). Now, one might argue that she too can be called a "widow" (*vidhavā*). This is not so, because it would contradict other Smṛtis. As Vasiṣṭha says, beginning with: "The wife of a deceased man shall observe vows for six months," and continuing: "Her father or brother shall cause her to be appointed [to raise offspring]" (VaDh 17.55–56). Now, one might say that even an unmarried woman is indeed a "wife of a deceased man" (*pretapatnī*) once her husband has died. Do not say so; for the term "wife" (*patnī*) does not apply prior to marriage. For thus is the rule of the venerable Pāṇini: "The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after *pati* when there is a connection with a sacrifice" (Pāṇ 4.1.33). Therefore, [the opponent's] assumption is baseless, given the consistency between the opening and the conclusion [of the text]. How then is this verse, "If of one [husband] she should die" (MDh 9.69), to be understood? It should be explained as referring to the *āsura* form of marriage. If, after the bride-price (*śulka*) has been paid for a maiden, the giver of the price should die, and she should so desire, then she should be given to her brother-in-law (*devara*) as before. If she does not, he should cause her to be appointed to the brother-in-law alone. Or, because of the use of the word "own" (*nija*) in the phrase "she should find a husband from among her own kin" (MDh 9.69), the "brother-in-law" (*devara*) is a uterine brother, and she must indeed be found through this procedure—whether by appointment (*naiyogika*) or by marriage (*vaivāhika*). But a half-brother (*sāpatna*) may do so with the consent of the girl. And so he says:

"If the giver of the nuptial fee should die after the fee has been given for a maiden, she should be given to his brother-in-law, provided the maiden consents" (MDh 9.97). However, when he dies before the fee has even been given, then upon his death, the maiden herself, being virtuous, should be given by her father to another according to the prescribed rule, if she so desires. As Vasiṣṭha says:
"If a bridegroom dies first after she has been given [in marriage] by water and word, but she has not yet been led away by the sacred formulas, that maiden belongs to her father alone. (VaDh 17.72)

From the mention of the word "at first," it is understood that even a girl who has been betrothed (*vāgdattā*) in the presence of a marriage ceremony remains a maiden (*akanyā*). Furthermore, the meaning of the statement, "If a maiden is forcibly carried off" (*VaDh* 17.73), is as follows: she is "carried off" (*prahṛtā*), which means defiled (*dūṣitā*), by virtue of the force implied by the prefix *pra*. And this must be seen as applying only to cases other than the Kṣatriya rite (*kṣātra-vidhi*), because defilement is impossible in that case. If she has not been consecrated with the sacred mantras (*mantra-saṃskṛtā*), then she should be given to another after having been made to undergo the prescribed penance (*prāyaścitta*). And once the penance has been performed, she is to be regarded as "just like a maiden" (*VaDh* 17.73). This, however, is an alternative rule (*kalpāntara*).
"When the husband has died, the maiden who has been consecrated solely by the mantras [is eligible for remarriage].

(VaDh 17.74). The meaning of this is as follows: according to local custom (*grāmadharma*), there may be a taking of the hand even prior to the formal marriage ceremony. If that "husband" has died, or if she remains one whose virginity is intact (*akṣatayoni*) before the taking of the hand, she is still entitled to undergo the sacramental rite of marriage again with another husband. However, in no case is there a second marriage for one who has already been wedded. As it has been said:
"Nowhere in the rules for marriage is the marrying of a widow mentioned. (MDh 9.65).
And likewise Baudhāyana says:
"If the husband should die when [the woman] has been released [from her vows] or even when the oblation has been offered," (BDh 4.1.16).

The meaning is: even when she has been given away [in marriage], even when the oblation has been offered, but not yet wedded. This very point clarifies what we have already described: "If she should be one whose virginity is intact" (BDh 4.1.16). Therefore, the Smṛti rule regarding *niyoga* does not concern a maiden (*kanyā*). What, then, is its subject matter? It concerns the case when the husband has died and there is a failure of progeny. Furthermore, because of the force of the prohibition, there is an option. Thus says the Vedic tradition: "Therefore, one man may have many wives, but for one woman there are not many husbands at once" (AitB 3.23). And from the prohibition of simultaneity, it is understood that they occur in succession. Likewise, from the statement "Whomever my father gives me to, him I shall not abandon as long as he lives" (ŚB 4.1.5.9), and from the mention of abandoning while he is alive, it is understood that *niyoga* exists when the husband is dead.
Who brings you two together in the dwelling place, as a widow brings her brother-in-law, or as a young woman brings her husband? (RV 10.40.2)

Thus, from this further passage of the *mantra*, the injunction (*niyoga*) is even more explicit. For when Indra had finally seen the two Aśvins after a long time, he said to them who were difficult to behold: "Where indeed are you two? Like a widow, does a woman—bringing a young man (*marya*), that is, a human being, to her bed as a place of joy—perhaps bring you [to hers], that is, serve you? By this, he makes the *niyoga* clear. And likewise Vasiṣṭha says: "At the hour sacred to Prajāpati, she should behave toward him as toward her husband" (VaDh 17.61). Therefore, the *niyoga* is irreproachable.

To this it is replied: The Smṛti rule regarding *niyoga* is not to be explained in this manner, because it contradicts established practice (*samācāra*) and because an option (*vikalpa*) is improper. How then? The Smṛti rule regarding *niyoga* concerns the Śūdra class. Why is this so? From the word of Manu: "A widow must not be appointed by the twice-born to another [man]" (MDh 9.64). This is a prohibition connected with the twice-born. The injunction, however, is general, being connected with the Śūdra. Therefore, there is no option. And thus it has been said:
"For this practice of treating [others] like cattle was censured by learned brahmins even for human beings while Vena was ruling the kingdom. (MDh 9.66)

The meaning is "even among humans, even among Śūdras. And such is the established practice (*samācāra*). As for the procreation of offspring by Vyāsa in the wives of Vicitravīrya, that is to be disregarded, just like the marriage of Draupadī. Alternatively, *niyoga* is permitted even for Kṣatriyas when their lineage is extinct, in order to protect the kingdom; and this applies only to kings, due to the exigency of the task and the word of Vyāsa. For kings, however, it must be caused to be performed by a Brāhmaṇa alone. This being so, the scriptural injunctions (*āmnāya*) also refer specifically to Kṣatriyas, such as: "I shall certainly not abandon him while he is alive" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 4.1.5.9). The meaning of the scriptural injunction is that one who is capable of living should not be abandoned. The statement, "Many [husbands] do not belong to one woman" (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 3.23), refers instead to the subject of re-consecration (*punaḥ-saṃskāra*); in that context, the word "husband" (*pati*) is used in its primary sense. However, the wording of the mantra should be explained as referring specifically to Śūdras. In this manner, other statements regarding the brother-in-law (*devara*) and so forth are also to be explained. And thus says Vṛddha-Manu:
This practice of resorting to another man upon the death of her husband is the duty of Śūdras alone;
yet it is practiced even by foolish and ignorant Kṣatriyas out of greed.
Having said this, he spoke:
"In this regard, the wise recite the verse proclaimed by Vāyu:
'There is no appointment for Brahmins [as officiants] when the husband has died, nor is there the performance of Vedic rites.'"
This is that verse:
"It is an improper act for Brahmins that a widow is appointed [to raise offspring],
or especially that she is wedded by her brother-in-law after her husband has died."
How then is this statement of Vasiṣṭha to be understood:
"One should never study [the Veda] with one's brother without a formal designation"? (This is not found in the VaDh.)

For by this [text], because of its connection with teaching, it is understood that Brahmins also have the authority for *niyoga*. To this it is replied: This is not correct, because the reasoning has already been stated. It is better to assume the sublation of a single [text] that has another purpose than to assume the futility of many [texts] that have no other purpose. Furthermore, this sentence refers to Kṣatriyas, because they alone have the authority for *niyoga* in times of distress (*āpad*). And it has been stated that this [authority] belongs to the Kṣatriya alone. Therefore, the construction is as follows: Even while a brother is teaching, one must not study. By whom? "By the non-designated" (*avyapadeśena*). That by which one is not designated is the "non-designated"; the meaning is "one of a different caste. For what purpose? It should be understood as "the cause for violating the Guru’s bed," because of approaching the wife of a brother's pupil; for "in times of distress, the husband is the brother-in-law" (*devara*). The term "husband" (*bhartṛ*) is used because of his capacity to support and his preeminence; since he becomes the brother-in-law in times of distress, the meaning is that he is appointed (*niyojyate*). Therefore, one must not study from him. The phrase "in times of distress" refers to even a single instance of distress; the plural is used for the sake of emphasis, so that the distress characterized by the extinction of the lineage may occur. Although it should have been said "one must not teach," it is said "one must not study" in order to indicate that [the child] is the son of the "field-owner" (*kṣetrin*). How, then, is its application to Brahmins justified? For *niyoga* is not possible between two uterine brothers. How so? If the one to be appointed (*niyojya*) is himself childless, then he should procreate on his own [wife]. If, however, he has a son, then...
Manu has declared that if among brothers born of the same father one should have a son, they all become possessed of a son through that son.

Because of this statement, since the lineage (*santāna*) is not yet exhausted, how could there be an injunction? However, if the subject matter concerns a Kṣatriya, there is no such contradiction. Or, if it were said that the subject matter concerns a woman with a co-wife (*sāpatnī*), that would be the same even for a Kṣatriya. But when the phrase "of those born of one [father]" means "born of one caste," then the subject matter being a Kṣatriya is quite clear. As for the statement regarding a Brāhmaṇa woman waiting for a period of time while her husband is away, that must be explained by distinguishing it as being for the purpose of going to her husband's presence, and not for the purpose of an appointment (*niyoga*). Therefore, the determination of the scope of the texts concerning *niyoga* is well-stated. Thus, the eligibility for *niyoga* has been stated for Śūdras. (69)

But when a Brahmin woman also acts in this way, then he who is charged with her protection shall deprive that unfaithful woman of her authority, confine her in a dirty place, provide her with nothing more than a mere morsel of food, treat her with contempt, and make her sleep on the ground. (1.70)

Thus, since she has no authority over the performance of religious duties even when her husband’s lineage is extinct, she remains indeed unfaithful while acting [in that capacity]. One should cause her to live in such a state—deprived of authority over the household, wearing coarse garments, lacking the purificatory rites bestowed by a husband, subsisting on a mere morsel of food, utterly humiliated, and sleeping on the bare ground. This alone is the penance; I shall not mention that which will be stated later, because an act undertaken out of delusion regarding the scriptures involves only a minor fault. Furthermore, according to another Smṛti, this constitutes a year-long penance.

Alternatively, if women were to take refuge with another out of their own independence, then they would be partakers of the fault. But when they are directed by their kinsmen out of greed for wealth or delusion, then the fault and the penance belong to them alone, and not to the women. Therefore, women are blameless. However: Soma gave women purity; Gandharva, a graceful voice; and Agni, the capacity to consume all things. Thus, women are indeed considered pure. (1.71)

The word *vai* (indeed) has the sense of emphasis. Since their purity—consisting of mind, speech, and body—has been restored by means of Soma and other rites, therefore these women are indeed faultless. The intention is that the fault belongs only to the men who carry out the *niyoga*. By this, it is stated that there is also an expiation for those who perform the *niyoga*, but it is not forbidden for the women; otherwise, the preceding verse would be rendered meaningless. That [expiation] should be understood to apply in cases of infidelity due to independence, whereas in the case of *niyoga*, because of their dependence, women are faultless. (71)

But where, then, does the fault of women lie, or where is their abandonment prescribed? It is said: Adultery [is a fault]; purification occurs at the time of menstruation; abandonment is ordained in the case of pregnancy, as well as in the killing of the fetus or the husband, and likewise in the case of a great sin. (1.72)

The fault of women arises from infidelity toward their husband; regarding this, an expiation has been prescribed, beginning with the words "one whose authority has been taken away" and so forth. Thus, even in the case of infidelity during the fertile period (*ṛtu*), if no conception occurs, there is indeed purification—this is the intended meaning. However, if conception does occur, abandonment alone is ordained; this is stated for the purpose of removing doubt. Likewise, in the case of killing the fetus, killing the husband, and other acts connected to mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*) such as the killing of a Brahmin, the word "abandonment" is to be supplied. Furthermore, "killing the fetus" includes the failure to conceive during the fertile period due to pride in one's conjugal fortune and the like. And so says Baudhāyana:

"She who, through disobedience to her husband, causes the miscarriage of her menses—having publicly proclaimed her as a destroyer of the embryo (bhrūṇahni) in the midst of the village, one should expel her from the house. (BDh 4.1.20). And the killing of the husband is based on a specific scriptural injunction, since it is established by the very mention of him among the great sins (mahāpātaka). Thus Gārgya says: "Women who have become outcasts (patita) are to be abandoned, as are those who have vowed to kill their husbands. Alternatively, this case of killing the fetus and the husband may be understood as referring specifically to Kṣatriyas and others. Therefore, in other cases, even if the fault is great, they are not to be abandoned. || 72 ||
What then?

A woman who drinks liquor, one who is diseased, a rogue, one who is barren, one who destroys wealth, one who speaks unpleasantly, one who gives birth only to daughters, and likewise one who hates her husband—such a wife may be superseded. (1.73)

She is to be superseded because of these and other such defects; the meaning is that she is not to be abandoned. Here, by the word *surā* (liquor), both *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* are included, because their abandonment is taught among the great sins (*mahāpātaka*). Even those who drink what is forbidden for Kṣatriyas and others are to be abandoned. A woman afflicted with disease is one seized by incurable diseases such as leprosy (*kuṣṭha*). A deceitful woman is one whose nature is to deceive. A barren woman is well known. The word "wealth" (*artha*), however, includes dharma and pleasure (*kāma*) as well; the meaning is "one who destroys the goals of human life" (*puruṣārtha*). One who speaks unpleasantly is well known. One who gives birth only to daughters is one who produces only female offspring. One who hates her husband is averse to sexual union. "Supersession" (*adhivedana*) means marrying another wife above her. After having pointed out these faults to them, it must be done, according to another Smṛti: "Having reproached a wicked wife, one should supersede her. (73)
But surely, supersession is also a form of abandonment, since she has no further function [in the household] once another wife is taken. Not so; for it is said:
"A superseded wife must be maintained; otherwise, great sin would ensue.
Where there is harmony between husband and wife, there the three aims of life flourish. (1.74)

The word *tu* has the sense of the word *api*; thus, the meaning is "even though she has been superseded. Or rather, it serves to emphasize; the meaning is that she must indeed be maintained [but] not approached. And if one does not abandon the fault, that [supersession] occurs; otherwise, there would be a great sin—meaning a mortal transgression (*mahāpātaka*). Why, then, is this instruction on supersession and so forth given? Because where there is harmony and unanimity between husband and wife, the three aims of life (*trivarga*)—characterized by dharma, artha, and kāma—attain growth; otherwise, however, the opposite would occur. Therefore, the performance of supersession and so forth is well-stated. || 74 ||
But why, having been wedded, should she not abandon her husband and resort to another? Because:
"Whether her husband is dead or alive, she who does not approach another man attains fame in this world and rejoices with him in the hereafter. (1.75)

The word *saha* is used in the sense of a comparison (*upamā*). Since praise is seen when one does not accept [a second wife], it follows by inference that there is fault in accepting her. The fruit in this life is fame, and the fruit in the next life is the attainment of heaven; otherwise, both would be reversed. Therefore, even if she has been superseded (*adhivinnā*), a husband must not be abandoned. || 75 ||
But a husband who is guilty of a fault may be abandoned in public; yet even toward such a man, other women must carry out his commands.
For this is the supreme duty of a woman: "The word of the husband must be carried out by women;
even if he is defiled by a mortal sin, he is to be waited for until purification. (1.76)

Even toward a husband who possesses faults, women must act upon his word without hesitation; this is the supreme duty (*dharma*) of women. Or, the word "supreme" (*para*) may be used for the sake of emphasis: this alone is the duty, meaning there is no other duty. And so says Manu:
"Whether he be lacking in character, acting according to his lusts, or devoid of virtues, a husband must always be served by a virtuous wife like a god. (MDh 5.154)

But when the husband becomes unfit for social intercourse due to the fault of a *mahāpātaka* (grave sin), what then? Even then, he is to be awaited until his purification. The particle *āṅ* should be understood as having an inclusive sense (*abhividhi*). By separating it from its connection with *apekṣya*, the meaning is: "even though he is tainted by a *mahāpātaka*. Consequently, he must not be abandoned even before his purification, starting from that point. And because of the word *sam* (in *saṃpratīkṣya*), she who is devoted to chastity (*brahmacāriṇī*) and intent upon him must wait for him. The general sense of the section is that, in every way, women must not abandon their husband, whether he be living or dead. And so Vyāsa says: "Women have the husband alone as their deity. (76)
And those women who serve their husbands in this manner with undivided devotion— by them, through effort,
[is attained] the attainment of endless worlds and heaven, along with sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons; for it is from the wife that these come.
Therefore, women should be enjoyed;
moreover, they must be supported and well protected. 1.77.

Since the attainment of the world (*loka*), the attainment of infinity (*ānantya*), and the attainment of heaven (*div*) occur respectively through sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, therefore women should be served. And so they say: "Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains infinity; and through the grandson of a son one reaches the realm of the Sun. (MDh 9.137)

"Loka" means the earth; "ānantya" means the intermediate space (antarikṣa); "divaḥ" means heaven (svarga). An alternative reading is: "lokānantyaṃ divaprāptiḥ. Its meaning is as follows: the attainment of heaven results from the performance of the Agnihotra and other rites, while the infinity of worlds results from the repeated practice thereof. And thus say the Carakas: "He who has sacrificed three times does not fall away from that world. Furthermore, the lineage consisting of sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons proceeds from this very cause. Since this is so, women should be served, and so forth, as previously stated. || 77 ||
It has been stated that women are to be approached. Since an unrestricted rule might otherwise follow, he says:
"The menstrual period of women consists of sixteen nights; during that time, one should approach them on the even nights.
He should remain as if observing celibacy, avoiding the sacred festival days (parvan) and the first four nights. (1.78)

The period of sixteen nights beginning from the appearance of the menses is designated as the *ṛtu*. During that time, women become capable of conceiving; therefore, one should approach them on those even nights. What would happen by doing so? He remains a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) indeed. This connects with the following verse which speaks of his constant [practice]. And this term *brahmacarya* refers to its fruit due to the contradiction [with the literal meaning]; the meaning is that he possesses the fruit of celibacy, which is the attainment of the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*). Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "Approaching [his wife] during the season and offering oblations according to the rule..."

"A Brahmin does not fall from the world of Brahmā" (VaDh 8.17). Or, even if he should go for some other reason while remaining in the state of studentship (*brahmacarya*), since he remains a student even while going, the meaning is that he does not fall away from his vows. And because this would lead to an over-extension of the rule, he says: "The *parvan* days, such as the new moon and others; one should avoid the first four nights of the [four] seasons. (78)
Furthermore:
"Proceeding in this manner, he should avoid a woman who is emaciated, as well as the asterisms Maghā and Mūla.
When the moon is in its full strength, a man shall once produce a son endowed with auspicious marks. (1.79)
"Emaciated," "weak," or "sickly. Others say it means "barren," as Bhṛgu states:

"If a twice-born man, even out of necessity for protection and without desire, approaches his superseded wife (adhivinṇā) even during her fertile period, he is purified by performing the Prājāpatya penance."

Furthermore, since the attainment [of the fruit] is for the sake of obtaining a son, that [attainment] is simply not applicable here. At the end, they recite: "and Maghā and Pauṣṇa. And so say the experts in calculation:
"The birth of women occurs in the tenth lunar mansion from the asterism of conception;
therefore, one should avoid that [asterism], as well as Revatī and Maghā."

Furthermore, because of the word *ca* ("and"), Revatī is not included; however, Mūla and the other [asterisms] must indeed be avoided because they constitute the *gaṇḍānta* junctions. Moreover, since the mention of Mūla is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), other such [junctions] should also be avoided, as this statement regarding their avoidance is based on other authorities. Furthermore: "When the Moon is well-placed, a man may once beget a son endowed with auspicious marks. The word "once" (*sakṛt*) is connected with the verb "should enter" (*saṃviśet*) from the preceding verse. Thus Manu says:
"One should avoid women on the eight censured nights and the other [inauspicious] nights;
for wherever he may dwell, in whichever stage of life, he remains a celibate student. (MDh 3.50)

Six nights are censurable: the first four, the eleventh, and the thirteenth. The other eight are not censurable. Thus, fourteen [nights] are to be avoided; the remainder consists of two nights. Among these, Manu’s intention is that one [of the two] is for the sake of a woman. However, the Teacher (Ācārya), considering the procreation of a son alone to be the mandatory duty (*naiyogika*), says "once. For this very reason, the conjunction (*ca*) in the phrase "and four" (*catasraś ca*) does not serve to include another night. The prohibition regarding "four" is intended to exclude other times. Or, let it be that the conjunction (*ca*) is indeed for the purpose of including another night, since there is an addition of meaning. Approaching [his wife] in this manner, he shall procreate a son endowed with auspicious marks (*lakṣaṇya*); [the father] should have semen exceeding that of the woman. Thus says Manu: "A male is born when the semen of the man is in excess" (MDh 3.49). In every way, without contradicting the scriptures, one should engage in intercourse according to the instructions of physicians, astrologers, and others, so that the birth of a son endowed with auspicious marks may occur—this is the meaning of the two verses. Furthermore, because "a son" (*putram*) is the object of the injunction (*uddeśya*), the number is not restrictive. Thus says Śaṅkha.
"For one who is established in sons and grandsons, who has many offspring, and who is living. Thus [it is said].

Furthermore, the wording of the Mantras shows that she has many sons: “May her womb not be empty; may she live; may she have [many] sons” (ĀpMP 1.4.8), and “Place ten sons in her, and make her husband the eleventh” (ĀpMP 1.4.6). As for the mention of even-numbered nights and so forth, there is no fault, as it is intended to indicate the gender of the offspring. Since the previous verse already establishes that women should be approached for the sake of a son, and thus access during the *ṛtu* period is already established, these two verses should be understood as having the purpose of restricting intercourse to once [per cycle], thereby precluding other nights within the *ṛtu*. The Mānava rule, however—"He should approach his wife during the *ṛtu*-period"—(MDh 3.45) must be explained as being for the purpose of a religious observance (*vrata*), because of the suffix *-nin* used in the word *abhigāmī*. Yet, in accordance with other verses, it is explained as a restriction for one desiring a son to approach only once. By this very reasoning, the Vāsiṣṭha rule is explained (VaDh 8.17). Because of the mention of a reward in the phrase "he should approach during the *ṛtu*-period," and in accordance with other Smṛtis such as "approaching during the *ṛtu*" (VaDh 8.17), it should be explained as meaning "once on an even-numbered night. As for the Gautama rule, some hold that "he should approach during the *ṛtu*" (GDh 5.1) is for the purpose of excluding non-*ṛtu* periods. However, since approaching would occur by implication whether during the *ṛtu* or not, and because another Sūtra begins with "or at all times, except when forbidden" (GDh 5.2), both Sūtras would otherwise be redundant, as the option would be obtained by implication alone. Therefore, that too must be explained as being for the purpose of a restriction. The subsequent Sūtra, however, merely restates the option of approaching outside the *ṛtu*—which is already implied—and serves the purpose of specifying "except when forbidden. This, then, is the traditional interpretation (*saṃpradāya*) here: one who has not yet fathered a son incurs a transgression if he does not approach during the *ṛtu*; but for one who has already fathered a son, there is no fault even in not approaching. Thus they say:

"But the eldest alone shall be the son; they know the others to be born of desire" (cf. MDh 9.107). Furthermore, since the injunction to procreate a son is made with reference to the fact that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) for each wife if one fails to produce even a single son, [the rule applies]. However, regarding sons born of women of a different caste (*asavarṇā*), there is freedom of will (*yāthākāmyam*), according to another Smṛti:
"He who, having already taken a wife, obtains a later wife by begging..."
"The fruit for the giver of the material substance is merely pleasure, but for the one who gives his own offspring, it is the lineage itself. (MDh 11.5)

This word *avara* refers to one who is not of the same class (*asavarṇa*), because [a man] has already taken a wife from his own class (*savarṇā*). That this is so has been stated previously. And Jātūkarṇa says: "One who has taken a wife from his own class should not desire another, lest the lineage pass to another. However, regarding the procreation of offspring, there is an option (*vikalpa*), because Manu has prescribed two nights, and because here [in our text] it is heard only once. But at a time other than the fertile period (*anṛtu*), intercourse occurs only out of desire for the woman, because of the commencement of the sūtra: "Or at all times" (GDh 5.2). Even during the fertile period (*ṛtu*), if the intercourse exceeds the prescribed time, it is equivalent to being outside the fertile period; thus, the settled rule is that intercourse occurs solely in accordance with the woman's desire. Now, one might argue that even during the fertile period, intercourse is properly motivated only by desire for the woman, because of the prohibition against being "of the nature of desire" (*kāmātmatā*) and because of a Vedic mantra: "And she indeed yielded her body to him, like a longing wife well-dressed to her husband" (RV 10.71.4). This shows that the inclination toward intercourse arises only from desire for the woman, for [the verse] says: "She entrusts her person to him with confidence, like a longing, desiring wife well-dressed to her husband, during the seasons. It is not so. This Vedic mantra is intended to indicate a dual restriction. Since there is a specific injunction for both the man and the woman to procreate a son, and since the tradition records a transgression (*pratyavāya*) for the failure of either to engage in intercourse, Baudhāyana says accordingly: [The text continues with Baudhāyana’s citation: "If a man does not approach his wife when she is in season, he incurs the sin of killing an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*) for each night. Likewise, if a woman, being fit and desiring a child, does not allow herself to be approached by her husband when he is in season, she incurs the same sin. Thus, the settled rule is that intercourse should take place according to the woman's desire, even during the fertile period. However, if she is not desirous, he should approach her only during the fertile period, in accordance with the scriptural injunction. But if she is desirous, he may approach her even outside the fertile period, in accordance with her wish. This is the established conclusion. Furthermore, the mention of the fertile period is merely illustrative; the essential point is the fulfillment of the woman's desire. For it is said: "A woman is the vessel for the production of offspring; therefore, one should always honor her. And: "When a woman is honored, she brings forth heroes; when she is not honored, she brings forth enemies. Therefore, the settled rule is that intercourse should be performed in accordance with the woman's desire. As for the statement that one should approach her only during the fertile period, that is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) intended to ensure the procreation of offspring. But if she is desirous, there is no restriction. This is the final position. "But for him who does not approach his wife when she is in her season and he is present, his ancestors lie within her menses during that month. (BDh 4.1.18). This applies to women as well.

"A wife who, by refusing her husband, causes her fertile season to pass in vain, shall be proclaimed in the midst of the village as a destroyer of the embryo and driven out from the house. (BDh 4.1.20).
Therefore, it is not appropriate to approach one's wife during her fertile season solely out of lust for her; this is the general direction of the rule. || 79 ||

Having thus stated the rule for approaching one's wife during her fertile period, he now says this because, since approaching is already established by necessity, there might otherwise be a sense of lack of restraint:
"Or he may act according to his desire, remembering the boon granted to women;
yet he must remain devoted to his own wife alone, since women are declared to be protected. (1.80)

The word *api* is to be construed with a shift in its position: *yāthākāmy api bhavet*. One whose desire is like that of a woman is a *yāthākāmī*; for even in the absence of a specific injunction, approaching [a woman] at will would otherwise be established. Alternatively, the word *vā* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), meaning "or rather, there is indeed freedom of will (*yāthākāmya*). Why? Because he remembers the boon granted to women: "May even those of us who are about to give birth tomorrow sleep with their husbands" (VaDh 12.24; 5.8). This verse indicates such a statement. The meaning of the verse is that out of desire for his wife, he may approach her even outside the fertile period (*ṛtu*). Furthermore, he should be devoted solely to his own wife. Why? Because women are declared to be protected. This has been stated: "They are to be maintained and well-protected" (YDh 1.77). And the protection of women consists essentially in being devoted to one's own wife; it does not consist in beating them and so forth, for by such means their ruin might even be brought about. Thus worldly people recite: "Gentleness toward Pāñcāla women. The two particles *ca* and *eva* serve to fill out the meter. Or rather, having displaced the order, it should be construed as: "Because women are declared to be protected indeed. The intention is that since the rule of devotion to one's own wife follows directly from the injunction of protection itself, no other separate injunction is required. Thus says Vasiṣṭha:
"The pleasure that arises from non-transgression is rooted in dharma. Thus [it is said].
Manu also says:
"One's own offspring, conduct, family, and even one's very self..."

"For by protecting his wife with effort, he indeed protects his own dharma" (MDh 9.7), and Gautama states: "The dharma consists in the protection of progeny and the prevention of social confusion" (GDh 8.3). Therefore, for the sake of protection, there is no fault in a man approaching his wife even outside her season out of desire, since he has heard the injunction regarding the husband; thus, [the position] is beyond reproach. || 80 ||
And because it is established that the attainment of endless worlds, as well as sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, comes from women— that women are to be served— for that very reason,
women must be honored by their husband, brothers, father, kinsmen, mother-in-law, father-in-law, brother-in-law, and relatives with ornaments, clothing, and food. (1.81)

Because the continuum [of one's life] is beneficial to all, and because women are the cause of that [continuum], they are to be honored by everyone; there is no dependence on other roots. The word *jñāti* refers to maternal uncles and the like; the word *ca* (and) refers to female friends and the like. || 81 ||

Thus, even while being honored by all, she should not be proud and must be frugal in her spending. Rather, with her household utensils well-kept, she should be skillful, joyful, and averse to wasteful expenditure.
Devoted to her husband, she should perform the salutation of the feet of her parents-in-law. (1.82)
And it would be so; this is the ellipsis. || 82 ||

And this is another [rule]: A woman whose husband is away from home should avoid games, bodily adornments, attending social gatherings, witnessing festivals, laughter, visiting the houses of others, and traveling abroad. (1.83)
And so Manu said:

"Drinking [intoxicants], association with wicked people, separation from her husband, wandering about, sleeping [at inappropriate times], and dwelling in another's house—these are the six things that corrupt women" (MDh 9.13). || 83 ||

But when she herself does not practice these [duties] due to lack of restraint, her feminine nature, or because she is honored by all her kinsmen, then who shall cause her to practice them? Or when the husband has gone abroad, is deceased, or has not yet been born, then who is her protector? To this he says: The father shall protect the maiden; the husband, the married woman; but the son, in old age. In their absence, the kinsmen [shall protect her]; for there is never independence for a woman. (1.84)
Or [it refers to] the time or the rite. Thus Manu said:
"For women there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even a fast;
by means of that service which she renders to her husband, she is exalted in heaven" (MDh 5.155).
Thus, he demonstrates that even with respect to action there is dependence on another. || 84 ||

[Objection: But if this is so, there would be no fault regarding women, because of the instruction for fathers and others to protect them. Or rather, in the absence of other protectors, if a failure of protection occurs, then the license of women to act as they please would follow as a consequence. [Reply: Foolish one, do not say so. "Deprived of her father, mother, son, brother, mother-in-law, father-in-law, and maternal uncles, she must not be without a husband; otherwise, she would become subject to reproach. (1.85)

This word *bhartṛ* (husband) applies to anyone who merely protects her. She may attend upon some other elderly woman, such as her mother or others, but she must not be independent. Or rather, she should go to where there is someone to protect her; otherwise, she would become an object of reproach in this world, and after death, she would fall into hell, precisely because of this reproach which can be inferred from the text. || 85 ||

But if this is so, since women are dependent on their husbands and he is independent, should he not employ all his wives equally in ritual acts? Not so. When another wife of the same caste exists, he should not have her perform duties pertaining to dharma. Among wives of the same caste, in rites prescribed by dharma, he should not employ one other than the eldest. (1.86)

The connection [of the verse] is: "While a wife of the same caste exists, one should not cause another to perform religious duties. Even among wives of the same caste, one should not cause another—the younger—to perform them without the eldest; and among those [wives of the same caste], it is according to seniority. In a rite (*vidhi*) such as the *agnihotra* and other rituals, and in a duty pertaining to dharma (*dharmya*) such as the inspection of the clarified butter (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*), that is to say, for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), one should cause even the younger wife to perform it, provided she is of the same caste. Even among wives of different castes, the explanation should follow the sequence of being separated by one caste (*ekāntara*) and seniority, and so forth. (86)

But if this were so, then if the younger wife were to die while the elder was still living, her cremation with the fire intended for the Agnihotra and other rites would not be possible. It is replied:
"Having caused his virtuous wife to be cremated with the Agnihotra fire, the husband shall, according to rule, take another wife and the sacred fires without delay. (1.87)

For the rule regarding the eldest wife applies to matters pertaining to the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), not to those pertaining to the person (*puruṣārtha*). Cremation is a *puruṣārtha*, because it is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the body. Therefore, if she has been virtuous (*vṛttavatī*), she must indeed be consecrated; that is to say, she is one who possesses the qualification (*adhikāriṇī*). Now, one might object: even among *puruṣārtha* rites performed by the husband, the eldest alone should be consecrated first. Let it be so; what is the harm? [The harm is that] in the case of the simultaneous death of two wives, there would be a loss of the funeral rite for the youngest, since the vessels and the fires have already been exhausted on the eldest. Furthermore, because the vessels are to be disposed of (*pratipādyatva*), no other set of vessels can be produced. As for the fires, it is simply impossible. Even in the case of a single funeral pyre (*ekacitikaraṇa*), the aforementioned cremation would be untenable. It is replied: This is an objection raised by one ignorant of the ritual science (*ayājñika*). Since fires are born of heat (*saṃtāpaja*), they retain the designation of *āhavanīya* even when produced from the heat of multiple sources. But surely, when one fire has been established through heating, the remaining fire is not an *āhavanīya*, because it is merely worldly (*laukika*). Who has told your long-lived self this? For a fire becomes "worldly" only when its ritual function (*apavṛktakarman*) has ceased. Since the fire was drawn out for the purpose of cremation, it should cease its function according to the object to be cremated; thus, there is no contradiction in the drawing out of the fires being intended for all objects to be cremated, as no distinction is made. The collection of vessels (*pātracaya*), however, belongs to the eldest alone, because of her primacy. And even though the vessels are a consecration of the body, they are not to be used [again], just like the upper half of the cake in the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. It is by this very fact that the younger wife is disparaged. Alternatively, the fires themselves constitute the consecration, while the collection of vessels is their disposal (*tatpratipatti*). Thus, the accusative case is seen in relation to the vessels: "He places the *juhū* ladle full of ghee in his right hand. In the phrase "they kindle with fires," the instrumental case indicates that the fires are the means of accomplishment, following the requirements of another ritual act. In the passage "she who is burned with the fires and the sacrificial implements," the instrumental is a restatement (*anuvāda*) because its meaning is already established. As for the statement regarding the "sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudha*), it is irrelevant because it is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Therefore, it is settled that as many wives as there are, all must be cremated with the fire used for the *agnihotra* and other rites. Some, however, maintain that the wife should not be cremated at all. But as for the argument based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the text, "They burn the one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) with the fires" (Śabara on PMS 4.1.9), that is contradicted by direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*), because the gender is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*) and the meaning of the nominal stem is possible. Thus, in the Kāṭhaka Śruti, after beginning with, "These are indeed the fires of the corpse which are maintained when the wife has died," it states clearly as a specific injunction: "Therefore, one should burn the wife with the fires. The statements of the authors of the Sūtras and others, being contrary to the Śruti, are to be disregarded. Enough of this digression; such injunctions inferred from explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the like should be rejected. Now, one might object: a wife of a different caste (*asavarṇā*) should not be cremated with the *agnihotra* fire, as Manu says: [Manu 5.167: "A wife of a different caste should not be cremated with the *agnihotra* fire; she should be burned with a common fire, or else she should be cast into water. This is incorrect. For Manu himself says: [Manu 5.168: "If a wife of equal caste dies before her husband, he may, having cremated her with the *agnihotra* fire, enter the fire himself. And furthermore: [Manu 5.169: "If a wife of a different caste dies before him, he should cremate her with a common fire and, having purified himself, enter the fire himself. Since these are contradictory, one must choose between them. However, the text of Manu is more authoritative because it is a direct injunction (*vidhi*), whereas the other is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Moreover, the word "common" (*prākṛta*) refers to the fire used for ordinary purposes, not to a fire that has lost its ritual status. Therefore, the conclusion remains: all wives, regardless of caste, are to be cremated with the *agnihotra* fire. As for the statement, "They burn the one who has maintained the sacred fires with the fires," since the gender is not intended to be significant and the meaning of the nominal stem is possible, it does not contradict the Śruti. Likewise, in the Kāṭhaka Śruti, after beginning with, "These are indeed the fires of the corpse which are maintained when the wife has died," it states clearly as a specific injunction: "Therefore, one should burn the wife with the fires. The statements of the authors of the Sūtras and others, being contrary to the Śruti, are to be disregarded. Enough of this digression. This is incorrect. For Manu himself says: [Manu 5.168: "If a wife of equal caste dies before her husband, he may, having cremated her with the *agnihotra* fire, enter the fire himself. And furthermore: [Manu 5.169: "If a wife of a different caste dies before him, he should cremate her with a common fire and, having purified himself, enter the fire himself.
