The statements of the authors of the Sūtras and others, being contrary to the Śruti, are to be disregarded. Enough of this digression. Now, one might object: a wife of a different caste should not be cremated with the *agnihotra* fire, as Manu says: [Manu 5.167: "A wife of a different caste should not be cremated with the *agnihotra* fire; she should be burned with a common fire, or else she should be cast into water. This is incorrect. For Manu himself says: [Manu 5.168: "If a wife of equal caste dies before her husband, he may, having cremated her with the *agnihotra* fire, enter the fire himself. And furthermore: [Manu 5.169: "If a wife of a different caste dies before him, he should cremate her with a common fire and, having purified himself, enter the fire himself. Since these are contradictory, one must choose between them. However, the text of Manu is more authoritative because it is a direct injunction (*vidhi*),
"A twice-born man who knows the law should have his wife—of the same caste, of such conduct, and who dies before him—cremated with the *agnihotra* fire and the sacrificial implements. (MDh 5.167)

Not so, because there is no distinction regarding the state of having maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). However, the mention of a wife of the same caste (*savarṇā*) in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra] is for the purpose of indicating eligibility (*adhikāra*). For through the attainment of sacrifice, everyone attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa, and thus there is equality of caste (*sāvarṇya*). Accordingly, the Vedic tradition states: "He who is born from sacrifices is indeed born as a Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, [if one were to interpret it otherwise], there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the sentence: "One should cause her to be cremated with the *Agnihotra* fire if she is of the same caste. Therefore, cremation is to be performed without such distinction. "One should take a wife and the sacred fires according to rule, without delay (*avilambita*). This means quickly. Alternatively, the word "without delay" should be understood as referring to the non-occurrence of an obstacle to one's own cause. If there is no obstacle, one should take a wife for the sake of the householder stage (*gārhasthya*). If there is an obstacle, one should enter another stage of life (*āśrama*). And for one who lacks a wife, the act of taking a wife has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). This is precisely the meaning of the term "according to rule" (*vidhivat*): if a suitable wife is not available, one should seek another. If the eligibility for taking a wife exists, one should take her, because there is no eligibility for others once one is endowed with both religious duty (*dharma*) and progeny (*prajā*). As for the statement, "In the absence of either, one should take a wife," this same occasion is appropriate for that as well, since it is impossible to marry after the consecration of the fires (*ādhāna*) has already been performed. And so they remember: "If one should marry before the consecration of the fires. Those learned in logic and ritual say: "Because it possesses potency, one should not employ it for the sake of a son. As for the statement, "When a wife has been brought and married, one should perform the consecration again," that refers to the domestic fire (*āvasathya*); enough of this digression. (87)
It has been stated that cremation is performed with the *vṛttavatī* and the *agnihotra*. What, then, is the definition of such a woman? To this he says:
"Devoted to the pleasure and welfare of her husband, well-conducted, and with senses restrained—she attains fame in this world and the unsurpassed state after death. (1.88)

This is the definition of a woman who possesses such conduct: she is devoted to the pleasure and welfare of her husband, not primarily concerned with her own beauty; she is virtuous in her behavior and is not overcome by desire and other passions. Only such a woman, in our view, attains fame and the right to perform sacrifices (*yajñādhikāra*) through her renown or through being celebrated. By virtue of the context, "fame" refers to the qualification for sacrifice, or sacrifice itself. And "the unsurpassed goal after death": since there is no other goal higher than this for her, it is "unsurpassed. This state, characterized by union with her husband and attainable through the combination of knowledge and action, is what she attains—thus it should be explained. (88)
Thus ends the section on marriage;
now begins the section on the discernment of castes and classes.
*** (Note: This sectional division occurs only in later editions.)

It has been stated [in verse 1.77] that "women should be served, maintained, and well protected for the sake of obtaining sons. Furthermore, the rule regarding marriage with a woman of equal caste (*savarṇā*) and the restriction on such unions have been established. To strengthen this very point and to define the castes (*jāti*), he says:
"From men of the same caste, born of women of the same caste, are born those of the same lineage (*sajātayaḥ*).
Through blameless marriages, sons are produced who increase the progeny. (1.89)

Since children of equal caste are born from those of equal caste only when they are begotten upon women of the same caste, and since these sons—born only of blameless wives wedded through the *brāhma* and other approved forms of marriage—discharge their debt to the ancestors by increasing the lineage, whereas otherwise there is a reversal resulting in the destruction of the caste; therefore, all that was previously mentioned, beginning with the rules for marriage, must be performed with great care. This is the meaning of the verse and the summary of the section’s purpose. (89)

Thus far, the rule regarding caste has been stated in the case of non-deviation from a wife of equal caste. Even in the case of deviation, it is better when the object is a man of superior caste; for: "A woman of the Brāhmaṇa caste bears a Mūrdhāvasikta to a Kṣatriya; a woman of the Vaiśya caste, an Ambaṣṭha;
and a Śūdra woman bears one called a Niṣāda, as well as a Pāraśava. (1.90)

It should be understood that there are two designations—*niṣāda* and *pāraśava*—for that single individual born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother. Why, then, is the second name *pāraśava* used? It is for the purpose of censuring sexual misconduct with a woman of a different caste (*asavarṇā*). Although he is produced from the seed of a Brāhmaṇa, because he lacks those [Vedic] sacraments, he is "a corpse even while living" (*pārayan eva śavaḥ*); this is the meaning. Thus Manu says: "Since he is a corpse even while living, he is therefore known as a *pāraśava*" (MDh 9.178).

However, for the purpose of praising even the most excellent transgression, a woman gave birth to a *mūrdhāvasikta*—one worthy of consecration—even from a *vipra*; this should be applied everywhere in the same manner. || 90 ||
Furthermore:

From a Kṣatriya, a Māhiṣya and an Ugra are born by women of the Vaiśya and Śūdra castes respectively; from a Vaiśya, a Karaṇa is born by a Śūdra woman. This is the rule recorded for those who have married women of their own or lower castes. (1.91)

From a Kṣatriya, by a Vaiśya woman, a Māhiṣya is born; by a Śūdra woman, an Ugra. But is this not contradictory, given the prohibition against marrying a Śūdra woman, since it is stated that "this rule is prescribed for those who are married"? Your Honor is ignorant of the meaning of the verse. [The term] "married" (*vinnāsu*) refers to women of a lower caste. This rule—that there is a loss of one's own caste—applies to those who are married; therefore, its meaning is that one should not marry a woman of a lower caste. For this very reason, even in the case of unmarried women, no other designation is obtained. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to apply a different designation in that case. Thus, the application of the word "rule" (*vidhi*) is intended merely as praise, implying that by marrying a superior woman or through such deviation, there is an elevation of caste. || 91 ||
Since superiority is observed through connection with a superior caste, lest there be a suspicion that the same applies even in the reverse order, he says:
"From a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Sūta; likewise from a Vaiśya, a Vaidehaka;
and from a Śūdra, a Caṇḍāla is born, who is despised by all religious duties. (1.92)
The Vaiśya woman bore to the Māgadha a son, and the Śūdra woman bore a Kṣattṛ;
furthermore, the Vaiśya woman begot upon the Śūdra a son known as an Āyogava. (1.93)

The connection with the cognition of the actual meaning is intended to demonstrate that the usage is beginningless. For this very reason, even when a single object is seen to have multiple names in other Smṛtis, one may infer the existence of such usage according to the difference of regions; however, one should not assume these to be merely technical (paribhāṣika) designations, since various kinds of names are observed even in the Vedas. || 92, 93 ||
Thus, first, when there is a connection with a superior [caste] in the inverse order (*prātilomya*), one attains the status of a *caṇḍāla* and so forth. Furthermore, in the direct order (*ānulomya*):
"From a *māhiṣya* father and a *karaṇī* mother, a *rathakāra* is born.
These should be known as 'non-existent' and 'existent' according to the inverse and direct orders. (1.94)

A son born to a Kṣatriya from a Vaiśya woman is a Māhiṣya; a son born to a Vaiśya from a Śūdra woman is a Karaṇī. From that Karaṇī woman, a Rathakāra is born by a Māhiṣya. He is authorized to perform the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires); therefore, it should be understood that there is an upward progression (*utkarṣa*) through the subsequent ages in the direct order (*ānulomya*), while there is a downward degradation (*apakarṣa*) in the inverse order (*prātilomya*), as this is intended to be illustrative. Thus he clarifies: "But those who are non-existent and those who are existent are to be known [respectively]. That is, in due order, those born in the inverse order are non-existent, and those born in the direct order are existent. Accordingly, Gautama states: "But one born in the inverse order is devoid of dharma" (GDh 4.25). || 94 ||
Furthermore:
"The excellence of birth is to be known as occurring in the fifth or even the seventh generation;
upon the reversal of karmas, there is equality, and as before, there is the distinction of high and low. (1.95)

The excellence of birth (*jātyutkarṣa*) is the excellence of caste (*varṇotkarṣa*), meaning that even a Kṣatriya may attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa. What is this "falling like a *kūśmāṇḍa*"? It is not so; the meaning is that the application of terms such as "Brāhmaṇa" occurs through the exclusion of the duties prescribed for other castes. [This happens] in the fifth or seventh generation. For a Kṣatriya, Brāhmaṇahood is attained in the fifth generation; for a Vaiśya, in the seventh. However, if he is born from a Kṣatriya, then for him too it is only in the fifth. This is faultless because, through the exclusion of the duties prescribed for the previous birth and the acquisition of the duties stated for the other caste, one obtains the designation of that [new] caste. If it is asked, "From what do the acquisition and exclusion arise?", it is from this very statement regarding excellence, and because the scripture (*śāstra*) is not to be questioned. Confirming that very point, he says: "In the reversal of duties, there is equality. The meaning is that when there is a reversal of the aforementioned excellence, in the absence of a change of the Yuga-cycle, the duties prescribed for one's original nature (*prakṛti*) alone prevail. If a Brāhmaṇa marries a Mūrdhāvasiktā, her daughter, and her granddaughter, then in the fifth generation there is eligibility for Brāhmaṇa duties. If, however, the Mūrdhāvasikta himself [marries] her, her daughter, and her granddaughter, then only Kṣatriya duties prevail. Furthermore, for those intermediate-born ones (*antaraprabhava*) as well, the higher or lower status according to the natural or inverse order should be applied by the same logic as before—this is the remainder [of the sense]. However, their specific designations are not mentioned here for fear of making the text too voluminous. In every case, in a mixture with a superior caste, there is an elevation of women; otherwise, the reverse is true. But for men, there is a degradation in both ways; this should be elaborated upon by commentators. And this is the path: in the natural and inverse orders, twenty-four "pseudo-castes" (*varṇābhāsa*) are produced among the four castes starting with the Mūrdhāvasikta. Including the six [original castes] themselves, that makes thirty. In the inverse order, it is exactly the same for the Sūtas and others; thus, there are sixty pseudo-castes. And so they record in the Smṛtis:

"By means of the inverse and direct orders of the castes, and by those born from them according to caste, sixty other [castes] are produced; however, from their further procreation, there is infinity. (95)
Thus ends the section on the distinction between castes and classes.
Now begins the section on the duties of the householder.

Having thus explained the general duties of the householder, the author now speaks regarding the rules for the sacred fire (*agni*), which is the foundation of the householder’s daily routine, as he intends to describe that daily practice.
A householder should perform the Smārta rites daily in the marriage fire, or else in the fire brought at the time of inheritance;
the Śrauta rites, however, he should perform in the Vaitānika fires.

The scriptural statement is for the sake of providing an illustration: just as a scriptural rite performed in another fire would be as if it were not a rite at all, so too would a Smṛti rite such as the *akṣata-homa* or the cooking of food. Furthermore, the marriage fire (*vaivāhika-agni*) exists after the fourth [rite], because the purpose of having a wife is already attained by that very fire, and because the qualification belongs to one who has a wife (*patnīvat*). Or, it refers to the fire brought at the time of the partition of inheritance; the word "also" (*api*) implies even when brought at another time, such as when a man with an existing wife marries another upon the death of his first wife. However, if he produces yet another wife while the first is still living, the success [of the rite] is established solely by the rule regarding the marriage fire. Thus says Gautama: "The fire begins with the wife, or with the inheritance" (GDh 5.7). Now, one might object: this is a rule regarding the time for one qualified for the formal establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*). We reply: No; for one who already possesses a fire, the qualification arises merely by the production of another wife. If it is argued that the qualification belongs to her alone, we say no, because co-operation (*sahatva*) is impossible. If it is argued that co-operation is achieved by conforming to her, we say no, because he already possesses the fire and because its abandonment is impossible. One might object: even so, how could one man be able to abandon the common property? Do not say so. Just as when the wife is menstruating, the sacrificer may perform the sacrifice alone by virtue of a scriptural injunction and her mere permission, so it is here; thus there is no fault. Likewise, she must be made to act in such a way that she does not create opposition to her own relationship [with the ritual]. Or rather, she simply lacks the property; why? Because of this very lack of qualification. We say: no, for the acquisition of property is not for the sake of the sacrifice, but for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). And that remains unimpeded even in the absence of qualification. For the Śruti says: "These women attain the lordship over the houses of others through their menstrual flow. Indeed, the connection with property does not depend on qualification. True; but that [property] belongs only to the previously married eldest wife. By transgressing her, even a remarried wife is not a mistress of the property, like a courtesan. One might object: when the cause for supersession (*adhivedana*) exists, how can the remarried wife be without ownership? It is said: for supersession is of two kinds, since it consists in the loss of either religious merit (*dharma*) or offspring (*prajā*). In the case of the loss of merit, the other [wife] would be the one [superseded], not the previous one. But in the case of the loss of offspring, how can there be a claim to religious merit? To this it is replied: Oh, what subtle insight the Teacher possesses! Supersession is prompted by the loss of merit or offspring; it does not, however, establish the status of being for her sake (*tādarthya*), because there is no proof for that. For being "for her sake" is one thing, and the prompting is another. In this regard, the meaning of the Smṛti is: "Upon the loss of either, one should take another wife. And because she is a wife (*dāra*), how could the property and other items prescribed for her purpose not belong to her? Therefore, there is no lack of ownership. As for the argument that the rite is performed only with her permission, that too is incorrect, because the original fire has been destroyed. If it is asked why it is destroyed, it is because the capacity to act as an agent (*kārakatva*) has departed. For the wife and the sacrificer must either be a single agent or distinct agents. In either case, the fire is destroyed by the introduction of a different substance, just like the fires of Agni and Soma. One might object: this defect would occur if there were entry into the agency; but we deny entry altogether. The difference is that destruction occurs once agency is established. We say: no, for entry cannot be prevented by mere whim, as the zeal for the fruit is equal. If qualification were preceded by agency, then it might be prevented by its impossibility; but when agency is preceded by qualification, entry is difficult to ward off. Consequently, from the destruction of the original agent, there is the destruction of the fire established therein. Thus, in the absence of any other cause, the production of fire occurs again only through marriage. And thus the Smṛti is rooted in logic: "When she is brought [as a second wife], he should establish the fires again. Enough with excessive discussion. Therefore, the word "also" (*api*) refers to another time, as we have stated. (96)
And this is another duty of that [twice-born]:
having finished reflecting on the body and performed the rules of purification, the twice-born man should perform the morning twilight devotion preceded by the cleaning of the teeth. (1.97)

This verse is intended solely for the purpose of the rules regarding the cleaning of the teeth (*dantadhāvana*), because it is a restatement of that which was already prescribed for the religious student (*brahmacārin*); and since that which is prescribed in that specific context is not prohibited and is common to all stages of life (*āśrama*). The syllables of the verse have their meaning quite straightforward. As for the statement, "One who is menstruating, one with matted hair, one whose teeth are covered in mud, one wearing a turban, or one with a topknot—these speak only the truth" (cf. ĀpDh 1.7.11), that refers to the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and similar occasions, because the rule of speaking the truth applies specifically there. And so says the Śruti: "One whose teeth are covered in mud performs the sacrifice. Vyāsa explains it thus.

"O dear one, using a tooth-stick on the new moon day, sexual intercourse on the fourteenth, and taking oil on the eighth destroys seven generations of one's family. Here, the word "second" (dvitīyā) should be understood in the sense of "seventh" (saptamī). 97.
Furthermore:
Having offered oblations into the fires, he should, with a concentrated mind, recite the mantras dedicated to the Sun-god;
he should master the meanings of the Vedas and various treatises as well. 1.98.

This section is commenced so that the long duration of the act of recitation (*japa*) does not result in the displacement of the time for the fire-oblation (*homa*). "Vedic meanings" refers to the commentaries on the *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas*. "Treatises" (*śāstra*) refers to grammar and the other sciences. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include other branches of knowledge. By this, it is made known that even one who has not fully mastered the knowledge of all duties (*dharma*) is eligible for the householder's stage of life. Alternatively, this injunction is for the purpose of memorization specifically for one who has already understood the Vedas and the treatises. Thus says Vyāsa: "By having understood the true meaning of the Vedas. (98)
And this is another [rule]:
he should also approach a lord for the sake of accomplishing his security and well-being;
having bathed, he should likewise gratify and worship the gods and the ancestors. 1.99.

*Yoga* is the acquisition of what has not yet been obtained; *kṣema*, however, is the preservation of what has been obtained. For that purpose, one should approach the Lord (*īśvara*). By this, he shows that the undertaking of ritual action is not for one who already possesses sufficient wealth; rather, even for one who has begun his ritual duties, there must be the daily acquisition of materials. For this very reason, the instruction regarding the fetching of fire is given at the very beginning. Furthermore, because of the mention of the purpose of *yoga* and so forth, this rule should be understood to apply specifically to one who lacks wealth. Moreover: "Having bathed, one should satisfy the gods and the ancestors with water; one should worship them with offerings of flowers and the like. By the word "and" (*ca*), the sages (*ṛṣis*) are also included. The force of the particle "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "having bathed only" (*snātvaiva*) indicates that this is the proper time even for acts intended for personal pleasure. Similarly, the word "thus" (*tathā*) refers to the manner [of the rite]: facing south, using the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors), on the ground, saying "May such-and-such be satisfied," and so forth. (Verse 99)
Moreover:

"To the extent of one's ability, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña), one should recite the Vedas, the Atharva-veda, the Purāṇas along with the Itihāsas, and the knowledge concerning the supreme self. (1.100)

This sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) was already mentioned previously in order to demonstrate that it follows immediately after the worship of the Vedas and so forth. The separate mention of the *Atharva*—even though it is a Veda—is for the purpose of ensuring its inclusion among the Vedas. Furthermore, one should recite the spiritual knowledge (*vidyā*), namely the knowledge of Brahman characterized by the Upaniṣads. And thus Gautama says: "The Upaniṣads are the Vedāntas; [their recitation] is for the destruction of sin" (GDh 19.12). The rest is straightforward. 100.
Now he describes the great sacrifices (mahāyajña) which are unique to the householder:

"The offering of bali, the svadhā-offering, the burnt oblation, the private recitation of scripture, and the hospitable reception of guests—these are the great sacrifices for beings, ancestors, gods, Brahman, and men. (1.101)

*Makha* is sacrifice (*yajña*). The five great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) for beings (*bhūta*) and so forth, beginning with the offering of oblations (*balikarma*), are to be performed in sequence; this is the understood remainder [of the verse]. And thus says the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "The five great sacrifices are indeed the great sessions (*mahāsatra*): the sacrifice to beings, the sacrifice to men, the sacrifice to ancestors, the sacrifice to the gods, and the sacrifice to Brahman" (cf. BDh 2.11.1). This injunction is intended to establish that these rites—though mentioned in direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣaśruti*) such as "Every day one should offer an oblation to the beings"—are nonetheless considered *smārta* (based on Smṛti), according to the statement: "Smārta rites are to be performed in the marriage fire" (YDh 1.96). || 101 ||

However, because it does not depend on the sacred fire (*agni*), the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*) may proceed at will. Since the sacrifices to the beings (*bhūta*) and the ancestors (*pitṛ*) also do not depend on the fire, their performance might otherwise follow; therefore, he says: "From the food remaining after the oblation has been offered to the gods, one should present the *bali* offering to the beings.
One should also cast food upon the ground for dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and birds. (1.102)

Since the *balikarma* is performed from the remnants of what has been offered to the gods, and the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*) is included therein because of the instruction regarding the utterance of *svadhā*, therefore, in the absence of fire, those two do not take place. All of this is to be understood specifically from the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. At this very time, one should cast food outside onto the ground for dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and others. The particle *ca* (and) is intended to indicate the sequence of the rites. The particle *eva* (only/just) is for the purpose of removing any doubt as to whether this should be done even before giving to a guest. Because of the connection with the cooking intended for the *vaiśvadeva*, there is no performance [of these rites] by one who maintains no sacred fire. Some, however, offer to the gods from that very food remaining in the vessel, and having performed the *balikarma* from the remainder, they cast whatever food is left outside. But that view is to be disregarded, because the washing of the vessel is prescribed as part of the *balikarma*. Furthermore, the mention of "food" (*anna*) here again is for the purpose of including other types of food. (102)
Having thus performed the rites ending with the giving [of food] to the crows and others,
he should then daily give food to the ancestors and to men, as well as water;
he should also perform his private Vedic recitation daily, and he should not cook food for himself alone.

By the rule, "Food should be given to the ancestors and humans," the *hantakāra* (the offering of food with the word *hanta*) is prescribed for the sake of both. Since the *svadhākāra* and the hospitable reception of guests have already been enjoined as *mahāyajñas* in the preceding section, what is here enjoined for the sake of the ancestors and humans is specifically another form of food-giving called *hantakāra*. Thus says Pāraskara: "Having set aside food and having offered water for washing (*avanejya*), he should give it to a Brāhmaṇa" (PārG 2.9.11). By the indicative mark of the word *avanejya*, he shows that it serves both purposes. Furthermore, one should give water every day for the sake of completing the sacrifices to the ancestors and humans; the ellipsis is "one must not omit this. Thus says the sacred tradition (*Āmnāya*): "Day by day one should give [water], even down to a vessel of water," and so forth. Alternatively, the word *api* has the sense of conjunction: one should give water every day as well. Moreover, one should perform the *svādhyāya* (Vedic study), i.e., the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), every day. From the word *ca* ("and"), it should be understood that the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*) and others are also included. The repetition of the mention of the *brahmayajña* and others is for the purpose of enjoining their daily performance. Consequently, because of their high importance, these must be performed even when one is unable to perform other rites. Furthermore, by the rule "one should not cook food for oneself alone," it is made known that cooking is intended solely for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice. Therefore, since it is a matter of Smṛti, it takes place in the *aupāsana* fire. Thus says Manu: "The householder [should perform] the daily cooking" (MDh 3.67); he mentions "cooking" in this very context. And the sacred tradition shows its purpose for cooking: "When he sacrifices to the gods, by that [act] humans eat. Otherwise, there would be a mere prohibition of something irrelevant. Thus it is established that for one who maintains no sacred fires (*anagnika*), there is no fault even if he cooks for his own sake. || 103 ||
Having thus offered the *hantakāra* (the portion for ancestors and men), then:

"Children, daughters living in the father's house, the elderly, pregnant women, the sick, and young girls, as well as guests and servants, having been fed, the husband and wife should eat the remainder. (1.104)

The word *saṃ* signifies eating according to one's rank. As Pāraskara says: "The household members, from the youngest to the eldest, shall eat according to their rank" (PārG 2.9.13). "Daughters who have been married" refers to those living in their own homes (*svavāsinī*). Because of that very mention, or because of the mention of "children" (*bāla*), which—like the logic of the stick and the cake (*daṇḍāpūpavat*)—implies the inclusion of unmarried girls, the separate mention of "those living in their own homes" is intended to indicate that there is no fixed order for them in that regard. The mention of the "pregnant woman" is for the sake of the wife. The inclusion of the term "afflicted" (*ātura*) is for the purpose of indicating that even if he himself is afflicted, he should eat first. The mention of the "guest" (*atithi*) serves a visible purpose. The word "and" (*ca*) includes those who have arrived as visitors. Having thus fed everyone, the husband and wife eat the remainder afterwards. Alternatively, it is for the purpose of precluding the necessity of cooking again when everything has been consumed. And so says the traditional law (*smṛti*): "When everything has been consumed, there is no further cooking. However, regarding the husband and wife themselves, there is no fixed rule of sequence; either the wife eats after [everyone], or, as Pāraskara says: "Afterwards, the master of the house and his wife; or the master of the house first" (PārG 2.9.14). || 104 ||
Now, he states the rule regarding the acquisition of food: "By the twice-born who eats, the food must be made 'not naked' and 'immortal' by means of *apośāna* both before and after. (1.105)

The word *tathā* (likewise) refers to the manner in which the *āpośāna* has already been performed; it prescribes another sipping (*ācamana*) as an ancillary part of the meal. For this very reason, by means of the expression "not naked" (*anagna*), it imitates the Vedic scripture: having introduced the passage with "What is my food? What is my clothing? (BĀU 6.1.14), it shows the sipping at both stages, stating: "Knowing this, learned Vedic scholars sip water before eating and sip water after eating. They consider that food to be nectar, making it 'not naked. Therefore, one who knows this should sip water before eating and should sip water after eating. Since this is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) based on the sipping alone as an ancillary, it must include all its constituent parts. However, worldly people, because of its obligatory nature, consider the duty fulfilled merely through the primary act itself, and thus perform only a single drinking of water; this is how it should be understood. (105)
Hospitality toward guests has been described. Now, who is qualified for the status of a guest? To this he says:
"To those belonging to the [social] classes, one should give according to one's ability and in due order;
even in the evening, a guest must not be turned away with mere words, but should be provided with grass and water. (1.106)

The meaning is that the gift given for the sake of hospitality is intended only for those belonging to the [four] social classes (*varṇa*), and not for those outside them (*apaśada*). In that regard as well, it should be explained as being according to the sequence of both class and quality. However, the instruction concerning the evening meal is mentioned here incidentally. || 106 ||

Immediately after giving the *hantakāra* offering, one should respectfully give alms to a mendicant who observes the vows; and at the proper time, one should feed friends, relatives, and kinsmen who have arrived. (1.107)

The term *bhikṣu* here refers to a mendicant ascetic (*bhikṣuka*), whereas the term *suvrata* intends the Paramahaṃsa because of his firm observance of vows; he is mentioned separately because he subsists on a single alms-meal. The word *ca* (and) is intended to indicate an excess of respect, or it may be for the purpose of including other types of mendicants. For the sake of compassion, one should feed friends and others who have arrived at the time of one's own meal, treating them with due honor. By the force of the word *ca*, it follows that cooking may be undertaken even outside of that time for their sake. Furthermore, the rule is that this applies only to those who have arrived at the proper time within the same village. 107.

In this manner, food should always be given with due honor to friends and others; furthermore, upon the arrival of a *śrotriya*, one should provide for him a large bull or a large goat. [One should offer] hospitable service, pleasant food, and truthful speech. (1.108)

The word "should be done" (*kāryam*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Because of the mention of "preparation," the slaughter of the great bull and so forth is permitted for that purpose. "Hospitality" (*satkriyā*) means the honoring of guests. "Service" (*sevanam*) means attendance; and he should perform that. He should provide food that is both savory and refined, and he should speak words that are pleasant and truthful (*sūnṛtam*). This should be applied according to the specific guest, either individually or collectively. || 108 ||
The case of approaching a Śrotriya who is not a relative has already been mentioned. But regarding a relative, [it is said]:

"However, those worthy of the Arghya reception are the Snātaka, the teacher, the king, a dear friend, one for whom one performs a marriage, and likewise the officiating priests at a sacrifice. (1.109)

The terms *snātaka* and *ācārya* are relative terms; otherwise, there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For he who initiates someone is that person’s *ācārya*, and he who has returned from that [initiation] is that person’s *snātaka*. A king is also a ruler of his own country, yet he is not [necessarily] a Kṣatriya. The word *prati* signifies distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). The word *tu* is for the purpose of restriction. They are to be honored with the *arghya* offering, the *madhuparka*, and so forth. “A dear one and one to be married”—the meaning is that they possess qualities equal to those [already mentioned]. However, officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are to be honored with the *arghya* specifically at a sacrifice, even before a year has passed. And thus says Gautama: “Before [the end of] a sacrifice or a marriage” (GDh 5.29). Furthermore, the word *yajña* here refers to a Soma sacrifice, according to the scriptural statement: “If one should sacrifice with Soma more than once a year. (109)

The hospitable reception of guests and learned Vedic scholars has been described; now its definition is stated: "A traveler is to be known as a guest, and one who has mastered the Vedas is a learned scholar (*śrotriya*).
These two are to be honored by a householder desiring the world of Brahman. (1.110)

The status of being a guest has been described according to the sequence of castes and in accordance with their qualities; in that very context, this specific distinction is made regarding the traveler. And thus says the Nigama:
"Because he stays for only a short time, he is therefore called an *atithi* (guest). (MDh 3.102).
The mention of the *śrotriya* (one learned in the Vedas) is for the sake of emphasizing the significance [of the guest]. The rest is straightforward. 110.

And this being so, with the intention that he should not always be like a traveler who is intent on tasting delicious food as a guest, he says: "One should have no taste for another's cooking except when invited by those beyond reproach;
one should avoid restlessness of speech, hands, and feet, as well as overeating. (1.111)

Even when invited by blameless persons, he should avoid overeating; the meaning is that he should go there solely out of compliance with their request, without feeling elated. Therefore, even while traveling, he should present himself as a guest only if he lacks the capacity to cook for himself; however, this would not apply in the case of a single village, even in times of distress. || 111 ||

Furthermore, one should follow as far as the boundary a learned guest who has accepted hospitality according to the rules; having done so, one should spend the remainder of the day with disciplined, beloved kinsmen. (1.112)

The word *saha* (together with) is to be understood as the ellipsis. There is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between *atithim* (the guest) and *śrotriyaṃ* (one learned in the Vedas). Nor is there any assumption of a [separate] word [for the latter]. Worship appropriate to the occasion should also be arranged for any other guest. And thus says Pāraskara: "They should honor mendicants and guests according to their worth" (PārG 2.9.12). Because of the expression "he sat down together," the seating [of the guest] takes place from the time of the removal of the sacred fires. || 112 ||
But having extinguished the sacred fires, and having performed the evening twilight devotions and offered oblations into those fires,
he should eat with his dependents and then go to bed without over-satiating himself. || 1.113 ||

This verse concerns the second time for eating. Since the rule for the first meal would otherwise apply in its entirety, the meaning is that one should eat together with the servants, not according to seniority. Consequently, there is no eating in between. Thus, the traditional teaching says: "Therefore they say, 'One should indeed eat only in the evening and in the morning,'" which he states precisely to prohibit eating at other times. || 113 ||
[Objection: But if this is so, since the sentence has another purpose, there would be no fault in eating when one is already fully satisfied. [Reply: True, it is so. However:
"One should not neglect virtue, wealth, and pleasure according to one's ability;
having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should reflect upon what is beneficial for oneself. (1.114)

True. This prohibition does not derive from the scriptures (*śāstra*). Rather, even wealth (*artha*) and pleasure (*kāma*) are certainly not to be abandoned, provided they do not conflict with *dharma*. Even in their transgression, there is indeed a violation of the scriptures. Furthermore, *dharma* itself would not attain the status of *dharma* if it were absolutely opposed to them. And so says Manu: "One should abandon wealth and pleasure" (MDh 4.176). Alternatively, by virtue of the context, this is intended solely to authorize the desire for sexual union (*saṃveśana*). Moreover, having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*—the final watch—one should contemplate the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) for one's own benefit, because that alone is beneficial in the ultimate sense, because no other time is prescribed, and because this particular time is appropriate. The mention of rising is for the purpose of concentrating the mind by withdrawing from worldly activities. For this very reason, the specific *muhūrta* is taught by that designation. However, according to the statement of Manu, contemplation of wealth and the like is also permitted when not in conflict [with *dharma*]: "One should contemplate *dharma* and wealth" (MDh 4.92). Why, then, is contemplation of the Supreme Self emphasized over *dharma* and wealth? Is it not the case that those two alone should be contemplated primarily, since they are also the causes of liberation (*apavarga*)? Not so. For it has been stated that [the Self] is beneficial in the ultimate sense and is taught by that specific designation. (114)
Furthermore:
"One is to be honored according to the sequence of knowledge, ritual action, age, kinship, and wealth;
even a Śūdra, if he possesses these in abundance, deserves honor on account of his advanced age. (1.115)

By "knowledge" (*vidyā*), specifically the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is meant. Otherwise, since one devoid of that [knowledge] lacks the qualification for ritual action (*karman*), the superiority of ritual action would be rendered groundless. Accordingly, Gautama, after stating that knowledge is inferior to age, declares their distinction: "But sacred learning (*śruta*) is weightier than all [others], because it is the root of Dharma" (GDh 6.21–22). How, then, can there be superiority of age? That word "age" (*vayas*) refers to the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśrama*), not to mere old age. For instance, having stated that one who has reached the tenth decade of life is to be honored by the gift of a path, he declares the *snātaka* alone to be more honorable than all others. In this context, however, the word "age" refers precisely to old age. Its honorability is also established by the Vedic tradition: "He who lives for a hundred years attains immortality even here" (ŚB 10.2.6.8). Furthermore, as for what was stated by Vasiṣṭha—"Learning, wealth, relationship, and ritual action are grounds for honor; each preceding one is stronger than the next" (VaDh 13.56–57)—that refers to wealth characterized by the study of the Vedas and the status of being a Brāhmaṇa.
Even this entire earth, he alone is worthy to rule. (MDh 1.105)

Thus, because external wealth is a cause [of respect], and in accordance with Gautama’s rule that “learning (*śruta*) is indeed weightier than all [other causes]” (GDh 6.21), one might object: “But even that [learning] is not distinct from ritual action (*karman*). Indeed, it is distinct, because learning residing only in a Brāhmaṇa is the cause of that [respect], and because of the statement, “And he should teach others” (MDh 10.2), it is beneficial to everyone. Ritual action, however, relies only on non-Brāhmaṇas, according to the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): “Therefore, in the Rājasūya sacrifice, the Brāhmaṇa sits below the Kṣatriya” (BĀU 1.4.11). Furthermore, the relationship mentioned by Vasiṣṭha is specifically that of the Brāhmaṇa [as teacher], not the matrimonial one, since the relationship of ownership (*svāmitva*) makes even Kṣatriyas and others worthy of honor as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). But the intention of the Teacher [Manu] is that only worldly wealth and both types of kinship [matrimonial and priestly] are meant. Thus Manu says: “Wealth, kinship,” and so forth (MDh 2.136). Are these alone the grounds for honor when residing in a Brāhmaṇa? No, it is said: “Even a Śūdra deserves honor in old age if these [qualities] are abundant. If they exist; but where, by fate, they do not exist, what can we do? The intention is that the honorability of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas is unimpeded. And thus Manu says: “Of the five [grounds of honor] among the three castes” (MDh 2.137). Or rather, it should be construed as: “By these being abundant, there is a greater degree of honorability. Moreover, the point is that even a Śūdra deserves honor in old age. 115.

The way must be yielded to the elderly, the burdened, kings, those who have performed the ritual ablution, women, the sick, ascetics, and wheel-turning monarchs; among these, O King, the one who has performed the ritual ablution is to be honored even by the king.

When there is a gathering of these [persons], such as the elderly and others, and when the path is narrow, one should step aside from the road for those who do not possess the aforementioned characteristics. However, the sequence among them is understood from other Smṛtis; as Vasiṣṭha says: "In a meeting of the elderly, children, the sick, those burdened with loads, women, and those in vehicles, the way must be yielded to each subsequent one" (VaDh 13.58). The word *nṛpaḥ* (the king) takes the genitive case in the sense of the agent (*kartari ṣaṣṭhī*), meaning that the king is to be honored by all of them—the elderly and so forth. Likewise, the Brāhmaṇa who has completed his studies (*snātaka*) is to be honored by the king. Thus Gautama says: "But by the king, [respect is due] to a Śrotriya" (GDh 6.25). Furthermore, according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha, "And by all [is respect due] to a bride being carried away" (VaDh 13.60), the groom is even more honorable than that [Brāhmaṇa]. Regarding the woman, they intend her specifically when she is pregnant, because of Gautama’s rule concerning those to be favored (cf. GDh 6.24); however, since the sick person is mentioned here [in the verse], this point requires further deliberation. *Cakrin* means one in a vehicle with wheels. The rest is straightforward. But where even a Śrotriya is to be honored by all, what need is there to mention one who knows the Veda? This is the application to the subject at hand. And this is the application to the context. As for the verse itself, its scope is already understood; it should be seen in the same way elsewhere as well. || 116 ||
But why, then, is only the Brāhmaṇa designated as a *snātaka*, when sacrifices and other rites exist for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya as well? True; however:
"Sacrificing, studying, and giving are [the duties] of the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya;
receiving gifts, as well as officiating at sacrifices and teaching, are additional [duties] for the Brāhmaṇa. (1.117)

Even these [means] intended for livelihood certainly become causes for pride. Alternatively, it has been stated that one should not abandon dharma and the other [aims] according to one's capacity. In that regard, sacrifice and the like are the means for accomplishing dharma for everyone; the acceptance of gifts and so forth are the means for accomplishing wealth according to one's qualification; and as for desire, it has already been explained—such is the construction [of the verse]. 117.
The primary duty of a Kṣatriya is the protection of the subjects; lending money at interest, agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing are prescribed for the Vaiśya. (1.118)

In the preceding [verse], because the word *tathā* (likewise) refers to another matter, because it speaks of primacy regarding the duties of a Kṣatriya, because of the formation of the compound "money-lending, agriculture, and trade," and because it alludes to the meaning of another Smṛti which states "tending cattle is remembered as the duty of the Vaiśya," money-lending and the others are common [to all] as secondary options (*anukalpa*). However, for the Vaiśya, even when these are performed by himself, they constitute his primary option (*svakalpa*) alone, according to another Smṛti. || 118 ||

Thus has it been stated regarding the twice-born. Now, as for the once-born—the Śūdra—he should live by serving the twice-born; if he cannot subsist by that, he may become a merchant, or he may live by various crafts while performing what is beneficial for the twice-born. (1.119)

For a Śūdra, the means for accomplishing dharma is solely the service of the twice-born; sacrifices and the like are not, because he lacks the injunction for Vedic study. That same service is also the means for acquiring wealth. However, when he cannot subsist by that, he may engage in trade—buying and selling—or live by various kinds of crafts. In every way, however, he should act for the benefit of the twice-born, for that alone is his means for accomplishing dharma. (119)
And this is another duty specifically for the Śūdra:

finding delight in his wife, being pure, supporting his dependents, and devoted to the performance of ancestral rites (śrāddha), he shall not neglect the five sacrifices by means of the mantra of salutation (namaskāra). 1.120.

Since he is not prone to adultery, he should be one who approaches his own wife according to his desire. He should be pure, performing ablutions and other such rites; he should support his dependents alone. He should perform the *śrāddha* rite at the proper time without reciting mantras, as well as the five great sacrifices (*pañca-mahāyajña*) every day. However, there is this distinction: he should employ only the word "namas" (salutation), and not the names of the deities. Because of the prohibition regarding [the use of] mantras, the relinquishment of the offering must indeed be made with reference to the deity. But in the *śrāddha*, even the words for the deities are employed because they are not among those prohibited from being used as mantras. (120)
Thus, the means for accomplishing dharma have been stated for the twice-born and for the Śūdra. Furthermore:
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, restraint of the senses, self-control, forbearance, uprightness, and generosity—these are the means for accomplishing dharma for all. (1.121)

The meaning is: "of all four castes. And so it has been said: "Non-violence, truthfulness, and non-stealing. Alternatively, the word "all" (sarva) may refer to those born in the inverse order (pratiloma). For the former [those born in the natural order], however, the inclusion would follow by the principle of the "stick and the cake" (daṇḍāpūpika). This being the case, the mention of "giving" (dāna) would not be redundant. But if it were intended to refer only to the Śūdra, the use of the word "all" would be inappropriate. There is no contradiction if it serves both purposes. || 121 ||
And he says this other [verse], which is generally applicable as appropriate for the sake of the subsequent section:
"One should likewise conduct oneself with a behavior that is consistent with one's age, intelligence, wealth, speech, dress, learning, birth, and actions—straightforward and free from deceit. (1.122)
Straightforward and not crooked; honest and not causing harm to others. || 122 ||
Now, in order to elaborate upon that very similarity, he says:
"A twice-born man who possesses more than three years' worth of grain may indeed drink the Soma;
he whose food supply lasts for one year should perform the rites preliminary to the Soma sacrifice. (1.123)
The verse has the purpose of describing optional rites (kāmyakarman), because otherwise it would contradict other Vedic texts. || 123 ||
Furthermore, regarding matters not performed out of desire:
"The Soma sacrifice, the animal sacrifice, and likewise the [sacrifice] at each solstice must be performed; as well as the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices every year. (1.124)

This verse is intended to distinguish between optional (kāmya) and obligatory (nitya) rites. Particles such as *ca* and others serve to indicate the scriptural injunctions (*śrauta-vidhāna*). Likewise, the word *tathā* is for the purpose of referring back to what has been stated in the scripture. And because these [rites] are obligatory, they must be performed according to their possibility. 124.
But for one who is absolutely incapable [of performing them], then:
"In the absence of these, a twice-born man should perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice;
he should not perform a rite with deficient ritual elements when the necessary materials are available, for it yields no fruit. (1.125)

One should not perform an optional rite (*kāmya-karman*) with inferior materials, because it yields its fruit only when the substance is present, due to the rule that all constituent parts must be assembled. Furthermore, the scriptural injunction for a sacrifice such as the *iṣṭi* even in the absence of Soma and other materials is intended to make known its mandatory performance under those circumstances. || 125 ||

And this being the case, since it is an obligatory rule, [the author] speaks when there arises the possibility of procuring a substance from somewhere: "By performing a sacrifice with what has been begged from a Śūdra, one is born as a Caṇḍāla;
by not giving what was obtained for the sake of a sacrifice, one is born even as a vulture or a crow. (1.126)

But surely, wealth is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), not for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). True. However, there is no fault, because that which a person acquires for the purpose of the sacrifice is indeed "for the sake of the sacrifice. Alternatively, this instruction is intended for the purpose of winning over desirable things. Even though it serves the person's own ends, there is a censure of begging from a *śūdra*. For one who begs from a *śūdra*, even sacrifices lead to sin, let alone anything else. The statement regarding its being for that purpose refers precisely to the aforementioned context; thus, there is no fault. The meaning is that even when the sacrifice is completed, he should give [the wealth] to the members of the assembly (*sadasya*) and should not use it himself. (126)
Now, for the sake of regulating the practice for his own welfare among those very persons under discussion, he says:

"Whether possessing grain in a granary or a jar, or having enough for three days, or even not enough for tomorrow; or he may live by gleaning ears of corn or individual grains—among these, each succeeding one is better than the preceding. (1.127)

The first word "api" (also/even) has the sense of "unbegged" (ayācita). The second, however, is for the purpose of stating the distinction between *sila* and *uñcha*. A *kusūla* is a granary measuring twenty *droṇas*; half of that is a *kumbhī*, for ten *droṇas* are traditionally known as a *kumbhī*, and a *kusūla* is twice that amount, according to the instruction of the learned. *Traihika* refers to grain sufficient for three days' use. *Aśvastana* refers to one who washes [the vessel] immediately [after eating]. *Sila* is the gathering of ears [of grain]; *uñcha* is the gathering of individual grains.

But is it not the case that this Smṛti contradicts Śruti because it conflicts with the performance of the Soma sacrifice and other rites? Nor is eligibility dependent upon one's means of livelihood, since the lack of wealth does not constitute an obstacle to eligibility.

It is said: Because of the statement "one should live," the restriction of one's livelihood (*vṛtti-saṃkoca*) is for the sake of living. Since acquisition through receiving gifts and other means is not prohibited even for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*), there is no contradiction. Alternatively, this should be understood as being like the case of the *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong celibate) and others. For the injunctions regarding the *agnihotra* and other rites do not operate by subverting the traditional rules on restricting one's livelihood, while abandoning the acquisition of wealth in which one has already engaged out of passion. If they did so operate, then the acquisition of wealth would have to be considered solely for the sake of the ritual; and in that case, the entire system of the scriptures (*sarvatantra*) would be destroyed. Therefore, the injunctions for the *agnihotra* and other rites refer specifically to livelihoods such as receiving gifts, and thus there is no contradiction. We shall explain this more precisely in the section defining the forest-dweller’s stage of life (*vanasthāśrama*). Furthermore, these modes of livelihood apply to one who has entered another stage of life. Thus Śaṅkha says, beginning with "After this, having procreated sons," and continuing: "The sequence of specific livelihoods characterized by the commencement of rituals is superior; or, having practiced agriculture and trade, one should resort to the forest. From this also, there is no contradiction. || 127 ||
Thus ends the section on the duties of the householder;
now begins the section on the duties of the *snātaka*.

Thus far, the restriction of livelihoods has been explained according to their increasing excellence for those whose passions have been eradicated by superior knowledge. However, regarding those who are still subject to passion, who desire abundant wealth, and who are inclined to acquire property in an unrestricted manner through the previously mentioned means such as receiving gifts, [the author] says:
One should not strive for wealth that conflicts with Vedic study, nor from improper sources; one should never indulge in what is forbidden and should always remain contented. 1.128

One should not abandon Vedic study half-finished and approach a lord for the sake of wealth; nor should one seek wealth from just anyone, such as from a Śūdra or from an ignoble source. Furthermore, when there is a simultaneous conflict between dharma and artha, one should not accept that artha which contradicts dharma. Accordingly, Āpastamba has prescribed the penance for killing a Brahmin even in the case of a conflict: "In the event of a collision between dharma and artha, this same [penance] applies to one who chooses artha" (ĀpDh 1.24.23). The concluding point—that one should always be content and not greedy—is intended to prohibit being motivated solely by desire. 128.

These [means of livelihood], beginning with officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) and ending with gleaning ears of grain (*siloñcha*), follow one's natural birth and belong to the first alternative (*kalpa*); these are not secondary alternatives (*anukalpa*). However, this [following method] is the alternative for times of distress (*āpadkalpa*) for all. "One who is suffering" (*sīdan*)—because of this expression—it is understood as an alternative for times of distress. "King" (*rājā*) means a Kṣatriya, or one who governs a kingdom while following the scriptures. "Pupil" (*antevāsī*) means a student. The rest is straightforward.
Furthermore:
One should not honor those who are hypocritical, those who rely on fallacious reasoning, heretics, or those who act like herons. (1.129)

The word *ca* (and) includes those who persist in forbidden occupations (*vikarmastha*) and others. As Manu says: "Heretics (*pāṣaṇḍinaḥ*) and those who persist in forbidden occupations... (MDh 4.30). One should not honor these people under any circumstances. And so Manu says: "One should not honor them even with a mere word" (MDh 4.30). A hypocrite (*ḍambhī*) is one who lives under the pretext of dharma. "Logicians" (*haitukāḥ*) are sophists. "Heretics" (*pāṣaṇḍinaḥ*) are the Kṣapaṇakas and others. One of "heron-like conduct" (*bakavṛtti*) is a deceiver, intent only on his own self-interest. As Manu says: "One who looks downward, a rogue... (MDh 4.196), and so forth. || 129 ||
Now he states other restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) of this very [path] in detail:
Wearing white garments, with hair, beard, and nails kept short, and being pure, he should not eat while looking at his wife, nor while wearing only a single garment, nor while standing. (1.130)

As for the statement that "her hair and dress are not fixed," that should be understood as referring to a *śūdra* woman upon whom one depends. Furthermore, one should not eat while looking at one's wife; rather, one should act in such a way that he does not eat while his wife is looking on. As Manu says:
"One should not eat together with one's wife, nor should one look at her while she is eating. (MDh 4.43)

In the traditional scripture (*āmnāya*) it is likewise stated: "Therefore, these human women swallow men as if they were prey. As for the statement in that same text, "Therefore, one should not eat in the presence of his wife," that is intended to prohibit sharing a single bed beyond the act of sexual union, according to the context. Such is also the established practice. The rest is clear. || 130 ||
One should not fall into doubt, nor should one speak unpleasantly without cause;
one should neither speak what is harmful nor what is untrue, nor should one be a thief or a usurer. 1.131

The repetition of the word "thief" is not without purpose; it serves to establish a connection with this [verse], or rather, it is for the sake of exclusion, as in the previous case where it was said, "the means of accomplishing dharma. || 131 ||
Wearing a sacred thread, carrying a staff and a water-pot,
he should circumambulate the gods, clay, cows, Brahmins, and trees from left to right.
One should possess the gold of Dakṣāyaṇa; for thus says the mantra-text:
"Neither the Rākṣasas nor the Piśācas overcome it, for this is the first-born vigor of the gods."
"He who wears the gold of Dakṣa's lineage. (RVKh 4.6.7a-b)

The repetition of the term *brahmasūtra* is for the purpose of excluding the girdle (*mekhalā*) and other such items. As for the staff (*yaṣṭi*), however, it serves the function of a staff (*daṇḍa*); therefore, it should be of that same measurement. The phrase "with a water-pot" (*sakamaṇḍalu*) expresses mere accompaniment, so it need not necessarily be carried by him personally. However, because of the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*), the staff and other items must indeed be carried by him personally. One is not called "possessing a staff" (*yaṣṭimān*) by means of a staff that remains in the house or is held by another; rather, the connection with "together with" (*saha-yoga*) is seen even when the object is situated elsewhere. And this [staff] is for a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), as Manu has stated: [Manu 2.48: "A staff, a water-pot, a sacred thread, a girdle, and a garment—these five are prescribed for a Brahmin. Thus, the staff and the rest are required for their respective functions. Furthermore, the mention of the staff here is intended to exclude the *tridaṇḍa* (triple-staff) and the like. For it is said: "One should always carry a staff made of bamboo, which is straight, unblemished, and pleasing to the sight; it should be free from knots and of a single piece, reaching up to the hairline. This indicates that the staff is to be used for the purpose of warding off danger and the like. Therefore, the staff is not an item for ascetics alone, but is rather a requirement for all students (*brahmacārins*). Thus, the staff and the rest are to be understood as being for the sake of a visible purpose. Consequently, the prohibition of the triple-staff and so forth is established. As for the water-pot, its use is for the purpose of purification and other rites. Hence, the water-pot is also required. Therefore, the rule regarding the water-pot is not restricted solely to the student stage, but applies generally. Thus, the staff and the rest are to be carried according to their specific purposes. Consequently, the prohibition of the triple-staff and the like is established. As for the water-pot, its use is for

"One should carry a bamboo staff, a water-pot containing water, a sacred thread, a Veda [manuscript], and two auspicious golden earrings" (MDh 4.36). Since the verb "should carry" (*dhārayet*) can also be understood in a causal sense, there is no contradiction in having someone else carry the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). One should perform circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*) of deities and the like. The word "deity" (*deva*) should be understood here as referring to an image used for worship. Furthermore, one should walk clockwise when clay and other such substances approach from the front. The term "tree" (*vanaspati*) refers to well-known sacrificial trees such as the *aśvattha* and others. || 132 ||
Furthermore:
One should not urinate in a river, in the shade, on a path, in a cow-pen, in water, or on ashes;
nor should one face fire, the sun, cows, the moon, the twilight, water, women, or the twice-born.

Since the requirement is already established by the mention of water itself, the mention of the river is for the purpose of including fields and other locations designated by that term. Furthermore, "shade" refers to shade that is habitually used for shelter, based on the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "not in shades that are habitually used for shelter" (VaDh 6.12). Likewise, Manu says:
"In shade or in darkness, by night or by day, one may always perform [the rite] facing whichever direction is comfortable, as well as when there is fear of injury to life" (MDh 4.51).

Thus, he shows that the prohibition applies only to the mere shadow. The word *saṃdhyā* is intended to prohibit the directions associated with sunrise and sunset, for it is at that time that urination is permitted. Furthermore, the word *mehana* should be understood to refer to the voiding of both urine and feces in both cases. And the fact that [the rule] is not explicitly mentioned even though it is relevant to the section on the student (*brahmacārin*) is for the purpose of making known that what is prescribed for all stages of life (*āśrama*) and is not contradictory may be practiced in all stages. Accordingly, Gautama says: "And this is not in conflict with those who follow the subsequent [stages]" (GDh 3.10). By the word "and" (*ca*), he indicates that what is stated for the other stages of life also applies to the student.

Now, one might ask: why is it not the case that [the rule] stated in the section on the *brahmacārin* is intended to apply to others as well, and thus its omission there [in the section on the *snātaka*] was unnecessary? For if the restriction regarding the directions for the *brahmacārin* were established, then the prohibition against the *snātaka* facing the sun and so forth would be logically consistent. Otherwise, how could one who faces north face the sun, such that it would need to be prohibited?

True; however, it has been stated that this is because [the rule] must be construed as a single syntactical unit with another *smṛti* text. And thus, Manu has prescribed the restriction regarding the directions specifically for the *snātaka*. How then is the prohibition against facing the sun to be understood? This should be seen as referring to cases such as confusion regarding the directions. For even when the directions are not known, a lack of restriction would naturally follow by implication; in that regard, it is said: "Not toward fire or the sun," etc. (133).

And this is another [rule]: One should not look at the sun, nor at a naked woman, nor at one who has engaged in sexual intercourse; nor should one, while impure, look at urine, feces, or the moon and stars. (1.134)

The prohibition against looking at the sun is always absolute and without exception. Nor [should one look] at a woman who has engaged in sexual intercourse; here, the word *ca* ("nor") serves to indicate a different state, as in the rule: "or when she is sneezing or yawning," and so forth (MDh 4.43). By implication, this prohibition applies to a woman belonging to another; however, the rule "not a naked woman" applies even to one's own wife. This is not contradictory elsewhere. Precisely for this reason, the nakedness of women for the purpose of applying unguents and the like is permitted. Furthermore, because of the prohibition against looking at Rāhu or the stars while impure, there is no fault at other times. The mention of Rāhu is intended to include eclipses of the moon and other such occasions. (134)
Reciting this entire mantra, "This is my vajra," one may go about unsheltered even when it rains; nor should one sleep with the head facing west.

And thus the sacred tradition (āmnāya) says: "Therefore, one should not go out unsheltered when it is raining. [The mantra] "May this thunderbolt of mine strike away evil" (PārG 2.7.7)—this indeed is the completeness of the mantra. It should be explained that when one goes while it is raining, then [the mantra] is used in this manner. || 135 ||
And this is another [rule]: One should not throw spittle, blood, feces, urine, or poison into water; one should not warm one's feet over a fire, nor should one step over it. (1.136)

The prefix *pra-* is used in the sense of intention, meaning "one should not do this. The word *ca* (and) serves to include spitting and other such acts even in the case of fire, and to indicate that other things mentioned in other Smṛtis are also prohibited. *Asṛk* means blood; *śakṛt* means excrement. The rest is clear. || 136 ||

Furthermore: One should not drink water from one's cupped hands; one should not wake a sleeping person; one should not play with dice or with those who destroy righteousness; nor should one dwell with those who are diseased. (1.137)

By the mention of water, milk and other liquids are not prohibited; others hold that the mention of water is for the sake of illustration. One should not wake a sleeping person by striking him or by acting according to one's own will. Thus says the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "Therefore, one should not wake a sleeping person as one would [wake] a draft-ox (*dhūḥ*). *Dhūḥ* means injury; one should not wake him by means of that. The meaning is "as if striking. And in this entire section on restraints (*yama*), the previously stated rule—"one should not do so without cause"—should be applied everywhere. Furthermore, the sacred tradition shows that [waking] may be done for another reason, having begun with: "He addressed him with these names," and after stating, "He did not rise," it prescribes the method of waking: "He woke him by rubbing him with his hand. (137)
And this is another [rule]:
one should avoid contrary actions, crossing a river by means of a ghost's smoke, and staying in the midst of hair, ashes, chaff, embers, or skulls. (1.138)

One should avoid hostile acts such as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). This prohibition is intended so that there may be no doubt regarding the prescribed rules. Crossing a river by means of one's arms is forbidden, according to the statement of Manu: "One should not cross a river with one's arms" (MDh 4.77). The mention of "river" is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*). Ashes and charcoal are mentioned separately because they are produced from cow-dung and wood respectively; this is for the purpose of making the distinction clear even in other contexts. The rest is straightforward. || 138 ||
Furthermore:
One should not point out a cow suckling her calf; one should never enter through any place other than the gate;
and one should not accept gifts from a king who is greedy and acts contrary to the scriptures. (1.139)

One should not report another's cow. This is because of another Smṛti text: "One should not report to another a cow suckling [her calf]" (GDh 9.23). Furthermore, since the cow is the agent, one must indeed report it when her udders are being pricked against her will. The repetition of the prohibition regarding the king—though already forbidden previously by the rule "He should not strive for gain from here and there" (YDh 1.128)—is for the purpose of elaborating upon that topic and as an introduction to demonstrating excessive censure. || 139 ||
Now he speaks of that very same excess of censure:
"In receiving gifts, the butcher, the usurer, the soldier, the prostitute, and the king are wicked ten times more than each preceding one, respectively. (1.140)
A *sūnā* is a wooden block for slaughtering animals; one who possesses such a block is a butcher (*sūnī*). A *cakra* is a snare. A *dhvaja* is the sign of a liquor-seller;
he should carry a banner for the sake of identification and may dwell within a village according to the established convention.
However, he must never give liquor to those of the lowest castes (*antāvasāyin*), except in times of distress.

Thus, from another Smṛti: *veśa* means appearance or sexual intercourse; she who lives by that is a *veśyā* (prostitute). And so Manu says: "And for those who live by their very appearance" (MDh 4.84). The intended meaning has already been stated. || 140 ||

Having thus explained the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) based on purposeful activity, he now speaks with the intent of describing those based on Vedic study; for the sake of introducing that subject, he says:

"The rite of commencing the study of the chapters (*adhyāya-upākarma*) is performed on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa under the asterism Śravaṇā, or under the asterism Hasta when the herbs have appeared, or on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa. (1.141)
Having thus commenced the Vedic chants and having studied them for four and a half or five and a half months,

the twice-born man should then perform the formal conclusion (utsarga) of the Vedas according to the rule at the edge of water, either under the asterism Rohiṇī in the month of Pauṣa or on the Aṣṭakā day. (1.142)

And here, the *Aṣṭakā* of the month of Māgha is intended. Thus says Pāraskara: "In the month of Pauṣa, under the asterism Rohiṇī, or on the middle Aṣṭakā, they should dismiss the lessons" (PārG 2.12.1). These two rites of the commencement (*upākarma*) and the dismissal (*utsarga*) belong to the teacher alone, because Pāraskara specifies [the agent] as such in the context of the *upākarma*: "as many a group of pupils as he may desire" (cf. PārG 2.10.17). The mention of the "twice-born" (*dvija*), however, is a restatement with reference to the pupils. Furthermore, this instruction is based solely upon the *Gṛhya-śāstra*, because of the expression "according to rule" (*vidhivat*). And according to rule, for any twice-born person who, having commenced and dismissed [the study], studies the Veda—known as *brahman*—either in its meaning or its text, for the sake of practice. 142.
There is a suspension of study for three days when a pupil, an officiating priest, a teacher, or a relative has died;
likewise at the commencement (upākarma) and conclusion (utsarga) of the Vedic term, and upon the death of a learned master (śrotriya) of one's own Vedic school.

In this context, the *guru* refers to the *upādhyāya*, not the *ācārya*. As Pāraskara states: "When the *guru* has died, one should enter the water [for ritual bathing] and abstain for ten nights. For a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*) who has performed the *sātnūnaptra* rite, [one should abstain] for three nights; for one who is not a fellow student, for one night" (PārG 2.11.7–9). This rule regarding the *ācārya* should be understood to apply when he is not the father. Following this same principle, the determination of other cases should also be made, and not arbitrarily. However, at the time of a sacrifice (*ṛtvik-samaya*), because of the mention of the *sātnūnaptra* rite, the rule would apply to other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) just as it does to the patron (*yajamāna*). For this very reason, in the case of officiating at a sacrifice where no *Soma* is used, the period is only one night. A "fellow student" (*sabrahmacārin*) is one initiated by the same *ācārya*, according to the rule: "Likewise for one learned in the Veda (*śrotriya*) of one's own branch (*sva-śākhā*). A *śrotriya* is one who studies the *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas*. Alternatively, there is a distinction between one who studies one's own branch and one who is a *śrotriya*; the word *śrotriya* also signifies one who has mastered the Vedas and so forth. In other instances, however, it is only one night. The word "likewise" (*tathā*) is intended to include the various types of non-study periods mentioned in other *smṛtis*. As Gautama says: "If [animals] such as dogs pass between [the teacher and pupil], there shall be fasting for three days and staying away from home," and so forth (GDh 1.58–59). The rest is clear. || 143 ||
Likewise:
"In the event of thunder at twilight, a hurricane, an earthquake, or the fall of a meteor;
and having completed the Veda, as well as having studied the Āraṇyaka for a day and a night. (1.144)

"Dyunisha" means day and night (ahorātra). And this is determined by specific rules: [one should fast] only during the night when there is thunder at twilight; "during the morning, only during the day in the rainy season, but otherwise there is a combination [of both]," according to another Smṛti text. And here, although "dyuniśam" is the subject matter further on, the explicit mention of "ahorātram" is used for the sake of clarity. || 144 ||
And likewise:
"On the fifteenth, the fourteenth, or the eighth lunar day; during an eclipse of Rāhu; at the junctions of the seasons; or having eaten, or having accepted a gift at a Śrāddha ceremony. (1.145)

The term *dyuniśam* (day and night) continues [to apply here]. The fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*) is included with respect to the fortnight, as is the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). Thus says Pāraskara: "On the day of the wind and on the new moon day, there is a cessation of study for all. An invitation for the sake of a *śrāddha* is called *śrāddhika*; there is a cessation of study even upon receiving such an invitation. Or rather, this undertaking refers to a *śrāddha* consisting of raw food (*āma-śrāddha*), because of the statement: "For the twice-born is declared to have his hand as his mouth" (MDh 4.177). And thus, the word *vā* has the sense of *ca* (and), meaning "whether having eaten or not having eaten. As for the three-night period during the eclipse of Rāhu (*rāhusūtaka*), that applies to study for the purpose of grasping (*grahaṇa*), not to study for the purpose of memorizing (*dhāraṇa*). Other heavy restrictions (*guru*) in this context should also be understood as applying specifically to the purpose of grasping, according to the distinctions in the texts of one's own branch (*sva-śākhā*) or other branches of the Kalpa. And so Manu speaks with the intention of referring specifically to memorization:

"A twice-born man should always diligently avoid only two occasions for the suspension of study: an impure place for Vedic recitation and himself when he is impure" (MDh 4.127). Furthermore, the traditional scripture states: "Therefore, a learned man should indeed continue to study while it is lightning, thundering, and crashing" (ŚB 11.5.6.9); this is intended solely for the purpose of retention, since there can be no suspension of study during the *brahmayajña*. 145.
When an animal, a frog, a mongoose, a dog, a snake, a cat, or a pig [enters the sacrificial fire], there is an interruption for one day and night; likewise when Indra falls or rises.

The word *tu* (but) serves to emphasize. It is for a full day and night (*ahorātra*) alone, not according to the previous arrangement. The animal is a goat, because of the wording of the mantra, "The ram is your animal," and because of the instruction regarding the ram in another *Smṛti*. The rest is clear. There is another reading: "during a great festival. And thus, on occasions such as the *Mahānavamī*, it lasts for a day and night. As for what was stated, "the festival begins after the meal," that refers specifically to festivals in general. However, in the case of the raising of the banner of Indra (*Śakra-ucchraya*), it is according to another *Smṛti*. || 146 ||
In the presence of the sound of dogs, jackals, donkeys, owls, the *sāman* chants, or the cries of those afflicted by arrows;
in the vicinity of impure substances, corpses, Śūdras, outcastes, cemeteries, or those who have fallen from their status—1.147.

*Kroṣṭā* means jackal; *bāṇa* means lute; *antya* means the lowest-born. Since the status of the "lowest-born" is already established by the mention of the Śūdra—just as in the case of the maxim regarding the stick and the cake—the specific mention of the *antya* is for the purpose of excluding those Śūdras who have taken refuge [in the community].
