There is no study when one is in an impure place, even if situated in a pure region, provided one is near an impurity or near a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). Although the status of the cremation ground is already established by the mention of "impurity," the explicit mention of the *śmaśāna* is for the purpose of avoiding it at a greater distance. And so says Āpastamba: "One should not study within the cremation ground, nor within the range of a throw of a yoke-pin (*śamyā*) in any direction" (ĀpDh 1.9.6). || 147 ||
Likewise: in a pure place, when one is oneself pure, during a downpour of lightning and thunder, after eating while the hands are still wet, inside water, at midnight, or in a great wind. (1.148)

During a rain of dust, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, during the fears of twilight or mist, when there is a foul odor, and when a learned man has arrived at the house—one should run [to greet him]. (1.149)
Nīhāra is mist. || 148, 149 ||
When there is the sound of donkeys, camels, vehicles, elephants, horses, or boats, or when trees grow on barren ground—
these thirty-seven occasions are known as temporary interruptions for study.

The mention of specific numbers is for the sake of distinguishing cases such as when there is a flash of lightning or a clap of thunder, when one has eaten with wet hands, when mounting a donkey, a camel, a vehicle, or a boat, and so forth. From the barking of a dog up to climbing a barren mound (*iriṇa*), these [interruptions] are temporary; the interruption lasts only as long as one remains in that state. A *iriṇa* is a saline wasteland. The phrase "they know these" is intended to introduce the opinion of others. Consequently, the intention is that one should seek out other occasions for the suspension of study mentioned in other Smṛtis and observe them according to the rules. || 150 ||

It has been stated that there is no study when a person of refined conduct (*śiṣṭa*) approaches. Since the term "refined" is listed alongside *śūdras* and others, one might suspect that some other kind of refined person—perhaps one who is unconventional or whose speech is unfit to be heard—is meant; to dispel this doubt, he says:
"One should not step on the shadow of a deity, a sacrificial priest, a *snātaka*, a teacher, or a king, nor on another person's [shadow];
nor should one step on blood, excrement, urine, phlegm, or the remains of an ointment. (1.151)

The word *chāyā* (shadow) here signifies appearance (*khyāti*). As in the expression: "Devadatta’s shadow is large. Therefore, one should not step upon the shadow of gods and others. In this regard, just as there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) when priests and such persons arrive—due to affection or being preoccupied with offerings like *madhuparka*—so too is there a suspension of study when another person of eminent qualities is present; this is the meaning. And thus says the sacred tradition (*Āmnāya*): "He who, knowing this, seeks to be a leader among his own people, he indeed becomes sufficient for his dependents" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.18). "But he who competes with one who knows this, he withers away right here and finally dies" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21). The mention of the gods is for the sake of high praise. However, because blood and the rest do not possess the quality of pervasiveness (*abhibhava*), there is a prohibition against standing upon them. *Rakta* means blood. *Viṭ* means feces. The rest is clear. Because of the proximity to the rules regarding suspension of study, it is by contrast that the impurity of a place is established through the defilement of the feet and so forth. Consequently, study is accomplished even on ground that has been smeared [with cow-dung] and the like. Others, however, maintain that one must not stand even in the bodily shadow of gods and others. That, however, requires further consideration. (151)

[Objection: But if this were so, would it not follow that there should be no suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) nor [the performance of] worship even when one who is not eminent has arrived, because of the statement: "A guest is a teacher for everyone"? [Reply: Not so.
"Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and those of royal lineage are never to be treated with contempt.
Until death one should desire prosperity; one should not touch anyone on a vital spot. (1.152)

The terms *vipra* and *kṣatriya* are restatements of the preceding verse and refer to learned Brahmins and kings. The word *ahi* (snake) serves as an illustration: just as a snake is not to be treated with contempt, so too are the eminent Brahmin and the king; the same applies to the Self (*ātman*). Therefore, one must not treat the Self with disrespect—by rising for it, by interrupting Vedic study (*anadhyāya*), and so forth—merely out of regard for anyone at all. The meaning is that such treatment should be accorded only to a learned Śrotriya. Thus Manu says: "In those kingdoms where ignorant men eat the food of the learned, they invite drought or great fear arises. (MDh 4.95)

He states the reason for not disparaging oneself as follows: "One should desire prosperity until death. However, this one should perform without exception by thinking, "One should not touch anyone on their vital spot. Another interpretation is that "one must never show contempt toward a Brahmin or anyone else. And so says the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva:
"Whether he be learned or unlearned, pure or impure, the one who does not bow to a Brāhmaṇa as is his due," [is a sinner].
"That evildoer, consumed by the fire of Brahmā’s wrath,
is to be punished and executed, and he does not belong to us"—
this argument is of no consequence, as it will be addressed later. 152.
Now, in connection with the topic of honoring, he speaks for the purpose of honoring the household deities (*gṛhadevatā*):
"From afar, one should discard remnants of food, feces, urine, and water from the feet.
This is for the sake of honoring the household deities; the word "from the house" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
One should always properly practice the conduct prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti. (1.153)
"This has been stated by me for the sake of illustration"; the intention is that other [rules] should also be sought from other Śrutis and Smṛtis. || 153 ||
And this other point follows from the very context of pride:
one who is impure from eating should not touch a cow, a Brahmin, fire, or food with his foot.
"Fire" means the sacrificial fire. "Food" refers to that which is being eaten, whether cooked or raw.
Furthermore:
one should not subject the subjects, such as cattle and other animals, to reproach or physical punishment.
The exception to this is:
"One may strike one's son and one's disciple. (1.154)

And by the word "ca" (and), one should also censure [the husband]. Or, the word "ca" has the sense of "wife" and so forth, because of their proximity and the understanding that they too are objects of censure. || 154 ||
This, however, is the summary of the instruction here:
one should diligently practice dharma through action, mind, and speech;
the words "not for the sake of wealth or pleasure" are to be understood as the remainder.
An exception to this is stated: "One should not practice even a dharma that is contrary to one's own welfare or loathed by the world. (1.155)

Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *ad* (to eat) here has the sense of "going" (*gati*). Thus, *asvantam* means "not well-gone" (*asugatam*), which is to say, "not well-ascertained. There is another reading: *asvantam*. Its meaning is exactly the same: "having a bad end" (*aśobhanāntam*). It is not beautiful at the end because it is not certain. The conclusion regarding that very point is: "hated by the world," and so forth. The word *tu* (but/however) serves to emphasize. Others, however, explain *asvantam* according to conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) itself as something opposed to other duties (*dharmāntara-virodhin*), such as "excessive Vedic study" (*svādhyāyātiśaya*). But that must be investigated further. Some say that *lokavidviṣṭam* refers to things like the killing of cows, which are not accepted by all people. But that is incorrect, because [if that were the case] the injunction would be purposeless. Therefore, those who know the world to be accomplished through action are the "knowers of the world" (*lokavidaḥ*), such as Manu and others; one should not practice what is hated by them. The meaning is that even if a practice appears to be a duty, one should not engage in it out of one's own pride if it has been censured by Manu and others. However, if it is not hated [by them], one may proceed without opposition. || 155 ||
In connection with the topic of those worthy of honor, he says something else as well:
"By mother, father, guests, brothers, kinsmen, relatives, maternal uncles, the elderly, children, the sick, teachers, physicians, dependents, and friends... (1.156).
Having avoided disputes with officiating priests, family chaplains, ministers, wives, slaves, and kinsmen, the householder shall conquer all the worlds. (1.157)

Therefore, the ellipsis is that one should not engage in dispute with these [five]. Furthermore, because there is a distinction in the specific grounds for engaging in dispute with each of them, the objection that their meaning would be redundant—like the "stick and the cakes" (the maxim of the stick and the cakes)—is avoided. || 156, 157 ||
And this other [rule] is stated in connection with the prohibition against showing contempt:
one should not bathe in the waters of others without having removed five lumps [of earth];
however, one may bathe in rivers, in natural pools, in lakes, and in ponds. 1.158.

If one were to bathe in public bathing places without first removing the mud, then the person who built them would be treated with contempt; therefore, even for the sake of conforming to their intentions, it is proper to remove the mud—this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, this is the procedure for bathing in the absence of rivers and the like. The word "ca" (and) is intended to include springs and other such sources. || 158 ||
In connection with the topic of what is to be honored, he says something else as well:
one should avoid the beds, seats, gardens, houses, and vehicles of others when they have not been given.

The word "adattāni" (not given) is a compound [meaning "things not given"]. The word "para" (other) has the sense of "excellent" or "distinct. One should not occupy beds, seats, pleasure gardens, dwellings, houses, and so forth that belong to another and are not common property. From the statement "not given," it is understood that one may occupy them if they have been authorized.
Moreover:
One should not eat the food of one who has neglected the sacred fires, except in times of distress. 1.159.

One should not eat the food of even a distinguished person who does not maintain the sacred fire (*aupāsana*), and—by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*)—also of one who possesses the faults about to be described. Others, however, explain the word "another" (*para*) as referring to anyone other [than a relative], and they connect this with the phrase "one should not eat what has not been given. That, however, must be further considered. (159)

Now, by way of further incidental discussion, he states that others as well have food that is unfit to be eaten: "Of the miserly, the bound, the thieves, the eunuchs, those who enter the stage [as actors], the hunters, the accused, the usurers, the courtesans, and those initiated into a guild... (1.160).

The ellipsis to be supplied is "one should not eat the food of these. A *kadarya* is one who is greedy. A *baddha* is one restrained by fetters and the like. A *cora* is a thief, well known. A *raṅgāvatārī* is a wrestler. A *vena* is an actor. An *abhiśasta* is one defiled by the accusation of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) or similar offenses. A *vārdhuṣī* is one who, having taken goods at a low price, sells them for a high price. A *gaṇikā* is a female slave. A *gaṇa* is an assembly. A *dīkṣita* is one consecrated prior to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice. Even among the twice-born (*dvijāti*), those defiled by such actions as these have food that is not to be eaten. 160.
Likewise:
[One should not accept gifts] from physicians, the sick, the angry, unchaste women, the intoxicated, and enemies;
nor from the cruel, the fierce, the outcaste, the vrātyas, the hypocritical, or those who eat the leavings of others. (1.161)

A *cikitsaka* is a physician; an *ātura* is one afflicted with an incurable disease; a *kruddha* is one who is constantly angry; a *puṃścalī* is a woman whose primary characteristic is her generative organ; a *matta* is one overcome by the intoxication of wealth and the like; a *vidviṣ* is an enemy; a *krūra* is one whose inner disposition is harsh; an *ugra* is one who acts with violence; a *patita* is one guilty of a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*)—the mention of one already established by the word "accused" (*abhiśasta*) is for the sake of emphasizing the gravity of the penance; this should be understood elsewhere as well; a *vrātya* is one who has fallen away from the *Sāvitrī*; a *ḍāmbhika* has been described [previously]; an *ucchiṣṭabhojī* is a Śūdra. (161)

[The impurity lasts for one day] for those whose wives have no heroic husbands, for goldsmiths, for those who have conquered their village by means of their wives, for village-priests, for sellers of weapons, for blacksmiths, for weavers, and for those who subsist by keeping dogs.

A woman without sons or a husband is called *avirā*. A goldsmith and his wife are well known as *strījitau* (conquered by women). A village priest is known among the Mālavas as a *vaiśvadevika*. An ironworker is a *bhastrerimaka* (?). A tailor is one whose livelihood is sewing. One who serves by performing lowly tasks such as washing feet is a *śvavṛtti*; or he is a *śvakaṇṭhaka* (a dog-necked one). || 162 ||
[One should not accept gifts] from a cruel man, a king, a dyer, an ungrateful person, one who lives by slaughter,
a washerman, a cultivator of the soil, one who lives with his father-in-law, or one who lives with a paramour.

A *nṛśaṃsa* is one who recites [the Vedas] without nobility (*anudārapāṭhaka*), or it is an epithet for a king; a *pārthiva* is a king; a *rajaka* is a dyer; a *kṛtaghna* is well known [as ungrateful]; a *vadhajīvī* is a killer or a rogue; a *celadhāva* is a washerman of clothes; *sudhā* is the material used for the consecration of temples and the like, and he who lives by that is a *sudhājīva*; one whose house (*veśma*) is together with a paramour (*upapati*) is a *sahopapativeśmā*; a *upapati* is a husband’s lover; by virtue of its connection to the house, the lover of a daughter-in-law is also included. || 163 ||
The food of those who have been mentioned as misers and the like must not be eaten, nor that of a seller of Soma, nor that of a slanderer, a liar, a wheelwright, or a bard. (1.164)

Regarding these [persons], such as the miserly and others: one should not eat only in their house; one should also not consume their food even when brought to oneself, nor should one accept it—this being understood from the force of the initial statement. Because of the use of the word "eṣām" (of these), the food of those who maintain no sacred fires may be eaten after it has been brought home and purified by sprinkling and other rites. And just as with the miserly and others, so it is with the sellers of Soma and the like. A *somavikrayī* is a seller of the *soma* creeper, or a seller of the fruit of sacrifice. The word *soma* is intended to indicate sacrificial acts in general. A *piśuna* is a wicked person who points out the vital secrets of others. An *anṛtī* is a speaker of falsehood on occasions involving harm to others. A *cākrika* is a drummer (*pāṭahika*). A *vandī* is a naked ascetic teacher (*nagnācārya*). The word "tathā" (likewise) is for the purpose of including other persons whose food is unfit to be eaten as mentioned in other Smṛtis. Alternatively, it should be understood that while the food of these must not be eaten, they themselves are not necessarily persons whose gifts must not be accepted. By the prohibition of food, there is permission for fruits, roots, and the like, even when brought from them. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "One may accept from these even firewood, water, fodder, roots, fruits, honey, protection, a vehicle offered spontaneously, a dwelling, a *śapharī* fish, *priyaṅgu* grain, garlands, perfumes, and meat" (VaDh 14.12). Or rather, this introduction is for the purpose of censure: it is not merely that their food must not be eaten; rather, the meaning is that even if eaten, it devours the eater himself. All alternative interpretations of the various explanations should also be examined elsewhere in light of other scriptures, and then accepted or rejected according to whether they are taken individually or collectively. In this way, particles such as *ca* (and), as well as words like *krama-bheda*, *anarthakatva*, or *śabdāntarārthatva*, should be applied to their respective places for the purpose of completing the meter. || 164 ||
Thus ends the section on the duties of a *snātaka*.
Now begins the section on what may and may not be eaten.

Having thus far declared the unfitness for consumption of food based on its connection to the absence of the *aupāsana* fire and other such factors, he now states that even food accepted as fit for consumption becomes unfit due to other causes.

Meat that has not been honored, meat obtained for no purpose, that which is infested with hair or insects, that which is turned sour, stale, or leftover from a meal, that which has been touched by a dog, or that which has been looked upon by an outcast; ||| 1.165 ||

Meat that has been cooked in vain, meat brought from a house where no fire is kept, and meat abounding in hair and insects—[in the case of the latter], according to the word "saṃ" (meaning "together"), one should remove the small [hair and insects], prepare it, and then eat it. Meat that has turned sour or has not been properly strained, even if prepared on that very day, is forbidden. The rest is clear. 165.

One should avoid food touched by a woman in her courses, food announced [beforehand], and food over which water has been sipped for rinsing; likewise, food smelled by a cow, food left over by birds, and food intentionally touched by the foot. (1.166)

The word *ca* has the sense of the word *tu*. The intention is that while there may be some remedy for those previously mentioned [faults], one should nevertheless avoid these [specific ones] altogether. A *udakyā* is a woman in her menses. *Saṃghuṣṭam*: as Vasiṣṭha says, "that which is called out by the question, 'Who shall eat? (*VaDh* 14.9). Alternatively, *saṃghuṣṭam* means food touched by a *udakyā*. *Paryācāntam* refers to that which has been sipped around on both sides in a single row, or the leavings belonging to one who has already sipped water. The rest is clear. Because of the expression "intentionally," food touched by the foot of a Brāhmaṇa when done unintentionally is indeed fit to be eaten. 166.
Furthermore:
Among Śūdras, the slave, the cowherd, the family friend, and the sharecropper—along with the barber and he who offers himself—are those whose food may be eaten. (1.167)

Although it should have been said "those whose food may be eaten" (*bhojyāḥ*), by the use of the expression "those whose food may be eaten" (*bhojyānnāḥ*) and by the context, their food is indeed only grain. However, for other Śūdras, even that [grain] is prohibited. Furthermore, slaves and the like must be one's own; otherwise, there would be an over-extension of the rule. (167)
Food that has stood overnight may be eaten if it is mixed with oil or fat and has been kept for a long time;
likewise, preparations of wheat, barley, and cow's milk are edible even if they are not oily.

The mention of "food" (*anna*) is for the purpose of excluding meat and the like; for meat that has stood overnight (*paryuṣita*) is indeed unfit for consumption. However, it is only food that has turned sour (*śukta*) by standing overnight that is unfit for consumption. Other things that have stood for two or three nights, or have been kept for a long time, are indeed fit for consumption even if they have stood for a long duration, provided they are mixed with oil or fat and have not undergone a change in taste or other qualities. In the preceding rule as well, the term "standing overnight" should be explained with reference to this very point. Because of the prefix *pari-*, that which has remained for a full day and night is understood; therefore, what is prepared in the latter part of the night is indeed fit for consumption. The rest is clear. (168)
Having thus stated the faultiness [of certain milk] by way of its cause, he now speaks in order to state it by way of its intrinsic nature:

"One should avoid the milk of a cow that is suckling, one whose calf has not yet passed ten days, or one with a dead calf; likewise the milk of camels, of single-hoofed animals, of women, of forest-dwelling animals, and of sheep. (1.169)

A *saṃdhinī* is one joined with another’s calf, or one who is pregnant. Others say she is one who calves only once. *Anirdaśā* means from the time of birth until ten nights have passed. However, others—on account of the prohibition [of cow's milk] in the rule "cow's *pīyūṣa*" (MDh 5.6)—assert that it refers to the period after that [birth] for ten nights. That is incorrect, because there is no specific distinction made; furthermore, the term *anirdaśā* depends on a limiting condition (*upādhi*), and the presence of milk itself is that condition. Thus Gautama says: "And the milk of a cow during the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) when she has not yet passed ten days" (GDh 17.22), thereby specifying the birth itself as the limit. The prohibition of *pīyūṣa*, however, is for the purpose of prescribing a more severe penance. Accordingly, he says: "One should avoid it with great effort" (MDh 5.6). *Avatsā* means one whose calf is dead or whose calf is lost; for the word *vatsa* denotes a young cow. Since this already establishes the prohibition of cow-milk, the explicit mention of "cow" is for the sake of prohibiting all milk whatsoever. Therefore, there is no fault regarding curds and the like. By the prefix *pari*, however, there is a prohibition of the products of camels and other such animals. If, however, there is a prohibition of the products of an animal that has not passed ten days anywhere else, then by avoiding them there is spiritual merit (*abhyudaya*). This same principle should be understood to apply elsewhere as well. The rest is clear. || 169 ||
Furthermore:
sacrificial offerings intended for deities, the śigru plant, red exudations from incisions, meat not consecrated by ritual, things grown from dung, and mushrooms; 1.170.

The *havis* for the deities refers to the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and so forth; others say it refers to the *bali* offering. *Śigru* is the *saubhāñjanaka* plant. "Red" means red-colored resinous exudations from trees. *Āvraścana* is a standing stump; if that is edible, it is to be avoided. By the word "and" (*ca*), its sprouts are also included. Thus says Manu:
"Red resinous exudations from trees, as well as those produced from cuttings... (MDh 5.6).

"Unconsecrated" refers to that which does not originate from an animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*). "Beans and the like" refers to those produced from soil (*viḍja*), such as *māṣa* beans. "Mushrooms" refers to unopened snake-canopy mushrooms (*sarpacchatra*). By the word "and" (*ca*), other things mentioned in other Smṛtis as unfit for consumption are also included. Furthermore, the mention of "oblation for a deity" (*devatārtha-havis*)—by way of indicating the category of things inherently impure—is intended to prohibit even that which is not an oblation but is well-known to be inherently intended for a deity. The mention of "unconsecrated meat" (*anupākṛta-māṃsa*) is likewise for the purpose of making known the inherent impurity of meat. (170)
This being the case, since meat would thus be prohibited from eating by its very nature, he speaks in order to specify certain exceptions:
"Carnivorous birds, the dātyūha, the parrot, peckers, the ṭiṭṭibha, the sārasa crane, single-hoofed animals, swans, and all village-dwelling birds. (1.171)

Carnivorous meat-eaters are birds such as vultures and the like. The word "birds" (pakṣin) is used here even though it occurs elsewhere in connection with impure birds, for the purpose of specifying these particular ones; or, like the mention of "single-hoofed animals," it refers specifically to birds alone. The *dātyūha* is the *saṃpātaka*. "Peckers" (*pratuda*) are those that eat by pecking, such as the *sūcīmukha* and others. "Single-hoofed" (*ekaśapha*) means those with one hoof, such as horses and the like. Their mention among the birds is so that village-dwelling animals, such as dogs and the like, may also be included. The rest is clear. || 171 ||
The koyaṣṭi, plava, cakravāka, balāka, and bakas, as well as scattered seeds;
and kṛsara, saṃyāva, pāyasa, apūpa, and śaṣkulī prepared in vain. (1.172)

The *koyaṣṭika* is the *meḍhraka*; the *plava* is the *śakaṭibala*. The *cakravāka* and others are well known. *Viṣkira* birds are those that scatter food with their feet before eating, such as the domestic cock (*kukkuṭa*) and others. Since the prohibition of the village cock is already established by the mention of "those living in villages," this present rule is intended for the sake of forest-dwelling birds. Even in that case, because of the statement of Āpastamba—"among the *viṣkira* birds, the cock [is forbidden]"—there is no prohibition against the *lāvaka* and similar species. *Kṛsarā* and other such dishes are well known. Their mention here is for the purpose of making known the penance required for eating them, as well as their inherent impurity. Consequently, there is a fault even for one who maintains no sacred fires (*anagni*) if he eats these for his own sake. Thus says Śaṅkha: "Having eaten *kṛsarā*, *saṃyāva*, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), cakes (*apūpa*), or meat in vain, one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) shall perform the *Prājāpatya* penance; for others, it lasts three nights."
Likewise: the *kalaviṅka*, the *kākola*, the *kurara*, the *rajjudālaka*, web-footed birds, the *khañjarīṭa*, and wild animals or birds that are unknown [should not be eaten]. (1.173)

The *kalaviṅka* is the village sparrow (*grāmacaṭaka*). Some say that it is mentioned again because there might be a suspicion that it dwells in the forest during the rains; however, that is incorrect, since it has already been designated as a "village sparrow. Therefore, its mention is for the purpose of emphasizing its excessive natural depravity. Consequently, this establishes that the meat of women and *śūdras* is also unfit to be eaten. Furthermore, this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for anyone who merely dwells in a village; such is the established practice. In this section, other repeated mentions should be explained in the same manner. The *kākola* is the hawk (*śyena*). The *kurara* is the *karañjaka*, which imitates sounds. The *rajjudāla* is the wild pigeon (*araṇyakapota*). The *khañjarīṭa* is a long-tailed bird well-known in the eastern regions; others identify it as the *śleṣmātaka*. This statement is intended to show that its fault is equal to that of [forbidden] meat. "Web-footed" refers to swans and the like. Its repetition serves the purpose already stated. An objection: "In that case, the mention of the *cakravāka* and others would be improper. It is for the sake of ensuring that, unlike the *kalaviṅka*, they do not serve as an elliptical indicator for all web-footed birds. For this very reason, birds such as the *caṭyā* are not prohibited for women and *śūdras*. The plural number in "of *khañjarīṭas*" is for the purpose of establishing their unfitness to be eaten by women and *śūdras* as well. Although their depravity was already established by the term "swans," the plural is used here so that this same principle may apply to other cases as well. The mention of the "unknown" is for the sake of an illustration: just as animals and birds that are not known to be fit for consumption by those habituated to eating meat are not eaten out of fear of death and other consequences, so too are those whose natural depravity is declared in the scriptures. (173)
Likewise:
"Having unintentionally eaten blue jays, red-footed birds, meat from a slaughterhouse, dried meat, or fish, one should observe a fast for three days. (1.174)

The plural number has already been explained. *Sauna* refers to meat from a slaughtered animal that is unfit; *vallūra* is well known [as dried meat]; some say it means putrid meat. Having unintentionally eaten these, as well as fish—beyond what will be prescribed later—one must observe a three-day fast along with [the primary penance]; the meaning is that it should be four days in total. Or, together with that [primary penance], there is a three-night fast. (174)
Likewise, it is only out of desire [that one incurs this].
Having eaten onion, village-pig, mushroom, village-cock, garlic, or leek, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (1.175)

*Gṛñjana* is similar to the onion (*palaṇḍu*) and is well known in the northern regions (*udīcya*). Since expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) are prescribed for garlic, *gṛñjana*, and onions, their prohibition is established by implication. However, the mention of village pigs (*viḍvarāha*) and so forth is for the purpose of prescribing expiation. A village pig is a domestic swine. *Chattrāka* refers to the *sarpacchatraka* (the mushroom). The word "and" (*ca*) serves to prohibit village-dwelling animals that are similar to the village pig. Thus says the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "Three kinds of animals, having been killed, are impure: the village pig, the ram, and the [wild] boar. The word "three" is already established by the recitation [of the text], but it is used here to specify the manner of impurity: only those of this class are impure, and not goats and the like. The particle "but" (*tu*) is intended to emphasize that this applies in every way to all castes (*sarvavarṇa*). The statement regarding expiation outside of the specific context is for the sake of its performance immediately following [the offense] in all cases. And this [expiation] is the *yaticāndrāyaṇa*.
"Having unknowingly eaten these six, one should perform the *sāntapana-kṛcchra* or the *yati-cāndrāyaṇa*; for the remaining [forbidden foods], one should fast for a day. (MDh 5.20).

However, the traditional interpretation (*saṃpradāya*) here is as follows: for eating food that is defiled by its source, such as being prepared without fire, one should observe a three-night fast if it was unintentional; but if intentional, a *prājāpatya* penance is required. As Manu has said:
"Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one should fast for three days;
but having eaten it intentionally, or having consumed semen, feces, or urine, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance. (MDh 4.222)

This same [penance] applies even to food that is unfit for consumption due to its specific cause (*naimittika*), because there is no difference in the context. However, regarding food that is inherently impure (*svabhāvaduṣṭa*), a four-night fast has been prescribed here for unintentional consumption. For intentional consumption, it is simply a *kṛcchra* penance augmented by recitations (*japa*) and so forth. Regarding onions (*palāṇḍu*) and similar items, the *yaticāndrāyaṇa* is prescribed for unintentional consumption; but for intentional consumption, the penance for drinking liquor (*surāpāna*) applies, both because of the statement [in the legal codes] regarding those who have fallen (*patita*) and because of the commonality of the act of eating. In that regard, the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* and the subsequent re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) mentioned by Vasiṣṭha in the rule "and in the case of ignorance of liquor" (VaDh 20.19) refer to this, and not to the penance for intentionally drinking liquor, because the latter involves the designation of being "fallen. This applies to a twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). For others, however, there is a fast for one day in the case of unintentional consumption, according to Manu’s rule: "In the case of the remaining [forbidden foods], he should fast for a day" (MDh 5.20). In the case of intentional consumption, it is three nights, based on the statement of Śaṅkha: "Three nights for the others. For unintentional consumption of onions and such, the *sāntapana* penance applies; but for intentional consumption, it is indeed an *atikṛcchra*, according to Vasiṣṭha’s rule: "In the case of eating onions and so forth, an *atikṛcchra*" (VaDh 14.33). Although an *atikṛcchra* has been prescribed for eating food that has been licked by a crow or other animals, it is nevertheless the same in this case as well, because of the consistency with other Smṛti texts. We shall discuss the principles for determining the scope of these rules in the section on penances. || 175 ||
Are all meats indeed inedible? No, it is said:
"Among five-toed animals, the porcupine, the iguana, the tortoise, the hedgehog, and the hare are edible; and among fish, the siṃhatuṇḍaka and the rohita are likewise edible. (1.176)

"Eatables" (*bhakṣyāḥ*) are those fit to be eaten. The five-toed animals (*pañcanakhāḥ*) are those beginning with the *sedha* and ending with the hare (*śaśa*). The word "and" (*ca*) includes the rhinoceros (*khaḍga*) and others. As for the Vasiṣṭha-smṛti: "Regarding the rhinoceros and the non-domestic pig, they dispute" (VaDh 14.47), the meaning is that they speak variously [of them] for the sake of praise in the context of *śrāddha* and other rites. Thus says Ātreya: "Infinite [merit is gained] by the meat of the rhinoceros. The mention of "five-toed animals" is for the purpose of excluding elephants and the like. Among fish, too, the *siṃhatuṇḍa* and others are eatable, but not the *sarpaśīrṣa* and others. The *siṃha* has a long snout and is long; the *tuṇḍa* is thick and thick-snouted; the *rohit* is red-colored. The word "for" (*hi*) indicates the reason. Since the satisfaction of the ancestors through the increase of months will be declared by means of the meat of fish and so forth, therefore fish are eatable. The purpose of stating the reason, however, is to make known their edibility specifically in the context of *śrāddha*. And thus says Manu: "The *pāṭhīna* and *rohit* are to be eaten first" (MDh 5.16). The word "also" (*api*) serves two purposes: first, so that the penance prescribed for five-toed animals may also apply when eating fish—"one should observe a fast for three days" (YDh 1.174); and second, to include the *sedha* and others in the *śrāddha*. || 176 ||
Likewise, the pāṭhīna and rājīva fish, as well as those with scales, may be eaten by the twice-born;
therefore, hear now the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat. (1.177)

The *pāṭhīna* and other such fish are well known. By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), the *pāṭhīna* and *rājīva* are also [permitted] specifically at a *śrāddha*. However, those with scales are permitted without distinction; the word "ca" (and) has the sense of the particle "tu" (but/however). Because of the mention of the twice-born (*dvijāti*), both what has been said and what will be said is for the sake of the twice-born alone, implying: "This must be performed even by the twice-born, how much more so by others. And because the meat of the *sedhā* and others is neither inherently defiled nor suitable for a *śrāddha*, therefore [the author says]: "Listen to the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat. "Avoidance of eating" (*bhakṣaṇavarjanam*) means the avoidance [of that which is] eating; the meaning is that eating is faultless. Alternatively, it refers to the avoidance of eating that has already become customary. The word "rule" (*vidhi*) signifies the manner [or method]. The address regarding the avoidance of meat is for the sake of showing respect. (177)
What, then, is that rule? To this he says:
"In a life-threatening emergency, at a funeral feast (śrāddha), when sprinkled with water [for consecration], or by the desire of a Brahmin;
having thus honored the gods and the ancestors, one who eats meat incurs no fault. (1.178)

But he who lives otherwise than this shall dwell in a terrible hell for as many days as there are hairs on the animal's body— that man of evil conduct who kills animals contrary to the prescribed rule. (1.179)

In the preceding verse, because of the two occurrences of the word *tathā*, there are two modes. One mode is: "in a life-threatening emergency (*prāṇātyaye*) and likewise at a *śrāddha* [one may eat] what has been consecrated (*prokṣitam*). The other is: "having honored the gods and the ancestors according to the desire of the twice-born (*dvijakāmyayā*). The meaning here is this: just as in a life-threatening emergency or during a sacrifice (*kratu*), one may eat meat even while restrained by fear of the sin of death, so too may one who is appointed to a *śrāddha*. Thus says Manu: "But being appointed, according to the rule" (MDh 5.35). From the expression "according to the rule," however, there is an exclusion of [eating out of] mere pleasure. Furthermore, although the mention of a "life-threatening emergency" serves as an illustration, it is nevertheless enjoined because that which is not yet established cannot serve as an illustration, and because it is not established [otherwise] except through scripture. Even regarding the "consecrated" (*prokṣita*) meat, if one does not eat it during a life-threatening emergency due to delusion, he would be slain by the animals themselves without ritual authorization; for by not eating consecrated meat, there is a deficiency in the sacrifice (*kratuvaiguṇya*). Therefore, the construction is: "He who, other than in a life-threatening emergency and so forth, kills animals unlawfully out of greed and the like, shall dwell in a terrible hell. And killing is of eight kinds, as Manu says: "The consenter, the carver," and so forth (MDh 5.51). Now, an objection: this word *prokṣita* denotes an excellent sprinkling (*prakṛṣṭasecana*). How, then, is the specific meaning understood? True. But this very thing is the excellence: namely, its being characterized by a scriptural injunction (*vidhānalakṣaṇatva*), and that occurs only in the context of a sacrifice (*kratu*). Furthermore, two things must be done elsewhere: one should perform the sprinkling, and one should eat what has been consecrated. But since that [sprinkling] is already established in the sacrifice, its inclusion for the sake of another [purpose] is not contradictory. Thus the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) shows this: beginning with "The fires of the sacrificer who offers oblations indeed decay," and continuing with "Now, for those who have these [fires], no other desire for meat exists, nor for him to whom these belong," [the text] demonstrates the attainment of meat only in the sacrifice and its non-attainment elsewhere, thereby illuminating that the word *prokṣita* has the sacrifice as its sole purpose. As for the other mode, beginning with "according to the desire of the twice-born," by eating [meat] in that way, one does not incur fault. || 179 ||
But if he should avoid it, then, even while dwelling in his own home, a Brahmin becomes a sage by the abstention from meat; he attains all desires as well as the fruit of the horse sacrifice. 1.180.

Because it is desired by the twice-born (*dvija*), the honoring of guests is called *dvijakāmyā*. There is no fault for one who eats the great bull and other such items brought forth by that [hospitality]. Likewise, there is no fault for one who eats the remaining meat after having performed the worship of the gods and ancestors (*devapitṛ-arcanam*) and the *śrāddha* rite. However, if one should even avoid this, then one attains all desires as well as the fruit of the horse sacrifice (*hayamedha*); such [passages] are to be applied here. And having considered the various ways of practicing the eating of meat, Manu said: "There is no fault in the eating of meat" (MDh 5.56). || 180 ||
Thus ends the section on what may and may not be eaten;
now begins the section on the purification of substances.

[Objection: But surely, such a rule for the consumption of meat is improper, because the impurity of the cause cannot be remedied; for meat is produced by dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and the like. [Reply: True, it is produced by dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and so forth; nevertheless, with the very intention of demonstrating that it is indeed not impure, [the author] speaks—by way of incidental discussion—for the purpose of establishing the purity of other substances as well when they are rendered pure through other causes. Alternatively, the commencement of the section on the purification of substances is intended to show that while all substances have a means of purification, this does not apply to those inherently impure, such as village pigs and the like. And since there is an expectation as to how a substance contaminated by an impurity such as a village pig might be purified, he says: *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* 1.186: *madyair mūtrapurīṣair vā ṣṭhīvanaiḥ pūyaśoṇitaiḥ / saṃspṛṣṭaṃ naiva śudhyeta punaḥpākena bhājanam // YDh_1.186* "A vessel touched by intoxicating liquors, urine, feces, spittle, pus, or blood is not purified at all; it must be purified by being fired again. *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* 1.187: *nāryas tu pātraiḥ śudhyanti somasūryāṃśumārutaiḥ / adbhir gātrāṇi śudhyanti manaḥ satyena śudhyati // YDh_1.187* "Women, however, are purified by their vessels [during menstruation], and by the rays of the moon and sun and by the wind; the limbs are purified by water, and the mind is purified by truth. *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* 1.188: *adbhis tu śudhyate śodhyaṃ nadī vegena śudhyati / rajasā strī manoduṣṭā saṃnyāsena dvijottamaḥ // YDh_1.188* "That which is to be cleansed is purified by water; a river is purified by its current; a woman defiled in mind is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born is purified by renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* 1.189: *vigair mṛdbhiś ca kāṃsyānāṃ śuddhiḥ plāvo 'yasām api / śuddhyet tuṣādibhir lohamaśmanaḥ kṣālanena tu // YDh_1.189* "The purification of bell-metal vessels is by acids and earth; that of iron is by immersion in water; metal is purified by husks and the like, and stone by washing. *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* 1.190: *tāmrāyaḥkāṃsyaraityānāṃ trapuṇaḥ sīsakasya ca / śaucaṃ yathārhaṃ kartavyaṃ kṣārāmlodakavāribhiḥ // YDh_1.190* "For copper, iron, bell-metal, brass, tin, and lead, purification should be performed as appropriate with alkaline substances, acids, and water. *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* 1.191: *bhasmanā śudhyate kāṃsyaṃ surayā yad upāhṛtam / surāmoditasaṃpṛktaṃ śudhyate tāpalekhanaiḥ // YDh_1.191* "Bell-metal is purified by ashes, as is that which has been touched by liquor; that which is permeated by the smell of liquor is purified by heating and scraping. *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* 1.192: *gaṇḍūṣaṃ pādaśaucaṃ ca kṛtvā vai kāṃsyabhājane / ṣaṇmāsāt tu parityāgaḥ kāṃsye syād bhasmasecanam // YDh_1.192* "After using a bell-metal vessel for rinsing the mouth or washing the feet, it should be discarded after six months; in the case of bell-metal, sprinkling it with ashes [is required]. *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* 1.193: *phalamūleṣu pakveṣu kāṣṭhaloṣṭhatṛṇeṣu ca / rajjucarmāsu ca strīṣu nityaṃ śaucaṃ parikṣayet // YDh_1.193* "In the case of fruits, roots, cooked foods, wood, clods of earth, grass, ropes, skins, and women, one should always examine the purity [of the source]. *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* 1.194: *adbhis tu prokṣaṇaṃ śaucaṃ bahūnāṃ dhānyavāsasām / prakṣālanena tv alpānām adbhir amalaiḥ smṛtam // YDh_1.194* "The purification of large quantities of grain and clothing is by sprinkling with water; but for small quantities, it is traditionally held to be by washing with pure water. *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* 1.195: *cailavat syād vikalpena celadhautādikarmaṇi / śāka-mūla-phalānāṃ ca dhānyavat śuddhir iṣyate // YDh_1.195* "In the matter of washing clothes and similar tasks, the same rule as for clothes applies optionally. For vegetables, roots, and fruits, purification is desired to be like that of grain. *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* 1.196: *kauśeyāvikayor ūṣaiḥ kutapānām ariṣṭakaiḥ / śrīphalair aṃśupaṭṭānāṃ kṣaumāṇāṃ gaurasarṣapaiḥ // YDh_1.196* "Silk and woolen cloth are purified by alkaline salts; blankets by *ariṣṭaka* nuts; fine cotton cloth (*aṃśupaṭṭa*) by bilva fruits; and linen by white mustard seeds. *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* 1.197: *kṣaumavac chaṅkhaśṛṅgāṇām asthidantamayasya ca / śuddhir vijānatā kāryā gomūtreṇaudakena vā // YDh_1.197* "The wise person should perform the purification of conch-shells, horns, bone, and ivory according to the rule for linen, either with cow-urine or with water. *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* 1.198: *prokṣaṇāt tṛṇakāṣṭhaṃ ca palālaṃ caiva śudhyati / mārjanopāñjanair veśma punaḥpākena mṛnmayam // YDh_1.198* "Grass, wood, and straw are purified by sprinkling; a house by sweeping and smearing with cow-dung; and an earthen vessel by firing it again. *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* 1.199: *somacarubhakṣayoḥ kṛte śuddhiḥ syād abhigh
Of golden and silver lotuses, of vessels for holding [liquids], of stones, of sugar, ropes, roots, fruits, garments, split bamboo, and skins. || 1.181 ||

The purification of vessels and cups by means of water is prescribed. The phrase "purification is prescribed" is the verb in this section and should be applied accordingly to each case. Regarding golden vessels that are free from stains, there is no impurity resulting merely from contact with something impure. As Manu says:
"A golden vessel free from stains is purified by water alone."
"A vessel made of lotus-fiber, one made of stone, and one made of silver, provided it is unadorned. (MDh 5.112)

*Rājata* means silver. *Abja* refers to conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and the like. *Ūrdhvapātra* refers to the sixteen-vessel cups (*ṣoḍaśipātra*) and so forth. *Graha* refers to the vessels for Indra-Vāyu and others. Since the term *graha* already establishes that these are tall vessels, the specific mention of them here is intended to include all such vessels; thus, the large wooden vat (*droṇakalaśa*) and others are also included by this. *Aśman* refers to grinding stones and the like. Vegetables (*śāka*) and so forth are self-evident. *Vidala* refers to bamboo and similar materials. In this entire section, even when only one of the two—either the original form (*prakṛti*) or its modification (*vikṛti*)—is mentioned, both are understood. Thus, Vasiṣṭha, after prescribing the carving of wooden objects, extends the rule by stating: "As with wood, so with bones" (VaDh 3.52). The Teacher [Yājñavalkya] likewise clarifies this very point by teaching that *rājata* and *aśman* are qualifiers of the vessels themselves. (181–2b)
Thus, for these common vessels used in Soma sacrifices, purification with water is prescribed when there is only slight defilement or when they are free from stains. But for those that are stained:
"The *caru* pot, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and vessels containing oily substances [are purified] with hot water. (1.182)

The repetition of the word "water" (*vāri*) is for the purpose of making known that it possesses the quality of heat (*auṣṇya*). Consequently, it is established that whatever is the means of purification for a substance, that very same thing, when modified by its qualities, serves as the means for that which is modified by defects. Thus, what was stated by Śaṅkha—namely, "for clothes, [purification is] steaming or cutting off that much"—is also established. Furthermore, the meaning of the words is clear, and the rest is self-evident. || 182 ||
If they are merely defiled by contact,

the purification of the wooden sword (sphya), the winnowing basket (śūrpa), the hide (ajina), grains, the pestle (musala), the mortar (ulūkhala), the fire-pan (anas), and of many garments that are joined together, is simply sprinkling (prokṣaṇa). (1.183)

Just as sacrificial implements such as the *sphya* and others, by the mere sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) at the time of the ritual, remove occasional damage (*upaghāta*), even so do things of this nature—such as beds and the like when combined for the sake of human ends, and garments when uncombined and worn by a person. The word "and" (*ca*) refers to parched grains (*dhānā*) and so forth. Thus the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) states: "Whatever among these a mantra-impure carpenter or anyone else unholy (*amedhya*) strikes, that very thing he makes holy (*medhya*) for them with water. This shows that when impurity might result from some other cause, holiness is restored by sprinkling. (183)
The minor injury has been described; now, however, regarding the major one:
the cleaning of tools made of wood, horn, or bone, and of those produced from fruit, as well as the wiping of sacrificial vessels with the hand during a sacrificial rite. (1.184)

This is the purification for items made of wood, such as *caru* vessels and the like. Some maintain that because they share the common nature of being wood, substances such as resin (*sarjarasa*) are also considered wooden; however, this requires further consideration. The form *saṃbhuvām* is derived from the root *bhū* preceded by the prefix *sam*, with the suffix *kvip*, followed by the genitive plural ending and the substitution of *āmyuvaṅ*. These refer to vessels made of gourd (*alābu*) and so forth. Their purification consists of scrubbing them with cow-hair; for those coated with a paste, it is by wiping. This applies specifically to sacrificial vessels once they have been purified. The mention of "with the hand" in the context of sacrificial rites is for another purpose: namely, that the hand of a Brāhmaṇa may also serve as a cause of purification, just like water. Consequently, purification occurs through the wiping of water-pots (*kamaṇḍalu*) and similar items. Furthermore, at the time of eating, even pure vessels must be wiped. Thus says the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "Therefore, when the serving of food has been prepared for men, one then wipes the vessels. By the word "then" (*atha*), it indicates that this refers specifically to those [vessels] that are already pure. (184)

In cases of excessive defilement, woolen cloth and thread are purified with water and cow’s urine containing salt; silk cloth with *śrīphala* fruit; and likewise, *kutapa* wool with *ariṣṭa* fruit. (1.185)

[The term *āvika* refers to] that made of wool (*ūrṇā*), whether it be woven with threads (*sautrika*) or not; [the term *kārpāsa* refers to] that made of cotton. Because the word *sūtra* (thread) is common to all, it includes silk (*kauśeya*) and the like. As for the rule, "of those made of wool by means of the sun" (cf. BDh 1.8.40), that concerns defilement resulting from usage. As for the statement of Bhāradvāja: "There is no purification required for beds, seats, mats, straw-mats, vehicles, cushions, pillows, bolsters, blankets, houses, grain, jewels, fruit, wooden planks, stones, things with many hairs, and wood that is not buried in the ground, nor for grass, chaff, ropes, children, except by sprinkling; some say that in the case of touching an outcast (*antya*), there must be bathing for the children," that concerns the matter of physical contact, because of the mention of "touching an outcast. However, in the case of contact with urine and the like, one should determine the appropriate purification according to the degree of fault, using water and cow's urine along with soil. For fine cloth (*aṃśupaṭṭa*)—which is a cloth for the eyes—one should use those same substances, water and cow's urine, together with the paste of *bilva*. A *kutapa* is a specific kind of blanket. The rest is clear. (185)

[It should be purified] with water and cow-urine alone. Linen [is purified] by re-boiling with white mustard seeds; earthenware [is purified] by re-baking. Since the mention of earthenware occurs under the heading of water and cow-urine, that too should be understood as a means of purification when there is only slight defilement. Furthermore, because of the word "again" (*punar*), this applies to what has been baked; however, unbaked [earthenware] is purified by baking, while that which cannot be baked is purified by the cleansing of the ground itself. And in the case of excessive defilement, there must be abandonment. As Vasiṣṭha says:

"An earthen vessel that has been touched by liquor, urine, feces, phlegm, pus, tears, or blood is not purified even by re-firing. (VaDh 3.59) Because of the word "touched" (*saṃspṛṣṭa*), that which is soaked with liquor and so forth must be discarded; it is not [discarded] merely from contact with a few drops. Furthermore, since impurity is declared [only] in the case of re-firing, it is indeed purified by the initial firing.
Even though they are almost always defiled, the hand of an artisan, merchandise, alms-food, and likewise the mouth of a woman, are pure. (1.186)

An artisan (*kāru*) refers to a potter and the like. Alms (*bhaikṣa*) refers to what is obtained from a religious student (*brahmacārin*) and others. The term "the face of a woman" (*yoṣinmukha*) includes even one of a different caste; the word "woman" is used here for the sake of its specific quality. As Śaṅkha says: "The hand of an artisan is pure, as are their tools. Substances produced in mines (*ākaraja*) are pure when sprinkled or washed. Edible things produced in mines, once they have been sprinkled with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), must be cooked again. The same applies to oily substances and liquids that possess oiliness. Sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) means washing; pouring over (*abhyukṣaṇa*) means merely sprinkling from above. The repetition of the word "pure" is for the purpose of making known that there is no defect in these because they are mine-produced. The repetition of the phrase "produced in mines" is for the purpose of indicating that this applies specifically to things like *kilāṭa* (coagulated milk) which are generally mine-produced, and not to items such as cakes or condiments. For those [mineral products] that have been cooked and sprinkled with clarified butter, there is a further cooking; for others, mere sprinkling suffices. In the case of oily substances, however, mere cooking is required. This should be applied accordingly to liquids like honey and the like that are fit for cooking and possess oiliness. (186)

However, according to the specific nature of the defect, purification of the ground occurs through sweeping, burning, the passage of time, or the treading of cows; likewise, a house is purified by sprinkling, scraping, and smearing, as well as by sweeping and plastering. (1.187)

This is because of the word "likewise" (*tathā*) and because of the sowing of other soil. Gautama states: "And the sowing of earth [purifies]" (GDh 1.32). *Mārjana* means cleansing, which is to say, the removal of much [impurity]. Regarding time, it refers to periods such as the rainy season; or in the case of ground occupied by a woman in her courses and so forth, until the time of her purification. However, regarding unoccupied ground, Bhṛgu says: "That which is smeared and traversed by a woman in her courses becomes pure once it is swept, or else it is purified when sprinkled with gold-water."
Sprinkling (seka) means pouring water over. Thus Yama has said:
"A drop of water the size of a cow's ear, as it falls upon the ground, purifies whether the area is covered with grass or not, provided that no stain is visible."
The house [should be cleaned] daily by sweeping and smearing; or, the word "house" (gṛha) refers to the walls, since elsewhere the purification of the ground has already been mentioned. || 187 ||
It has been stated regarding food that is not fit for consumption; however, regarding food that is fit for consumption:
"If food has been smelled by a cow, or is defiled by hair, flies, or insects, water, ashes, or even earth should be thrown into it for the sake of purification. (1.188)
Because they are not fit for food, [the purification] applies to those items defiled by the leavings of food or their stains.
The purification of tin, lead, and copper is by means of alkaline substances, acids, water, and earth;
that of bell-metal and iron is by means of ashes; and the purification of liquids is by means of overflowing.
By the word "tu" (but), it is indicated that this rule for the purification of an object applies elsewhere as well, in cases of minor defilement. || 189 ||
But regarding urine, feces, and the like:

that which is smeared with impurities is purified by earth and water until the odor is removed. That which is commended by word, that which is washed with water, and that which is unknown [to be defiled] are always pure. (1.190)

This is the rule for the purification of all substances. Regarding the mention of "fragrance," some maintain that when there is defilement by odorless phlegm and the like, the removal of stains should be accomplished with water alone. That, however, must be reconsidered, as Manu has said: "In all purifications of substances, earth and water should be applied as long as the odor and the stain caused by it do not depart from the object smeared with impurity" (MDh 5.126).

Furthermore, as for what was stated by Śaṅkha: "For metallic objects defiled by a corpse, semen, urine, or feces, there shall be smelting, scraping, or wiping twenty-one times with ashes"—this is to be understood as applying when one is unable to remove the odor and other such impurities. For even with ashes, it is only those whose odors have been removed that are not in conflict [with purity]; and wiping applies only to contamination by dry, impure substances. This, however, is the conceptual rule regarding the purification of common substances: whatever is not known to be defiled by a specific authoritative means, and which is praised by words such as "this is indeed beautiful" upon the heart's conviction, or which has been washed with water or sprinkled—that should always be understood as pure beyond doubt. (190)
Thus water has been described as a cause of purification. Furthermore, this is their purity:
Water on the earth that remains in its natural state and satisfies the cow is pure;
likewise is meat fallen from the mouth of a dog, a *caṇḍāla*, a carnivorous beast, or the like. (1.191)

Some maintain that water fit for bathing and so forth, which satisfies a cow, is [pure]; however, that is incorrect, because of the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "Even from a small pool, there may be waters sufficient to satisfy a cow" (VaDh 3.35). Water that is in its natural state and is not corrupted by the addition of odor, color, taste, or other qualities is pure even if it has entirely entered the ground. Thus says the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "Speech indeed departed from the gods; it entered the waters. Those gods sought speech from the waters. The waters said to them: 'Whatever is inauspicious among our offspring and among others, purify that; then we shall give back speech. The gods said, 'So be it. Having begun thus, it continues: "That which is the sun is the *brahmayajña*; Savitṛ, who is all the deities, should purify [the waters] daily with rays purified by the *brahmayajña*. Therefore, on that very day they are considered pure for the sake of purification. Therefore, whatever may be subject to doubt, one should touch it with water; it becomes pure. At night, [speech] entered Varuṇa; therefore, one should not take [water] at night. Or, one should take it over a fire while reciting, 'From every abode... Nor is there any fault even in the case of modifications such as camphor, because of the mention of impurity in the rule: "by those corrupted by odor and so forth" (VaDh 3.36). By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), meat also is pure only when in its natural state. Consequently, it should be understood that if it is struck down [killed] by a Caṇḍāla or similar person, there is indeed a fault. || 191 ||
And just as water remains pure even when there is suspicion of defilement, so too are these things:
a ray of light, fire, dust, shadow, a cow, a horse, the earth, and wind;
droplets, flies, and a calf while suckling are pure to the touch. (1.192)

The rays of the sun, fire, dust stirred up by the wind, the shadow of the body of a *caṇḍāla* or similar person, cows, horses, the earth, the wind, the drops of water driven by it that are not touched [by anything impure], and flies that frequent unclean things, are pure when touched. Furthermore, the mouth of a mother’s calf is pure when it is suckling; the mention of the "calf" is intended to include all suckling animals, as the underlying principle is the same. In every respect, the scripture is not to be subjected to mere rationalistic scrutiny. (192)

Objection: But does not the statement that cows and horses are pure imply that buffaloes and the like must be impure? Not so; this is for the sake of praising specific qualities, not for the purpose of exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*). What is the quality? It is said:

"The goat and the horse are pure in their mouths, but neither the cow nor [the human] is so; dirt from the nails is not [pure]; and roads are purified by the rays of the moon and sun and by the wind" (1.193).

By the word "and" (*ca*), it is understood that other things of this same nature are also purified by touching *soma* and the like. Thus says the Vedic mantra: "Agni is the purifier; may he purify me, as well as Vāyu, Soma, Sūrya, and Indra" (ĀpŚr 12.20.6). Therefore, the summary of the teaching is that this [method of purification] applies specifically to those for whom no other means of purification has been prescribed. || 193 ||
For even when there is a suspicion of impurity:
"Droplets from the mouth are pure, as are drops from the final sipping of water;
likewise, the beard within the mouth and what is stuck between the teeth are pure once they have been dropped. (1.194)

The repetition regarding droplets (*vipruṣ*) is for the purpose of making it known that, once their impurity is understood through direct perception, they are indeed impure in other instances as well. Furthermore, the rule of Gautama, "if they do not fall upon the body" (GDh 1.41), refers to the case of another person; this [present rule], however, is for one's own self—this is the distinction. Yet, if there is clear perception [of impurity], there is certainly a fault even in the case of one's own [droplets]. Moreover, droplets that fall away are pure. Thus says Vasiṣṭha:
"Furthermore, those droplets which have fallen on the feet of one who is causing another to wash, are to be known as equal to those situated on the ground" (VaDh 3.42).

For this very reason, the accomplishment of *ācamana* is established even by one who has not been invited; and thus Āpastamba says: "Or he whom one who is pure (*prayata*) causes to sip water" (ĀpDh 1.15.3). Beard that has entered the mouth is pure. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that the smearings on the beard are also pure, according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "There is no smear on the beard" (VaDh 3.40). And because of the scriptural mention of its being on the beard, this applies only when it is impossible to remove it. Regarding what is stuck to the teeth: "having discarded it, one is then pure," and also "while swallowing. It should be understood that if something is not perceived with effort at the time of sipping water, then after swallowing it or discarding it, one becomes pure by that very act of *ācamana*. In this very context, some recite this verse:
"Roads, mud, and water touched by outcastes, dogs, or crows are purified by the wind alone, as are structures built of baked bricks. (YDh 1.195).
However, since that has already been covered by the preceding [verse], it is of no further consequence here. 194.

The interruption [of the previous rule] was already mentioned following the preceding sipping of water (*ācamana*). Since that other sipping of water has not been taught elsewhere, he now states it for the purpose of instruction:
"Having bathed, having drunk, after sneezing, sleeping, eating, and walking on a road, as well as after changing one's garment—one who has already sipped water should sip water again. (1.195)

Because of the instruction "having sipped water" (*ācānta*), another rule for the procedure of sipping water must be inferred in accordance with other *smṛtis* regarding other occasions such as bathing and so forth, as well as in cases of touching what is impure (*ucchiṣṭa*) and the like. On the basis of that [inference], the subject matter of this verse is: "one who has already sipped water should sip again during bathing and similar acts. Therefore, in other instances, there is only a single sipping of water. Regarding "wandering on a road" (*rathyā-prasarpaṇe*), because of the prefix *pra*, the sipping of water applies only when one has not washed [the feet], and not in every case. Furthermore, the sipping of water occurs only upon changing one's garment (*viparivarte*), and not merely upon loosening and readjusting it. Some, however, desire the sipping of water at both the beginning and the end; that, moreover, is to be deliberated. The rest is clear. This, then, is the traditional interpretation (*saṃpradāya*) here: the rule for sipping water according to Kātyāyana is of various types, because sipping water serves purposes such as purification and the destruction of inauspiciousness. For instance:
Purification following the discharge of urine and so forth serves as the means for accomplishing rites such as sacrifices;
it is occasional purification after sneezing and the destroyer of sin when speaking what is sour (or unpleasant).
For the sake of dharma at the Ganges and other such sites, for the attainment of perfection when setting out on a journey,
and for the removal of the afflictions caused by the gaze of cruel-eyed beings, one should [perform this].
Through other Smṛtis, through established practice, through traditional scripture, and by such means as these,
those who desire to know reality should always discern that [truth].

In that regard, for one who has touched something requiring purification or sipping water (ācamana), as well as for one who has touched such a person, purification consists of sipping water alone. However, there is no fault for another [who touches the latter]. And so they record in the Smṛti: "One who is touched by someone defiled by food remnants becomes impure only by himself; another who touches him does not become impure. This rule applies to all substances. Thus it is said.

But for an insentient object, there is sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). As Śaṅkha says: "One who is impure while holding an object should set it down and sip water; by sprinkling it with water, the object becomes pure. The Vedic scripture also states: "Whatever may require investigation [for purity], that should be touched with water. However, there is no fault in touching an insentient object that has been touched by one who is impure, because of the statement: "This rule applies to all objects. But for things that are neither humans nor living beings, there is simply an absence of defect. By this very principle, the various types of bathing (*snāna*) are to be explained in detail. This much, however, is the distinction: even regarding the purpose of purification, there is a twofold division based on the distinctions of sexual intercourse, contact with a woman in her courses (*udakyā*), and so forth. In the case of contact with a woman in her courses or one who has been touched by her, there must be a bath and the washing of the object. In the case of sexual intercourse and similar acts, however, there is sipping of water (*ācamana*) and sprinkling. And this applies only to an object that is human or capable of being washed or purified by bathing; for that which would perish [by such treatment], such as a sick person or a book, there are only sipping and sprinkling. As Baudhāyana says:
"Having understood the place, the time, as well as oneself, the substance, the purpose of the substance, the justification, and the state, one should determine the purification. (BDh 1.8.53)

And this is the ultimate truth here: this [rule] is merely an elaboration upon other Smṛtis. As Manu says: "Purification should be performed according to the requirements" (MDh 5.114). Although it concerns the purification of specific metallic objects, it applies to all things. Thus, when there is contact with a Caṇḍāla or similar outcast, and the general rule for washing all substances would apply, there is this specific rule: metallic objects should be rubbed with ash twenty-one times; those that have been used once should be scraped, and those used for a long time should be polished. This should be applied similarly to cases involving urine, garlic, use by a Śūdra, and so forth. As for earthenware, however, if touched by a Caṇḍāla, garlic, and the like, it must be fired again. In the case of contamination by urine and such, or use by a Caṇḍāla and the like, it must be discarded. If birds such as crows nest in it, it should be circumambulated with fire. If contaminated by their excrement and the like, it must be fired again. Similarly, for wooden objects, one should apply washing, sprinkling, scrubbing, scraping, planing, discarding, and so forth. For woven cloth, if there is contact with a Caṇḍāla and the like, small items should be washed; those used once should be cleaned appropriately with husks and the like, or with earth and water. If they are defiled by garlic and the like, or pervaded by urine and the like, if the stain cannot be removed, one should cut away only that portion. If they are pervaded by flour-based substances (paiṣṭī) and the like, or if they have been used for a long time by a Caṇḍāla and the like, they must be discarded. If they change color, they should be steamed. For all substances, however, after restoring their respective original colors, they should be washed with earth and water. For objects made of lotus, stone, bone, ivory, or gems, if they have been used by a Śūdra and the like, or touched by garlic and the like, they should be wiped and then washed with water and cow's urine; however, if they have been used for a long time, they must be discarded. But very costly items are not to be discarded at all, based on the statement: "Gold [is pure] even from impurity" (MDh 2.239). And it has been said: "Place, time... (BDh 1.8.53), and the Manava verse: "That which is to be purified is purified by earth and water" (MDh 5.108). In all cases where no specific purification is prescribed, one should determine the appropriate method based on the presence or absence of a coating. For large quantities of grain, clothing, beds, and the like, if there is contact with a Caṇḍāla and the like, they should be sprinkled. If an object that requires bathing is merely touched, it is sprinkled; but if touched while one is impure from eating, nothing further is required. Grass, wood, dry cow-dung, roots, fruits, and the like brought by a Caṇḍāla and others should be sprinkled. However, if one touches them without having sprinkled them, one must bathe. Fresh cow-dung and the like are purified by drying, or by being sprinkled with gold-water. In the case of contamination by urine and the like, for grains, one should discard what was touched and purify the remainder by circumambulation with fire and so forth. Regarding the indefinite contact with dry excrement and the like, Āpastamba states: for rice, wash and dry them; for husked grain (taṇḍula), discard them. For liquids, if the vessel is defiled, transfer them to another vessel and heat them. In the case of contact with garlic and the like, remove the liquid and pour it over. If there is a suspicion of contact with non-edible or non-falling-off substances, boil the liquid to be cooked; then, after pouring it over, throw gold or the like into it. Oil and ghee, if touched by the impurities of food remains, should be used after placing them in water. This should be understood to apply to those [liquids] capable of being drained in measures of a Droṇa or an Āḍhaka, even in the case of contamination by dogs, crows, and the like. For wells and the like, if the defect is removed by drawing out the water, gold and the like should be thrown in. Salt and honey produced by Pulkasas and others are purified by burying them in the ground. And for all substances, purification occurs simply through the discarding of the contaminated part.
Whatever object has become impure through contact with the impure shall attain purification from it by means of its absolute abandonment.

This is because of another Smṛti text: for all substances, even the smallest amount, there must be renunciation [of the defiled part]. However, regarding cooked foods, if they are touched by food-leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*), even small amounts require sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "While engaged in eating edible foods... (VaDh 3.43). Even upon touching the leavings of a Śūdra, [sprinkling is required], because of the instruction that what has been touched by a woman in her courses (*udakyā*) is unfit for consumption. Upon touching garlic and the like, however, one should remove only a tiny portion and purify the rest with a process similar to that for grain; but for a very small amount, there is simply renunciation. If a dog, crow, or similar creature has licked a quantity less than a *droṇa* or an *āḍhaka*, it must be discarded. But if it has stepped on it, one should remove only the portion directly touched and purify the remainder like grain. If urine or the like is discharged into food already taken into the mouth, the purification is as before. If a Śūdra who has taken food becomes defiled by leavings, one should purify it by sprinkling with *Kūśmāṇḍī* verses after performing the ritual preparation. In cases of defects in all types of food, one should use them after consecrating them by reciting the Sāvitrī verse one hundred and eight times and performing the ritual preparation. In all these cases, one must consider the "place and time. Wherever there is a pang in the heart, that must be discarded, since self-satisfaction is also a cause of purity. In the case of dried cakes and the like, only that specific part should be removed. Things contaminated by extremely impure substances must be discarded. When a vessel is defiled, the food inside is treated like the liquid. In the case of contact with Caṇḍālas and others, cooked food must be discarded entirely. For cloth, rope, split bamboo, and leather, the purification consists of cutting off only that part and so forth. For the skins of animals such as the *kukuṇṭha*, dyeing is required when there is contact with urine and the like. In all cases, one should not use items that have not been dyed according to this rule. Regarding the purification of shoes, it is done appropriately with earth and water. This too should be understood from the statement of Śaṅkha: "For cloths, as for cloths, and for grains, down, chowries, skins, grass, hair, cane, bark, and so forth, [purification is] with earth, ashes, cow-urine, alkaline water, and water. The inclusion of "and so forth" is for the sake of items such as the *kutapa* blanket. By the word "grass," palm leaves are also included, since the word "grass" applies there as well due to its being a plant. Upon touching wood buried in the ground that has been handled by a Caṇḍāla or similar person, there is no fault. As Āpastamba says: "One should consider oneself pure while touching other things on a heap of grass, provided one is already pure; likewise regarding grass and wood buried in the ground" (ĀpDh 1.15.13–14). And Vṛddhagārgya says: "Wood and stone slabs that cannot be lifted by many are equal to the ground. This also includes door-panels, mats, ladders, and so forth attached to the house, because of the word "likewise. Some, however, desire the sprinkling of ladders; but that is incorrect due to the statement of Vṛddhagārgya. The general principle is: "By the sight of the sun, purification occurs for earth, bricks, mud, and all mechanical devices. This is the direction. In all cases, purification is indeed the word of the Brāhmaṇas, according to another Smṛti: "Whatever learned Brāhmaṇas versed in the Vedas declare, that one should respect as purity. Enough with further elaboration. Here, the original source texts are not cited for fear of excessive length; however, a few are cited for the sake of illustration. As Hārīta says: "Purification with water is appropriate for gold, silver, conch-shells, mother-of-pearl, and the like, due to their natural qualities and color. For those stained by oily substances, scrubbing with the powder of barley, wheat, black gram, peas, and lentils, and washing with water; for copper, with acid and salt; for bell-metal (*kāṃsya*), with ashes; for iron, with rubbing with stone and oil; for gems, with rubbing and scrubbing with stone; for stones that have stains, with scrubbing with sand; for wooden objects, scraping; for earthenware, heating over fire; for fruit vessels, with a cow-hair rope and water; for cotton and hemp, with alkali and hot water; for linen and silk, with *putrañjīva* and sour gruel; for skins, with *putrañjīva* and buttermilk; for silks, with the paste of *bilva* fruit and white mustard; for woolen cloth, with buttermilk, anthill earth, and mustard; for heavy woolen cloth, with rubbing using oil, flour, and fermented grain; and for all metallic objects that are excessively defiled, purification is by fire. There is renunciation of earth, wood, and leather [if heavily defiled]. Some say there is only the cutting off of that specific part in the case of clothes, or rather not, because of their common use. 'Clothing is for common use,' say the Teachers. Therefore, the purification of all clothes is only through the removal of the contamination. The purification of skins is like that of cloth. For leather bags, dyeing; for products of the cow, such as milk, by means of fire; for purchased items, by circling with fire and sprinkling; for curds and the like, by sprinkling; for rice, by circling with fire and threshing; for barley and wheat, by sprinkling; for husked grain, by winnowing; for pulses, by rubbing, splitting, and grinding; for vegetables, roots, and fruits growing on the ground, by winnowing and washing; for those not growing on the ground, by picking them up; for stalks of sugarcane, by cutting and washing; for sacrificial liquids and oblations, by their own prescribed rules; for *sruva* ladles, by hot water; and for *caru* pots, by cooking. For oily substances mixed with salt, and for grass and wood touched by outcastes (*pulkasas*) and the like, purification is by the sight of the sun. Likewise for bricks that have been broken into pieces. And in cases of touching, smelling an unpleasant odor, hearing, seeing, or mentioning [impurity], and when food is defiled by hair, ants, and the like, it becomes pure by being touched with water and any one of the following: gold, silver, ashes, copper, diamond, lapis lazuli, cow-hair, skins, or Darbha grass.
