Purification occurs through mantra-sprinkling, circling with fire, and the sight of the sun when large quantities of food are defiled, or by the permission of Brāhmaṇas. Or, having removed only that portion and having had it smelled by a goat, it becomes pure. In cases of extreme defilement, there is renunciation, as is the case for liquid substances. Water on the ground is pure, except where there has been the arrival of something inauspicious. To this effect there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: 'The speech of the gods departed,' and so forth. Furthermore, they cite here:"
"But if even one of the purified vessels is damaged, that purification applies only to that vessel and by no means to the others.
A calf is pure when it sheds its urine; a dog is pure when it catches game.
All mines are pure, as is the *śakuni* bird when it has shaken down fruit.
Likewise: "By the treading upon them by cows, by burning, by digging, and by being rained upon..."
"By sweeping, by smearing, and with the passage of time, the ground is purified by these means.
Furthermore, ground defiled by a *caṇḍāla* does not produce a state of ritual impurity (*aprāyatya*) requiring a bath; for it has been said:
"Flies, droplets, women, the earth, water, and fire [are naturally pure]."
A cat, a ladle, and the wind are always pure;
just as a torrent of impurity flowing through a river acquires the qualities of that river and becomes endowed with those very qualities.

"Likewise, food and drink that has arrived according to the prescribed rule does not become defiled when it has been passed through the vessel of a twice-born person. Other Smṛti texts may be cited and analyzed in this manner; enough of this digression.
I have here provided this purification of the meaning of the words,
for it is generally intended for the benefit of the world;
therefore, it should be accepted as a path worthy of faith.
It is to be elaborated upon by many wise men. || 195 ||
Thus ends the section on the purification of substances. Now begins the section on giving. [Objection:

But surely this purification has been described as pertaining only to a limited number of substances, whereas its scope is infinite. How, then, is it to be understood when not explicitly stated? [Response: This has indeed been stated in the verse concerning the assembly (*pariṣad*): "Whatever even a single Brāhmaṇa who knows the inner self (*adhyātma*) may say, that is in every way the Dharma, free from doubt" (cf. Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.9). Moreover:
Having performed austerities, Brahmā created the Brāhmaṇas for the protection of the Vedas,
for the satisfaction of the ancestors and the gods, and for the preservation of dharma.

In this way, there is both the protection of the Veda and the preservation of the Dharma, provided that one understands the meaning of the Veda in its entirety. Furthermore, the statement regarding creation and so forth is intended to show that the capacity of the effect exceeds [the capacity of] the cause. || 196 ||
But even so, one might object that a Brāhmaṇa who has merely acquired knowledge might not necessarily speak [the truth]; therefore, he says:
"Brāhmaṇas who are devoted to sacred learning and study are the source of all;
among them, those devoted to ritual action are superior, and among them, those who contemplate the supreme self (adhyātma) are indeed the best. (1.197)

The Brahmins are the masters of the entire world; and they are masters only by means of instructing in the Dharma, and not otherwise. Thus Manu says: "A Brahmin should know the means of livelihood for all according to the rule, and he should proclaim them to others, and he himself should likewise abide by them" (MDh 10.2).

Is this greatness [of theirs] due to birth alone? No, it is said; it belongs only to those who are devoted to sacred learning and study, because others do not possess the status of instructors. That they are "devoted to ritual action" and so forth has already been explained in the verse concerning those worthy of honor (mānya). || 117 ||
And why is there such progressive excellence? Because:
"Neither by knowledge alone nor even by austerity is one a worthy recipient; where conduct and both of these exist, that indeed is proclaimed a worthy recipient. (1.198)

And here, by the word *tapaḥ* (austerity), it is specifically *jāti* (birth) that is intended, following the context of the creation [of the four varṇas]; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even Kṣatriyas and others would be worthy of honor. Therefore, where learning (*vidyā*), austerity (*tapaḥ*), and conduct (*vṛtta*)—that is, practice—are present, that is the "worthy recipient" (*pātra*) for the means such as giving. And since all of that [learning, austerity, and conduct] exists in the knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*), along with the excellence of qualities such as dispassion (*vairāgya*), therefore he alone possesses the highest excellence in every respect. Alternatively, the word *tapaḥ* may be used in its primary sense [of asceticism]. The mention of *jāti* [as birth] follows from the word "and" (*ca*) and from the introductory context. || 198 ||
And because such a brahmin is a vessel for the world by virtue of being its protector, therefore:
"Cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and so forth should be given with honor to a worthy recipient;
nothing at all should be given to an unworthy recipient by a wise person desiring his own welfare. (1.199)

"To a worthy recipient" means: one should give everything that has been honored [with respect]. And it is said: "He who would accept what has been honored... (MDh 4.235). However, if the recipient is not worthy, one who desires his own welfare should not give anything at all; by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," this includes even food and other such things. Furthermore, those who know the supreme self (*adhyātmavid*) certainly do accept food and so forth; therefore, their status as recipients (*saṃpradāna*) is established. Now, an objection is raised: a Brāhmaṇa should not be examined, because it is heard in scripture that examining him constitutes a sale of the Veda; and since knowledge cannot otherwise arise, how can there be an understanding of who is a worthy recipient? It is replied: in this matter, the means is purely worldly. 199.
Furthermore, if he were to accept it, even the consideration of its faults would result in his own downfall; for him, there is simply no qualification [to receive gifts]. Why? Because:
"A gift must not be accepted by one who is deficient in learning and austerity.
For this reason:
By accepting it, he leads both the giver and himself downward. || 1.200 ||
The word "tu" (but) has the sense of restriction; the rest is clear. || 200 ||
And because it is so, therefore:
One should give every day to a worthy recipient, especially on auspicious occasions;
even when asked, one should give according to one's ability, purified by faith. (1.201)

Every day, one should bring unasked-for food and give it in a worthy vessel. Thus says the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "Day by day one should give, beginning with a vessel of water," and so forth (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 11.5.6.2). Likewise, [the text] "Taking gold, he approaches the *Āgnīdhra* priest" shows that the gift is brought forward. Similarly, beginning with "He who is indeed known and of a known lineage is one who has a father and is descended from his forefathers," it concludes, "He who gives even a few sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to one who is known, by those he conquers greatness"—this shows that the giving is specifically for a worthy recipient (*pātra*). On special occasions such as eclipses of the planets and so forth, one should especially give more abundantly, and this too without being asked. Furthermore, one must give even when requested by the ten types of *snātakas*, beginning with those seeking offspring (*sāṃtānika*). One should not show contempt simply because they have asked; rather, one should give with respect, purified by faith (*śraddhā*), according to one's capacity, in accordance with one's own wealth, and in accordance with the qualities of the recipient. Thus Manu says: "One should know these ten to be *snātakas*" (*Mānava Dharma Śāstra* 11.2). || 201 ||
The gift of cows and other animals has been mentioned; he now describes the details of that procedure:

"A milch cow, with horns adorned with gold, hooves with silver, well-behaved, covered with cloth, accompanied by a bronze milking vessel, and provided with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), should be given. (1.202)
A gift that is honored is a "gift with honor" (sadakṣiṇā). From the word *dakṣiṇā*, it follows that a great abundance of gold should be provided. || 202 ||
And this is not the only way of giving gifts. What then?
"The giver of this [cow] attains heaven for as many years as there are hairs on her body;
if she is a Kapila cow, she delivers even further, up to the seventh generation of his lineage. (1.203)

When given according to this very procedure, especially [on specific occasions], this same method applies even to the daily (nitya) rite, because no other has been taught and because it is required. This should be applied similarly elsewhere as well. Alternatively, regarding what was stated—that it is "especially" for the occasional rites (*naimittika*)—this is the specific detail that has been declared. However, it should be understood that for the daily rite, one should give with due respect as is appropriate. || 203 ||
Or one that is not tawny;
by giving a cow with her calf and a bronze vessel as large as its hair, according to the aforementioned ritual, the donor attains heaven. 1.204.

For as many hairs as there are on the calf, for that many *yugas*—that is, years—he who gives [the cow] attains heaven; this is to be construed with the phrase "giving, the donor attains heaven. Furthermore, the wording of the mantra is: "O Aditi, you are two-headed" (*aditir asy ubhayataḥ śīrṣṇī*, TS 1.2.4.2). [The cow is] "two-faced," meaning she is about to give birth and has already delivered her calf. [She is given] according to the previously mentioned procedure regarding the golden horns and so forth (YDh 1.202). || 204 ||

Thus far, the specific manner [of giving] has been described. Even in the absence of that, by giving a cow in any way whatsoever—whether it be a milch cow or even one that does not yield milk—the donor shall attain heaven, provided the animal is healthy and not afflicted. (1.205)
The meaning of this verse is clear. || 205 ||

But for one who does not even possess a single cow, [the following acts] are equal to the gift of a cow: massaging the weary, attending to the sick, worshiping the gods, washing the feet of the twice-born, and clearing away the remnants of their meal. (1.206)
The verse has been stated [in prose] above. || 206 ||
And indeed, according to what is possible, by giving land, cattle, food, clothing, water, sesame seeds, clarified butter, shelter,
a dwelling, gold, or a draft animal, one is glorified in heaven. (1.207)
A *naiveśika* is wealth or a daughter for the purpose of marriage. A *dhurya* is a draft ox. The rest is straightforward. 207.
And indeed, in accordance with one's wealth:
by giving a house, grain, fearlessness, sandals, an umbrella, garlands, ointments, a vehicle, a tree, water, or a bed, one becomes supremely happy. (1.208)

A *yāna* is a cart and so forth. Water suitable for watering trees is *vṛkṣajala*. The rest is clear. In this entire section, the determination of the specific excellence of the fruit is based on the wealth of the donor. As it has been said: "This sacrifice is not equal to a measure (*prastha*) of barley-meal. And the traditional teaching (*āmnāya*) has indeed been stated: "He who, even though possessing [wealth], gives only a few... and so forth (cf. Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.201 comm.). Furthermore, the excess resulting from external wealth pertains to the purpose of [protecting] Brāhmaṇas and others through the gift of fearlessness by staking one's own life. And the traditional teaching: "Therefore, even if one should lose everything in a total ruin, as long as he lives himself, they say there is no destruction [of his merit]" (?)—this shows the secondary importance of wealth. Thus, in all cases, the distinction is to be determined. 208.
Thus far, the duty of giving common to all has been described for one who possesses wealth. But as for the wise Brāhmaṇa—for him, the Brahman consisting of all dharmas is superior to all other gifts;
by bestowing that, he attains the world of Brahman, never to fall away. (1.209)
The meaning of this verse is clear. || 209 ||
And this being so:
"Even though he is capable of receiving gifts, he who does not accept them attains those abundant worlds that belong to those whose nature is generosity. (1.210)
The meaning is: "by the very act of bestowing [it upon a worthy recipient]. Therefore, one should accept [a gift] thinking, "I shall not give it away. Thus say the worldly wise:
"For it is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off. From this, it should be understood that the renunciation of accepting gifts is indeed superior. || 210 ||

And even when one has turned away [from accepting gifts], the following should not be refused: *kuśa* grass, vegetables, milk, fish, perfumes, flowers, curd, earth, meat, a bed, a seat, grain, and water. (1.211)
The verse has been stated [as follows]: || 211 ||
Thus, it is established that vegetables and the like are not to be rejected; the same applies to gold and other such things.
Even that which is brought unasked may be accepted from one of evil deeds, except in the case of an unchaste woman, a eunuch, an outcast, or an enemy. (1.212)

A *kulaṭā* is one who wanders among families; she is an unchaste woman. By the word *tathā* ("likewise"), the hateful person is also included, or else it refers to those types of persons from whom gifts should not be accepted. Similarly, others such as Śūdras and the like, who resemble eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍa*) and are disqualified [from Vedic rites], are also meant. As for the statement of Gautama: "And by that [gift], his subsequent accumulation is for that purpose" (GDh 10.62–63), that should be understood as referring to a Śūdra who has taken refuge [in the Vedic path]. Even for these [Śūdras], there is the authority to accumulate wealth beyond what is necessary for their livelihood, solely for the purpose of giving. It should be understood that this very point is expressed by the phrase "his accumulation is for that purpose. || 212 ||
Thus, the acceptance of what is brought unasked has been explained. But even after asking:
"For the sake of honoring guests with liquor, for the sake of serving one's teacher, and indeed for the sake of one's own subsistence, one may accept from anyone. (1.213)

The word "all" (*sarva*) here should be understood as referring to unchaste women and others, following from the preceding verse. As for the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "One who wishes to support his wife for the sake of his teacher, or who desires to honor the gods and guests, may accept gifts from anyone; however, he himself should not satisfy his own needs with them" (VaDh 14.13).

Thus, this is for the purpose of providing an exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding unchaste women and others. And so it is stated in that very same work: "One may accept water and other such things even from these" (VaDh 14.12). By this pronoun (*etad*), these very individuals are referred to. Furthermore, the distinction must be elaborated that this is for the sake of preserving one's life, and not for the sake of enjoyment, and so forth. || 213 ||
Thus ends the section on giving.
Now begins the section on ancestral rites (*śrāddha*).
Giving has been specifically described in relation to various occasions; as to what those occasions are, he says:

The new moon day, the Aṣṭakās, the occasion of prosperity, the dark fortnight, the two solstices, the abundance of materials and Brahmins, the equinoxes, and the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign. (1.214)
The Vyatīpāta yoga, the Gajacchāyā, the eclipses of the moon and the sun,
and a personal inclination toward performing a Śrāddha— these are proclaimed as the times for Śrāddha.

Although the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) and the *aṣṭaka* days are included within the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), they are mentioned separately out of great respect. In the same manner, the scriptural injunctions regarding the sun’s transit (*saṃkrānti*), the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), the solstices (*ayana*), and so forth, are to be applied accordingly. "Substance" (*dravya*) refers to items such as the *vārdhrāṇasa* (the meat of an animal killed by a wild beast) for the sake of the *śrāddha*, while items such as the "two-headed" cow (*ubhatomukhī*) are for the purpose of giving (*dāna*). The excellence of the Brahmins has been described and will be further discussed. The "elephant shadow" (*gajacchāyā*), however, is something distinct, occurring in proximity to the *vyatīpāta* yoga: "If the Moon is in the lunar mansion of Maghā (*pitrya*) and the Sun is in the constellation of Hasta, on the thirteenth day during the rainy season—that is the 'Elephant Shadow'."

And because of this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*): "These times for the *śrāddha* have been proclaimed. The mention of the *śrāddha* is intended to illustrate [the timing of] gifts and other such acts as well, since there is no distinction in the context. Thus they say: "A gift on the day of the new moon yields a hundredfold. These occasions are effective even when taken individually. Alternatively, the word *śrāddha* may be used in its own primary sense; this is a rule regarding its time. Because of proximity and because this very time is required for giving as well, it should be understood that the time is not contradictory, in accordance with other *smṛtis*. Regarding the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), the *śrāddha* is prescribed without qualification. As Jātūkarṇi says: "Now, the *śrāddha* is performed in the latter fortnight everywhere without distinction; or specifically in the month of Nabhasya (Bhādrapada), due to both scriptural authority and logical possibility. And the Vedic tradition clarifies this very point in passages such as: "Now, wherever the sun moves southward, it is then directed toward the ancestors," and so forth. Or rather, that [dark fortnight] is more praiseworthy. Here, its status as an occasion is universal, according to the Vedic text: "And eating every month [is prescribed]. Jātūkarṇi’s statement should also be interpreted in this same way. (214, 215)
Having thus described the perfection of time, he now speaks of the perfection of the recipient:

"One who is foremost among all the Vedas, a learned scholar (*śrotriya*), a knower of the Veda, young, a knower of the meaning of the Veda, a singer of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, and one who knows the *Trimadhu* and *Trisuparṇa* [hymns]. (1.216)

A sister’s son, a priest, a son-in-law, a person for whom one sacrifices, a father-in-law, a maternal uncle, one who has performed the three *Nāciketa* fire-sacrifices, a daughter’s son, a pupil, a relative by marriage, and a kinsman; || 1.217 ||
Brahmins who are devoted to their duties, devoted to austerity, who maintain the five fires, who observe celibacy, and who are devoted to their fathers and mothers, are the perfection of the śrāddha.

*Agrya* means one who goes at the head; *śrotriya* among all the Vedas, such as the Ṛgveda and others, means one who knows them or has mastered the Vedas (*vedapāraga*). A *vedavid* is one who has mastered a single branch (*śākhā*) of the Veda. *Yuvan* means young. A *vedārthavit* is one who knows the treatises (*śāstra*) such as Mīmāṃsā. A *jyeṣṭhasāman* is one by whom the vow (*vrata*) known as the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*—which belongs to the Chāndogya—has been performed; the same should be applied to the subsequent terms as well. A *trimadhu* is one who knows the *Atharvaṇa* [portion]. A *trisuparṇaka* is one who knows the *Bāhvṛcya*. A *svasrīya* is a sister’s son. The *ṛtvij* (priest) and others are well-known. A *trināciketa* is one who has performed the *Ādhvaryava* vow, or one who has thrice piled the sacrificial fire (*agnicayana*). A *śiṣya* is one who has been instructed; a *snātaka* is one who has completed his studies. A *saṃbandhin* is a relative such as a brother-in-law. *Bāndhavas* are maternal cousins and the like. *Karma-niṣṭhas* are those who maintain the *Agnihotra* throughout their lives. *Tapo-niṣṭhas* are lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika*), wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*), and so forth. A *pañcāgni* is an *Agnihotrī* or a forest-dweller (*vanastha*). A *brahmacārin* is a student (*upakurvāṇaka*). Those devoted to father and mother are those who are dedicated to them. The word "and" (*ca*) includes those mentioned in other Smṛtis, such as reciters of the *Smṛtidroṇa*. Because the sister’s son and others are related by kinship, and because Kṣatriyas and others have the right to perform the *Śrāddha*, when there is a possibility of including those castes, he says: "Brāhmaṇas are the perfection of the *Śrāddha*" (*śrāddhasaṃpadaḥ*). They are called *śrāddhasaṃpadaḥ* because they bring about the success of the *Śrāddha*. According to the *Bahvṛca* tradition, even those with reversed [order] are included. It should be understood that the sister’s son and others, even if they possess few virtues, are not fallen from their sacraments (*saṃskāra*). The repetition of the word "Śrāddha" is for the purpose of indicating that they are worthy recipients (*pātra*) due to the excellence of their qualities in the act of giving. (216–218)
Are all these Brāhmaṇas to be fed indiscriminately at a Śrāddha? We say: "No," because:

"One who is diseased, one with deficient or redundant limbs, one who is one-eyed, one born of a remarried woman, one who has broken his vow of chastity, a Kuṇḍa or a Golaka, one with deformed nails, and one with black teeth. (1.219)

One who teaches for wages, one who is cruel, one who defiles a maiden, one who is falsely accused, one who betrays a friend, a slanderer, a seller of Soma, and one who marries before his elder brother—these are [excluded]. (1.220)

One who abandons his mother, father, or son; one who eats from a base vessel; the son of a Śūdra woman; the husband of a woman previously married to another; a thief; and one whose actions are corrupt—these are censured.

The sick person is one overcome by an incurable disease. The *avakīrṇin* is one who has committed a breach of celibacy for which a penance has been prescribed, since he is censured specifically due to the wickedness of his action. As for the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, as Manu says: "Two types of sons, the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*, are born from the wives of others;
the *kuṇḍa* is born when the husband is alive, while the *golaka* is born when the husband is dead" (MDh 3.174).

A *parivindaka* is one who takes a wife while his elder brother remains unmarried. An abandoner of a mother is one who does so under any circumstances; an abandoner of a father or son is one who does so without cause. A *kuṇḍāśī* is one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa*, a *golaka*, or similar outcasts. A *vṛṣalātmaja* is one whose offspring is a *vṛṣala*, that is, the child of a *śūdra* woman. A *parapūrvā* is a remarried woman (*punarbhū*); her husband is a *parapūrvāpati*. A *stena* is a thief. Although the status [of these as unworthy recipients] is established by the mention of their wicked deeds, the term is stated again for the sake of specifying the various types. The rest is clear. (219–221)
Thus, on the day before, a self-possessed and pure person should invite blameless Brahmins to the meal for those of faith;
and those invited must remain restrained in mind, speech, and body. (1.222)

The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is for the sake of indicating his specific qualities; consequently, it is precisely for a visible purpose that one who possesses such qualities is invited on the day before [the sacrifice]. For others, however, there is no contradiction even in inviting them on the very day of the rite. || 222 ||

Now, on the day of the *śrāddha*, having honored those who have arrived with a welcome in the afternoon, he— holding the *pavitra* grass in his hand and after they have sipped water (*ācamana*)— should cause them to sit upon their seats. (1.223)

Because of the word "saṃ" (together), one should honor them by rising from one's seat oneself and other such acts; and because of the expression "having arrived," there is no fault even if the invitation was performed by another. "Purifying" refers to the spreading of *darbha* grass and so forth. And because of the mention of having sipped water (*ācānta*), the act of washing their feet is not to be performed by oneself. However, one should personally seat them on the seats as is appropriate, with regard for those who purify the row (*paṅktipāvana*) and others. The mention of "seats" beforehand is for the purpose of preparing the seats. Thus he says: "When the seats have been prepared, provided with *barhis* grass, according to the rule" (cf. MDh 3.208). || 223 ||
What, then, is the manner of seating? It is said:

for the rite of the gods (daiva), one should seat an even number according to one's ability, and likewise for the rite of the ancestors (pitrya), an odd number; in a secluded and pure place that slopes toward the south. (1.224)

The word "tathā" (likewise) signifies the manner [of action], such as facing the east and so forth; and "capacity" (śakti) should be understood as characterized by the absence of deficiency. || 224 ||
Restrained in mind, speech, and body, and according to their capacity and lack of deficiency,
two [seats] should be placed for the gods in the east and three for the ancestors in the north, or one for each;
the same applies to the maternal grandfathers, or the rite for the Viśvedevas may be performed as a single common offering (tantra).
And thus Manu has said:
"In the rite for the gods, he should feed two; in the rite for the ancestors, three; or one in each case.
Even if he is very wealthy, he should not be overly attached to a large number."
"Hospitality, place and time, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins—these five are destroyed by prolixity; therefore, one should avoid it. (MDh 3.125–26).

Having thus prescribed the ritual for the ancestors (*pitrya*) up to the point of seating, he extends [the rule] by stating: "In the same way, all [details] such as the time and so forth must be accomplished for the maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*s). Consequently, since the possibility of performing nothing at all might arise, an exception is made based on one's capacity: "Or one may perform the *vaiśvadevika* rite as a single performance (*tantra*). The word "or" (*vā*) also serves to indicate an alternative procedure, according to another *smṛti*:
When there is only one Brahmin and no second is found,
having appointed him for the sake of the ancestors, one should appoint the fire for the sake of the gods.
The second [verse]: "If one should feed only a single person at a śrāddha, how should the rite for the gods (daiva) be performed?
Having set aside a portion of food from all that has been prepared into a vessel..."
"Having placed [the offerings] in a temple of the deities, one should then perform the *śrāddha*;
one should cast that food and other offerings into the fire, or give them to a celibate student (*brahmacārin*). Thus it is said.

Now, this is considered here: what is this that is called *śrāddha*, and who has the authority (*adhikāra*) for it? In this context, although the word *śrāddha* is etymological (*yaugika*), it is not an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*). This is because faith (*śraddhā*) is already established through other means, as stated in the verse: "But [one should give] purified by faith according to one's ability" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.202). Furthermore, since the term is already in common usage, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) due to the inference of its etymology. Therefore, it is established that this is simply a name, like the *agnihotra* and other such rites. And that [name] applies specifically to the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍadāna*), not to the feeding of Brahmins and so forth, based on the Vedic scripture: "That which he bestows upon the ancestors" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.16). "Bestowing" (*niparaṇa*) is indeed the offering of the rice-balls, not the feeding of Brahmins and so forth, in accordance with the observation of usage in passages such as "He should bestow upon all" (*sarvebhya eva nipṛṇīyāt*). Objection: But usage such as "Devadatta is a *śrāddha*-eater" is also observed. True; however, that is merely figurative (*aupacārika*). If one asks how this distinction is made, it is by the principle: "Or rather, those established in the scriptures [are authoritative], because they are based on that" (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.3.9), and because we observe its usage in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*. As Jaimini said: "If it is argued that it is like the *śrāddha*" (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 6.8.16). Moreover, it is not perceived in the daily feeding of Brahmins for the ancestors when no rice-balls are offered; and from the statement "One should give the rice-ball, one should take the wealth," we see that the connection with the ancestors belongs to the offering of the rice-balls alone. Usages such as "If one should feed only one at a *śrāddha*" are to be understood as being based solely on the purpose of that [offering]. Vyāsa also indicates that the rice-ball is primary, because he mentions the rising of the ancestors' hands specifically during the offering of the rice-balls. Thus, by virtue of the Vedic scripture and in accordance with other Smṛtis, the status of being a *śrāddha* is established for the offering of the rice-balls alone. The purpose of this deliberation is so that, in the absence of the aforementioned Brahmins, the performance may proceed with the rice-balls alone. Where, then, is this offering of the rice-balls to be included—among sacrifices (*yāga*) and the rest? Some say it is not included in any of them. Others hold that this is a distinct activity called "bestowing" (*niparaṇa*), characterized as a renunciation (*utsarga*). It can indeed be called a "gift" (*dāna*), because it culminates in the transfer of ownership to another. For in the original injunction, the ancestors are indeed the recipients (*saṃpradāna*), as seen in "one should give to the ancestors" and "one should give the rice-ball. Objection: But here the meaning of "giving" is untenable, because a relationship of ownership residing in the ancestors is impossible, and because the qualification belongs to one whose father is deceased (*preta*). As Kātyāyana says: "He gives to the deceased" (Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra 4.1.23); and Manu likewise.

"However, if one's father has passed away, but the grandfather is still living," and so forth—by such passages, [the texts] show that the offering is indeed for the deceased (*preta*s). This is true. We shall explain later how even the *preta*s can function as the recipients (*saṃpradāna*). But how are these very statements [to be understood]?
"While the father is still living, one should offer to the ancestors alone."
Or else, at a śrāddha ceremony, one may cause even a brahmin to partake as one's own father.
"But if one's father has passed away, yet his grandfather is still living, he should pronounce his father's name and then proclaim the name of his great-grandfather. (MDh 3.220–221)

Likewise, there is this other [text]: "If father and son should both be maintainers of the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), the son should give to those same [ancestors] to whom the father gives. Some say that because of the contradiction, these [other rules] are to be disregarded; for such is the Vedic tradition (*āmnāya*): "So-and-so, this is for you" (ŚB 2.4.2.19), and likewise, "for the father of the sacrificer," and so forth (ŚB 2.4.2.19). Having considered this very point, Kātyāyana says: "But [the offerings] beginning with the father are obligatory" (KātŚr 4.1.27). Furthermore, the eligibility for others [is established] by direct scriptural statement (*vacana*). And the citation of the Vedic tradition, "one does not give beyond one who is living" (KātŚr 4.1.27), is made with reference to one whose father and others are still living. Or else, these [rules] pertain to the *śrāddha* performed for the sake of the student's return home (*samāvartana*) by one whose father is living. This applies to him as well.

"One should not perform Vedic rites without having offered the Śrāddha to the ancestors"—since this [rule] applies specifically to one who lacks the sacred fires (*anagnika*), it follows by implication that he indeed has the entitlement to perform the Śrāddha. If it is asked, "What is the reason for this distinction?"—the answer is that one who possesses the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) but whose father is still living has no entitlement to the Śrāddha because he lacks entitlement to the Piṇḍapitṛyajña; for it is said: "One should perform the monthly and subsequent Śrāddha, which is the *Piṇḍānvāhāryaka*. (MDh 3.122)

Because it is stated [in the scriptures] that this is an ancillary (*aṅga*). If that is so, then let it also apply to the *śrāddha* rites performed on the first day of the waning moon (*aparapakṣa*) and so forth. No; because those are modifications of the *pārvaṇa* rite, and because that [the *pārvaṇa*] has the deceased as its object, and because a modification (*vikṛti*) is to be performed according to the model of the archetype (*prakṛti*). If that is the case, then the same principle would apply to the *samāvartana* ceremony as well. True; however, the statement that it applies to that [ceremony] is made out of a desire to avoid its being purposeless. Since the avoidance of purposelessness is achieved by that much alone, there is no over-extension [of the rule]. Furthermore, even in the absence of the sacred fires (*agni*), the ritual procedure for the fire-offering (*agnaukaraṇa*) belongs to that [deceased] alone, by virtue of the inherent capacity [of the rite].
"But in the absence of fire, one should place [the offering] directly into the hand of a Brahmin" (MDh 3.212).

On account of this general principle, it is appropriate that other similar cases also belong to that same category. Thus far, the determination of the scope has been stated. However, this [verse] appears to be intended by the Blessed One as a *pūrvapakṣa* (an opponent's view). For how could the Blessed One have failed to consider the direct Vedic scriptures? And so he said: "Or rather, the Grandfather (Brahmā) should eat that *śrāddha*," thus spoke Manu.
Or, with their permission, he may perform it himself at his own will. (MDh 3.222)

This is its meaning: Manu stated the passage beginning with "But while the father is living" (MDh 3.220) and ending with the word *iti* (cf. MDh 3.286), but he did not himself perform it. Rather, having been permitted by that very same learned grandfather—who, having reflected upon the meaning of the scripture, deemed it appropriate—he should have performed what was fitting by himself. Thus, even the Vedic tradition (*āmnāya*) shows that what is merely stated but not performed is indeed something not to be done, as in: "The virtuous indeed engaged only in inquiry; they did not perform what he had done. The intention is that authority (*prāmāṇya*) consists only in performance, not in mere verbal statement. As for the rule, "If both father and son should be maintainers of the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*)," that must be understood as referring to the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) during a sacrifice (*kratu*), because of the mention of the *āhitāgni*. And thus, for that specific purpose, there is the traditional legal text (*smaraṇa*) of the ritualists: "To those very ones to whom the father would give, so also the son" (cf. Haradatta on ĀpG 8.21.4). Therefore, for one whose father is living, even the *āvasathya* fire and other rites are to be devoid of the *śrāddha*; enough of this digression. However, regarding the bath of initiation (*snāna*) and marriage, the established tradition (*saṃpradāya*) is that even for one whose father is living, the performance of the *śrāddha* occurs just as it does for the father.

It is established that the *piṇḍadāna* is the *śrāddha*. However, the qualification [for its performance] must be stated. Now, it has been said that one who possesses the sacred fires (*agnimān*) and whose father is deceased is qualified for the *śrāddha*. If this were so, then the case of one whose father has committed suicide would also follow as a possibility; yet that is incorrect. As Manu says:

"For those born of illicit unions or of mixed castes, for those who persist in wandering asceticism (*pravrajyā*), and for those who have abandoned their own lives, the water-rites (*udakakriyā*) shall be withheld. (MDh 5.89)

Thus, because the performance of water-libations (*udakakriyā*) for those of this class [of deceased persons] is prohibited in all such *smṛti* texts, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is precluded. Consequently, due to the absence of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, there is no entitlement to perform the *śrāddha*. To this it is replied: The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is not the cause (*nimitta*) for the *śrāddha*; rather, it is the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and other such times. [Objection: But the time is prescribed for one who is entitled to the *amāvāsyā* rite; however, the entitlement to the *śrāddha* belongs only to one whose father has undergone *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Otherwise, it would follow that the *śrāddha* must be performed even prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. [Reply: Let it follow so, if you say. No, because of the prohibition. As Manu says: *(Manu 3.247–248)* "Until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is performed, one should offer the *piṇḍas* separately for each individual. Once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, one should offer them together with the ancestors. And: *(Manu 3.250)* "One should not perform the *śrāddha* for a single person alone; one should always perform it for three generations, or for four, including the father. Therefore, the *śrāddha* is indeed performed before the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. However, because of the prohibition against water-libations, the *ekoddiṣṭa* is excluded. And since the *ekoddiṣṭa* is excluded, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*—which is dependent upon it—is also absent. Thus, there is no entitlement to the *śrāddha*. This is the conclusion.

"But for a twice-born person who has died, until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has been performed, one should offer a *śrāddha* without [an offering to] the gods, feed [the guests], and present a single *piṇḍa*. (MDh 3.247)

But is not the *ekoddiṣṭa* also indeed a *śrāddha*? True; however, we have stated that one lacks the entitlement to perform the *pārvaṇa*. If that is so, does the other [the *ekoddiṣṭa*] not also belong to one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*)? It does belong to him, but not for one whose father has not yet been made a *sapiṇḍa*. The distinction is that the *ekoddiṣṭa* belongs to him even in that case. Therefore, there is no entitlement to the *śrāddha* in the absence of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Others, however, having derived it from some source, recite this verse:
"For twice-born men such as those who are outcasts (*patita*), for whom the ritual of water-libations is forbidden..."
"After one year has passed, one should perform all the funeral rites for the deceased. Thus [it is said].

However, this [objection] is to be investigated because its basis is unclear. On this point we say: Manu and others have prohibited only the *pretakriyā* (the rites for the deceased); they have not prohibited the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to perform the *śrāddha*. If it is argued that [the son-in-law has no entitlement] because of the absence of *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, we say no, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For when, by chance, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has not been performed, there would likewise be no entitlement [to the *śrāddha*]. Furthermore, the performance of *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* after one year is untenable, as there is no scriptural injunction for it. In this regard, the following might be thought: either that rite must be performed out of season, or else entitlement [to the *śrāddha*] must be stated to exist even in its absence. Now, if the performance of a rite whose time has passed is to be done by everyone without distinction—since it is prompted by the *śrāddha* itself, just like the invitation of Brahmins—then its being a cause for lack of entitlement is indeed established, since it is observed that [the *śrāddha* occurs] even in the absence of that [rite]. Furthermore, a daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) does not perform *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for his maternal grandfathers, yet he does perform the *śrāddha*. But surely, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the mother is desired to be performed together with her own maternal grandfather; so how can it be said that the daughter’s son does not perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*? In the procedure for *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, beginning with the statement "there are four vessels," it is said: "three for the ancestors (*pitṛs*), one for the deceased (*preta*). The connection there is between the deceased and the three ancestors, not between the entitled person and the ancestors; this would be consistent. And the maternal grandfathers are indeed the "ancestors" (*pitaraḥ*) of the mother. Therefore, it is logical that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be performed with them alone.

To this it is replied: This might be so if the term *pretasya* were a qualifier of the ancestors (*pitṛ*). However, since *pretasya* is heard in connection with the vessel (*pātra*), it is not capable of being understood as a qualifier of the ancestors. Therefore, the phrase "of the ancestors" (*pitṝṇām*) must be construed as referring to those [sons] who are entitled [to perform the rite]. Furthermore, if the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* were performed together with the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*), it would be entirely purposeless. For first of all, the descendants of the maternal grandfather’s lineage would not offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) for her, because there is no scriptural instruction to that effect. Nor would the descendants of the person entitled [to perform the rite] do so, because they have absolutely no connection with the maternal grandfather to whom the entitlement belongs. Thus, it is established that the daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) does not perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the maternal grandfathers. Nor do those who have been made *sapiṇḍa* by one person become *sapiṇḍa* through another. Now, one might argue that since the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is a post-mortem sacrament (*saṃskāra*), it benefits everyone once performed by anyone. This is not so. For this rite is a benefit to the deceased, not a sacrament; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to postulate an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Its status as a benefit is established like other *śrāddhas*, and its exclusion from the list of sacraments, as well as the absence of explicit scriptural statement to that effect, confirms this. If this were the case, every son would have the entitlement, as there is no distinction between them; thus, the instruction based on the mere existence of a son would not be restricted. Therefore, the entitlement of one person is not established by the act of another. Consequently, the superior view is that the entitlement exists even in his absence. Moreover, the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) by sapindas and others is prescribed in the event of the absence of a son. That would be impossible if the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* had already taken place. Therefore, they do not perform that either, because it is impossible for one who has no son. As Pāraskara says: "In the performance of the rice-balls, the deceased of the ancestors shall be the first, provided he has a son" (PārG 3.10.50). For them, there is only an injunction for the *śrāddha* alone, not an injunction for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Furthermore, there is the offering of a rice-ball to the mother together with the maternal grandfathers; yet the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is not applicable there. Therefore, it is established that even upon the cessation of that [son], the entitlement does not cease. It should be understood that the statements of Manu and others find their fulfillment solely in the prohibition of the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, and do not serve as a counter-argument to the *śrāddha*. In this way, the direct Vedic text regarding the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* remains unobstructed; otherwise, it would be sublated by the conflict with the Smṛti, which would be improper. Thus, the proof of what was stated is established. When, however, the verse beginning with "those for whom the water-rite is prohibited" (*niṣiddhodakakalpānām*) is taken as authoritative, then let the performance be according to that. In any case, the rule regarding the existence of the *śrāddha* remains. As for what was said—"the rite of non-*sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*" (MDh 3.247)—that should be understood as applying prior to a year. After that, however, the *śrāddha* proceeds even for one who has not been made *sapiṇḍa*. Why is this? Because the instruction "or when a prosperity (*vṛddhi*) occurs" applies specifically before the year; the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is not an integral part (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha*, as there is no evidence for it. How, then, is it known that this rule applies only before the year and not after? From the conformity with other Smṛtis. As Pāraskara says: "For one year, separately, one [ball]" (PārG 3.10.52). And where even the attainment of a year is doubtful, how can there be such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? Kātyāyana also, by using the word "full" (*pūrṇe*) in "when the year is full," indicates that it is not after that. Otherwise, since "year" (*saṃvatsare*) would suffice, the word "full" would be redundant. Therefore, since the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is impossible after a year, the statement "the rite of non-*sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*" (MDh 3.247) is intended to prohibit the *śrāddha* only prior to the year. Thus, the argument is faultless.

This, however, must be considered: should one who does not maintain a sacred fire (*anagnika*) perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, or only one who maintains a sacred fire (*sāgnika*)? It is logical that it is the latter, because for the former, the performance of all constituent parts of the rite is impossible. For him, there is no offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), nor is the oblation pertaining to the sacrifice to the ancestors (*paitṛyajñika-homa*) prescribed in a common (*laukika*) fire. (MDh 3.282)

Because of this statement, it is understood from this very fact that since the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire) is absent, even one who maintains no sacred fires (*anagnika*) may perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite. This being the case, we reply: the entitlement (*adhikāra*) applies without distinction. Otherwise, the instruction regarding the year (*saṃvatsara*) would indeed be purposeless. First, he who possesses the sacred fires performs [the rites] beforehand. But if one who maintains no fires were to perform them after establishing the fires (*ādhāna*), then, because he lacks entitlement to the preceding *śrāddhas*, he must perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* itself. If, however, out of fear of deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) he does not perform it, then—since one whose father has not yet been *sapiṇḍīkṛta* lacks entitlement to the *śrāddhas* for a year, and since the domestic fire (*āvasathya*) depends on those [rites]—the rule regarding the establishment of the fire would be impossible. Therefore, even for one who maintains no fires, there is entitlement to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Now, why does a religious student (*brahmacārin*) not likewise perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*? Because there is no instruction to that effect. For only the *ekoddiṣṭa* is prescribed for him, and not the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and so forth, since only the funeral rites (*śavakarman*) are permitted for him. Thus, there is no contradiction. But why is it that for one who establishes the domestic fire on the eleventh day after the father's death, the performance of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* does not necessarily precede it? Because of an exception (*apavāda*) by another scriptural statement. As Yama says:
"The rite should be performed on the anniversary of death every month for a year, and likewise annually; however, the first [rite] is performed on the eleventh day."

This is precisely the purpose of the statement regarding the first [rite]. Consequently, it is established that for him as well—just like one whose father is living—the establishment of the domestic fire (*āvasathyādhāna*) is devoid of the *śrāddha*. Now this must be considered: when one performs this *mātāmaha-śrāddha*, is it only then that it is performed in this manner, or should it also be performed thus as a regular (*nitya*) obligation? Since an extension (*atideśa*) is applicable in both ways, a doubt arises. When the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached that "it is only when one performs it that it is done thus," it is replied: because there is no other injunction and because this [text] is non-specific, it is a regular obligation. Objection: In that case, the praise of the son would be inappropriate, for if the daughter's son (*dauhitra*) were to perform the *śrāddha* just as the son does. Reply: It is not so. The praise is with respect to the daughter, not even with respect to the daughter's son, because she herself is not entitled to perform the *śrāddha* for her own father; and because she performs the *śrāddha* for her father-in-law together with her husband. However, there is no distinction between the daughter's son and the grandson. Objection: Why then is he not the inheritor of the estate (*rikthagrāhin*)? Reply: We shall state the specific rule regarding the division of the inheritance later on. But in the case of sons such as the adopted (*dattaka*), because of their primary status, the performance of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and other rites must be done for the biological progenitor alone; for the other [the adoptive father], only the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is required. Now, is this *śrāddha* a single one with two deities, or are there two separate ones? When the lack of a restrictive rule is reached, we say there are two. For this is the very injunction: "The *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfathers is separate from that of the paternal ancestors, and likewise for the maternal grandfathers. In that context, the meaning is simply that "one should also perform the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfathers," and not that there is a non-distinction between the *śrāddhas*. Moreover, the rule "or the *vaiśvadeva* portion is common (*tantra*)" (YDh 1.227) would be applicable only if a distinction were possible; otherwise, the commonality would be inherent by nature, rendering the instruction useless. Objection: But a single *śrāddha* is also observed: "One should perform the *śrāddha* for the mother and the maternal grandmother together with the paternal ancestors. Reply: That refers to the *tarpaṇa* (libation), not to the *śrāddha*. For it is said: "The *tarpaṇa* for the mother is performed together with the paternal ancestors. Furthermore, the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather is performed separately from the *śrāddha* for the paternal ancestors, as stated: "The *śrāddha* for the paternal ancestors is performed on the new moon day, and the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather is performed separately. Therefore, it is established that the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather is indeed distinct. Thus ends the section on the *mātāmaha-śrāddha*. Now follows the section on the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Regarding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of one who has died childless: "If a man dies childless, his brother, or his brother's son, or a *sapiṇḍa*, or a *gotraja*, or a *bandhu*, or a *samānodaka*, or a *mātṛ-bandhu*, or a *mātula*, or a *mātāmaha*, or a *pitṛ-vyasana* (paternal relative), or a *jāmātṛ* (son-in-law), or a *śiṣya* (disciple), or a *ṛtvij* (priest)—any one of these, having bathed and purified himself, should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* after having fed Brāhmaṇas. Here, the term "childless" (*anapatya*) means one who has neither a son nor a wife pregnant with a son. The mention of the "brother" is illustrative (*pradarśana*); the sense is that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be performed by anyone among those previously mentioned, starting with the brother. The phrase "having bathed and purified himself" indicates that the performer should bathe and perform the *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water). The word "then" (*tataḥ*) implies that this should be done after the *ekoddiṣṭa* has been performed. The word "Brāhmaṇas" is used in the plural to indicate that at least three should be fed. The word "having fed" (*bhojayitvā*) implies that they should be fed with food accompanied by meat, as the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is a *pariṣecana* (concluding rite) involving meat. The word "purified" (*śuciḥ*) means that the performer should be free from impurity (*aśauca*). The word "should perform" (*kuryāt*) means that he should carry out the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite. "Likewise, one should offer water for rinsing the mouth to the maternal grandfathers as well. (YDh 1.240). This is indeed seen [in the text]. However, it is obtained by implication (*arthaprāpta*), because there is no difference in place, time, and so forth. And when something is obtained by implication, it is not proper to assume a further function of the word. Therefore, it is established that there is a distinction between the *śrāddha* rites and a unity of procedure (*prayogatantratā*). The practical purpose (*prayojana*), however, is that there is no obstruction to the eligibility (*adhikāra*) of one whose father is living and whose mother is deceased.

Now, is this *mātāmaha-śrāddha* intended only for the mother, the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*), and the maternal great-grandfather (*pramātāmaha*)? Certainly; for the word *mātāmaha*, when used in the plural, is logically explained in this very way: "the mother and the two maternal grandfathers" (*mātā ca mātāmahau ca mātāmahāḥ*). But surely it could also be explained as "the maternal grandfather and the two paternal great-grandfathers" (*mātāmahaś ca pramātāmahau ca*)? Furthermore, [it is stated]: "She has entered into oneness with her husband in the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), in the lineage (*gotra*), and also during the period of impurity (*sūtaka*). Because of this difference in lineage (*anyagotratva*) from the mother, an offering together with the maternal grandfather would indeed be improper. Moreover, her *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is traditionally prescribed to be performed together with the women [of her husband's family].
"One should perform the *sapiṇḍana* with the mother by means of her husband’s lineage and name;
silently, one should separate the ancestors from the two *piṇḍas* of the couple by means of *kuśa* grass.
For this reason as well, that [offering] is not connected to the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*). Furthermore:
The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā) should first offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his mother;
the second to her father, and the third to his own paternal grandfather.

In this way, the instruction regarding the offering of the *piṇḍa* would be meaningful; otherwise, it would be purposeless since [the result] would be obtained in that very manner [by default]. Furthermore, the offering by a man and a woman together in one place is improper. Moreover, there would be a lack of consistency (*vairūpya*) in the word "maternal grandfather" (*mātāmaha*), as it would be designating both a father and a daughter. Therefore, it is proper that [the offering be made] to the maternal grandfather and the others alone.

To this it is replied: The cognition of the maternal grandfather occurs precisely through the medium of the mother, not independently of her, because the suffix is prescribed after the nominal stem *mātṛ* itself. In that case, when the word *mātāmaha* is uttered, it first causes the mother to be understood. And one must state a reason for the sublation of what has already been cognized. Nor is it proper to sublate what has been cognized on the grounds of [the requirements of] the daughter and so forth, because words are the authoritative means of knowledge (*śabdapramāṇaka*). As it is said: "For the paternal grandfathers are satisfied by what is given, even more so than by the increase of months. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.255)

Thus, the term *pitāmaha* (grandfather) includes both the father and the great-grandfather; likewise, the term *mātāmaha* (maternal grandfather) should be understood accordingly. As for the scriptural injunction that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is to be performed together with women, that is intended for the purpose of the *ānvaṣṭakya* offerings and not for the *śrāddha*, since you yourself do not accept it [as applicable here]. Furthermore, a fault that is equal for both parties should not be leveled against one alone. Moreover, since motherhood is identical for both [the father and the maternal grandfather], it would indeed be improper to say that one should not perform the *śrāddha* for the mother. And it is illogical to exclude the maternal grandfather and others who are understood through their connection [to the mother] by bypassing her, as there is no reason to bypass the first [relative] when they are equally related. As for what was said:

"The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra) should first offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his mother" (MDh 9.140)—this should be understood as intended to establish that the son of an appointed daughter possesses the status of a grandson (pautra). Thus it has been said:
"By him [the son of an appointed daughter], the maternal grandfather becomes the possessor of a grandson; he should offer the funeral cake and inherit the property" (MDh 9.136).

We shall explain the division of inheritance more thoroughly later. Therefore, it is established that the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* (ancestral rite for the maternal grandfather) begins precisely with the mother. || 225 ||
Thus, having seated the Brahmins at both Śrāddhas— either by a single performance (tantra) or by repetition—
and having given them water for washing their hands as well as Kuśa grass for seats,
he should, being permitted, invoke the Viśvedevas with the verse beginning "viśvedevāsaḥ. (1.226)

The meaning is "for the sake of the *viṣṭara* seats," that is, for the sake of the seats. Having asked the leader of the row or all of them, saying, "I shall invoke the Viśvedevas," and being permitted by them, he should mutter this *ṛc*: "O Viśvedevas, come hither" (*viśve devāsa āgatā*, RV 1.3.7). This alone is the invocation, and nothing else. || 226 ||
Then,
having scattered barley grains over a vessel containing a purifier (pavitra),
and having poured water with the verse "śaṃ no devīr," one should pour barley grains with the formula "yavo 'si. || 1.227 ||
With the mantra "yā divyā," one should pour the *arghya* offering into their hands.

The scattering [of barley] is performed by sprinkling them around [the vessel] in a clockwise direction. By the force of the word *atha* ("then"), that which is stated in other Smṛtis should be understood here as well. Having recited the mantra, "O Viśvedevas, hear this," one should place two blades of *pavitra* grass into a vessel made from a sacrificial tree or similar material, according to the injunctions of other Smṛtis, provided that such a vessel is available. Then, having poured water into it with the verse, "May the divine waters be auspicious to us" (RV 10.9.4), and having scattered barley grains with the formula, "Thou art barley; ward off [evil]" (TS 1.3.1.1), one should place the *pavitra* blades into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa and pour the *arghya* water with the verse, "That which is celestial... (TB 2.7.15.4). The mention of "in the hand" is intended to exclude [the use of] another vessel, as some other Smṛtis prescribe pouring the water through an intervening vessel. Because of the specific term *arghya*, flowers should also be added. The plural number in "in the hands" (*hasteṣu*) refers to the Brāhmaṇas [who may be more than one]; however, the *arghya* offering itself is only one. 228.
Having thus presented the *arghya*,
one should offer water, perfumes, incense, and the gift of garlands, together with lamps.

Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) and circumambulating the ancestors counter-clockwise, he should offer double-folded kuśa grass to the ancestors with the verse beginning "uśantas tvā. (1.229)
Having invoked them, he should recite the mantra "May they come to us" with their permission;
he should substitute sesame seeds for the purpose of the barley, while the remaining rites, such as the *arghya* offering and so forth, are to be performed as before.

The reversal of the order of incense (*dhūpa*) and garlands (*mālya*) is for the sake of conforming to the meter. Furthermore, from the mention of *apasavya* (leftward) and *apradakṣiṇa* (non-circumambulation), it is understood that there is a reversal in the *vaiśvadeva* rite. The word *tataḥ* signifies a reason; thus, for that reason—characterized by the citation of scriptural authority such as, “The *prācīnāvīta* [wearing mode] belongs to the ancestors; this southern direction indeed belongs to the ancestors; the ancestors face away,” and so forth—the meaning is that the practice of *apasavya* and the like is for the sake of the ancestors. Consequently, all of this is established from the very beginning for the ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*). It should be understood that in the phrase “of the ancestors” (*pitṝṇām*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the Brahmins intended for them. Although the Teacher has described the sequence according to sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*)—from the seating with *darbha* grass to the lighting of the lamp—for the sake of brevity, nevertheless, in accordance with proximity to the principal act (*pradhāna*), the sequence according to individual items (*padārthānusamaya*) is more appropriate. Therefore, in the *vaiśvadeva*, there is the seating with *darbha*; then, in the ancestral rite, the same follows. In this way, the *arghya* offering and so forth should also be applied accordingly. The preparation of the *arghya* and other offerings is according to the number of deities and so on, not according to the number of Brahmins. This is because of another Smṛti text stating, “One should prepare three *arghya* vessels for the ancestors. Thus, even if there is only one Brahmin, three *arghya* offerings must be made. And when there are many Brahmins, only a single *arghya* is to be given to all, because all the Brahmins represent the three ancestors. The rest is clear. (227–230)
But having offered the *arghya* to the ancestors and having placed their remnants in a vessel according to the rule,
he turns the vessel face down with the words "This is the seat for the ancestors. (1.231)

Having placed the remnants of these *arghya* offerings into a single vessel, he should turn that vessel face down upon the ground with the mantra: "Thou art the place for the ancestors (*pitṛbhyaḥ sthānam asi*). The long reading, "sthānam āsi," is for the sake of conforming to the meter. || 231 ||
Then,

intending to offer it in the fire, he takes up food soaked in clarified butter and asks for permission, saying, "Do so. Having been permitted with the words, "Do so," he makes an offering into the fire as in the Pitṛyajña.
With a concentrated mind, he should offer the remnants of the oblation into vessels,
especially those made of silver, as they may be obtained.

Taking food soaked in clarified butter and having asked, "Shall I offer in the fire? he should offer two oblations with a stirring-ladle (*mekṣaṇa*) as in the *pitṛyajña*, saying, "To Agni Kavyavāhana. The mention of "Agni" is so that for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), the offering may take place in the *aupāsana* fire and not in the *anvāhāryapacana*. He should pour the remainder of the offered food into the vessels of the Brahmins—preferably silver ones, which have been washed according to custom; if those are unavailable, into vessels containing silver; if even those are unavailable, into others. Others, however, explain that when a few silver vessels are available, they should be used for those who purify the row (*paṅktipāvana*), because of the word "especially" (*viśeṣataḥ*). Nevertheless, there is no fault [in this view]. And the giving of the remainder of the fire-offering (*agnaukaraṇa*) is for those invited for the ancestors, not for those invited for the *vaiśvadeva*; this is because the fire-offering is connected to the ancestral rite. The word "but" (*tu*) is for the sake of restriction. Therefore, it should be understood that the remainder must necessarily be set aside, and not that there is a gift of what remains [only] if it exists. However, because of the mention of the "remainder of the offering," its omission follows in the absence of an oblation. (232–233)
But the other [rite] is preceded by the divine [mantras].

Having offered the food, one should consecrate the vessel with the mantra, "The earth is the vessel"; then, having recited "Idam Viṣṇuḥ," one should cause the guests to place their thumbs into the food. (1.234)

The repetition of the word "food" (anna) is solely for the purpose of placing the thumb upon the remnant of the *agnaukaraṇa* offering; and because of that contact, the grasping of the vessel (*pātrālambha*) should also be understood to occur at that very point. Since there is no distinction in the substance of the gift, one should grasp the vessel after having given food to all [the ancestors]. Although one ought to say, "The earth is your vessel" (*pṛthivī te pātram*), it is stated as "The earth is the vessel" (*pṛthivī pātram*) in accordance with the requirements of the meter. || 234 ||
Having thus served the food and provided the *āpośana* water, he should then recite the *Sāvitrī* together with the *Vyāhṛtis*, and the three verses beginning with "madhu vātā.
Having caused them to say, "Eat as you please," they too should eat while remaining silent. (1.235)

By the use of the word "api" (also), it is implied that one should also personally remain restrained in speech. Regarding the matter of eating, however, it is according to one's pleasure; the meaning is that they should eat whatever they like and in whatever order suits them. || 135 ||
Now, must one eat food that is strictly undetermined? No, it is said:
"One should offer food that is desirable and fit for oblation, free from anger and without haste;
having likewise recited purifying mantras and the previously mentioned prayers until satiety. (1.236)

Because of the word *tu* (but), the recitation (*japa*) itself must be performed by [the performer] personally; however, the serving of food (*pariveṣaṇa*) is to be done by another. In this way, the duty of the wife is also fulfilled in the *śrāddha*. The mention of "food" (*anna*) is for the sake of cooked food; the word "and" (*ca*) is for the sake of roots, fruits, and so forth. "Desirable" (*iṣṭa*) means what is intended by the Brāhmaṇas or what is prescribed by the scriptures, such as *kāla-śāka* and other vegetables. The mention of "sacrificial food" (*haviṣya*) is for the purpose of excluding split pulses (*vidala*) and the like. Thus Vyāsa says: "But he who, not knowing, serves the *śrāddha* with split pulses—Rākṣasas plunder that; such is the ancient Vedic revelation."

"Bharadvāja says that one should not give split pulses (*vidala*), with the exception of black gram (*māṣa*), adzukī (*āḍhakī*), and green gram (*mudga*). The word *tathā* (likewise) is intended to include the methods of serving, eating, and reciting mentioned in other Smṛtis. And so Śaṅkha, having begun with: 'Having strewn grass-blades (*darbha*) with their tips pointing south around the fire, one should offer oblations,' continues: 'Sitting on the ground with knees bent, meditating on the ancestors in his mind, he should then, free from envy, offer abundant food as desired—sesame seeds, meats, vegetables, soups, *kṛsara*, milk-rice, cakes, parched grain, honey, ghee, curd, and milk. While the Brāhmaṇas are eating, they should not speak of merits or defects, nor touch one another, nor praise one another. They should not say 'the food and drink are abundant,' nor speak of anything unpleasant, except by means of hand gestures. As long as the food is warm, the ancestors eat it, except for roots, fruits, and drinks. With sacred grass in hand, sitting upon *darbha* blades, one should mutter the *madhuvātīya* hymns. The *pavitra* is the Dharmaśāstra," and so forth. Likewise Vyāsa says:"
"As long as they eat warm food, and as long as they eat with speech restrained, for so long do the ancestors eat, until the qualities of the oblation are mentioned.

Likewise, elsewhere: "The Rākṣoghna verses, the Pāvamānī verses, the Puruṣasūkta," and so forth. All of this should be understood as intended to complete the manner implied by the word "tathā" (thus). || 236 ||

Having thus recognized that they are satisfied, he himself should then recite the mantra previously mentioned— characterized by the *vyāhṛtis*, the *sāvitrī*, and so forth— and taking some food, he should ask, "Are you satisfied? and having obtained their consent regarding the remainder,
he should scatter that food upon the ground and offer water once for each.

Having taken food and asked the Brahmins, "Are you satisfied? and having been told by them, "We are satisfied," he should offer the remaining food to them alone and seek their permission, saying, "Let it be used as you wish"—the meaning is that he should obtain their consent. The particle *ha* is for the sake of emphasis, because another Smṛti states: "He should do exactly as they say" (MDh 3.253). Having thus obtained permission regarding the remainder, he should scatter on the ground that food which was taken up, but not upon the Darbha grass. Furthermore, he should give water to the Brahmins one by one, but not before the inquiry concerning their satisfaction; this is the meaning. || 237 ||
In this very manner, having offered water,
he should take all the food that has been prepared, along with sesame seeds, and facing south,
offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) near the remains of the meal, according to the ritual of the Pitṛyajña.

The prefix *upa* signifies the taking of portions; the meaning is "having taken portions from all the food. The phrase "like the Piṇḍapitṛyajña" is intended to include the use of a single-cut blade of grass (*sakṛdācchinna*), the sprinkling of water (*avanejana*), and other such details. However, this is the distinction: [the offering] is accompanied by sesame seeds and made near the remains of the meal. The mention of "pindas" (balls of food) is for the purpose of excluding the giving of threads (*sūtra*) and other such items. The prefix *pra-* is for the purpose of prohibiting the eating of the middle pinda. || 238 ||

Just as this offering of rice balls (piṇḍa) is made for the fathers, so too should one give it for the maternal grandfathers; thereafter, one should provide water for sipping (ācamana). Then, having caused the benediction (svasti) to be recited, one should likewise offer the water for inexhaustibility (akṣayyodaka). || 1.239 ||

Since the extension [of the rules] from the preceding case is already established, this repetition is for the purpose of ensuring that the modification (*ūha*) is performed according to the specific requirements. As for the establishment of the sequence, it follows simply from the textual recitation (*pāṭha*). Having offered water for sipping (*ācamana*) to all, one should then perform the recitation for well-being (*svastivācana*); one should cause each person to say, "Say 'May there be well-being!'"—the word "thus" (*eva*) implies that even Kṣatriyas and others should perform the recitation because of the injunction. Furthermore: "One should offer inexhaustible water mixed with sesame seeds, and one should cause them to say, 'May it be inexhaustible! (239)

Is the offering of inexhaustible water (*akṣayyodaka*) to be performed immediately after the benediction? No, it is said: having first offered the inexhaustible water, and then—having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability—one should utter the word *svadhā*. Being authorized with the words "Let it be recited," [the officiant says]: "Let the *svadhā* be uttered for the ancestors (*prakṛta*). (1.240)

The example for the utterance of *svadhā* is: "I shall cause the *svadhā* to be recited. Having been authorized by them with the words "Let it be recited," he should say, "Let the *svadhā* be uttered for the ancestral fathers (*pitṛs*) and the maternal grandfathers (*mātāmahas*) present here. (240)
Then they too should say, "Let there be *svadhā*. When this has been said, one should pour water upon the ground.
As he gives the water, he should likewise say, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased. (1.241)

By the mention of the *bhūmi* (ground), *kuśa* grass is excluded. The word "then" (*tataḥ*), however, means that one should look [at the water] after the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. And from this, it is understood that [one looks] with the mantra "ūrjaṃ vahantī" (VS 2.34). While giving water to the Brāhmaṇas who have partaken of the *vaiśvadeva* offerings, he himself says: "May the Viśvedevas be pleased. He should not cause them to recite this, because of the explicit statement "he says" (*āha*). || 241 ||
And this other [prayer]:
"May our donors increase, as well as the lineage of the Veda;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give. (1.242)
Having repeatedly spoken affectionate words and having prostrated, one should dismiss [the guests] with joy, saying "Vāja-vāja," beginning with the ancestors. 1.243.
The intention is that the dismissal alone is preceded by the ancestors, while everything else is preceded by the gods. || 242–243 ||
And he should do this:
having turned face upwards that vessel for the ancestors into which the remnants were previously placed in the *arghya* vessel, he should dismiss the Brahmins. (1.244)
The mention of the vessel for the paternal ancestors is intended to exclude the vessel for the maternal ancestors.

Having thus dismissed the Brahmins and having circumambulated them clockwise, he should eat what was consumed by the ancestors; remaining celibate and self-restrained, he should spend that night together with the twice-born.

The word *syāt* (should be) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. The mention of *pradakṣiṇa* (circumambulation) is for the purpose of excluding the counter-clockwise circumambulation (*apradakṣiṇa*) that would otherwise apply because the rite is intended for the ancestors (*pitṛ*). The phrase "he should eat what has been served by the ancestors" is intended to exclude eating elsewhere, or to preclude cooking again. Consequently, having first performed the daily rites such as the *hantakāra* offering, one should then understand that the *śrāddha* is a constant obligation. "With a restrained soul (*niyatātmā*), he should remain celibate (*brahmacārī*) with the Brahmins throughout that night. The use of the word "that" (*tām*) implies an excess of effort to ensure celibacy even during the fertile period (*ṛtu*). The particle *tu* is for the purpose of removing doubt. Furthermore, the expression "restrained soul" is intended to indicate that there is no deficiency (*avaiguṇya*) even if the Brahmins do not maintain celibacy, or it may be intended to prohibit study (*anadhyāya*). As for what was stated previously—"one who is self-possessed and pure"—that is intended to indicate that only one who is certain of the afterlife is qualified for this rite. Alternatively, it should be understood as applying to all cases without distinction. The mention of "pure" in various places is for the sake of external purity (*bāhya-śauca*). The mention of "composed" (*samāhita*) is for the sake of one-pointedness of mind. The terms "free from anger" and "not hasty" are intended to prohibit anger and other natural impulses that might arise in one who is fasting and oppressed by hunger. In this manner, other [injunctions] should also be distinguished according to their specific purpose. Furthermore, other Smṛti texts implied by the need for explanation should be cited as supporting evidence (*jñapaka*) everywhere.

"Having performed a *śrāddha*, he who, being agitated, should eat at another's *śrāddha*," and so forth. Due to the fear of excessive length, these [passages] have not been cited from the text. || 245 ||
Having introduced the *śrāddha* as being of universal application, he now states the instruction regarding its modifications:
"In this manner, having performed the circumambulation, they worship the Nāndīmukha ancestors at the rite of prosperity (*vṛddhi*);
the offerings consist of balls (*piṇḍas*) mixed with curd and jujube fruits, and the rites are performed with barley. (1.246)

Just as the *śrāddha* has been described for the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) and other such occasions, it is exactly the same for the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* (rites of prosperity) as well. However, this is the distinction: from the very beginning, one should perform the entire *śrāddha* after having circumambulated [the site] clockwise (*pradakṣiṇa*). The mention of "clockwise" is also intended to exclude the "counter-clockwise" (*apasavya*) mode and so forth. Why is this so? Because the text says, "they sacrifice" (*yajanti*). This is its meaning: here, the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) are [regarded] as deities (*devatā*), not as recipients (*saṃpradāna*). Consequently, since the ancestors also possess the status of deities, the ritual duties of the deities—such as wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavīta*) and so forth—are what apply, and not the duties pertaining to the ancestors, such as wearing the thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) and so forth. And thus says Vyāsa:
"For the gods, assuming the form of the ancestors, indeed eat the food. Thus [it is said].

This is the distinction: in rites such as "I shall invoke the ancestors," the term *nāndīmukha* must be employed. However, the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) should be done by name and lineage alone. Furthermore, the rice-balls should be made mixed with curd and *karkandhū* (the *karkandhū* is the jujube fruit). Because of the mention of "mixed," the rice-balls are to be made with food itself; barley is to be used in place of sesame seeds. Since barley would already be obtained by virtue of the rite being for the gods, this specific mention indicates that sesame seeds are also to be used in the *vaiśvadeva* portion. Consequently, it should be understood that in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), namely the *vaiśvadeva*, the use of sesame seeds is optional. Moreover, because it is for the gods, the utterance of *svadhā* is omitted. The actual ritual procedure, however, should be explained in detail. Now, an objection may be raised: was not the *śrāddha* also previously taught in the context of prosperity (*vṛddhi*) in the verse, "The new moon, the *aṣṭakā*s, and prosperity... (YDh 1.214)? True.
