But there is a distinction: the rule given here applies to that *śrāddha* known as *ābhyudayika* which is performed when prosperity is the occasion, such as at the commencement of the return home from studentship (*samāvartana*) and so forth. On the other hand, that which is performed when prosperity has actually occurred—characterized by the birth of a son and the like—is governed by the previous rules. Alternatively, in those various contexts, the term "prosperity" (*vṛddhi*) is used merely to denote the occasion; here, however, it should be explained as an instruction regarding the specific method of performance. || 246 ||
Now he describes another type of modified *śrāddha*:
"The *ekoddiṣṭa* is devoid of the gods; it has one *arghya* offering and one *pavitraka*;
it is indeed without the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the *agnaukaraṇa*, and is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). (1.247)

That which is performed with reference to a single deceased person is the *ekoddiṣṭa*. It is in every respect the same as the preceding [rites]. However, this is the distinction: it is devoid of the ritual for the Viśvedevas, and there is only one *arghya* offering. Furthermore, there is only one *pavitra* (purifier) therein. From this very fact, it is understood that elsewhere there are two *pavitras*. Since the singularity of the *arghya* is already established by the fact that there is only one deity, the mention of it is for the purpose of prescribing the number of *pavitras*. From this also, it is understood that the preparation of the *arghya* is determined solely by the number of deities, not by the number of Brahmins, nor should it be suspected that there is no fixed rule. And this is another distinction: it should be devoid of the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire). If it is asked, "From what is this obtained?"—because this is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). Since the *Pārvaṇa* rite is characterized by the *apasavya* mode as its means, this [rite] should be like that; the meaning is that it is not like the *Abhyudayika* rite performed when [the ancestors] are present. || 247 ||
And this is another distinction:
at the dismissal of the Brahmins, in place of the word "akṣayya" (imperishable), one should say "upatiṣṭhatām" (may it stand near);
they should say "abhiramyatām" (may you be pleased), and they should reply, "We have been pleased."

In place of [the formula] "May they attend upon [you]," one should say "May it be inexhaustible. And at the dismissal of the Brahmins, instead of saying "Vāja-vāja," one should say "May you be pleased. Furthermore, there is this distinction here: the Brahmins should say, "We are pleased. The word *ha* has the sense of restriction; the meaning is that this alone should be the case, and not "Vāja-vāja. Thus it is made known that, except for a specific substitute, there is a sublation [of the original rule]. || 248 ||
Furthermore, this other modified *śrāddha* for the deceased should be performed either on the anniversary of the day of death, when a full year has passed, or even earlier due to some other cause.
One should prepare four vessels joined with scented water and sesame seeds;
for the purpose of the *arghya* offering, one should pour the vessel of the deceased into the vessels of the ancestors. (1.249)

One should prepare four vessels containing scented water and sesame seeds: three for the ancestors (*pitṛs*) and one for the deceased (*preta*). For what purpose? For the sake of the *arghya* offering. Consequently, by this substitution, the ordinary *arghya* is set aside. Then, that vessel of the deceased should be poured out into the vessels of the ancestors in three parts. Regarding this, some explain the word *preta* as referring to the great-great-grandfather (*vṛddhaprapitāmaha*), deriving it from the etymology “he has gone away (*itaḥ*) in an excellent manner (*pra-*)”; they then pour his vessel into the vessels of the father and the others. However, that is not correct, because it contradicts other *smṛtis*. Pāraskara states: “In the preparation of the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*), the first among the ancestors shall be the *preta*, provided he has sons” (PārG 3.10.50). Furthermore, there is no possibility of doubting that the great-great-grandfather is without sons. Nor is it logical to pour [the vessel] into a more recent ancestor, as it would contradict the Vedic tradition: “The ancestors have turned away,” which speaks of them as if they were once united and then departed. Moreover, the word *preta* is used in its primary sense through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), as seen in its employment everywhere. Even if an etymological derivation (*yoga*) exists, it should be understood as applying to that same primary sense; it is not proper to override conventional usage merely because an etymological possibility exists. In this manner, one should dispel such errors. (249)
Should one sprinkle [water] silently? No, it is said:
with the two verses beginning "Those who are equal," the remainder, such as the *arghya* offering and so forth, is as before.
This *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for a single ancestor applies to women as well. 1.250.

With the two verses beginning with “*ye samānāḥ*” (VS 19.45), one pours [the remaining water] into the vessels for the ancestors. The remainder is as before, according to the *pārvaṇa* rite; that is the meaning of “one should perform. Why is this so? Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the three vessels. Furthermore, the mention of the *arghya* is for the sake of illustration; therefore, the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is also exactly like this. And thus says Kātyāyana: “By this very [rule], the rice-ball is explained. This *śrāddha*, known as *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, which is distinct from both the *ekoddiṣṭa* and the *pārvaṇa*, is to be understood here. The application of this specific name is for the purpose of establishing the rule that the offering of the rice-balls occurs together [with the ancestors] from this point forward. “The *ekoddiṣṭa* is also for a woman”—that is, it also pertains to the mother. But the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is for the father alone; such is the meaning. And this is a prohibition against performing the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the mother together with the maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*), because the offering of the rice-balls is performed together with them. However, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* with women [her own female ancestors] certainly does exist, according to other *smṛtis*. Alternatively, the meaning of the statement “this *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is an *ekoddiṣṭa* even for a woman” is as follows: some teachers teach (*upadiśanti*) it as being for one person (*eka-uddiṣṭa*); thus, this *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* exists even for a woman. In any case, there is no prohibition against the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* with women. || 250 ||
Intending the two time-periods for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* mentioned in another *Smṛti*, he says:
"For one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* takes place before the completion of a year, one should also give food along with a water-pot to a twice-born man for the duration of that year. (1.251)

Since it might follow that giving [gifts] separately after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is prohibited, this verse is intended as an exception (*apavāda*). The mention of "twice-born" (*dvija*) refers specifically to Brāhmaṇas because of their connection with the act of giving; the use of the locative case for the sense of the dative is due to metrical requirements. (251)

But is it the case that for one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, there is no separate *piṇḍa* at all? Indeed, this follows from the very designation [of the rite]. To this, there is an exception:
"And on the anniversary of death, the monthly [śrāddha] must be performed for a year;
likewise, every year, the śrāddha should be performed just like the monthly ones. (1.252)

On the very day one has died, one should perform the *śrāddha*. The word "day" (*ahaḥ*) here refers to the lunar date (*tithi*). Consequently, on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*) or whichever date one died, on that very same date one should perform it. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that it should also be performed on the day of the funeral rites (*saṃskāra*). This indicates that the *śrāddha* is to be performed on the day of the rites, as evidenced by the statement: "Then, after a year, one should give food to the deceased (*preta*) on the day he became a *preta*. This is because the word *preta* denotes the person who is to undergo the funeral rites. Why is this so? Because although one could have said "to the dead" (*mṛtāya*), the text says "to the deceased" (*pretāya*). This is established both by traditional law (*smṛti*) and by sacred scripture (*āmnāya*). Likewise, Pāraskara states: "Those who have touched the *preta* shall not enter the village until the appearance of the stars" (PārG 3.10.35); thus, he shows that the word *preta* refers to the person undergoing the rites. Manu also [states this].
"Those who have touched a corpse are purified in one day, in one night, and in three nights respectively. (MDh 5.64).
Likewise, regarding the touching of a corpse, bathing alone has been prescribed.
"Having touched a corpse, or even one who has touched it, one becomes pure by bathing. (MDh 5.85)

And the traditional scripture (*āmnāya*) states: "This indeed is the supreme austerity—that they lead the deceased to the forest, that they place the deceased upon the fire. This shows the use of the word *preta* specifically in the context of the performance of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*). [Objection: But this is the reverse, since the instruction to lead [the body] to the forest applies to one who is already *preta*. [Reply: Not so; for elsewhere it is designated thus: "Whoever dies, he is a corpse (*śava*). Therefore, the word *śava* refers merely to one who has died, whereas the word *preta* refers to one who is to be consecrated by the rites. Consequently, the meaning of the rule "on the day the *preta* occurs, he should be consecrated" is precisely this. In that regard, the Teacher’s mention of the "day of death" is so that there may be no omission of the *śrāddha* for one who has not yet been consecrated. And here is the settled rule (*vyavasthā*): for one who has not been consecrated, [the rite is on] the day of death; for another, only on the day of the consecration. However, for one whose both [dates] are unknown, he should perform it on the very day when those authorized [to know] truly perceive his death, as that is the only possibility. Otherwise, there would be a general omission of the *ekoddiṣṭa* which is prescribed without distinction. Should one perform the *śrāddha* only within the ten-day period? No, we say. The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of restriction: [one should perform it] every month, and not only within the ten days. For how long a time? Until the end of the year. Beyond that, however, only once a year. The word "and" (*ca*) is for the sake of including those killed by weapons and others on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, as well as for the three-fortnightly periods and so forth. Since there is the contingency of offering separate rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) for one who has undergone the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, he says: "One should perform the *śrāddha* as if it were the monthly [rite]. The word "indeed" (*vai*) is for the purpose of setting aside the conventional name [of *ekoddiṣṭa*]. The word "as" (*artha*) is for the purpose of prescribing the manner. The meaning is: "just as the monthly rite is prescribed, so [should it be done]. And from that, the meaning of the verse is that just like the prescription for the monthly rite, the *ekoddiṣṭa* exists even for one who has undergone the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. [Objection: But is it not the case that the "monthly" rite is said to be the *pārvaṇa* itself?
"The wise know the monthly *śrāddha* for the funeral cakes as the *anvāhārya*.

Because of this statement regarding the monthly [rites], it is not so [that the *anvāhārya* applies to all months]. For if that were the case, it would follow that even prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the rite would be performed according to the *pārvaṇa* model; and in that regard, it would contradict [the rule]:
"But for a twice-born who has passed away, the ritual act of *asapiṇḍīkaraṇa*... (MDh 3.247).

Thus, if it were otherwise, the rule for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* performed at the end of the year would be rendered meaningless; furthermore, since the matter would already be established by the name itself, the verse would be purposeless. Therefore, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite mentioned in other Smṛtis is what should be understood by the term "monthly" (*māsika*). Accordingly, Yama says: "After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, except on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight and until the annual anniversary, one should not perform any *ekoddiṣṭa*."
Likewise:
"Every year, however, reverence must be paid to one's mother and father;
one should perform a śrāddha without [invoking] the gods and offer a single pinda. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, regarding Manu’s statement beginning with "the rite of *asapiṇḍa*," which says:

"But when the *sapiṇḍa* rite has been performed for him according to the law, the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) must be performed by his sons according to this very same procedure" (MDh 3.248).

The instruction "by this very [method]" refers to the *pārvaṇa* rite taught in proximity; therefore, it should be understood to apply to occasions other than the annual anniversary. Likewise, this also applies:

"In whatever case there is an offering of these [ancestors] after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, that should be entirely like the *pārvaṇa*, except for rites for prosperity (*abhyudaya*) directed toward the ancestors."

Thus, even that [rite] is to be performed only on occasions other than the annual anniversary (*pratisaṃvatsara*). Alternatively, the rule of Manu also pertains specifically to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa*. By the phrase "by this very [procedure]," because it is the most proximate, the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* alone is understood, and not the procedure for the *pārvaṇa*, because the latter is remote; furthermore, since the term *āvṛt* (procedure) can apply to the *ekoddiṣṭa* as well. For what purpose, then, is this statement? It is so that there may be no suspicion that the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) is to be done together, based on the name "Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa. Otherwise, since that would already be established by the preceding verse and by the name itself, the commencement of this rule would be entirely redundant. Therefore, in the phrase "but in the rite involving the rice balls together," the word *tu* has the sense of "but" (*apiśabdārtha*), or it serves to exclude doubt; the meaning is that one should not be deluded merely by the name, and thus even for one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, the rite must be done by this very procedure of the *ekoddiṣṭa*. This being the case, since the *ekoddiṣṭa* would otherwise apply at all times, the injunction of the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha—based on the force of the rule and the words of the Teacher such as "on the day of death" and so forth—is established such that the *ekoddiṣṭa* occurs only on the annual anniversary and similar occasions, while on other occasions it is indeed like the *pārvaṇa*. As for the statement, "Wherever there is the offering of these [rice balls]," that refers to matters such as the *prācīnāvīta* (wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder), and not to the number of three rice balls, because of the exception: "except in the case of prosperity rites (*abhyudaya*). Furthermore, from the plural "of these" (*eṣām*), it is understood that wherever the offering of many [rice balls] directed toward the ancestors is prescribed, there it is so; it does not mean that wherever there is an offering, there must be many. And the mention of "ancestors" (*pitṛ*) is solely for the purpose of excluding the deceased (*preta*). Thus says Bhṛgu:
"Every year, however, reverence should be paid to one's mother and father;
one should perform a *śrāddha* without [invoking] the gods, feed [the Brahmins], and offer a single *piṇḍa*.
Thus it is enjoined that "year after year, food should be given to the deceased (*preta*). Others, however, having derived this verse from some source, recite it as follows:

"He who joins a deceased person for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed with a separate rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) becomes a destroyer of the ritual injunction and is born as a slayer of his ancestors. Thus [it is said].

But this [interpretation] is of no consequence because its basis is unclear. Furthermore, even for this [view], the scope is already stated, since the reasoning has been expressed. Alternatively, this too is intended solely to clarify the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite. This is its meaning: he who, out of delusion, does not join the deceased—who, having been made a *sapiṇḍa*, is entitled to a single *piṇḍa* according to the rules for the deceased—at the annual anniversary and other times into a separate *piṇḍa*, violates the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure by that very delusion, and so forth. Or rather, "separate *piṇḍas*" refers to that [rite] in which there is a separation of *piṇḍas*, namely the *pārvaṇa* itself; and joining [the deceased] is possible only in that case, not in the *ekoddiṣṭa*, because the act of joining requires a second [recipient]. Moreover, the commencement [of the rule] is appropriate when the offering of *piṇḍas* together is applicable; otherwise, it would be without cause due to the absence of such an occasion. Enough of this digression. (252)
The specific distinctions for all types of ancestral rites (śrāddha) have been stated up to the point of offering the rice-balls (piṇḍas). Now, he states what is common to all:
"One should give the rice-balls to cows, goats, or Brahmins, or else throw them into fire or water;
while Brahmins are present, one should not wipe away the remnants of the twice-born. (1.253)

One should give the *piṇḍa* to Brahmins and others, or cast it into fire or water; one should not dispose of it according to one's own whim. While the Brahmins have not yet risen, one should not wipe away the remnants of the food intended for the ancestors from the Brahmins. The second mention of "twice-born" (*dvija*) is for the sake of specifying the Brahmins intended for the ancestors. And this is the final alternative. However, when one has the capacity, the rule of Vasiṣṭha applies:
"One should not wipe away the remnants until the sun has set. (VaDh 11.22)

[Objection: Surely this should have been stated even before the mention of the *vaikṛta-śrāddha* (the modified śrāddha). [Response: True; however, this introduction is for the purpose of ensuring that the subsequent ritual acts (*pratipatti*) do not take place. From that, the non-performance of the pouring of the remnants (*saṃsrava*) and so forth is established. Furthermore, since what is about to be described is common to all, the materials such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) would also serve all purposes. Otherwise, because of the instruction that they are for the sake of pleasing the ancestors, there might even be a suspicion of their absence in rites such as the *ābhyudayika* (prosperity rites). Moreover, due to the connection with specific desires (*kāma*), those rites based on lunar days and so forth become applicable to all purposes; otherwise, they would apply only to the archetype (*prakṛti*), since the fruit is not extended [to the ectype]. Such is to be understood as the purpose of the difference in sequence. || 253 ||
What, then, are the foods for the purpose of pleasing the ancestors? These are said to be:
"By means of sacrificial food (haviṣya) one satisfies them for a month; by milk-rice (pāyasa), for a year;
and by fish, deer, sheep, birds, goat, and the meat of the spotted deer. (1.254)
The ancestors here are indeed satisfied by the offerings of the flesh of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, the boar, and the hare, respectively, as the months increase. (1.255)

Satisfaction for one month is achieved by means of sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) such as *vrīhi* rice and the like; [satisfaction] lasting from two or three months up to eleven months is achieved by fish and other [meats] ending with the hare; but by means of cow’s milk-rice (*pāyasa*), satisfaction lasts for a year. And so Manu says:
"But for a year [one is satisfied] by cow’s milk or by milk-rice" (MDh 3.271).

The mention of the "grandfather" (*pitāmaha*) should also be understood as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) and others, since there is no distinction in the context. "Fish-eaters" are well known. "Lamb" (*aurabhra*) refers to sheep. "Fowl" (*śākuna*) means that which comes from birds killed for food. "Pārṣata" is the meat of the spotted deer (*pṛṣat*). "Eṇa" is simply a young black antelope; others say it is a different species. "Ruru" is a large-horned deer. "Boar" (*varāha*) is a pig. "Hare" (*śaśa*) is well known. Furthermore, following the statement regarding satisfaction, one should infer a rule for the giving of gifts according to the literal description, rather than concluding that the ancestors remain satisfied for a year merely by the gift of milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and thus omitting the performance of the *śrāddha*. (254–255)
But these are for the sake of extreme satisfaction:
the flesh of rhinoceros, large-scaled fish, honey, the food of sages, the flesh of iron-eating insects, black pot-herbs, and the meat of the vārdhrīṇasa crane. (1.256)
Whatever one who stays at Gayā gives, all that attains infinity;
likewise on the thirteenth day of the month and under the Maghā asterism, there is no doubt. (1.257)

*Khaḍga* refers to the *gandhaka* (fragrant) meat. Some say that *mahāśalka* is the *śarabha* (a kind of deer), but that is incorrect because of the scriptural mention of its impurity (*amedhya*). Therefore, *mahāśalka* should be understood as a specific type of fish. *Munyanna* refers to *śyāmāka* (millet) and similar grains. *Loha* is a red goat. The use of the word *āmiṣa* (meat) is for the purpose of removing any suspicion regarding the ritual slaughter of an animal. *Vārdhrāṇasa* is an old goat; others say it is the *kaṅkaṇāhi* snake. The repetition of the word *māṃsa* (meat) is for the sake of praise. Thus says the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "This indeed is the supreme food, which is meat. The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and if he is at Gayā" (*gayāsthaś ca*) serves to include other times such as the *maghā* asterism. However, in the subsequent [verse], the meaning is one of option (*vikalpa*), indicating that even if the whole set is not obtained, one may give each individually. From the use of the word "all" (*sarva*), the meaning is that whatever else one gives here, that too reaches the ancestors in an inexhaustible manner. Because this is stated without doubt, it should be understood that the result is established through this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) itself, rather than being merely a figurative praise. (256–257)

Having thus explained the *śrāddha* pertaining to specific places and times as being based on scriptural injunction (*naiyogika*), he now speaks with reference to the attainment of desired objects (*kāmasaṃyoga*):
"A daughter, those who seek a daughter, and excellent cattle, as well as sons;
gambling, agriculture, trade, and likewise animals with cloven and uncloven hooves. (1.258)
The giver of a Śrāddha always obtains sons endowed with Brahmanic luster, gold, silver, and base metals, preeminence among kinsmen, and all desires. (1.259)
Indeed, from the first day of the lunar fortnight onwards, excluding the fourteenth day,
offerings are presented there for those who have been slain by weapons.

The meaning of these three verses is as follows: at all times, on the lunar days beginning with the first (pratipad) and ending with the new moon (amāvāsyā), excluding the fourteenth day, one should understand that there are fourteen respective fruits, beginning with the acquisition of a daughter, in due order. By performing a *śrāddha* on the first day (*pratipad*), those desiring a daughter—both those seeking to find a bride and those wishing to marry her—obtain her. The same principle should be applied to the subsequent days. "Cattle" (*paśavaḥ*) refers to goats and the like. "Principal sons" (*mukhyāḥ sutāḥ*) refers to those born of a Brāhmaṇī wife and others. "Excessive profit" refers to gains in gambling, agriculture, and trade. "Two-hoofed animals" (*dviśapham*) are cows and the like; "one-hoofed animals" (*ekaśapham*) are horses and the like. "Possessing spiritual luster" (*brahmavarcasvinaḥ*) means those endowed with sacred learning and study. Gold and silver are well known. "Base metals" (*kupya*) refers to copper utensils and the like. "All desires" (*sarvakāmāḥ*) are those already mentioned in the context. The rest is clear. (258–260)
In this same way, this [attainment] also occurs through union with desire alone:
heaven, progeny, vigor, heroism, as well as land and strength;
sons, preeminence, good fortune, offspring, and the status of a distinguished son. (1.261)
The turning of the wheel [of Dharma], sons, power over kinsmen, as well as freedom from disease, fame, freedom from sorrow, and the supreme goal—these he bestowed. (1.262)
He who offers a śrāddha according to the prescribed rule bestows wealth, knowledge, success in medicine, base metals, cattle, goats and sheep, horses, and long life.
From Kṛttikā to Bharaṇī, he who is a believer, full of faith, and free from pride and envy, shall obtain these desires. (1.264)

These four verses also are to be explained as before. There are exactly twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), beginning with Kṛttikā and ending with Bharaṇī. Correspondingly, there are just as many fruits, beginning with heaven (*svarga*), each of which is to be applied in due order. By performing the *śrāddha* at all times under the asterism of Kṛttikā, one attains heaven. In the same way, the attainment of offspring and other results is to be applied for Rohiṇī and the others. The words beginning with "hi" (for/indeed) are for the purpose of completing the meter. This is to be explained similarly for the preceding [verses] as well. Furthermore, it should not be thought that because these are presented as fruits, they constitute a means for those who have already engaged in gambling and other prohibited acts by transgressing their injunctions. The rest is clear. (261–264)

Now, does this *śrāddha* yield fruit only for the performer, or is it also beneficial for the ancestors? We say it is for the sake of both, because it is understood as such. For the satisfaction of the ancestors has been stated, as well as the attainment of desires by the performer. True, it has been stated; however, that [satisfaction] is untenable. How indeed can the satisfaction of ancestors who have entered various kinds of wombs according to their own karma be possible? This objection is not to be raised, because this matter is established by the authority of scripture. Furthermore: "The ancestors, the sons of the Vasus, Rudras, and Aditis, are the deities of the *śrāddha*."
Being gratified by the śrāddha rite, they bring satisfaction to the ancestors of human beings.

The Vasus consist of those beginning with Agni and ending with the Nakṣatras; the Rudras consist of the eleven [organs] beginning with Prāṇa; the Ādityas are the twelve months. These eternal entities are the Pitṛs. It is these alone who should be understood as the deities of the Śrāddha; therefore, there is no contradiction. If this is so, what follows for the human Pitṛs? It is said: when these gods, the Vasus and others, are pleased, they gratify the Pitṛs of humans—wherever they may reside—by bestowing the essence of the Śrāddha offering. Since they pervade all living beings, their capacity to satisfy the Pitṛs in all states of existence is not contradictory. Furthermore, since it is accepted that all deities, such as Agni and the rest, have subordinate deities within them, there is no contradiction. It was previously stated, with this very intention, that the Pitṛs constitute the recipients (*saṃpradāna*). Since it is enjoined that "one should give to the Pitṛs," the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) which establish the rationale for that injunction must also be regarded as authoritative. Therefore, one should not harbor an obsession with false objections based on the fallacious arguments of sophists. Now, it might be argued that the Vasus and others are not actually enjoined as the deities. If one says, "This very [injunction] is their injunction," then the status of the Pitṛs as the previously enjoined deities would be lost. To this it is replied: there is no contradiction because the Vasus and others are designated as the deities (*devatā*), while the Pitṛs are the recipients (*saṃpradāna*). The term *devatā* is used instead of *devāḥ* merely for metrical completion, or perhaps its use is redundant. Since the word is derived from the root *dā* (to give), it is understood that the Vasus and others are the givers. Thus, the meaning becomes this: whatever the agent desires to give to the Pitṛs, the Vasus and others, by virtue of their omnipresence, are capable of giving that to the Pitṛs wherever they may be. Therefore, the position is faultless. Moreover, because they are called "givers" even to the Vasus and others, it should be understood that they certainly experience satisfaction. Alternatively, the Pitṛs have two forms: their form as transmigrating beings (*saṃsārin*) and their form as Vasus and others. Among these, those who have attained the state of Vasus and others provide satisfaction to other transmigrating beings because of their power of ubiquity (*vibhutva*). Where the Pitṛs are connected as deities in rites such as the *Abhyudaya-śrāddha*, their status as deities is precisely through their form as Vasus and others. However, according to the specific injunction, they are addressed by name and lineage. One should understand that eligibility for the rite belongs to one who knows this. Or rather, this verse has another purpose: the Vasus and others are also indeed deities of the Śrāddha. In that regard, the following application of the subject matter is established: one who does not know the names of the ancestors should give to the three beginning with the Vasus; or, in the case of an *abhyudaya* rite, one whose father is still living; whereas another [ordinary person] should give to the three ancestors starting with the father. Thus says Āśvalāyana: "One who does not know the names [should say] 'father, grandfather, great-grandfather'" (ĀśŚr 2.6.24). This shows the eligibility of one who does not know the names. There is an option based on two Smṛtis: either addressing them with the words "Vasu" and so on, or with the words "father" and so on. This being the case, the injunction "one should give" is justified as an original injunction (*utpatti-codanā*) following the recipient established by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). And thus, it should be understood that when the Pitṛs are nourished by the Śrāddha performed by learned sons, they themselves—even if they were not performers of merit—attain the status of Vasus and others. (265)
And having reached that [state],
the grandfathers (pitāmahas), being pleased, bestow upon men longevity, wisdom, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, happiness, and likewise sovereignty. (1.266)
The verse has an unclear meaning. || 266 ||

Thus, this *śrāddha* must necessarily be performed by those who hate their ancestors as well, according to the teacher’s opinion, on lunar days such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) and others, in accordance with the injunctions and within one's capacity. However, in the case of incapacity, it should be understood that [the rite] is omitted.
According to this rule, one should perform the *śrāddha* here three times a year—during the winter, summer, and rainy seasons—and the *pañcayajña* daily. (MDh 3.281)

The statement regarding the five great sacrifices (*pāñcayajñika*) is for the sake of illustration. Just as, in accordance with direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), one must perform the five sacrifices daily—even when lacking the capacity—as stated in "Every day one should give [alms] such as a vessel of water" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 11.5.6.2), so too has this been declared by the author of this Smṛti through its own rule: "While living here in the householder stage, even one who is utterly incapable for three years must perform this without hesitation. And this ritual procedure applies specifically to the maintainer of the sacred fires (*agnihotrī*): "Even if he is utterly incapable, there is no Śrāddha for a twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires without the New Moon sacrifice" (Manu Dharmaśāstra 3.282).

The phrase "not without a *śrāddha* on the new moon day" (*na śrāddhena vinā darśe*) involves a transposition of case endings; otherwise, there would be an inconsistency. Furthermore, for one who does not even maintain the *aupāsana* fire, he is simply not entitled to perform the *śrāddha*. For it is said:

"The oblation pertaining to the sacrifice to the ancestors (*paitṛyajñika*) is not prescribed to be performed in a common (*laukika*) fire. (MDh 3.282) In the absence of that [fire], there is a deficiency in the *śrāddha*. However, this alternative procedure applies to everyone only in cases of extreme incapacity.

"Whatever fruit one obtains by bathing with a concentrated mind and satisfying the ancestors with water, by that alone one attains the entire fruit of the performance of the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña)" (MDh 3.283)—thus says Manu. And Kātyāyana states: "One should not let the latter fortnight pass without [offering] even vegetables; there is a Vedic injunction that there must be eating every month" (PārG Śrāddhasūtra 1). The traditional teaching (*saṃpradāya*) is that this refers to the rites of the latter fortnight. The ultimate truth, however, is that one should perform the *śrāddha* in every way according to one's capacity and without deceit.

But why was the *Śrāddhakalpa* for the Mānava [tradition] not composed by the Teacher? Because its purpose is the same, and the objective is attained through this very [text]. Furthermore, it is not necessary for every single thing to be stated by every single author of a *Smṛti*, for that would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the uselessness of the multiplicity of *Smṛtis*. Not so. Whatever duty is mandatory for a person at a particular time must be remembered by all; otherwise, there would be the consequence of mutual dependence (*sāpekṣatva*). [Objection: But surely, only he who has perceived a thing is capable of remembering it. [Reply: O you who do not understand the nature of a rememberer! Not so. For how could one who has not understood the entire meaning of the Veda teach it? Or, even if he were to teach it, how could his words be accepted by the learned? Moreover, Manu and others are held in high esteem; therefore, they must have been experts in the entire meaning of the Veda. And since the understanding of another [tradition] arises from their teaching, there is no contradiction in the performance [of rites]. [Objection: If this is so, then everything should be taught by every rememberer. [Reply: Certainly. Then why is there no teaching [of certain things]? Due to other causes. Just as the Teacher did not state the *Mānava-śrāddha* because its purpose was the same, so too Manu did not state the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* because it was optional (*vaikalpika*). If it is asked, "Why is it optional?", it is precisely because of this non-mention by Manu. As for what was said regarding its obligatory nature (*nityatva*), that was with the Teacher's intention. Such options (*vikalpas*) are to be observed. And by that very word "ca" (and) and so forth, the inclusion of matters mentioned in other *Smṛtis* is intended. However, where inclusion is impossible, then in a *Smṛti* intended for practical application (*prayoga*), that which is not mentioned should be regarded as optional. But in a *Smṛti* intended for a secondary quality (*guṇārtha*), since it is directed toward something else, the mention of the essential form (*svarūpa*) is not the primary concern; this has already been stated in the passage beginning, "The speakers of the Dharmaśāstras... In any case, having considered the various compositions of the *Smṛtis* to be authoritative beyond doubt, everything of this kind should be explained after discerning it according to its proper application. Therefore, it is established that the objection regarding the uselessness of the multiplicity of *Smṛtis* is indeed not a valid objection.
Thus has this ancient Śrāddhakalpa been composed, its interior filled with a composition of clear, formidable, and distinct reasoning;
and Vivasvat [taught] it directly to Yājñavalkya.
Śrāddhadeva, who was conversant with the rules of the ancestral rites, spoke thus.
Thus ends the section on ancestral rites (śrāddha);
now begins the section on the ritual procedures for Vināyaka and others.

Thus, the faithful recipient has been described, as well as the connection with the specific occasion (*nimitta*). However, this must be addressed here: why, then, do these fruits such as heaven not arise immediately after the ritual action? If it is argued that this is because heaven is to be experienced by means of a particular body, then it would follow that sons and other such results must also arise immediately; and who would find this undesirable? [Objection: But it is simply because they are not observed to do so. [Response: Not so. Their non-observation is due to another cause, and not because the actions fail to produce them. What, then, is that other cause? It is said:
In ancient times, Vināyaka was appointed by Rudra and Brahmā for the sake of presiding over the Gaṇas and for the accomplishment of success despite obstacles to one's actions.

By the word *vināyaka*, delusion (*vyāmoha*) is meant here. For it leads (*nayana*) a person toward contradictory actions for the sake of obstructing karma or for the sake of success, whether through existence or non-existence; thus it is denoted by the term *vināyaka*. It was appointed by Rudra—meaning by Brahmā, the creator of the body—to preside over the host (*gaṇa*) that causes decline by instigating anger and other such states. Alternatively, the term *vināyaka* denotes the accumulation of innate unwholesome karma. That too, leading humans in various ways toward the production of its own fruit, is indeed a *vināyaka*. And this [delusion], currently employed by a prior power denoted by the terms Rudra and Brahmā to create obstacles for karma engaged in yielding its fruit, has proceeded specifically for the sake of sovereignty over the hosts of living beings by virtue of its strength; the meaning is that it completely blocks the operation of one's own will. Thus says Vyāsa:
"O best of the Pāṇḍavas, that previously performed karma which human beings do not remember in this world is designated as 'fate' (daiva). Thus [it is said].

"Created by the gods" means created by the divine; this should also be applied here [to the phrase] "by Rudra and by Brahmā. Alternatively, Rudra is anger (*krodha*), and Brahmā is the scriptural injunction (*vidhāna*). In that regard, since the Veda (*brahma*) was disregarded by one afflicted by anger, this Vināyaka known as Anger has now been appointed by that very same Veda—which, due to its prior unwholesome nature, manifests in such a form; thus it should be construed. Or, let Vināyaka be a deity itself in accordance with the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*); however, from the perspective of his qualification (*adhikāra*), there is no contradiction with his eternality. || 267 ||

But how is a man's connection with past unwholesome karma to be understood? To this he says: "Learn the symptoms of one who is afflicted by that: in his dreams he plunges excessively into water and sees shaven-headed men. (1.268)
He wears saffron-colored garments and mounts carnivorous beasts;
he dwells together with outcastes, donkeys, and camels. (1.269)
While walking, he likewise imagines himself followed by others;
dejected and with his undertakings frustrated, he desponds without cause. (1.270)
Even in the waking state, these [experiences] should be understood as being caused by previously committed unwholesome karma, like the condition of having deformed nails and so forth. (268–270)
But this is very clear here: it is caused by the influence of past unwholesome karma.
Afflicted by that, the prince does not obtain a kingdom;
nor does the maiden obtain a husband, nor offspring, nor even a fetus. (1.271)
It should also be applied that a pregnant woman does not [give birth to] an offspring, nor does a woman in her menses [conceive] a fetus. || 271 ||
Being a learned Vedic scholar, he does not obtain the status of a teacher; likewise, as a student, he does not obtain study.
The merchant does not obtain profit, nor does the farmer obtain a harvest. (1.272)

It should be explained that even one who is a *śrotriya* (learned in the Vedas) and endowed with scriptural knowledge does not obtain the status of a teacher; and likewise, a disciple—even if pure, excellent, vigilant, and possessed of the qualities of a disciple—does not obtain a teacher or the opportunity for study. This is stated by way of illustration. In every case, when someone who is understood from either scripture or worldly experience to be fit for something does not obtain it, it should be concluded that he is afflicted by past unwholesome karma. || 272 ||
But here is the resolution: his ceremonial bath (snapana) should be performed on an auspicious day according to the prescribed ritual,
after he has been smeared with a paste of white mustard seeds mixed with curd.
With his head anointed with all medicinal herbs and all fragrant substances,
and seated upon an auspicious throne, he should have the twice-born pronounce auspicious blessings.

The connection is that the ceremonial bath (*snapana*) should be performed in such a manner. "Auspicious day" (*puṇyāha*) refers to an astrological conjunction characterized by the strength of the moon and other favorable factors. "Anointing" (*ucchādana*) means rubbing with unguents; and that [should be done] with a paste of white mustard seeds ground immediately. From the word "but" (*tu*), it follows that the head should also be anointed with that same [paste]. And from the word "likewise" (*tathā*), there is rubbing with the scents of all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhi*). The word "all" (*sarva*) refers to the scents of all medicinal herbs that have not been specifically prohibited. "Bhadra-seat" (*bhadrāsana*) is a beautiful seat. "Recitation for well-being" (*svastivācana*) is the giving of gold and other gifts to Brahmins. (273–274)
Furthermore:

From a horse-stable, from an elephant-stable, from an anthill, from a confluence, and from a pool—one should cast earth, yellow pigment (rocanā), fragrant substances, and guggulu into the water. (1.275)
The water which has been drawn from the lake by four men of a single caste in jars should likewise be placed upon a red bull’s hide, along with the auspicious throne.
Conceptualization occurs according to its respective application. 275–276.
These, however, are the mantras for the ritual bathing:
"The thousand-eyed, hundred-streamed [water], made purifying by the seers—with that I sprinkle you; may the *pāvamānī* verses purify you. (1.277)
King Varuṇa gave you fortune; Sūrya and Bṛhaspati gave you fortune;
Indra and Vāyu gave you fortune; and the Seven Seers bestowed fortune upon you. (1.278)
Whatever misfortune is in your hair, in the parting of your hair, or on your head; whatever is in your forehead, your ears, or your eyes—may the waters always destroy that for you. 1.279

The bathing with the three jars is performed with each mantra individually using three mantras; however, by the fourth [mantra], because there is no distinction, it is performed with all the mantras. The meanings of the mantras, however, are to be understood from the commentators. (277–279)
Thus, first, even with the four pitchers;
for one who has bathed, one should offer mustard oil with a ladle made of udumbara wood into the head,
while grasping the kuśa grass with the left hand.
The word "ca" (and) signifies the manner [of action], such as bending the right knee and so forth. || 280 ||
These, however, are the mantras for the oblation:
one should recite *mita*, *saṃmita*, as well as *sālakaṭaṅkaṭa*, and the prince *kūśmāṇḍarājaputra*, accompanied by the word *svāhā*. (1.281)

There are four Vināyaka mantras; these are indeed the names of the four. In that regard, the recitation (*japa*) and the offering-rite (*balikarma*) are performed with [the names] ending in *svāhā*, or the offering-rite may be performed using their very own forms. And this is the method of application: *mitāya svāhā*, *saṃmitāya svāhā*, *sālakaṭaṅkaṭāya svāhā*, and *kūśmāṇḍarājaputrāya svāhā*. By means of the two words "and" (*ca*), he shows the distinction between *mita* and *saṃmita*; and because the other two are formed as compounds, he shows their lack of distinction due to the absence of such a [separate] word. Therefore, there are exactly four mantras. || 281 ||
Thus far, the ritual is performed within the house itself. Hereafter, however:

having spread *kuśa* grass everywhere upon a winnowing basket at a crossroads, one should offer [the oblation] with the names [of the deities] and with *bali*-mantras accompanied by salutations. (1.282)

The names are *mita* and so forth; the *balimantras* are those prescribed for the offering of oblations, such as the salutations (*namaskriyā*) and others. For here there is a connection with the characteristic mark of the *bali*, namely: "Homage! I take this oblation to them. And in the ritual of attendance (*upasthāna*), because Ambikā is seen and because they are feminine mantras, these very [mantras] are appropriate. At the crossroads, there is the spreading of *kuśa* grass, not of a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*). The rest is clear. || 282 ||
What, then, should be placed in that winnowing basket?
Cooked and uncooked rice, as well as rice mixed with sesame paste; likewise, cooked fish and raw fish, and meat—only these [should be offered]. (1.283)

"Prepared" means husked; "unprepared" means unhusked. Because of the word "and," rice (*odana*) is likewise of two kinds. Flesh also consists of exactly these two: cooked and raw; such is the meaning. || 283 ||
Furthermore:
variegated and fragrant flowers, as well as the three kinds of liquor; radishes, fried cakes, and buns, and likewise garlands of *oḍḍeraka* flowers.
Having offered all this with [their respective] names and bali-mantras. || 284 ||
Immediately after, having offered a full *añjali* as the *arghya* with a paste of *dūrvā* grass and mustard seeds,
using the very same mantras as before.
Then one should worship Ambikā, the mother of Vināyaka.

And here, Ambikā is said to be the intellect (*buddhi*); for she generates unwholesome causes such as greed and the like. Alternatively, Ambikā is the goddess herself, the wife of Rudra, by virtue of her permanent office; thus, there is no fault in either interpretation. || 285 ||
This, however, is the mantra for the ritual attendance:
"Grant me form; grant me glory; grant me fortune, O Bhavati. Grant me sons; grant me auspicious prosperity; and grant me all my desires. (1.286)
Having performed the service in this manner, one should then,
wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands, perfumes, and unguents,
feed the Brahmins and also give a pair of garments to the teacher.
The guru is the one who performs the ritual bathing; the rest is clear. || 287 ||
Having thus worshipped Vināyaka and the planets according to the prescribed rite,
one obtains the fruit of one's actions and attains unsurpassed prosperity.

Because this rite is intended for the destruction of impurity, the attainment of the fruit of action by one whose impurity has been exhausted is irreproachable. Even he who appears to be a performer of meritorious deeds attains unsurpassed prosperity after performing this; therefore, it must certainly be performed by him as well, according to the scriptural injunction: "Until death, one should desire prosperity" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.152). Furthermore, the procedure for the worship of the planets, which will be described later, should be observed. || 288 ||
But for one who, even in this way, should not obtain the fruit of his actions, there is this further means:
by constantly performing worship of Āditya, as well as Tilakasvāmin and Mahāgaṇapati, he shall attain success. (1.289)

And this Smṛti is without distinction; the procedure for worship is to be understood as being for the sake of the accomplishment of all men, by virtue of the force of the word "always" (sadā). The rest is clear. || 289 ||
Thus ends the section on the ritual manual for Vināyaka and others.
Now begins the section on the pacification of the planets (*grahaśānti*).

It has been stated according to the injunctions that the planets are to be worshipped for the sake of accomplishing one's actions without obstacles. Desiring now to explain that procedure, and for the sake of accomplishing the ritual application even independently, he states another qualification [of the practitioner] in connection with specific desires.
One who desires prosperity, or one who desires peace, or one who desires rain, long life, and nourishment, or likewise one performing malevolent rites, should undertake the sacrifice to the planets.
By the word "again," it is meant that after performing [the rite] for the sake of removing obstacles, one performs it again for the sake of fulfilling desires. || 290 ||

What, then, are these so-called planets? The Sun, the Moon, the Son of Earth (Mars), the Son of the Moon (Mercury), Bṛhaspati (Jupiter), Śukra (Venus), Śanaiścara (Saturn), Rāhu, and Ketu—these are remembered as the planets. || 1.291 ||
Are these [images] being worshipped while remaining in the sky? No, it is said:
"The planets should be fashioned in this order from copper, crystal, red sandalwood, gold, silver, iron, and lead. (1.292)

Both Mercury (Budha) and Jupiter (Bṛhaspati) are to be made of gold; Ketu, however, by virtue of proximity, is to be made of lead alone. From the use of the word "these" (imaḥ), it is understood that they are in human form. Alternatively, the understanding of their forms arises from the historical narratives found within the explanatory passages (arthavāda). || 292 ||
However, depending on one's capacity, in the absence of copper and so forth,
[the deity] should be drawn with gold on a cloth or within fragrant mandalas;
this applies to all ritual manuals (kalpas).
Garments and flowers should be offered according to their respective colors.
Fragrances, offerings, and incense mixed with guggulu should be given;
their color is to be understood as being identical to the color of the image, such as copper or other materials, according to its specific hue.
And for all the planets, beginning with the Sun,
caru offerings accompanied by ritual manuals (tantra) must be performed for each respective deity.
"Possessing tantras" means having a single tantra; from the word "and" (ca), it should be understood that the ritual of worship applies to each [tantra] individually. || 294 ||
These, however, are the primary mantras for all purposes;
the verses beginning with "ākṛṣṇena," "imaṃ devāḥ," "agnir mūrdhā divaḥ kakut," and "udbudhyasva" are proclaimed respectively. || 1.295 ||
"Bṛhaspate atyāyaṃ," "tathaivānnāt parisrutaḥ," "śaṃ no devīḥ," and likewise "kāṇḍāt ketuṃ kṛṇvan"—these [verses] as well. 1.296.
And since there might be an attachment to using any tree whatsoever for fuel due to the commonality of all being *pākayajña* sacrifices, he states an exception:
"The *arka*, the *palāśa*, the *khadira*, the *apāmārga*, then the *pippala*, the *udumbara*, the *śamī*, the *dūrvā*, and the *kuśa* grasses are the fuel sticks in their respective order. (1.297)
Now, for the sake of specifying the number, he says:
"In this case, one hundred and eight or indeed twenty-eight oblations of each [substance], combined with honey, clarified butter, and curd, are to be offered. (1.298)

Alternatively, this unprecedented *samiddhoma* (oblation of fuel-sticks) is enjoined as a subsidiary (*aṅga*). Consequently, it should be performed with the same mantras as before at the end of the consumption. According to the traditional teaching (*saṃpradāya*), this injunction for the *samiddhoma* is optional (*vaikalpika*) in conjunction with the oblations of cooked rice (*caru*). || 298 ||
In both cases, however, [the offerings should be]:
rice with jaggery, milk-rice, sacrificial food (haviṣya), rice cooked with milk and ṣaṣṭika grain, rice with curd, sacrificial oblation, cakes, meat, and variegated rice. (1.299)

A wise man should give this food to the twice-born according to the sequence of the planets, honoring them with due ceremony and according to the prescribed rite, either according to his capacity or as it may be obtained. 1.300.
These two verses have clear meanings. (299–300)
Having thus fed the Brahmins, he should give to them respectively as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās): a cow, a conch shell, a bull, gold, a garment, a horse, a black cow, iron, and a goat. || 1.301 ||
And their magnitude is relative to their capacity.

Thus, first of all, the worship of all the planets has been described for the purpose of pacifying obstacles and for the fulfillment of desires. However, according to the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), even a single planet [may be worshipped]:
whichever planet is in an unfavorable position for someone at a particular time, that person should worship it with effort.
Why?
A boon was granted to them by Brahmā: "When you have been worshipped, you shall worship [others]."
And each individual worship also possesses the very characteristics of the procedure as previously described. || 302 ||

Furthermore, he states the reason for the worshipfulness of the planets, both individually and collectively: "The rise and fall of kings depend upon the planets; so too do the existence and non-existence of the world. Therefore, the planets are most worthy of worship. (1.303)
The meaning of this verse is clear. || 303 ||
Thus ends the section on the pacification of the planets (*grahaśānti*).
Now begins the section on the duties of kings (*rājadharmaprakaraṇa*).

But who is this so-called "lord of men" (*narendra*), whose fall and rise depend upon the planets? Is it not well known that the term *narendra* refers to a king? Does it refer to a Kṣatriya? Certainly. And so it has been said:
"The primary duty of a Kṣatriya is the protection of the subjects. Thus it is said;
and it has been stated by the Self-Existent One:
"By a Kṣatriya who has duly received the Brāhmaṇical consecration..."
"The protection of all this must be carried out according to the rule.

(MDh 7.2) However, there is this distinction: the right to sovereignty belongs only to one endowed with qualities such as consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and the like, not to every mere Kṣatriya, because of the Vedic tradition: "He created the king from the head; he who is consecrated on the head shall be the king. Nor, this being so, does it follow that the king is subject solely to destiny (*daivatantra*), since falling and rising depend upon the planets; for what then? [The king should be] one of great energy, liberal, grateful, and a servant of the elders.
Disciplined, endowed with goodness, of noble birth, truthful in speech, and pure. || 1.304 ||
Not procrastinating, possessed of mindfulness, with a retinue that is not mean-spirited, righteous, firm in devotion, wise, heroic, and a knower of secrets. (1.305)
The lord of men was likewise trained in the protection of his own domains through the science of logic and the science of government, as well as in the science of commerce and the triple Veda.

The word *syāt* (should be) is to be understood as the ellipsis. One who possesses great energy (*mahotsāha*) is one desiring victory (*vijigīṣu*). One who is "large-eyed" (*sthūlalakṣa*) is a liberal giver. One who is grateful (*kṛtajña*) recognizes favors; he is not solely intent on his own self-interest. One who serves the elders (*vṛddhasevitā*) is one who serves those advanced in knowledge and age. One who is humble (*vinīta*) is not arrogant, or rather, by virtue of his sound policy, he cannot be led astray by anyone. One endowed with courage (*sattvasaṃpanna*) is entirely free from despondency. One of noble birth (*kulīna*) is born of a great lineage. [Objection: But surely this is impossible, because [success] depends upon fate (*daiva*). [Reply: True. The meaning is that he should emulate a king of noble descent. One whose speech is truthful (*satyavāk*) is faithful to his word. One who is pure (*śuci*) is purified through all tests of integrity. One who is not dilatory (*adīrghasūtra*) acts swiftly in every respect. One who possesses memory (*smṛtimān*) is reflective and of a nature that does not forget. One whose retinue is not mean (*akṣudrapariṣatka*) has a following like that of swans (*haṃsa*). And so says Śaṅkha: "A swan does not have a retinue of vultures; however, a vulture may well have a retinue of swans. By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), other types of subjects are included. One who is righteous (*dhārmika*) is a performer of duties as prescribed. One of firm devotion (*dṛḍhabhakti*) is one who wins over others through devotion, or one whose devotion is unwavering toward those in whom he has taken refuge, such as gods, Brahmins, and teachers. One who is wise (*prājña*) knows how to distinguish between the essential and the non-essential in all matters. A hero (*śūra*) is one who, having violently agitated the entire circle of enemies, remains undaunted even when facing them. One who knows secrets (*rahasyavid*) understands the application and conduct of all forms of concealment regarding friends, enemies, neutrals, and those seeking victory or standing in the middle, as well as the methods for testing ministers and other constituents of the state; he is one whose eye is the secret, unerring network of spies (*cāracakṣus*). One who knows the inner self (*adhyātma*) knows its secret; the meaning is that he possesses profound reflection (*prasaṃkhyāna*). A protector of his own vulnerabilities (*svarandhragoptā*) conceals all his own weaknesses and exposes the flaws of others. He is trained (*vinīta*) in logic (*ānvīkṣikī*), the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*), the various arts of livelihood (*vārtā*), and the three Vedas (*trayī*). Logic (*ānvīkṣikī*) is the science of reasoning capable of investigating all invisible matters. The science of government (*daṇḍanīti*) consists of the exertion of one's own power to cause the rise or fall of oneself or others as appropriate, or it is to be applied by inflicting appropriate punishment upon those deserving of it. Others, however, say that *daṇḍanīti* refers to a specific branch of dialectics (*tarka*). The three Vedas (*trayī*) are characterized by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman. Thus, he should be endowed with qualities such as great energy and so forth, and not one who has cast the burden upon fate out of a false sense of merit. Whether he be another person or even an enemy, one possessing qualities like great energy is to be considered difficult to overcome; conversely, one lacking them is easily managed—this is the summary of policy (*naya*). For example: one who lacks royal lineage, is greedy, has a mean retinue, whose subjects are disaffected, who acts unjustly, is unapplied, addicted to vice, lacking energy, acting at random, without foresight, and constantly harmful, and so forth. In every way, he should act so that the group of adversaries, due to the opposite of the perfection of qualities like great energy, becomes easy to manage, while he himself, as a conqueror (*vijigīṣu*), becomes capable of seizing the entire circle of the earth, free from dependence on others, and able to destroy the enemy's realm. Since tradition (*smṛti*) is rooted in positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), everything—whether explicitly stated or unstated—should be discerned and explained as appropriate. And since the lord of men should possess these qualities, it is not contradictory for one who already possesses a stable kingdom to acquire further virtues. (304–306)

Even though he possesses such qualities, one should not be so excessively proud as to think, "What need is there for a minister? Rather, he who indeed possesses such qualities should appoint ministers who are wise, hereditary, steadfast, and pure;
with them he should deliberate on affairs, then with a Brahmin, and finally by himself. (1.307)
And so Manu says:
"Even an action that is easy to perform is difficult for one person alone;
how much more so a kingdom of great consequence, especially when lacking assistance? (MDh 7.55).
And the mention of the "minister" is intended to include all counselors. Thus he says:
"He should appoint as many men as are required for his duties—men who are untiring, skillful, and discerning. (MDh 7.61)

This statement is intended for the purpose of appointing a prime minister (*pradhānamantrin*); however, in practice, there is no contradiction in appointing others. Furthermore, because the purpose is visible (*dṛṣṭārthatvāt*), the appointment of others occurs precisely when the status of being a minister does not belong to anyone else. Now, if one should obtain a kingdom that belongs to his father or another, and if he considers the former ministers to be inferior to himself or otherwise unsuitable for that kingdom, then, in order to avoid provoking the subjects (*prakṛti*), he should appoint all other ministers who possess such qualities. The prefix *pra-* (in *pramantrī*) signifies excellence or superior consideration according to the logic already stated. And they [the ministers] should be wise, discerning, and hereditary (*maula*). "Hereditary" (*maula*) means those worthy of the kingdom; the sense is that they are capable of expanding and protecting the realm. Alternatively, they are those known from the root—meaning those of noble lineage—or those who have come down through the succession of the root; for even if they have been displaced from their offices, they do not initiate opposition due to their excessive loyalty or because they are restrained by the "whip of the family" (*kulāṅkuśa*). They are steadfast, capable of enduring all calamities, loyal to no other, and initiators of virtuous undertakings. They are pure, having been proven honest through the tests of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and fear. This is mentioned merely as an illustration; in every case, the appointment of counselors (*saciva*) must be performed after investigating them thoroughly according to worldly custom and the scriptures, and in accordance with their respective capacities and offices. As Bṛhaspati says:

One who knows his own duty (*svadharma*), is devoted, pure, not arrogant, industrious, knowledgeable of place and time, skilled in policy (*nīti*), the Vedas (*nigama*), and history (*itihāsa*), free from vices, gentle, trained in the treatises on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*), certain in his judgment regarding the conduct of elephants, horses, and men, as well as the duration of days and nights, and who understands the relative strength and weakness of his own and the enemy's forces—such a person should be the commander-in-chief (*senāpati*) appointed over the army. One born of a noble family, industrious, gentle, noble-minded, courageous in battle, brave, loyal, incapable of being divided, who knows the distinctions among foot-soldiers, and is skilled in interpreting gestures and facial expressions—such a person should be the chamberlain (*pratihāra*). One who knows the forest breeds, seasons, lineages, suitability, qualities, age, and character [of elephants], who understands their capture, movement, and training, who is free from fear, and whose mind is emboldened by victory—such a person should be the superintendent of elephants (*hastyadhyakṣa*). One who knows the breeds of regions, suitability, qualities, physical marks, and the equipment of weapons for horses, who is exceedingly capable, pure, not arrogant, and suitable [for the task]—such a person should be the superintendent of horses (*aśvādhyakṣa*). One who knows the points of alliance, its breaking, and its consolidation, who is loyal, pure, clever, possessed of a good memory, knowledgeable of place and time, handsome, skilled in the course of policy, wise, eloquent—such a person should be the envoy (*dūta*). One born of a high lineage on both sides, pure, learned in the treatises of Manu, Bṛhaspati, and Uśanas, skilled in the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*) and other fields, free from deceit, not crooked, unaffected by honor or dishonor, fearless, certain in his judgment regarding what ought and ought not to be done, incorruptible, purified by all tests of integrity, and possessing secret counsel—such a person should be the minister (*mantrin*). One who is unchangeable, with unimpaired senses, majestic, fortunate, pleasant-faced, not miserly, vigilant, clever, and who, for the sake of protecting courtesy and conduct, acts as a judge in doubtful legal cases—such a person should be the provincial governor (*uparika*). Thus it is said.

In this manner, those appointed over the treasury, the harem, the kitchen, the bedchamber, and so forth, should be examined and assigned their duties according to their merit. Having thus appointed all his ministers according to their respective capacities in accordance with the treatises of Bṛhaspati and Uśanas, and having deliberated with them on common matters as appropriate—discerning both individual and collective opinions—the king should thereafter deliberate, together with a learned Brāhmaṇa who possesses the qualities of a great minister and is privy to the highest secrets, upon the seed of policy (*nayabīja*), which is endowed with the sixfold strategy (*ṣāḍguṇya*), leads to great prosperity, and yields manifold results. Then, through trust in that [Brāhmaṇa], he himself, having risen during the latter part of the night, should carefully discern that very matter and, without procrastinating, should swiftly carry it out. Thus, the seed of total exaltation has been stated in brief; having discerned it, it should be explained in detail. Enough of this digression. (307)
By the very logic previously stated:

"And he should appoint as his domestic priest one who is renowned for his learning, skilled in astrology, and likewise proficient in the science of government (daṇḍanīti) as well as the Atharvāṅgiras [Veda]. (1.308)

By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), there is also the possession of the aforementioned qualities. A "knower of fate" (*daivajña*) is one who knows the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), or one who knows the connection between past actions and their results; that is, one who has risen ever higher by knowing: "This result of such an action is being experienced today, but later there will be a remedy. He must also be proficient in the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*). By the word "and" (*ca*), he should also be skilled in the three Vedas (*trayī*), in investigative logic (*ānvīkṣikī*), and in the various arts of livelihood (*vividhavārtā*). This [set of qualifications] is common to ministers as well. However, this is his specific distinction: he should be proficient in the *Atharvāṅgirasa* for the sake of rites for pacification (*śāntika*), nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), and so forth. One should deliberate with him on matters according to the facts. Furthermore, all ministers are to be tested by him specifically through the test of integrity regarding dharma (*dharmopadhā*). Thus, the examination of all ministers should be carried out by others as well, using specific tests appropriate to each position; such is the summary of political ethics (*nītisaṃkṣepa*). || 309 ||
And this is a further, distinguished duty of the king:
for the sake of performing rites prescribed by revelation and tradition, he should likewise choose officiating priests and duly conduct sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees. (1.309)

By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), it is understood that the domestic priest (*purohita*) also [should be appointed] solely for the sake of performing rites prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. And this selection of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should be seen as occurring at the very beginning, prior to the actual performance of the ritual. The meaning is that one should perform sacrifices according to the rules, and not in an arbitrary manner. "Abundant sacrificial fees" (*bhūridakṣiṇā*) refers to gold and other items in great quantity; or, the quality of being "abundant" may be applied in comparison to the gifts given to the spectators (*prasarpaka*). || 309 ||
Even apart from sacrifice, one should give enjoyments and various riches to the Brahmins. Why? Because:
This is an inexhaustible treasure for kings: that which has been bestowed upon the Brahmins.

“Enjoyments” refers to food, drink, and so forth. The word “and” (*ca*) includes fearlessness, honor, and the like. “Wealths” refers to the various kinds of gold and other riches. The second “and” indicates the diversity of the recipients. Thus says Manu: “A gift given to one who is not a Brahmin is equal,” and so on (MDh 7.85). The rest is clear. || 310 ||
Furthermore, for the sake of encouraging the practice of giving,
he says: "Because it is unspilled, free from distress, and untainted by expiatory rites,
therefore..."
It is said here that what is offered into the fire by a brahmin is superior to [what is offered] from the presence of Agni himself.
"Should that which was previously acquired and set aside for times of distress be given from the treasury itself? It is said: "No;

one should seek to acquire wealth through righteous means, protect what has been acquired with effort, constantly increase what has been protected, and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients. (1.312)
The meaning of this verse is clear. || 312 ||
Thus, in the case of gold and other such items, the process ends with the act of giving. However, there is this distinction regarding the gift of land and the grant of a fixed income (nibandha):
having given land or having established a fixed income, one should cause a written deed to be executed.
Why?
The king [acted] for the sake of identifying future minor rulers. || 1.313 ||
The *nibandha* is an inexhaustible treasure. The rest is clear. || 313 ||
But should this be done according to the characteristics of a written edict (lekhyalakṣaṇa) that will be described later? No, it is said. What then?
"Having inscribed upon a cloth or a copper plate his own lineage and himself, marked with his own seal, the wise ruler [should issue the grant]. (1.314)
He should cause a stable edict to be issued, specifying the dimensions of the land received, describing the boundaries of the gift, and completed with his own hand and the date. 1.315.

The mention of "cloth" is for the purpose of excluding birch-bark (*bhūrja*). Because of the word "around" (*pari*), [the document] must be marked with the seal of the hand of the messenger of wisdom (*prajñādūta*), the camp, the encampment, the name of the place, and so forth. At the very beginning, the three ancestors should be inscribed; because of the mention of their lineage, women are included as well. Immediately after that, oneself. Then, the dimensions of the gift: "In this place, a village named so-and-so," and so forth. Then, having described the non-confiscation of the gift: "This is the fruit of giving; this is the fruit of confiscating: the giver of land dwells in heaven for sixty thousand years."
Both the one who seizes it and the one who consents to it shall dwell in hell for that very duration.

And so forth. He should cause a firm establishment of the land’s tenure to last as long as the moon and stars, marked with the names of the scribes, bearing his own hand-signature, and intended to prevent the grief of future minor kings, by means of the "allocation of fissures" (*chidranyāsa*). It must be done in such a way that, in every respect, even future rulers shall not alter this very edict. (314–315)

But surely, one might object, the gift of land is improper because it entails the contraction of the kingdom. O you who are ignorant of the conduct of kings, do not say so! For a king must always be adept at increasing the three goals of life (*trivarga*). He should take refuge in a region that is pleasant, suitable for cattle, providing a good livelihood, and of the *jāṅgala* type; there he should construct fortresses for the increase of his people, treasury, and himself. (1.316)

The plural form "durgāṇi" (fortresses) is intended to signify the various types of fortifications. As Manu has said: "One should dwell in a city by taking refuge in a desert-fortress, an earth-fortress, a water-fortress, a forest-fortress, a man-fortress, or a mountain-fortress."
"But with every effort, one should take refuge in a mountain fortress;
due to its many advantages, the mountain fortress is praised above these [other types].
(MDh 7.70–71), and so forth. 316.
Having thus established fortresses and occupied that territory,
he should appoint therein supervisors who are expert, skillful, pure, and diligent in matters of revenue, labor, and expenditure. (1.317)
There is nothing here that is hidden, as it were. || 317 ||

Thus far, the rule regarding the acquisition of wealth within one's own kingdom has been stated. Now, he states an exception to the prohibition against seizing the property of others when it becomes necessary:
"There is no duty for kings higher than this: that wealth acquired in battle is given to the Brahmins, and constant fearlessness is granted to the subjects. (1.318)
The intended meaning is "from what was acquired in battle. || 318 ||
Now, since the two prohibitions—"one should not fall into doubt" (YDh 1.132) and "one should not harm any living beings"—might lead to the contingency of not engaging in battle at all, he says:
Those who are slain in battles for the sake of land, without turning their backs and with weapons that are not treacherous, go to heaven just like performers of sacrifices. (1.319)

*Āhava* means battle. The mention of "land" (*bhūmi*) is intended as an illustration for the army, the treasury, and so forth. It should be construed as "fighting with non-deceptive weapons. "Deceptive" (*kūṭa*) refers to things such as arrowheads smeared with poison. The mention of "weapons" (*āyudha*) is intended as an illustration for all types of weaponry. The rest is clear. || 319 ||
Furthermore, he spoke again to encourage the rules of combat and the various modes of battle formation:
"The steps taken by those who retreat when broken are equal to sacrificial rites;
the king takes the merit of those who were slain while fleeing. (1.320)
For since it was gathered solely for the purpose of battle, this is indeed appropriate. || 320 ||

This being the case, since violence is generally applicable in battle, he speaks for the purpose of providing an exception: "One should not strike one who claims 'I am yours,' nor a eunuch, nor one who is unarmed, nor one who has joined another's side, nor one who has turned away, nor even a spectator of the fight. (1.321)

The word "ca" (and) includes those who have met with calamities such as weapons and the like. "Nirhetih" means not fighting. "Parasaṃgataḥ" means fighting with another [while being attacked]. The rest is clear. || 321 ||
Thus far, then, has been the summary of royal policy. Now follows the king's daily duties:
Having performed his protection, he should rise and personally inspect income and expenditure; thereafter, having seen the legal cases and bathed, he may eat according to his desire. (1.322)

Protection is of two kinds: divine and human. That characterized by the worship of gods and Brahmins and other such auspicious acts is divine; that consisting of being surrounded by men equipped with well-tested and raised weapons is human. And so says Bṛhaspati: "Having awakened and risen to the sound of Vedic recitation, conch shells, hymns, and the proclamation of an auspicious day, and having performed the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), he should mentally pay homage to the gods, ancestors, and Brahmins; then, surrounded by those who have been tested for integrity regarding virtue, wealth, pleasure, and fear, and by those who hold weapons honestly and are trustworthy, he should be attended by his immediate retinue," and so forth. In accordance with urgent matters of great importance, he himself should oversee income and expenditure and judicial proceedings according to the rules to be described hereafter. Then, having bathed and performed the worship of the gods, ancestors, and others, he should enter the inner apartments and eat food that has been thoroughly examined according to his desire. (322)

Thus has been described the method for acquiring wealth according to the established order of one's own and foreign kingdoms. Now, as for that wealth, should it be offered to the worthy recipient (*pātra*) immediately upon its production, since the purpose of its acquisition is for that end? Having raised this question, he says: "Gold brought in by officials should be deposited in the treasury;
then, having inspected the spies, he should dispatch messengers in consultation with his ministers. (1.323)

Whatever has been brought by those occupied with all administrative duties should be deposited in the treasury itself and not given out; for that very reason, it is said: "One should deposit what is increased among the worthy recipients" (YDh 1.312). And having eaten daily, being free from fatigue and with a confident mind, he should inspect the spies already stationed there as well as those sent on various missions and those yet to be dispatched. For this is the summary of political science (*nīti*): indeed, every day, the king—being diligent, skilled in secret signals, and vigilant—must observe those of many kinds belonging to all stages of life (*āśrama*) and all heretical sects (*pāṣaṇḍa*), including those wearing sectarian marks (*liṅgin*), who are stationed in foreign or domestic kingdoms under the guise of various sciences, and who are concealed by the disguises of the blind, the mute, the lame, the deaf, the insane, and so forth, either by proclaiming themselves to be primarily full of curiosity or by establishing a reputation for being intent on wishing to benefit all beings. Alternatively, he should appoint a single person, such as a dwarf or a hunchback, who is well-tested, trusted, and renowned for being exceedingly beloved by him, to engage in the work of spying. He, in turn, should repeatedly report the entirety of the news concerning the king’s constant network of dispatched spies. Having thus observed the spies, he should, in accordance with the determination of their purpose, dispatch messengers on all matters as appropriate, joined by his chief ministers.
