Following the policy of the six measures of statecraft (*ṣāḍguṇya*), he must daily and vigilantly sow this seed of prosperity, which moves in diverse ways. || 323 ||
Since secrecy of counsel is the seed of prosperity, he should therefore move about at his own will, either alone or in the company of ministers;
having inspected the troops, he should deliberate with the commander-in-chief. (1.324)

Moving about at will and not disclosing secret counsel even to the Prime Minister—or rather, having the inspection of spies and such conducted only in the company of ministers in whom confidence has been established—is intended to mean that the lack of secrecy in counsel leads only to failure. The regulation of these two [freedom and secrecy] must be consistent with political expediency (*naya*). Even all ministers, though repeatedly and thoroughly tested, must be examined again and again; and one should engage in affairs as appropriate only with those who have been tested. Furthermore, having carefully inspected the various components of the forces—elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, weapons, armor, and so forth—in the presence of the Chief of the Army and the Commander-in-Chief, he should then deliberate skillfully upon the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) according to the sequence previously described. The intention is that the determination of peace, war, and the other measures depends precisely upon the state of the army, the treasury, and other resources. || 324 ||
Nor does the exclusive focus on wealth necessarily entail the abandonment of other human goals. What then?
"Having performed the twilight devotions, he should listen to the secret speech of spies;
he may enjoy himself with songs and dances, and he should likewise recite his own sacred study. (1.325)

He should enjoy himself with songs and dances, and may even indulge his desires; he should also recite his private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). The meaning is that he must not neglect his duties (*dharma*). Alternatively, this half-verse has a further purpose: to show that even in great calamity he remains free from despondency, being solely intent on reflecting upon his established tasks. Thus, for the sake of concealing his own misfortune or for lulling others into security, he should—without any agitation—enjoy himself with songs and dances, and likewise recite his *svādhyāya*. From the word "and" (*ca*), it follows that he may also engage in hunting. (325)
Furthermore: He should go to sleep to the sound of musical instruments, and likewise wake up in that same manner;
having awakened, he should contemplate the scriptures as well as all his duties.

To prevent the hearing of mantras from one who is dreaming, the threefold arts—consisting of dance, song, and instrumental music—should be employed in their proper places for as long as he sleeps. The word "and" (ca) is intended to include the sounding of praises and the like. In this way, even desire that has arisen becomes restrained, as does wealth. Having slept and awakened, free from fatigue, he should determine all matters with skillful wisdom through his proficiency in the three goals of life (trivarga). || 326 ||
And having thus carefully established the manifold principles of policy,
he should then respectfully dispatch spies among his own people and those of others,
while being greeted with blessings by the officiating priests, the family chaplain, and the teachers.

He should dispatch spies during the very last watch of the night to his own established circles of spies. Furthermore, he should dispatch spies with great respect toward those ministers of enemy kingdoms who have been won over by his skill in policy. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that he should also send spies among forest-dwellers and those situated within his own circle. Thus says Viśālākṣa: "Desiring victory and possessing far-reaching vision, the king should always honor those from the wilds through spies stationed in the wilds, and likewise those situated in the circle through such [spies]. (327)
Having thus dispatched his spies and offered oblations into the sacred fires, and being greeted with benedictions by the officiating priests and others, he should enter the assembly hall. Then,
having seen the astrologers and physicians, he should bestow cows, gold, land,
as well as household goods and houses upon those learned in the Vedas.

Having consulted with astrologers and physicians, having observed the configuration of the planets as they relate to his own body, and having understood specific omens, he should give cows, gold, and so forth to those learned in the Vedas according to their merit and in accordance with that [observation]. The rest is self-evident. || 328 ||
And this is another summary of essential policy for the acquisition and maintenance of a kingdom:

A king should be patient toward Brahmins, straightforward toward those who are affectionate, and wrathful toward his enemies; he should be like a father to his circle of servants and to his subjects. (1.329)
He is affectionate because he is bound solely by disinterested affection; he is straightforward, meaning he is not crooked. The rest is clear. || 329 ||
But why is this so?
Because, while protecting [the people] according to justice, he takes a sixth part of their merit.
Why?
For the righteous protection [of subjects] is superior to all forms of giving. (1.330)
By whom, then, are the subjects oppressed, such that this effort is required? It is said:
by rogues, thieves, evildoers, violent criminals, and the like;
and the subjects must be protected when oppressed, especially from scribes (kāyastha). (1.331)
The "body-dwellers" are passion and the other afflictions; others say they are scribes. 331.
If, however, the king does not provide protection from such [evils] as these,
then whatever sin the subjects commit while remaining unprotected,
for that the responsibility falls upon the king.
The word "might be" (syāt) is to be supplied.
Why?
Because he collects taxes (karān). 1.332

But how, then, should the king learn of the afflictions of his subjects? Has it not already been stated that he should appoint "supervisors who are experts in their respective fields" (YDh 1.317)? If it is asked, "What should be done when these very officials themselves act corruptly?", it is replied: "Having learned through spies the conduct of those appointed over the realm, he should always honor the virtuous, but put to death those who are the opposite. (1.333)
But when wicked people, having united with the supervisors and being greedy, should maltreat virtuous people, then he should also banish them,
having deprived those who live on bribes of their wealth;
as for those who are virtuous, [he should protect them].
He should always provide shelter for those learned in the Vedas with the six kinds of gifts, with honor, and with respectful treatment.

The mention of the *śrotriya* is for the sake of providing an illustration; or rather, the meaning is that one should provide shelter even through gifts and other means only to *śrotriyas*, and not even to ill-behaved people who pay taxes. || 334 ||
Since this is so, therefore:
The king who increases his own treasury from the kingdom by unjust means shall, before long, lose his royal fortune and go to ruin along with his kinsmen. (1.335)
But why is it precisely this? Because:
"The fire born from the torment and suffering of the subjects does not cease until it has consumed the king's lineage, his fortune, and his life. (1.336)

The intention is that due to such a great offense, they might even kill him by striking him with a single clod of earth; for the destruction of the treasury, the army, and so forth is certain, since those depend upon him as their root. 336.

"But surely, if there is oppression even in a foreign kingdom, this same fault applies. "O you who are ignorant of what is dharma and its opposite, do not say so! Whatever dharma belongs to a king in the protection of his own kingdom, he obtains that entire merit when bringing a foreign kingdom under his control. (1.337)
Such is the nature of things; however, the intention here is that no further fault need even be suspected. || 337 ||
However, whatever conduct, custom, or tradition is established in a family, that very same thing must be maintained when one has come under their power. (1.338)

The phrase "without contradicting the Dharma" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Although protection [of the king] would follow from [the king being] one's own [master], this statement is made for the sake of [stating] a specific quality. || 338 ||

How, then, is success in another kingdom achieved? We say: by means of counsel (*mantra*). For the treasury, the army, and so forth, are dependent upon it. And therefore: "Since the kingdom has its root in counsel, one should keep that counsel well-guarded, such that others do not know its actions until the emergence of their results. (1.339)

Since counsel alone, when well-determined and well-guarded, is the cause for the acquisition, maintenance, and increase of one's own and others' kingdoms, it must therefore be kept secure through both determination and secrecy; for in the opposite case, there is the danger of total ruin. Furthermore, even when the fruit has arisen, the counsel should not be disclosed, because it might be repeated in that same manner. People, inferring the cause from the observation of the result, might—driven by curiosity—fail to determine the specific details. Therefore, the concealment of counsel must be strictly observed in every way toward both friends and enemies alike. For the powers of energy (*utsāha*) and lordship (*prabhu*) are dependent solely on the power of counsel; indeed, even in the absence of those two, success is seen to occur through the power of counsel alone. Thus, effort must be made to guard it. (339)

What, then, is that which is to be deliberated upon? It has been stated [to include]: the deployment of spies through movement in various directions and the dispatching of envoys; the employment of agents disguised as mendicants, ascetics, householders, merchants, and forest-dwellers; the investigation of the network of secret reports; the elimination of mendicants and others employed by enemies; the construction of forts and other works; the entrusting of deposits; the consideration regarding princes; and the conduct within the inner apartments—these and many other such matters. Furthermore, this other point:

The enemy, the friend, and the neutral party—the one immediately adjacent, the one beyond him, and the one further still—this circle of states (*maṇḍala*) should be considered in due order, employing the strategic means beginning with conciliation (*sāman*). (1.340)

For one who desires victory, the king whose territory is adjacent is the enemy; beyond him is the ally; and beyond that is the neutral king. Thus is this circle of states situated, and it should be dealt with as appropriate through conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and force. 340.
But why is there an application of conciliation and the other [means] according to what is appropriate? Because:
"The means are conciliation, generosity, sowing dissension, and likewise punishment;
and precisely because they are means."
Those who are correctly applied will succeed; however, punishment is a resort only when there is no other way.

Conciliation (*sāman*) is both verbal and physical. Generosity (*dāna*) consists of accepting what is being given without anger and giving away one's own property. Sowing dissension (*bheda*) is the inciting of a rift between those who are united. Force (*daṇḍa*) is the subduing by means of violence. These [means] should be employed individually or collectively as appropriate. When the first three expedients have failed, force is to be used. In this regard, the enemy is of three kinds: natural (*sahaja*), artificial (*kṛtrima*), and the immediate neighbor (*bhūmyanantara*). The immediate neighbor can be subdued only by force. Likewise, a friend is categorized as natural, artificial, or the neighbor of the neighbor (*anantarapara*). The neighbor of the neighbor is within the scope of conciliation and bribery. Conciliation alone is to be used toward neutral parties. Those on the side of the enemy are always to be divided. Such methods, following various applications like the purification of materials, are governed by the rule for the employment of conciliation and the rest, having considered "the place, the time, and likewise oneself" (BDh 1.8.53). || 341 ||

Having duly deliberated upon these constituent elements of sovereignty, beginning with the sovereign himself, the seeker of victory—possessing well-guarded counsel—should appropriately employ these strategic means: peace, war, marching, halting, seeking refuge, and the double policy. (1.342)

A treaty for the mutual benefit of both parties through the exchange of gold and other assets is a *saṃdhi*. Sometimes it yields fruit for both immediately; sometimes it yields fruit for one immediately and for the other in the future. Thus Manu says:
"Whether involving joint military action or otherwise, a treaty characterized by two aspects should be understood as being connected to both the present and the future" (MDh 7.163).

In this manner, the two-fold nature of war (*vigraha*) and the other [strategic means] should also be illustrated. War is the opposite of peace (*saṃdhi*). Marching (*yāna*) is the movement toward enemies when there is an excess of superior strength. Remaining stationary (*āsana*) is the state of not undertaking action. Double-dealing (*dvaidhībhāva*) is the employment of the seeds of both peace and war. Seeking refuge (*saṃśraya*) is taking shelter with another when one has been depleted. Peace is made when one is currently depleted but expects future prosperity; in the opposite case, it is war. Both may also result from the obstruction of a friend. One who is depleted, out of regard for a friend and in consideration of the power of his own forces, should gradually pacify his enemies and maintain his position through remaining stationary. Furthermore, one who is depleted and besieged should divide his army into two parts and employ the seeds of both [peace and war]. However, when all resources are exhausted or due to a calamity within his own forces, he should quickly seek refuge with a king who is of noble birth, powerful, non-greedy, righteous, supported by his ancestors, and surrounded by a multitude of friends. In every way, he should propitiate that very king through conciliation (*sāma*) and the bestowing of gifts (*upapradāna*). Thus it is said:
"One should always serve with every effort that [king] who effects the suppression of both his subjects and the enemy's forces, just as one serves a teacher. (MDh 7.175).

But when he is endowed with the powers of counsel (*mantra*), energy (*utsāha*), and sovereignty (*prabhu*), then, having made arrangements for the territory to be attacked (*yātavya*), he should march against the enemy. And so they say: "When two neighboring kings are both overcome by calamity, one should not march against them; rather, one should march against that very enemy. || 342 ||

Whether proceeding at the request of an ally or by his own will, he should march against a foreign kingdom when it is properly endowed with [favorable] conditions according to the rules for future undertakings; that is, when the enemy is weak and his own self is joyful, possessing well-trained mounts and men. (1.343)
The meaning of this verse is already explained. || 343 ||

[Objection: But in that case, this entire undertaking is useless, since we observe reversals even for those who are most prosperous; and so it was seen in the case of Suyodhana during his expedition against Virāṭa. And it has been said: "The rises and falls of kings depend upon the planets" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.303). Therefore, because sovereignty is dependent on fate, we consider this Smṛti to have its very root destroyed. [Reply: O you ignorant of human effort! It is not so. Success is established in both fate and human effort; the intention is not that it depends on fate alone.
Furthermore, Your Majesty has not yet defined the nature of destiny; for it is said:
"In that regard, destiny is the manifestation of human effort from a previous life. (1.344)
The meaning is that only the human effort belonging to a previous birth is called "fate" (daiva), and nothing else. || 344 ||

[Objection: But even so, the exposition of the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) is indeed useless. [Response: It is said: For this would be the case only if everything were dependent solely upon fate (*daiva*); however, when it is said:
"Some goals of men are accomplished through fate, some through force, and some through human effort (*puruṣakāra*)."
In that case, the implication is that this objection is not to be raised. Furthermore: "But their source is the power of the Puruṣa. (1.345)

The meaning is that among those [factors]—fate, chance, and human effort—it is human effort alone that is the source (*yoni*) or cause. Even "chance," which refers to an extraordinary resolve such as the propitiation of a *vetāla* and the like, is also simply an extraordinary form of human effort; this is the meaning. Therefore, it is well said: "But their source is human effort. (345)
But even so, our objection remains unrefuted! Oh, how truly extraordinary is Mātṛmata’s discernment! Behold:
"Just as a chariot cannot move with only a single wheel, so too destiny does not succeed without human effort. (1.346)

For even those things that are perfectly endowed with destiny (*daiva*) do not transcend the established order of objects. Food, even when brought near, never enters the mouth without effort (*vyāpāra*). If it is argued that effort itself comes from destiny alone, we say no; for destiny is also preceded by that [effort], as was stated previously that the word "destiny" refers to past action (*karman*). If it is argued that this [past action] too is due to another destiny, then there would be an infinite regress (*avyavasthā*). If it is argued that let it be so, as it is faultless because it is beginningless (*anādi*), we say no; for it would follow that it is causeless (*nirnimitta*). And if that were asserted, the independence of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) would remain unestablished. Furthermore, it is logical to postulate the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) in accordance with what is seen, not by contradicting what is seen. Moreover, in this way, the authority of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) would be undermined. And if another cause were postulated, the postulation of the unseen would be unavoidable. Therefore, it is established that this entire teaching is appropriate because of the primacy of human effort. 346.

If, however, while engaged in an expedition for equal results with an ally, the enemy—being hemmed in—is unable [to resist] and offers up territory and so forth, then why should one not accomplish one’s own purpose by outmaneuvering the ally? For Manu has also said: "So that allies, neutrals, and enemies do not outmaneuver him," and so forth (MDh 7.180), as well as, "He should provide for his own welfare" (MDh 7.57). [The opponent replies: "O you who are unskilled in distinguishing between dharma and its opposite, do not speak thus! For the acquisition of an ally is better than the acquisition of gold or land."
Therefore, one should strive for its attainment; being composed, one should protect the truth. || 1.347 ||
Composed, he possesses direct knowledge of the welfare of both worlds. || 347 ||
Furthermore:
The sovereign, the minister, the people, the fort, the treasury, the army, and likewise the allies—these constituent elements (prakṛtis) are said to constitute the sevenfold kingdom. (1.348)

The sovereign is the king; the minister is the counselor; the people are the subjects; the treasury is the accumulation of wealth; the rod is the force consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; and allies and fortresses have already been mentioned. These are indeed the seven constituent elements (*prakṛti*). It is with reference to these that the kingdom is said to have seven limbs; therefore, the meaning is that just as the self, the ministers, and the other constituent elements must be protected with effort, so too must the allies. || 348 ||

Thus, having somehow obtained through both destiny and human effort a kingdom that is possible to acquire due to a multitude of various merits from the past and through the possession of diverse qualities in this life—a king who is wise, learned, and true to his word—should, upon attaining it, inflict punishment upon the wicked. Why? Because:
For Dharma was created of old by Brahmā in the form of the rod of punishment.

Having obtained that kingdom which is so difficult to acquire, the king—being intent on attaining the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*) through the impartial application of all forms of punishment—should, after careful consideration, inflict appropriate punishment upon those who are incorrigible. He must not, out of excessive soft-heartedness, cause a wound to his own heart. This very thing called punishment was created and ordained by Brahmā through the Veda for the sake of benefiting the entire multitude of living beings within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). The word "formerly" (*pure*) is used to encourage its practice without doubt due to its beginninglessness. Thus says Gautama: "Then, by the remainder [of his merit], he attains a distinguished country and birth" (GDh 11.29), and beginning with that, "Those who act contrary to this perish in all directions; the instruction of the teacher and punishment protect them. Therefore, the king and the teacher are beyond reproach" (GDh 11.30–32). And the Sacred Tradition (*Āmnāya*) says: "In the beginning, this world existed as one—the gods and humans. When the gods were unable to make humans their own through favors, they vanished. Prajāpati said to them: 'Who will protect the subjects on earth? You have all disappeared. If unprotected, the subjects, afflicted by unrighteousness (*adharma*), will abandon the giving of gifts and the livelihood that belongs to us. Those gods said to Prajāpati: 'Let us make a king in human form; taking the form from Soma, the splendor from Āditya, the prowess from Indra, victory from Viṣṇu, liberality from Vaiśravaṇa, and restraint from Yama... and so on, until: 'He said: "Make Dharma itself my companion; then I shall protect the subjects. Then they made Dharma his second [companion]. That Dharma, in its essential nature, is punishment (*daṇḍa*). Therefore, such a king should inflict punishment even upon his father. With Dharma I shall consecrate him for sovereignty, for the state of Indra, and for the world of Brahmā. I am the lord of one who acts thus. (349)
And since such is the nature of this punishment,
it cannot be administered by one who is greedy and of undisciplined mind.
By whom, then, can it be administered?
By one who is true to his word, pure, well-assisted, and wise.

But for what purpose is this effort? Because: "Being employed according to the scriptures, it would gladden the entire world, including its gods, asuras, and humans; otherwise, however, it would cause distress. (1.351)
Since the joy and the wrath of the entire world depend upon punishment, the intended meaning is that effort must be exerted in the administration of punishment. || 351 ||
Since this is so, therefore:
Unjust punishment destroys the world, heaven, and fame;
but just punishment brings a king heaven, fame, and victory. (1.352)
The world consists of the acquisition of foreign kingdoms and the stability of one's own kingdom; the rest is clear. || 352 ||

And because the attainment of heaven and other rewards results from proper punishment, therefore: "Whether it be a brother, a son, one worthy of honor, a father-in-law, or even a maternal uncle—there is no one who, having deviated from his own duty, is exempt from being punished by the king. (1.353)
Having reflected thus:

"The king who punishes those deserving of punishment and causes those deserving of death to be executed properly, would by that merit have performed sacrifices accompanied by hundreds of thousands of sacrificial fees. (1.354)

The intention is that just like violence for the sake of a sacrifice (*kratvarthahiṃsā*), violence against thieves and others is also indeed righteous (*dharmya*). The *Rājasūya* has a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of a hundred thousand; the plural number is used because there are many such sacrifices. Alternatively, the *Agniṣṭoma* and other rites have a fee of a hundred, while the *Abhijit* and others have a fee of a thousand. The rest is clear. (354)

Having reflected thus, for the purpose of establishing the distinction between those who deserve punishment and those who do not, and between those who deserve death and those who do not, the king, surrounded by his assessors, should personally examine the legal cases daily, each yielding fruit equal to that of a sacrifice. (1.355)

"Separately" means individually. Alternatively, the connection is that "separately" [refers to] a fruit equal to a sacrifice; the meaning is that by punishing each one [offender] individually, one obtains the fruit of a sacrifice. || 355 ||

Thus the procedure for corporal punishment has been stated. Now, in order to state the measure of monetary punishment (*arthadaṇḍa*) in relation to the middle and lowest degrees of violence (*sāhasa*) and so forth, he says:
"A particle of water suspended in a sunbeam is known as a *trasareṇu* (a mote of dust).
Eight of those are a *likṣā* (nit), and three of those are called a *rājasarṣapa* (mustard seed). (1.356)

The dust that is seen like water within a sunbeam, when perceived through the notion of duality, is called a *trasareṇu*. It is termed *trasareṇu* because it moves about as if trembling (*trasta*). Eight of those particles combined constitute a *likṣā*. Three of those are called a *rājasarṣapa*. This same principle should be applied to the subsequent measurements as well. || 356 ||
Three *gaura* are one *yava*; three medium *yava* are one *kṛṣṇala*; five *kṛṣṇala* are one *māṣa*; and sixteen *māṣa* are one *suvarṇa*.
A *pala* is proclaimed to be four or even five *suvarṇas*, as both usages are observed; its determination depends on the specific purpose at hand. || 357 ||
Thus, first, the measurement of gold has been stated up to the limit of a *pala*. Now, regarding silver:
two *kṛṣṇalas* make one silver *māṣa*, and sixteen of those make a *dharaṇa*. (1.358)
Ten *dharaṇas* make one *śatamāna*, which is indeed a *pala*.

Two *kṛṣṇalas* make a silver *māṣa*. Sixteen *māṣas* make a *dharaṇa*. Ten *dharaṇas* make a *śatamāna*; when calculated, that is exactly four gold *suvarṇas*, and thus it becomes a *pala* measured by a *pala*. || 358 ||
Thus the measurement of silver has been stated. Now, regarding gold alone:
four *suvarṇas* make a *niṣka*; a copper coin weighing one *kārṣika* is a *paṇa*. (1.359)
A fine of eighty thousand paṇas is called the highest amercement (uttamasāhasa);
half of that is declared the middle amercement (madhyama), and half of that is remembered as the lowest amercement (adhama).

As for what was stated—that a *pala* consists of four *sauvarṇikas*—that very same unit has a second designation, namely *niṣka*. A *karṣa* of copper, however, is designated as a *paṇa*. A *karṣa* consists of sixteen *māṣas* and eighty *kṛṣṇalas*. This is demonstrated [by the text]: "A fine of ten thousand *paṇas*, plus eighty, is the highest *sāhasa*. This very thing denoted by the word *paṇa* is the eighty *kṛṣṇalas*. The mention of copper is illustrative; it applies to gold and silver as well. The *kārṣika-paṇa* is to be applied depending on the specific type of fine. A *sāhasa* multiplied by a thousand is the highest *sāhasa* fine. Alternatively, "plus eighty" (*sāśīti*) means that which exists together with eighty; the meaning is "one thousand plus eighty. Half of that is the middle *sāhasa* fine. Regarding the word "recorded" (*smṛta*), the meaning is that this rule is derived from the *Śāstra* and not from any other source of authority. The assignment of these designations is for the sake of practical usage within one's own *Śāstra*, so that these very terms may be employed in the statements concerning fines such as the highest *sāhasa*. (359–360)

Now, should the punishment for all offenses be applied according to the scale of the highest fine and so forth? No, it is said: "Reprimand by word, then censure, the fine of wealth, and likewise corporal punishment—these should be applied individually or collectively, according to the gravity of the offense. (1.361)

The punishment of speech (*vāgdaṇḍa*) consists merely in the naming of the offense. The punishment of reproach (*dhigdaṇḍa*) is censure. The punishment of wealth (*dhanadaṇḍa*) has already been described. The punishment of death (*vadhadaṇḍa*) is corporeal. The word "likewise" (*tathā*) refers to such purposes as exorcism (*uccāṭana*). The rest is clear. || 361 ||
And here is the summary of the principles of legal procedure:

Having ascertained the offense, as well as the place, the time, and the strength [of the offender], and having also considered age, occupation, and wealth, one should determine the punishment. (1.362)

The repetition of the word "offense" (*aparādha*) is for the sake of providing an illustration. The intention is that just as the determination of punishment is made after knowing the offense and in consideration of it, so too is it determined in consideration of place, time, and other such factors. The repetition of the word "having known" (*jñātvā*) is for the purpose of reopening a legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) in accordance with *dharma*, even when the case has already been decided. The rest is clear. || 362 ||

Thus, having assembled his court, the king Sudhāman— resplendent, exceedingly radiant, a source of delight, and possessed of valorous character— like the sun, impartial toward his subjects, sustains the entire world through his administration of justice.
Whatever true matter has not been recorded by me here for fear of excessive prolixity,
that should be discerned by commentators from the oral traditions.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Bālakrīḍā*, a commentary on the *Dharmaśāstra* composed by the supreme venerable Yājñavalkya and written by Viśvarūpa.
The Chapter on Legal Procedure (Vyavahārādhyāya): Now begins the section on General Principles.

It has been stated that a king desiring victory and wishing to attain the accumulation of prosperity should, through diligent effort, seize the kingdoms of his enemies and expand his own realm. Furthermore, it has also been stated that the kingdom must be protected even from those who are the most formidable enemies—namely, fraudulent spies, wicked agents, and bandits. Now, for the purpose of discerning the methods for their eradication, the author introduces the exposition of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*).
Free from anger and greed, the king should examine legal cases together with learned Brāhmaṇas, in accordance with the Dharmaśāstras. (2.1)

But has this not already been stated previously at [YDh 1.355]: “Having reflected thus, the king”? True; however, this undertaking is for the sake of [attaining] excellence (*guṇa*), so that the primary aim should not be the mere desire to accumulate a treasury. The meaning is that the king should examine legal disputes solely in accordance with the *dharmaśāstra*. Furthermore, [he should do so] together with learned Brāhmaṇas. Even though the Brāhmaṇas possess the status of expounders (*pravaktṛ*), their utility lies solely in being assistants to the king. The king alone, however, is the judge (*draṣṭṛ*) because he possesses the power to inflict punishment and grant favor. For this very reason it is said: “free from anger and greed. Even though he is capable, he must act in accordance with the *dharmaśāstra*; the meaning is that he must not conduct the legal process otherwise under the influence of anger and the like. Although the legal process is a single entity, the plural number is used in view of its own specific subdivisions. As Manu says: “Of these, the first is non-payment of debt” (MDh 8.4), and so forth; and Nārada says: “It has four feet and pervades four [spheres]” (NSm Mā 1.8), and so forth. || 1 ||
And since the Dharmaśāstras hold primacy in the administration of justice, for this reason:
The king should appoint as members of his court those who are perfected in Vedic learning and study, of noble birth, speakers of truth, and who are impartial toward both enemy and friend. (2.2)
The verse has been stated in prose. || 2 ||

And because the king’s own practice of overseeing legal proceedings is based on a visible foundation, even though it serves an invisible (transcendental) purpose, he should— after considering the gravity or lightness of the cases according to their requirements— appoint a Brāhmaṇa learned in all the laws to act as judge in place of himself when, due to the pressure of business, he is unable to oversee the lawsuits personally, together with the members of the court. (2.3)
He too, because he occupies the position of a king, must be entirely free from anger and other such passions. || 3 ||
And for this very reason:

"Whether out of passion, hatred, or even fear, those members of the court who act contrary to the law or fail in their mindfulness shall each be punished with double the amount of the fine in dispute. (2.4)

Those who act contrary to the matters declared in the legal codes (*smṛti*) due to passion and other such motives shall each be fined double that amount. By the inclusion of the word "and others" (*ādi*), the intention is that this also applies to those who wish to lead the meaning of the *smṛti* astray. Furthermore, the king or his representative shall be fined double the total fine imposed upon all the members of the court (*sabhyas*), because the judicial decision depends upon them. For this very reason, there is the distributive repetition "each individually" (*pṛthak pṛthak*). Each member of the court shall be fined double the amount of the dispute, and the king shall be fined double that [total]. Thus he will state later. (4)

Now, should litigants be brought to trial by the king or his officers after he has sought them out? No, because it is prohibited. As Manu says: "Neither the king himself nor his officer should initiate a legal case" (MDh 8.43). How, then, does the commencement of a lawsuit occur? It is said:
"When one who has been oppressed by others brings a matter before the king through a path that deviates from the traditional law and custom, that indeed constitutes the basis for a lawsuit" (2.5).

For that alone is the basis for legal procedure (*vyavahārapada*) which someone might describe as "corrupted by an external path devoid of traditional law (*smṛti*) and custom (*ācāra*), and disconnected [from truth]"; the intention is not that one should personally initiate the legal action oneself. And so says Nārada:

"But the plaintiff, having determined his own strength, impelled by his own interest, and having reached a certainty regarding the matter to be accomplished, shall cause the *pūrvapakṣa* (the initial claim) to be written down. (NSm Mā 2.1)

*Smṛtyācāra* refers to conduct prescribed by the *smṛtis*. Alternatively, this may refer to the intention behind family customs (*kuladharma*) and so forth. The phrase "by others" is intended to exclude disputes between teacher and pupil. Thus says Nārada:
"Between teacher and pupil, father and son, husband and wife, and master and servant—among these who are united [in such relations], no legal dispute is recognized."
One [man] together with many, as well as women and servants.
And so forth. And Kātyāyana says:
"A plaint that is contrary to the state, one that has been rejected by the king, or one that is confused by multiple points, does not succeed."
And so forth. "To be traversed by conventional usage" means that it is to be defined through conceptual determination. || 5 ||
When the plaintiff has thus made his representation, the king, having summoned the defendant without guile with the consent of the plaintiff, the defendant, and the members of the court,
shall have the defendant write down in his presence a document according to what was stated by the plaintiff,
marked with the year, month, fortnight, day, names, caste, and other identifying characteristics. (2.6)

The phrase "as reported" (*yathāveditam*) is for the purpose of making known the offense as qualified by its duration, motive, and so forth. A "year" (*samā*) is a full year; a "month" (*māsa*) is clear; "half of that" (*tadardham*) is a fortnight (*ardhamāsa*). The inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*) is for the purpose of defining the details of the formal statement (*bhāṣā*) in accordance with other *smṛtis*. As Kātyāyana says: "Having reported the time—namely the year, month, fortnight, and lunar day—as well as the place of writing, the subject matter, and the location, caste, and physical appearance [of the parties]."

The measure of the object to be accomplished, the substance, the number, and likewise the name of the self; the names of the kings in sequence, the residence, and the name of the person for whom the rite is performed.
"One should formulate [the plaint] by sequentially proclaiming the names of the ancestors, the injury, the plaintiff and the defendant, the evidence of the case, the time, and the fortnight.

These items, having been examined according to reason, should be written down either individually or collectively. Furthermore, one should first write them on the ground, correct the plaint, and only afterwards proceed with the formal filing of the document. As it has been said:
One should rectify matters that are excessive and supplement those that are deficient;
one should establish them on the ground for as long as the legal position remains firm.

Those who know the subject (*pakṣa*) understand it to be that which is free from defects of the proposition, is the object to be proven, is endowed with valid reasons, is certain, and is established in the world.
And so forth. As for the defects of the thesis (*pratijñā-doṣa*), as it has been said:
"The king should avoid a thesis that is unestablished, defective, meaningless, purposeless, impossible to prove, or contradictory."
He who does not wish to act with justice for me, or even acts unjustly,
and likewise does not cause it to be recorded in writing— his case shall not succeed.

And so forth. And Nārada says: "In the course of oral proceedings, the defendant shall not present his answer until the plaintiff has cleared up [his claim] as far as the matter he intends to state. (NSm Mā 2.7)

The intention here is that there is no occasion for quibbles, futile rejoinders, and the like; thus, as before, one should cause [the opponent] to hear what is properly formulated and committed to writing. || 6 ||
The reply to the matter heard must be written in the presence of the plaintiff.

"Matter heard" (*śrutārtha*) means that which has been both heard and is a substantive matter; if there is a reply corresponding to that, then it should be written. Otherwise, the intention is that there is certain defeat. The phrase "in the presence of" (*saṃnidhau*) is for the sake of an immediate decision. This should be understood as pertaining to urgent matters, because it is so.
Then the plaintiff shall immediately have a document prepared that establishes the proven facts of the case.
The meaning is that one should not let time pass [without acting]. || 7 ||
But why is there an effort to state the proof for the meaning of the thesis? Because:
"When that [proof] is established, one attains success; otherwise, the opposite occurs.
And it has been said:
"The essence of legal proceedings is declared to be the plaint;
upon its failure, the plaintiff loses, while he who crosses over it becomes the defendant" (NSm Mā 1.6).
For this very reason, the argument advanced by the logicians—that the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is not an integral part [of the syllogism]—is also refuted.
For this fourfold judicial procedure has been set forth for use in legal disputes. (2.8)

The phrase "by means of logic (*nyāya*) and scripture (*āgama*)" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Thus, it consists of four parts: the proposition (*pratijñā*), the subsequent proof (*sādhana*), and the final determination (*nirṇaya*). Otherwise, it would not be so. Therefore, the intention is that the process of debate proceeds precisely according to the sequence of the proposition. || 8 ||

But surely, when one who has been told, "This man has wronged me," returns that very accusation against him without having first settled his own claim, then this sequence of procedure is not logical. True; for that very reason [the author says]: "One should not bring an accusation against another without having first settled one's own accusation; nor should one lead an accused person, who has not been charged by another, into a state of agitation. (2.9)

One should not bring a charge against a plaintiff without having first resolved one’s own charge, for that would lead to an infinite regress and the failure of the legal proceeding. For this very reason, even one who is being charged by another must not be charged in return. Nor should one deny a matter that has been stated by oneself. || 9 ||
The exception to this is as follows:
"But in cases of mutual assault and verbal abuse, one may bring a counter-charge;
in both instances, a guarantor capable of resolving the matter must be secured. (2.10)

One should not bring a charge of *sāhasa* (violence) or similar offenses without first having exhausted one's own efforts; this is the meaning of "this very method constitutes the determination in that case. Furthermore, in all disputes, when an immediate decision cannot be reached, a guarantor (*pratibhū*) capable of resolving the matter must be taken from both parties. || 10 ||
But when one party has been defeated according to the legal process, then: "If he denies [the claim] and is proven [guilty], he shall pay the debt to the king and an equal amount as a fine;
the one who brings a false accusation shall pay double the amount of the claim. (2.11)

*Nihnava* means concealment or denial. In that case, when the matter has been made clear, one must pay as much as requested by the creditor; and an equal amount to the king. But when one makes a false accusation, then twice the amount requested by the accuser must be paid as a fine to the king alone—this is the meaning. || 11 ||
But is there an immediate determination of legal proceedings in every case? True; that is indeed logical. Nevertheless:

"In cases of violence, theft, verbal or physical assault, a false accusation of a capital crime, and regarding women, one should litigate immediately; in other matters, the time may be according to one's wish. (2.12)

*Sāhasa* (outrageous violence) is that which is done suddenly and forcibly, without even investigating the conclusion, relying solely on one's own strength. *Steya* (theft) and *pāruṣya* (assault/abuse) he will describe later. *Go'bhishāpa* is an accusation involving the killing of a cow; the mention of "cow" is for the sake of illustration, as it refers to the accusation against all horned animals. *Atyaya* is a matter for which there is no capacity to wait for time. And where women are the parties involved, one should settle the dispute immediately because of the contradiction in waiting for time; the meaning is that one should bring the litigation to a conclusion. However, in other cases such as the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇādāna*), one may indeed wait for time, or it depends on the desire of the court (*dhruvādhikaraṇa*). As Nārada has said: [The verse from Nārada follows here.]
"Because disputes are complex and because memory is momentary, one may, out of a desire to know the truth, take as much time as desired regarding debts and other such matters. (NSm Mā 1.38) || 12 ||

Surely, the activities of men are of many kinds. In that regard, if one person, due to unskillfulness in verbal expression suited to legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), appears like a liar even when the matter is true; while another, clever in deceitful dealings, appears like a speaker of truth even when the matter is false; and consequently, the effort to determine legal procedure would indeed be useless—this is true, provided there were no means for ascertaining discrimination. But there certainly is such a means: "He goes from place to place and licks the corners of his mouth."
His forehead perspires and his face turns pale. || 2.13 ||
With parched mouth and faltering speech, he speaks much that is contradictory;
he does not honor his words or his eyes, and he even distorts his lips. (2.14)
If one undergoes a change from their natural state through actions of mind, speech, or body during a legal proceeding or when testifying, that person is declared to be corrupt. || 2.15 ||

Even if, through skill in the ways of worldly convention or by relying on some assistant, one produces an impression that appears to be virtuous, nevertheless, he who possesses such signs as these is proclaimed to be corrupt. The use of the word "proclaimed" (*parikīrtita*) is for the purpose of making known the certainty of his corruption. Furthermore, one whose cleverness is clearly understood is to be determined [as corrupt] by such signs; however, this may indeed occur even in another person who lacks presence of mind or who has been intimidated by rogues. Therefore, it is faultless [to conclude] that these signs must be established by distinguishing them in this manner. *Sṛkvaṇī* refers to the corners of the mouth. The phrase "he does not honor speech or sight" (*vākcakṣuḥ pūjayati no*) is the grammatical split. The meaning is that he does not offer respect to either speech or the eyes. Respect for speech consists in the firm confidence in one's own words; respect for the eyes consists in the firm confidence in one's gaze. *Oṣṭhanirbhujana* is the distorting of the lips in various ways, or licking them with the tongue. The rest is clear. (13–15)

Furthermore, when two parties are in conflict over a legal matter and possess the capacity to settle it by relying solely on their own strength—even without reporting it to the king—must they nevertheless necessarily report it to the king? Yes; this is indeed proper. For it is said:
"He who settles a disputed matter on his own authority, he who absconds, or he who says nothing when summoned—he is declared defeated and liable to punishment. (2.16)

Just as one who, having been summoned by the king, flees and perishes, or one who, having gone into the presence of the king, says nothing despite possessing esteemed eloquence, would be defeated and liable to punishment—likewise, he who, without establishing a certainty through legal reasoning regarding a matter contested by the opponent, should instead settle it arbitrarily and independently, is also defeated and deserves punishment; such is the intended meaning. || 16 ||

Thus, first of all, where there are witnesses, the decision depends entirely upon them; in their absence, or in the case of their contrary testimony, it depends on signs such as their departure to another country and so forth. But where both parties have witnesses or signs such as departure to another country and so forth, how is it decided? It is said: "When witnesses exist for both sides, the witnesses belong to the plaintiff; when the initial claim has been refuted, they belong to the defendant. (2.17)

In what case, then, is there the possibility of witnesses for both parties? It is where the defendant (uttaravādī) counters the lawsuit by means of a plea of denial (*pratyavaskandana*). For example, when one person says, "My property was taken by this man at such a time and in such a place," and another replies: "True, if that is so; however, I shall prove by means of witnesses that at that time I was in another country, away from the specified location. In that situation, if witnesses are accepted for both sides, the witnesses should belong to the plaintiff alone (*pūrvavādī*), because the proceedings of the lawsuit proceed primarily on his basis. But where the initial claim has been rendered invalid, there the witnesses should belong to the defendant alone. For example: "It is true that he spoke exactly as he did; however, I have already returned it to him, and thus I shall prove this by means of witnesses. (17)

But when he should again defeat him by means of this same method of counter-objection (*pratyavaskandana*) as before, how would that be? Not so. If such a succession of superiority and inferiority were allowed, there would be no finality at all. What then is the solution? Only by the introduction of a higher stake (*abhyadhika-paṇa*) can the legal proceeding be brought to a conclusion; otherwise, there would indeed be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). And therefore: "If a dispute should be accompanied by a stake, one should cause the loser to pay the stake, as well as a fine, and the money itself to the creditor. (YDh 2.18)

The fine and the stake must be paid to the king. "Svapaṇa" means a stake of one's own; the meaning is that it is the stake which a wealthy person has made in order to turn back the legal proceedings. However, the king should cause the wealth itself to be paid to the creditor alone. The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of including other forms of punishment, such as verbal censure (*dhig-daṇḍa*) and so forth. Thus far, the rule regarding the confusion of witnesses has been stated. But what about when there is a confusion of signs, such as perspiration on the forehead? In that case as well, since the Smṛti texts concerning signs and the like are rooted in inference, the determination of the legal proceeding depends entirely upon the correct ascertainment of inference. || 18 ||

In every respect, however, the king should conduct legal proceedings by setting aside deception and relying on the truth; for legal procedure indeed has its origin in falsehood and is based solely upon artifice. And so it was said by Nārada:
When men were single-mindedly devoted to Dharma and speakers of truth, there was then no legal dispute, nor hatred, nor even envy.
"When Dharma has perished among men, legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) has been set in motion; and the king, the wielder of the rod, has been made the judge of those legal procedures. (NSm Mā 1.1–2).
The meaning is that unrighteousness (*adharma*) predominates in legal proceedings.
And since this is so, therefore:
"Even a fact, if not presented, is lost in legal proceedings. (2.19)
Otherwise, a matter is decided through the path of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*). As it has been said:
"Māṇḍavya, though not a thief, became a thief by virtue of legal procedure" (NSm Mā 1.36).
Therefore, the meaning is that a king who has diligently eliminated fraud and the like, and who is solely devoted to truth, should be proficient in legal proceedings. || 19 ||

If, however, one who has been charged with multiple matters initially says "no" to everything, but later admits to some part in some manner, should he be made to pay only that much? No, it is said: "When a defendant denies a written claim and is proved on one part, he must be made by the king to pay all the amounts; but what was not previously declared shall not be taken. (2.20)

If he has written down [the claim] by way of denying multiple items and reported it to the king, yet later denies it, and if that [denial] is subsequently proven regarding even one part [of the claim], then he must be made to pay all the amounts along with the fines. However, if it was not written down, then even if such [a denial] occurs, he is not to be fined. Alternatively, there is another interpretation of the rule "he is not to be seized if he has not reported [the debt]": the king should make the debtor pay the entire amount to the creditor, but he is not to be fined; the meaning is that this applies even if [the denial] was not intended [by the debtor]. || 20 ||

"Surely, even if he is not intended by him [the king], he must still be punished because he has committed an offense; for such cases are indeed the very sources from which a king derives revenue. Otherwise, the king’s power of punishment would apply only in rare instances. Do not say so. For it is an established principle: "In a conflict between traditional law (smṛti) and logic (nyāya), logic prevails in legal proceedings; however, in a conflict between the science of statecraft (arthaśāstra) and the science of dharma (dharmaśāstra), the science of dharma is more powerful. (2.21)

If there were conformity with the *Arthaśāstra*, then this might indeed be so. But since the *Dharmaśāstra* alone is authoritative, then the accumulation of wealth that is contrary to it is superior. [Objection: If this is the case, then even in a situation where there is the appearance of truth regarding an untrue matter, the fault would accrue to the king; as in the case of the execution of Māṇḍavya and others, for according to the *Smṛti*, punishment is ordained only for those who have actually committed an offense. And in that case, even if an offense is legally established, because it does not exist in reality, the person is not at all an offender. Nor is there any other basis for the decision of a legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, this is a dilemma. [Response: There is no dilemma here. When there is a conflict between *Smṛti* and *Nyāya*, *Nyāya* is stronger. Why? Because of the legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*). The meaning is that otherwise, the functioning of legal proceedings would be impossible. Alternatively, in a conflict between *Smṛti* and *Nyāya*, *Smṛti* alone is superior, not *Nyāya*, because *Nyāya* functions through legal proceedings. A legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) is a "various carrying away" (*vividham avaharaṇam*), meaning it is full of artifice. And such a proceeding must not be accepted even if it contradicts the scriptures. For the established rule is that the *Dharmaśāstra* is more powerful than the *Arthaśāstra*. The other [the *Arthaśāstra*] is merely conventional (*aparamārtha*). This very interpretation is the superior one. The operation of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) follows the thing as it exists; the thing does not conform to the operation of the means of knowledge. Once the thing is established, the comprehension of the means of knowledge follows it; thus there is no fault. Others, however, explain this verse differently: "In a conflict between two *Smṛtis*, *Nyāya* is stronger because it conforms to the actual practice (*pravṛtti*) of legal proceedings. But where there is a conflict between the *Arthaśāstra* and the *Dharmaśāstra*, the *Dharmaśāstra* is stronger. As it is stated in the section on legal proceedings (*vyavahāra-prakaraṇa*) in the *Arthaśāstra*: [text follows].
"There is no fault whatsoever for the slayer in killing an *ātatāyin* (one who comes with intent to kill)," so it is said (MDh 8.350).
Furthermore, in the section on penance (*prāyaścitta*) in the *Dharmaśāstra*:
"No atonement is prescribed for the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa," so it is said (MDh 11.89).

In that regard, because the Dharmaśāstras possess greater authority, it would follow that there is a fault in killing an *ātatāyin* (an aggressor); however, since that [position] is irrelevant to the present context and lacks any basis in authoritative evidence, it is not at all correct. 21.
Nor is it necessarily the case that even for those who are intent upon reality there is an absolute absence of means for realizing the ultimate truth; for it is said:
"Written documents, possession, and witnesses are proclaimed as the means of proof.
In the absence of any one of these, one of the divine ordeals is prescribed. (2.22)

For when the realization of reality occurs through visible means such as written texts and the like, then everything is well. But if those means are absent—either individually or collectively—or even if they exist, they are not sufficient to bring satisfaction, then there is no contradiction, because the realization of reality arises through one or another of the divine methods to be described hereafter. || 22 ||
Furthermore: In all disputes whatsoever, the subsequent legal act is stronger;
however, in the case of a pledge, a gift, or a purchase, the prior act is more powerful. (2.23)

In all disputes that have not yet been decided, a subsequent legal action characterized by *divya* (ordeals) is indeed stronger, because it provides an infallible determination. However, in cases such as mortgages (*ādhi*) and the like, the prior action—such as documentary evidence—is stronger, because an ordeal is impossible there. For instance, when property deposited with Devadatta is enjoyed by Yajñadatta’s sons, they lack the support of an ordeal due to their lack of personal experience [with the transaction]. Alternatively, this verse refers specifically to documentary disputes; in all such disputes involving documents, a subsequent documentary action is stronger because it involves a greater number of examinations and thereby eliminates fraudulent fabrications. But in the case of mortgages and so forth, since the object is held by another, the prior action is superior due to the primacy of the original document—this is the meaning. (23)
But regarding possession:
"For land, loss occurs after twenty years for one who sees it being enjoyed by another but does not speak; for wealth, loss occurs after ten years. (MDh 8.147)

The intention is that if one, even while seeing [one's property] being enjoyed by others who have no connection to it, should say nothing for such a length of time, surely it would not belong to him. However, the restriction regarding the period of time must be understood as being rooted in the Veda itself. [Objection: But this is improper, since the loss of the object occurs merely through non-assertion. [Reply: In that case, this too must come from the Veda. Since the loss of property occurs even through neglect, the intention is that what is being enjoyed by others should not be neglected. Now, does the other person possess any connection to ownership? The Teacher’s view is that, at least for the former owner, there is a loss. Furthermore, the other person has no ownership at all, because he proceeds to enjoy the property with the very notion that it belongs to another. If this is so, then there is no fault on the part of the king at that time. That is true. But then, let it belong to the king alone, since the instruction regarding loss refers to the original owner, and such property goes to the king. Alternatively, it should be returned to the former owner himself, because there is no reason for the cessation of his ownership. The Smṛti rule is indeed consistent even when based on visible grounds; it is merely a prohibition against neglect. The mention of "loss," however, serves only as a censure, its purpose being to indicate that the neglecter is unfit to engage in legal transactions. That alone is appropriate here; otherwise, there would be the abandonment of what is heard in scripture and the assumption of what is not heard. Enough of this digression. (24)
Would it then follow that, due to equanimity (*upekṣā*), one would be unfit to engage in any worldly transaction whatsoever? True;

with the exception of property placed under a boundary, deposits, and the wealth of the simple-minded or children, as well as the wealth of sealed deposits, the king’s women, and Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*). (2.25)

The intention is that, in the case of pledges and the like, possession (*bhukti*) is not at all a cause for forfeiture. First, a pledge (*ādhi*) is made precisely for the purpose of enjoyment. A boundary (*sīmā*) is enjoyed in various ways due to the negligence of those who guard it. A deposit (*nikṣepa*) is [not lost] because it has been handed over; likewise for the property of the mentally disabled and children, due to their incapacity. He will discuss the open deposit (*upanidhi*) later. Royal wealth is [not lost] because it belongs to many. And the property of women is [not lost] because of their lack of independence. For those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), it is because of their dependence on other occupations. The word "likewise" (*tathā*) signifies a similar category. The meaning is: in every case where possession is possible even in the absence of ownership, there, the enjoyment resulting from that [possession] is not a cause for forfeiture. || 25 ||
Since the enjoyment [of property] arises from other causes such as deposits and the like, therefore:
The king shall cause the one who misappropriates deposits and the like to pay the wealth to the owner, and a fine equal to that amount to the king, or otherwise according to his capacity. (2.26)
Having given wealth to the creditor, an equal amount must subsequently be paid to the king; or rather, the meaning is that it should be according to his capacity. || 26 ||

And because the loss of a right does not occur merely through enjoyment, therefore: "Title is superior to possession, except in the case of possession inherited through prior succession. "Title" (āgama) refers to a written document (*lekhyam*). That is more powerful than possession, because it is certain; otherwise, possession could arise even without a title. However, when there is a prior succession, possession is more powerful, because it is possible for a document—even one set aside by another document—to remain in force due to negligence. Possession by three generations constitutes "prior succession. Furthermore, since it is possible for a document to remain in force even when it has been sublated by a prior claim through means such as concealment of its destruction.
In that regard: "Even in the case of scriptural tradition (āgama), there is no strength at all where even a slight enjoyment [of the object] is absent. (2.27)
The meaning is: it would not exist—that is, the establishment of the written document would not occur—without that much [of the requisite]. || 27 ||
And because possession through succession is stronger than scriptural title, therefore:
"But he by whom the title was made must, when sued, produce it;
neither his son nor his grandson need do so, for in that case possession is more weighty. (2.28)

The son of the document-drafter shall not clear up defects in the document, for he does not know the nature of the document as well as his father did; however, the wealth [in question] does not belong to that son. But for the son of that [original owner], there may be both the wealth and the title, because it has already been stated that in such a case possession is more authoritative than the document—this is the intended meaning. || 28 ||
But why is a son born of a written document not an heir to the wealth? Because:
"Possession attains the status of proof through a pure title;
possession lacking a pure title does not attain the status of proof. (2.29)

Because of ignorance regarding the true nature of the document, there would be merely the removal of its defects; however, the intention is that ownership itself cannot exist without valid evidence. The meaning is that validity belongs only to possession (*bhoga*) accompanied by a pure title (*viśuddhāgama*), and not to mere possession alone. || 29 ||
Moreover:
"If one who was possessed of the property should have died, his heir shall recover it; in that case, possession is not a valid ground when it is devoid of a legal title. (2.30)

For if one who is engaged in clearing up a defect in a document should die or pass away, then the one entitled to receive his wealth should clear it up. And this refers to the case of the document's author; for others, there would simply be the seizure of property. Because in that case, possession devoid of a legal title (*āgama*) is not a cause for ownership, since even if such possession were established, it is fallible—this is the meaning. || 30 ||

But if, even when a document or the like is defective, its maker does not remove those defects, then how [should the matter proceed]? Regarding such a case, reporting to the king has been prescribed in the passage beginning with "by a path deviating from the Smṛtis and established custom. For this very reason:

"The king, officials in charge of legal affairs, guilds, then trade associations, and finally families—each preceding one among these is to be known as more authoritative than each succeeding one in the judicial procedure for men. (2.31)

Since the king alone is capable of conducting legal proceedings because he possesses power, he is the most authoritative in the administration of justice. Others, too, become either weak or strong depending on their respective capacities. Therefore, it should be understood that the cases of litigants proceed to the king precisely according to the sequence of *kula* (family) and so forth. *Pūga* refers to associations such as groups of Brahmins; the rest is clear. (31)

And by virtue of his authority alone, the king or the judge and others appointed to adjudicate those matters shall set aside legal proceedings brought about through force or fraud, as well as those conducted by women, at night, inside a house, outside [the house], or by enemies. (2.32)
The meaning of this verse is clear. || 32 ||
Furthermore:

A legal proceeding initiated by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by disease, beset by calamity, a child, or terrified, as well as one that is unrelated [to the facts], is not established. (2.33)
"Intoxicated" means excessively joyful or arrogant; "insane" refers to one possessed by spirits and the like; the rest is clear. || 33 ||
Furthermore:
"The king, having disciplined families, castes, guilds, assemblies, and even provinces that have strayed from their own dharma, shall establish them on the right path. (2.34)

Families (*kulāni*) are households. Castes (*jātayaḥ*) are the social classes, such as the Brāhmaṇas and others. Guilds (*śreṇayaḥ*) are associations of artisans. Clans (*gaṇāḥ*) are groups consisting of Brāhmaṇas and others. A district (*janapadaḥ*) refers here to the people residing in a fortified area; the intention is that even they, if they deviate from their own duty (*svadharma*), should be punished by the king. Alternatively, "district" may refer to all other people. In any case, the intention is that everyone who deviates from their own duty should be punished by the king. (34)
And because the king is the foremost authority in the administration of legal proceedings and is the wielder of the rod of punishment, therefore:
Property lost and then found must be restored by the king to the owner; if he cannot prove his ownership by signs, he deserves a fine equal to the value of that property. (2.35)

If something lost by someone has been found by the king or another person, and the owner requests it, then, having asked what it is and how many in number it consists of, it should be restored after investigating whether the claimant is non-deceptive. If he does not prove it to be so, he shall be fined an amount equal to the value of the property. || 35 ||
What then is to be said regarding a treasure-trove or the like that has no owner? It is said:
Upon finding a treasure-trove, a king shall give half to the twice-born; however, a learned twice-born man may take it all, since he is the master of everything. (2.36)
By the statement "He is the lord of all," it is made known that even in the absence of acceptance and so forth, there exists a relationship of ownership. || 36 ||
When a treasure has been found by someone other than the rightful heir, the king shall take a sixth part;
if it is discovered without having been reported, he shall be made to pay that [treasure] and also a fine.

The meaning is: by another Brāhmaṇa who is not learned (*anabhirūpa*). However, Gautama’s rule—"The discovery of a treasure-trove is the property of the king" (GDh 10.43)—refers to non-Brāhmaṇas; the meaning is that whatever discovery of a treasure-trove occurs, all of it belongs to the king. And so, having stated, "Not [the property] of a Brāhmaṇa who is not learned," he says: "Some say that even a non-Brāhmaṇa who reports it shall receive a sixth part" (GDh 10.44–45). But a Brāhmaṇa who takes it without reporting it, even if he is learned, should be punished after taking everything, according to his capacity. However, a learned man, because of the statement "He is the lord of all," does not incur guilt even if he takes it without reporting it. || 37 ||
And because the king possesses sovereignty over such things as treasure-troves that have no owner, for that very reason:
"The king must restore property stolen by thieves to the people of the realm. Why? Because:
For he who gives it away incurs the sin of that person to whom it belongs. || 2.38 ||

For it is by virtue of being a protector that the king’s authority extends over [lost property] such as a treasure-trove. The underlying intention is: if he is a protector, why should he not restore what belongs to another that has been stolen by thieves and the like? The mention of the "country" (janapada) is for the sake of inclusivity; the meaning is that it does not apply to a Brāhmaṇa alone. And so Bṛhaspati says: "What has been stolen by thieves must be recovered and restored to everyone; if it cannot be found, it should be paid from his own treasury. One who does not restore it shall incur the guilt of a thief," and so forth. (38)
Thus ends the section on general principles (*sāmānyanyāya*).
Now begins the section on the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*).

Having thus described the nature of legal procedure in general, he now introduces it specifically according to the sequence of the titles of law (*vyavahārasthāna*), beginning with the non-payment of debt. Among these, the non-payment of debt was declared by Manu and others to be the first; therefore, that alone is discussed first.
With a pledge, the interest shall be one-eightieth part each month;
otherwise, according to the order of the castes, it shall be two, three, four, or five percent per hundred. (2.39)

Although the eightieth part has been stated without distinction, nevertheless, this applies only to the Brāhmaṇa. For others, however, the calculation of interest is by an increase of one quarter [per varṇa]. Thus says Bṛhaspati: "For the others, [interest is] by a gradual increase of one quarter. Otherwise, the intention is that in the absence of a pledge, the interest is two or three percent. Regarding this stated measure of interest, one should not take more than this; however, there is no contradiction in taking less. (39)
By this same rate of increase, the maximum interest on livestock and female animals is eightfold; likewise, that on clothing, grain, and gold is fourfold, threefold, and twofold respectively. (2.40)

The "increase" (*vṛddhi*) of cattle and women refers to their offspring when they have been pledged for the enjoyment of the fruit; that [offspring] shall belong to the creditor. By the word "but" (*tu*), the meaning is that it is only the progeny, and no other form of interest. The phrase "of cattle and women" is intended to exclude the offspring of male cattle. Alternatively, it should be construed as "of cattle and female slaves. Regarding sugarcane juice and the like, the maximum interest is eightfold. For clothes, it is fourfold; for grain, threefold; and for gold and so forth, twofold. And according to the rule of the eighty-part share and so on, by the same amount of time in which gold becomes twofold, grain and the like reach their own double measure. (40)

But beyond the four castes: those living in the wilderness shall pay ten percent, and those by the sea a hundred percent; or else, all [merchants], regardless of their caste, may pay the interest they themselves have agreed upon. (2.41)

"Those who travel through wildernesses" (*kāntāragāḥ*) are forest-dwellers or those who go there. "Ocean-farers" (*sāmudrāḥ*) are those who engage in maritime trade. They should pay ten percent or twenty percent per month. Alternatively, "those who go to the wilderness" (*kāntāragāḥ*) refers to those who go to the state of being outcasts from their caste (*varṇāpaśadatva*); that is the meaning. "The ocean" (*samudra*) is that which exists with a seal (*mudrā*), namely the domain of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*); those who transgress it are, by way of figurative indication (*viparītalakṣaṇā*), "ocean-farers" (*sāmudrāḥ*), meaning those who persist in improper occupations (*vikarmasthā*). Or else, they should pay interest as agreed upon between themselves; this applies to all, including Brāhmaṇas and others, even among all outcaste classes—this is the meaning. By the word "or" (*vā*), he indicates that this is an alternative rule for Brāhmaṇas and the rest in times of distress (*āpadkalpa*). (41)

And by means of this interest, one who recovers his property from a debtor shall not be censured by the king; but if he goes to the king while the debt is being recovered, the debtor shall be made to pay that wealth and be fined for it. (2.42)

When a matter has been brought forward according to the law and clarified through the means of proof, the king must not say anything by his own will. However, if while being investigated he should report it to the king, then he shall be punished and made to pay that wealth; "to the creditor" is the understood remainder. || 42 ||
Now, if several creditors should simultaneously demand payment from a single debtor, then this is the order:
the debtor shall pay the creditors according to the sequence in which the debts were contracted;
however, he shall pay first to a Brāhmaṇa, and immediately after that to the king. (2.43)

A debt must be paid by the debtor to those of the same caste according to the very order in which they were mentioned; in the case of different castes, it must be paid according to the order beginning with the Brāhmaṇa. The word "tu" (but/however) indicates that even when the caste is the same, the order depends on qualities and other such factors. || 43 ||
But a debtor who has acted in opposition [to the creditor] shall be reported to the king immediately. And in that case:
"The king shall cause the debtor to pay ten percent on the amount proved;
however, the creditor who has recovered his property shall be made to pay five percent. (2.44)

The debtor shall be compelled by the king to pay the entire amount to the creditor; and the king himself shall take a tenth part from that very debtor. The creditor, moreover, shall give a fifth part of the amount recovered as a gratuity to the king. *Uttamarṇika* means the creditor. The rest is clear. 44.
In this manner, one should first cause a wealthy person to pay. However, as for one who is not wealthy:
"One may compel a man of low birth who is impoverished to perform labor for the sake of the debt;
but a Brāhmaṇa who is impoverished should be made to pay gradually, according to his means. (2.45)
The meaning of this verse is clear. || 45 ||
And likewise for one who gives according to the original agreement:

if a person does not accept their own wealth when it is being given back after having been lent, that [debt] shall be deposited with a neutral third party; it does not increase beyond that point. (2.46)

Because of the expression "one's own wealth" and because of the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), this refers to the case of a nearby creditor; otherwise, however, the intention is that it indeed increases. || 46 ||
This sequence for the repayment of debt applies when there is a creditor present. But in his absence:

The heir to the estate shall pay the debt, and likewise the one who takes the wife; the son shall pay it if he has not inherited other property; and for one who dies without a son, the heir to the estate shall pay. (2.47)

Since debts follow the inheritance, those who take the inheritance alone shall pay them without hesitation. However, in the case of one who is destitute of wealth, he who takes his wife by appointment (*niyoga*) shall pay. And this refers to non-Brahmins, because for them alone is there the possibility of their wives going to another man. The phrase "and likewise" means that just like the taker of the property, the taker of the wife shall also pay without distinction; the intention is that the same property belongs to the one who is devoid of wealth. It is precisely from this extended application (*atideśa*) that the taker of the wife and others are to be understood as liable only in the absence of an heir. "A son whose wealth is not dependent on another. A son whose wealth is not dependent on anyone else—that son shall pay. The meaning is: provided that the wealth has not been taken by another. Now, it was already established previously that a son shall pay only for one who is destitute of wealth, since a debt follows the wealth. Why then is it stated again, "whose wealth is not dependent on another"? Do not say so; even previously, this was explained in accordance with this very term. This [present statement] is merely a reinforcement based on the extended application. Alternatively, if among many sons one should take the paternal wealth with the consent of the others, then the liability for the debt would be equal for both the taker of the wealth and the others, since the others have also voluntarily combined their own shares. To dispel this doubt, he says: "A son whose wealth is not dependent on another. Only that son upon whom the wealth depends shall pay; not another, even if he is a consenter. From this very point, it is known that sons shall pay the debt according to their respective shares. Or the eldest may pay more, because a distinction is seen in the division of the inheritance—this is the general direction. In every way, the connection to the debt follows the connection to the acquisition of wealth. Likewise, even for one who is sonless, others who are heirs to the property are the ones who bear the debt; the intention is that they also incur the liability for the debt. And so says Kātyāyana.
"The debt must be paid by the heir; in his absence, by the wife;
and in her absence, by the sons; and in their absence, by other heirs to the estate in due order. Thus [says the law]. And Bṛhaspati also:
"Among those who take away wealth, a wife, or sons, the liability for debt follows the order in which they appear;
in their absence, it falls successively upon the other heirs. (BṛSm 10.106–7)

Alternatively, there is another meaning for the phrase *ananyāśritadravya*: when the father has died, if one's paternal inheritance (*paitṛkaṃ rikthaṃ*) has been deposited with someone else for some reason such as being entrusted, that person is one whose property is held by another (*anyāśritadravya*). The reason for the rule that he should not pay his father’s debt without first recovering that [inheritance] is precisely this: “of the heir of one who has no son. The ellipsis is to be supplied as “but others also exist. The intention is: as long as he does not obtain even the rightful paternal inheritance, why should he pay the debt? It should be understood that all these points have been correctly explained based on other Smṛtis, just as Kātyāyana says:
