"As long as a son does not obtain existing paternal property, the debtor shall not be made to pay, even if [the creditor] is very wealthy. (KSm 563) || 47 ||
Thus, first of all, the paternal debt must be paid. But how is it with debts contracted by a brother or others? In that regard also:
"If a debt has been contracted for the sake of the family by those who are undivided, the heirs shall pay it when the head of the household has died or gone abroad. (2.48)

A "family member" (*kuṭumbī*) is one who exists within the family, such as a brother or others. Whatever debt has been contracted for the sake of the family by such a person must be paid by all those who share in the inheritance (*rikthabhāk*), provided they remain undivided, whether that person has died or is away on a journey. The term "undivided" is used because even among those who share in the inheritance, division is possible. (48)

But even when there is no partition of property, a wife shall not pay what was contracted by her husband or son, nor shall a father pay what was contracted by his son; likewise, a husband shall not pay what was contracted by his wife, except for the sake of the family. (2.49)
An exception to this rule is stated:
"The husband shall pay the debt of a cowherd’s wife, a liquor-seller’s wife, an actress’s wife, a washerwoman’s wife, or a hunter’s wife, because their livelihood depends upon him. (2.50)

A *gopa* is a cowherd; a *śauṇḍika* is a liquor-seller; a *śailūṣa* is an actor; a *rajaka* is a washerman of clothes as well as a dyer; and a *vyādha* is a hunter. These must pay even a debt contracted by their wives, because they are under the authority of their wives. And so says Nārada: "Their livelihood depends on her, and their family is supported by her" (NSm 1.16). The statement of the reason is made so that others of this same kind may also be included. || 50 ||
But with respect to the lack of distinction in being merely human beings:
a woman shall pay a debt that was contracted by her husband, or one that she herself incurred; other than these, a woman is not liable to pay. (2.51)

The intention is that even when husband and wife possess undivided property, a woman must not pay [a debt] except in cases such as those involving a voluntary agreement (*abhyupeta*). Why, then, would there be any possibility of women incurring debt independently, or why would there be any possibility of their paying it? For the author will indeed speak of women possessing independent wealth in the verse: "That which was given by a pleased husband" (NSm 1.24). It is not contradictory for women to incur debt for the purpose of personal maintenance; it is precisely in this context that the connection of women with debt is established. || 51 ||
But it is stated elsewhere as well:
"Even when the father has gone abroad, is deceased, or is overwhelmed by calamity, the debt must be paid by the sons or grandsons, provided it is established by witnesses in case of denial. (2.52)

When the father has died or is away abroad, the son and others should wait twenty years before paying the debt; or, if he is overcome by calamity, the debt must be paid by the sons and others. The word *api* (even/also) is used in the sense of "in this manner. The meaning is that even in other such circumstances—such as when [the father] has fallen ill or suffers from an incurable impairment of his faculties—the debt is to be paid. Likewise, in the case of denial, if the father is hostile, then the debt must be paid by the sons and others once it has been proven by witnesses. For he too, due to his altered state and incapacity, is indeed unfit [to manage the estate]. It should be understood that in these conditions, the paternal inheritance must also be taken by the sons and others, just like the debt. (52)

There is an exception to this: "A son shall not pay for what was incurred through liquor, passion, gambling, fines, or taxes, nor for gifts made in vain; such is the law regarding paternal debts. (2.53)

What was promised by a father while he was in a state of sound health must be paid by those who inherit his property when he is no longer healthy; however, the intention is that what was promised while he was himself unwell need not be paid. This verse is intended to elaborate upon the various types of such "unwell" states. Furthermore, on account of specific scriptural injunctions, the following must not be paid: the remainder of a fine or a tax; the price for liquor that has been drunk but not yet paid; what was promised to women out of lust; what was lost at gambling; the remainder of a fine or similar dues; and likewise, "vain gifts" (*vṛthādāna*)—that is, whatever is determined here to have no fruit in the next world. *Śulka* refers to a gift due to the king on a road. A "vain gift" is one not enjoined by the scriptures. The rest is clear. (53)
The manner of discharging a debt has been stated. Now, in order to determine who may be a debtor, he says:
"Suretyship, debt, and witness-hood among brothers, between husband and wife, and between father and son, are indeed not recorded as permissible when they are undivided. (2.54)

Among brothers and others who are undivided, there exists no mutual relationship of debt, witnesshood, or suretyship. By that very principle, when there is doubt as to whether they are divided or undivided, the determination is made by means of witnesses and other such evidence. And the mention of "husband and wife" here is intended to demonstrate the absence of witnesshood and so forth among other co-heirs who are undivided, because division is impossible between them. (54)
In what matter, then, is suretyship prescribed? Suretyship is ordained for appearance, for confidence, and for payment.
But if the first two fail, they must be made to pay; in the case of the other, even the sons are liable. (2.55)

The surety for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) is for the purpose of ensuring attendance when there is a fear of escape, and for the purpose of inspiring confidence where there is distrust. The surety for payment (*siddhārtha-pratibhū*) is established by the giving of the object; this is prescribed for the purpose of removing doubt. Let there be no doubt on the part of one who either gives or causes to be given [the debt] when it has not been received. In that regard, if the two sureties for appearance—having failed and being in default—when the debtor is [unable to pay], they themselves must be made to pay, but not their sons. However, the intention is that the sons of the other—the surety for payment—must also pay. The word "also" (*api*) is intended to include other heirs (*rikthabhāj*). Now, one might object: is not the surety for appearance also merely for the sake of providing confidence? This is not so. Even for one who has provided confidence, non-appearance can indeed occur due to some other cause. Or rather, the mention of the surety for appearance should be understood as being for the purpose of making him a payer when the debtor has died. And thus says Bṛhaspati: "In case of misfortune, having caused the person for whom he stood sure to be produced, the surety must again be made to pay" (BṛSm 10.79). And this rule applies only to those cases where a surety for appearance is appointed after gaining confidence through the delivery of the object. Thus says Nārada:
"When debtors fail to repay or when the evidence is contested, the guarantor shall pay that debt; likewise, he shall pay it if the debtor fails to appear. (NSm 1.105).

The remainder of the sense is "when appearance is possible. Since appearance is impossible for one who is dead, Nārada’s intention is that this rule applies only to those who are living. Regarding the contingency of alternative options, the determination of the scope has already been stated. || 55 ||
He clarifies the meaning of the preceding verse:

"Where a guarantor for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or a guarantor for trust (*prātyayika*) has died, their sons shall not pay the debt; however, those who stood as sureties for payment (*dāna*) must pay. (2.56)

The intention is that, by the force of the commencement of the subsequent verse and from the mention of "the deceased," the sons must search for the living [father] according to their ability. || 56 ||

But when there are many sureties for a single debtor, they shall pay the money according to their respective shares; however, among those who stand in the same position of liability, the creditor may collect as he pleases. (2.57)

If there are many sureties, they should pay the debt in proportionate shares. However, among those who stand under a single liability (*ekacchāyāsthita*), one may cause the entire debt to be paid—either collectively or individually—at the creditor's will. Those who share a single liability are sureties by virtue of being joint borrowers; they are not users of the property. This very point is clarified by the use of the pronoun "among these" (*eṣu*) in the verse. (57)
And because he does not enjoy the substance [of the debt]:
"Where a surety is made to pay the wealth to the creditor publicly, that wealth must be repaid by the debtors at double the amount. (2.58)

According to the statement of Prakāśa, that which has passed into the hands of the surety must be paid back doubled; however, the intention is not that this applies to whatever may be owed to the creditor. Furthermore, this verse concerns the subject of gold (hiraṇya). || 58 ||

But regarding livestock and so forth: grain for female animals should be returned with interest at three times the original amount; clothing should be given back fourfold, and likewise, liquids eightfold. (2.59)

The word "tathā" (likewise) signifies with honor and so forth. The meaning is that whatever maximum interest has been declared for a given [debt], that interest, along with the principal and accompanied by due honor, must be paid to the surety. || 59 ||

There are two causes for confidence: the surety (*pratibhū*) and the pledge (*ādhi*). As it has been said: "In this matter, there are two causes for confidence: the surety and the pledge" (NSm 1.103). Of these two, the surety has been explained. Now, as it follows in the sequence, the pledge is discussed: "A pledge shall perish when the debt has doubled, if it is not released;
one made for a fixed time perishes at the expiration of that time, but one to be enjoyed for its produce does not perish. (2.60)

That which is deposited for the purpose of gaining trust, such as gold and the like, is a pledge (*ādhi*). It is of two kinds: that which is to be guarded (*gopya*) and that which is not to be guarded (*agopya*). Among these, a guarded pledge is sometimes made with a temporal limitation, such as: "If he does not release me within this much time, this [pledge] shall be forfeited to me. Sometimes, however, it is indefinite; it would be forfeited when the debt has doubled, provided it is not paid. The other type [the non-guarded pledge] is also forfeited by the same temporal limitation. Therefore, he says: "A pledge to be enjoyed for its fruit (*phalabhogya*) is not forfeited. That pledge whose fruit is enjoyed is a "pledge to be enjoyed for its fruit. The "fruit" is the interest (*vṛddhi*). The rest is clear. (60)
Furthermore:
Interest on a pledge for use ceases when it has been used or when its value has increased;
likewise, if it is lost or destroyed—except by act of God or the king—it must be restored. (2.61)

The interest of one who enjoys a pledge (ādhi) shall perish—this is the remainder [of the sense]. The word *atha* in the phrase "or when there is benefit" (*sopakāre 'tha*) has the meaning of the particle *api*. The meaning is that even in the case of a pledge that provides benefit, there shall be no interest. A cow or similar animal that is capable of carrying, milking, and so forth, is "one that provides benefit. It is mentioned separately because of the possibility of doubt regarding its modification. "Bhāvita" means when it has been acknowledged by the enjoyer, or when it has been enjoyed by him, as established by witnesses, in this manner: "This was enjoyed by him. If the pledge is lost or destroyed—except in the case of destruction caused by divine calamities such as fire or by royal authority—it must be restored to the debtor. Destruction (*nāśa*) refers to the loss of its essential form; however, "destruction" (*apahāra*) here refers to its disappearance. The rest is clear. || 61 ||

When a pledge has been offered by a debtor, its validity is established through acceptance; even if it is being preserved, if it becomes worthless, another pledge must be provided, or the debtor shall pay the money to the creditor. (2.62)

Even for that which has been surrendered, its status as an object of enjoyment would be established through acceptance. However, if—even while being guarded with effort—it reaches a state of worthlessness; that is, if it becomes valueless despite being maintained, then another pledge must be provided. Alternatively, at this juncture, the debtor may become a possessor of wealth, or the creditor may receive the wealth along with interest, or another pledge must be made; such is the intended meaning. [62]
But when a pledge is not being utilized at all and is held merely as a security, then:
He shall cause the debtor to pay the money lent on the basis of a pledge of good conduct together with interest;
however, he shall cause the value of an article pledged as a token of truth to be returned twofold. (2.63)

He shall be made to pay the debt along with interest incurred through a pledge for conduct (*caritrabandhaka*); the meaning is that he is not to be released merely by the arrival of the creditor. In other cases as well, when a transaction based on trust has occurred and money was handed over as a token of good faith (*satyaṃkāra*), that which was deposited must be returned twofold by one who breaks his word. However, for the one who provided the token of good faith, there is simply the loss of that [money] due to his breach of faith. As Kātyāyana says: "In a breach of a token of good faith, one should cause twice the amount to be paid;
but for one who does not act [accordingly], there is the loss of that [token]; such is the purpose of the token of good faith" (KSm 541). || 63 ||

But when the debtor presents himself having brought the property along with the interest, then: "The pledge must be released to the one who has presented himself; otherwise, he shall be fined. If the creditor is absent, he may obtain the pledge after depositing the money with a member of the debtor's family. (2.64)

If a creditor, having brought the property along with the interest, does not release the pledge to one who has presented himself, he shall be subject to punishment. However, when the money-lender is absent, then, in his absence, he may take possession of the pledge by depositing the property with that person's family; the meaning is that he should take it without hesitation. In this manner, having deposited the property with the family of the creditor, the pledge should be seized. 64.
Or it may remain there at its value fixed at that time, without interest;
or, with the consent of the debtor, he may sell it in the presence of witnesses. (2.65)

That for which the value was fixed at that time is "tatkālakṛtamūlya. If there should be a decrease from the [original] value, then the creditor must pay that value which was fixed at that time; by this rule, the pledge remains in the creditor's possession free of interest. However, when the debt has doubled and the debtor is absent, then, having announced it at that time, he may take the pledge without hesitation—that is, he may sell it in the presence of witnesses even without the debtor's consent. || 65 ||
For the purpose of increasing the principal, the creditor may continue to enjoy the pledge from the first day of its use;
however, when the debt has doubled, then indeed the pledge must be released once twice the amount of the original money has been recovered from the proceeds of that pledge. (2.66)

Once the wealth has been received, the pledge must be released; the intention is that its forfeiture—characterized by the failure to repay the doubled amount—should not occur before that point. || 66 ||
Thus ends the section on the non-payment of debts. Now begins the section on deposits (*upanidhi*).
Following the discussion of pledges (*ādhi*), the deposit is treated next because it shares the common characteristic of being entrusted in trust.
When an object contained in a vessel is handed over into the hand of another without being specifically described, that substance is called *aupanidhika*; this is the remainder of the sense.
In that same way, it must be returned. || 2.67 ||

Having stated that something is deposited somewhere with an unspecified nature in the possession of someone else, saying, "This must be guarded by you," the word *hasta* signifies possession. The meaning is "having placed" or "having cast down. Thus, that which is designated as a *aupanidhika* (sealed deposit) must be returned exactly as it was received. || 67 ||

But as for the property that was deposited, he shall not be made to pay for it if it has been stolen by the king, by fate, or by thieves; however, if it is not returned when demanded, he shall be made to pay the value and a fine equal to that amount. (2.68)

One who has not committed an offense shall not be made to pay for property stolen by kings and others. If a fault exists—meaning if, when the item is sought and requested, it is not returned or delivered, and there is a fault characterized by theft, plunder, and so forth—then he must be made to pay the stolen property; and he must also pay to the king a fine equal to that amount. The rest is straightforward. 68.
If one makes use of a deposit for his own livelihood without the owner’s permission, he shall be fined and made to pay that property along with its interest.
This same rule applies to articles borrowed for a specific purpose, those entrusted for delivery to another, deposits, and pledges. (2.69)

That which is borrowed for the sake of a specific purpose; that which belongs to another, such as household utensils and the like; that which is deposited (*anvāhita*)—meaning something else handed over when one lacks the capacity to provide a pledge (*ādhi*); or that which, in the course of receiving a gift, was brought in as an accessory even though it had not been obtained [as a gift], such as a bowl; a deposit (*nyāsa*), which is a substance of a specified nature entrusted for the purpose of protection; and a sealed deposit (*nikṣepa*), which is what has been placed into the hand of another to be delivered to yet another person—in these cases, too, including those beginning with "borrowed," this same rule pertaining to sealed deposits (*upanidhi*) is to be understood to apply. (69)
Thus ends the section on deposits;
now begins the section on witnesses.

In all matters, such as the recovery of debts and the like, the means of establishing proof (*vyaktihetu*) are documentary evidence (*likhita*), witnesses (*sākṣin*), and possession (*bhukti*). Among these, possession applies to immovable property, while in other cases, documentary evidence and witnesses apply. Accordingly, Nārada says: "Documentary evidence and witnesses are the two means of proof that bring about clarity" (NSm 1.103), stating this with the intention of referring to them generally. Therefore, when it has been stated that the plaintiff and defendant must establish their respective positions through witnesses, documents, or both, it remains to be explained what the characteristics of witnesses and documents are. Regarding this, the witnesses are first described.
They were ascetic, charitable by nature, of noble birth, and speakers of truth;
they held righteousness as their primary concern, were upright, possessed of sons, and endowed with wealth.
Witnesses should be known as at least three in number, devoted to the performance of the five great sacrifices;
they may be of the same caste and class, or all may serve for all purposes.

Austerity and the other qualities are the grounds for determining their reliability as speakers of what they have perceived. How so? For how could one who is disinterested, solely intent on accomplishing the welfare of the next world, engaged in austerity, charity, and the like, and whose wisdom surpasses that of other men, speak a falsehood for the sake of another—a lie that contradicts both the seen and the unseen and relies upon a wrong path? This is the intended meaning. Those who are truthful because they prioritize Dharma through austerity, charity, and so forth; or those who are of noble birth out of fear of bringing disgrace upon their lineage; or those who possess sons and wealth out of fear of losing them; or those who are upright by nature and, being incapable of speaking beyond what they have perceived, do not speak otherwise—these should be known as witnesses, provided they are at least three in number. "At least three" (*tryavara*) means those of whom three is the minimum; that is, starting from three onwards. "Should be known as witnesses" implies that they are rooted in direct perception. The meaning is that witnesses should be scrutinized with precision according to their characteristics, such as direct observation and the like. Regarding the phrase "devoted to the performance of the five sacrifices" (*pañcayajñakriyāratā*): the injunction for performing the five sacrifices is indeed for the purpose of expiating the unavoidable violence committed daily. Therefore, the intention is: how could those who are engaged in removing even unavoidable violence ever, by their own inclination, engage in false testimony like those who follow unjust ways? Other Smṛti texts concerning the classification of witnesses should be explained in this same manner. As for the eleven types of witnesses mentioned by Nārada according to the distinction between those who have been formally appointed (*kṛta*) and those who have not (*akṛta*) (NSm 1.129), that was stated for the sake of instructing simple-minded people out of friendship. That [distinction] should be understood from that very source: "according to caste" (*yathājāti*). Alternatively, the word "caste" (*jāti*) refers to the specific castes of human beings and women. As Nārada has stated: "In guilds, the members of the guild," and so forth (NSm 1.135). And there is testimony according to *varṇa*, such as Brāhmaṇas and others. Or, since all are denotable by the term "caste" (*jāti*), there is no contradiction in using the feminine gender even when referring to *varṇa*. The word "again" (*punaḥ*) is used in view of the context. It means that in the absence of other witnesses, or in view of the matters to be discussed hereafter, all may be witnesses for all, as in: "Everyone is a witness in cases of adultery" (YDh 2.74). (70–71)
But when there is a contradiction with the stated rule:
"Women, the elderly, children, gamblers, those intoxicated, the insane, the accused, stage performers, heretics, forgers, and those with impaired faculties [are excluded]. (2.72)

An outcast, a relative, one who has received a benefit, a kinsman, an associate, an enemy, a thief, one who commits violence, one whose fault has been observed, and one who has been dismissed—these are non-witnesses. (2.73)

The meaning is that those for whom there is no cause—either seen or unseen—for their perceiving the matter as it truly is and for their speaking of the facts as they have been seen, or where such a cause exists in the opposite case, are not witnesses. Furthermore, all those mentioned in the section on those whose food should not be eaten (*abhojyānna*), such as those who maintain no sacred fire (*agnihīna*) and so forth, should be understood as unfit to be witnesses. The mention of a woman here is intended as an illustration of them; as it has been said: "And [the testimony] of women who have no male protectors" (MDh 4.213). It is she alone who is intended here as well. However, the testimony of a woman who has a protector and is under his authority is indeed admitted in some cases, as stated by Svayambhū: "Women shall give testimony for women" (MDh 8.68). A *raṅgāvatārī* is a wrestler. The rest is clear. Regarding those whose food should not be eaten, Nārada spoke with the intention that their lack of qualification as witnesses is established by logic itself:
"Neither those connected by financial interest, nor friends, nor companions, nor enemies;
nor those whose faults are known, nor those afflicted by disease, nor those who are corrupt— these should not be appointed [as witnesses]," having said this, then:
"Slaves, the deceitful, the exhausted, the elderly, women, and children are those who are despised.

(NSm 1.160) Thus, all those whose food is not to be eaten have been enumerated. Furthermore, the grounds for being disqualified from witnesshood based on other authorities have been elaborated, as follows:
"A child [is disqualified] due to ignorance; a woman, due to lack of understanding; and a forger, due to the habitual practice of evil."
"Relatives may speak [the truth] out of affection, while an enemy speaks it for the sake of revenge.
(NSm 1.173) Also, in some cases, it is by virtue of a statement; as it is said:
"Those such as Vedic scholars [are witnesses] by virtue of their testimony, while those such as thieves [are excluded] because of the perception of defects. (NSm 1.138)
In every way, by this method and through both reasoning and scripture, the witnessed and the unwitnessed should be elaborated upon. 72–73.

Furthermore, depending on the place, time, and other circumstances, even a single person who knows the law may serve as a witness if he is acceptable to both parties. In cases of adultery, verbal assault, and physical violence, everyone is a witness. (2.74)

A single person who is approved by both the plaintiff and the defendant and possesses extraordinary qualities may serve as a witness; by the use of the word "even" (*api*), two may also be permitted. The repetition of the term "witness" is intended so that there may be testimony even in cases such as adultery (*saṃgrahaṇa*) based solely on direct observation. Although no specific distinction was stated [in the previous rule], children and others shall not be witnesses because they lack the capacity for speech regarding the perception of the actual facts. And thus says Nārada:
"Even those who are declared here to be non-witnesses, such as slaves, rogues, and the like, may become witnesses when the gravity of the matter requires it."
Having stated: "But in all cases of violence, such as theft, adultery, and so forth,
as well as in verbal and physical assault, one should not examine the witnesses," he says:
"Among these, neither a child, nor one who is alone, nor a woman, nor a deceitful person, nor a relative, nor an enemy should give false testimony. (NSm 1.172)

Therefore, testimony by two or more persons—excluding children and the like—is not contradictory. Alternatively, the phrase "not one" (*naika*) is not a prohibition against a specific number; rather, this is a prohibition against a single person *per se*. Just as a single woman is prohibited [as a witness] by the rule "and a woman who is not accompanied by a male relative" (*yoṣitaṃ cāvīrām*), so too should it be explained that a single man devoid of a woman is unfit. Consequently, it should be understood that testimony in cases such as adultery (*saṃgrahaṇa*) belongs only to groups of at least three. And precisely because this is rooted in logic, even this prohibition from Nārada may be overridden by those who are exceedingly skilled in inference. To this effect is the text of Svāyambhuva:
"In the absence of a woman, the task may be performed by a child, an elderly person, a pupil, a relative, a slave, or even a hired servant" (MDh 8.70). Furthermore,
the attainment of certainty through inference is described in that very same context:
"One should recognize that the speech of children, the elderly, the sick, and those with agitated minds is unsteady when they give testimony while speaking falsely" (MDh 8.71).
In this manner, the distinction between logic and scripture should be elaborated elsewhere as well in the section on legal procedure. 74.

"But even so, what if no one gives testimony in a legal proceeding involving witnesses that has become thus difficult? True; for that very reason he says: 'If a man fails to give testimony regarding a debt, the king shall cause him to pay the entire debt along with a fine equal to the principal on the forty-sixth day. (2.75)

Even if a person who is healthy should fail to give testimony even within three fortnights, he must then be compelled by the king to pay the debt along with a fine of ten percent (*daśabandhaka*). "Along with a fine of ten percent" means together with an additional tenth part; that is to say, an amount exceeding one-tenth [of the principal]. The mention of "debt" (*ṛṇa*) is intended to indicate all types of legal disputes. (75)
Moreover: "That lowest of men who does not give testimony even though he knows it, is indeed equal to false witnesses in both his sin and his punishment. (2.76)
The phrase "even though he knows" (*jānann api*) shows that the formal injunction (*niyoga*) is not intended [to apply here]. And so says the Self-Existent One (*Svayambhū*):
"In a case where anyone might observe or hear something that is not recorded, even when questioned therein, he should speak it exactly as seen and exactly as heard. (MDh 8.76)
Since there is a transgression in failing to speak, the meaning is that it must be spoken by one who knows it, even if appointed for that specific time. || 76 ||
Perjurers are those who speak falsely. He shows what their sin is by means of another passage:
"He shall cause the witnesses, standing in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant, to hear [the following]:
'Those worlds which belong to the perpetrators of mortal sins (pātaka) and likewise to those who commit great sins (mahāpātakin)... (2.77).
Whatever worlds belong to those who set fire to dwellings and whatever worlds belong to those who kill women and children—all of those he attains who gives false testimony. (2.78)

According to other Smṛtis and logical reasoning, the judge himself—being likewise purified, facing either east or north, self-restrained, and having focused his one-pointed attention in the forenoon—in the presence of the plaintiff, the defendant, and the members of the court, should cause [the oath] to be heard by reciting: "Those worlds which are for the doers of heinous sins... The rest is clear. (77–78)
Having thus caused him to hear [the truth], one should question him as is appropriate according to his specific nature. However, if he is ignorant of the Dharma, one should awaken him in this way:
"Whatever merit you have performed throughout hundreds of previous births, know that all of it belongs to him whom you defeat falsely. (2.79)
When this has been said, let those who speak according to their experience testify;

in the case of a conflict among witnesses, the testimony of the majority prevails; if they are equal in number, that of the virtuous; and if there is a conflict even among the virtuous, the statement of those possessing the highest qualities should be accepted.
And thus they whose words have been examined:
he whose witnesses declare his claim to be true shall be the victor; for him whose witnesses speak otherwise, defeat is certain. (2.81)

Because the term "claim" (*pratijñā*) is used without qualification, victory should be understood to occur only when the truth of the entire matter of the claim is established; otherwise, there would be defeat. And so says Nārada:
"In regard to place, time, age, substance, quantity, form, and caste—wherever there may be disagreement, even that testimony [is invalid] otherwise. (NSm 1.212)
And regarding the claim involving many matters:
"Where witnesses state a matter that is either deficient or excessive, that too should be understood as unstated; this is the traditional rule for witnesses. (NSm 1.213)
Therefore, victory is certain only when the entire meaning of the proposition is true, because legal tradition (vyavahārasmṛti) is rooted in logic. || 81 ||
Even when testimony has been given by witnesses, if others who are more virtuous,
or twice as numerous, should state otherwise, the former witnesses shall be considered false.

And thus, when false testimony has been made manifest by the witnesses, or when the litigants themselves have been shown to be practitioners of fraudulent legal proceedings, the king should, without hesitation, punish them individually:
"The forgers and the witnesses shall be punished;
the property [of the litigants] shall be fined double the amount in dispute, but a Brāhmaṇa shall be banished. (2.83)

One who engages in fraudulent transactions or is a forger shall be punished. Furthermore, each witness individually shall be made to pay twice the value of the disputed property. However, a Brāhmaṇa who fails to pay the fine, even if he possesses his full wealth, shall be banished from the kingdom. Thus says the *Svāyambhuva*:
"One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is involved in every kind of crime; rather, one should expel him from the kingdom with his entire wealth intact and unharmed. (MDh 8.380)

In the event of a threat of execution, or when a punishment is not to be imposed, the Brahmin should be banished from the kingdom with all his wealth; however, the meaning is that neither corporal punishment nor any other form of restraint should be inflicted upon a Brahmin. || 83 ||
But a witness who was summoned by another to give testimony, yet— overcome by darkness— denies it when about to depart or at the point of death,
shall be made to pay eight times the value of the property; however, in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, he shall be banished.
Therefore, one must necessarily speak testimony that is truthful. || 84 ||
An exception to this rule is stated:
"But where the death of those belonging to the [first three] castes would otherwise occur, there a witness may speak untruth.
To purify himself from that sin, the twice-born must perform the *sārasvata* oblation. (2.85)

The intention is that for a Śūdra, however, [the rule applies] to acts such as giving gifts (*dāna*). Those belonging to the four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, are called *varṇins*. In a case where, if a witness speaks the truth, death would result for them, there the witness ought to speak untruth. Even though it is faulty, the speaking of untruth is accepted on account of the abundance of merit. And so Gautama, having stated: "There is no fault in speaking untruth if life is dependent [on it]," says: "But not for the sake of the life of one who is more sinful" (GDh 13.25–26). This statement regarding the absence of fault should be understood as referring to a minor fault, because of the force of the injunction for penance (*prāyaścitta*). And this is merely what is established by logic, stated for the purpose of instructing those of dull intellect. Furthermore, by the injunction of penance, its necessity is declared here. Elsewhere also, having considered the gravity or lightness of the sin, its performance and the penance for its removal should be undertaken so that it may be averted. And because it serves another purpose of Dharma, even this [act] committed intentionally should be regarded as if it were unintentional. But in the *Svāyambhuva* [Smṛti]:
And they should sacrifice to Sarasvatī with sacrificial porridges (caru) dedicated to the goddess of speech,
thereby effecting the supreme atonement for that sin of untruth.

"Or one should offer clarified butter into the fire according to the prescribed rule with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* verses, or with the verse beginning with 'ud' addressed to Varuṇa, or with the three-verse hymn addressed to the Waters. (MDh 10.105–06)

Thus, regarding the fourfold expiation that has been prescribed, it should be understood as applying respectively according to the social classes (varṇa), following the order beginning with the Śūdra, in accordance with their specific designations. Furthermore, the expression "with carus" is used so that the performance of the caru may occur once for each individual Śūdra. From this very permission of expiation for falsehood, it is understood that for a king, the neglect of those deserving of execution is mandatory. However, it should be concluded that witnesses, by the mere instruction of expiation, are exempt from royal punishment. (85)
Thus ends the section on witnesses.
Now begins the section on written documents.
Immediately after witnesses, the written document is discussed, because there is no difference between them in terms of being a means of proof for specific individuals.
Whatever matter has been settled by mutual agreement through their own consent, a document should be executed for it, containing witnesses and beginning with the name of the creditor. (2.86)

Whatever matter—such as a debt, a purchase, a gift, or a sale—is settled by mutual agreement between the creditor and the debtor, having been determined with its nature, number, quantity, interest, and due date clearly established, a document should be executed to ensure its non-dispute. This document, accompanied by witnesses possessing the aforementioned characteristics, must be capable of removing any future doubt. Its procedure is as follows: it should begin with the creditor; that is, the creditor’s name comes first in relation to the debtor, not in relation to time or other factors. (86)
And thus follows this sequence:
it should be marked by the year, month, half-month, day, lunar mansion, birth, and lineage; and by the name of one's fellow student, oneself, and one's father. (2.87)
When the matter is concluded, the debtor shall record his own name by his own hand: "What is written above is approved by me, the son of so-and-so. (2.88)
And the witnesses, being unequal [in number], should each write by their own hand, preceded by the name of their father, saying: "I, so-and-so, am a witness here. (2.89)

In this regard, they should write: "I, so-and-so, am a witness. This means three unequal [witnesses]. Others, however, due to a confusion regarding the word division (*cheda*), say there are two, interpreting it as "equal" (*samāḥ*). That is incorrect because it contradicts the statement of the *Bahvṛca* school. Nor is it reasonable to claim that the passage intends four witnesses, for there is the explicit statement: "But in a written document, at most three. (87–89)
He who is illiterate or a debtor should cause his own statement to be written down by another witness, in the presence of all the witnesses. (2.90)
A debtor or a witness who is illiterate shall have his own opinion or testimony recorded by a scribe or another witness in the presence of all the witnesses. (90)
Then, at the end, the scribe should write: "This has been written by me, [Name], the son of [Name], having been requested by both parties. (2.91)
The expression "finally" (antataḥ) is stated for the purpose of precluding anything further, since [the limit] has already been reached. || 91 ||
But what, then, is the purpose of recording it with one's own hand? It is said:
"Even without witnesses, a document that has been written by one's own hand is held to be valid evidence in its entirety, except when it was produced through force or fraud. (2.92)

For witnesses are intended for the purpose of securing the debtor's admission; if he should admit it even with his own hand, [the lawgiver] considers the utility of witnesses to be minimal. And this should be understood as referring to cases such as those involving a written acknowledgment (*upagata*). || 92 ||
And that which is pure by reason of its being free from fraud:
"A debt recorded in a document must be paid by only three generations of men; however, a pledge is enjoyed only so long as that debt is not repaid. (2.93)

That debt which is "entered in writing"—meaning recorded in a document—must be paid by exactly three generations of persons; that is to say, by the debtor himself, his son, and his grandson. The word *tu* (but/however) serves to exclude others. And so says Nārada:
"The debt incurred by a grandfather, which has been received in due order without interruption and cleared by the sons, the grandsons must pay; it ceases with the fourth. (NSm 1.4)

The exception to this is as follows: "But a pledge is used; it does not cease [to belong to the owner] until the fourth year. Is it then without limit? No, indeed; rather, it lasts only so long as that which is to be paid has not been returned. || 93 ||
But when a document has been moved from the debtor's country to another country, or has deviated from its original form, he states the procedure for that case:
"When a document is located in another country, or is illegible, or lost, or erased, or likewise stolen, or torn, or broken, or burnt, one should cause another document to be executed. (2.94)

The king, or else the creditor and debtor with one another—this is the intended meaning. A defect in the document (*lekhyadoṣa*) is that which arises while it is being written due to negligence; that is a "badly written" document (*durlekhya*). An "effaced" document is one where the letters have been rubbed out. A "torn" document is one damaged by mice and the like. A "split" document is one that has been ripped. The word *tathā* (and so forth) signifies "of such a kind. The rest is clear. || 94 ||
If there is a suspicion of error regarding the very nature of the document, what is the means of determination here? It is said:
"But that which is written in one's own hand for the sake of clarifying a doubtful matter [is established] by means of reasoning, acquisition, performance, marks, connection, and title. (2.95)

"Of doubtful meaning" (*saṃdigdhartha*) means that the matter itself is doubtful; a document for which the purpose is the purification of such doubt is described as such. The sense is that in the determination of a doubtful matter, that [document] alone is the authority. And if that [document] were written in one's own hand, then it is indeed pure. But in case of doubt, a determination must be made through reasoning (*yukti*) and other means. Reasoning (*yukti*) consists of such factors as: "At that time, Devadatta had need of wealth, and Yajñadatta was then lending his own capital," and so forth. Attainment (*prāpti*) is the fact that both were residing in the same place at that time. Action (*kriyā*) refers to the fact that this scribe is known to be non-deceptive and that these are his documents. A mark (*cihna*) includes a seal, a specific type of script, and so on. Absence of force or fraud (*balopadhyādyabhāva*) is the connection (*saṃbandha*). Consistency with the characteristics of a document (*lekhyalakṣaṇayoga*) is the source (*āgama*). The impossibility of false testimony and the like is the logical ground (*hetu*). Thus, it should be understood that a document examined by means of reasoning and the other factors is authoritative. (95)

And thus, on the back of a document whose validity is established by logic and scripture, the creditor shall cause to be written what has been received from the debtor; or he may give a receipt marked with his own hand. (2.96)

Whatever price or other item he might give, that should be written on the back of that very document. Or the creditor may give something else, marked with his own hand, to the debtor. Otherwise, even if given, it would be as if not given. || 96 ||
But when the debt has been paid in full, he should tear up the document; or for the sake of clarity, he should have another one executed.
Furthermore, whatever debt was contracted in the presence of witnesses must be repaid in the presence of witnesses. (2.97)

Having paid the debt, one should tear up the document for the sake of purification—that is, for the purpose of clearing [the obligation] so that there is no further reproach. Alternatively, however, one may cause another [document] to be made, or indeed a different document must be executed; this is an option according to the debtor's wish. But even apart from a document, that which was received with witnesses must be returned with witnesses, because it must be cleared [of the debt]. In every case, when a matter is documented, purification comes from another document; and when it involves witnesses, it comes from other witnesses. The meaning is that exactly as the object was received, so must it be returned. (97)
Thus ends the section on written documents. Now begins the section on divine ordeals (*divya*).
When there is an absence of written documents and the like, or when [the debtor] is unable to satisfy [the creditor], [an ordeal may be administered].

The balance, fire, water, poison, and the sacred ordeal (kośa) are the divine tests for the purpose of purification in this world; these are to be employed in cases of grave accusation when the accuser has placed his head [as a stake]. 2.98.
By saying "in cases of great charges," [the author] indicates that the taking of oaths applies to cases that are not of great charges. And so says Nārada:
"Truth, vehicles, weapons, cattle, seeds, gold, the feet of deities and ancestors, and meritorious gifts."
"Thus these oaths have been declared by Manu for minor causes;
however, when there is an accusation of a grave sin, the procedure of divine ordeal is proclaimed. (NSm 20.2, 4).
"In a major accusation" means in an accusation of a great sin (*mahāpātaka*) and so forth. The rest is clear. 98.
"Is the plaintiff necessarily required to provide a surety? This is the general rule:
by mutual consent, one party may act as surety while the other provides the head;
however, even without a surety, one may proceed in cases of treason against the king or in matters involving mortal sin. (2.99)

Either the defendant or the plaintiff may undergo the ordeal by their own choice; the other shall provide the head (as a stake). If the matter of the accused turns out otherwise [than claimed], then he who employs the ordeal with such a resolve as, "May this wealth of mine, or my entire property, or this limb, or my head, go to him," is called a *śirovartī* (one who provides the head). However, in cases involving treason against the king or suspicion of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), there may indeed be an ordeal even without a head-stake. The rest is clear. || 99 ||

But when there is no suspicion of a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) or similar grave offense: "In legal proceedings concerning the affairs of the king, those who are pure shall never undergo the ordeal of the plowshare, nor the balance, nor likewise the poison, beyond a thousand [paṇas]. (2.100)

The word *para* signifies "for the sake of"; for example, *brāhmaṇaparam asya dravyam* means "his wealth is for the sake of the Brāhmaṇas. [Regarding the phrase] "less than a thousand [palas], there shall be no ploughs and such," the meaning is that for amounts below a thousand, these [ploughs and other tools] are not to be employed. However, in matters concerning the king, even when the charges are small, they "shall carry out" (vaheyuḥ), which means they shall perform [the work]. Regarding the phrase "always pure": those who are constantly pure and whose purity is never suspected due to divine providence alone shall be the ones to perform it; the meaning is that even those whose impurity might be suspected are not to do so. || 100 ||
And this being so:
for a debt of a thousand, one should have the scales and other instruments made in a treasury even for a small amount;
one who is pure should be made to pay fifty, while one who is impure shall be subject to punishment. (2.101)
The meaning of this verse is clear. || 101 ||
Is the divine ordeal to be performed immediately? No, he says. What then?
Having summoned one who has bathed with his clothes on and fasted since sunrise, he should cause all the divine ordeals to be administered in the presence of the king and Brāhmaṇas. (2.102)
The mention of the presence of the king and others is for the purpose of conveying the gravity of the matter. || 102 ||
Nor should all divine ordeals be administered to everyone indiscriminately. What then?
The balance is for women, children, the elderly, the afflicted, the lame, Brahmins, and the sick; fire or water for a Śūdra; or seven barley grains for one undergoing the ordeal by poison. (2.103)

The mention of "women and so forth" is for the sake of including Kṣatriyas and others. Regarding the rule, "For one who is not a Śūdra, fire or water [is the ordeal]," it means that for one who is not a Śūdra, either fire or water may be used. This is an option based on specific conditions (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*). The meaning is that for a Kṣatriya there is fire, for a Vaiśya there is water, but for a Śūdra there are seven grains of barley, or else poison, or water, or fire. Alternatively, "for one who is not a Śūdra, fire or water" means for those born of the Kṣatriya and other castes. Consequently, for Kṣatriyas and others, there is an optional choice (*icchā-vikalpa*) among fire and the rest. However, according to other Smṛtis, a detailed arrangement based on place, time, and other factors is to be devised. (103)

The defendant, possessing the previously mentioned restraints and having performed the rites of auspiciousness and benediction, stands before the scale according to the characteristics described in other Smṛtis.
Having been brought before the scale by experts skilled in weighing, he ascends the balance; once made equal to the counterweight, the lines are marked and he is lowered. (2.104)

The ellipsis is to be supplied as "he shall perform the rite that is about to be described. One who is accused (*abhiyukta*) is one who has been charged in a legal dispute. When he has ascended the scale and is observed by experts in weighing by means of the balance being level with the counterweight (*pratimāna*), then, having made marks for the purpose of identification such as "this limb is at this spot," he should be lowered. Experts in weighing are goldsmiths and others. The counterweight is a basket (*piṭaka*) filled with sand and clods of earth, situated on the other side of the beam. The rest is clear. (104)
Having descended and stood facing north:
"O Tula, you are the abode of truth, fashioned of old by the gods;
therefore speak the truth, O auspicious one, and release me from my doubt. (2.105)
"If I am a doer of evil, O Mother, then lead me downward;
if I am pure, lead me upward," thus he should consecrate the balance.
If, when weighed, he rises upward, then there is purity; otherwise, however, the opposite is the case. As for that which is stated in the *Nāradīya*:
"If, when weighed, it increases, it shall be pure; of this there is no doubt.
But if it remains equal or decreases, it would not then be pure.
(NSm 20.12) This statement regarding purity based on descending [in weight] should be understood as referring to the case of the aforementioned consecration with mantras. 105–6.
The Scripture on Holding a Heated Iron Ball:
Having examined the two hands after they have been rubbed with rice grains, one should then place seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree upon them and wrap them with thread. (2.107)

Having rubbed his hands with rice grains, and having marked them with scratches to clearly demonstrate the burns for one who has taken the heated iron, he should place seven *aśvattha* leaves between his hands for concealment, wrap them seven times with a thread, and have the accused stand facing east near the person in the circle who is about to hand over the heated iron ball; this latter person, a skilled blacksmith who has taken up the heated iron ball, should be positioned there. || 107 ||
The other, observing the previously mentioned rules, facing north and gazing at the iron ball with palms joined in reverence, should say:
"O Purifier, you alone move within all beings;
O Seer, like a witness to merits and sins, declare the truth for me. (2.108)
The blacksmith also,
when he has been told "his," shall quickly place fifty palas of even iron, heated to the color of fire, upon both of his hands. (2.109)
Taking it up, he should walk slowly for exactly seven mandalas;
each mandala should be known as sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in extent, with an equal interval between them.
If the fire is extinguished, or if the grain is crushed, or if it is not burnt, he shall attain purification;
but if the sacrificial ball falls in between, or if there is doubt, he shall take it up again.

Having shown his hands with the marks impressed upon them, and then having crushed the rice grains—without any visible signs of burning, free from the marks such as perspiration on the forehead that indicate defeat, and liberated from suspicion of trickery and the like—he shall attain purification. However, in the event of doubt regarding the burning or the falling of the ball of rice, the procedure should be understood to be performed again after three nights or seven nights, in accordance with other Smṛti texts. The rest is clear. (109–11)
Possessing the very same restrictions mentioned previously, he shall go to water presided over by a king and a Brāhmaṇa; then,
having sworn an oath over the water, saying, "O Varuṇa,
protect me through truth," he shall enter the water while standing in it up to his navel and grasping the thighs of the two.

Having consecrated the water with the mantra ending in "O Varuṇa, protect me by truth," he should enter the water while holding with both hands the thighs of a very firm and strong man who stands waist-deep in the water. The repetition of the word "water" is for the sake of emphasis. 112.
If a swift man could simultaneously draw an arrow released by a man of middling archery skill from a bow of middling quality as it sinks [into the water], and if,
after the other has departed, he should see the submerged body, he would attain purification. (2.113)

When three arrows have been shot without being submerged, having stationed a very swift man near the middle arrow, another very swift man shall run from the vicinity of the water toward the location of the arrows at the very moment of immersion. When he has gone, the one previously stationed shall take up the arrow and return in the same manner; if he sees the submerged limb of the person standing in the water, yet not located in a different place, then he attains purification—this is the explanation already provided. 113.

A Śūdra or other such person, possessing the previously mentioned restrictions, standing near the king or a Brāhmaṇa, shall take a quantity of poison according to the measurements prescribed in another Smṛti, determined by the time, and consecrate it with the mantra:
"O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā, established in truth and righteousness. Protect us from this curse; by truth, become nectar for me. (2.114)
Having spoken thus, one should consume the Śārṅga poison produced from the snowy mountains;
when it has been digested without its characteristic effects, one should declare that person to be purified.

The word *evam* (thus) has the sense of "in this manner"; it means that for one who is not authorized for or ignorant of the mantras, this very meaning should be expressed through synonymous terms so that it may be understood. The mention of *śārṅga* (the horn) is for the purpose of removing poison of weak potency; the mention of *hema* (gold) is for the purpose of excluding [poisons] such as *kālakūṭa*. The rest is clear. || 115 ||

If the purpose is minor, or out of personal preference, one who maintains the previously mentioned rules should go into the presence of a king or a Brahmin, worship fierce deities, and fetch their bathing water; having made [the person] listen to the ritual instructions, he should cause them to drink three handfuls of that water. (2.116)

Having worshipped the fierce gods, beginning with the Ādityas, according to the proper ritual procedure in order to bring them face to face, and having taken their bath-water, he should cause the accused person to hear this: "Do not think that this is like drinking ordinary water for the sake of quenching thirst and the like. Reflecting that this [water] will be difficult to ward off—afflicting the liar even for hundreds of future births with calamities such as poverty and leprosy—he should say, "Do not do so," provided there is no reliance on truth, and then have him drink three handfuls. 116.

To explain how the manifestation [of the truth] occurs here, he says: "If, until the fourteenth day, no terrible calamity caused by kings or divine forces befalls anyone, he shall be purified; of this there is no doubt. (2.117)

If there is no immediate burning of the forehead or the like, nor the appearance of perspiration on the forehead, and if no severe calamity caused by fate or the king occurs within fourteen nights, then purity is to be understood as certain beyond doubt. This should be understood as the meaning of the verse, serving as a supplement to all ordeals. The intention is that if there is no immediate burning of the forehead or the like, and if no calamity caused by fate or the king occurs before the fourteenth night, then purity is certain; otherwise, the opposite is the case. And so it is stated in the *Svāyaṃbhuva* [Smṛti]:

"He whom the blazing fire does not burn, whom the waters do not cause to float, and who does not quickly meet with misfortune—he should be known as pure in his oath" (MDh 8.115). The phrase "and does not quickly meet with misfortune" is to be construed in conjunction with the preceding [conditions], such as not being burned by fire and so forth. Furthermore, by the force of the word *ca* ("and"), [the absence of] perspiration on the forehead and other such signs are also included. Since it is possible for non-burning and the like to occur through deception or other obstructions, the inclusion of the second indicator—"and does not meet with misfortune"—is not contradictory.

But surely this divine test (*divyasmṛti*) appears to have an unmanifested root, because it is not an object of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the like, precisely because it is designated as "divine. Furthermore, it is not an object of scripture (*āgama*), because it is not something produced [by human agency]. For the scope of scripture is not "this comes from that," but rather "by means of this, that occurs. How then is it said that "heaven results from sacrifice"? Because there is an instruction regarding what must be done by one desiring heaven, and because that [desire] would be contradicted if [the sacrifice] were not a means [to that end], one understands that sacrifice and the like are the means; thus it is said, "heaven results from sacrifice. In that case, here too, the instruction for the divine test might be for the purpose of purification, just like an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). True, if it were merely an instruction for performance. But here, on the contrary, it is stated that for one who has not been burnt by the heated iron ball, there is a further communication of faultlessness. That would seem inappropriate.

It is said: there are indeed two types of injunctions (*codanā*). For one who is suspected of theft and the like, if he confesses, there follows the application of penance or royal punishment; if he does not confess, however, there is the performance of the ordeal by balance and so forth. And in this case, when the rising upward [of the scale] occurs, the legal procedure regarding his innocence must be carried out. Consequently, it follows by implication that purity is not attained without the rising upward. For this very reason, even in the absence of a perceptible indicator, the establishment of innocence is achieved through the mere performance of oaths and the like. However, the spiritual fault (*doṣa*) pertaining to the next world remains for him. Thus it has been said: "The divine ordeals (*divya*) are for the sake of purification in this world" (YDh 2.98). The meaning is: "only in this world, not in the next. [Objection: In that case, would there not be the undesirable consequence of purity even when there is obstruction by fraud and the like? [Reply: No, because of the prohibition. As Bṛhaspati says:

"The king should cause [the accused] to be confined there for three or five nights, guarded by his own men, on suspicion of trickery. (BṛSm 8.37) Therefore, only a pure legal proceeding—free from trickery and the like—is valid for ascending [to heaven] and so forth; or, when there is suspicion of the presence of trickery and the like, provided no misfortune from gods or kings has occurred. But as for ultimate purity and impurity, where would they be of use? Consequently, its being rooted in the Veda is not contradictory. And thus says the Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa:

"O Somya, they bring a man, seized by the hand, saying: 'He has stolen; he has committed theft. Heat the axe for him! If he is the doer of that deed, then he makes himself false. Being one whose intent is falsehood, having concealed himself with falsehood, he grasps the heated axe; he is burned, and then he is killed. But if he is not the doer, then he makes himself true. Being one whose intent is truth, having concealed himself with truth, he grasps the heated axe; he is not burned, and then he is released. (ChU 6.16.1)

Other instances such as these, which are based on the application of ordeals like the balance (*tulā*), should also be sought out and cited. In this context, it is prescribed that one who is suspected is released—provided he is not burnt—by taking hold of the axe, and that his legal status be declared non-defiled; other matters, such as the occurrence of burning and so forth, are merely restated. For this reason as well, the aforementioned basis in the Veda is not contradicted. Alternatively, let its Vedic character consist simply in its conformity to what is heard [in scripture]. Even regarding its specific form, its authority in such cases is entirely uncontradicted, just as it is for the sentences of the Upaniṣads. We shall explain how this is so later on. This being the case, following the historical accounts (*itihāsa*) related by Vyāsa and others, the postulation of deities—such as the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) and others—who reside within the balance and act as witnesses to the universe, as presiding authorities, is also not contradictory. And thus, there are deities known through the words of mantras (*māntravarṇika*).
"O Purifier, you alone move within all beings"—thus it has been said.
Likewise, even in the *Svāyaṃbhuvamanu*, the presiding presence of the deity as following truth and dharma is demonstrated. As he says:
"For in ancient times, when Vatsa was falsely accused by his younger brother..."
"Fire did not burn even a single hair of him, for he was a witness to the world through truth. (MDh 8.116)

*Spaśaḥ* means a spy; that is to say, a witness. Alternatively, let it be that [the authority of the *Divya-smṛti*] is based solely on inference (*anumāna*). For one who is faultless yet suspected of being faulty—just as fire does not burn [in the case of] mica and the like due to the non-perception of burning—the pure inference derived from the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) established through the operation of beginningless and non-deviant worldly practice is indeed unimpeded, just as the inference of the absence of smoke from the absence of fire. Therefore, the fact that the *Divya-smṛti* possesses a valid basis is also logically established; this is the general direction of the argument. [Objection: But if this were so, divine ordeals (*divya*) would not apply to a future matter, because the presence or absence of malice (*dauṣṭya*) would be unestablished. [Response: Who says otherwise? [Objection: How then is there the practice of drinking from the *kośa* (sacred water) and so forth regarding a future matter? [Response: That is merely a manifestation of a truthful resolve (*satya-saṃkalpa*), intended to ensure the censure of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) for those who deviate from it. However, by acting contrary to one's resolve, the fault of falsehood (*anṛta-doṣa*) remains certain. Enough of this digression. (117)
Thus ends the section on divine matters.
Now begins the section on the partition of inheritance:
[concerning] property acquired in the various ways previously described.
If the father should make a partition, he may divide the sons according to his will; either he may give the eldest a superior share, or they may all be equal sharers. (2.118)

For when one wishes to enter another stage of life (*āśrama*), or for the sake of ensuring the practice of dharma by virtuous sons, or out of curiosity, he may divide his property among his sons—that is, he may provide them with shares. According to his own will, he should give to each son as much as he desires to give; it is not according to the sons' will. The meaning is that the father should not be compelled by his sons to make a division or to establish a specific restrictive rule. For this very reason, he may, out of propriety, endow the eldest with the best share—whether less or more than the others—or he may make all of them equal sharers. In that case, it should be exactly as the father wishes; thus, this rule concerning the sons is faultless. (118)

If he should give equal shares regardless of [the husband's] affection, qualities, and so forth, solely out of impartiality, then the wives whose *strīdhana* was not given by the husband or the father-in-law must be made sharers of an equal portion. (2.119)

In the case of equal distribution of shares, the wives whose husbands have died—namely, daughters-in-law, granddaughters-in-law, and wives—should be made entitled to their husbands' shares, provided that their husband or father-in-law did not personally give them *strīdhana* (woman’s property). Alternatively, those to whom no *strīdhana* was given should be made recipients of a share equal to the *strīdhana*. According to another Smṛti text stating, "The woman's inheritance shall not exceed two thousand [paṇas]," this much alone should be given even when the wealth is abundant; and even when it is small, it must be given as an equal share. Others, however, assert that childless women are entitled to equal shares on the grounds of their being eligible for *niyoga* (levirate marriage). But that is incorrect because *niyoga* is no longer possible. For those for whom *niyoga* is still possible, it is proper that they receive only a share corresponding to *niyoga*. (119)

If one who is capable of maintaining his own family and performing religious duties does so without depending on paternal property and yet remains indifferent to it, he may be separated from the estate after being given something;
this is recorded as the law for those whose shares were divided unequally by the father. (2.120)

Even for one who does not strive [for a share], a separation should be effected by performing some slight act of respect so as not to cause discord at a later time. But surely, even in this case, if he should say: "The entire portion was not received by me; let that be given to me," then there would indeed be a conflict. We say: there is no such conflict. Why? Because of the phrase "of sons divided unequally by their father"—this is the ellipsis. The meaning is: "Dharma is declared to be that which is performed by the father"; that very law of partition which was made by the father is what is remembered as ordained. Therefore, there is no conflict. || 120 ||
But by their own right, after the death of both parents, the sons shall divide the inheritance and the debt equally.
The daughters shall take the remainder of the mother's estate after the debt has been cleared; in their absence, the heirs in the line of succession [shall take it]. (2.121)

After clearing off the debt, the sons shall divide the remaining inheritance of their parents after [the latter's] passing. The mention of "sons" (*suta*) is for the purpose of including the *aurasa* (legitimate) son. "Parents" (*pitarau*) means the mother and the father; the meaning is "after those two parents have died. After the father’s passing, they shall divide the paternal estate, and after the mother’s passing, the maternal estate. Even in the absence of an inheritance, they shall pay the debt proportionally according to their respective shares. And since equality is stated regarding the payment of the debt, it is understood that there is also equality in the division [of the estate]. As for that which is stated in another *smṛti*:
The eldest shall receive a twentieth part as his preferential share, as well as the best item from among all the property. (MDh 9.112)

When such an inequality in the division [of property] is understood, it should be known as occurring through the mutual consent of the brothers. Others, however, describe the scope of the texts concerning unequal division as being dependent on merit (*guṇa*), considering that [merit] to be for the sake of ritual action (*karma*). But that is understood to be improper, because the substance [of the inheritance] is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). As for those statements regarding the seizure of property and so forth in the event of the non-performance of the *Agnihotra* and other rites, they are intended for the punishment of persons who act unjustly, not for the purpose of establishing that the substance is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). Therefore, inequality in division is indeed by the will of the brothers themselves. As for the statement by Gautama that one who acts unjustly has no share, even that is to be explained merely as an instruction based on the opinion of others (*paramata*), according to the expression "some say" (*ekeṣām*, GDh 28.40); this is the general direction. Just as the sons of a father are sharers of the wealth in equal shares, so too are the daughters of a mother. However, they should divide the remainder from the debt; but they should not pay the debt even for a mother who is herself without wealth. For the sons, however, their connection to the mother is not at all absent—it is not non-existent—but rather, it exists in the absence of those daughters. The meaning is that the "succession" (*anvaya*) belongs to the sons. Others, however, explain that in the absence of those daughters, the succession belongs to her [the mother's] own line. But that is incorrect, because of the Vedic mantra: "He did not leave that inheritance to the sister" (*na jāmaye tān vo riktham āraik*). If it is argued that this refers to the paternal wealth, we say no, because of the mention of the connection to the mother in the phrase: "If the mothers generated the carrier" (*yadī mātaro janayanta vahnim*). Here, "mothers" (*mātaraḥ*) refers to women; "carrier" (*vahni*) means a son fit to carry [the lineage]. The meaning there is that the son alone is the heir, not the woman. And from this very mention of the "carrier," the lack of property for the impotent (*klība*) and others who are incapable of marriage is established. If it is asked, "In that case, let it belong to the sons even when there are daughters," we say no. Because of the Smṛti rule, "The daughters of the mother," and because of the conformity with the Vedic mantra and other Smṛtis, the meaning is that the nature of the inheritance belongs to the daughters themselves. Therefore, it is settled that in their absence, it goes to the sons. (121)
And among those who live together,

[the property] acquired by one himself, provided there has been no depletion of the paternal estate, as well as what is obtained through friendship and what is received at marriage, shall not belong to the co-heirs. (2.122)

Whatever else has been acquired without depleting the paternal estate—such as that obtained from a friend (*maitra*) and that received at marriage (*audvāhika*)—belongs to the acquirer alone and shall not belong even to the other heirs. That which is obtained from a friend is *maitra*; that which is received at a wedding is *audvāhika*. Even if obtained through the depletion of paternal wealth, gifts from friends and the like are indeed indivisible, because of the force of the initial context. Others, however, maintain that only those things such as gifts from friends, when acquired without depleting the paternal estate, are indivisible, according to the maxim of "the specific subsuming the general. But that is improper, since marriage itself must be accomplished by means of common property. (122)

But when there is no distinction such as [the order of] affection and so forth, an equal division is prescribed for the distribution of property arising from a common source; however, for those who have multiple fathers, the allotment of shares is determined according to the father. (2.123)

That property whose origin, acquisition, and possession are common [to all] is described as such; in that case, regarding the property where the origin is common, [the text says]: "But the division. The word "but" (tu) has the sense of restriction. The meaning is: there is indeed a division. And that [division] is recorded as being equal even when there is an excess of suffering for one [member], such as from the body; the meaning is that it is ordained as equal. Is the division always equal for all heirs? No; it would be equal only among brothers. "But for those who have different fathers," such as the sons of paternal uncles and so forth, the determination of shares is according to the father—that is, according to the father's own division. This implies that for brothers, the division is first equal; once the division has been made, the sons of any one [of them] shall divide his share into sub-portions (aṃśāṃśataḥ). For the intention is that the grandsons' right to the grandfather's property is through the father, and not by themselves as the fathers were. || 123 ||

Now, does ownership arise from partition, or does partition occur when ownership already exists? They say that ownership arises from partition; otherwise, the scriptural injunctions regarding the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) and so forth for one whose son has been born would be contradicted, because the relinquishment of property is impossible when wealth is held in common. Furthermore, the Smṛti rule regarding partition by choice would not exist [if ownership were not established prior to partition]. Nor is it reasonable to say that performance [of rites] occurs through the son's consent, since one who is merely born lacks the capacity for consent. To dispel such doubts and others like them, he says: "Land acquired by the grandfather, or a mortgage, or even property..."
In that case, there would be equal ownership for both the father and the son. (2.124)

The meaning is that regarding land acquired by the grandfather, or a mortgage, or an imperishable endowment (*akṣayanidhi*), or any other property whatsoever, the sovereignty of the father and son over it must be understood as equal and beyond doubt. The use of the word "of both" is intended to indicate that ownership remains undivided. The separate mention of land and so forth should be seen as due to its indivisibility or its permanence. As for the objection regarding the contradiction with ritual practice (*anuṣṭhāna*) and the like, that is of no consequence, since such practice can be accomplished even with property acquired by oneself; or rather, let the performance of rituals take place after dividing the property at that very time. However, the Smṛti rule regarding division by choice should be understood as applying to one who possesses property acquired by himself. Therefore, it is established that division occurs when there is [separate] ownership. 124.
And since partition occurs only when there is property, therefore:
even after partition, a son born of a wife of the same caste (savarṇā) is entitled to a share.
Or rather, his share may be determined from what is visible, after deducting income and expenses. (2.125)

If a son is born after the partition has been made while the mother’s menses have not yet ceased, he too certainly has a connection to the property; therefore, it is said that [the right to share] exists only when there is ownership (*svatva*). For if the connection to ownership were established by the act of partition itself, then the connection to the property for one born after partition would not be possible. But in this case, he indeed has a connection to the property. Hence, the term "ownership" (*svatva*) is used. Therefore, this verse is commenced to distinguish that point: "Even after partition, a son born of a wife of equal caste is entitled to a share. The word "should be" (*syāt*) is to be supplied. Although there is no distinction [in his status], it should be understood that he is entitled to a share of the father's inheritance. As Gautama says: "One born after partition [shares] the paternal [estate]" (GDh 28.29). Furthermore, even one born after partition, if the father is without wealth, shall receive a share from the visible property of the brothers alone. However, this is the distinction: [it must be] free from income and expenditure. That which he himself has acquired is "income" (*āya*); that portion of the property which has been consumed from it is "expenditure" (*vyaya*). The meaning is that the property, cleared of income and expenditure, is to be divided equally with the one born after partition. (125)
He clarifies this very point:
"If one recovers property that was taken and had come into his possession by succession, he need not give it to the heirs; the same applies to what has been acquired through learning. (2.126)

If one who has already been divided recovers, by his own effort and with the consent of the other heirs, property inherited from his father and ancestors that had been interrupted in its enjoyment at the time of partition, he need not give it back to those co-heirs born after the partition (*vibhaktaja*) at the time of a subsequent division. This also applies to what is obtained through learning; the word "and" (*ca*) implies what is obtained through friendship and so forth. It has already been stated that this refers to what remains after deducting income and expenses. (126)
Furthermore:
whatever has been given by the parents to anyone shall belong to that person alone. This is the rule regarding the partition among those born after partition while the parents are still living.
When dividing [the estate] after the father's death, the mother also shall receive an equal share.

A mother who possesses no property of her own shall also receive a share equal to that of a son; and this term "mother" (mātṛ) should be understood as referring to any wife of the father, since there is no distinction made regarding their relationship to the father. || 127 ||
Furthermore:
"But those who have not been consecrated should be consecrated by their brothers who have already been consecrated;
and the sisters, having given a fourth part from their own shares, [should be consecrated]. (2.128)

The *saṃskāra* (sacramental rite) refers to marriage. That [rite] must be performed for brothers who have not yet been consecrated by those brothers who have already been consecrated. Alternatively, having set aside wealth sufficient for that purpose, the remainder should be divided.
