From this very point it is understood: the accomplishment of marriage proceeds from common property; and that marriage-related wealth, even if subject to depletion, belongs exclusively to those who acquired it. Therefore, the brothers and sisters are to be consecrated from the common property alone. However, if there should be little wealth or none at all, then one should set aside a fourth part from one's own share for the sake of the sisters, and the rest should be divided equally. || 128 ||

Thus, the division is equal for those of the same caste; but for those of different castes: "The sons of a Brāhmaṇa, according to their respective castes, shall receive four, three, two, and one shares; the sons born of a Kṣatriya shall receive three, two, and one shares; and the two sons of a Vaiśya shall receive two and one shares. (2.129)

When a Brāhmaṇa has sons by wives of the four classes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇī, then the property shall be divided into ten parts, six parts, and three parts respectively; and according to the order of the Brāhmaṇa and the others, they shall receive four, three, two, and one shares. That is to say: four shares for the Brāhmaṇa, three for the Kṣatriya, two for the Vaiśya, and one for the Śūdra. The same rule applies to those born of the Kṣatriya caste: three shares for the Kṣatriya, two for the Vaiśya, and one for the Śūdra. Likewise for one born of the Vaiśya caste: two shares for the Vaiśya and one for the son of the Śūdra wife—such is the settled rule. Now, it may be objected that for the twice-born there can be no son by a Śūdra wife at all, because marriage with her is forbidden. True; however, the intention is that this rule for distribution applies in the event that one proceeds [to marry her] due to a misconception regarding the meaning of the Smṛti texts. (129)
But even though they do not receive equal shares, the settled rule is:
"Where property is seen to have been taken from one another by those who have already divided, they shall divide that again into equal portions. (2.130)
The statement regarding stability is free from doubt for the purpose of attaining equal distribution. || 130 ||
This is the law of partition for legitimate sons born of the wife. But in their absence:

"A son begotten by means of *niyoga* in the field of another by a man who has no son of his own is, according to the law, the heir to the estate and the giver of the funeral oblation (*piṇḍa*) to both. (2.131)

But surely, because the appointment (*niyoga*) is prohibited for a Brāhmaṇa, this [rule] cannot be undertaken by him; it must then be for the sake of a Kṣatriya or others. It is not that the appointment is prohibited for a Brāhmaṇa, but rather for a Brāhmaṇī. Therefore, a son produced by another would not belong to the Brāhmaṇa [husband]; however, there is no lack of procreative capacity for a Brāhmaṇa with respect to a Kṣatriya woman or others. Thus, this alternative rule is entirely consistent in the absence of a legitimate son (*aurasa*). || 131 ||
What are the characteristics of the legitimate son? It is said: The legitimate son (*aurasa*) is born of the lawful wife; equal to him is the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāsuta*).
The son of the field (*kṣetraja*) is one begotten upon the wife by a kinsman of the same lineage (*sagotra*) or by another. (2.132)

A woman of the same caste (*savarṇā*), consecrated by the *brāhma* or other forms of marriage, is the lawful wife (*dharmapatnī*). A son begotten by himself upon her is the legitimate son (*aurasa*). The statement regarding his equality [with others] is intended to indicate his superiority over the *kṣetraja* and other types of sons. The nature of the appointed daughter (*putrikā*) is to be understood from another *smṛti*. As for the *kṣetraja*, however, he is one begotten through the practice of *niyoga* upon the wife (*kṣetre*), who is the husband's field, by a kinsman of the same lineage (*sagotra*) or by another. (132)

Even in the absence of a formal appointment (*niyoga*), a son born secretly in the house is considered a "secret-born" (*gūḍhaja*) son; a son born of an unmarried girl is considered a "maiden-born" (*kānīna*) son, the son of his maternal grandfather. (2.133)
But these two should be understood as belonging to the mother's caste, due to the lack of knowledge regarding the father. || 133 ||
And likewise:
A son born of a woman who has been either unwounded or wounded [in marriage] is a *paunarbhava* son;
he whom the mother or the father gives away becomes a *dattaka* son. (2.134)

A *paunarbhava* is one born of a woman who, after her husband has died, has not lost her virginity (*akṣatayoni*) and has not been consecrated by another [man], or one born of a woman whose virginity has been lost (*kṣatayoni*). As it is said: "Having lived with others, she enters the household of that very [man]" (cf. VaDh 17.19). [An adopted son] is given by his parents—that is, by the father or the mother—with their permission. And so Vasiṣṭha says: "But a woman shall neither give nor receive a son, except with the permission of her husband" (VaDh 15.5). An *dattaka* is one given by his parents in accordance with the law (*dharmeṇa*). 134.
One who is purchased from those two is a "purchased" son; one who is made by himself is an "artificial" (kṛtrima) son;
one who has given himself is a "self-given" (svayaṃdatta) son; and one born of a pregnant bride is a "son received with the bride" (sahoḍhaja). (2.135)

But one who is sold for a price by those two, his parents, who have the authority to do so, is called the "purchased" (krīta) son of the buyer. The word "but" (tu) serves to indicate that, by analogy with the given daughter (*dattakanyā*), the mother likewise lacks independence. One who is destitute of both mother and father and is accepted as a son is the "artificial" (*kṛtrima*) son. One who has given himself in this very manner is the "self-given" (*svayaṃdatta*); he is so called because he himself has given himself. These sons, beginning with the adopted (*dattaka*), are to be understood as being of equal status according to other Smṛti texts. As for the son born of a pregnant bride (*sahoḍhaja*), he is one whose conception occurred while the mother was in the womb during her marriage; he is to be recognized as the son of the husband and belongs to the caste of the mother. || 135 ||
If one who has been abandoned by his mother and father is somehow taken up [by another], he shall be an *apaviddha* son;
that is to say, he is designated as an *apaviddha*.
The giver of the funeral cake and the receiver of the inheritance among these are determined by each succeeding one in the absence of each preceding one. (2.136)

Among these sons—beginning with the *aurasa* and taught in their respective order—it should be understood that in the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent one is the giver of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) and the receiver of the share. However, when a preceding son exists, only a mere subsistence allowance is to be assigned for the sake of compassion toward the subsequent ones. Thus says the *Svāyambhuva*:
"The *aurasa* son alone is the master of the paternal wealth;
however, he should grant a livelihood to the others for the sake of compassion" (MDh 9.163).

The mention of the *aurasa* son is intended as an illustration for all types of sons born of the wife (*kṣetraja*, etc.). The meaning is that he alone who, by virtue of being the *aurasa* son, is the heir to the inheritance, shall take the entire paternal wealth; for the sake of kindness toward the others, he should provide them merely with subsistence. As for the specific rule regarding the division of the *kṣetraja* son’s share when an *aurasa* son exists: "When dividing the paternal inheritance, the *aurasa* son should give a sixth part of the father's wealth to the *kṣetraja* son, or even a fifth. (MDh 9.164)
Thus it has been said again:
"The legitimate son of the body and the son begotten on the wife are the two heirs to the father's estate;
but the other ten, in their respective order, are sharers in the family name and a portion of the inheritance. (MDh 9.165)

Thus, in this context, the *kṣetraja* son is intended specifically as the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*). But is he not indeed equal to the legitimate (*aurasa*) son? True; for by that very same author it has been stated: "They are both sharers in the father’s inheritance. How then [is it said] that "he receives a sixth or even a fifth share"? This refers specifically to the wealth of the biological father. For since he is equal to the legitimate son with respect to his maternal grandfather, he is entitled to the entire share [of that grandfather's estate]. However, with respect to his own biological father, he is excluded because he was procreated for the sake of another. It is with reference to this very point that the Vasiṣṭha-smṛti states: "The son of an appointed daughter is the third [in the order of heirs]" (VaDh 17.15). A woman is given by her father to another man solely as a field (*kṣetra*) for the purpose of producing offspring; therefore, he can be called her *kṣetraja*. Furthermore, because the biological father also produces him for the sake of another, his connection to the woman is merely through the "field" in the sense of being consecrated [for procreation]; thus he bears the designation *kṣetraja*. In that regard, his entitlement to the father’s inheritance as something distinct from the legitimate son refers to the maternal grandfather, while the inequality of shares refers to the biological father—thus there is no contradiction. As for the alternative between the fifth and sixth shares, there is an option according to the will of the legitimate son. In other cases as well, the determination of unequal shares is to be understood in exactly this way. Therefore, it is established that in the absence of the preceding [son], the succeeding one has a connection to the property. As for this passage from the Svāyambhuva [Manusmṛti]:
The legitimate son of the body, the son begotten on the wife, the adopted son, the made son, the son secretly born, and the son cast off— these six are both heirs and kinsmen.

The son of an unmarried girl, the son received with a bride, the purchased son, the son of a remarried woman, the self-given son, and the son of a Śūdra woman—these six are kinsmen who do not inherit. (MDh 9.159–160)

What is the meaning of this? The five [sons], beginning with the *kṣetraja*, share in the inheritance even when the *aurasa* (legitimate son) exists; however, those beginning with the *kānīna* (maiden-born son) do so only in the absence of the former. By this, the rule of Vasiṣṭha is explained. And so says Śaṅkha: "Two shares for the father, two indeed for the *aurasa*, three for the *kṣetraja* and the son of the appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*), and one each for the others. The statement "three for the *kṣetraja* and the *putrikā-putra*" implies that each of these two receives one and a half shares. Furthermore, because of the statement regarding the division by the father, these [latter sons] share in the inheritance while the father is still living, provided the *aurasa* exists. But after [the father's death], according to the teaching of the Teacher (Ācārya), the established rule is that the subsequent ones have the right of succession only in the absence of the preceding ones. As for the mention of a different order, that should be understood as an option based on the father’s own will. In his absence, however, the order is exactly as stated by the Teacher. In this manner, other statements concerning partition of this same kind should also be interpreted. (136)
In order to demonstrate that all these, beginning with the adopted son (dattaka), belong to the same caste (sajātīya), he says:
"This rule has been declared by me regarding sons of the same caste;
even one born to a Śūdra from a female slave shall, if born of desire, be a sharer of the inheritance. (2.137)

By stating, "This rule has been declared by me," he demonstrates that those rules mentioned in other Smṛtis have their application in other contexts. And this has already been explained: namely, that this conceptualization of the priority and posteriority of the connection to property applies only when the father has passed away; whereas while he is alive, the arrangement of partition follows what is stated in other Smṛtis. He clarifies this very point: "When the father is dead, this arrangement of partition has been determined by us because it was difficult to determine otherwise. By stating, "But while he is alive, even a son born of a Śūdra slave-girl shall receive a share by the father's wish," he shows a disregard for the detailed determination [of other cases]. (137)
And by his own wish alone:
"If the father has died, the brothers shall make him a sharer of half [the estate].
One who has no brothers shall take everything, except for the son of a daughter. (2.138)

The use of the word "half" (*ardha*) is intended to indicate a smaller share. Thus Bṛhaspati says: "If a son born of a Śūdra wife cohabits with his brother after the father has died, they should give him merely a share equal to that of an attendant, provided he is obedient" (BṛSm 26.83). In this case as well, this rule applies to one who acts in violation of the scriptures—just like the sons of twice-born men born of Śūdra wives—and does not imply an inference of a rule for taking a Śūdra woman as a concubine; thus there is no fault. However, in the absence of daughters or their sons, a man without brothers shall inherit everything by the king's permission, according to the very words of Bṛhaspati: "The king shall take all the property of one who leaves no heir, or [he may give it] by his permission to a son born of a concubine, so say some. Precisely because of this mention of the absence of a daughter’s son (*dauhitr*), it follows that even among the twice-born, in the absence of a son, the daughter’s sons are the heirs to the wealth. For this very reason, the rule regarding the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather is logically established. (138)
Thus, first, the rule for a Śūdra has been stated according to the Vaiśeṣika school. But without distinction [of caste], it is as follows:
"The wife, the daughters, the parents, the brothers, their sons, a kinsman born of the same lineage (gotraja), a relative, a pupil, and fellow students. (2.139)
In the absence of these, each subsequent one among them becomes the heir to the wealth of the deceased who left no son; for this rule applies to all castes. (2.140)

In this context, the term *patnī* (wife) refers to one who has conceived. Thus Vasiṣṭha states: "Now follows the division of inheritance among brothers; and as for those women who may be childless, [the division continues] until they obtain a son" (VaDh 17.40–41). This shows that pregnant women are entitled to the inheritance. Furthermore, because of the expression "childless," the word *putra* (son) here serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the fetus itself. Alternatively, even a daughter may be considered a "son" once she is born, so that she may inherit. Accordingly, Gautama, after stating "and the wife of one who is childless" (GDh 28.21), says "or she may seek to obtain seed" (GDh 28.22). By this, he makes it known that the mention of the "woman" is intended to include the pregnant woman. And the daughters referred to are specifically appointed daughters (*putrikā*). Thus, the *Svāyaṃbhuva* [Manu] speaks with reference precisely to the appointed daughter.
"As the self is, so is the son; the daughter is equal to the son. While she remains as one's own self, how could another take the wealth? (MDh 9.130)

However, in the event of fear regarding the birth of a son or in the absence of offspring, the entitlement belongs to them. The plural number is for the purpose of indicating the plurality of appointed daughters (*putrikā*). The word "and" (*ca*) serves to indicate that there may also be a connection with property through desire by way of conjunction. The particle "only" (*eva*) is for the purpose of restriction in every instance. "Mother and father" (*pitarau*) [is a dual compound]; the use of a copulative compound (*dvandva*) despite their joint entitlement is for the purpose of ensuring that each one individually obtains [the inheritance]. Even when indicated as a copulative compound, the mother has priority. As it is said: "The mother of a son who is childless shall obtain the inheritance."
"And when she too has passed away, the father's mother shall take the wealth" (MDh 9.217).
In every respect, this is the specific scope for the case where there is no offspring and no descendant of a descendant (*anaptya*). But is it not also the case that:
"The father shall take the inheritance of one who has no son, or the brothers themselves" (MDh 9.185)?

This should be understood as applying when the mother is absent. How so? From the statement of Śaṅkha: "The property of one who has died without a son goes to his brothers; in their absence, the parents shall take it, or the eldest wife. This refers to a uterine brother, intended for a case where there is no wife or daughter possessing the characteristics previously described. Furthermore, if there were another wife of the father, then in her absence the parents [would take it]; in that situation, the father alone should come first, according to the rule that "the father shall take the property of one who is sonless," or else the eldest wife with his consent, but if he does not consent, then the eldest wife. The word "eldest" (*jyeṣṭhā*) signifies one of the same caste (*savarṇā*). Or rather, all [wives] may [take it] if they are of the same caste, because of the word "or" (*vā*). By this, the following is also explained:
"If among brothers one should die without offspring or should renounce the world, his brothers shall divide his property, excluding the woman's property. (NSm 13.24)

Regarding sons born of Kṣatriya women and others, however, this is the scope of the rule: "In the absence of the mother, the father's mother shall take the wealth. The word *tathā* in the phrase "the brothers likewise" (*bhrātaras tathā*) has the sense of "in the same manner"; it includes all types of brothers, such as those from different mothers and so forth. Their sons should be understood in the same order; likewise, the *gotrajas*—those related through the sapinda, the samānodaka, the single male ancestor, or the single ṛṣi—should be understood in their respective order. "Kinsman" (*bandhu*) refers to the maternal uncle and others. The "teacher" (*ācārya*), although not explicitly mentioned here, is included by implication due to his close association with the father. The "pupil" (*śiṣya*) is one who has been initiated (*upanīta*). A "fellow-student" (*sabrahmacārin*) is one initiated by the same teacher. For these, the right of succession belongs to each subsequent one in the absence of each preceding one. The rest is clear. (139–40)
Thus, the rule for the distribution of inheritance based on caste has been stated. Now, that based on the stages of life (āśrama) is being declared:
For forest-dwellers, renunciants, and students, the heirs in order are the teacher, a virtuous pupil, a spiritual brother, and one who shares the same sacred site (tīrtha). (2.141)

The lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) is intended here. A "dharma-brother" is one connected to the same teacher; a "fellow-pupil" (ekatīrthin) is one connected to the same stage of life (āśrama). The rest is clear. As for those other than the lifelong celibate, the forest-dweller, and the ascetic, the previously mentioned rule for distribution applies by default. || 141 ||
But a reunited coparcener shall give and take the share of one who is reunited, as well as of a uterine brother; this applies both to one who has been born and to one who has died. (2.142)

One who, having been divided, lives again in union with his father or brother by reuniting their property for some other reason, is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* (one reunited). In that case, if among those living together—father and sons—a son is born to the father, a share must be given to him as well, and [the property] of the deceased [father] must be taken [by him]. And a uterine brother [takes the share] of a uterine brother; this, however, should be understood to apply to the case of division according to the mother, and refers to one born after partition (*vibhaktaja*) when the father is without wealth. As for the rule of Gautama: "Now, regarding the division of reunited property: among the deceased, it belongs to the eldest" (GDh 28.27), here the word "eldest" refers to the father himself. In the absence of another uterine brother, he is the heir to the wealth of the deceased sons and of those brothers not reunited with him. Thus it has been said: "The father shall take the property of one who is sonless" (MDh 9.185). Others, however, say that the word "eldest" refers to the brother. That, however, requires further consideration. The rest is clear. 142.
In this regard, others recite this verse as a commentary on the preceding one:
"The uterine brother who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* shall take the wealth; the non-uterine brother shall not take it.
Even if he is not a *saṃsṛṣṭin*, the uterine brother shall take it, but not one born of another mother. (2.143)

Even if he is commensal (*saṃsṛṣṭin*), one born of a different mother does not share in the wealth when a uterine brother exists; rather, the meaning is that only the uterine brother, even if not commensal, is the heir to the wealth. || 143 ||
But those who are indeed entitled to the inheritance shall be the brothers and their sons of such a nature;

however, one who is outcast, his son, a eunuch, a cripple, one who is insane, an idiot, a blind man, and one suffering from an incurable disease must be maintained, but they are to receive no share. (2.144)

His son is one born of a degraded person (*patita*). A madman is one possessed by a planetary spirit (*graha*). An idiot (*jaḍa*) is one who is perpetually devoid of intelligence. One afflicted by incurable diseases such as leprosy is one suffering from an untreatable illness. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include those mentioned in other *smṛtis*, such as the deaf and so forth. The rest is clear. Some hold that the mention of the lame and others is for the purpose of indicating all those who are disqualified from performing the *agnihotra* and other rites; however, that is incorrect, because property is for the sake of the person, and we see that even one who is unlearned and disqualified is indeed entitled to property. As Gautama says: "A learned man may, at his pleasure, not give what he has earned himself to those who are unlearned," and "Those who are unlearned shall divide [the estate] equally" (GDh 28.30–31). Therefore, their lack of a share is due solely to this prohibition, and not because of their disqualification. Or rather, their lack of a share is due to their connection with the signs of great sins (*mahāpātaka*) committed in another birth. However, the traditional doctrine (*saṃpradāya*) holds that the grandfather’s property belongs to the blind and others provided they have not fallen from caste. It should be understood that this is merely a statement of propriety regarding the inability to employ property beyond mere maintenance, based on their physical incapacity. And thus says the *Svāyaṃbhuva*:

"If the eldest or the youngest should be deprived of his share from the distribution, or if either one should die, his share is not lost. (MDh 9.211). By this, [the author] shows that when there is an inability to utilize the share obtained, an appropriation [of it by others] occurs as a matter of propriety; for this very reason, it is said, "his share is not lost. And thus, these [categories] are themselves without shares. 144.
But their sons born of their own wives (aurasa) and those born of their fields (kṣetraja) are entitled to shares, being free from fault;
and their daughters must be maintained until they are given away to husbands. (2.145)

However, sons such as the *aurasa* (legitimate), *kṣetraja* (born of the wife), and others, being faultless, are indeed entitled to a share even for those who are lame or otherwise disabled. Even for the impotent man, sons such as the *kṣetraja* and others certainly exist. Their sons and their daughters—specifically appointed daughters (*putrikā*)—must be maintained by those who inherit the property of the lame and others; they must be supported with food, clothing, and so forth, until they are provided with suitable husbands, and they must be honored by them with the status of mistress of the household. || 145 ||
Furthermore:
"The childless wives of these [husbands] who are of virtuous conduct must be maintained; however, those who are unfaithful or likewise hostile shall be banished. (2.146)

Even women who are not unfaithful, if they act perversely by relying on their own property or wealth and live according to their own independent will, are likewise to be banished. By the use of the word "ca" (and), the intention is that they [should be banished] specifically while still possessing their rightful share of women's property. || 146 ||

What, then, is a woman’s property? It is said: That which is given by her father, mother, son, or brother; that which is received at the nuptial fire; and that which is received upon supersession—this is declared to be a woman’s property. (2.147)

What is obtained at the time of marriage in the presence of the sacred fire (*adhyagni*); what is received as a gift upon taking a second wife (*ādhivedanika*), whether given to the superseded wife or for the purpose of supersession; and, by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), ornaments and so forth mentioned in other legal treatises (*smṛti*)—this is to be understood as *strīdhana* (woman’s property). || 147 ||

In this regard, the distinction is as follows: "What was given by relatives, as well as the nuptial fee (śulka) and the subsequent gift (anvādheya), when she dies childless, her kinsmen shall obtain that. (2.148)

That which is given by the father and others is *bandhudatta*. That which is given for the purpose of taking a second wife and so forth is *śulka*. That which is given as a subsequent gift (*anvādheya*) is that which is given to be enjoyed by the lineage. When she dies childless, her kinsmen—the uterine brothers—shall take this. And thus says Gautama: "The dowry of a sister belongs to the uterine brothers after the mother's [death]" (GDh 28.25). This rule stated by the Teacher applies only after the mother’s [death]. || 148 ||
But apart from the nuptial fee and so forth: "The wealth of a childless woman belongs to her husband even in the four [marriages] beginning with the Brāhma;
if she has borne children, it belongs to her daughters; in the remaining [marriages], it goes to her father. (2.149)

Whatever woman’s property exists in the four types of marriage beginning with the Brāhma, that belongs to the husband if she has not borne children; if she has borne children, it belongs to the daughters alone. (149)

In connection with the discussion of the Āsura and other forms of marriage, this is stated: Having taken wealth from the groom, if one then gives away the girl and subsequently takes her back, he shall be fined and made to pay the expenses along with interest; if she has died, he may take back what was given after deducting the expenses incurred by both parties. (2.150)

Having given away a maiden, if he takes her back, he shall be punished by the king; furthermore, he shall be made to pay the husband the expenses along with interest. But if she has died, the husband shall recover what was given [to her] after clearing off the depletion caused by his own purposes and that incurred for her father. 150.
Having thus spoken incidentally, he states the subject at hand:
"In times of famine, for the sake of religious duties, or during illness or imprisonment, a husband is not required to give back to his wife the property she received from him. (2.151)

It is understood from the word *bhartṛ* (husband/master) that a brother or other relative may also give [the property], even if it has been seized during a famine or similar crisis. "Seizure by force" (*saṃpratirodhaka*) refers to taking [property] through confinement, thinking, "If he does not give it right now, he will not leave. Others say it means the siege of a city. The rest is clear. || 151 ||
Furthermore:
He shall give an equal amount as a compensation for supersession (*ādhivedanika*) to a wife who has been superseded.
If no woman's property (*strīdhana*) has been given to her, half of that [compensation] is prescribed. (2.152)

To her whom he has married, he must give an amount equal to whatever wealth was spent during the marriage ceremony, provided that no separate property (strīdhana) had previously been given to her; however, if it had been given, then half of that amount should be given. This rule is to be understood as applying to a woman who has been superseded by another wife, except when such supersession is caused by a specific legal ground for taking a second wife. || 152 ||
Thus has this division of inheritance been described. But if someone should deny the partition by saying "I am undivided," then, when the question arises as to how that is to be determined, he says:
"In the case of a denial of partition, [it is established] by means of the cognizance of kinsmen and relatives, witnesses, and written documents;
and by means of the management, enjoyment, and acquisition of shares, houses, fields, and purchases. (2.153)

In the event of a denial regarding partition, the proof of partition must be established by means of kinsmen and others. A "kinsman" (*jñāti*) refers to a maternal uncle and so forth; a "relative" (*bandhu*) refers to the son of a paternal uncle and so forth. For these are generally involved in the process of partition and are usually present nearby. Alternatively, there may be other witnesses, or a written document that serves as proof of the partition. As Bṛhaspati has said:
"A document should be prepared by the brothers who have partitioned among themselves, recording the transaction for the purpose of mutual notification.
Or, blameless witnesses should be appointed by those making the partition to ensure there is no contradiction. (BṛSm 26.148)

Or else, there may be a witness, or a mutually perceived mark of partition, or a written document for the purpose of establishing the terms of the gift and so forth. Likewise: "By means of gifts, houses, fields, and dowries. "Gift" (*ādeya*) refers to the act of giving and receiving. "House, field, and dowry" (*gṛhakṣetrakayautaka*) refers to the establishment [of separate status] through the individual possession of distinct fields, houses, and so on. And thus Nārada says:

"Brothers who have divided their inheritance may act as witnesses, sureties, or in matters of giving and receiving; those who have not divided may never do so under any circumstances. (NSm 13.39) || 153 ||
Thus ends the section on the partition of inheritance.
Now begins the section on disputes concerning boundaries.

It has been stated how to resolve doubts regarding fields and other properties situated separately; however, it remains to be explained how such disputes should be handled when they concern the very boundaries of those fields and other properties. To this, it is said:
In a dispute concerning the boundary of a field, the neighbors, elders, village assemblies, cowherds, farmers, and all others who frequent the forest shall be the witnesses of the boundary. (2.154)

In a dispute or doubt concerning a boundary (*sīmā*), the neighbors (*sāmantas*)—those who own fields on all sides of the disputed plot—the elders (*sthaviras*), and the guilds (*gaṇas*) such as those of the *Cāturvaidyas* and others, [should decide it], for they too are knowers of the boundaries. As Bṛhaspati says: "Having granted the land, the king should demarcate it under the supervision of *Cāturvaidyas*, merchants, water-distributors, all the villagers, the local headmen (*mahattaras*), and the owners' men; or he should issue a formal edict (*śāsana*)" (BṛSm 19.5). Therefore, the guilds are authoritative in a boundary dispute. Furthermore, the cowherds (*gopas*)—the mention of cowherds being intended to include all animal keepers—as well as other farmers (*kṛṣāṇas*) who are experienced plowmen (*vṛddha-hālikas*), and all forest-dwellers such as hunters and fowlers. (154)

And those established by the king and the Brahmins should lead [the boundary] to its limit, characterized by these: ground, charcoal, husks, trees, embankments, anthills, depressions, bones, shrines, and so forth. (2.155)

Chaff, charcoal, and the like are concealed marks; depressions, elevations, trees, and the like are manifest marks. By means of these, they should establish the boundary; that is, they should clearly define this boundary by means of such marks. The rest is clear. || 155 ||
Or the neighboring lords of the land, four, eight, or ten in number, acting together as a united community, wearing red garlands and garments, shall lead the boundary markers.

“Equal” means impartial. “Equal villages” (*samagrāmāḥ*) refers to those villages which are equal; the word *vā* has the sense of *ca* (and). The previously mentioned boundary-markers, such as the field-adjacent neighbors (*kṣetrasāmanta*), and others who are equal village-dwellers—among these, there should be four, eight, or ten. The phrase “or else” (*atha vā*) indicates an alternative option mentioned in other legal codes (*smṛti*). “Three, two, or one” is also possible. They should lead [the boundary] while wearing red garlands and garments and carrying earth on their heads. That is, they should wear wreaths of red *karavīra* and other flowers, and be dressed in red clothes; they should place earth (*mṛd*) upon their heads. Although no specific caste is mentioned here, this applies only to the twice-born (*dvijāti*). As for Śūdras, Bṛhaspati says: “If a Śūdra should be the leader, having adorned him with the ornaments of a eunuch and smeared his face with the ashes of a corpse, having made five finger-marks on his chest with the blood of a goat (*āgneya-paśu*), and having tied intestines around his neck, he should hold a clod of earth from the boundary on his head with his left hand. (BṛSm 19.6) In this context, the “goat” (*chāga*) is the animal related to Agni (*āgneya*). The “ornaments of a eunuch” include red rags and similar items. The rest is clear. || 156 ||
And these are the ones who establish the boundary;
however, if they speak falsely, they shall each be punished by the king with the middle amercement.
In the absence of signs of knowledge, the king is the one who determines the boundary. (2.157)

The word *tu* (but) serves to indicate certainty. When false testimony has been established—either because the aforementioned signs have proven inconsistent or because other signs have been observed—the king shall punish them with the middle amercement of five hundred *kārṣāpaṇas* each. This is so that the king’s command regarding the boundary may be carried out in his presence. The meaning is that when secret or manifest signs of knowledge are absent, the king himself, acting by his own will, becomes the establisher of the boundary. || 157 ||

This rule for the boundary of a field that has been stated is to be understood as applying to pleasure groves, temples, villages, water reservoirs, gardens, houses, and even to the flow of rainwater. (2.158)
And regarding fields and so forth whose boundaries have been declared:
"In the case of breaking a boundary, as well as in the seizure of a field, and in the transgression of a limit, the punishments are indeed the lowest, the highest, and the middle. (2.159)

The term "fines for violence" (*sāhasadaṇḍāḥ*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the context]. For violating established boundaries (*maryādābheda*), the first fine of violence (*prathamasāhasa*) is two hundred and fifty [paṇas]. For seizing a field (*kṣetraharaṇa*), however, the highest fine of violence (*uttamasāhasa*) is one thousand and eighty paṇas. For overstepping a boundary (*sīmātikramaṇa*), the middle fine applies. || 159 ||
And since there are cases where one might otherwise take away another's field or property, he says:
"But a dam that causes little harm and brings about benefit should not be prohibited;
a well on another's land may take away [the value of] that land if it has little area but provides much water. (2.160)

A *setu* (watercourse) is the diversion of the flow of water already set in motion within a dug channel into another path; this is the meaning of *kulyā*. If a channel being led through the middle of one field to irrigate another field causes little damage and is beneficial because it results in an abundance of harvests for the whole, then it should not be obstructed by the owner of the [first] field. This is well known even among cowherds: "A well with much water may take away [the moisture of] another's land, even if its own field is small. By the phrase "a well may take away," it is meant that a well, when led as a channel through a small field for the purpose of irrigating another field, takes away the land belonging to another. From this common saying, we understand that such a watercourse (*setu*) is not to be prohibited. Alternatively, there is another meaning: if a well being dug in someone’s field should have little damage [to the field] but yield much water, then while being dug, it "takes away" the land of the field-owner by virtue of its benefit to the king. (Verse 160)

And this being so, since it might follow that one could proceed with constructing a watercourse even without the landowner’s permission, he says: "If a person constructs a watercourse on a field without even informing the owner, the enjoyment of the produce belongs to the owner; in his absence, it belongs to the king. (2.161)

If a cultivator, having been provided with a field by his master and having marked it out with a plow, should—out of anger or other motives—not cultivate it himself or cause it to be cultivated, then, in response to the question of what should be done in such a case, [the author] says: "Even if a field has been struck by the plow, he who neither cultivates it nor causes it to be cultivated shall be made to pay the value of the crop that would have been produced from it, and the master shall cause the field to be cultivated by another. (2.162)
Thus ends the section on disputes concerning boundaries.
Now begins the section on disputes between owners and herdsmen.
If, however, cattle should cause damage to crops due to the fault of the herdsman or the fault of the owner, how should it be handled in that case? For in that matter also:
A buffalo that destroys standing crops shall be fined eight māṣas;
a cow shall be fined half of that, and a goat or sheep half of that again. (163)
A twentieth part of a kārṣāpaṇa is a māṣa. The rest is clear. || 163 ||
"If they flee after having caused damage, it is thus; but if they remain right there, then:
'For those who remain after having eaten [the fodder], the fine for staying is double.
This same rule applies to them even in a *vivīta* (pasture-land); for donkeys and camels, it is equal to that for buffaloes. (2.164)

For those who have eaten [the crops] and are sitting or staying overnight, a fine double that previously mentioned amount shall be imposed; however, for those staying overnight, it is fourfold according to another Smṛti text. And that which has been determined regarding damage to a field applies equally to these animals such as buffaloes even in a *vivīta* (pasture); the meaning is "in exactly the same way. Furthermore, in a *vivīta*—that is, a field used for grazing cattle—a donkey or a camel is equal to a buffalo. In this manner, the calculation of fines for elephants and other animals should also be made in accordance with the degree of injury. 164.

And like the punishment for a king's offense: as long as the crop is destroyed, the owner of the field shall receive the fruit [of his loss]; the herdsman shall be beaten, but the owner of the cow deserves the previously mentioned fine. (2.165)
Here is the exception:
there is no offense regarding a field located on a path, at the edge of a village, or within a pasture,
provided it is unintentional.
This is the division [of the verse]. When buffaloes and other animals have entered by mistake a field located either at the edge of a village or at the edge of a pasture, there is no offense.
Regarding the determination of intent, however, it is said:
"If one acts according to their own will, they deserve punishment like a thief. (2.166)
Either the protector or the master; or perhaps both. 166.
Even apart from the vicinity of the aforementioned villages and such places:

"A bull set at liberty, cattle for sacrifice, a cow that has recently calved, a cow that is traveling, those whose herdsman is absent, and those overwhelmed by divine or royal power—these must be released [from liability]. (2.167)
The interpretation that those whose protector is overwhelmed by the king of fate (destiny) are to be released is a strained construction. The rest is clear. || 167 ||
This is the mutual obligation between the owner and the herdsman:

the herdsman shall return the cattle entrusted to him in the evening exactly as they were given; likewise, one who has received wages must be made to pay for those that have perished or been lost through negligence. (2.168)

A cowherd who has received a fixed wage, or one to whom wages have been paid, shall return in the evening the animals that were entrusted to him in the morning. Because of the requirement of returning them, there is no fault if they are lost when not returned; and the mention of "cowherds" (*gopa*) is intended to include all animal-keepers, as it begins with the word "animals. Those animals which have died or been lost through negligence or neglect must be made good by the keeper alone. (168)

Regarding what has not been reported to the king, that which was stated previously applies; however, in the case of reporting it, a fine is prescribed for the keeper in the event of loss due to his negligence: thirteen and a half paṇas, and the value of the property itself must be paid to the owner. (2.169)

When it has been reported to the king that "the destruction here has occurred due to the fault of the keeper," a fine of twelve and a half paṇas is imposed on the keeper; and it has been stated that this is prescribed when there is little suspicion [of negligence]. || 169 ||
Furthermore:
By the consent of the village, or by the authority of the king, a twice-born man may take grass, fuel, and flowers from anywhere as if they were his own. (2.170)
The meaning of this verse is clear. || 170 ||
Furthermore: "The boundary between a village and its fields shall be one hundred bow-lengths;
that of a market town (karpaṭa) shall be two hundred, and that of a city (nagara) four hundred. (2.171)
A *karpaṭa* is that which possesses the characteristics of both a village and a city; the rest is clear. || 171 ||
Thus ends the section on disputes between owners and herdsmen.
Now begins the section on sale by one who is not the owner. The relationship of ownership regarding goods has been explained; now he demonstrates the sale by one who is not the owner.

One shall recover one's own property sold by another; the fault lies with the purchaser if the sale was not made public. Upon seeing an article sold by someone other than the owner, the owner may take it back. And the fault belongs to the purchaser if the purchase was not made public. However, in the case of a public purchase, there is merely the loss of the price, but no fault of theft. Where, then, does the fault lie? It lies in taking from a low person, such as a slave or the like; likewise, if taken in secret or concealed, and if taken for a low price, because of the suspicion of theft.
And at an improper time, he is a thief. (2.172)
And in the absence of the [proper] time, he becomes a thief; the meaning is that he would be a purchaser. And so says Nārada:
"The owner of the property shall recover goods sold by one who is not the owner;
the purchaser is cleared of guilt through a public purchase, but there is theft if it was done in secret."
"One who purchases [a slave] in secret from a non-owner or from a person who is not his own, for a low price and at an improper time, shall incur the fault of that transaction. (NSm 7.2–3) || 172 ||
Furthermore:
Having recovered property that was lost or stolen, one should cause the thief to be apprehended;
or, if there is a lapse of time or place, one should seize it oneself and restore it [to the owner]. || 2.173 ||

Having discovered or found property that has been lost or stolen and is being held by another, he should cause the possessor to be seized by the king’s officers for the purpose of a legal determination, identifying him as "this man is the thief. However, if one fears the absence of royal officials or the loss of the proper time and place, then he may seize the property himself and hand over the thief to the king. [Objection: But surely this need not be stated, since it follows from the very nature of things. [Reply: True; however, this is intended to make known that there is no fault for one who seizes independently and delivers the thief. Another interpretation: having acquired lost or stolen property by purchase, when the owner requests it, he should cause the seller to be seized. The meaning is that he should pay the price. Or, in case of the loss of time or place, even after seizing it through an open purchase, he should hand it over himself. The intention is that even in such a case, there is no fault. || 173 ||

And when the thief has been identified by the king, purification is attained through the production of the seller; the owner recovers his property, the king receives a fine, and the purchaser recovers his price from whoever was the seller in that transaction. (2.174)

Having pointed out the seller, the buyer is proven innocent; at that time, the owner gains possession of the property, the buyer recovers the price from the hands of the seller, and the king receives the fine—this is how it should be understood. (174)

But how, then, is ownership understood? It is said: "Ownership of lost property is established through title and possession; otherwise, a fine of five times its value shall be imposed upon the king for failing to investigate it. (2.175)

One must establish that a lost property which has come into another's hand is indeed one's own, either by means of documentary evidence such as a written deed or by means of open and undisputed possession for a long time. Therefore, if one claims "this is mine" in a manner other than these two ways, a fine shall be imposed equal to a fifth part of the disputed property. Furthermore, that property, if the other party cannot likewise establish it as his own through the two aforementioned modes of proof, should be understood as forfeited to the king. (175)
Since this is so, therefore:
"He who recovers property that has been stolen or lost from the hand of another, without having reported it to the king, shall be fined ninety-six paṇas. (2.176)
The meaning of this verse is clear. || 176 ||
Furthermore:
If property that has been lost or stolen is recovered by customs officers or local guards, the owner shall recover it within one year; after that time, the king shall take it. (2.177)
Within one year, the owner may take it back; after that, the king may take it. || 177 ||
As a reward for the king,
one should pay four *paṇas* for a single-hoofed animal, five for a human, two each for buffaloes, camels, and cattle, and one-quarter each for goats and sheep. (2.178)
Thus ends the section on sale without ownership. Now begins the section on the non-delivery of what has been given.
In connection with the giving of rewards, the general rule regarding gifts, even those for transcendental purposes (*adṛṣṭārtha*), is stated.

One may give away property without detriment to one's own family, except for one's wife and sons; however, when there is a lineage remaining, one's entire estate must not be given, nor that which is dependent upon others. (2.179)

The word *sva* (one's own) is intended to exclude sons and others who have been separated [from the family estate]. Furthermore, "non-opposition" (*avirodha*) should be understood as characterized by the sufficiency of mere food and clothing. The mention of "wife and sons" is for the purpose of including all kinsmen, those supported by religious duty (*dharmopanatādi*), and so forth. The meaning is that one must not give away one's entire property while there exists a lineage, even if it remains as separate households. Regarding the phrase "and that which is to be given," "to be given" refers to deposits and the like to be returned; it refers to property that belongs to oneself but is held in trust by another, is common to others, or is dependent on another. There is an alternative reading: "and that which has been promised" (*yac ca pratiśrutam*). This means that which has been promised to another as something to be given. And thus says Nārada:

That which has been entrusted for delivery, that which has been borrowed, a pledge, that which is held in common, a deposit, one's wife and children, and one's entire property when there is offspring; [these should not be divided].
"Even when a person is beset by dire distress, the teachers declare that certain things must not be given away: namely, those which have already been promised to another. (NSm 4.4–5) || 179 ||

But for those things that are fit to be given and distinct from what is not to be given, the acceptance should be public, especially in the case of immovable property. Likewise, what has been promised as a gift must be given; once given, one must not take it back again. (2.180)

As for the statement that "a gift should not be made public," that refers to the act of giving, whereas this [present rule] refers to the act of receiving; thus there is no contradiction. The rest is clear. || 180 ||
Thus ends the section on the non-delivery of what has been given. Now begins the section on rescission of purchase. Sale by one who is not the owner has been defined, as well as sale by the owner.
The examination of seeds, iron, draft animals, gems, women, milch cattle, and men shall take ten, one, five, seven days, one month, three days, and half a month respectively. (2.181)
Whatever has been purchased or sold after the period of examination is considered unimpaired. However, the *Svāyaṃbhuva* states:
"If, after having purchased or sold a commodity, one should have remorse in this matter, he may give back or take back that commodity within ten days. (MDh 8.222)

Thus, having examined it, it should be inspected after purchase. The periods for the examination of seeds and other items follow a sequence beginning with ten days. Ten days is the period for seeds such as wheat; one day is for iron. The mention of "iron" is intended to indicate all metals such as copper and the like. This same principle should be applied to draft animals and so forth: "draft animals" refers to oxen and the like; "jewels" refers to emeralds and the like; "women" refers to female slaves and the like; "milch animals" refers to cows and the like; and "men" refers to male slaves and the like. (181)
Furthermore: Gold is not diminished when placed in fire; silver [loses] two palas for every hundred;
tin and lead [lose] eight; copper [loses] five; and iron [loses] ten.

Gold thrown into the fire for the purpose of refining does not diminish; that is to say, it remains exactly as it was. In the case of silver and other metals, there is a loss of two palas and so forth for every hundred palas. In this manner, goldsmiths and others shall not be made to pay for what has been consumed [in the process]. || 182 ||

When thread is supplied for the manufacture of cloth by means of looms and the like, there shall be an increase of ten palas per hundred [palas] in the case of woolen and cotton fabrics; in the case of medium quality, a reduction of five palas is prescribed, while in the case of fine fabric, a reduction of three palas is considered appropriate. (2.183)

In one hundred palas [of wool], there shall be an increase of ten palas for both woolen and cotton [thread] when the thread is thick; however, in the case of medium [thread], the meaning is that the increase shall be five palas less than the aforementioned increase; but for fine [thread], the increase is three palas. And so Nārada, having stated an increase of ten palas, says: "For these of medium thickness with thick thread, the [increase is] one hundred and five; but for those that are very fine, it is three palas" (NSm 9.14). || 183 ||
There is an exception to this rule:
"In the case of leather and woven hair, a loss of one-thirtieth is recognized;
however, there shall be neither loss nor increase in the case of silk or bark-cloth. (2.184)

*Carman* refers to leatherwork such as *kuruṇṭha* and the like; *romabaddha* refers to woven fabrics such as *dūṣyapaṭa* and the like. In the case of these, there is a loss of one-thirtieth due to cutting. However, for *kauśeya* (silk) and *vālkalaya* (bark-fiber cloth), there is no change at all. *Kauśeya* is made from *trasarī* (silk-worm cocoons). The rest is clear. || 184 ||
Having considered the loss according to the proportional increase [of the price], as in the case of clothes and other goods by washermen and others;
and having understood the place, the time, the usage, and the relative value of the lost items, those who are experts shall declare what must be paid—of this there is no doubt. (2.185)

Whether it be produced in one’s own country or another country, whether it be old or recent, used or unused, difficult to obtain or easy to obtain—having thus ascertained the relative strength or weakness of the lost article, those experts skilled in knowing the relative strength or weakness of goods shall state its value; the owner who caused the loss shall pay that amount without hesitation. And if he does not pay, he must be compelled to do so by the king. Thus, when an item has been purchased after such examination, there arises for the buyer the possibility of punishment from the king and other consequences if he deviates from the truth. It is established that even if the seller deviates from the truth, he does not recover what was sold. And likewise says the Svāyambhuva [Smṛti]:
"But after ten days, one should neither give nor cause [the goods] to be given;
both he who takes them and he who gives them shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king. (MDh 8.223) || 185 ||
Thus ends the section on rescission of purchase.
Now begins the section on service after having entered into an agreement.
He speaks next for the purpose of providing an exception to this.
One who has been forcibly enslaved by thieves and even sold is liberated by providing for his master’s life, by sharing his food, or even by paying his ransom. (2.186)

One who has been forcibly enslaved despite the absence of any cause for slavery such as being born in the house, or one who has been sold into slavery by thieves into the hands of another, must be released. In this case, there is no liability for the purchaser. Furthermore, even one for whom a cause for slavery exists is released from servitude if he liberates his master from a life-threatening danger by means of a firm resolve to sacrifice his own life. As for the *bhaktadāsa* (slave for food), he is released by abandoning that service or by paying a ransom; by the use of the word "also" (*api*), the favor of the master and other such means are included. (186)
This is an exception regarding the attainment of release from slavery:
"One who has fallen from the religious life becomes a slave of the king for as long as he lives. Slavery exists according to the direct order of the castes, not in the inverse order. (2.187)

One who has returned from renunciation (*pravrajyā*) shall become the slave of the king; and in this case, there is no release even by saving the life of the master. Furthermore, even a Brāhmaṇa who has fallen from renunciation shall become the slave of the king, even through the inverse order (*prātilomya*). However, in other cases, slavery among the castes occurs only through the natural order (*ānulomya*). As in the passage, "He was released from a great debt" (NSm 5.25), and so forth, it should not be understood as occurring through the inverse order. From other *smṛti* texts, the causes for slavery—such as being born in the house—and the methods for liberation from slavery should be sought. It is established that in all cases, there is an absence of slavery through the inverse order. Where there is a conventional slavery agreed upon by both parties, or something else, that should be carried out exactly as such. (187)

Since this is so, therefore: Even when he has mastered the craft, the apprentice shall remain in the teacher's house for the prescribed period; having received his food from the teacher, he shall offer the fruits of his labor to him. (2.188)

An *antevāsī* is one who has entered into the status of a pupil for the purpose of learning a craft (*śilpa*). When he remains after being formally bound by the agreement, "I must dwell in your house for such a length of time to learn the science of the craft," even if he should have already acquired the knowledge in the interim, he must nevertheless reside in the teacher's house for that stipulated period. It should be understood that the teacher must provide him with food, clothing, and so forth, and whatever he earns through his craft, he must hand over to the teacher alone. (188)
Thus concludes the section on the failure to serve after having made an agreement.
Now begins the section on the breach of agreements (*saṃvidvyatikrama*).

In connection with the non-alteration of what is conventionally defined, he introduces the performance of collective action as a preliminary topic (*upodghāta*) for the further purpose of resolving disputes regarding conventions.

Having established a place for them in the city and settled the Brāhmaṇas there, the king should provide those learned in the three Vedas with a means of livelihood and say: "Let your own duty be observed. (2.189)
As it has been said:
"In that regard, one should construct fortresses for the sake of increasing the people, the treasury, and oneself. (YDh 1.317)

Thus, this undertaking is solely for the purpose of prescribing these duties. Having established a secure position within his fortified city, the king—having stationed Brāhmaṇas there for the sake of protection during future times and having settled them as a community—should provide those who have mastered the three Vedas (*traividya*), namely Brāhmaṇas of virtuous conduct who have reached the further shore of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas, with a means of livelihood (*vṛtti*) and say: "Let your own duty (*svadharma*) be observed. A "livelihood" (*vṛtti*) is the cause of subsistence; the meaning is that he should grant them wealth consisting of villages, houses, fields, inexhaustible treasures, and so forth, established for their support. "One's own duty" (*svadharma*) refers to the non-deviation from the duties pertaining to caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*). Furthermore, it includes the guidance toward the right path through instruction whenever the king acts otherwise. The rest is clear. (189)
Furthermore: "Moreover, that which is conventional and does not conflict with one's own dharma, as well as any law enacted by the king, must also be protected with effort. (2.190)

One's own duty (*nijadharma*) is that which is declared in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. Furthermore, whatever conventional rule (*sāmayika*) may exist—whether it conforms to wealth and other interests without contradicting that [duty], or is established by one's own regulations, such as the penalty for failing to appear when summoned to a court—that too must be properly protected with effort by the King. Moreover, whatever law has been established by a king remains exactly as it was placed in its own location, even in other locations established by subsequent kings, such as the placement of Vedic schools (*brahmaśālā*), processions, festivals, and so forth. And thus says Nārada:
"Whatever is their duty, whatever their work, and whatever the rule for their attendance..."
"And whatever provision for their livelihood one might authorize, that should be done accordingly.

(NSm 10.3) Regarding the statement "the law is enacted by the king," the repetition of the word *dharma* implies that it is not to be observed merely because it was made by another king; rather, the intention is that it must be followed precisely because it is consistent with *dharma*. And thus Nārada, while summarizing the laws of guilds (*samūha*), says:
"Whatever enactment may be defective, being not established by traditional scripture..."
"Even if it has already begun, a king who desires his own welfare should cause it to be stopped. (NSm 10.7) || 190 ||
"He who seizes two shares [of the produce] under the pretext of protection, or he who violates the agreement— having confiscated all his property, the king shall banish him from the realm. (2.191)

He who should misappropriate the property of a corporation (*gaṇa*), or violate the agreement or convention established by the group that is not contrary to the Dharma—the king, having confiscated his entire property, shall banish him from the realm. Having confiscated that property, he shall restore it to the corporation itself; he must not take it for himself. From the use of the word "having done" (*kṛtvā*), it is understood that the king is merely the agent and not the appropriator. This prohibition is intended in the same way in the *Svāyaṃbhuvamanu*:
"One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is guilty of every possible crime."
"He should banish him from the kingdom, with all his wealth and unharmed. (MDh 8.380).

Therefore, the surrender of the collective [fine] is faultless. In this same manner, the payment of fines and so forth for the sake of the collective should be applied in other cases as well. || 191 ||

[Objection: But surely this property of a collective (*samūhadharma*) is untenable, because it depends upon persons whose intentions are diverse. [Reply: Not so; for it is possible for there to be a single intention with respect to the task at hand. Furthermore: "The speech of one who speaks for the benefit of the group must be carried out by all—whether they be members of the assembly or someone else."
Whoever acts contrary to that rule shall be made to pay the first fine. 2.192.

The meaning is "for the sake of the corporation alone. Indeed, the king must protect the laws of the corporation with great effort, because through the increase of dharma, the corporation is of service to the king. || 192 ||
Since this is so, therefore:
"He should dismiss those who have come for the business of the assembly once their business is accomplished";
the remainder of the sense is that he should do so quickly, even by setting aside other matters.
Having honored him with gifts, respect, and hospitality, the lord of the earth—

But surely, since giving culminates in the acquisition of ownership by another, and since individuals in a collective lack individual ownership, a collective cannot possess the characteristics of a group capable of acquiring distinct ownership; therefore, the gift of a collective is indeed untenable. For this very reason, when property belonging to a corporation (*gaṇa*) is being requested, people say: "This is not yet ours. Likewise, even for officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the relinquishment (*utsarga*) of their fee is intended toward the assembly (*pariṣad*). Thus, some maintain that the designation "giving" is used figuratively only with respect to the mere relinquishment. If that were the case, there would be no fault in misappropriating the property of a collective, yet such a fault is indeed recognized because of the observation of punishment. Therefore, this must be explained. Regarding this, other self-styled scholars, like the heretics (*pāṣaṇḍin*), describe it thus: "The injunctions regarding punishment and so forth have only visible purposes. Even so, the practice of giving to a collective for the sake of *dharma* would be entirely without foundation.

To this it is replied: It is true that the individual members of the collection lack ownership (*svatva*). But who can deny the connection with ownership for the collection itself? As for the claim that the collection is not something distinct [from its members], that is exactly so. It is precisely the members themselves, by virtue of being delimited by a single effect and being mutually dependent, that attain the state of being a "collection. And it is possible to say that the connection with ownership belongs to each one of them while they are thus mutually dependent. Nor is there any injunction regarding the giving of such things; for from the statement that cows and other items constitute an undivided sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), it is understood that even many individuals may be connected to the act of giving. Furthermore, the giving is enjoined to a Brāhmaṇa, and it is not the case that something should be given only when it is dependent [on others]. Nor is this a delusion consisting in the conceit of ownership, since no sublation (*bādhā*) is perceived. In this regard, one might ask: "How can the giving be accomplished if all the members of the collection are not present? That too is incorrect. Because the recipients are connected with ownership only while they remain mutually dependent, and because of the force of the agreement (*samaya*), the priests and the sacrificer are like the body, senses, and mind [functioning as a whole]. Just as in the case of a sacrificer who is traveling abroad, their presence is maintained through the power of the agreement and the mental focus, and because it is enjoined by scripture, the status of the group is identical to that of the priests and the sacrificer. As for the statement that the members do not own [the object], that intends to express their independence [from one another]. Since the distribution is prescribed, the relinquishment of the priests to the assembly (*pariṣad*) remains entirely unimpeded, even if there were no formal logic [for it otherwise]. As for those who think that because giving to individual members is impossible, there must be a division of the fee among the priests—[we reply that] in cases such as "the horse is the fee," where the substance is a single unit, division is impossible; and since it is improper to pay a price for it, their position is quite awkward. Enough of this digression. (Verse 193)
Having kept this very principle in mind, he said:
"One who has been dispatched on a collective task shall deliver whatever he may obtain;
if he does not deliver it himself, he should be made to pay eleven times as much. (2.194)
And because their collective status is based upon scriptural authority,
those who know the Vedas, who are pure and free from greed, should be the deliberators on legal matters;
furthermore, according to another Smṛti, they should be numbered at sixty-four or other such counts.
The words of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be carried out. || 2.195 ||
The phrase "by all the members of the assembly" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 195 ||

This rule which has been declared for the assembly of Brāhmaṇas applies also to guilds, merchant associations, heretical sects, and corporations. The king shall protect them from internal dissension and maintain their traditional way of life. (2.196)

A *śreṇi* is a guild consisting of a group of artisans such as laborers; a *naigama* is a group of merchants such as caravan leaders; *pāṣaṇḍas* are a collection of heretics such as those who use incense (*guggulu*); a *gaṇa* is a corporation of traders. Others say it is a group of elephant-riders and the like. Alternatively, the word *gaṇa* has the sense of defining a *pūga* and other such groups. And so Nārada says:

"In regard to heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*), merchants (*naigama*), guilds (*śreṇi*), corporations (*pūga*), military bands (*vrāta*), and assemblies (*gaṇa*), the king shall protect their conventions both in the fort and in the countryside. (NSm 10.2)

In this context, *naigama* refers to a group of Brāhmaṇas; *pūga* refers to a group of villagers and the like; and *vrāta* refers to a group of weapon-bearers. Furthermore, their mutual distinctions—whether among the members of the group themselves or between the groups—must be protected by the king. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that he must also prevent legal proceedings that oppose other associations, kings, and so forth. Thus says Nārada: "Whatever is contrary to the king, whatever is detrimental to the constituent elements [of the state], and whatever is obstructive to wealth—he shall cause that to be turned away from them."

The king should remedy such conflicts as "forming secret alliances," "bearing weapons against those who are not enemies," and "inflicting mutual injury" (NSm 10.4–5). Furthermore, he should protect the livelihood previously established for them, provided it is not contrary to dharma; by the use of the word "and" (ca), the intention is that he should also cause their prosperity himself. 196.
Thus ends the section on the breach of agreements.
Now begins the section on the non-payment of wages.

In connection with the preceding discussion on conventions, the author speaks in order to declare the legal punishment for any deviation from the customary conduct between an employer and a laborer based on their agreement.
If one who has received wages abandons his work, he shall pay double the amount;
if he has not received wages, the work shall be made equal [to the value of the wages], and the tools must be protected by the servants. (2.197)

The meaning is that if one has received wages, he shall perform twice as much work as the contracted labor; if he has not received wages, the work must be made to be performed by paying him the full contracted wage. Furthermore, whatever tools have been entrusted to all laborers for the purpose of performing the work, having been paid their wages, must be protected by them. As Nārada says:
"Whatever implements for the work have been entrusted to them for the sake of the task, those must be protected with trustworthiness and never by any deceitful means. (NSm 6.4)

Likewise: "Having promised to perform work, one who does not do it after having received wages by force, or one who, having received wages, does not work, shall pay double the wages. (NSm 6.5) || 197 ||

If, after the work has been performed, the employer—under the pretext that no agreement was made regarding wages—should be unwilling to give anything at all, then how should it be handled? To this requirement, he says:
"But the king shall compel him who causes work to be done without having fixed the wages to pay a tenth part of the profit from trade, cattle, or crops. (2.198)

And the ellipsis is that he should not give [the goods] himself. It should be understood that for one who engages in trade, cattle-rearing, or agriculture without having first made a formal agreement, he is entitled to a tenth part of the increase produced by those activities. || 198 ||
Just like a laborer directed by his master,

he who exceeds the prescribed place and time, or performs the work otherwise than ordered— in such cases, it shall be at the master's discretion whether an additional wage is to be given for the extra work performed. (2.199)

If work is performed otherwise than as prescribed by the master regarding place, time, and so forth, the master has the freedom to determine the payment of wages. Furthermore, it should be understood that if the laborers perform more work than required due to exceptional diligence, the master may, at his own discretion, grant them an additional amount. || 199 ||
However, there is an exception regarding the forfeiture of wages when one abandons work before it is completed:
"He shall receive wages for as much work as he has performed, provided both parties have been free from deceit; if there was deceit, [he shall receive] only for what was actually done. (2.200)

The meaning is "according to his wish. Even the employer, if he causes the work to be done through deceit, must be made to pay the wages as they were agreed upon, in accordance with another Smṛti text. || 200 ||
And likewise through deceit:
"The carrier shall be made to pay for goods lost through no fault of the king or the gods;
and he who causes an obstacle to the journey shall be made to pay double the wages. (2.201)
And like a laborer, the master as well [is liable for the loss].

When the journey has begun, he should abandon a seventh part of the fee on the way; if he abandons it at half the distance, he must pay the entire fee, and so too the one who causes the abandonment. 2.202.
Even the owner who abandons [the work] must be made to pay the laborers according to the sequence of the seventh part and so forth for the portions already undertaken; the rest is clear. || 202 ||
Thus ends the section on the non-payment of wages. Now begins the section on gambling and betting.
In connection with the topic of disputes, [the author] describes the legal proceeding concerning gambling and betting, which is the single cause of all disputes.
The keeper of the gambling house shall take five percent as interest from a fraudulent gambler, but ten percent from any other. (2.203)

The word *tu* (but) serves to emphasize. The intention is that the *sabhika* (the master of the gambling house) receives only the increment on the stakes as they fall, and nothing else such as the face-cloth (*mukhapaṭṭa*) or other items designated for his own use. "Falling" means that which has flowed out from the hand of the *sabhika*—namely, the wealth of the defeated players intended for the game, as well as the gaming equipment such as dice; all this "falling property of the *sabhika*" the master of the circle of gamblers shall take. How much? Five percent (*pañcakaṃ śatam*). This is for the winner of the rogue-gamblers, by reason of the gaming equipment. For the other, the defeated player, it is ten percent (*daśakaṃ śatam*), by reason of his own wealth that was employed [in the game]. || 203 ||

And for the sake of his own interest alone, the king should protect him properly; he should give the king the share as agreed, cause the winner to recover what was won, and give it to the victor—being truthful in speech and patient. (2.204)

The meaning is: as it has been established, as it has been defined, or as it has been determined in another Smṛti. For example, in the *Bṛhaspati-smṛti*: "The king’s interest on gambling shall be ten percent from the keeper of the gaming house, or it may be according to agreement. (BṛSm 27.3)

Furthermore, whatever has been won by gamblers, the keeper of the gambling house (sabhika) shall cause that to be recovered from those who have lost. And as for the winner, the keeper of the gambling house himself, having become truthful and free from deception, being patient and feeling regret, should give it back; this is how it should be understood. || 204 ||
Just as it was done;
when the king's share has been obtained and the assembly of gamblers is well-known, one should cause the winner to pay the debt in a place where there is a presiding court, but not otherwise. (2.205)
Furthermore:
"For they alone are the observers of legal proceedings and the witnesses; those who play with fraudulent dice or by means of deception shall be branded with a mark and banished by the king. (2.206)

These two verses have a clear meaning. Now, it might be argued that this gambling was prohibited by the Self-existent One [the Creator], for it has been said: "This gambling and betting are open theft" (MDh 9.222).
And so it has been stated:
"One should prohibit gambling in the kingdom, whether it be secret or open.

Thus [it is said]. In the Veda as well, there is a prohibition: "Do not play with dice" (RV 10.34.13). True. However, since this person engages in it by transgressing that prohibition, this rule is like the Śyena sacrifice and so forth; thus there is no contradiction. As for the Manava code, it prescribes punishment because of its conflict with Dharma, or because it has various aspects. || 206 ||

But for the sake of another purpose, gambling with a single stake may be permitted as a means of discovering thieves; this same rule is to be understood as applying to betting on living creatures and to challenges to combat. (2.207)

A single entrance with a single path, situated in one location and supervised by royal spies and others for the purpose of identifying thieves and other "thorns" among the subjects—though this is of the nature of unrighteousness (*adharma*), it results in great prosperity because it serves as a means toward another form of righteousness (*dharma*). Therefore, the intended meaning is that it must indeed be carried out. Alternatively, regarding those who, even in times of distress, abandon all their own duties and are solely devoted to gambling, the statements concerning punishment and so forth found in the *Svāyaṃbhuvamanu* (the Laws of Manu) are to be understood as referring to them. By this, the practice of heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*) and similar systems is explained. Furthermore, the rule described here for gambling called *dyūta*, which consists of playing with dice and the like without using living beings, is to be understood as applying equally to what is termed *samāhvaya*—gambling with living beings such as cocks or rams where a wager is placed—provided it is under the supervision of a master of the gaming house (*sabhika*) and involves the payment of royal taxes and so forth; this is the intended meaning. (207)
Thus ends the section on gambling and betting.
Now begins the section on verbal assault.

This section is commenced immediately after the legal proceedings concerning gambling, because gambling generally gives rise to verbal and physical abuse, and because both share the common characteristic of being causes of ruin. Furthermore, since verbal assault is the causal basis for physical assault, it is discussed first.

If one insults those who are deficient in limbs, those with impaired senses, or those afflicted by disease, by means of praise that is true, false, or otherwise, he shall be fined twelve and a half paṇas. (2.208)

Those with deficient limbs are the lame and so forth; those with impaired senses are the one-eyed and so forth; and the diseased are those overcome by leprosy and other ailments. If one should insult them—provided they are themselves innocent—with harsh speech that is true, such as by pointing out their existing sensory deficiencies due to mere caprice; or even if the speech is untrue, such as insulting a non-one-eyed person by saying, "O one-eyed man!"—or otherwise, by means of the ear or words of excessive praise, speaking to a well-known fool, saying, "O knower of the four Vedas!"—he shall be fined thirteen and a half paṇas once the matter has been reported to the king.
