Furthermore, according to another Smṛti, he must also be made to appease the person insulted. (208)
And specifically regarding the reporting to the king:
if a man swears, "I shall approach your sister or your mother," the king should compel him to pay a fine of twenty-five [paṇas]. (2.209)
And this is the rule for punishment regarding those of the same caste and equal qualities. || 209 ||
Furthermore, regarding inequality in qualities and social status:

half [the fine] for those of lower status, double for the wives of others and for those of higher status; the imposition of punishment must be carried out according to the superiority or inferiority of caste and class. (2.210)

The word "having ascertained" (*nirūpya*) is to be supplied [as the remainder of the sentence]. For those of lower status in terms of caste, qualities, and so forth, the fine is half of that stated previously, starting from thirteen-and-a-half *paṇas*. And for women belonging to others, it is double. The word "other" (*para*) has the sense of "superior. Women married by others who are superior—either by virtue of their qualities or their caste—are "women belonging to others" (*parastriyaḥ*); [the fine applies] when they are insulted. [The same applies] to men or women who are superior in qualities, caste, and so forth. The mention of "half" and the mention of "double" both serve to indicate the appropriate fine in each case; this is what he demonstrates. The intention is that the infliction of punishment must be carried out according to what is fitting, having considered the relative superiority or inferiority of caste and birth, whether by way of deficiency or excess. Furthermore, since the word "birth" (*jāti*) is based on the cause of birth, it should be understood here as indicating age or qualities. (210)
He clarifies this very point by means of an illustration:

"In cases of defamation involving the inverse order of castes, the fines are four, three, and two-fold; for those at the end of the castes in the direct order, they are half of that respectively. (2.211)

The Śūdras are those at the end of the castes. For their slander when uttered in the reverse order (pratiloma), the punishment prescribed for the sequence beginning with the Brāhmaṇa should be calculated as fourfold and so forth. The same principle should be applied to Vaiśyas and Kṣatriyas, even when there is an excellence of qualities and the like among those born of the intermediate [mixed] castes in the direct order (ānulomya). However, in the case of the direct order, the punishment is reduced by half; that is, it is a reduction of half from the aforementioned punishment. In the case of slandering a Śūdra, the punishment for the master is half, for the Kṣatriya it is a quarter, and for the Brāhmaṇa it is a half-quarter. The same should be applied to the direct order when there is excellence of qualities and the like. || 211 ||

But in the case of verbal abuse involving a threat of killing, the fine for verbal injury to the arms, neck, eyes, or thighs shall be one hundred panas; for injuries to the feet, nose, ears, hands, and so forth, it shall be half of that. 2.212.

If one who is capable of doing so says, "I shall cut off your arms and other limbs," a fine of one hundred [paṇas] (śatya) must be imposed. That which is accomplished by means of a hundred is "śatya"; the meaning is that he is to be fined one hundred. However, if the threat is to cut off his feet or other such parts, half of that—meaning fifty—is the fine. The word "and others" (ādi) refers to the breaking of teeth and so forth mentioned in the section on assault (daṇḍapāruṣya). The thigh-bone is called *sakthi*. The rest is clear. || 212 ||
The previously mentioned statement regarding the cutting off of arms and so forth applies to one who is capable [of performing the act].
However, one who is incapable, upon speaking thus, shall be fined ten *paṇas*.
Likewise, a capable person shall be made to provide a surety for his protection. (2.213)

For one who speaks with mere deceit while being incapable of performing the act, the fine is ten paṇas; but one who is capable shall be made to pay the previously mentioned fine. Furthermore, he must provide a guarantor (pratibhū) capable of removing fear and ensuring security. || 213 ||

In the case of an insult such as "You are a killer of a Brahmin" or "You are a killer of a cow," or for an insult involving an act that causes loss of caste, one should be punished with the middle amercement; but if the insult is connected to a minor offense (upapātaka), he should be made to pay the first amercement. (2.214)
Likewise:
For the insult of those learned in the three Vedas, a king, or a deity, the punishment is the highest amercement;
for castes and guilds, it is the middle amercement; and for villages and districts, it is the first amercement. (2.215)

The mention of the "king" (nṛpa) is intended as a general indicator for the teacher, father, Vedic scholar, and others as well. Furthermore, the word *pūga* here denotes a mere group (*gaṇa*). Consequently, the meaning is: "of groups of castes," that is, of assemblies consisting of members belonging to specific castes, such as the Kṣatriyas and so forth. The rest is clear. || 215 ||
Thus ends the section on verbal assault (*vākpāruṣya*).

Now begins the section on physical assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*). Because physical assault is preceded by verbal assault, it is commenced immediately after. Physical assault consists of striking with the hand or other means. In that regard, if one strikes someone in a secluded place and then falsely claims, "I did not strike him," or if, due to an excess of wickedness, one inflicts a wound or similar injury upon oneself and falsely attributes it to an innocent person—anticipating how this might be resolved, the author says:

But when a person has been killed without witnesses, the legal case must be investigated by means of marks, logical reasoning, and scriptural tradition, out of fear that false evidence might have been fabricated. (2.216)

In a case where there are no witnesses, when a person is struck by injuries such as wounds and so forth, or when there is doubt regarding those marks due to the fear of malicious persons who might forge such signs, the legal proceeding itself must be examined—either by the king personally or in the presence of learned men—according to the previously stated principle and by means of the four pillars of justice following logic and scripture. It should be understood that this verse, which is common to all titles of law (*vyavahārapada*), is cited here for the purpose of recognizing the gravity of the matter. 216.
Furthermore:

"In cases where no punishment has been prescribed by all those great-souled ones through oversight, there the wielder of the rod must determine the matter and carry out the infliction of punishment. (2.217)

One should not fail to reach a definitive conclusion due to the error of non-mention; rather, the intention is that one must determine the application of punishment and the amount of fine in every case by examining the nature of both parties—whether stated or unstated—through their qualities and so forth, as well as their connections and so forth, in accordance with the degree of injury. || 217 ||
He elaborates on this very point as a mere illustration:
"For touching [another] with ashes, mud, or dust, a fine of ten paṇas is prescribed by tradition;
for touching [another] with impure matter, the heel, or spittle, double that is prescribed. (2.218)

Even regarding that which is pure, if ashes, mud, or dust are thrown upon it when it has been rendered faultless, a fine of ten paṇas is prescribed by tradition; thus, even though the amount is small, it is not contradictory according to the traditional law (smṛti). However, in the case of contact with impure substances and the like, the fine is double that—meaning twenty paṇas. The mention of "spittle" is intended to include other impure substances similar to spittle; consequently, a higher penalty is established for urine, feces, and so forth. || 218 ||
And as for that which was stated:

"In the case of women of equal status, the penalty is the same; in the case of superior women, it is double; in the case of inferior women, it is half; there is no punishment if [the act] is committed through delusion, intoxication, and so forth. (2.219)
This has already been explained. || 219 ||

And there is this other distinction: a limb that causes pain to a Brahmin may be cut off from one who is not a Brahmin; however, if he merely raises his weapon, the first amercement is the punishment, and if he touches him, it is half of that. (2.220)

If one raises [the hand] but does not let it fall, the punishment is the first amercement. If, while raising the hand for the purpose of striking, one touches the body of a Brahmin out of confidence—provided he is not a Brahmin—the punishment is half that amount. The rest is clear. 220.
But when the intent is not excessive:
"If a hand or a foot is merely raised, the fines shall be ten and twenty [paṇas] respectively; but if they strike one another with a weapon, the middle amercement applies to all. (2.221)

The word *tu* (but/and) serves to restrict each term individually: [the fine is] ten [paṇas] when only the hand is raised, and twenty [paṇas] when only the foot is raised. Thus, there is the establishment of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) in the case of a combined action. This should be understood similarly in other cases as well. And this applies when all castes possess equal qualities and so forth. However, if a weapon is raised, the punishment is the middle amercement (*madhyama-sāhasa*). || 221 ||

But when there is equality of caste and so forth, for pulling at the feet, hair, garment, or hand, the fine is ten paṇas; for causing pain, pulling, smearing with collyrium, wrapping up, or stepping on the feet, the punishment is one hundred [paṇas]. (2.222)

For pulling at, shaking, or roughly seizing the feet, hair, or garments, the fine shall be ten paṇas. However, for causing pain by dragging, or by smearing [the body] while wrapping it around the neck or other parts and then placing one's foot upon it, the offender shall be fined one hundred [paṇas]. "Smearing" (āñjana) means making [the body] darkened or discolored. "Causing pain by dragging and smearing" (pīḍākarṣāñjana) refers to dragging with force while smearing. By "smearing" (āñjana), the meaning is "having wrapped [it] and brought [the victim] under control through discoloration. The rest is clear. || 222 ||
In the case of mere equality [of injury]:
"A man who causes pain with wood and such implements, even without blood, shall be fined thirty-two *paṇas*; if blood is seen, the fine is double. (2.223)
The meaning is "of blood" (asṛjaḥ), that is, of the red liquid (lohitasya). The rest is clear. || 223 ||
But in the case of inferior objects:
"For breaking a hand, a foot, or a tooth, for cutting off the ears or the nose, for piercing a wound, and likewise for striking one who is nearly dead, the middle amercement shall be imposed. (2.224)

For since it has been stated that merely raising a weapon [constitutes an offense] in the case of equality, this [penalty] should be explained as pertaining to the case of an inferior person. The rest is straightforward. 224.
Likewise:
"In cases of obstructing movement, food, or speech; piercing the eyes or other [senses];
and breaking the neck, arms, or thighs, the punishment is the highest fine. (2.225)

In the case of an assault that obstructs movement and so forth, or which pierces each of the seats of the sense organs such as the eyes, or which pierces the neck and other such parts, the punishment is the highest amercement (*uttamasāhasa*). "Obstruction of movement" refers to fainting. "Obstruction of eating" refers to the inability to eat due to excessive trauma. "Obstruction of speech" refers to the inability to utter sounds. The "neck" (*kandharā*) refers to the vessels (*sirā*) moving within the throat and shoulders. The rest is clear. (225)

Throughout this entire section, however, for many who strike a single person, the fines shall be double those as previously stated; that which was taken away during a quarrel must be restored, and the fine shall be double that amount. (2.226)
The meaning is "from that which has been taken away through a quarrel. It should be understood that this must be given to the one who was struck, in addition to the royal fine. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"But for the one who was struck, the fine is that prescribed for assault;
when [the property] is stolen, another fine double that is imposed, and the royal fine is even greater than that. (BṛSm 21.14)
As for that which is stated in the *Nāradīya*:
"Whichever virtuous person among men these [officials] might transgress, he alone shall administer the punishment; the king does not incur the guilt of that punishment. (NSm 15.14–16.1)

This should be understood as referring to the case of Śūdras. For in the case of a grave offense committed by Śūdras, the king must not accept a monetary fine. What then? Without reporting it [to the king], they themselves should discipline them with a severe monetary fine. But if it is reported to the king, there shall be only corporal punishment. And thus he says immediately thereafter: "For these are stains among men; their wealth consists of stain.
Therefore, the king should have them executed; he should not punish them with a monetary fine" (NSm 15.15–16.1).
The rest is clear. || 226 ||
Furthermore:
He who causes pain shall be made to pay the expenses incurred for its removal, as well as the fine prescribed for that particular quarrel. (2.227)

If someone should cause injury, he must pay the expenses incurred until the victim has been properly restored and freed from suffering; these are the expenses arising from the restoration (*samutthānaja-vyaya*). By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is also implied that the costs for reporting to the king and for the legal proceedings are included. Furthermore, the aforementioned fine shall be paid to the king. If the offender does not pay voluntarily, he shall be compelled by the king to pay. The rest is clear. (227)
Now, because of its commonality with physical assault, he describes the legal procedure for violence:
A ferryman who takes a land toll shall be made to pay ten paṇas;
this same penalty applies to a Brāhmaṇa for failing to invite his neighbors [to a feast]. (2.228)

For a ferryman who collects the king’s due toll from a traveler on land, and for a Brāhmaṇa who, out of pride, fails to invite a suitable neighboring Brāhmaṇa [to a feast], the fine is ten paṇas. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" here is intended to include members of all three higher castes, as it is based on their specific qualities; furthermore, because such acts are committed out of arrogance, they constitute *sāhasa* (an offense of violence or willful injury). 228.
And likewise out of sheer insolence;
for striking, as well as for breaking, cutting, or causing the collapse of a wall, one shall be made to pay five, ten, or twenty paṇas, respectively, as well as the cost of repair. (2.229)

If a neighbor’s house is struck with stones or other projectiles out of malice, he shall be made to pay five *paṇas*. Likewise, if a breach is caused by such a strike or by intimidation, he shall be made to pay ten *paṇas*. But in the case of cutting, that is, splitting it in two, or the collapsing of a wall, he shall pay twenty *paṇas*. Furthermore, for the purpose of restoring what has been damaged, he shall give compensation to the householder; in all these cases, this is because of his reckless violence. (229)

If one throws into another's house property that causes suffering or even property that is life-threatening, he shall be made to pay sixteen *paṇas* in the first instance and the middle amercement in the second. (2.230)
Substances that produce suffering are thorns and the like; those that take life are snakes and the like; the rest is clear. || 230 ||
In the case of causing pain, drawing blood, or likewise cutting off a limb or a branch,
the fine for small animals shall be two paṇas and upwards in successive order.

The word "double" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. In cases of drawing blood, cutting a branch, or cutting a limb, the penalty increases twofold for each subsequent offense. "Branches" (*śākhā*) refer to the horns, ears, tail, and so forth; "limbs" (*aṅga*) refers to the eyes and other such parts. "Small animals" (*kṣudrapaśu*) refers to goats and the like. The rest is clear. || 231 ||

But for those belonging to others: "In the case of cutting off the male organ or causing death, the middle amercement and the price [of the animal] must be paid; for large animals, the fines in these instances are double. (2.232)

In the case of one's own animals, the fines—starting from two *paṇas* for the lowest, up to the middle and highest—are to be applied according to the specific circumstance; however, in the case of another's animals, it should be understood that both the fine and the value [of the animal] must be paid. "Large animals" refers to cows and the like. For these, in the aforementioned circumstances involving the shedding of blood or causing pain, the fines prescribed as starting from two *paṇas* should be doubled according to the specific circumstance. || 232 ||

For trees planted in a grove that are possessed of ownership, when their sprouts, twigs, branches, trunks, or entire bodies are torn apart, the fines for trees that provide livelihood are twenty times doubled. (2.233)

The "trees providing livelihood" (upajīvyadrumāḥ) are mango trees and the like. For cutting their sprouts, the fine is twenty paṇas. For cutting branches and so forth, the penalty is to be calculated by doubling for each successive stage. A "sprout" (prarohaḥ) is a young shoot. "Branchlets" (śākhikāḥ) are small branches. The rest is clear. || 233 ||

And also for those trees that provide a livelihood: for trees grown on a shrine, in a cemetery, at a boundary, at a holy place, or in a king’s palace, as well as for a tree of renown, the fines are double. (2.234)
The pippala and other such trees are renowned for their power to dispel quartan fever and similar ailments. The rest is clear. || 234 ||

But for the cutting down of shrubs, clusters, bushes, creepers, spreading plants, medicinal herbs, and climbing vines that grow near a shrine or similar site, the fine shall be half of what was previously prescribed for those same locations. (2.235)

For the cutting of shrubs (*gulma*) and other plants grown in the aforementioned places such as sacred groves (*caitya*), half-fines should be prescribed according to the sequence previously stated for sprouting and so forth, starting from the single-fold fine mentioned before. A *gulma* is [a plant] such as the *guñjā*; a *guccha* is [a plant] such as the *kunda*; a *kṣupa* is a bush such as the *jāti*; a *latā* is well known; a *pratāna* is a creeper (*vallarī*); *grāmyā oṣadhayaḥ* are cultivated herbs; and *āraṇyā vīrudhaḥ* are wild creepers. (235)

Thus ends the section on assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*). Now begins the section on violence (*sāhasa*). Since theft (*steya*) committed by force is also indeed violence, the punishment for theft does not apply here. What then?
Sāhasa (violent crime) is defined as the forcible seizure of common property;
the fine for such an act is twice its value, but if the offender denies it, the fine is fourfold. (2.236)

When common property belonging to two parties is forcibly seized by one of them after having overpowered the other—that is considered *sāhasa* (violence) by the great seers because of its forcible nature; therefore, the punishment for theft does not apply there. Rather, the intention is that the punishment for violence (*sāhasika*) shall be double the value of the stolen goods. If, after having forcibly seized it, he denies the act, the fine is four times the value. The mention of seizing common property is for the sake of illustration; whatever else is done as a forcible theft or otherwise, all that is indeed *sāhasa*. And so says Nārada:
Whatever act is performed impulsively by those arrogant of their strength is called *sāhasa* (violence); here, *saha* is said to mean strength. (NSm 14.1) || 236 ||
By another as well, by way of being the instigator:
he who causes a violent act to be committed shall be made to pay double the fine;
but he who, having said "I will give," causes it to be done, shall pay four times [the fine]. (2.237)

The one who causes [the work] to be done shall be made to pay double the previously mentioned fine. However, it should be understood that he who, having spoken thus, should cause it to be done—saying, "Let this be done; if any obstacle should arise here, then I myself will see it through"—is to be fined four times the aforementioned double fine. || 237 ||
And because of their very recklessness:

one who insults or bypasses those worthy of the *arghya* offering, one who strikes his brother’s wife, one who fails to deliver what has been entrusted, and one who breaks into a house by the sea (or a house with a vaulted roof). (2.238)
For those who cause injury to neighbors, guild members, and others, the penalty is fixed at fifty paṇas for each of them. (2.239)
These two verses have clear meanings. (238–9)
Likewise:
one who approaches a widow against her will, one who does not run to the aid of someone crying out for help, one who cries out falsely, and a Caṇḍāla who touches members of the highest castes; 2.240.
One who feeds Śūdras or renunciants at rites for the gods or the ancestors; one who makes an improper oath; and one who performs the duties of an unfit person—[these are excluded]. (2.241)
One who obstructs the virility of bulls or small animals, one who denies a common property, and one who causes the destruction of a maidservant's fetus [are liable]. (2.242)

Father and son, sister and brother, husband and wife, teacher and pupil: he who abandons any of these, provided they have not fallen from their status, shall be subject to a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. (2.243)
These four verses as well have a clear meaning. 240–3.

If a washerman wears another person's garment for the purpose of cleaning it, he shall be made to pay three *paṇas*; but if he sells, buys, pledges, or requests it [without authorization], he shall pay ten *paṇas*. (2.244)

"Parāṃśukam" means an excellent garment. For wearing such a garment [stolen], the washerman's fine is three *paṇas*. In this manner, for garments of middle or inferior quality, the calculation of the fine involves a reduction of *paṇas*. Likewise, the specific application [of the fine] depends on the frequency of the offense. However, in cases of selling and so forth, it should be understood that the owner receives the value [of the garment] and the king receives the fine. "Apakraya" (selling below cost) refers to handing over the goods [for a price lower than their value]. "Ādhamanam" refers to pledging [the garment as collateral]. The rest is clear. || 244 ||

Thus has the rule regarding punishment been declared for cases involving admissible legal proceedings. However, in the case of inadmissible proceedings initiated by brothers and others—such as disputes between father and son—the witnesses shall be fined two hundred panas.
Furthermore, whoever stands as an intermediary between those two shall also be fined eight hundred panas. (2.245)

In every case of a dispute between father and son or similar parties where the legal proceeding is not to be accepted [as valid], those who may be witnesses or observers—since the definition of a witness applies to them—shall be fined two hundred paṇas. Furthermore, he who causes estrangement among father, son, and others shall also be fined eight hundred paṇas; or alternatively, he who acts as a mediator between that very father and son, meaning one who engages in deceptive dealings. Both of these cases are appropriate because they do not involve a contradiction [of the law]. (245)
For the sake of establishing his own intended legal transactions:
"One who forges scales, royal edicts, measures, or coins, and whoever deals with these [falsified items], shall be made to pay the highest fine. (2.246)

The mention of "edicts" (*śāsana*) is intended to include the characteristics of all types of written documents. "Measures" (*māna*) refers to the *setikā*, the *prastha*, and so forth. The rest is clear. || 246 ||

But even if he knows the truth, if out of greed or other motives he declares a non-counterfeit coin to be counterfeit, or a counterfeit coin to be non-counterfeit, that examiner of coins shall be made to pay the first amercement. (2.247)
The word "tu" (but) is intended to indicate that in the case of gold, rubies, and so forth, there is an additional punishment.
Whether through ignorance or through error,
a physician practicing falsely shall be made to pay the first fine among those levied for offenses against animals.
In a human court, he shall be made to pay the middle fine; in a royal court, the highest fine.

Animals include those of inferior castes and animals; Vaiśyas and Śūdras constitute the human class; and Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas constitute the royal human class. For a physician who practices in this manner [of deception], the punishments range from the first amercement upwards. This is stated for the sake of illustration; it should be understood that in every case, the punishment must be determined according to the actual nature of the treatment and the specific injury caused by the physician. || 248 ||
But he who makes a false claim regarding caste,
or who binds one who should not be bound, or releases one who should be bound, or who engages in improper legal proceedings, shall be made to pay the highest fine. (2.249)
One who has not attained legal capacity is one whose status is not made clear by legal procedure; the rest is clear. || 249 ||

If one should take an eighth part [of the goods] through fraud, by means of skillful deception, or even by using false weights or measures, he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred; this amount is prescribed for both increase and decrease. (2.250)
This also must be determined with regard to the value of the stolen property; the rest is clear. || 250 ||

One who, desiring to cause a buyer to be deceived by means of similarity and other such tricks, puts inferior goods among merchandise such as medicines, oils, salt, perfumes, grains, or molasses, shall be made to pay a fine of sixteen *paṇas*. (2.251)
"Inferior" means of low value; "straightforward" means otherwise. || 251 ||
This is said with the intention of referring to the buyer's ignorance of the true nature of the commodity:
"For selling clay, leather, gems, thread, iron, wood, bark, or cloth by falsely representing them as being of a superior kind, the fine shall be eightfold. (MDh 2.252)

One who sells clay and other such materials by representing them as being of a superior quality when they are not shall be fined eight times the aforementioned sixteen paṇas. The rest is clear. || 252 ||

But if someone, having shown an item such as camphor contained within a casket, should effect a pledge or a sale by substituting another casket or by means of artificial fabrication, then for that fraudulent dealer who brings about either a pledge or a sale—whether it be the exchange of the casket or the substitution of a high-quality commodity with a counterfeit one—the following determination of punishment shall apply: "Whether it be the exchange of the casket or the substitution of a high-quality commodity with a counterfeit one, for one who effects either a pledge or a sale, the determination of punishment shall be made. (2.253)
The meaning of this verse has already been explained. || 253 ||
Is the determination of the fine based on one's own judgment? No; he says: "But when a *paṇa* is stolen, the fine is fifty; for a *paṇa*, it is said to be one hundred;
for two *paṇas*, the fine is two hundred; but as the value increases, the fine increases accordingly. (2.254)
The intention is that, however, in the case of a substance whose specific nature is not specified, the determination of the punishment should be according to its value. || 254 ||

Thus far, the instruction regarding individual transgressions has been stated. Now, he states the instruction regarding artisans and others acting in concert: "For artisans and craftsmen who act together to fix a price that causes distress—whether for the purpose of lowering or raising the price—a fine of one thousand paṇas is prescribed. (2.255)

When artisans and craftsmen, acting together with a single mind, cause obstruction or inflict suffering upon other artisans or the goods produced by them, they shall be fined one thousand *kārṣāpaṇas*. This fine is to be imposed when there is a decrease or an increase in the price of their craft. Those who manufacture vessels and other articles themselves and then sell them are "artisans" (*śilpins*), such as brazier-makers and the like. Those, however, who merely produce houses and other structures for others are "craftsmen" (*kāru*s). It should be understood that this fine applies when they cause a decrease or an increase in the price—either to prevent entry for visiting artisans or due to the excessive demands of the employer—at which time this punishment is to be levied. (255)

For the very reason already stated: "If merchants, having banded together, withhold merchandise at an improper price, or sell it [at such a price], the prescribed fine is the highest amercement. (2.256)
By what price, then, is the sale of commodities conducted? It is said:
the sale or purchase is carried out at whatever price is fixed by the king every day.
The word "kārya" (to be done) is understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
And as for that daily price determined by a skilled merchant appointed by the royal court, why is there a resale of goods purchased at that price? Because:
"Or rather, the sale of merchants is traditionally held to be for the sake of profit. (2.257)
From the statement "it is remembered," it is understood that selling [the property] even by means of acquisition is lawful. || 257 ||
But is the calculation of profit for merchants merely arbitrary? No, it is said. How then?
"A merchant dealing in goods from his own country may take five percent;
but ten percent on foreign goods, provided he buys and sells immediately. (2.258)
The meaning is that whoever is the immediate buyer or seller of a particular commodity shall take a tenth or a fifth part of its value. || 258 ||
But should the king fix the price arbitrarily? No, he says:
"Having established the expenses arising from the commodity upon the commodity itself, the price should be fixed so as to be beneficial to both the buyer and the seller. (2.259)
Thus ends the section on rash acts.
Now begins the section on the non-delivery of what has been sold.
Following the context of buying and selling, he now addresses the matter of the non-delivery of goods after sale.

If one who has received the price does not deliver the merchandise to the buyer, he shall be made to pay it with interest; or, if the buyer has gone to another region, he shall be made to pay the profit derived from that region. (2.260)

If, after paying the price, the buyer does not take the merchandise, then the fault lies solely with the buyer; otherwise, however, the fault lies solely with the seller—this is the intended meaning. || 260 ||
But when the price has been paid: "If the merchandise is damaged by the king or by an act of God, the loss belongs solely to the seller who, having been asked for it, does not deliver it. (2.261)

It has been stated that if one who has been asked, "Hand over this merchandise to me," fails to hand it over, any loss incurred therein belongs to the seller alone. However, if the merchandise should become defective due to a royal prohibition or due to a natural calamity such as drought, then whatever loss of value occurs must be understood to belong to the seller alone. || 261 ||
For it was indeed intended by the seller himself;
however, if what was sold into another's hand is defective, yet sold as if non-defective, the fine in that case shall be double its value. (2.262)

But he who sells again what has already been intended for sale by another purchaser, or who, considering it non-defective, sells what is actually defective, shall be fined double the value of the commodity; and the value of the commodity must be returned to the purchaser. The rest is clear. 262.
Now he demonstrates the scope of rescission regarding purchase and sale:
"A merchant who understands the loss and profit of commodities shall not exercise the right of rescission after having purchased; if he does so, he is liable to a fine of one-sixth. (2.263)

The price of commodities increases or decreases due to factors such as the movement of the moon. A merchant who understands this should, after determining the loss or gain, purchase or sell provided there is no conflict; otherwise, he should not feel regret. If he does so [regretfully], the king shall impose a fine of one-sixth of the commodity's value. The rest is clear. || 263 ||
Thus ends the section on selling without delivery.
Now begins the section on partnership (saṃbhūyasamutthāna).
Following the context of trade, he describes partnership.
When merchants perform work for the sake of profit through association, their gain and loss shall be according to the value of the goods or as determined by their agreement. (2.264)

Having pooled all the gains together, a division should be made according to the nature of the goods. Since the gain depends upon the value [of the goods] or upon the labor [performed], it is "according to agreement"; that is to say, a mutual convention or a boundary has been established. The rest is clear. || 264 ||
If those who have made such an agreement act according to their own will in a manner contrary to established custom; or if what was forbidden is used, or if it is lost through negligence;
he shall restore that, and the guardian shall receive a tenth part as compensation for the loss. (2.265)

The remainder [of the verse] means: that which is prohibited, not specifically enjoined, or not practiced by other merchants. Furthermore, whatever has been lost through negligence, the protector must restore that; this is done regardless of any consideration for the loss. However, in the case of a calamity (*viplava*), the protector who guards the property shall receive a tenth part of the profit from the guarded goods; this is the meaning. || 265 ||
Now he describes the duties pertaining to the king:
"From the casting of the price, the king shall take a twentieth part as toll;
that which is prohibited, what is fit for the king, and that which has been sold [as such], belongs to the king. (2.266)

Whatever price was set and established by the king, from that very price, after deducting the royal fee (*argha*), a twentieth part of the sale proceeds is due to the king. This fee, known as *śukla*, may be paid by both the buyer and the seller together, or mutually between them, or by either one according to their agreement. Furthermore, whatever property such as elephants or other goods—which has been prohibited by the king or is fit for the king—has been sold without having been reported or declared to the king, all of that must be understood to belong to the king alone. (266)

He who, for the sake of evading royal duties or customs duties, falsely declares the quantity of merchandise and the like while departing from the customs station, shall be made to pay eight times the amount; this applies also to one who engages in fraudulent buying or selling. (2.267)
Now, when those who have entered into a commercial partnership suffer the loss of one of their number, should that person's property be seized by the other merchants? No, it is said. What then?
"When one has gone to another country or died, his heirs, kinsmen, or relatives shall take that property; if they do not come forward, the king shall take it. (2.268)

When a deceased person has gone to another country, his heirs shall take his share—purified by [the accounting of] income and expenditure—and divide it according to the rules; but in the absence of such heirs, the king shall take it. Why, however, is this stated again? Because there is a prohibition regarding the payment of debts. As Gautama says: "Surety-money, trade-duties, tolls, liquor, gambling-debts, and fines do not devolve upon sons" (GDh 12.41). Since the connection with wealth is like that of a debt, one might suspect that it is only right for him to have no share; it is for the purpose of removing this doubt that this is said. The rest is clear. || 268 ||
This rule applies to masters, servants, and others who have come together and engaged in work with one another:
they should abandon one who acts dishonestly or fails to provide profit; one who is incapable should have the work performed by another.
By this same rule, the conduct of officiating priests, farmers, and laborers is declared.

Mutually, masters, laborers, members of an assembly, and so forth, should abandon one who is deceitful, crooked, or unfaithful, as well as one who is devoid of profit. However, one who has begun a task, even if personally unable, should have his own work or that of the assembly performed by another who is not antagonistic. This very rule which has been stated regarding collective enterprise should also be understood to apply to the performance of duties by officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others as determined by this same principle. Nevertheless, the detailed expansion regarding the specific performance of officiating priests and others should be sought from other *Smṛti* texts. The rest is clear. 269.

Thus ends the section on partnerships (*saṃbhūyasamutthāna*). Now begins the section on theft (*steya*). If, however, someone should steal and depart with property acquired through hardship—whether by means of individual gifts and the like, or through officiating at sacrifices and the like in partnership—how is he to be identified? And what should be done to him once he is identified? In response to this inquiry, the author speaks in order to define the nature of a thief: [The verse follows: *yo vai bhūtvā svayaṃ stenaḥ...* (He who, having himself become a thief... [and so forth].* *Note: The specific verse is not provided in the source text, but the commentary introduces it as the definition of a thief.*
A thief is apprehended by his captors through stolen goods, or by a footprint, or due to the transgression of a prior deed; in the same way, one who dwells in impurity [is apprehended]. (2.270)

The thief is apprehended by the seizers through the identification of his thievery by the owners of the stolen goods; or else by the "loptram"—the stolen property—or by the footprint (*pada*) which is skillfully traced from the place of the theft; or by his prior conduct, due to the suspicion of having committed a crime of theft; as well as by other signs establishing thievery mentioned in other *smṛtis* that will be described hereafter, such as "impure residence" (*aśuddhavāsaka*). One whose residence is impure is an "impure-resider," meaning one whose origin is unknown and who dwells in the houses of greedy men, prostitutes, and the like. (270)
And like pickpockets and the like,
others too may be suspected on account of the concealment of their caste, name, and so forth,
as well as those addicted to gambling, women, and drink, and those whose faces and voices appear parched and altered. (2.271)

Those who inquire about the property and houses of others while moving about in secret, those who have no income yet spend lavishly, and those who sell goods that do not exist—[these are to be suspected]. (2.272)

Since this Smṛti is rooted within the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), its explanation must be carried out by discerning it in accordance with those very means. As for the meanings of the individual words, they have already been stated literally. 271–272.
And according to the principle already stated:
"If one caught on suspicion of theft does not clear himself, he shall be made to restore the stolen property and be punished with the penalty for a thief. (2.273)
The determination of punishment should be made as appropriate, in accordance with other Smṛti texts. || 273 ||
When the theft has been made manifest by the thief or others,
the king shall cause the thief to restore what was stolen and then have him executed by various forms of death.
The intended meaning is that this includes corporal punishments mentioned in other Smṛtis— such as the extraction of eyes and so forth— as well as life-ending methods like impalement on a stake.
Thus [he should treat] one who is not a Brahmin. But how should he treat a Brahmin?
Having branded him as a Brahmin, he should banish him from his own kingdom. (2.274)
"With its mark" means branded with the footprints of a dog or the like. The rest is clear. || 274 ||
But how is it when no killer, thief, or the like is found despite diligent investigation?

Regarding the case of one who has been killed or whose property has been stolen: "The fault lies with the village headman if [the perpetrator] has not departed, provided there are signs of the tracks and so forth having been pursued. This is the implied meaning.

"But on the road belonging to a pasture-keeper" means near the vicinity of a pasture and so forth; the word "but" (*tu*) is intended to indicate that others who are capable [of apprehending thieves] are likewise liable for the offense according to their proximity.
"For one who recovers stolen goods from a thief, [the fine is] in a non-pasture area" (2.275).

In the absence of the previously mentioned conditions, the fault lies solely with the one who recovered the stolen property. The intention is that, in every case, the king must recover the stolen goods by diligent search. Alternatively, when the property has been stolen and the thief, possessing the goods, has been killed, and the property is not recovered, the question arises as to whose fault it is; in this regard, the rule regarding the village headman and so forth is the same as before. || 275 ||
But when the village headman is not present, the village itself shall provide the path within its own boundary, or wherever the path leads;
likewise, five villages outside the ploughed land, or even ten villages. (2.276)
The word *sva* (own) means wealth or kinsmen. That area where bipeds, quadrupeds, and so forth constantly move about is one's own boundary (*svasīmā*). The rest is clear. || 276 ||
But regarding specific types of thieves and others, he states the method of execution:
"Those who capture prisoners, as well as those who steal horses and elephants, and those who commit violent assaults—such men he shall impale upon a stake. (2.277)
The word "tathā" (likewise) signifies a manner or type. The mention of "man" is intended to include non-Brāhmaṇas as well. The rest is clear. || 277 ||
However, depending on the specific nature of the object and other factors:

for the first offense, the one who committed the theft shall be deprived of his hands and the one who broke the seal of the knot shall be deprived of their hands and thumbs; for the second offense, they shall be deprived of one hand and one foot.

An *utkṣepaka* is one who throws off [the king's] garment; a *granthibhedaka* is a cutpurse. Both of these, for the first offense, shall have their "hand-clasp" (*karasaṃdaṃśa*) deprived. The "hand-clasp" refers to the fingers; they shall be deprived of those, or alternatively, the "hand-clasp" refers to the hollow of the hand (*karasaṃpuṭa*); they shall be deprived of that. The meaning is that one hand shall be amputated. For the second offense, however, one hand and one foot [shall be amputated]. The rest is clear. (278)
Regarding this corporal punishment which has been described, as well as the monetary fine mentioned in other Smṛtis—in all such cases, this concise summary of the principles of justice is common:

"In the seizure of small, middling, or great property, the punishment shall be according to the value; in the administration of punishment, one must carefully consider the place, time, age, and capacity [of the offender]. (2.279)
The phrase "even elsewhere" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 279 ||
Furthermore:
"If one knowingly provides a thief or a murderer with food, shelter, fire, water, incantations, or implements, the highest fine shall be imposed. (2.280)

For one who knows that "this man is a thief" or "he is a violent assailant" and yet gives food and other provisions to such a thief or violent assailant, the punishment is the highest fine (uttamasāhasa). The rest is clear. || 280 ||
For stealing from women who are not unchaste, [the punishment is as prescribed]. For causing an abortion by the use of a weapon, and for causing a miscarriage, the highest fine is ordained;
likewise, for the killing of a woman, the highest or even the lowest form of corporal punishment applies to the man.

In the case of causing the death of a Brahmin woman or a weapon-wound to a fetus, the highest punishment must be inflicted; that is to say, execution. Whether the person is a superior Brahmin or an inferior Śūdra and so forth—the word "also" (api) implying even a middling person such as a Kṣatriya—the intention is that any man who causes the death of a woman is surely liable to execution. And so says Kātyāyana: "One who causes an abortion, one who strikes a Brahmin woman with a weapon, or one who kills an innocent woman—even a Brahmin is to be put to death. (KSm 806) || 281 ||

But even apart from theft, one should cause a woman who administers poison, one who kills a man, or one who destroys a dam— provided she is not pregnant— to be cast into the water bound to a stone. (2.282)

A woman who administers poison under the pretext of medicine and the like—by the use of the word "ca" (and), a man as well—is [to be punished]. The particle *eva* (only) is intended to indicate that there is no other way to avoid killing her. Even though there is no actual killing, the meaning is that she who employs the means for death through poison and so forth must be killed. A "woman who kills a man" (*puruṣaghnī*) is one who becomes the cause of a man's death due to excessive addiction to another man, whether by force or otherwise. And she who, out of fear of relatives and others, causes an abortion and says "I am pregnant"—her they call "one who is not pregnant" (*agarbhiṇī*). Thus it is stated in another Smṛti: [The verse continues: "One who kills a man, one who drinks liquor, one who steals gold, one who breaks her vow, one who destroys an embryo, and one who kills a woman—these six must be killed without hesitation. And: "One who kills a man, one who destroys an embryo, one who drinks liquor, one who steals gold, and one who breaks her vow—these five are equal to those who kill a Brahmin. And: "One who kills a man, one who destroys an embryo, one who steals gold, one who drinks liquor, one who breaks her vow, one who reviles her husband, and one who abandons her husband—these seven are equal to those who kill a Brahmin. And: "One who kills a man, one who destroys an embryo, one who steals gold, one who drinks liquor, one who breaks her vow, one who reviles her husband, one who abandons her husband, and one who reviles her elders—these eight are equal to those who kill a Brahmin. And: "One who kills a man, one who destroys an embryo, one who steals gold, one who drinks liquor, one who breaks her vow, one who reviles her husband, one who abandons her husband, one who reviles her elders, one who reviles the gods, and one who reviles the Vedas—these ten are equal to those who kill a Brahmin. And: "One who kills a man, one who destroys an embryo, one who steals gold, one who drinks liquor, one who breaks her vow, one who reviles her husband, one who abandons her husband, one who reviles her elders, one who reviles the gods, one who reviles the Vedas, and one who reviles the king—these eleven are equal to those who kill a Brahmin. And: "One who kills a man, one who destroys an embryo, one who steals gold, one who drinks liquor, one who breaks her vow, one who reviles her husband, one who abandons her husband, one who reviles her elders, one who reviles the gods, one who reviles the Vedas, one who reviles the king, and one who reviles the teacher—these twelve are equal to those who kill a Brahmin. And: "One who kills a man, one who destroys an embryo, one who steals gold, one who drinks liquor, one who breaks her vow, one who reviles her husband, one who abandons her husband, one who reviles her elders, one who reviles the gods, one who reviles the Vedas, one who reviles the king, one who reviles the teacher, and one who reviles the fire—these thirteen are equal to those who kill a Brahmin. And: "One who kills a man, one who destroys an embryo, one who steals gold, one who drinks liquor, one who breaks her vow, one who reviles her husband, one who abandons her husband, one who reviles her elders, one who reviles the gods, one who reviles the Vedas, one who reviles the king, one who reviles the teacher, one who reviles the fire, and one who reviles the sun—these fourteen are equal to those who kill a Brahmin. And: "One who kills a man, one who destroys an embryo, one who steals gold, one who drinks liquor, one who breaks her vow, one who reviles her husband, one who abandons her husband, one who reviles her elders, one who reviles the gods, one who reviles the Vedas, one who reviles the king, one who reviles the teacher, one who reviles the fire, one who reviles the sun, and one who reviles the moon—these fifteen are equal to those who kill a Brahmin. And: "One who kills a man, one who destroys an embryo, one who steals gold, one who drinks liquor, one who breaks her vow, one who reviles her husband, one who abandons her husband, one who reviles her elders, one who reviles the gods, one who reviles the Vedas, one who reviles the king, one who reviles the teacher, one who reviles the fire, one who reviles the sun, one who reviles the moon, and one who reviles the stars—these sixteen are equal to those who kill a Brahmin. And: "One who kills a man, one who destroys an embryo, one who steals gold, one who drinks liquor, one who breaks her vow, one who reviles her husband, one who abandons her husband, one who reviles her elders, one who reviles the gods, one who reviles the Vedas, one who reviles the king, one who reviles the teacher, one who reviles the fire, one who reviles the sun, one who reviles the moon, one who reviles the stars, and one who reviles the planets—these seventeen are equal to those who kill a Brahmin. And: "One who kills a man, one who destroys an embryo, one who steals gold, one who drinks liquor, one who breaks her vow, one who reviles her husband, one who abandons her husband, one who reviles her elders, one who reviles the gods, one who reviles the Vedas, one who reviles the king, one who reviles the teacher, one who reviles the fire, one who reviles the sun, one who reviles the moon, one who reviles the stars, one who reviles the planets, and one who reviles the constellations—these eighteen are equal to those who kill a Brahmin. And: "One who kills a man, one who destroys an embryo, one who steals gold, one who drinks liquor, one who breaks her vow, one who reviles her husband, one who abandons her husband, one who reviles her elders, one who reviles the gods, one who reviles the Vedas, one who reviles the king, one who reviles the teacher, one who reviles the fire, one who reviles the sun, one who reviles the moon, one who reviles the stars, one who reviles the planets, one who reviles the constellations, and one who reviles the seasons—these nineteen are equal to those who kill a Brahmin. And: "One who kills a man, one who destroys an embryo, one who steals gold, one who drinks liquor, one who breaks her vow, one who reviles her husband, one who abandons her husband, one who reviles her elders, one who reviles the gods, one who reviles the Vedas, one who reviles the king, one who reviles the teacher, one who reviles the fire, one who reviles the sun, one who reviles the moon, one who reviles the stars, one who reviles the planets, one who reviles the constellations, one who reviles the seasons, and one who reviles the months—these twenty are equal to those who kill a Brahmin. And: "One who kills a man, one who destroys an embryo, one who steals gold, one who drinks liquor, one who breaks her vow, one who reviles her husband, one who abandons her husband, one who reviles her elders, one who reviles the gods, one who reviles the Vedas, one who reviles the king, one who reviles the teacher, one who reviles the fire, one who reviles the sun, one who reviles the moon, one who reviles the stars, one who reviles the planets, one who reviles the constellations, one who reviles the seasons, one who reviles the months, and one who reviles the half-months—these twenty-one are equal to those who kill a Brahmin. And: "One who kills a man, one who destroys an embryo, one who steals gold, one who drinks liquor, one who breaks her vow, one who reviles her husband, one who abandons her husband, one who reviles her elders, one who reviles the gods, one who reviles the Vedas, one who reviles the king, one who reviles the teacher, one who reviles the fire, one who reviles the sun, one who reviles the moon, one who reviles the stars, one who reviles the planets, one who reviles the constellations, one who reviles the seasons, one who reviles the months, one who reviles the half-months, and one who reviles the days—these twenty-two are equal to those who kill a Brahmin. And: "One who kills a man, one who destroys an embryo, one who steals gold, one who drinks liquor, one who breaks

"She who, having caused her own fetus to fall, should say 'I am not pregnant,' the king shall cause her to be thrown into the water, as well as the paramour and the woman who causes the death of a man. *Setu* means a dam, a small canal, or a bridge; or it refers to a boundary. The rest is clear. 282.

Regarding the manner of execution for those who administer poison to their husband and others, he says: "One who gives poison or fire, or one who causes the death of her husband, her teacher, or her own child, shall have her ears, hands, nose, and lips cut off and then be put to death by oxen. (2.283)
The "guru" refers to the father-in-law and others; "one's own" refers to brothers and so forth. The rest is clear. || 283 ||

This method of execution by means of poison or arson is for the purpose of accomplishing a killing; however, regarding the death of a husband or others where the perpetrator is currently unknown, he now describes the manner of investigation for the accomplishment of such an unidentified murder:

"Immediately after someone has been killed under suspicious circumstances, his sons and kinsmen should be questioned about the quarrel [that preceded it], as well as his women who were infatuated with other men, individually. (2.284)

Immediately after the killing, and swiftly, the sons and kinsmen of the slain person must be questioned: "With whom did he previously have a quarrel? Who was it that provoked him with harsh words? Furthermore, his wives must be asked whether any of them were ever attached to another man. In this manner, the relatives should be questioned individually. Alternatively, those women among the neighbors and others who are known to be devoted to other men should be questioned one by one. Or, his own wives—the co-wives—should be questioned among themselves regarding any attachment to another man. Since the truth of this matter must be based on other means of proof, an investigation should be conducted accordingly. (284)
Furthermore:
"Or perhaps he went with someone desiring a woman's livelihood or wealth;
or one should slowly question people near the place of death. (2.285)

Furthermore, his sons and others should be questioned as follows: "What was his desire regarding women and so forth? Did he ever have any connection with another's wife? What was his livelihood? What wealth did he desire, or what was attached to his person? With whom did he leave the house? Who was his friend? Because the minds of wicked people are of many kinds, everything of this sort must be inquired about. Furthermore, the people nearby—cowherds and others—in the place where he was struck down should be questioned slowly: "Who was seen by you here at that time? In this way, through skill in inference, the killer is to be sought out. Here, the "killer" is mentioned merely as an illustration; it should be understood that this method of investigation applies to all those who commit wrongful acts. (285)
Likewise, those who search for assassins and those about to be mentioned—
namely, those who set fire to fields, houses, villages, forests, or enclosures,
as well as one who approaches the king's wife— shall be burned by a straw fire. (2.286)
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of including those who are learned in the Vedas and women; the rest is clear. || 286 ||
Thus ends the section on theft.
Now begins the section on sexual intercourse with women (*strī-saṃgrahaṇa*).
In connection with the offense of approaching the wife of a king, he states the rules for *saṃgrahaṇa* concerning women in general who are under the protection of another.
A man shall be apprehended for adultery when he is caught by the hair with another's wife, or by means of signs born of passion, or likewise when both parties admit it. (2.287)

The mention of "man" is for the purpose of emphasizing the man's excessive self-restraint. The phrase "seizing by the hair" is intended to include seizing by means of mechanical devices. Or [the offense is established] by marks produced through passion, such as nail and tooth wounds, or when there is mutual consent between the two. 287.

When the act of abduction has been made manifest either through skill in inference or by direct perception, the highest fine shall be imposed for abducting one of the same caste, while the middle fine applies in the case of abduction in the natural order of castes. In the case of abduction in the inverse order of castes, there shall be death for men and the cutting off of the nose and other features for women. (2.288)

In cases involving distinctions such as *ānulomya* (acting in accordance with the order of castes) and so forth, the determination of fines for property or fines for corporal punishment should be established as appropriate in accordance with other legal codes (*smṛti*). It should be understood that this was stated by the Teacher merely as an illustration. The rest is straightforward. || 288 ||

But when either one does not desire it, whether it be the man or the woman, [the following constitute adultery]: touching the waist-knot, the breasts, the upper garment, the navel, or the hair; conversing at an improper place or time; and staying together in private. (2.289)
A woman who has been forbidden [from intercourse] shall be fined one hundred [paṇas], and a man who does so shall be fined two hundred;
if there was no such prohibition, their punishment shall be the same as that for adultery (saṃgrahaṇa).

A woman who, though forbidden by a man, touches his waist-knot (*nīvī*) or other parts of his body, speaks to him at an improper place or time, or stays with him, shall be fined one hundred *paṇas*. A man who, though forbidden by a woman, does the same shall be fined two hundred *paṇas*. However, if both act out of mutual desire, the penalty for adultery (*saṃgrahaṇa*) as previously stated applies to both. The *nīvī* is the region around the waist-knot or the girdle. Speaking with the intention of being private is "speaking at an improper place or time. The rest is clear. (289–90)
Since abduction is closely related to the act of seduction, he mentions the abduction of a maiden as well by way of incidental discussion:

"But for one who abducts an adorned maiden of the same caste, the highest fine shall be imposed; otherwise, the lowest. However, in the case of abduction from a higher caste, death is ordained. (2.291)
Adorned and prepared for the wedding; the rest is clear. || 291 ||
Only with maidens; there is no fault if they are willing and of a lower caste, but otherwise it is a base offense.
However, for defiling [a maiden], the hand shall be cut off if she is of the highest caste, and likewise, there shall be death.

There is no offense in defiling and carrying off girls who desire it, whether they be of the same caste (*savarṇā*) or of a lower caste (*anuloma*), because this falls within the scope of the *gāndharva* form of marriage. As for the lesser punishment prescribed for carrying off an unadorned girl, that refers to cases where she is not desirous of it. However, in the case of defiling a girl by having sexual intercourse with her against her will, the cutting off of the hand is the penalty; otherwise, according to other *smṛti* texts, the cutting off of a finger is prescribed. But in the case of defiling a girl through a *pratiloma* union (with a man of higher caste), death alone is the penalty. The word "likewise" (*tathā*) indicates the methods such as being impaled on a stake mentioned in other *smṛtis*. The rest is clear. || 292 ||
The punishment for the defiler has been stated; but as for the girl to be defiled:
"A woman who defiles [another] shall be made to pay one hundred [paṇas], but she who makes a false accusation shall pay two hundred.
One who has intercourse with animals shall be made to pay one hundred, and he who has intercourse with a low-caste woman or a cow shall pay the middle amercement. (2.293)

A maiden who has been defiled by approaching her as a woman is called a "woman" (*strī*). When such defilement has occurred, she is to be punished with a fine of two hundred [paṇas]. However, if one should falsely claim that she has been defiled when she was actually undefiled, then he shall be fined two hundred for making a false accusation. For sexual intercourse with animals other than cows—such as horses and the like—he is to be fined one hundred. But for one who approaches a woman of a lower caste (*anuloma*) or a cow, the middle amercement is the penalty. The mention of a "lowly woman" is intended to serve as an illustration for the application of punishment to cows and other animals as well; otherwise, since this has already been stated previously, it would result in mere redundancy. Therefore, the determination of punishment for one who approaches animals and the like should be applied based on the specific nature of possession, just as in the case of women. (293)
And likewise,

in the case of female slaves who have been taken into one's household, or those who are dependent, even if they are women with whom intercourse is permitted, a man shall be made to pay a fine of fifty paṇas. (2.294)

Female slaves are those who perform labor as servants; even in their case, there is a punishment for one who approaches them by forcing them to neglect their master's work. Furthermore, among women with whom intercourse is permissible—even for Śūdras and others—this applies to those whose husbands have died, to the wives of brothers, and to those not yet initiated (by marriage) such as those offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). The mention of the masculine gender is intended to indicate that women such as those kept in confinement (*avaruddhā*) and so forth are subject to half the fine. [294]
If one approaches a female slave by force without having paid the price, a fine of ten paṇas is prescribed; if she is unwilling and many men do so, each shall be fined twice twelve paṇas. (2.295)
If many men approach a single female slave against her will, each shall be punished with a fine of twenty-four paṇas. || 295 ||
But without distinction:
for one who approaches a woman in a place other than the womb, or who urinates upon a man, the fine is twenty-four paṇas; the same applies when approaching a female ascetic. (2.296)

The insertion of the penis into the mouth, feet, or other [orifices] of a man is "penetration by a man. A woman who has been abandoned by her kinsmen due to her unchastity is a "female wanderer" (pravrajitā). The rest is clear. || 296 ||
But this applies to the three higher castes when it is done intentionally.
However, upon approaching a woman of the lowest caste, one should brand him with the mark of a headless trunk (kabandha) and banish him;
likewise, a Śūdra who approaches a woman of a higher caste should be branded. But for a man of the lowest caste approaching a woman of a higher caste, the punishment is death. (2.297)

This term "last" (*antya*) refers to the Śūdra as one who is base and outcast. A member of the three higher castes who has sexual intercourse with such a woman—an outcast woman of the last caste—should be branded with the mark of a headless trunk (*kabandha*) and banished from his own kingdom. A Śūdra, however, should likewise be branded, but he is not to be banished. This [penalty] should be understood to apply to one who does not perform penance or who acts intentionally or repeatedly. Consequently, the non-banishment of the Śūdra is for the purpose of making it known that he becomes a slave; having been made a slave, he should then be made to perform penance. But in the case of an outcast of the last caste having intercourse with an Ārya woman, such as a Śūdra woman and so forth, there is indeed death [as the penalty]. In this manner, the detailed exposition of the nature of adultery, the means of its recognition, and the various forms of punishment should be carried out. (297)
Thus ends the section on adultery with women. Now begins the section on miscellaneous matters (*prakīrṇaka*).
That which was not mentioned in the preceding sections is now stated for the purpose of completing the legal procedures previously determined.
Whoever writes a royal edict deficient or excessive, or who releases an adulterer or a thief, shall receive the highest punishment. (2.298)

The statement regarding the royal edict is for the purpose of defining the characteristics of all written documents. Whether it be the one who causes the document to be written or the scribe himself, whoever commits a defect in the writing such as omission or excess, or whoever wishes to release a person—such as an adulterer—who has been surrendered for custody, shall be punished with the highest fine. || 298 ||

He who, relying on the favor of the king, forcibly defiles a Brahmin with forbidden food through acts of violence, shall be punished with the highest fine; for a Kṣatriya, the middle fine; for a Vaiśya, the first fine; and for a Śūdra, half of that. (2.299)
This penalty is to be understood as applying to those things that cause loss of caste when consumed, such as garlic and the like; the rest is clear. || 299 ||
But because of their engagement in secret theft:
"A dealer in counterfeit gold and a seller of forbidden meat shall have three limbs cut off and be made to pay the highest fine. (2.300)

Counterfeit gold refers to that which is colored by incense and the like. Forbidden meat refers to that originating from dogs, jackals, and so forth. The monetary fine is determined specifically with regard to the particular nature of such items. The deficiency of three limbs should be applied both individually and collectively; the two hands and one foot constitute the three limbs. The rest is clear. || 300 ||

But because it was undertaken unintentionally, there is no offense for one who says "go away" when a four-footed animal has been struck; likewise for striking with wood, clods, arrows, stones, or engaging in hand-to-hand combat. (2.301)

"There is this vicious ox and so forth; hurry to move away"—for an owner who speaks thus, there is no fault regarding an offense committed by his quadruped. And such indeed is the meaning of this [verse]. In the case of two people throwing wood or the like, or being enraged in a wrestling match, it is understood from the word "tathā" (likewise) that there is indeed fault only when there has been no prior provocation. || 301 ||
And precisely because it was unintended:
"When damage is caused by a vehicle whose nose-rope is severed, or whose yoke is broken, or which retreats backward, the owner incurs no fault. (2.302)

It is joined with oxen and so forth that lack the [signs] such as "naṣṭa" (lost) and the like, and whose noses have been cut. The word "tathā" (likewise) has the sense of "in this manner. The rest is clear. || 302 ||

If a master is capable yet fails to release a bull or other animal that has been seized and is being harmed, he shall be made to pay the first *sāhasa* fine; likewise, if there is a cry for help, he shall be made to pay double. (2.303)
The word "tathā" (likewise) is for the purpose of understanding that specific punishments are to be determined in accordance with the specific nature of the offense; the rest is well known. || 303 ||
But if one falsely accuses a thief who is actually concealed by greed or other motives, saying "He is a thief," he shall be made to pay a fine of five hundred panas;
if he releases him after having used his wealth for his own livelihood, he shall be made to pay eight times that amount.

For one who, having passed by the actual thief, accuses another who is not a thief as being the thief, the fine is five hundred [paṇas]. It has been stated that for one who releases a thief after having profited from his property, the punishment is the forfeiture of that very property used and an eightfold fine; the rest is straightforward. || 304 ||
But by way of summary execution:
one who speaks what is displeasing to the king, as well as one who reviles him, and likewise one who divulges his secret counsel—the king should cut out their tongue and banish them. (2.305)
But by reason of sheer audacity alone,
the punishment for one who sells the limbs of a dead body, for one who strikes his teacher, and for one who ascends the bed or seat of a king is the middle amercement. (2.306)
Moreover:
For one who pierces two eyes, for one who issues commands hostile to the king, and likewise for a Śūdra living as a Brāhmaṇa, the fine is eight hundred [paṇas]. (2.307)

The mention of "two eyes" is intended to characterize all the sense organs. This should be understood as referring to sacrificial animals. One who is hated by the king is "hated by the king. The rest is clear. || 307 ||

Regarding this entire path of legal procedure that has been described, this following rule is common to all and depends upon the king: "But when a legal case has been wrongly decided by the king, the members of the court, together with the winner, shall each be fined double the amount in dispute. (2.308)
Since this has already been stated previously, its restatement here is intended to show that the King himself, acting as the observer, applies an exceeding effort. || 308 ||

Just as one who has been defeated is liable to a fine for making a false statement, so too is he who, though defeated according to the law, thinks "I am not defeated"; having won him back when he has returned, the king shall cause him to pay double the fine. (2.309)
The meaning of this verse is clear. || 309 ||
Even if a king has not personally imposed a legal punishment according to justice for any matter related to civil litigation, such as the non-payment of debts, having brought that case before Varuṇa,
he himself shall give thirty times that amount to the Brahmins. (2.310)

Even a fine that has been lawfully imposed by a king, if for some reason it was not actually collected due to affection or other such motives, he himself should multiply that amount thirtyfold, announce it to Varuṇa in the presence of water—meaning with reference to Varuṇa—and then give it to the Brahmins according to the previously mentioned rules for giving. Since this Smṛti rule is rooted in Vedic injunction (*codanā*), it should be explained that there is sin (*pratyavāya*) in failing to perform it or in performing it otherwise. Alternatively, if a fine was collected by a king unjustly, even if it is impossible for another to cause him to pay it back, one should multiply that amount thirtyfold, announce it to Varuṇa, and give it to the Brahmins. Or else, if a fine was collected by a king lawfully, one should, by implication, personally multiply that very amount thirtyfold and give it to the Brahmins. All of this must be understood as entirely justifiable, in accordance with the Śruti and Smṛti. (310)
Having made his entire circle resplendent, dyed by his first rising,
this exceedingly powerful King-Sun constantly protects the earth.
Thus, with his own weariness from vice dispelled and the conduct of his enemies overturned,
the king swiftly uprooted all thorns and became, like Hari, the most desired abode of Fortune.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Bālakrīḍā*, a commentary on the *Dharmaśāstra* composed by Viśvarūpa, authored by the supreme venerable Yājñavalkya.
The Chapter on Expiation;
now begins the Section on Impurity.

The removal of thorns (*kaṇṭakoddharaṇa*) has been described in various ways throughout the section on legal procedure (*vyavahāra-prakaraṇa*) as a duty of kingship, because it is the cause for attaining prosperity that is unfailing and sincere. Furthermore, the duties common to all castes (*varṇas*) across two stages of life (*āśramas*) have been stated. Now, although another stage of life is relevant at this point, it is set aside; instead, the author introduces the purification of the deceased (*preta-śuddhi*), which is a residual matter belonging to the preceding stage of life. But why is the description of the other stage of life, though relevant, postponed? It is so that the funeral rites (*pretakriyā*), which are prescribed as pertaining to the mere caste (*varṇa-mātra*), may occur independently of that [other stage], and so too may other modes of disposal for the body, such as carrying it to the forest. As it is said: "This indeed is the highest austerity: that they carry the deceased to the forest" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.11.1). Therefore, he now describes the funeral rites specifically according to the particular stage of life (*vayo'vasthā-viśeṣa*).
One should bury a child less than two years old and should not offer water for them thereafter;
as for others who have died, they should be followed by their kinsmen to the cremation ground. (3.1)

A child who has died before reaching two years of age should be buried in a pit after being dug; no cremation or other water-libation rites (udaka-kriyā) should be performed for it. Since there is a cessation of water-libation rites, the meaning is that the kinsmen should not follow the corpse. However, another [child] who dies after two years should be followed to the cremation ground; the meaning is that cremation and other water-libation rites must be performed for him. As for the text of Svāyambhuva:
"Kinsmen, having adorned a deceased child under two years of age, should place it outside on pure ground, except for the collection of the bones."
"No cremation with fire should be performed for him, nor should the water-rite be performed;
having abandoned him in the forest like a log, his kinsmen should simply pass three days [in mourning]. (MDh 5.68)

That [statement] is for the purpose of prescribing specific durations for the period of impurity (*āśauca*). Following this principle, the phrase "they should place [it]" implies that burial alone is intended there. Furthermore, it is stated in that very same [text]: "The water-rite (*udakakriyā*) should not be performed by relatives for one who has not reached three years of age;
however, they may perform it for one whose teeth have emerged, or once the naming ceremony (*nāman*) has been performed" (MDh 5.70).

Thus, this [statement] should be understood as being intended solely for the injunction of performing rites such as cremating the body under optional circumstances. As for the rule in the *Pāraskara-gṛhyasūtra*, "When a child of two years has died, the impurity belongs only to the mother and father" (PārG 3.10.2), that should be seen as referring to the touching of the body because it is an ancillary part of following the corpse. As for that which is stated in the *Svāyambhuva-smṛti*:
"For men whose tonsure ceremony (*caula*) has not been performed, impurity is declared to last one night" (MDh 5.67).

Thus, this [period of impurity] prior to the naming ceremony should be understood as lasting until one year has passed. Beyond that, however, whether the tonsure (*caula*) has been performed or not, it lasts for three nights until the initiation (*upanayana*). As it has been said: "For those whose tonsure has been completed, purification is desired after three nights" (MDh 5.67). The commencement of these two statements is intended to provide an option regarding cremation according to the specific circumstances: the option for cremation applies for two years after the naming ceremony; beyond that, cremation is mandatory. The rest is clear. || 1 ||
And he for whom the rite of cremation is prescribed,

if he has been initiated (upeta), should be burned with the common fire by those reciting the Yama-sūkta and the Gāthās, according to the procedure for one who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni), as the case may require. 3.2.

The *sūkta* dedicated to Yama, as well as the verses (*gāthā*) dedicated to Yama recited individually by Brāhmaṇas—both of these should be recited by the kinsmen. He who is entitled to the cremation rite is to be burned; any other person is to be burned with a common (worldly) fire. One who has been initiated (*upeta*) or invested with the sacred thread (*upanīta*) is to be burned according to the ritual procedure associated with the maintenance of the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), provided that the purpose is served and the essential elements are not omitted. He should be burned according to what is possible; however, according to another Smṛti, there is an omission of the mantras. And if the domestic fire (*śālāgni*) is available, the cremation is performed with that. || 2 ||

And having thus cremated [the body] according to their respective status, the kinsmen, facing the direction of the ancestors, enter the water from the seventh or even the tenth day with this [verse]: "May the sin burn away from us. (3.3)

Relatives who are connected by *sapiṇḍa* relationship up to the seventh generation, or by *samānodaka* relationship up to the tenth, shall descend into the water for the sake of the water-rites such as bathing, and perform their bath facing south while reciting the verse, "May our sin be burnt away" (*Ṛgveda* 1.97). The phrase "they descend" (*abhyavayanti*) is intended to mean merely a single immersion, as it excludes actions such as rubbing the body with earth. Thus says Śaṅkha: "Having descended into the water facing south and having immersed themselves once, they shall not perform rubbing. As for what is stated elsewhere regarding the rule for *samānodaka* relatives—"when the birth or name is unknown" (*Manusmṛti* 5.60)—that should be understood as a mere restatement based on propriety, in accordance with the mention of the ten generations. || 3 ||
