For just as [the water-rite] is performed for kinsmen even in the absence of the status of *samānodaka*, so too is the water-rite performed for maternal grandfathers, teachers, and married daughters; the water-rite may be offered at will for friends, married sisters, maternal cousins, fathers-in-law, and officiating priests. (3.4)

The meaning is that the water-rite (udakakriyā) should be performed for maternal grandfathers and others in exactly the same manner. "Unmarried" refers to girls who have not been given away in marriage, or those who have been given away; or it may refer to the wives of brothers and so forth. Regarding friends and others, however, the rule is "water according to one's desire" (kāmodakam); this means that the offering of water is to be performed according to one's own wish. Furthermore, the word *prattā* here denotes a woman living in her father’s house (svavāsinī). The rest is clear. || 4 ||
And those kinsmen who have descended into the water for the purpose of the water-rite, having bathed and being permitted by other Smṛtis such as the *Saṃyukta*,
silently pour water once, pronouncing the name and the lineage (*gotra*).
This is for the sake of clarity.
And even among those who are sapinda relatives,
students and outcasts shall not perform the water libation.

Furthermore, the terms *brahmacārin* and *patita* should be understood, according to other Smṛtis, as referring respectively to forest-dwellers (*vanastha*) and others, and to heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*) and others, as appropriate to each case. || 5 ||
Having stated the exception regarding [the impurity] as being caused by agency, he now states the exception regarding it as being caused by instrumental occasion:

"Those who have taken refuge in heresy, thieves, those who kill their husbands, those who go with [any man] according to their desire, those who drink liquor, and those who commit suicide—these do not partake in the impurity rites nor in the water libations. (3.6)

The word "likewise" (tathā) refers to those born of void or mixed unions mentioned in other Smṛtis. Since it has been prohibited for heretics and the like to partake in impurity merely by being the cause [of death], it should be understood that for students and others, the prohibition applies solely on account of their being the agent [of the act]. The rest is clear. || 6 ||
Those kinsmen who are authorized [to perform the rites] should,
once they have crossed over [the water] after the water-libations have been offered and are seated upon soft grass,
address those who have bathed with ancient historical narratives. (3.7)

When they have performed the water-libations and bathed again, others engaged in worldly affairs, stationed in their respective places as prescribed, should console them for the sake of alleviating their grief by means of historical narratives such as the slaying of Abhimanyu and other ancient accounts concerning other men.
He elaborates upon this very same refutation:
"He who seeks a core in human existence, which is as pithless as the trunk of a plantain tree, is utterly deluded; it is like a bubble of water. (3.8)
Furthermore: If this body, which was composed of five elements, has returned to its fivefold state, what cause for lamentation is there in that, since it arose from one's own actions? (3.9)
Behold: the earth, the ocean, and the gods all go to destruction; how then will the world of mortals, which resembles foam, not go to destruction? (3.10)
Furthermore:
Since the deceased, being powerless, must consume the phlegm and tears shed by his kinsmen, one should not weep; rather, funeral rites should be performed according to one's ability. (3.11)
"Intending for the deceased," with the understood addition: "according to one's own injunction. || 11 ||
Thinking, "In this manner, when worldly people have uttered their reproaches, they have indeed spoken rightly," they should go home with the children leading the way;
having placed the children in front, they should go as far as the door of that house where the deceased lies, and then [proceed].
Having chewed neem leaves, they remained restrained at the door of the house.
"Having bitten with the teeth" means having torn it apart. || 12 ||
And even in the absence of food,
having sipped water, they should enter [the village] after touching fire, water, cow dung, and white mustard seeds, and placing their feet slowly upon a stone. (3.13)

The remainder [of the rule] is that it should be done starting from the youngest. Since fire and the others serve the purpose of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), and because of the word "together" (*sam-*) [in the compound], they are to be touched only when combined. The rest is clear. || 13 ||

And from another Smṛti: having entered the house, they should remain for three days on a bed of ashes without eating at all. But if that is impossible, they should eat what is purchased or obtained and sleep separately on the ground.
Furthermore:
Food should be given to the deceased for three days according to the ritual procedure of the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña).

Having purchased [the food] with a three-night deadline, or having obtained it through trade and other means, they should eat it. And the *brahmacārins* should each sleep on the ground. For the sons and others, according to their respective eligibility and degree of proximity, the *śrāddha* should be performed even without the preliminary rites such as the washing mentioned in the *Pitṛyajña*; rather, food should be given directly to the deceased by addressing the deceased himself with the mantra: "O deceased one, bathe here" (*PārG* 3.10.28). || 14 ||
Water and milk should be placed in an earthen vessel for one day in the open air;
"in a vessel" is the understood remainder of the sentence.
Even when there is a cause for ritual impurity (*āśauca*) that renders one ineligible [for the rite], [the offering should still be performed] by all the kinsmen.
And the rites based on the three sacred fires should be performed, because they are seen in the revealed scripture (śruti). 3.15.
This is clear in meaning. || 15 ||
And as for what was stated, "Having sipped water, then [approaching] the fire and water" (YDh 3.13),
this refers to the rites pertaining to entry and even the touching of the deceased for those who so desire.
It is the same as with others. The word *icchatām* (of those who desire) is the division [of the compound].
For others, purification occurs at that very moment through bathing and self-restraint. 3.16.

The meaning is that for others—those who follow the corpse but are not its bearers, and those who do not share the same water-relationship (*asamānodaka*)—there is purification immediately, at that very moment, through the bathing, self-restraint, touching of fire, and so forth that will be described hereafter. However, if there is no desire to carry the bier, for the bearers of the corpse, Pāraskara states: "Those who have touched the corpse shall not enter the village until the appearance of the stars; if it is at night, until the appearance of the sun" (PārG 3.10.35–36). But when there is no visible motive such as affection, Parāśara declares immediate purification for the bearers of the corpse.
Those twice-born who carry a deceased brahmin who is without a protector obtain,
step by step, the fruit of a sacrifice in its proper sequence.
"And for those who perform auspicious deeds, there is no impurity whatsoever, nor any sin; by immersing themselves in water, their immediate purification is ordained. (PSm 3.39–40) || 16 ||
Moreover,

even after carrying out the funeral rites for his teacher, sub-teacher, or father by means of oil and other such substances, one who observes a vow remains a vow-holder; he must not eat food from a mat (or coarse food) nor dwell together with them.

The meaning is that even after carrying out the funeral rites for an *ācārya*, an *upādhyāya*, or one's parents according to the rules for the deceased, a student (*vratī*) or celibate student (*brahmacārī*) does not fall away from his vows. However, this is the specific distinction: he must not eat food from a mat (*kaṭānna*) nor dwell together with those sapinda relatives and others. From this very point, it is understood that there is a loss of the vow (*vratahāni*) in other cases. The intention is that one should not perform acts such as carrying the mat together with the sapinda relatives of the *ācārya* and others; for if one does so, there is indeed a violation of the vow (*vratalopa*). || 17 ||

For those who perform the water-libation rites, as well as for the *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas*, the impurity caused by a death is declared to last ten nights or three nights, as the case may be. For a child less than two years old, the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) belongs to both parents; however, it belongs to the mother alone. (3.18)

For ten nights for the *sapiṇḍas*, and for three nights for those related by water (*samānodakas*). The word "or" (*vā*) in both cases is intended to provide an option according to the rules found in other *smṛtis* regarding periods of four nights, a half-moon (*pakṣiṇī*), and so forth, as appropriate. "Impurity caused by a corpse" (*śāvam āśaucam*) refers to the state of impurity resulting from a death. Regarding this, some hold that the period begins from the time of death even before the funeral rites (*saṃskāra*). The Teacher refutes this by saying, "it is said [as follows]. The intention is that after the water-libations have been performed, others who attend to worldly affairs—such as *sapiṇḍas* and others—being asked about the period of impurity regarding the corpse, are told to observe the rule of ten nights and so forth. Consequently, the period should begin precisely from the time of the funeral rites. However, in their absence, the rule from other *smṛtis* applies, beginning from the time of death; such is the settled conclusion. Furthermore, even though not explicitly stated, for a child less than two years old, the same rule applies equally to both *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas*; the word "should be" (*syāt*) is to be supplied. As for birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), it primarily belongs to the mother alone; therefore, the rule regarding the number of nights equal to the months of pregnancy and so forth, following miscarriage, should be applied for her sake alone—this is the intention. Alternatively, this verse is intended to prescribe the limit for touching the body. For those ranging from the Śūdra to the Brāhmaṇa, touching the body occurs at one-third of their own respective period of impurity, measured by ten nights and so forth. Thus, for a Śūdra it is ten nights, and for a Brāhmaṇa it is three nights. By the word "or," five nights and four nights are prescribed for Vaiśyas and Kṣatriyas respectively; thus, like the case of a corpse, the lack of impurity regarding touching the body is expressed. For a child less than two years old, there is an absence of touching the body for both parents, as it constitutes one-third of their own period of impurity. However, birth-impurity belongs to the mother alone. And so says Vasiṣṭha: [End of provided text]
"There is no impurity for a man during childbirth, provided he does not come into contact [with the woman];
for it is the menstrual flow that causes impurity there, and that does not exist in the man" (VaDh 4.23). || 18 ||
Now he states the duration of the period of impurity:
"For a Brāhmaṇa, the impurity caused by a death lasts ten days;
for a Kṣatriya, twelve days; and for a Vaiśya, fifteen. (3.19)
The period of impurity for a Śūdra on account of a death is said to be thirty days; if another birth or death occurs in the interval, he becomes pure after the remaining days. (3.20)

In the phrase "but for a Brāhmaṇa ten days," the word *tu* (but) is intended to exclude any longer period. "Death and birth-impurity" (*pretasūtaka*) refers to the impurity lasting ten nights caused by death and that caused by birth; the meaning is that for a Brāhmaṇa, impurity exists for a duration of ten nights on account of both death and birth. In the phrase "or fifteen for the Vaiśyas," the word *vā* (or) should be understood as applying without distinction everywhere, serving to indicate an option regarding other limits mentioned in other Smṛtis. Furthermore, the mention of "death and birth" in connection with the Śūdra is for the purpose of excluding those of lower castes (*varṇāpaśada*) who are not Śūdras. Regarding birth and death, since they are of the same nature, if another birth or death occurs during the interval, purification is achieved simply by the remainder of the previous period of impurity. Thus, another Smṛti states: "If there is a simultaneous occurrence of birth and death, purification is by the first [period] until three nights remain; if it is less [than three], one completes the three nights; if it occurs before sunrise, it is three nights; but if it has already risen [the sun], then it is as previously stated. The rest is clear. (19, 20)
Furthermore, what does this [text] state?
"In the case of a miscarriage, the nights equal in number to the months [of gestation] are the cause of purification;
if the husband has gone abroad, the remaining time [of the period of impurity] shall apply; once that period is full, one becomes pure by offering water libations. (3.21)

In the case of a miscarriage, the period of impurity lasts for as many days and nights as there have been months [of pregnancy]. And this applies specifically to the mother alone. For the *sapiṇḍas*, however, it is only three nights, according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "In the event of a miscarriage, the impurity for the *sapiṇḍas* is three nights" (VaDh 4.34). If the relative was away when the news arrived, the impurity shall last for the remainder of the time from the moment of learning the news. But if the full period of impurity—ten nights or more—has elapsed, one becomes pure by offering water; that is, by the three-night rite prescribed in connection with the offering of water. Alternatively, in accordance with other *smṛtis*, it should be applied thus: if a full year has passed, one becomes immediately pure after offering water. || 21 ||
But for all castes without distinction, however,
there is purification by a day's fast for unmarried girls and young boys,
as well as for the teacher’s pupil, a fellow student of the Veda, a maternal uncle, and a learned Śrotriya. (3.22)

The word *ahaḥ* (day) denotes a day-and-night (*ahorātra*), because in the subsequent verse the expression "that day" (*tad ahar*) is used again to refer specifically to that duration. However, the phrase "but [the day] for those to whom a maiden has not been given" (*ahas tv adattakanyāsu*) should be understood in reference to the formal giving of a girl by means of water or speech. The particle *tu* (but) indicates an alternative arrangement regarding those who have already been given away (*pratta*) and so forth. An *antevāsī* is a student of a craft. And because of his close proximity to him, the term "teacher" (*guru*) is applied to the teacher of that craft as well. An *anūcāna* is a teacher who merely recites [the texts]. A maternal uncle (*mātula*) is the brother of one's mother. A *śrotriya* who is "not fully accomplished" (*anupasaṃpanna*) means one who is not a resident neighbor or similar [local connection]. For the primary teachers and others, however, one should consult what is stated in other *smṛtis*. || 22 ||
And by virtue of there being no distinction between all castes,
that day is the cause of purification for those who are not legitimate sons, for wives who have gone to others, and likewise for the king in whose realm one resides. (3.23)

The statement regarding one who has no son should be understood as referring to cases such as those of an *dattaka* (adopted son), because it concerns the exclusion of the connection between seed and field. Regarding women connected to another as wives—meaning those who have come [to the house] and are kept in confinement (*avaruddhā*)—and regarding a Kṣatriya king who conducts himself according to justice and serves as the cause for their residence: by the word "likewise" (*tathā*), there is a determination of the aforementioned types and so forth. The meaning is that in the event of the death of these persons, that very day is the cause of purification, not a full day and night. || 23 ||
He states [the following] as an exception to the previously mentioned rules for impurity, which would otherwise apply by virtue of being a sapinda:
"For those who have killed a cow, a king, or a Brahmin, and for those who commit suicide—whether by means of fasting, weapons, fire, poison, or other such methods—if they did so intentionally. (3.24)

In the case of those killed by cattle and other such means even against their will, impurity (*āśauca*) shall last for as long as it takes to see [the event]; *akṣa* here means the sense organ, and by extension, its function of perception; thus, the meaning is "as long as there is sight. Consequently, purification occurs upon the cessation of sight. Furthermore, by the mention of impurity, it is made known that even the act of seeing [the killing] must not be performed. And in the case of suicide committed by one's own will through fasting (*prāya*) and other such means, the impurity lasts for exactly that duration. The word "by oneself" is used to exclude the cases involving Brahmins and others. *Prāya* refers to walking along a great highway. And the Vedic tradition (*āmnāya*) shows the acceptance of self-destruction out of sheer desire for the sake of making it known: "If he should kill me, he will scatter the sacrifice after it has been drawn apart," and so forth (ŚB 11.8.4.2). || 24 ||
And because of being interrupted by other duties:
"For kings, there is no impurity when they are killed by lightning, or when they die in battle for the sake of cows or Brahmins, provided the lord of the earth does not desire it [otherwise]. (3.25)

For the sake of protecting kings and lords of the earth, there is an absence of impurity (*āśauca*). For that purpose, whoever—such as a judge (*prāḍvivāka*) or others—the king desires to be free from impurity, for him also there is an absence of impurity. However, it should be understood that in the case of those struck by lightning and the like, although they are faultless, [impurity is absent] because of a specific scriptural statement; whereas in the case of those killed for the sake of cows, Brahmins, and so forth, it is due solely to the excellence of their meritorious death. || 25 ||
Now he speaks regarding those who follow [the corpse]:
"A Brahmin must never follow a dead Śūdra;
the word 'anywhere' (kvacit) is used to indicate that even in times of distress (āpad), one must not follow him."

But as for a kinsman who is to be followed in death—whether he be a relative or not, or one of the same caste—even after following him, bathing in water, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter, one becomes pure. (3.26)
The word "ambhas" (water) refers to the act of bathing outside; the rest is clear. || 26 ||

And even when sapinda-relationship exists, there is no impurity for officiating priests, for those who have been consecrated, while performing a sacrificial rite, nor likewise for those observing the vow of sattra, for celibate students, for givers, and for knowers of Brahman. (3.27)
Immediate purification is prescribed in cases of giving a gift, at a wedding, during a sacrifice, in battle, during a national calamity, and even in times of dire distress. (3.28)

The mention of the *ṛtvij* (officiant) and the *dīkṣita* (initiate) is intended to remove impurity even before the commencement of the sacrifice, by virtue of their engagement through the mere act of selection (*varaṇa*) and initiation (*dīkṣā*). The phrase "while performing sacrificial rites" is intended to include even those who are not *ṛtvij*s, such as the *camasādhvaryu*s and others. A *satrin* is well known [as one engaged in a long sacrificial session]. An *ādiṣṭaprāyaścittī* is one under a vow of penance. A *brahmacārī* includes both the *upakurvāṇaka* (the student who returns home) and the *naiṣṭhika* (the lifelong student). A *dātā* is one who constantly engages in the giving of gold and other gifts. A *brahmavid* is, by virtue of his qualification for that purpose, a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), or one solely devoted to its meditation. The word "likewise" (*tathā*) refers to forest-dwellers (*vanastha*) and others. And in cases such as giving gifts and so forth—where the action is undertaken with ancillary acts like facing a Brāhmaṇa associated with that gift—and in the event of the ruin of a kingdom or other regional upheaval, or in any other sincere and dire calamity, "immediate purity is ordained" is stated for the purpose of removing doubt. (27–28)

Having thus described the impurity caused by death, he now states the specific exceptions concerning the impurity caused by birth (sūtaka): "But regarding the birth-impurity of parents, it belongs to the mother; that [impurity] is certain from the appearance of the blood. That day is not defiled, because it is the cause of the birth of the ancestors. (3.29)

*Sūtaka* is that which renders one unfit for physical contact due to the connection with the seed and blood of the parents; it does not apply to *sapiṇḍas*, because that [unfitness] is impossible for them. If this is so, then it belongs to the mother alone, because of the appearance of her blood. "Dhruvam" means certain. And thus says the *Svāyambhuva*: "For all, there is impurity on account of death (*śāva*), but for the parents, there is *sūtaka*.
The *sūtaka* shall belong to the mother alone; the father becomes pure by touching water. (MDh 5.62)

The word *śāva* is intended to convey the absence of touching the body [of the deceased]. Furthermore, even with regard to that impurity (*āśauca*) characterized by the disqualification from giving gifts and other rites—which is common to all *sapiṇḍa* relatives—the day on which a son is born should not be defiled. For what purpose? Because of the birth of the ancestors, the fathers and so forth; the meaning is: because of the occasion for a *śrāddha* rite on account of the birth. And from the prefix *pra-*, it is understood that there is no fault even for those who eat [the food]. (29)

But this is a general rule applicable to all men: "If he is touched by those who have had sexual intercourse with a woman in her courses or by those who are impure due to death or birth, he shall bathe; if he is touched by them, he shall perform ritual sipping (upaspṛśet).
He shall also mutter verses containing the word 'water' and recite the Sāvitrī mantra once mentally. (3.30)

A *udakyā* is a woman in her menses; those who are impure (*āśaucin*) are persons unworthy of physical contact. One touched by them should bathe. However, if one has intentionally had sexual intercourse with them and is then touched by them, one should bathe and then perform ritual sipping (*upaspṛśet*) while reciting the *ābliṅga* verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā. The meaning is that one should sip water (*ācāmet*). Having sipped water and having mentally recited the *Sāvitrī* once, one should be understood to become pure.

However, this must be considered here: how is the scope of these various mutually contradictory statements regarding impurity (*āśauca*) to be determined? For instance, by the Self-Existent One (*Svayambhū*), four alternatives were presented in the verse: "Impurity due to death (*śāva-āśauca*) lasts ten days" (MDh 5.59); here, "ten days" [is one], while by the phrase "or until the collection of the bones" (MDh 5.59), "four days" is indicated; and by the phrase "or three days, or even one day" (MDh 5.59), "three days" and "one day" are shown. Likewise, by Parāśara: "For a Brāhmaṇa, impurity due to death is said to last three nights."
"For a Kṣatriya it is ten days, and for a Vaiśya it is indeed eleven. Thus [it is said].

Gautama also stated, having begun with: "The impurity due to death (*śāva-āśauca*) lasts ten nights for *sapiṇḍas* who are not officiating priests, initiated for a sacrifice, or celibate students," and then continued: "For a Kṣatriya it is eleven nights, and for a Vaiśya twelve nights" (GDh 14.1–3). Vasiṣṭha also said: "A Brāhmaṇa [is purified] in ten nights, a Kṣatriya in fifteen nights, and a Vaiśya in twenty nights" (VaDh 4.27–29). As for the Śūdra, a full month is prescribed everywhere. Regarding this, some explain the scope of these rules based on the force of the commencement of other verses, taking into account conduct, Vedic study, and so forth.
"A Brahmin who is endowed with the sacred fires and the Vedas is purified in one day," and so forth.

However, that is not entirely correct; for if the purification in one day and so on were stated in consideration of conduct and other factors, then in both cases [of a death or birth], food would not be eaten from the family for ten days.
Giving, receiving, sacrifice, and the study of sacred texts cease.

Statements such as these would otherwise be entirely untenable. Furthermore, Gautama, by prescribing a ten-night period while excluding those who have already performed the *dīkṣā* (initiatory rites) and others, indicates that this rule applies specifically to those possessed of [proper] conduct (*vṛtta*) and so forth. Thus, in all other *smṛtis*, impurity (*āśauca*) consists precisely in the lack of entitlement to Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) and other such duties; and for one who lacks that [entitlement], the lack of entitlement is established by its very nature—so what would impurity accomplish? Likewise, Dakṣa, having introduced the ten-fold view of *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) beginning with immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*), stated: "For one who is diseased, for one who is miserly, and for one who is always burdened by debt..."
Especially for one who is devoid of ritual action, a fool, and one who is conquered by women.

"For one whose mind is attached to vices, who is perpetually dependent on others, and who is devoid of faith and renunciation, impurity shall last until the end [of the body] as ashes. The intention is that for those of such a nature, whose condition is established by their very disposition, impurity persists until death; they do not fall within the scope of the rules governing ritual impurity (*aśauca*).

How, then, is this verse to be understood: “A Brahmin is purified after one day” (PSm 3.5)? This should be viewed as a deprecatory explanatory statement (*nindārthavāda*), similar to the rule regarding impurity ending with the cremation of the body; it serves merely to praise those whose livelihood and other qualities are excellent, following the context of the passage, and because it would otherwise contradict other Smṛtis and logical reasoning. For there is no contact with the sacred fires for one who is devoid of Vedic knowledge. There is no contradiction, however, if it is taken as a statement of praise. The same applies to the verse concerning the son of Parāśara: “For Brahmins who bear the name [only], the period of impurity shall be ten days,” and so forth, which should be applied accordingly. Others, however, say:
When the teeth have appeared, when they have fallen out and reappeared, and when the tonsure ceremony has been performed; (MDh 5.58)

According to this verse, they state that the rule is determined with respect to the stages of life (*vayo'vasthā*). One whose teeth have emerged is "one whose teeth are grown" (*dantajāta*); one born after him is "born later" (*anujāta*), meaning he would be after the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) but before the eruption of the teeth. Beyond that, one who is less than three years old is "one whose teeth are grown. But beyond that, prior to the initiation (*upanayana*), he is "one for whom the tonsure (*caula*) has been performed. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that he is also "one for whom the initiation has been performed. Among these—starting with those for whom the initiation has been performed—the rule regarding the alternatives of ten days and so forth is established. However, because a three-night period is prescribed for one for whom the tonsure has been performed, this [system] is indeed improper, both there and elsewhere, due to the force of the commencement of other scriptural statements as appropriate. Furthermore, these conceptualizations follow one's own intellect; nor is this consistent with the definition of Vedic injunction (*codanā-lakṣaṇa*). What, then, is the correct method?

It is said: for all four alternatives refer specifically to the *sapiṇḍas*. Indeed, *sapiṇḍatā* itself is of exactly four kinds, as it has been stated: "The cessation of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) occurs at the seventh or the fifth [generation]" (GDh 14.13). Because the meaning of the Sūtra can be construed in both ways—as "when [the relationship] has ceased" and "while it is still occurring"—it follows that the cessation of the rice-ball occurs either at the fifth or sixth, or at the seventh or eighth person. For this very reason it was said: "But *sapiṇḍatā* ceases at the seventh person" (MDh 5.60).

When the seventh [generation] has passed, it ceases in the eighth; the meaning is that it does not proceed further than that. Thus, having considered this fourfold *sapiṇḍatā*, the application of the rules for impurity—such as ten days (*daśāha*) and so forth—is determined according to proximity. Consequently, the systematic arrangement of the rules regarding three days, a morning and evening, one day, or immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) for the four types of *samānodaka* relations becomes logically established. If it is asked how the cessation of the *piṇḍa* offerings is determined, it has been stated, beginning with: "In the offering of the *piṇḍas*, if he has sons, the deceased father shall be the first among the ancestors," and concluding with: "It ceases at the fourth" (PārG 3.10.50–51). Therefore, the cessation of the *piṇḍa* occurs on the fifth day for one whose father is deceased; likewise, on the sixth for one whose father is living, on the seventh for one whose grandfather is living, and on the eighth for one whose great-grandfather is living—this is the systematic rule. Furthermore, for sons living together, the impurity is caused solely by the father; however, when they live separately, it applies to each individual. And thus Parāśara speaks precisely with the distinction of residence in mind.
"For those who have withdrawn from social contacts, there is neither impurity due to death nor impurity due to birth. Thus it is said.

In this manner, the determination of the rules for impurity (*āśauca*) based on the status of *sapiṇḍa* and *samānodaka* should be applied to all castes. Alternatively, the application of the scriptural statements follows the specific birth of the Brāhmaṇa and other classes; and according to the rule, "The rule of purification shall be like that of a Vaiśya" (MDh 5.140), when multiple options arise even for a Śūdra, they should be applied as before. Because of the statement, "of those who live according to the law" (MDh 5.140), this [extended period] refers only to the Śūdra who is dependent on the twice-born (*dvijāti*); however, for another [Śūdra], the *sapiṇḍa* relationship extends only to eight generations, and his mode of purification lasts for one month. But for Kṣatriyas and others, because the scope is determined by the birth-class of the Brāhmaṇa and so forth, the *sapiṇḍa* relationship for the Brāhmaṇas and others extends to only three generations. Thus says Śaṅkha: "The *piṇḍa*, however, recurs among three. And the rule for impurity is individual, according to the statement: "Those who share the same *piṇḍa* have separate purifications. Consequently, regarding uncles, their sons, and so forth, the impurity is equal to that of one's own father and so on; but for those living together, it is equal to that of a father. Thus it has been said.

"But when the master has died, the purification for the slaves and for sons born of women of lower castes shall be equal to that of the master; however, this applies except in the case of the mother's separate property (*yautaka*). As for the father, moreover:

"When there is one husband for women of the various castes in the direct order of classes, the periods for birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and death-impurity (*mṛtaka*) are ten days, six days, three days, and one day, respectively. Thus it is said.

In this manner, the determination of the scope for all rules regarding impurity (*āśauca*) is established. However, if one must necessarily determine the scope even with regard to livelihood (*vṛtti*) and so forth, then it is better to do so specifically with regard to particular types of livelihood, such as those who live from day to day (*aśvastana*) or those who live for three days (*traihika*), because that serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). As for the statement in Gautama’s Dharmasūtra, “And for kings, because of the conflict of duties” (GDh 14.45), which prescribes immediate purity (*sadyaḥśauca*), that should be understood as applying only to those who have already commenced the *brahmayajña* (Vedic recitation), since the reason is explicitly stated there. Or rather, just as in the case of those who live from day to day, the engagement in teaching (*adhyāpana*) applies to Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). In this way, for those such as *satrin* (sacrificers) and *vratin* (those under vows), the cessation of impurity should be understood as occurring only in respect to those specific acts; this is the general direction. Impurity due to birth (*sūtaka*) should likewise be applied according to this extension (*atideśa*). Others, however, consider *sūtaka* to be an extension of the ten-day period alone. But that is of no consequence, as it lacks a scriptural basis (*aśābdatva*). As for the argument that the extension of the ten-day period applies here because of the contingency of a single day for the mother, because of custom, and because it avoids contradiction with the touching (*samālambhana*) and other rites prescribed in other Smṛtis for the ten-day period—that is essentially worthless (*phalguprāya*), because it would lead to the contingency of four days and so on based on the specific limit of *sapiṇḍa* relationship for both parents. Therefore, just as in the case of impurity from death (*śāvāśauca*), the determination of the rule here must follow the extension [of the ten-day period]; thus, it is faultless. As for the statement, “Impurity due to birth shall belong to the mother alone,” that has already been explained as being for the purpose of prohibiting the touching of her limbs. As for what follows...
But having discharged semen, a man becomes pure simply by touching water;
however, due to the connection arising from seminal emission, he should observe impurity for three days. (MDh 5.63)

Thus, that [rule] should be understood as referring to a Śūdra, either in connection with a kept slave-girl (*avaruddhadāsī*) or through the practice of *niyoga*. Regarding the case of a kept slave-girl, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*upaspṛśya*) after the birth of a son or similar event, one becomes pure immediately. However, regarding the *niyoga* perspective, the principle is "for three days due to the seminal connection" (*baijikād abhisaṃbandhāt tryaham*). As for the three statements concerning a maiden (*kanyā*), they are recited according to a specific arrangement of subject matter (*viṣayavyavasthayā*), and thus there is no contradiction. For example: "In the case of an immature maiden, however, immediate purity (*sadyaḥśauca*) is ordained."

According to this statement, it should be understood as referring to cases where the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) has not been performed. The rule, "But [on the day] for unmarried girls" (YDh 3.22), applies when the girl has had the tonsure performed but has not yet been given away in marriage. However, when she has been given away, the rule of Manu applies: "Those to whom she was given shall be purified after three nights, and those by whom she was given shall be purified after one day and so forth;
but her uterine kinsmen are purified according to the very procedure already stated" (MDh 5.72).

Because of this statement. Others, however, describe a ten-night period according to the very method already mentioned. As for that which appears through a strained interpretation in accordance with one's own school, it is indeed improper because it contradicts logic, established practice, and other Smṛtis. The statements regarding those who have gone abroad or are deceased, concerning the periods of three nights, a night and day, one day, or immediate purification, must be explained solely in accordance with the specific rules governing *sapiṇḍatā*. Regarding the case of maternal uncles and others, [the text says]: "One becomes pure after three nights in the case of the mother’s close kinsmen" (MDh 5.101).

According to this statement, the three-night period applies only to the one who performs the removal of the corpse; for others, however, it is only the *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night). The one-day period, moreover, applies specifically to cases such as a maternal uncle (*sāpatna*) and the like. And apart from the *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas*, in all other cases, the expression "impurity" (*āśauca*) should be understood as referring merely to the state of fasting and wearing unadorned clothing due to a resemblance to [actual] impurity, and not as a cessation of eligibility for sacrifices and other rites. As it is said: "When a fellow student has died, fasting for one day is prescribed. (MDh 5.71)
Thus, by virtue of the context and established usage, the systematic determination of all statements is accomplished in every respect; so, enough with this digression. || 30 ||

Having thus explained everywhere and in every way the rules for impurity caused by clearly manifest signs of cognition, he now states in general terms the cause of complete purification for one whose nature is impaired—due to the natural affliction of ignorance—whether it concerns the self, the senses, the body, or its instruments:
Time, fire, action, earth, wind, mind, knowledge, austerity, water, remorse, and fasting—all these are causes of purification. (3.31)

Fire is an example of brilliance (*tejas*); clay is that of earth (*pṛthivī*); while water and air are mentioned by their very nature. These four great elements (*mahābhūta*), beginning with earth, are the means for purification—either individually or collectively as appropriate—of external implements composed of them. As for time and action, they are the means for the purification of the external and internal self, as well as the collection of the senses; [they are also the means] for the mind and the other senses. Regarding the mind, he will speak later; the remaining factors, such as knowledge (*jñāna*) and so forth, belong to the self. Thus, it should be understood that all these are causes of purification everywhere, either according to their specific application or without distinction. This restatement is intended as a summary for the purpose of briefly restating all the means of purifying one's own objects, whether located in one's own place or elsewhere. (31)
To clarify this very point, he elaborates by means of a systematic classification of objects:
"The gift of those who have not performed their duty purifies through its flow; for a river, it is the current that effects purification;
for that which is to be purified, it is clay and water; and for the twice-born, it is indeed renunciation. (3.32)
Austerity is for those who know the Vedas, patience for the wise, and water for the body (*varṣman*);
*varṣman* here means the physical frame. And so says Svāyambhuva: "The limbs [are purified] by earth and water" (cf. MDh 5.109). || 32 ||
Moreover: "Recitation is said to be for those whose sins are concealed; truth is said to be for the mind. (3.33)

Austerity and knowledge are the purification of the elemental self; wisdom is the purification of the intellect; and through the knowledge of the Lord, the supreme purification of the Knower of the Field is attained. (3.34)
These three verses, whose meaning is clear, should be regarded as sūtras for the forthcoming sections on the Upaniṣads and the section on expiations (prāyaścitta). || 33–34 ||
Thus ends the section on impurity (*āśauca*).
Now begins the section on duties in times of distress (*āpaddharma*).
To provide a detailed analysis of the rule, "Purification for those who have committed forbidden acts comes through giving" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.32), he says:

In times of distress, a twice-born man may live by the work of a Kṣatriya, or even that of a Vaiśya; but having crossed over that difficulty and secured his livelihood, he should abandon that path and establish himself on the [proper] path, purifying himself.

Through the *kṣātra* occupation—consisting of duties such as the protection of subjects—a Brāhmaṇa or a Vaiśya may subsist; or through the *vaiśya* occupation, the two preceding castes [the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya] may subsist. Even though these are not their own prescribed duties (*akārya*), in times of distress characterized by the impossibility of one’s own livelihood, such subsistence is indeed lawful (*dharmya*). Furthermore, because they are mentioned among the "twice-born" (*dvija*), it is explained that the duties of the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya are common to all three castes insofar as they involve verbal instruction. Thus says Nārada: "For them, there exists neither a superior nor an inferior occupation; for, having set aside the two lowest occupations, those two are common to all. (NSm 1.54)

And because it is an improper act, it is like a calamity. Having emerged from that calamity and having purified himself by giving away the remaining wealth according to the rules, he should establish himself on the very path characterized by his own [brahminical] livelihood; the intention is that he should not take delight in that very occupation of a Kṣatriya or others. || 35 ||
And even when fallen into distress, [he may accept]:
fruits, woolen cloth, *soma*, humans, cakes, creepers, sesame seeds, boiled rice, liquids, alkaline substances, curd, milk, ghee, and water. (3.36)
Weapons, fermented liquor, beeswax, honey, lac, and the grass of the sacrificial altar;
earth, leather, flowers, blankets made of goat hair, hair, buttermilk, poison, and eraka grass. (3.37)
Silk, indigo, salt, meat, single-hoofed animals, hemp, vegetables, fresh herbs, oil-cakes, cotton, and perfumes—these likewise [are forbidden]. (3.38)
Even while making a living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, he should never sell sesame seeds;
for the sake of dharma, sesame seeds may be exchanged for an equal amount of grain. (3.39)

Even for a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya living in times of distress through the occupation of a Vaiśya, fruits and other items mentioned in the three verses [of Manu 10.90] are not to be sold. Since these are prohibited for them, it is understood that for a Vaiśya they are not forbidden. "Fruits" refers to mangoes and the like. "Stones" refers to rocks, slabs, rubies, and so forth. "Linen" refers to cloth made from flax, such as sacks and the like. *Soma* and others are well known. "Climbers" refers to wild medicinal herbs. *Apūpas* are small cakes. *Tila* (sesame) and others are clear. "Water" refers to water either standing in a reservoir or drawn out. However, the fetching of water for a price in order to irrigate crops by bringing it to a field should not be suspected of being "selling water," because it is for the purpose of another action. "Weapons" refers to swords and the like. *Āsava* is the juice of dates and similar fruits. Although already prohibited as a "liquid" (*rasa*), its mention again is for the sake of a specific penance due to its being designated by a different term; this alone is more logical, as the prohibition follows the specific meaning. *Madhu* is intoxicating liquor. *Ucchiṣṭa* is well known. Or, *madhu* may mean honey, and *madhūcchiṣṭa* refers to beeswax. The word *atha* is used to indicate a difference in the objects denoted. The genitive case in *barhiṣaḥ* is used to indicate a change in grammatical number. Consequently, although the word *barhis* generally means "grass," here, following its technical refinement, it serves to prohibit all sacrificial implements such as the *sruk* ladle and others. "Earth" and other items are well known. The application is the same as the explanation of "water. There is no fault regarding earth because it is a different substance. Furthermore, in this context, only what is explicitly mentioned is to be taken, since milk and curds are mentioned separately. *Viṣairakā* means "poison-water"; those fish and others originating therein. *Kauśeya* is silk cloth. *Nīlī* is indigo, whether in the form of a pill or having entered into cloth and so forth, or even pure. Salt, meat, and others are well known. "Single-hoofed" refers to animals with one hoof, such as horses and the like. "Causes" are the means of killing, such as poison and so forth. Since vegetables are taught elsewhere to be sold, here one should understand that *nālikā* and similar items are inedible. "Fresh herbs" refers to those standing in the ground and not yet cut; however, those damaged by axes, weapons, and the like are not prohibited. *Piṇyāka* is oil-cake. *Tūla* is derived from the *śalmali* tree and others. "Fragrances" are camphor and the like. The word "tathā" (and so forth) includes items mentioned in other Smṛtis, such as hemp cloth (*śāṇa*). However, sesame seeds produced from one's own cultivation through farming and the like may be sold by one who does not follow the Vaiśya occupation for the sake of dharma, or by a Vaiśya through exchange with other grains. Otherwise, there is sin in selling sesame. Thus it has been said:

"He who uses sesame seeds for any purpose other than giving as food or as an ointment becomes a worm in excrement and sinks there along with his ancestors" (MDh 10.91). Or, at his own will, a Vaiśya may sell sesame seeds after having produced them himself through cultivation. (36–39)
Moreover:
salt, lac, and daughter-in-law are forbidden items for sale; milk, curd, and liquor, however, cause one's caste to degenerate. (3.40)

How then is the sale of Śunaḥśepha and others to be understood? It is solely because such an act is prohibited by the Śruti that [the text] praises Śunaḥśepha by way of censuring his father and others. Alternatively, the meaning is that in every case, even in times of distress, [one may do so] for the sake of protecting one's own life. (40)
He clarifies that very point:
"A Brahmin who, having fallen into distress, accepts or eats from whatever source available, is not defiled by sin, for he is equal to fire and the sun. (3.41)

Just as fire, even when present in the houses of outcasts and the like, or the sun, which exists everywhere with impartiality, remains faultless; so too a Brāhmaṇa, having reached a time of distress through activities such as silent recitation (japa) and thereby regained his body, becomes capable of exhausting the sins he has accumulated. Thus, like the sun, his wandering at will is not contradictory. 41.
Since this is so, therefore:
Agriculture, craft, wages, learning, usury, a cart, a mountain, service, marshland, a king, and begging—these are the means of livelihood in times of distress. (3.42)

Agriculture and the other [means] are eleven modes of livelihood that serve as causes for overcoming calamities, according to their availability. These are mentioned merely by way of illustration; the intended meaning is that, in every respect, there is nothing that should not be done in times of distress. Agriculture is well known. Craft (*śilpa*) refers to painting and so forth. Wages (*bhṛti*) is performing work for others in exchange for a monthly salary or similar remuneration. Scholarship (*vidyā*) is teaching for a fee. Lending at interest (*kusīda*) is lending capital. The cart (*śakaṭa*) is the driving of carts for hire. The mountain (*giri*) is a hill; subsisting upon it means living off the sale of its grass, wood, and so forth. Service (*sevā*) is well known. The marshy region (*anūpa*) is the bank of a river or similar place; subsisting upon it means living off the sale of vegetables and other produce grown there. The king (*nṛpa*) is the monarch; subsisting upon him means living off his gifts. Alms (*bhaikṣa*) is of two kinds, distinguished by whether the food is prepared or unprepared. (42)

Precisely because calamities are so difficult to overcome, one who is hungry after fasting for three days may take wealth from a non-Brahmin; having received it, he must report it according to the law when questioned by an authority. (3.43)
The meaning is: "due to the absence of disagreement regarding its essential nature, magnitude, and so forth. || 43 ||
And thus, because he has not acted perversely even when attacked by the king,
the king, having ascertained his conduct, lineage, character, learning, education, and sons, shall provide him with a righteous livelihood from his own household. (3.44)

Having examined his means of livelihood and so forth, both individually and collectively, the king, in accordance with those merits, should further consider other matters from his own treasury and establish for him a permanent livelihood that is righteous—that is, not contrary to dharma—such that he does not fail in his duties, whether visible or invisible, performed according to his station. Thus ends verse 44.
Thus ends the section on duties in times of distress.
Now begins the section on the duties of forest-dwellers.

Thus far, two stages of life have been described. Now, the third stage, the forest-dweller's stage (*vānaprasthāśrama*), which comes in due order for one who has enjoyed the householder's stage, possesses wrinkles and grey hair, has established a lineage, and is detached from sense-objects, is being discussed. Previously, however, following the logic of the scriptural tradition that "one may dwell in whichever [stage] one desires" (*VaDh* 7.3), the position of renunciation immediately after the student life (*brahmacarya*) consisting of Vedic study was set forth. In this regard, the position of cumulative practice (*samuccaya*) is now stated.

But is it not reasonable that one who, due to an excellence of dispassion (*vairāgya*), has no regard for taking a wife and so forth, should renounce his current stage of life (*āśrama*) and accept another? However, for one who has taken a wife, whose mind is drawn by desire, and who is bound by the scriptural injunction (*śruti*) "as long as one lives," the transition to another stage of life—following the meaning of a *smṛti* that contradicts that injunction and is thus unauthoritative—is indeed ill-founded. If, on the other hand, it is argued that this occurs precisely through the power of dispassion, that is incorrect; for the meaning of the scripture is determined at the very time of initiation (*pratipatti*), and not even in the midst of the performance of the ritual being executed.

But surely, just as for one who is qualified as a seeker of desire but whose desire has ceased—even in the midst of the performance—there is a withdrawal from it due to the lack of qualification, so it would be here as well. Moreover, even for one who is alive, qualification extends only to the completion of the performance; because in that case, when another full-moon day arrives, there is a conclusion of the previously commenced performance, and since qualification is not understood to apply to a new performance due to an excess of dispassion, [the ritual does not continue].

Not so. For it is logical that for one who possesses desire (*kāmin*), the qualification (*adhikāra*) is understood to apply only to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) which serves as the means toward a fruit; and when the desire for the fruit has ceased, that [qualification] ceases. However, for one who is alive, the sacrifice and other acts do not have their status as a means apart from the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*), nor does the status of being the person to be enjoined (*niyojyatva*) cease, because living does not depart. Furthermore, because the wife has already been procured, no distinction residing in her can be asserted here, as was previously stated. As for the difference or non-difference in performance (*prayoga*), they are simply irrelevant because the cause of qualification (*adhikārahetu*) has not departed. Here, due to a contradiction with direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*), the forest-dweller stage (*vanasthāśrama*) is indeed improper in sequence. For this very reason, Gautama said: "The teachers [hold] that there is only one stage of life (*aikāśramya*), because the householder's state is directly enjoined" (GDh 3.36). Regarding this, others say that the stage of the forest-dweller and so forth occurs at the end of the *Puruṣamedha* sacrifice, following the direct injunction. For instance, having introduced the topic with "Then, having superimposed the fires upon himself," it says, "He should go to the forest without looking back," and so on. But even that is mostly useless, since the commencement of the Smṛti rules for the forest-dweller and others is made without such specification. As for the statement regarding [the life-span] ending in old age (*jarāmarya*), it is based on an indicative mark (*liṅga*); an inference of an injunction requiring another principle contradicts the direct injunction. Therefore, this must be explained. To this it is replied: It has already been stated before that the scriptural rule for "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*) applies to those whose wives are procured by desire and the like. And when desire has departed, wives cannot be procured by means of the Agnihotra and other rites if they are not motivated by that desire. And in the absence of that [desire], for those who have already taken a wife and for whom the rule "as long as one lives" has fulfilled its purpose, why should there not be another stage of life for those who are no longer qualified by that rule?

But surely, injunctions do not impel the production [of things]; rather, since once produced—such as a wife (*dārā*) and so forth—their own nature does not perish even when the cause of their own production has ceased, there is no contradiction for the injunctions regarding eligibility (*adhikāra*) even if they depend upon such things. For it is not the case that when desire ceases, wives cease to be wives; otherwise, for one who has many wives, the cessation of the desire for a single wife would entail his becoming wifeless, which would contradict the *smṛtis*.

We do not say that one becomes "without a wife" (*apatnīka*) merely because of the loss of desire due to the cessation of sexual impulse. What then? A woman is indeed a *dravya* (property/possession). The rite of marriage (*vivāha-saṃskāra*) is the cause for making her one's own. And the making of things one's own depends either on the purpose for which they are used or on their essential nature, according to the intention of the possessor. In this regard, if one whose mind is utterly drawn by desire first considers the injunction for life-long [performance] and then takes a wife through the act of marriage for the sake of her very essence, doing so for all time, then she is taken until death. However, for one whose mind is only slightly drawn by desire, the taking of a wife is for a limited purpose—either until the appearance of wrinkles and grey hair, or for the sake of progeny, since the purpose of marriage is the production of a son; thus, the limit is as stated. Furthermore, because he lacks a wife, the scriptural injunction for life-long [performance] is non-binding for him, just as it is for one who has not yet married. Therefore, there is no need to even suspect a contradiction with that [scripture]. Regarding the determination of the limit for possession, however, the scripture concerning "as long as one lives" remains indifferent precisely because it pertains to the qualification of one who has already married. Thus, the Smṛti rule regarding the combination of the four [orders of life] is also not contradictory in its sequence. Likewise, the statement that one should remain until old age (*jarāmarya*) is supported by a basis as a Smṛti root because it provides a necessary limit; otherwise, being without a basis, it would be meaningless. The teaching of Gautama—"The teachers [hold] that there is only one order of life"—should be explained by accepting the life-long option, meaning that the status of a householder is prescribed in that way specifically for those who have taken a wife out of direct desire. And thus, because the limit is reached, there is simply an absence of a wife. Consequently, in this view, since sons and others are appointed as protectors, the [scripture] prompts the acceptance of one's own wife; and since a choice is possible due to the difference in subject matter, the life-long scriptural injunction applies without distinction. As for the sacrificer of human sacrifices (*puruṣamedha*), since there is an instruction to go to the forest according to his wish, and since both [the life-long and the temporary options] are directly perceived, resorting to a specific arrangement of subject matter is not contradictory. For one who has a wife, becoming a forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*) is certainly not contrary to the Śruti, just like the options of the Yāyāvara and others. Therefore, in this view, the resorting to the forest is only for one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*), and not the kindling of fires according to the rules for a wandering ascetic (*śrāmaṇaka*). But if the life-long option is accepted, then upon the occurrence of old age or the death of the wife, or when desire has ceased and such [marriage] is impossible, does the qualification for forest-dwelling still exist? For one whose longing has perished, it certainly exists because there is no longer a cause for taking a wife or the like. But for the other [who still desires], it must be considered.

Another says: For one who, at the very time of marriage, has determined, "I shall also abide in another stage of life (āśrama)," his union with a wife is indeed limited by that [intended] period; and accordingly, his entitlement to livelihood is also wiped away at that very moment. But for one who has determined from the outset that his union with a wife lasts until death, and whose entitlement to the Agnihotra and other rites follows from that determination until death—even if his desire [for worldly life] has perished—since his resolve has not departed, how could there be for him an adoption of another mode of life when he is constrained by the scriptural injunction regarding livelihood? Thus they record in the Smṛti:

"One may again perform the taking of a wife and likewise the re-establishment of the sacred fires" (MDh 5.168). This point must be considered. Our position is that there is, in every respect, a combination of the stages of life (*āśrama-samuccaya*), and this is indeed logical; however, the traditional teaching (*saṃpradāya*) holds that the previously mentioned [view] alone is superior. As for the phrase "again the taking of a wife," its scope is restricted solely to those who have not entered another stage of life; such is the general direction [of the argument].
Considering that the practice of the forest-dwelling stage of life is unimpeded in either case, he introduces it:
"Having entrusted his wife to his son, or followed by her, he becomes a forest-dweller, practicing celibacy, maintaining the sacred fires and the domestic fire, and remaining patient. (3.45)

The word *syāt* ("should be") is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Regarding the statement, "Austerity is the means of purification for those who know the Vedas; forbearance for the wise" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.33), he now elaborates upon that. *Vānaprastha* is the name for one belonging to a specific stage of life (*āśrama*). He may at some time go to the forest together with his wife according to the logic previously stated, or having entrusted his wife to his sons and others. And when he is accompanied by his wife, the intention is that even while living in the forest followed by her, he should remain a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) alone. In the alternative view, however, this need not be stated at all, as it follows from the context of his capability. The phrase *sāgniḥ* ("with the sacred fires") refers to those who maintain the three sacrificial fires (*vaitānika*). *Saupāsana* means joined with the *āvasathya* fire. The rest has already been explained. || 45 ||
And this is his specific distinction:
self-possessed and maintaining a beard and hair, he should constantly satisfy with uncultivated produce the sacred fires, the ancestors, the gods, guests, and his dependents. (3.46)

In the view that one may go [to the forest] while maintaining the sacred fires (*sāgnika*), the injunction regarding food not produced by plowing is intended as a means for performing the *agnihotra* and other rites. In the alternative view, however, this mention is for the purpose of illustrating such practices as those prescribed in the *Vaikhānasa-śāstra*. Furthermore, the word "likewise" (*tathā*) in both views serves to include specific modes of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth according to that scripture. The rest is clear. || 46 ||

And for the sake of honoring guests and other such purposes, he should accumulate wealth for a day, a month, six months, or likewise for a year; what has been accumulated should be spent during the month of Āśvayuja. (3.47)
The word "likewise" (tathā) is for the purpose of indicating that there is no fixed rule regarding the period prior to one year.
Furthermore:
"Self-controlled, bathing at the three periods of the day, and abstaining from receiving gifts"—
the intention is that he should not accept even those things prescribed [for him], because they would be impossible to refuse.
And always: devoted to sacred study, habituated to giving, and intent on the welfare of all beings. (3.48)
But for the sake of maintaining himself,

he may subsist by using his teeth as a mortar, eating only what ripens naturally in due time, or grinding with a stone; likewise, he should perform the rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, as well as other ritual acts, using fruits and oils.

One who prepares a mortar by means of his teeth is a *dantolūkhalika*; the meaning is that he eats food together with its husks. Alternatively, he may be an *aśmakuṭṭaka*, meaning one who makes food free of husks by processing it with a stone. All such alternatives are to be applied according to one's capacity. The mention of eating what is ripened by time is intended to exclude what is ripened by fire. By virtue of this constant practice, he should perform rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti—such as those requiring clarified butter—using the oils of fruits like the *akṣa* and others which are not prohibited. The same applies to the activities ordained for a forest-dweller in the scriptures; the meaning is that he should act precisely in the manner prescribed therein. || 49 ||
And according to his own capacity:
he should pass the time with Cāndrāyaṇa fasts, or always subsist on Kṛcchra penances; or he may eat when a fortnight has passed, or when a month has passed, or when a day has passed. (3.50)
Furthermore, the statement "having gone" is intended to allow for an option according to one's capacity, even apart from the time already mentioned. The rest is clear. || 50 ||
And always with heedfulness:
he should sleep on the ground at night and spend the day on his tiptoes;
or else by means of standing, sitting, and walking about, or again by the practice of yoga. (3.51)

"At night" is for the purpose of excluding [the practice] during the day. "With the foreparts of the feet" means with the toes raised. "Standing and so forth" are clear. "Practice of yoga" is that which will be described hereafter. "Again" refers to [starting] from the foreparts of the feet and so on; the meaning is "repeatedly resting. || 51 ||
And according to one's capacity:
"In the summer, standing amidst five fires; in the rainy season, sleeping on the bare ground;
and in the winter, wearing wet clothes—or else one should perform penance according to one's strength. (3.52)
The mention of "on a leveled spot" (sthaṇḍila) is for the purpose of excluding obstructions; the rest is straightforward. 52.
For one dwelling in the forest, this alone is the supreme duty, the very essence of all hermitages:
he who pricks him with thorns and he who anoints him with sandalwood paste—he remains equal toward both, neither angry nor pleased. (3.53)
"Vitudati" means he pierces or causes pain with various thorns and the like; in this manner, as described, one should maintain the forest-dwelling stage of life (vanasthāśrama). || 53 ||
Or, having assimilated the sacred fires to himself, dwelling among the trees and eating moderately, he should beg for alms only for the sake of sustenance at the dwellings of forest-dwellers. (3.54)

And when the wife of one who has a co-wife dies, the cremation of that very wife—who constitutes half of his own self—with the sacred fires is itself the "internalizing of the fires" (*ātmasamāropaṇa*). However, this rule applies to another person who has entered the stage of life (*āśrama*) but is either incapable or possesses an excess of dispassion (*vairāgya*); by this alone, it should be understood that the undertaking [of the path] begins from the very outset. || 54 ||
But in the absence of another forest-dweller (vānaprastha), he should, restraining his speech, eat eight morsels of food brought from the village.

The word "having brought" is intended to exclude going to the village at times other than the time for begging alms. "Restraining his speech" is intended to mean not conversing with the people of the village; however, since restraint of speech is already established regarding the act of eating itself, it need not be stated [again].
When there is an excellence of dispassion or an excellence of knowledge,
one who subsists on air alone should proceed toward the northeast until the body is completely worn away.

"Eating air" means fasting. "Until the exhaustion of the body" (*varṣma*)—*varṣma* meaning the body—means until the exhaustion of the body. Since no specific fruit connected to this stage of life (*āśrama*) is taught, and because it is difficult to practice, it is understood that this stage of life is obligatory (*naiyamika*). Furthermore, because the practice of yoga is taught and it serves as a means to liberation, it is a means for attaining isolation (*kaivalya*). And thus says the traditional authority (*āmnāya*): "All these [ascetics] attain worlds of merit; he who is established in Brahman attains immortality" (ChU 2.23.1). || 55 ||
Thus ends the section on the duties of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). Now begins the section on the duties of the ascetic (*yati*).

Thus, through the performance of the duties as prescribed, by the neglect of prohibited matters, and by the arising of dispassion (*vairāgya*), one whose correct knowledge has been produced, who desires no further [rebirth] in the Supreme Brahman, and whose longing for the taste of all worldly pleasures has been cast aside, acts according to his own spontaneous inclination.
Having performed the sacrifice in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee (sarvavedasadakṣiṇā) either from the home or from the forest,
at its conclusion, having performed the Prājāptya rite, he should deposit those fires within himself.

Having studied the Vedas, performed recitations, fathered sons, given food, maintained the sacred fires, and offered sacrifices according to his ability, one should then direct the mind toward liberation; it cannot be otherwise.

The nature of the Prājāpatyeṣṭi sacrifice and the method of the internal transfer of the fires (*samāropaṇa*) are to be understood from the scriptures concerning the rules for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). "One should set the mind on liberation" means that one should enter the fourth stage of life (*āśrama*). The word "but" (*tu*) serves to emphasize that this must follow the sequence of having studied the Vedas and so forth; it does not mean otherwise. Since the meaning "not otherwise" is already established by the force of the context, its mention here is a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended as praise. Thus says the *Svāyaṃbhuva* [Manu]:
"A twice-born man who, without having studied the Vedas, without having procreated sons, and without having performed sacrifices, desires liberation, goes downward. (MDh 6.37)

Now, one might object: "Granted that renunciation (*pārivrājya*) may not be appropriate for one who has not studied the Vedas, but what contradiction is there if he does so in the absence of sons and other [obligations]? This has already been stated: "The householder's life is for those possessed of passion alone. Therefore, if even one who has taken a wife were to resort to renunciation without making any effort toward the birth of sons and so forth, then—due to the transgression of the purpose of the injunction—it is indeed correct that "he who desires liberation goes downward. However, with reference to those free from passion, it has already been said: "He may dwell in whichever [stage] he desires" (VaDh 7.3). The rest is clear. 56–57.

Devoted to the welfare of all beings, tranquil, carrying the triple staff and the water-pot, delighting in solitude, he should wander forth as a mendicant and resort to a village only for the sake of alms. 3.58

“Beneficial to all beings” (*sarvabhūtahita*) means one who is beneficial through non-malice toward all beings, even those who cause harm. Alternatively, by perceiving the non-difference from the Self (*ātman*), one becomes non-malicious because of the state of being the Self of all beings. “Beneficial” (*hita*) and “tranquil” (*śānta*) stand in the relationship of qualifier and qualified; for one may be beneficial yet untranquil due to transgression and the like, or, according to the systems of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, one may be beneficial yet not tranquil. To exclude such cases, it is said “beneficial and tranquil. Alternatively, “beneficial” refers to one who does not initiate violence (*hiṃsā*), and “tranquil” refers to one who does not initiate [mere] favor (*anugraha*). Thus says Gautama: “One who neither initiates violence nor favors” (GDh 3.24–25). Regarding the “triple-staff” (*tridaṇḍin*), it refers to the staff of mind, speech, and body, as in: “The staff of speech, then the staff of mind,” and so forth (MDh 12.10). It is understood that the connection with the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and other items follows precisely from the possession of the triple-staff. “He who delights in only one” (*ekārāma*) means he who delights solely through delight in the Self (*ātmarati*). Thus, having severed desire for the village and become constant in the forest of wandering mendicancy (*parivrajyā*), he should resort to the village only for the sake of alms; the intention is that he should not stay in the village for even a moment at any other time. || 58 ||
Free from attachment, he should wander for alms in the evening, unobserved, in a village devoid of other mendicants, seeking only enough for his sustenance. 3.59.

One should wander about heedfully so that, even though one has completely conquered the senses, one does not become negligent due to the sight of women and other such objects. *Bhaikṣam* means a collection of alms; from this follows the avoidance of food from a single source. *Sāyāhne* means in the afternoon; [he should beg] then. *Anupalakṣitaḥ* means not making oneself known by means of learning and so forth for the sake of obtaining alms—this is the meaning. And even in the afternoon, it should be when the village is deserted by all other mendicants. *Yātrāmātram* means merely for the purpose of sustaining the body. *Alolupaḥ* means not greedy or lustful. Alternatively, two types of wandering mendicants are intended here, and the two-fold nature of their begging rounds is described. In that regard, by the phrase "one should wander about heedfully," which prohibits eating at a single place, the practice of begging is prescribed for one characterized by the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) and other signs. By the other [phrase], the instruction regarding "merely for sustenance" and "single food" is given for the mendicant of knowledge (*jñāna-bhikṣu*), who is not characterized by the triple staff and other signs. Furthermore, the instruction regarding a different time is given by the phrase "in a village deserted by those mendicants characterized by such signs. Thus says Gautama: "Seeking alms, he should enter the village at the last [hour]; he should wander about until he has finished [his meal]" (GDh 3.14–15). He says this specifically with the intention of referring to a single meal. Otherwise, he would have simply said "seeking alms" (*bhaikṣārthī*). Moreover, the expression "at the last [hour]" is a statement of time only in relation to other mendicants. As for what was stated by Saṃvarta:

"Having collected eight alms and washed them, one should remain silent at night"—this [rule] refers to the case characterized by specific qualifications. For the other [type of ascetic], however, there is indeed only a single alms-meal. And thus says the Śruti: "Now another wandering mendicant (parivrāj), clothed in a single garment, shaven-headed, using his stomach as a bowl, dwelling constantly in the forest, seeking alms. By this, he clarifies exactly this point. || 59 ||
However, according to their respective suitability and established rules:
"The vessels of an ascetic are made of clay, bamboo, wood, or gourd;
water is their means of purification, as well as scrubbing with cow-hair. (3.60)
The vessels of an ascetic, such as those made of clay and so forth, are for the purpose of begging and eating. The word "and" (ca) implies leaf-cups and other such items. The rest is clear. || 60 ||
And thus, having become permanently dispassionate, or having adopted the life of a wandering mendicant according to the previously mentioned sequence,
then— having restrained the collection of his senses, having abandoned passion and hatred,
and having cast off fear for all living beings— the twice-born man becomes immortal. (3.61)

The attainment of the supreme Brahman is the state of immortality. The mention of "twice-born" is for the sake of Brāhmaṇas, because renunciation is prescribed for them alone. The rest is straightforward. 61.

Furthermore: "But the purification of the intention to act must be especially undertaken by the mendicant, because it is the cause for the arising of knowledge and for the attainment of independence. (3.62)

The intention (*āśaya*) is the body; its purification must be accomplished through the conquest of the vital breath (*pavana*) and other means by a mendicant of knowledge (*jñānabhikṣu*), and especially by any other mendicant—meaning, by a wandering ascetic (*parivrājaka*) characterized by such qualities. For the intention is purified only when it serves as the cause for the arising of knowledge; this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, [this purification is necessary] for the sake of attaining independence and for the accomplishment of powers such as entering another's body (*parakāyapraveśa*). || 62 ||

Now, is it the case that here the ultimate goal consists solely in exercising independence through the purification of one's intentions and so forth? No, it is said in reply. Because independence is merely a cause for conquering the world up to that of Hiraṇyagarbha, and because it is subject to decay and thus a cause of saṃsāra, its very nature is suffering. Therefore, one should not be satisfied with merely exercising independence for the sake of attaining unsurpassed bliss. What then? One must contemplate: "Dwelling in the womb, as well as the states of existence born of karma; mental agonies and physical diseases; old age and the transformation of form. (3.63)

Existence through thousands of births, and the reversal of the pleasant and unpleasant—these are to be perceived by means of the yoga of meditation; subtle, the Self is situated within the self. (3.64)

For the afflictions beginning with dwelling in the womb extend up to the state of Hiraṇyagarbha; having observed these and become dispassionate through reflecting on their true nature, one should rise [from worldly involvement] and, by means of the yoga of meditation in the manner to be described, correctly perceive the subtle Supreme Self as abiding non-differently within the individual self (vijñānātman). The intention is that the entire Karma-kāṇḍa must be regarded as lacking in essence. The rest is clear. 63–64.
Since this is so, therefore:

"The stage of life (āśrama) is not the cause of dharma, for that [dharma] would exist even when being performed [by others]. The intention is that even the adoption of a stage of life is essence-less, because it is included within the category of ritual action (karman)."
Therefore, one should not do to another that which is unwholesome for oneself. 3.65.

One should not practice that which is unwholesome for the supreme, non-dual Supreme Self—that is, action (*karman*) and the like, which are the causes of *saṃsāra*. Rather, the meaning is that one should constantly perform the profound meditation (*nididhyāsana*) upon the Supreme Self through the yoga of meditation alone. [Objection: If this were so, would it not result in acting merely according to whim, since action is not being accepted? [Reply: Not so. For the non-acceptance of action is on account of its purpose being the next world; that is, one does not perform prescribed (*vihita*) action so that such action, when performed, might initiate the next world. However, it is precisely the performance of what is prohibited (*niṣiddha*) that initiates the next world; therefore, with the desire to avoid that, one must conduct oneself regarding prohibited things exactly in accordance with the prohibitions. (65)
If this is so, then with the view that even for those who have renounced action (karmasaṃnyāsins), everything except prohibited matters is not contradictory, [the author] says:
"Truthfulness, non-stealing, freedom from anger, modesty, purity, wisdom, fortitude, self-restraint, control of the senses, and knowledge—this is declared to be the universal dharma. (3.66)

Even though truthfulness (*satya*) and the other virtues are positive injunctions (*vidhi*), they do not contradict [the state of renunciation] because they consist in the avoidance of falsehood and so forth, which belong to the category of prohibited acts. *Hrī* means modesty; its mention as something to be avoided is intended to ensure that it never arises again, or there is no contradiction even if it is to be practiced. This modesty of the wise person is indeed great: that the connection with birth—which, through dependence on others, brings the afflictions of dwelling in the womb and so forth—is itself a cause for shame.
