Purity (*śauca*), moreover, being of three kinds, is taught as something to be practiced precisely because it is conducive to liberation (*apavarga*). *Dhī* is wisdom (*prajñā*). *Dhṛti* is fortitude (*dhāraṇā*). *Dama* is the endurance of dualities (*dvandva-sahiṣṇutā*). Control of the senses (*saṃyatendriyatā*) is self-evident, or it may be defined as meditation characterized by withdrawal from the manifold world of forms (*rūpa-prapañca*). *Vidyā* is the direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) of Brahman. Intending to show that all this—truthfulness and the rest—is taught as an auxiliary to that [realization] and is thus not contradictory even for those who have renounced ritual action (*karma-saṃnyāsins*), he says: "This dharma beginning with truthfulness is declared to be universal. It is universal (*sārva*) because it belongs to all. It is said to be "declared" (*udāhṛta*) for the purpose of illustration; it should be understood that other practices such as wandering for alms (*bhikṣā-ṭana*) are also applicable to all and non-contradictory. Therefore, the intention is that even for the *paramahaṃsas*, there is no license to act according to whim (*kāmacāra*). Thus, the stage of the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka-āśrama*) has been well-stated, including its various distinctions such as the secondary characteristics (*upalakṣaṇa*).

In this regard, some who harbor ill-will toward these various types of wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya) consider wandering mendicancy to be defined solely by its external characteristics. Thus it has been said by Dakṣa:
"He who does not possess these characteristics is neither one who requires penance nor one belonging to a stage of life (āśramin)."

Vasiṣṭha also begins with: “The wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), having given the gift of fearlessness to all beings, shall set forth” (VaDh 10.1), and after stating the collection of his duties, concludes: “Wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavītin*), with a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in hand, pure, and avoiding the food of a *śūdra*, a Brāhmaṇa does not fall from the world of Brahman” (VaDh 10.31). It has already been stated that the association with the water-pot and other items occurs precisely through the possession of the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*). Therefore, it is difficult to maintain that the wandering mendicant is not characterized by these [marks]. As for the verse regarding the wandering for alms (*bhikṣāṭana*), it has been explained in quite another way. Furthermore, other Smṛtis apart from the well-known ones such as those of Svāyambhuva and others, because their basis is unclear, are to be disregarded when they conflict with this [text]. Moreover, even here, purity is a duty common to all, and the sacred thread is an accessory of purity; therefore, it too must serve every purpose. If this is so, how could the absence of it in the case of the wandering mendicant be suspected? For this reason also, [the objection] is simply untenable. And the contradiction with established practice remains exactly as it is; this is the general direction [of the argument].

To this it is replied: For it has already been stated that wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) for the sake of liberation has knowledge alone as its means; therein, ritual action (*karman*) serves no purpose. As for the wearing of the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) and so forth on the basis of scriptural injunction, that too refers only to the initial stage of wandering mendicancy. But for the other [type of renunciant], there is no acceptance of the restrictive rules of the stages of life (*āśrama*), because he belongs to the side of those who maintain the necessity of ritual action. And it has been said: "The stage of life (*āśrama*) is not the cause of *dharma*. As for the Vasiṣṭha-smṛti passage: "Wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavītin*), with a water-pot in his hand... (VaDh 10.1), that too refers only to one who has not renounced ritual action. How is this known? Because, having begun with "Shaven-headed, free from the sense of 'mine,' without possessions" (VaDh 10.6), the text subsequently presents a different alternative by specifying: "He should eat whatever he obtains in a Brāhmaṇa family" (VaDh 10.24). Furthermore, since the opening statement "Shaven-headed, free from the sense of 'mine,' without possessions" (VaDh 10.6) prohibits the total possession of the sacred thread and other such items by those who have renounced ritual action, it is for this very reason that there is a subsequent counter-exception (*pratisedha*) regarding the sacred thread and so forth for the sake of the other [type of renunciant]. Otherwise, since these would have been obtained precisely because they are not contradictory, such a statement would be inconsistent. Nor should it be suspected that the counter-exception applies without distinction, because they are presented according to a specific sequence. For otherwise, this would have been stated immediately after the counter-exception regarding clothing, namely: "Clad in a single garment or in a deerskin" (VaDh 10.9–10). However, there is no contradiction when there is a difference in type, since the use of the word "or" (*vā*) is justified only through a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*); thus, there is no room for improper optionality (*vikalpa*). Moreover, in another Smṛti, the fixed rule for the stages of life is quite explicit:

Now, another type of wandering mendicant (parivrāj), clothed in a single garment, shaven-headed, using his stomach as a bowl, and constantly dwelling in the forest, may enter a village for alms when he is unable [to subsist otherwise], provided it is late in the evening, circumambulating from left to right and free from doubt. His begging for alms should include all social classes, with the exception of those accused of crimes and outcasts. Wearing no sacred thread (yajñopavīta), being devoted to purity, he may at will carry a single staff made of bamboo.

And so forth. Furthermore, the traditional scripture (*āmnāya*) states: "Having renounced, they then wander for alms" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.5.1). By this prohibition of all desires, it demonstrates the renunciation of ritual action (*karma*). Likewise, after stating, "Having mastered both childhood and wisdom, one then becomes a sage" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.5.1), it says: "Then, having renounced, one should master both silence and non-silence" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.5.1). The intention is that, having cast aside both "non-silence"—which is prescribed for other stages of life—and "silence"—which is prescribed for this stage—one who is solely devoted to knowledge immediately thereafter becomes a *brāhmaṇa*, a *paramahaṃsa*. Thus, it shows the non-applicability of the [standard] stages of life (*āśrama*), saying: "By what would he be a *brāhmaṇa*? By whatever he may be, by that he is just such [a person]" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.5.1). Here, there is no designation of a rule regarding the stages of life, because the prescription of the stages of life belongs to the side of ritual action (*karman*). Otherwise, due to contradiction, there would be nothing but inconsistency. Therefore, it is well said: "The stage of life is not the cause of dharma," and so forth. As for the claim that the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is obtained as an auxiliary to purification (*śauca*), that must be understood as referring only to cases where the thread already exists; for even in its absence, the purification of women and others is not obstructed. And how the sacred thread and so forth are not required has already been stated. Consequently, even such deprecatory explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are to be seen as referring only to existing circumstances.

"Without the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), or even with the sash and topknot loosened, and without having washed one's feet, one does not become pure even by performing the *ācamana* rite. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even a student (*brahmacārin*) who has removed his topknot would be impure. Therefore, since the sacred thread and other such items are limbs of purification only when they are already present, there is no fault. In this manner, all [conflicting] statements should be reconciled. Furthermore, from other Smṛtis—such as those of Viṣṇu and others—one must accept the specific distinction of the fourfold types of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*). Thus, wandering mendicancy has been described as having liberation as its purpose.

This is now considered: from what cause, moreover, is this instruction on the liberation of the bound self? If bondage were intrinsic, then its eradication would be impossible, and thus [the teaching] would be flawed. If it were due to another cause, that too is untenable because Brahman is pure. Furthermore, if even for the pure [Brahman] there were an adventitious cause of bondage, then the effort toward liberation would be entirely useless, since such [bondage] could occur even for one who is liberated.

True, if there were an acceptance of a causal agent (*hetu*). However, since the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) arises from ignorance (*avidyā*) by virtue of its nature as a non-apprehension of reality (*tattva*), there is no room at all for such an objection. Furthermore, there is no other entity distinct from the Self (*ātman*) that could be known through valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and thus designated as the cause of bondage. Indeed, the empirical discourse of bondage and so forth is entirely untenable when considered in relation to the Self alone. Yet, due to ignorance, even in the case of a single object, there appears a manifestation of duality—like the moon—caused by non-apprehension. The established position of those who know Brahman is that, in reality, there exists no other entity whatsoever apart from Brahman. How then is it that the cognizing selves (*vijñānātman*) are perceived as manifold? It has already been stated that this is caused solely by ignorance. (66)
Explaining this very point at length, the Lord of Yogins said:
"Just as sparks issue forth from a heated lump of iron, so indeed do all selves emerge from the Self. (3.67)

But is it not the case that, in this way, the status of the individual selves (*vijñānātman*) as being derived from the supreme self (*paramātman*) has been stated as being inherent? Just as sparks issue forth from a red-hot iron ball due to its very nature, without depending on any other cause, so too do the individual selves proceed from the supreme self—this is the meaning [of the passage].

Not so; for the position that [the world] is the material cause (*upādāna*) has already been refuted. What, then, is the meaning of this? It is that this phenomenal world (*prapañca*) arises from ignorance (*avidyā*) even though it is non-different from Brahman. Just as, although the sparks are non-different from the fire-ember which is impermanent, a distinction appears as sparks and the relationship of material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyatva*) manifests due to the non-apprehension of their identity, exactly so, although the individual selves (*vijñānātman*) are non-different from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), they appear as distinct and as its effects due to the non-apprehension of reality. Thus, there is no fault. Furthermore, we shall explain later how, even in this view, the systematic arrangement of merit, demerit, and so forth—which rests upon duality—is possible, and how there is no contradiction with the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*). || 67 ||
Thus, he elaborates on how the self, through ignorance, revolves in this cycle of existence—which is the cause of manifold sufferings—in an uninterrupted stream.
In that regard: "The self indeed performs some action by itself, some by its own nature, and some, consisting of merit, demerit, and rebirth, through habituation. (3.68)

In this context, the conscious self (*vijñānātman*), situated within this manifold of duality (*dvaitaprapañca*), performs actions of its own accord: some are performed according to scriptural injunctions; some arise spontaneously from birth alone, such as the sucking of the breast; and some arise from habit, such as dwelling in the forest after having emerged [from it]. That which consists of existence (*bhavātmaka*) includes both that which is of the nature of merit and demerit (*dharmādharmātmaka*), like the sucking of the breast, and that which is of the nature of existence distinct from merit and demerit. Alternatively, it should be understood that it "consists of existence" because, by means of merit and demerit acting as instrumental causes, it serves as the seed of *saṃsāra*. Furthermore, since merit and demerit are included within ignorance (*avidyā*), their status as the seed of *saṃsāra* is due solely to delusion; this must be understood through the lens of Brahman’s state of non-attachment (*niḥsaṅgatva*). But how do we understand that Brahman is non-attached? Because Brahman is unborn (*ajātatvāt*). [Objection: Is it not the case that the Self is indeed born? [Reply: No, because it exists even prior to birth. (68)

How, then, is there the designation "born," or how can there be existence prior to birth? It is said: The Imperishable is the cause, the agent, the knower, Brahman, the possessor of qualities, and the controller; though unborn, it is proclaimed "born" because of the assumption of a body. (3.69)

"What is this [meaning of] 'due to the assumption of a body'? It means: because of the comprehension of its distinction [from the Self] by way of being a body. And although Brahman is imperishable (*akṣara*), agency and so forth are possible for it precisely through the cause of that comprehension of distinction; likewise, through being the knower (*bhoktṛ*), one attains Brahman-hood by the arising of perfect knowledge and the attainment of the Supreme. Conversely, even for one who is under the sway of qualities such as passion and hatred, the connection with birth remains unsevered. Therefore, it is logically established that [the soul] is "born due to the assumption of a body through ignorance. || 69 ||
Now, due to the excess of ignorance, he elaborates upon the assumption of a body:
"Just as at the beginning of creation he emits space, air, light, water, and earth—each possessing one additional quality—so too does he assume them, even though he himself is unborn. (3.70)

For just as the Lord Prajāpati, desiring to emit creatures at the initial creation following the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), emits the gross elements beginning with space and ending with earth—endowed respectively with one, two, three, four, and five qualities of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—for the sake of the manifestation of the world; even so does this [Self], favored by merit and other factors in every birth, take up [the body] for itself. The meaning is that even though it is "non-existent" (*abhavan*), that is, not being produced, it takes up [the body] for the sake of the manifestation of a physical form. Now, it might be argued: "In the creation following the great dissolution, [the elements] are certainly not accepted as being already condensed [into bodies], because that would entail defects such as the impossibility of a creator being present. Such an objection could indeed arise if [the world] were ultimately real (*pāramārthika*). However, regarding this play of phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) characterized by ignorance (*ajñāna*), an objection based on logical inconsistency is simply not to be raised. Furthermore, if scripture (*āgama*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) even with respect to its own nature, then it is improper to assert a contradiction with another means of knowledge regarding a matter established by a scripture whose purport is none other than that very thing. Alternatively, this verse is intended solely to refute the views of others. For just as a creator, according to those who accept him, produces space and the other elements at the beginning of creation for the sake of establishing bodily activity, even so, although there is no creator, and although [the Self] is "non-existent"—meaning unborn—it "takes up," that is, assumes [the body] in accordance with the phenomenal expansion rooted in ignorance, for the purpose of the designation "birth. (70)
And just as the manifold diversity of the body is based solely on ignorance and not on any real entity, so he explains in detail:
"By the oblation the sun is nourished; from that comes rain, and then the plants.
That food, in the form of essence, becomes semen. (3.71)

For it is precisely for the sake of fulfilling its own function that the sun is nourished by the oblation as a secondary result. Thus it is stated in the *Jābāli-praśna* of the Śruti, beginning with: "Do you know how... by the oblation to space," and continuing: "In this very fire, the gods offer semen; from that oblation, the person comes into being" (ChU 5.3.1–9). || 71 ||
By stating that even eternal entities are described as being produced, he clarifies that this is merely a conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*):
"In the union of a woman and a man, when the semen and blood are pure,
the Lord simultaneously takes up the five elements, himself being the sixth" (3.72).

The purification of the semen and blood is to be understood from the medical treatises (*bhiṣak-śāstra*) through the removal of putrid odors and other defects. This word "elements" (*dhātu*) refers to the great elements (*mahābhūta*), such as space and the rest; these are five. One takes them along with oneself as the sixth. Regarding the phrase "along with oneself as the sixth": just as there is a designation of appropriation for the self—which is in fact absolutely non-distinct [from the body]—based on delusion, treating it as if it were distinct, so too should it be understood for space and the other elements. (72)
To further strengthen this very point, he speaks again at length:
"The senses, the mind, the vital breath, knowledge, life-span, happiness, fortitude, retention, impulse, suffering, desire, and indeed the ego-sense. (3.73)
Effort, form, and appearance, as well as likes and dislikes, existence and non-existence—all this is born of his own self for him who desires a beginning for that which is beginningless. (3.74)

The meaning is this: all these things, beginning with the sense organs, appear as if distinct from that very stainless Brahman—which is without beginning—due to the excessive delusion of one who desires a beginning for that which has no beginning; though they are non-different from the Self, they appear as if different. Furthermore, even for one who has attained the state of a conscious self (*vijñānātman*), this diversity characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth, must be understood as being born of the Self itself, following its own *dharma* and *adharma*. This is to be applied everywhere: just as the sense organs are unimpaired in some cases but their opposite in others. "Sense organs" refers to the eyes and so forth, as well as the hands and so forth. The mind is mentioned separately because it possesses a dual nature. "Vital breaths" (*prāṇa*) and so forth are well known. Although *dhṛti* (fortitude) is a form of pleasure, it is mentioned separately because it is metaphorically treated as the cause of that pleasure. "Sustenance" (*dhāraṇā*) and "impulsion" (*preraṇā*) refer to the body or other objects. "Pain" is well known. Desire and egoism are mentioned together in a compound because they share a common cause. "Effort" (*prayatna*) is the natural engagement in specific actions. "Form" and "appearance" (*ākṛti-rūpa*) are well known. They are combined into a compound because they are of a single nature due to being innate. "Voice" (*svara*) means sound, and its mention serves as an illustration for the perception of all objects. "Becoming" (*bhava*) is transmigratory existence; "non-becoming" (*abhava*) is liberation. Moreover, we shall explain later how the discourse on non-duality is ultimately real and conducive to liberation. Since its manifestation is based on delusion, there is no contradiction in describing the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) in every instance. (73–77)
And he elaborates upon the connection of Brahman, delimited by ignorance, with a body, as well as its nature:
"In the first month, it exists as a mass of moisture, a congealing of the elements;
in the second month, it becomes an *arbuda*; but in the third month, it is endowed with limbs and sense organs. (3.75)

The seed that has been infused becomes moistened and unconsolidated in the first month; such is the state of that embodied being as "become moisture" (*saṃkledabhūta*). The elements (*dhātu*)—the great elements (*mahābhūta*) manifested in their specific forms—are blended together in him; thus he is "blended with the elements" (*dhātuvimūrcchita*). In this way, through the sequence beginning with the *kalala* and reaching the stage of the *arbuda* in the second month, in the third month he comes to possess the distinct locations for the limbs and the sense organs. || 75 ||
Now he analyzes the conjunction of the limbs and the sense organs:
from space [come] lightness, subtlety, sound, the sense of hearing, and likewise strength;
from wind, however, [come] propulsion, movement, expansion, and even dryness. (3.76)
Fire, however, has visibility, digestion, heat, and the illumination of form;
from water come taste, coolness, moisture, cohesion, and softness. (3.77)
The self perceives the odor of the earth, as well as the sense of smell, heaviness, and form; therefore, it vibrates in its entirety during the third month.

From the great elements such as space (*ākāśa*), the Self—desiring to enter into transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) and thus following the expansion of ignorance (*avidyā-prapañca*)—takes up qualities such as lightness in accordance with the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), as well as objects such as sound, and the sense organs such as the ear. Therefore, it should be understood that [the Self] moves about, bound by karma and falling within the sphere of dualistic worldly activity. Furthermore, since this matter is rooted in other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and because the Smṛti is of secondary authority (*apara*), one should not insist upon the distinction that the sense organs and so forth are composed of material elements (*bhautika*) or are products of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). Moreover, their substrates (*adhiṣṭhāna*) are space and the other elements; however, the powers of the sense organs are to be understood as having the Self as their object, because they follow after cognition. The rest is clear. (Verses 76–78)
And according to the medical treatises:
"By not granting her longings, the fetus may incur defects, deformity, or even death; therefore, that which is pleasing to the woman should be provided. (3.79)

*Dauhṛda* is the longing for specific foods and so forth. The rest is clear. Even though [this longing] follows from other means of knowledge, it is mentioned here in order to make known that its non-fulfillment constitutes a fault. || 79 ||
Thus, in the third month, the limbs and sense organs are gradually joined;
in the fourth, there is stability of the limbs; in the fifth, the production of blood; and in the sixth, the emergence of strength, complexion, nails, and body hair. (3.80)
Furthermore:
Endowed with mind and consciousness, pervaded by channels, sinews, and vessels, in the seventh and eighth [stages] he possesses skin and even memory. (3.81)
From the word "ca" (and), it should be understood that in the sixth [moment] as well, the conjunction of the mind and so forth occurs indeed by the power of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). || 81 ||
But because his vital energy (ojas) flows away again toward the womb and again toward the nurse, even though his sense faculties are fully developed,
the fetus born in the eighth month is deprived of life. (3.82)

For when the embryo of a certain creature has been fully developed in one womb—that is, in another mother—it is in that very eighth month that its birth occurs. Because its vitality (*ojas*) and life-force (*prāṇa*) then rush toward and migrate into another embryo from the previous one, and into another mother-womb from the previous mother, it is for this reason that one born in the eighth month is deprived of life; the meaning is that such a child does not survive. || 82 ||
When the eighth month has been completed auspiciously,
in the ninth or tenth month, he is expelled by powerful winds of birth, like an arrow through the opening of a machine, accompanied by feverish distress.

Because it is rooted in other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the mention of "the ninth month and so forth" is intended as an illustration for other months as well. The description of birth as being dependent on others—by means of "powerful winds of labor"—is for the purpose of intensifying world-weariness (*vairāgya*) through its shameful nature. He clarifies this very point with the words, "through the opening of the machine, afflicted by fever. This same method of explanation should be applied to subsequent passages as well, such as the description of the number of bones and so forth. (83)
This very play of ignorance is further elaborated:
its body is sixfold; indeed, it possesses six layers of skin; likewise, its limbs are six, and its bones number exactly three hundred and sixty. (3.84)

Do not foster false adornments and the like by superimposing upon this little body the status of being an instrument for the fulfillment of desires. This body, as it is perceived, is not merely a collection of causes for delusion; rather, it is a limitation (*avacchedaka*) for that undivided Brahman in order to assume the state of transmigratory existence. It exists in six ways—namely, earth and the other elements, as well as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)—thus consisting of sixfold modifications. Since these [elements] cover and maintain the six layers of skin, such as pus, blood, and so forth, the meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that one should not harbor attachment to this [body]. Furthermore, there are six limbs: the head, the two arms, the trunk of the body, and the two thighs. The word "tathā" (likewise) signifies a manner; that is to say, it is of such a nature as to be a corpse. The rest is straightforward. || 84 ||
Now he establishes that there are three hundred and sixty bones:
"Together with the sockets, there are sixty-four teeth; the nails are twenty;
and the digits of the hands and feet—these constitute their four locations. (3.85)

The sockets are the jaw-bones; the bones are the thirty-two teeth, thus making sixty-four. Together with the twenty nails and the twenty skeletal bars (śalākā) of the hands and feet, along with the four locations where the hands and so forth reside, there are one hundred and eight. The "skeletal bars of the hands and so forth" refers to the bones at the roots of the fingers; the "locations" are those upon which they are established. The rest is clear. (85)
Likewise: there are sixty bones in the fingers; two in the heels; four in the ankles; four bones in the forearms; and exactly that many in the shanks. (3.86)

The meaning is "four. Because the hands are mentioned separately, the word *aratni* here should be understood as distinct from them. Thus, together with the previous [limbs], there are one hundred and eighty-two. 86.
One should point out two each arising from the kneecaps, the thighs, the pelvic plates, and the shoulders; as well as the axle-pin at the *sthālūṣaka* and the two hip-plates. (3.87)

One should point out two skull-bones in each knee, likewise two flat bones in each thigh, one in each shoulder, and the axles and so forth; these, counted as pairs, amount to sixteen, which together with the previous [bones] make two hundred minus two. The *akṣa* is the hip bone; the *sthālūṣaka* are its fastenings; the rest is clear. 87.
There is one bone in the pubic region, forty-five in the back, fifteen bones in the neck, and the collarbones and the jaw together form a single unit. (3.88)
Together with these sixty-three, there are two hundred and sixty-one [bones]. The junction of the arms and shoulders is the *jatru* (clavicle). The rest is well known. 88.
At its base are two frontal bones, the cheekbones, the nasal bone, and the jawbone; together with the side-plates and the occipital protuberances, there are seventy-two [bones]. (3.89)

At its base are two bones of the forehead; there is one bone that connects the cheek and the nose, which is called the *gaṇḍanāsāghanāsthi*. These four, together with the seventy-two [previously mentioned], make seventy-six. (89)
There are two temples, four skull-bones, and likewise seventeen bones for the chest; such is the collection of bones in a person. (3.90)
That which was stated in the previous summary—"one hundred and sixty"—is now complete. || 90 ||
The qualities of these very great elements (mahābhūtas), beginning with earth and ending with space, which constitute the body,
are known as the objects— namely, smell, form, touch, and sound—
and they are also the perceivers of these [objects].
The nose, the eyes, the tongue, the skin, and the ear are the sense organs.

Following the sequence of the body, this word [“ear”] is used figuratively for the seats of the sense organs; the word “ear” (śrotra) refers to the physical ear-cavity due to the force of the word “but” (tu). The rest is straightforward. 91.
But these—the hands, the anus, the generative organ, the mouth, and the feet as the fifth—one should know to be the organs of action; and the mind is of the nature of both. (3.92)

The mention of "mouth" intends to include the palate and other substrata of speech. The mention of the "fifth" is for the purpose of making known that there is no difference [in function] between the hands and so forth. The rest is well-known. || 92 ||
Furthermore:
The navel, the vital energy (*ojas*), the anus, the semen, the blood, the two temples, as well as the head, the heart, and the throat—these are indeed the abodes of the life-force (*prāṇa*). (3.93)

The seats of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—that is, of life-force (*jīvana*) and longevity (*āyus*)—are the navel and so forth. Their utility lies in the thorough knowledge [of them] for the sake of purifying the inner disposition (*āśaya*). The same should be applied to what follows as well. *Ojas* is the essence of food (*annarasa*), which initiates the flow of blood and other bodily constituents. The rest is clear. (83)
By virtue of their connection with the internal cavities:

the omentum (*vapā*), the site for removing the omentum, the navel, the *kloman*, the liver, the spleen, the small intestine, the kidneys, the bladder, and the receptacle of feces (*purīṣādhāna*). (3.94)
The stomach, the heart, the small intestine, the rectum, and the abdomen—this is declared to be the expansion of the abdominal cavity. (3.95)

The *vapāvahanana* is the binding of the omentum to the intestines. As for the *kloman*, the liver (*yakṛt*), and so forth, they are to be understood from dictionaries or from the medical treatises (*bhiṣak-śāstra*) of meat-sellers. As it is said:
"They call the *tilaka* the *kloman*, and likewise the *tālakhaṇḍa* the liver.
And similarly:
The receptacle of undigested food (āmāśaya) is said to be below the large intestine (pakvāśaya) and above the navel.
And so forth. || 94–95 ||
Even when divided part by part, though it remains undivided:
the two pupils, the eyes, the two frontal globes, the two ear-lobes, the two temples, the two ears, the two tusks, the two gums, the two lips, and the two hollows of the loins. (3.96)
The groins, the testicles, the kidneys, the two masses of phlegm, the breasts, the uvula, the buttocks, the arms, the shanks, and the thighs with their calves. (3.97)
The palm of the belly, the top of the bladder, the chin, the nape of the neck, and the hollow at the base of the neck—these are the locations here in this body. (3.98)

The *kanīnike* are the pupils of the eyes; the remaining parts are the eyes themselves. The two pieces of skin that cover them are the *kūṭe*. The *karṇaśaṣkulī* is the clearly visible outer ear; the holes therein are the *karṇaputrakau*. The *dantāveṣṭau* are the gums surrounding the teeth. The *kakundarau* are the hollows of the buttocks. The *vaṅkṣaṇa* is the joint of the thighs. The *vṛkkau* are located above the testicles. The *upajihvikā* is at the root of the tongue. The fleshy protuberances on both sides of the anus are the *sphijau*. The *vasti* is the bladder situated within the anus. The rest is well known. (96–98)
In this very body, the four eye-sockets, the feet, the hands, and the heart— these nine apertures are indeed the abodes of the vital breath (prāṇa). (3.99)

The "fourfold path" refers to the four organs of perception—namely, the ear, nose, tongue, and skin. These five, beginning with the eye, are the sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*). The hands and feet are the objects of the organs of action (*karmendriya*). The word "and" (*ca*) includes the remaining [organs]. The heart is the mind (*manas*). These eleven organs, excluding the hands and so forth, as well as the nine apertures, are primarily the abodes of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). There are seven apertures in the head, along with the anus and the generative organ, thus making nine apertures in total. || 99 ||
Furthermore: there are exactly seven hundred veins, nine hundred sinews, two hundred arteries, and five hundred muscles. (3.100)

The vessels that discharge blood are the *sirās*. The *snāyu* (ligaments) are well known. The *dhamanīs* are indeed those *sirās* which carry the vital air (*vāyu*); they become thick when filled and thin when emptied. The *peśīs* (muscles) are indeed those *sirās* that carry fat (*medas*). This [classification] is stated in a gross measure for the purpose of medical practice according to the scriptures. 100.

Now, for the sake of mastering the vital winds (vāyu) and perceiving their subtle dimensions, he says: "Twenty-nine hundred thousand, as well as nine hundred and fifty-six vessels are specified; they are designated as *dhamanīs*. (3.101)
The verse has been stated [as follows]. || 101 ||

Those wise ones who are skilled in the intent of the Yoga scriptures and desire to know the true nature of the body should understand that there are three hundred thousand [hairs] on the head and beard;
the remainder [of the verse] implies this is according to the count of individual hairs.
Furthermore: there are one hundred and eight vital points (marmas), as well as two hundred joints (saṃdhis). || 3.102 ||

The term "vijñeye" (in the object of cognition) is to be supplied [to the verse]. The word "tathā" (likewise) is intended to indicate the various alternatives regarding the dimensions of hair and so forth mentioned in other treatises; this is to be explained throughout the entire section on number. || 102 ||
And because the measurements mentioned in other treatises are subject to variation, [the number] is as follows:
fifty-four crores, sixty-seven hundred thousand, and half [a lakh], along with the pores of perspiration. (3.103)

[Objection: Is it not the case that this measurement of the number of hairs and so forth appears like a stake driven into the middle of the earth by a rogue—due to being stated arbitrarily and because of mutual contradiction, merely on the grounds that no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) is perceived? [Reply: True, it is so; for the Smṛti has as its purpose the censure of the body. However, there is no fault, because such things are possible even through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as established by ancient knowers of Brahman who performed superlative meritorious deeds. 103.
He clarifies this very point:
"The atoms, being divided, are reckoned by means of the winds; if these were different [from the mind], who indeed could know the established nature of these entities? (3.104)

Sanatkumāra and others are the disciples of Vāyu; they are the "Vāyavīyas. By them, those specific numbers which have been mentioned by us are calculated. If, however, there are other even more subtle atoms beyond these that constitute further numerical distinctions, let them be; there is no fault, because who indeed knows their ultimate measure? The intention is that something is stated merely according to faith and as far as it can be understood. Furthermore, it should be applied thus: "Who indeed knows the manifold and diverse arrangement of beings and living creatures? (104)
And according to the traditional scriptures alone:
"Nine añjalis of rasa are to be known, ten of water, seven of feces, and eight of blood are proclaimed. (3.105)

This measurement of the elements should be understood as pertaining to one who is healthy and fully developed. As for what has been stated by some, following their own reasoning, that "urine and feces are indeterminate," that is not to be challenged here, because it refers to the state of a newborn who has not yet reached full development. || 105 ||
And with palms joined in reverence:
"Phlegm is six [palas], bile five, urine four, fat three, and adipose tissue two; marrow is one and a half, and the brain is half of that. (3.106)
One añjali at the waist and half an añjali on the head; thus, there are one and a half añjalis. || 106 ||
"Only so much phlegm-essence, only so much semen—this body is thus unstable; he who strives for liberation [should renounce it]. (3.107)

*Ojas* has been explained; that very *ojas* which is the cause of phlegm (*śleṣman*) is "phlegmic *ojas*" (*śleṣmaujaḥ*), and the meaning is that there is exactly one and a half handful (*añjali*) of it. Likewise, there is exactly one and a half [handfuls] of semen. Thus, for that field-owner (*kṣetrin*) who is a doer of merit, who has produced dispassion, whose desires have been severed, and whose body (*varṣma*, *śarīra*)—which has been described as unstable, impermanent, perishable, most terrible, difficult to perceive, and the cause of saṃsāra—exists for the sake of liberation and for the purpose of entering the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśrama*), he has accomplished his duty; this is the meaning of "having done what was to be done" (*kṛtakṛtya*). || 107 ||
What, then, is the method of liberation here by which there would be no further rebirth? It is said:
"Seventy-two thousand channels named *hitā* have issued forth from the heart; in their midst is that which has the luster of the moon. (3.108)
The mandala is his, and situated in its center is the Self, motionless like a lamp.
Having known that which is in the center, one is not born again. (3.109)

It should be understood that this name "beneficial" (*hita*) is indeed literal, because they are capable of removing cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). The word *hi* has the sense of a reason; since they are the cause for the excellence [of the self] by virtue of being the means for the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇātman*), therefore they are called "beneficial. Among them, that lunar-mansion-like orb (*maṇḍala*) residing within the heart, which is accessible only through meditation—within that, the Self is clarified by the analogy beginning with "like a lamp. The meaning is: having known this very Self which is perceived in the center of the heart-mandala, one is not born again in the wheel of cyclic existence, but is indeed liberated. Now, an objection might be raised: since the Self is omnipresent (*sarvagata*), its designation as being in a specific location is improper. This is not so. This is an instruction regarding the path of perception, not an instruction regarding the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the Self. For this very reason, there is a further specific designation: "having known that which is in the center. The analogy of the lamp, however, is due to the fact that [the Self] is not illuminated by anything else and is all-pervasive. Just as even though the light of a lamp is undivided, because it is perceived in one place due to its greater intensity, there is a designation of delimitation such as "this is right here," so too is the conceit of delimiting the Self [in the heart]. This is the intended meaning. (108–9)
But for the sake of its correct discernment: "The *Āraṇyaka* which I obtained from the Sun, and the *Yoga-śāstra* proclaimed by me, should be known by one who desires Yoga. (3.110)

By the words "I [attained] from the Sun," and so forth, he indicates that this is the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*. From the instruction on the knowledge of the *Āraṇyaka*, it is understood that this meaning is to be grasped from the Veda alone and not from anything else. Furthermore, by the passage beginning with "I [attained] from the Sun," it is illuminated that even from the Veda, [this knowledge must be received] from a teacher through the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). And this being the case, the Smṛti is not rendered purposeless; rather, its purpose is to serve as an auxiliary to the meaning of the Veda. The intention is that one who desires to bring about the perfection of yoga should know that "the Yoga-śāstra also has been proclaimed by Me. The intention is that what is proclaimed by Me is in accordance with the meaning of the Veda, and not contrary to it like that which was spoken by the Buddha and others. Thus it has been stated by the Self-existent One (*Svayambhū*):

"He who examines the Vedic proclamation of Dharma with reasoning that does not contradict the scriptures of the Vedas knows Dharma, and no other" (MDh 12.106). "Ārṣa" means belonging to the Ṛṣis; they are the knowers of Brahman, and this [proclamation] belongs to them, being for the purpose of realizing the nature of Brahman. The rest is clear. 110.
Now he elaborates upon the method of meditation that is in accordance with the Vedas:
"Having made the mind, intellect, memory, and senses have no other object, the Self is to be meditated upon—He who resides in the heart as the Lord, like a lamp. (3.111)

The meaning is as follows: "non-other" (*ananya*) refers to the Self (*ātman*), because nothing else exists apart from it. Having made the mind, intellect, memory, and senses have that [Self] as their object, one turns them away from having anything else as their object. But in what part of the body must the mind, intellect, and so forth abide for there to be this state of having no other object? To this he says: "in the heart" (*hṛdaye*). For when the activities of the senses are restrained in the heart through the cessation of external objects, then the mind also—following along with them—becomes free from conceptual construction (*akalpaka*), even while remaining in its own location, because it has turned away from its own objects such as pleasure. And since memory and cognition are dependent upon that [mind], they abide in the Self; thus, the establishment of the mind, intellect, memory, and senses as having the Self as their object is achieved. Therefore, one should meditate upon the Supreme Self—the Lord, the imperishable—who, though undivided like a lamp, appears as divided due to having the Self as its object when the collection of senses is fully restrained in the heart; this is how the passage beginning with these words is to be construed. (111)

"Is it not the case that this appears difficult to accomplish because the collection of the senses is so hard to restrain? True, it is difficult; yet it is not impossible. For behold: just as a man sings a *sāman* chant with focused attention, so too does one who is attentive attain the Supreme Brahman through practice. (3.112)

What is impossible here? For it is observed that those who chant the *sāman* with a concentrated mind can distinguish, even when it is difficult to perceive, the singing of the *rathantara* and other melodies superimposed upon various *ṛks*, such that they do not lose the integrity of the *sāman* chant, thinking "this is the *sāman* here. And just as a man, though his mind is attached to external objects, can nevertheless sing the *sāman* attentively, so too one attains even the Supreme Brahman through the practice of meditation (*dhyāna*). Therefore, one must apply effort in this matter; this is not at all impossible—thus should the opponent's objection be refuted. And so it has been said:
"Having seen the overflow of the ocean caused by a single drop on the tip of a blade of grass, one who has cultivated their intellect should not think that anything is impossible. (112)

For this very reason, Nārada and others who are experts in the Gītā-veda consider song to be the means for yoga—which is the cause for attaining the Supreme Brahman by means of restraining the senses—and they record [the following]:
"The Aparāntaka, Ullopya, Madraka, Prakarī, as well as the Auveṇaka, Sarobindu, Uttara, and the Gītikās. (3.113)
The *ṛggāthā*, the *pāṇikā*, the *dakṣavihitā*, and the *brahmagītikā*—these are called *geya* because they are characterized by the practice of singing them. (3.114)

These seven *gītikās*, beginning with the *aparāntaka* and others, consist for the most part of the basic subject matter (*vastu*) and its subdivisions (*pādabhāga*), and are distinguished by their respective objects; they are to be understood from the science of song (*gānaśāstra*) itself. For example:
"Now, the *vastus* are six, seven, or five, as well as the *aparāntaka*" and so forth. Likewise:
First, there is the *ullopyaka*, which is then joined with measures (*mātrā*) and descents (*patana*).

Such extensive treatises as these are not elaborated upon here for fear of excessive prolixity. Likewise, the distinction between the *vastu* (the subject matter), the *mātrā* (metrical units), the *pāda* (quarters), and the *bhāga* (parts) should be sought from those very sources. For example: “The *vastu* itself consists of six *mātrās*,” and so forth. Regarding the term *ṛggāthā*, it refers specifically to those *ṛks* sung by Brahmā on his divine lute. Similarly, the *gāthā* is that sung by Kāśyapa Prajāpati. The *pāṇikā* is that composed and sung by Dakṣa Prajāpati; this is the meaning. The *brahmagītikā* is a song for the purpose of praising Brahmā. All of this, bearing the aforementioned designations and possessing the characteristics described by Nārada and others, is to be sung because of its utility for the path of yoga (*yogamārga*). Furthermore, since its intent is directed elsewhere [toward the ultimate goal], one should not be overly attached to the mere instruction. Alternatively, by virtue of the traditional authority of Nārada and others, and because it is mentioned here in this context, its basis in the Vedas (*vedamūlatva*) may be inferred; thus, there is no fault. (113–4)
Furthermore, with the intention of [referring to] Nārada and others, he says:
"One who knows the true principles of playing the lute, who is proficient in the *śrutis* and *jātis*, and who knows the rhythmic measures (*tāla*), attains the path of yoga without effort. (3.115)

Śruti, consisting of sound, should be understood as being of twenty-two kinds, which determine the measurement of musical notes (svara). Jāti, however, is of eighteen kinds, beginning with Ṣaḍja and the others. Tāla is a specific measure consisting of the falling of time-units. The rest is clear. || 115 ||
Moreover:
even if one who knows the song does not attain the supreme state through yoga,
nevertheless—
Having become an attendant of Rudra, he rejoices together with him.
And by this, it is indicated that Rudra is the presiding deity of song. || 106 ||

Having stated this as a digression, the Teacher, now desiring out of great affection to favor the entire world of living beings by clarifying this very reality of the Self, introduces the sages who prompted the composition of the treatise as his interlocutors:
"The Self is said to be beginningless, and its beginning is the body;
the entire world arises from the Self, and the Self originates from the world. (3.117)
The remainder [of the argument] is that this has already been stated in such passages as "the sign, the syllable, and the agent" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.69). || 117 ||

Since this causal relationship between the world and the self is thus untenable, how is it that we—including gods, asuras, and humans—are so deluded? Tell us: how was the world produced, and how did the self come to be within it? (3.118)
How indeed is this contradictory relationship between cause and effect? To resolve this contradiction, tell us—that is, explain it to us—this is the meaning. || 118 ||
Now the Lord of Yogins gives them this reply:
"For that person who is seen when this web of delusion is cast aside has a thousand arms, feet, and eyes, and possesses the splendor of the sun in its thousands. (3.119)
He is indeed the Self, the sacrifice, the omniform Prajāpati;
as the Virāj, he attains the state of the sacrifice in the form of Soma.

The exposition in the form of a dialogue has already been explained by way of commentary; do not fall into delusion regarding this. Having removed the web of delusion following the false cavils of wicked logicians, one perceives—through direct perception itself, aided by the reasoning to be stated—the Person who is distinct from the entire phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*), who is experienced within the inner self (*pratyagātman*) in an immediate form, and in whom all appearance of duality has been dispelled. What are His characteristics? He is characterized by "a thousand hands and feet," and so forth. That very Self is the Sacrifice (*yajña*); and the word "Sacrifice" refers to the great elements such as Earth and the rest, which are its cause—the meaning is that Earth and the other elements are also He alone. But how can He alone be both the Self and the Sacrifice? Because He is the Universal Form (*viśvarūpa*) and the Lord of Creatures (*prajāpati*). Since all beings are the forms of this undivided Self, He is "Universal Form. For this very reason it was said: "with a thousand hands and feet," and so on. The word "thousand" signifies "many" and does not denote a numerical limit; though He is non-different due to His connection with infinite species and forms, He is seen divided in a thousand ways, like the space within jars and the like. "Radiant as the sun" means He is self-luminous. And because He Himself creates offspring through differentiation, He is the "Lord of Creatures" (*prajāpati*) and the "Virāj. Having become food, He attains the state of being the Sacrifice—that is, the instrument of sacrifice—in the form of Soma and the like. (119–20)
And therefore:
"That supreme essence which arises from the renunciation of substance and deity, having fully satisfied the gods, [satisfies] the sacrificer with its fruit. (3.121)
Having been joined with the wind, the Soma is then led by the rays;
it is brought to the solar abode ordained by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.

This subtle and supreme essence, which consists of the oblation—arising from the renunciation of substances and deities, following the perception of sacrificial materials such as Soma, being common to all, and serving as the cause of the universe—having thoroughly satisfied the gods, joins the sacrificer with the fruit [of his action] through its specific nature by virtue of the performance of the injunction; then, through its common nature, it is cast into the wind by means of the *Samiṣṭayajus* formula, "Svāhā! Let it be placed in the wind," according to the vision of the Vidyā. It is led by that wind to the Moon, to the lunar orb. And from there, by the grace of perception through the solar rays alone, it is led to the solar station, as established by the mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) of the *Ṛgveda* and other scriptures, and so forth. This very point is also stated in a *Ṛk*: "Him whom the imperishable ones drink, the imperishable one... (TS 2.4.14.1), and so on. (121–22)

And that sacrificial essence which has reached the solar abode and is gathered as the cause of the world— that Sun creates that maṇḍala, the supreme nectar, from which there is the birth of all beings, whether they are of the nature of eaters or non-eaters. (3.123)

That which is the essence of sacrifice (*yajño rasaḥ*)—that maṇḍala is that Supreme Self, the Sun. As it has been said: "The Sun is the Self of the moving and the stationary" (RV 1.115.1). That Sun emits—that is, releases—that supreme nectar, the water which constitutes the cause of the world; such is the meaning. He further qualifies that very water: "That from which there is the birth of all beings," and so forth. "Of those whose nature is eating and not-eating" means of the stationary and the moving. || 123 ||
That sacrificial essence which has reached this state as water, having become the fruit, attains the status of Virāj in the form of food;
from that food, again sacrifice, again food, again the ritual—thus does this wheel revolve without beginning or end. (3.124)

From that food, by the same path as before, the sacrifice—which is common to all—is produced again; and from that sacrifice, by that very same path beginning with the wind, the Virāj and food are produced again; and from that food, likewise again, the ritual (kratu) or sacrifice arises, and from that again food. In this way, this seed of the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) of the omniform Brahman revolves in the manner of a wheel, being without beginning or end. Consequently, there is no contradiction even though they stand in a relationship of mutual cause and effect. || 124 ||
Having observed this wheel, which revolves without beginning or end, we have declared:
"The self is without beginning; there is no origination of the inner self.
But the person is a composite entity, born of delusion, desire, aversion, and karma. (3.125)

If the self (*ātman*) is beginningless, how can there be such worldly conventions as "he is born" or "he dies"? It has been stated: "He is called 'born' because of the assumption of a body" (YDh 3.69). In the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), however, the self is beginningless; the intention is that for it there is no intermediate origination or birth. If it is asked why the assumption of a body occurs for the stainless Brahman, [the answer is: there is no connection with a body for the imperishable Supreme Self (*paramātman*), for He is indeed unattached to a body. But this other person (*puruṣa*), distinct from Him, who is inseparable from Him and inherent in the body, becomes subject to the designation "birth" when, through the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā-vyāmoha*), he is joined by action (*karman*) characterized by both common and specific qualities due to desire and aversion. Thus it should be understood. || 125 ||

Therefore, this very Supreme Self, consisting of the high and the low and having both form and formless aspects, is he who is proclaimed as the primordial deity Maya, whose self is the thousandfold. From his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet, the social classes (varṇas) were produced in their respective order. (3.126)

Because of his connection with activities such as reciting the Vedas and eating through the mouth, and because of his preeminence and priority, the Brāhmaṇa is said to be "born from the mouth"; likewise, because of his connection with arm-related activities such as protection, he is said to be "born from the arms," and so forth. This must be explained away as a figurative elaboration (*prapañcanīya*), since for Brahman there is no literal mouth or other limbs in an ultimate sense. 126.
In this very way, through the connection with the effects of his feet and other limbs as the foundations and so forth:
from his feet the earth was born; from his head the sky arose; from his nose the vital breaths; from his ears the quarters; from his skin the wind; and from his mouth the fire. (3.127)

Because he is manifested through mental vision, from his mind the moon was born, and from his eye the sun; from his loins came the intermediate space and the world with all its moving and stationary beings. (3.128)

The word *jaghana* means the navel and so forth. One should apply [the interpretation] as follows: "The world, including all that moves and is immobile, was born from that very Brahman," and so on. The rest is straightforward. || 128 ||
When the nature of the Supreme Self has been thus described, the sages raise an objection:
"If this is so, O Brahmin, how is it that he is born in sinful wombs?
How can he, who is the Lord, be joined with undesirable states? (3.129)

And why does one who is endowed with the instruments [of perception] not know his prior cognition? Furthermore, why does one who is omnipresent not feel the sensation [experienced by another], even though he too is omnipresent? (3.130)

If, in this way, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is without beginning or end and imperishable (*akṣara*), then, O Brahmin, we ask you: how does it undergo birth in sinful wombs, subject to the power of others? If it is thought that this is due to association with undesirable things such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, that too is subject to further inquiry: since God (*īśvara*) is also independent, how is he associated with undesirable states? Now, if the intention is that [this occurs] because, as a transmigrating self (*saṃsāryātmatā*), prior knowledge has ceased, that too is incorrect. How can there be the state of being a transmigrating self for that which is stainless? And even if it were of that nature, why would there be no prior knowledge, given that it is still endowed with the instruments (*karaṇa*)—such as sight and the rest—which exist in the form of powers (*śakti*) and are inseparable from it? If it is argued that [knowledge is absent] precisely because of the interruption caused by the state of being a transmigrating self, then the consequence would be total ignorance (*ajñatva*). If it is argued that knowledge arises because the nature of the all-pervading Supreme Self is never lost, then, in that case, why does that Lord, though being all-pervasive, not perceive—that is, not know—the sensations and cognitions of pleasure and so forth contained within all bodies? This is the meaning. (130)
When the sages have thus urged him, the Blessed One speaks this reply:
"Through the faults born of the actions of mind, speech, and body, this living being goes to the state of the lowest animals and immobile things, wandering through hundreds of births. (3.131)

Regarding what was asked—how one is born into evil wombs—the answer is this: through the defects arising from the actions of mind, speech, and body, one passes through hundreds of births, being produced among various species as the lowest animals, birds, or immobile beings. However, this very point should have been stated first: how it is that the Self of Brahman itself becomes transmigratory. That question, however, has already been largely resolved by the description of the sacrificial cycle—which is both common and specific—as being without beginning or end; therefore, it is not further considered here, as it would be as useless as one who, seeking the means of extraction for someone fallen into a well, goes about searching for the manner of their fall. || 131 ||
Moreover: "Just as the states of embodied beings within their bodies are infinite, so too are the forms of those possessing bodies here in all wombs. (3.132)

For it is indeed mental states alone that serve as the causes of vocal and bodily actions. Thus also says the sacred tradition: "Now, this person consists of volition" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.6.3.1). And just as there are infinite causal states belonging to embodied transmigrating selves existing within their bodies, so too are there infinite effects in the form of [physical] forms belonging to these embodied beings existing here. Consequently, because of the connection with infinite mental states, just like the nature of the Supreme Self, the beginninglessness of transmigrating selves is established. || 132 ||

If the connection with another womb results from karma, then for one who lacks the qualification for a particular womb—such as that of an animal—the connection with that womb would not be possible. True; this might indeed be so if Vedic rituals were to have results only in this life. But when, in fact:
"The ripening of some karmas occurs after death, while for others it occurs both in this world and in the next."
The implication is that this objection is therefore not to be raised.

Furthermore, the knowledge of entitlement has no utility whatsoever in the production of the fruit of action there; what then? It is the state [of being entitled] that is the operative factor there. (3.133)

The intention is that even an action that is not fully understood through its mere existence certainly produces a fruit. "Ripening after death" refers to fruits such as heaven; "in this very life" refers to rain and so forth; "indeterminate" refers to cattle and the like. The rest is straightforward. || 133 ||
Now he elaborates upon this causal relationship born of karma:
"Coveting the wealth of others, likewise brooding over what is undesirable, and being intent on what is false, one is born in the lowest wombs. (3.134)
It should be understood that through mental defects such as coveting the property of others, one is born in the lowest wombs, such as those of the Caṇḍālas and similar castes. || 124 ||
But through defects of speech— a man who speaks untruth, a malicious person, and one who indulges in irrelevant prattle— is born among beasts and birds. (3.135)

Furthermore, by the use of the word "mānava" (human), it makes known that this [prohibition] rests upon the human being as such. And the mention of "beasts and birds" is for the purpose of characterizing all species of animals. The rest is straightforward. 135.

But through bodily faults of action— being devoted to taking what is not given, consorting with the wives of others, and being a violent injurer according to improper rules— one is born among stationary beings. (3.136)
Furthermore, due to the possession of an excellence of sattva-qualities:
"One who knows the Self, who is pure, self-controlled, ascetic, has restrained senses, performs dharma, and knows the Vedas, goes to the wombs of the gods. (3.137)

He who knows the Self, is devoted to purity and other virtues, and is a knower of the Vedas—he is of the nature of *sattva* and goes among the divine wombs; the meaning is that he attains the state of a deity through his actions. || 137 ||
But due to an excessive connection with *rajas*:
"He who delights in unwholesome actions, who is restless, enterprising, and sensual—he, being of *rājasa* nature among men, attains birth after death. (3.138)

The word *sat* denotes the eternal (*nitya*). That which is an eternal duty, such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice and the like, is the "real" (*sat*) action; other than that, the "unreal" (*asat*) action is that which is performed for the sake of desire (*kāmya*). One who is primarily devoted to that [unreal action], who is undisciplined and fickle-minded, who is enterprising—meaning primarily intent on worldly undertakings—and who is attached to objects of desire such as enjoyments, is of the *rājasa* type. Because he is an experiencer of the fruits based on the human species, he is born among humans after death; the meaning is that as a mortal, he is unworthy of divinity characterized by immortality. || 138 ||
But due to an abundance of demerit, by their very nature, one who is prone to sleep, cruel, greedy, an atheist, a beggar,
as well as negligent and of broken conduct, becomes a tamasic being among the animals. (3.139)

That threefold nature of each [state], such as the *sāttvika* and the rest, which was described by the Self-born One, has not been elaborated upon here because it was presented merely for the sake of illustration. (139)

And thus, because the existence in saṃsāra is rooted in the state of the mind, one who is possessed by passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas), wandering here, and joined with undesirable states of being, enters into saṃsāra through the mental [faculties] alone. (3.140)

Due to the paucity of *sattva*, being overwhelmed by *rajas* and *tamas*, and because of dependence on others, he wanders right here in this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) and repeatedly encounters that very cycle again, joined with undesirable mental states; the meaning is that he does not attain liberation. || 140 ||
And because its *sattva* is overwhelmed by *rajas* and *tamas*, it is severed from omniscience despite being of the nature of consciousness.
For just as a tarnished mirror is incapable of reflecting forms and light, so too the self whose faculties (*karaṇa*) are unripened is incapable of knowledge. (3.141)

For just as a mirror, despite the presence of light, is incapable of perceiving forms due to the impairment by dirt, so too the cognizing self (vijñānātman), when immature and its faculties unrefined due to the impairment by *rajas* and *tamas*, is incapable of right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). Thus, the objection raised—namely, "How can there be an absence of prior knowledge even for one possessing the instruments [of perception]?"—is refuted. || 141 ||
And for this reason, even when the capacity for production is not yet severed,
just as in an unripe *kaṭurohiṇī* fruit, the sweet taste, though present, is not perceived.
Such is the analysis.
Likewise, even in oneself, there is no cognition when the faculties are unripened. (3.142)
Even the urvāru fruit is like that which is to be split; the rest is clear. || 142 ||
Regarding what was said—"Why does he, though omnipresent, not experience sensation that is omnipresent? (YDh 3.130)—the author speaks this to resolve that objection:
"The embodied soul experiences sensation, which has everything as its locus, within its own body;
but the disciplined yogin, who [is present] in all, does not undergo sensation. (3.143)

Because the production of consciousness occurs only in one's own body, since that body is the locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*), therefore—even though [the Self] is omnipresent—it does not perceive cognitions residing in all substrates. However, when the yogin has perfected the knowledge born of yoga, then, being joined in *samādhi* and remaining in his own body, by the power of the yoga of touch (*sparśayoga*), he knows the feeling—the cognition—residing in other bodies, even though it rests in other substrates; having removed the notion of difference through another self, he perceives it while established in his own Self. This is the meaning. The word "but" (*tu*) is displaced and connected with the negative particle (*na*): "but he does not obtain the feeling. What is meant is this: he indeed perceives it, but he does not obtain it; the meaning is that he does not enjoy the fruit of consciousness, such as pleasure and so forth. But how can there be non-enjoyment of pleasure and so forth for one who is non-different from the knower? There is no contradiction, because the enjoyment of the fruit is accomplished through karma, and karma—which conforms to difference—has its locus in the cognitional self (*vijñānātman*). || 143 ||

But how can that which is one alone possess both differentiated and undifferentiated states? It is so because it is perceived in that very way through both reasoning and scripture. For instance: "Just as space, though one, appears distinct within jars and other vessels, so too the Self, though one, appears manifold, like the sun reflected in various receptacles of water. (3.144)

For just as even though space is one, it maintains both the notion of unity and differentiation when delimited by objects such as jars, yet there is no confusion of properties that follow from those differences, so too should it be understood for Brahman. And thus it has been said:
"Just as when one jar-space is joined with dust, smoke, and so forth, not all [spaces] are joined [with them], so it is with the self regarding pleasure and pain" (Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 3.5).
Likewise, it is said by others as well:
"When the release of even a single one among jars filled with smoke is performed by uprooting [the breath], there the stainless sky arises. (144)

If, then, just as in the case of the sun, Brahman—though itself undivided—appears as divided due to limiting adjuncts such as water and so forth, then duality would not be established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), since it would be based on delusion; [the author] refutes such an objection.
"Brahman, space, air, fire, water, and earth are the constituent elements (*dhātavaḥ*).
The remainder [of the sense] is that these are indeed ultimately real (*paramārthasatya*). As it has been said:
"The Lord simultaneously takes up the five elements as his own sixth" (YDh 3.72).
In this regard, just as these five elements are the ultimate reality, so too are these worlds, this Self, and from that [Self] proceeds all that is moving and unmoving. (3.145)

The word *loka* signifies the body; the meaning is that "lokas" are bodies. Therefore, because it is non-different from the Self, the world—including both the moving and the unmoving—follows the conventional usage of distinction like the space within a jar or similar objects; this is the meaning. But how could the Self, being indeed non-different [from itself], produce the body and so forth? It has been stated: "by the favor of specific states of being. (145)
Furthermore: Just as a potter makes a jar from the conjunction of clay, a staff, and a wheel, or as a house-builder constructs a house with grass, clay, and wood; || 3.146 ||
Just as a goldsmith [fashions] a form by taking up mere gold, or a silkworm [produces] a cocoon through the union with its own saliva. (3.147)

The intention is as follows: having thus taken up the instruments (karaṇas) in various births here, since the necessity of the causal complex (sāmagrī) is to be understood through its effects, the conceptualization must follow that observation. Just as a variety of causal complexes is perceived in the case of a jar, a house, and so forth, and just as a silkworm and the like produce cocoons and such by means of saliva and other instruments, yet in the production of those [cocoons], the self alone possesses both agency and instrumentality; likewise, for Brahman too, who possesses the instruments of karma and so forth produced from the great elements and so on, there is the production of bodies and the like, but in the creation of those instruments and so forth, the self alone possesses both agency and instrumentality. || 146–7 ||
He demonstrates this:
"The Self alone, having brought forth the instruments, creates itself. (3.148)
Thus; and the meaning is that the instruments, having come together, themselves become the agent and the instrument.

But surely this conviction regarding the self, which follows upon the search for ultimate reality, is mutually contradictory—being based on both the conscious and the unconscious, on unity and multiplicity, and on the nature of the supreme and the subordinate. For instance, if Brahman is non-dual according to reason and scripture, then the conventional usage of difference must be based solely on delusion, like the appearance of the sun in various water-vessels due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). On the other hand, if the conventional usage of difference is real, how then can the self have a connection with a body that is distinct from it? Furthermore, we do not perceive any essential nature of the self apart from the great elements (*mahābhūta*), since consciousness can be explained as a property of the aggregate of elements, just like the power of intoxication in wine. Moreover, even the great elements themselves remain to be proven for the Proponent of Consciousness (*vijñānavādin*), because the cognition of blue and so forth is possible as being merely forms of knowledge. Therefore, this must be explained.

To this it is replied: An external object is indeed perceived; how can it be denied? It is not the case that its existence is established merely by being a form of cognition, for that would entail the consequence of there being no consciousness at all; for it is not possible for there to be self-consciousness of itself by itself. Furthermore, the cognition of the grasped and the grasper is independent of any cause for their difference. Oneness, however, must be postulated through superimposition, as well as the absence of forms [in the cognition]. Nor are conceptual constructions possible that contradict actual experience. Nor does the falsity of waking cognitions follow from the falsity of dreams and the like, because the distinction between waking and dreaming is established by something other than themselves; and even when there is the conceit of remembering what has been forgotten, the object of memory has an external basis. Now, if it be argued: "How could a distinct object produce consciousness? Or, if it did produce it, why is there not a simultaneous awareness of all objects?"—that too is not a valid objection, since the production of knowledge follows from the connection between the sense organ and the object. Nor is there momentariness for the external object, because its identity is determined through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), and because no cause for its destruction is perceived in the interval; furthermore, since the arising of an effect depends on a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), objections regarding the impossibility of sequence or simultaneity do not apply even if the object were stable. This is the general direction of the argument. If this is so, then since the object exists exactly as it is perceived, the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are certainly real. As for the claim that if those elements are real, then because they possess the nature of a composite, the production of consciousness would lead to the consequence of *nairātmya* (selflessness)—just like the power of intoxication—that too is of no consequence, because the self is established precisely through the experience of the external object, just as the external object is experienced. (Verse 148)
Moreover: "The great elements are real, and the self is likewise so; otherwise, who could see with one eye what was seen by the other? (3.149)

The intention is that just as the great elements, such as earth and so forth, are real because they are being experienced, so too the self is indeed real because it is the experiencer. Otherwise, if cognition were a property of the elements, who—apart from an experiencer—would see with one eye what was previously seen by another eye, thinking, "This is that very same thing seen before"? Who would then connect [the two perceptions]? Such is the intention. (149)
He clarifies this very point further:
"Who indeed recognizes speech when it is heard again after having been heard before?
Whose is the memory of past objects, and who is the creator of dreams? (3.150)
This is for the sake of conceptual proliferation. || 150 ||

Moreover, the realization of the true nature of the self occurs through direct experience alone; what need is there for reasoning in this matter? For it is one whose mind is overwhelmed by *rajas* and *tamas*, who is inflated with egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) due to birth, form, age, conduct, learning, and so forth, and who is attached to objects such as sound through action, mind, and speech. (3.151)
The intended meaning is that this very [cognition], which is immediate and self-cognizing, is not the Self. || 151 ||

Furthermore, he who has attained perfection through yoga indeed realizes Brahman—which is non-conceptual, immediate, and non-dual. As for the other, who is conceited due to the arguments of bad logicians, his mind is full of doubt as to whether the fruit of action exists or not;
for even one who is unperfected imagines himself to be perfected. (3.152)

Even that one who fancies himself a sophist, whose mind is doubtful and overwhelmed by darkness, when he thus speculates out of excessive cleverness as to whether the fruit of action exists or not, then he necessarily considers the self to be established and certain as distinct from the body—meaning that even though [the distinction] is not yet proven, he does so regardless of the Yoga philosophy. As for what was said—that if the great elements are real, how can there be a connection of a distinct self with the body—that is not even a valid objection, because the great elements themselves are non-different from the nature of the self. If it is argued that this is indeed an objection because the reality of the conscious self follows from experience, we say no, because another cause is possible. (152)
For instance: "My wife, children, and ministers; I am theirs"—thus he remains, his mind always perverted regarding things that are beneficial and harmful. (3.153)
He was impartial toward the learned and the ignorant, as well as toward the primordial nature and its transformations;
he was intent on fasting, entering fire, and leaping into water.
One who behaves in this way, whose self is undisciplined, and who possesses false attachments, is bound by action through hatred, delusion, and desire. (3.155)

The intended meaning is as follows: one who behaves as described in these two verses—one who possesses the dogmatic adherence to the objections of false sophists, who is undisciplined, and who, though distinct from action—which consists of both common and specific types—as well as from mental hatred and delusion, and from the desire for excessive sensory enjoyment—is nevertheless bound. One who stands in a relationship of mutual benefit and service, thinking "my wife, children, and so forth" and "I belong to them"; one who has perverted cognition regarding things that are beneficial or harmful, whether their purpose is seen in this life or in the unseen (transmigratory) realm; one who falsely imagines what is beneficial or harmful in purely worldly matters, and likewise in other cases; one who is ignorant of the distinction between the Knower and the known, between the one who knows the meaning of the Vedas and the ignorant false sophist, and between primordial nature (*prakṛti*) characterized by *rajas* and *tamas* and its transformations (*vikāra*); and one who, due to the conceit of having a sense of duty, exerts himself in practices such as fasting unto death—such a person of this character is bound. This has been explained. (153–155)
And thus, for one who has entered this most terrible cycle of existence (saṃsāra), this is the instruction on the method for casting off the body:
service to the teacher, discernment of the meaning of the Vedas and scriptures, the performance of their prescribed duties, association with the virtuous, and auspicious speech. (3.156)
Avoiding the sight and touch of women, beholding the Self in all beings, renouncing possessions, and wearing worn-out saffron robes. (3.157)
Restraining the senses from their objects, casting off sloth and laziness, a thorough enumeration of the body, and seeing evil in worldly activities. (3.158)
Free from passion and darkness, through purity of being, desirelessness, and tranquility—one who is thoroughly purified by these means becomes fit for the essence and attains immortality. (3.159)

By these means—beginning with the service of the teacher—which have been described in these three and a half verses, one who is thoroughly purified and characterized by *sattva* attains *yoga* and, through the knowledge of liberation (*kaivalya*), becomes immortal; that is to say, he attains the state of Brahman.
