The rest is clear. 156–9.
Liberation has been stated to result from yoga. But how that very yoga comes about is now explained:
"Through the presence of the recollection of reality, through union with the *sattva*, through the complete destruction of karmas, and through proximity to the virtuous, yoga proceeds. (3.160)

The principles (*tattva*) are earth and the others; the recollection of the principles (*tattvasmṛti*) is the perception of their non-difference from the Self in accordance with the scriptures. From the presence—that is, the arising—of that recollection of the principles, and because of the conjunction with *sattva* through the absence of *rajas* and *tamas*, and because of the exhaustion of karmas performed in previous lives through meditation and other means, and because of the proximity—that is, the connection—with the virtuous (*sat*), the yoga characterized by the attainment of supreme bliss proceeds; thus it should be explained. || 160 ||
And even if, despite being disciplined, one should somehow fail to attain the supreme state due to negligence, nevertheless, as an incidental result at least:
"He whose mind, upon the dissolution of the body, abides in the Lord with its essence established in purity, shall, with unimpaired memory, truly attain the recollection of his former births. (3.161)

At the time of death, when the body dissolves, he whose mind is unattached to sense objects, established in *sattva*, independent of a lord, and unsubdued by passion and the like—he, with his memory unimpaired, shall go after passing away to the state of remembering past births; that is, he shall attain the recollection of former lives. And from that, through once again connecting with yoga, he indeed becomes immortal; such is the intended meaning. || 161 ||
Moreover, one is joined with only those virtuous and non-virtuous actions performed by oneself;
for just as Bharata maintains his body through various colors, so too the self assumes a body born of karma while assuming diverse forms. (3.162)

This verse serves as a summary. Bharata is an actor. Just as he assumes various forms for his body according to the specific roles he plays, so too the *vijñānātman* (the conscious self), born of karma, performs various auspicious and inauspicious actions and brings about birth in diverse wombs; this is the meaning. || 162 ||

"But surely, even if one possesses the memory of past births, since only one with unimpaired limbs has the capacity to perform dharma and other duties, a means [to attain that state] should be taught for that very purpose. It is replied: "The statement of a means is not required here, because the state of having unimpaired limbs is natural. For it is said: 'By defects of time, karma, and the seed of the self, and likewise by those of the mother, deformity of the embryo is observed; indeed, there is no loss of limbs at birth. (3.163)

The defect of time (*kāladoṣa*) consists in approaching [the wife] at forbidden times such as during the night. The defect of the rite (*karmadoṣa*) is either a deficiency or a non-performance in rites such as the impregnation (*garbhādhāna*). The defect of the self (*ātmadoṣa*) consists in coveting another woman who is undesirable. The defect of the seed (*bījadoṣa*) consists in its being scanty and so forth. The defect of the mother (*mātṛdoṣa*) is the contemplation of another man. The intention is that through such defects there occurs a transformation and deformity of the embryo, but not a loss of limbs by birth or by nature. || 163 ||
As for what was asked—how the imperishable Brahman could undergo transmigration—it is said in response:
"Never has this Self been previously liberated from egoism, mind, movement, the fruit of action, and the body. (3.164)

For that Supreme Self, which is eternally established and consists of supreme bliss, is indeed one; whereas this [individual self] is another. Even when there is non-differentiation from Him, the cognitional self (*vijñānātman*) is, by its very beginninglessness, delimited by the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth, and is not separated from the body. And it is precisely for the sake of this [self's] attainment of non-difference from the Supreme Brahman that the Blessed One’s effort is directed toward the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). 164.
And if, regarding this very path of instruction for attaining the supreme, there should be an obstacle due to illness, it is said in that regard:

"The donor, the truthful one, the patient, the wise, the performer of auspicious deeds, the master of his senses, the ascetic, and the one devoted to yoga—such a person is not overcome by diseases. (3.165)
The verse has been stated [in prose] above. || 165 ||

But surely, since action—which consists of both common and specific elements—is without beginning or end, just as the connection with the body is beginningless, so too it must be endless. Consequently, because of the resulting impossibility of liberation, the effort to explain it would be entirely futile. It is said in reply: "Just as the persistence of a lamp depends upon the wick, the vessel, and oil, and its modification is likewise observed, so too is the untimely destruction of the life-force. (3.166)

For if the cause were beginningless, the effect would indeed be beginningless, but not necessarily endless simply because the cause is endless. Indeed, the destruction of the effect does not necessarily follow from the destruction of the cause, since we observe its destruction even while the cause still exists, due to other factors. Thus, for instance, the persistence of a lamp and the like—which are produced by the combination of a wick, a support, and oil—lasts as long as those causes remain; yet, modification occurs through another instrumental cause, such as impact by wind. In the same way, for the Self, which is connected to a body that is the product of karma, there may be the cessation of life at an untimely moment—even though that [connection] has not been severed—due to another factor such as the realization of reality (*tattvāvabodha*). This means that there is the cessation of the subtle limiting adjuncts (*liṅga*) and so forth. Even in the case of worldly existence, the cessation of a person’s body should be understood in this very same way, resulting from the convergence of karma with intense fruits and the like. (166)
Now he elaborates upon that means for the attainment of reality, which results in the exhaustion of the vital breaths:
"Infinite are its rays, like those of a lamp situated in the heart—white, black, tawny, blue, brownish-yellow, and reddish. (3.167)

That which was previously explained as being situated in the heart like a lamp, to be meditated upon through *nididhyāsana*—the means for attaining that [lamp] are the infinite rays, the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*), which manifest it and possess colors such as white and so forth. Here, "white" (*sitā*) refers to the stainless, supreme attainment; and because they are the means to that, the channels are designated by that same term. This should be applied similarly to the *kadru* and other [colors]. There is only one white [channel]; all others are non-white. Their detailed expansion consists of the *kadru*, the blue (*nīla*), and so on, to be applied according to their relative proximity. The word *kadru* signifies a contemptible movement and serves as a qualifier for blue and so forth, rather than denoting a color itself. Thus, "blue with a contemptible movement" is *kadrunīla*, and "yellowish-brown with a contemptible movement" is *kadrupiṅgalā*; this should be applied accordingly. "Yellowish" (*āpītāḥ*) means green (*haritāḥ*). And thus says the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "In that [space], they say there is white, and also blue, yellowish-brown, green, and red" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.9), and so forth. || 167 ||
And that which serves as the means for attaining the Supreme is the white ray called Suṣumṇā; straight from the heart, it extends upward toward the head.
Among those [rays], one stands above; having pierced the solar orb and transcended the world of Brahmā, by that [ray] one goes to the supreme goal. (3.168)

Whether through the practice of optional meditations (*kāmyopāsana*) or by the principle of offering everything to Brahman (*brahmārpaṇa*), he who is established in action— by means of that other hundred rays of his which are directed upwards— he attains the abodes of the hosts of gods. (3.169)
The Vasus and so forth are the classes of deities; the rest is clear. || 169 ||
But he who is of a passionate nature, driven by desire, indeed moves according to his own karma;
with those reins that are of many forms, downward-pointing, and of dull luster, he wanders here helplessly for the sake of experiencing the fruits of his actions. (3.170)
The verse has been explained. || 170 ||

Having thus reflected upon this nature of Brahman as both the higher and the lower, and seeing that every effort other than the realization of the Self is purposeless, the Lord of Yogis spoke these words to urge you on, O sages: "Exert yourselves somehow according to your own capacity to know the Self—by means of the Vedas, the scriptures, and realized knowledge; through birth and death, through mental absorption, through coming and going, and indeed through truth and falsehood. (3.171)

[They judge] by means of welfare, pleasure and pain, and by auspicious and inauspicious actions; by the knowledge of omens and portents, and by the results arising from the conjunctions of the planets. (3.172)
By the movements of the stars and constellations, by those born of water, and even those born of dreams;
likewise, by space, wind, light, water, earth, and darkness. (3.173)
Even through the passing of Manvantaras and Yugas, or by the power of mantras and medicinal herbs,
one cannot perceive the Self, which is the eternal cause of the world and ever-present.

In every possible way—by means of the Vedas and so forth, up to the power of mantras and medicinal herbs—you should strive to know the Self according to your capacity. The intention is that you should exert effort toward self-knowledge to the best of your ability. Even when the means such as the Vedas are unavailable, one should not become lax regarding self-knowledge on the grounds that it is impossible to achieve, whether through birth and death, or through omens, the knowledge of birds, or the powers of mantras and herbs; for the undertaking is directed solely toward the necessity of attaining self-knowledge. One should not, however, be overly obsessed with mantras, herbs, and the like. By the Vedas, which serve as the means to the knowledge of reality (*tattva*); by the *śāstras*, such as grammar and other sciences; by those accompanied by various forms of knowledge such as history (*itihāsa*); by another birth, meaning that if one lacks the capacity for discernment in this life, one may do so in another; and by "until death," meaning with lifelong and intense application. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that there is no failure even after hundreds of other births. By "great affliction," meaning even with great mental distress. By "going," meaning by traveling to other lands; by "not going," meaning by remaining in one place. The word "thus" (*tathā*) refers to other such modes. By "truth," meaning by the realization of the unity of the Self (*ekātmya*); by "untruth," meaning by imagined modes of worship such as the four-armed form; by "the auspicious," meaning by the state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*); and by "pleasure and pain" and "good and evil deeds"—the word "and" here implies the inclusion of pleasure and so forth, thus meaning by the state of householdership (*gārhasthya*). Pleasure is the enjoyment of perfumes, garlands, and the like; displeasure is the observance of restraints (*yama*) and disciplines (*niyama*); good deeds are the *agnihotra* sacrifice and others; evil deeds are the *sarvasvāra* sacrifice and others, which, though prescribed, are considered evil due to their connection with death, and because of incapacity, they lead to the production of another body capable of knowledge, which is useful for the present context. By the knowledge of omens and so forth, one should observe the time of prosperity and, without despondency, engage again and again; "omens" include the throbbing of the right eye and the like, as well as the northern solstice (*udagayana*). "Knowledge of birds" is the knowledge of the cries of crows and the like. "Planetary conjunctions" refer to the strength of the moon and so forth. "The movement of stars and constellations" refers to the affliction of one's birth constellation by malefic planets. "Water-born" refers to pilgrimages and the like. "Dream-born" refers to the seeing of desired dreams. The word "even" (*api*) is used as before to indicate the possibility of these being means. And by "space" and so forth—meaning, according to the Puranic view, by the darknesses (*timira*) that arise or are produced, which obscure the true nature of the Self as the Sun, and which are likewise removed in the manner described therein. And by the knowledge of the wheel of time (*kālacakra*) through the attainment of other Manvantaras and Yugas. Know the Self by means of the power of mantras and herbs, which are causes for the stability of wisdom. Of what characteristics? Existing always, meaning existing eternally, devoid of reference to the three periods of time. This has already been explained as being the cause of the universe. Nor is this matter concerning the characteristics of the Self extremely remote and to be accepted merely on the authority of scripture; rather, another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) has been stated here: "As the great elements are real, so too is the Self" (YDh 3.149). 171–4.
Furthermore, for the sake of summary, he clarifies that very point out of friendship:

Egoity, memory, intelligence, aversion, intellect, happiness, fortitude, the transition between different senses, desire, and the opening and closing of the eyes and life—[these are the marks of the Self]. (3.175)
The creation of objects in a dream, the impelling of the mind, its movement, the blinking of the eyes, consciousness, effort, and the grasping of the five elemental constituents; 3.176.
Since these signs of the Supreme Self are perceived, therefore there exists beyond the body the embodied one, the all-pervading Lord. (3.177)

*Medhā* is an excellence of wisdom (*prajñā*). *Dhṛti* is retention (*dhāraṇā*). The transition from one sense organ to another, which is the mental review of what has been grasped by a different sense organ, is the movement of the senses. That retention of the body through will—that is, its relinquishment—is *icchā-dhāraṇa*. The creation of various existing beings within a dream is the *svapna-sarga*. Thus, the Vedic scripture also says, beginning with "There are no chariots there," and continuing, "Then he creates chariots, yoked horses, and paths" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.10). *Preraṇa* (impulsion), however, belongs to the mind even in the waking state. *Agati* (non-movement) of the mind occurs in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). *Nimeṣa* (closing of the eyes) is an indicative mark for all bodily movements. *Cetanā* (consciousness) resides within. *Prayatna* (effort) is of every kind. *Ādāna* (taking up) is grasping according to the three types of action. It pertains to the five elements, having the five elements such as earth and so forth as its object. Since these [qualities] are perceived as signs of the Supreme Self, being distinct from the attributes of the material elements, therefore there exists a Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), the embodied one (*dehin*) distinct from the embodied one residing in the body, who is all-pervading, supreme, the Supreme Self, the Lord, ungraspable by action, blissful, undecaying, and immortal—this is the meaning. Furthermore, in this context, the fact that [the qualities] do not depend on the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, and the logical possibility of taking up the great elements and so forth, are signs of the Supreme Self intended to show non-difference. However, it should be understood that the remaining [qualities], although common to the individual self (*vijñānātman*), are mentioned incidentally for the purpose of establishing that Brahman is both the higher and the lower self. The rest is clear. (175–7)

Now, by means of following the designation "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña), he clarifies the distinction between the field and its knower, as well as the status of Brahman as both the higher and the lower:
"The sense organs together with their objects, the mind, the organs of action, as well as the ego-sense, the intellect, and the elements beginning with earth. (3.178)

The sense organs are the eyes and so forth. Their objects are form and the rest. Ego (ahaṃkāra) is the self-referential awareness within the inner self, unmingled with any other cause, and having the intellect as its instrumental basis. Intellect (buddhi) is the activity that serves as the cause and fruit of experience. By the word "and" (ca), the Unmanifest (avyakta), known as Pradhāna, is included; however, this is not the Unmanifest as conceived by the Sāṃkhyas—which consists of the state of equilibrium among the qualities of sattva and the rest—but rather that which is the common causal ground of the universe. This has been stated in the passage: "The essence produced from the renunciation of substance and deity... (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.121). As for sattva and the others, they are indeed qualities of the Self. The rest is clear. || 178 ||
This field consists of these twenty-four principles.
The unmanifest Self is declared to be the knower of this field;
He is the Lord of all beings, being both existent and non-existent, and both the manifest and the unmanifest. (3.179)

The Lord, who exists as the presiding controller and the enjoyer of the fruits of this [universe] consisting of twenty-four principles, and who is bound by karma while abiding in the unmanifest (*avyakta*), is thus designated as the "Knower of the Field" (*kṣetrajña*) by those who know Brahman. And so Vyāsa says:
"Those who know that speak of him who knows this as the Knower of the Field" (BhG 13.1).

Alternatively, the term *avyakta* (unmanifest) should be construed as a qualification of the Self (*ātman*). Its meaning is that it is unmanifest, being unmixed with form and other qualities. However, the distinction between these two is as follows: the Lord who is the master of all entities consisting of the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Furthermore, the word *bhūta* (being), by virtue of denoting existence in general, refers to the knower of the field as well. And this [Self], while being the Supreme Self, is both existent and non-existent; it is designated as "existent" in its aspect as the knower of the field and as "non-existent" in its aspect as the nature of the Supreme Self. But in the ultimate sense, that which is both existent and non-existent—all that is indeed He alone, whose nature consists of both existence and non-existence, because it is perceived exactly in that way. Thus says the Vedic tradition: "Verily, there are two forms of Brahman: the formed and the formless" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.1). || 179 ||
Now he shows the sequence of the origin of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña):

"The origin of the intellect (buddhi) is from the Unmanifest; from that, the emergence of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra); from that, the elements beginning with space are born, each possessing one additional quality. (3.180)

In the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptāvasthā*), when all consciousness has undergone a great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), the intellect (*buddhi*) arises from the unmanifest (*avyakta*) due to karma, which is the cause of experience. Then, upon awakening, through the realization within the individual self (*pratyagātman*), the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) comes into being. In the same way, through engagement with external objects, there arise space and the other elements, possessing one, two, three, four, and five qualities respectively—this is the meaning. Furthermore, the sense organs and the mind, impelled by their capacity to grasp those [objects], undergo a transformation into their nature and thus become identical with them; the mind, in particular, consists of both the existent and the non-existent according to its own objects from the very beginning. This process is to be applied everywhere, even in the *Purāṇas* and other texts, in the descriptions of creation and dissolution. (180)
Furthermore, those which have been described here as the great elements (*mahābhūta*)—beginning with space, wind, fire, water, and ending with earth—possess one additional quality each.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their respective qualities.

In the subsequent passage, the word "and" (*ca*) serves the purpose of compounding the preceding qualities; thus, even though it is not explicitly stated in the phrase "and taste" (*rasaś ca*), it should be understood there as well for the sake of the meter.
And regarding creation:
whatever is dependent upon something else, that dissolves back into that very thing. (3.181)
And because the qualities dissolve into the elements, the qualitylessness of the Supreme Self is established. || 181 ||
Now he summarizes the aforementioned matter in its entirety: "I have told you how the Self creates itself, even though it is the Lord, through the ripening of the three kinds of karma. (3.182)
The meaning of the verse has been explained as stated. || 182 ||

The unmanifest (*avyakta*), which is called *pradhāna*, consists of the ripening of the three-fold karma; it is unseen and is the seed for the engagement in saṃsāra. However, this is not according to the intention of other systems [of thought], where it is characterized by the equilibrium of the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva* and so forth. For *sattva* and the others are not the qualities of *prakṛti*. What then?
"Sattva, rajas, and tamas are proclaimed to be the qualities of that very [unmanifest] itself; they are not [qualities] of the self (*ātman*), but of *prakṛti*. This is the meaning.
If this is so, how then is the distinction between bondage, liberation, and so forth established? It is said:
"For he, possessed by rajas and tamas, revolves like a wheel. (3.183)

The intended meaning is that through the destruction of that [bondage], by virtue of the connection with the quality of sattva, one is indeed liberated upon abiding in one's own true nature. || 183 ||
Now, in order to conclude the discussion on the higher and lower Brahman, he says:
"This Puruṣa who is both without beginning and with a beginning, the Supreme, is declared to be accompanied by modifications and perceivable through the subtle body (liṅga) and the senses. (3.184)

The Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) appears to have a beginning due to its connection with the modifications such as the Great Principle (*mahat*), which constitute the characteristics of the Field; however, he who is the beginningless and stainless Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is described as being graspable by the subtle body (*liṅga*) and the senses because of his dual nature. It should be understood that this Blessed One, though appearing in both modes, is in reality the Supreme Self alone, whose universal form consists of both the existent and the non-existent. The intention is that one should not be deluded in this matter. The construction is as follows: the subtle body and so forth—namely, egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and the rest—are to be understood as having the Self as their object, while the senses, such as the eyes and the rest, are to be understood as having primordial nature (*prakṛti*) as their object. || 184 ||

Regarding this [self] which is distinguished as the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), he describes the path—indicated by external signs perceived by the senses—which is the cause of its ascent and descent:
"The path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) and that which lies between the path of the immortals (ajavīthī) and the star Agastya;
by that path those who maintain the *agnihotra* sacrifice go toward heaven, desiring offspring. (3.185)

Following the passage beginning with “the other hundred rays of his” (YDh 3.169), which names the paths, this external path is mentioned as an illustration of that very [subject]: that which lies between the Ajavīthī and Agastya is the path of the ancestors (*pitṛyāṇa*). By that path go those who maintain the *agnihotra* fire, those desiring progeny, those devoted solely to ritual action, and those who worship the year (*saṃvatsara*). This same principle should be applied to the other paths as well. For in the Purāṇas, many paths or tracks belonging to the divine Sun in the sky are heard of; among them, the Ajavīthī is immediately adjacent to Agastya. The rest is clear. (185)
Moreover: Even those who are devoted to generosity and endowed with the eight qualities correctly, they too go by that very path, being dedicated to the vow of truth. (3.186)
Compassion toward all beings, patience, freedom from envy, and so forth—these are the eight qualities of the self (*ātma-guṇa*). The rest is well known. 186.
And by this path, there is the world of the gods;
therein are eighty-eight thousand sages who are householders, who return again to this world, who serve as seeds, and who promote the Dharma. (3.187)

The word "they remain" (*tiṣṭhanti*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. For in that world known as Janasthāna, eighty-eight thousand householders (*gṛhamedhinaḥ*), who have conquered the worlds through their ritual actions such as the *agnihotra* and so forth, and who are the seeds of *saṃsāra*, having been dissolved [in heaven], act to uphold the Dharma; they go there by means of the *agnihotra* and other rites. Furthermore, because they turn toward this world again for the sake of propagating the Dharma, they are to be explained as "those who return" (*punarāvartinaḥ*). || 187 ||
By the same path as that of the Devayāna,
the seven Ṛṣis and the Nāgavīthi are situated, having taken their resort in the world of the gods;
there dwell just as many sages who have abandoned all undertakings.
This also is as before. || 188 ||

And that world which lies between the Seven Sages and the Nāgavīthi— those who have gone there by means of austerity, celibacy, renunciation of attachment, and wisdom, remain there until the dissolution of all beings. (3.189)

But surely, since the Veda has action as its purpose and there is no other means of valid cognition [to confirm it], this description of the paths and so forth appears to be without foundation. True, if the authority of the Veda were restricted solely to its capacity for enjoining action. However, its authority is indeed admitted even with respect to its own nature (the state of being).
For: "The Vedas, the Purāṇas, the sciences, the Upaniṣads, as well as verses, aphorisms, commentaries, and whatever else exists as speech anywhere—[all these constitute the source]. (3.190)
The recitation of the Vedas, sacrifice, celibacy, austerity, self-control, faith, fasting, and constancy are the causes for the knowledge of the Self. (3.191)

If ritual action (*kriyā*) alone were the meaning of the Veda, being caused solely by the performance of rituals, then there would be no focus on the essential nature (*svarūpa*). But when the accomplishment of the injunction (*niyoga*) is the sentence-meaning, then its accomplishment occurs only through the comprehension of one's status as the person to be enjoined (*niyojyatva*). Only for one who has realized the nature of the Self (*ātman*) can there be the fulfillment of the injunction. Consequently, the realization of the nature of the Self is indeed the meaning of the Veda; thus, the authority of the Veda is established in the essential nature itself. Furthermore, it was stated that the Veda’s authority lies in the "task to be done" (*kārya*), because linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) is based on such tasks. However, it is not possible for something intended for another (*parārtha*) to be a task to be done. For what person acting with deliberation would perform a task for the sake of another? Therefore, a task to be done is only for one's own sake. And since there is no purpose for the Self other than the knowledge of its own nature, that alone remains as the task. Thus, the ultimate authority of the Lordly Veda resides in that alone. As it has been said: "For the injunction (*codanā*) is able to make known an object of such a kind—past, present, or future" (TV on PMS 1.1.2, p. 15). The meaning is that it makes known the nature of the Self of such a kind. Accordingly, the prohibition of other senses is appropriate precisely because they have that [Self] as their object: "There is nothing else whatsoever, no other sense" (TV on PMS 1.1.2, p. 15). Otherwise, since there would be no possibility of attaining that [Self] through the meaning of an injunction, the prohibition would be entirely arbitrary. Therefore, the authority of this scripture must lie in the very nature of Brahman. And that alone is the ultimate reality of the meaning of the injunction. As for the communication of tasks such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice, that should be understood as being the meaning of subordinate sentences (*avāntara-vākyārtha*), intended for the removal of ignorance required for that [realization], and serving as a means thereto. Since it is not an object of other means of knowledge, it participates in the designation of a "task. If this is so, then the designation of a "task" is not contradictory even in the presentation of the nature of the path and so forth; this is the general direction. He shows this: "Since the Vedas and the Purāṇa," etc. All these are causes for the knowledge of the Self, because the determination of linguistic competency is established precisely through the intent toward that [Self]. Therefore, the authority of the Veda is unimpeded even regarding the essential nature. And thus, the tradition (*smṛti*) concerning the paths and so forth also possesses an irreproachable basis in the Veda; this is the intention. The word "and" (*ca*) in "and the Purāṇa" includes the meaning of the Itihāsas. "Knowledge" (*vidyā*) refers to Mīmāṃsā and the like. The separate mention of the Upaniṣads is to show that they constitute a distinct portion of the Veda dedicated to that [purpose]. Likewise, "verses" (*ślokas*) are the very mantras that serve as aphorisms (*sūtra*) for the Upaniṣads, such as: "That subtle, ancient, and wide-spread path... (BāU 4.4.8). Their separate mention is precisely to indicate their status as Upaniṣadic aphorisms. The explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and so forth are the commentaries (*bhāṣya*) intended to explain those [aphorisms]. This extensive elaboration of the Upaniṣads is due to their preeminence. Furthermore, "whatever consists of speech anywhere": the meaning is that even in the world, the competency of words is established only through intent toward the Self. And thus, the efforts of the four stages of life (*cāturāśramya*), such as the recitation of the Vedas, are for that very purpose. Thus says the sacred tradition: "The Brāhmaṇas seek to know that very Self through the recitation of the Vedas... (BāU 4.4.22). "Recitation of the Vedas" (*vedānuvacana*) is the repetition of what was taught by the teacher; this refers to the first stage of studenthood (*brahmacarya*). "Sacrifices" (*yajña*) is an indication of the householder's stage. "Studenthood" (*brahmacarya*) here means lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhikatva*). "Austerity" (*tapas*) and "self-restraint" (*dama*) refer to the forest-dweller's stage (*vānaprastha*). "Faith, fasting, and constancy" refers to the wandering mendicant's stage (*pārivrājya*), according to the statement: "Eight mouthfuls are the meal of a sage" (ĀpDh 2.9.13). Or, the word "fasting" (*upavāsa*) may mean eating light food. The rest has been explained. (190–1)
Since this is so,
therefore he is indeed to be meditated upon through all the stages of life (*āśrama*) in this very manner;
the intended meaning is that all undertakings have him as their ultimate goal.
Moreover: "Furthermore, it should be seen, reflected upon, and heard by the twice-born. (3.192)

The word "of the twice-born" (dvijāti) is intended to show that [the study] is for the purpose of the second birth, namely the initiation ceremony (upanayana). He is to be "seen" through perception and other means; he is to be "heard" from scripture; he is to be "reflected upon" by means of reasoning. The change in the order [of these verbs] is due to metrical requirements. He is to be "meditated upon" (nididhyāsya) so as to be directly realized through the path of yoga. || 192 ||
And those who follow the two previously mentioned paths—
those twice-born ones who, having resorted to the forest hermitage, know this [truth] in such a manner and worship it with supreme faith. (3.193)

The forest itself is the "forest-dweller" (*āraṇyaka*). According to the context, those who know it thus [know] here the intermediate nature of Brahman, such as Hiraṇyagarbha and so forth. The rest is clear. || 193 ||
And those who know this proceed in due order through the flame, the day, the bright fortnight, the northern solstice, the world of the gods, the sun, and the lightning. (3.194)
Then a person born of the mind approaches them and makes them inhabitants of the world of Brahmā;
for them, there is no return here again.

This path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi-mārga*) pertains to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); according to the capacity of one's meditation (*upāsana*), it is the cause for gradually conquering various worlds, as elaborated by the authors of the *Purāṇas*. Indra is praised [as] the one belonging to lightning (*vaidyuta*) due to mental contemplation (*abhidhyāna*). This very one is the inner self, the mental person (*mānasa-puruṣa*). And "non-returning" here means attaining that state. Regarding this world of transformation existing within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), there is no returning again. The rest is clear. (194–5)
And by remaining on the path of the Ajavīthī:
"Those men who have conquered heaven through sacrifice, austerity, and gifts, [travel] through smoke, the night, the dark fortnight, and the southern solstice. (3.196)
The world of the ancestors, the moon, the sky, the wind, the water, and the earth—
they arise here in this sequence, and in this very way they go forth again.

Having attained the state [of dissolution] by means of the sequence beginning with smoke and ending with the moon, according to the principle just described, they then reach the earth again by the sequence beginning with space. Thereafter, being elevated once more, they should be understood to assume the state of the seed of saṃsāra through a cycle like that of a wheel. The rest is straightforward. 196–7.
One whose mind is struck by demerit due to being excessively overwhelmed by passion and darkness,
and who does not understand these two paths of the self,
shall become either a venomous serpent, a moth, an insect, or a worm. (3.198)

And for that person whose impurities have been exhausted, once they somehow attain a state suitable for sacrifice and other rites through the arising of merit, there is the attainment of further excellence. "Dandaśūka" refers to those inclined to bite, such as snakes and the like. The rest is clear. || 198 ||
Now, out of great friendship, he describes the tradition of the path of yoga, which is the means for attaining the Supreme Self:
With the feet turned upward and placed upon the thighs, one should rest the left hand upon the right;
slightly raising the face and supporting it with the chest. (3.199)

With eyes closed, established in the quality of goodness (sattva), not touching tooth against tooth, with the tongue fixed motionless against the palate, the mouth closed, and perfectly still. (3.200)
Having fully restrained the collection of the senses, sitting on a seat that is neither too low nor too high,
one should undertake breath control (prāṇāyāma) twice or even thrice.

In accordance with other *yoga* treatises, *prāṇāyāma*, characterized by exhalation (*recaka*) and so forth, is to be understood. The rest is clear. These [postures] such as the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) and others, being causes for the concentration of the mind, are established as limbs of *yoga* precisely because they are already implied by their purpose. Therefore, some maintain that one-pointedness is not contradicted even otherwise. And thus it has been said by Dakṣa: "There is no exertion regarding the lotus posture," and so on. However, that is indeed improper because the scripture functions as a restrictive rule (*niyāmaka*). The statement of Dakṣa, on the other hand, is not contradictory because it is intended to praise the conquest of the senses. (199–201)
Having thoroughly purified himself through breath-control (prāṇāyāma),
the wise man, maintaining his concentration (dhāraṇā), should fix his self upon that Lord who resides in the heart like a lamp. 3.202.

That very Supreme Self—which resides in the heart like a lamp, not illumined by anything else but existing as the illuminator of all, and in whom the external phenomenal world has ceased—is the object of meditation. Established in the heart, that which is to be contemplated through seeing, hearing, reflecting, and so forth, the wise one, maintaining concentration (*dhāraṇā*) and higher synthesis (*prasaṃkhyāna*) directed toward that state, should maintain his own self therein solely as the nature of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*), even though Brahman possesses a dual nature. Having realized the essential nature of Brahman as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) who possesses both natures, he should maintain himself there as the Supreme Brahman, whose nature as meditator and object of meditation has ceased. And he should perceive within himself that stainless, fearless, non-returning, immediate Bliss, which is beyond all designations; thus the exposition should be elaborated. 202.

The meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) of the Supreme Brahman, who is the perfected yogi and the nature of the inner path-attainer, has been described; now, the characteristics of that very qualified practitioner must be stated, and therefore he says:
"Invisibility, memory, luster, vision, as well as knowledge through hearing, and the entry into another's body after casting off one's own body. (3.203)
The creation of objects at will is indeed the characteristic mark of perfection in yoga;
when yoga is perfected, one who casts off the body is fit for immortality.

Invisibility (*antardhāna*) is the state of being unperceivable by others. Memory (*smṛti*) is the non-forgetting of what has been understood through meditative concentration (*samādhi*); the meaning is that there is a constant realization of it exactly as it was, without interruption. Radiance (*kānti*) is the departure of hunger and other such afflictions. Vision (*dṛṣṭi*) is unimpeded perception regarding the future and so forth. Sound is called "the ear" (*śrotra*) because it is perceivable by the ear; "knowledge of the ear" (*śrotrajñatā*) is the knowledge of its objects. Likewise, this means without dependence on the study of the Vedas (*vedānusaṃdhāna*) through sound. Regarding the body: having cast off one's own specific body—which is produced by particular karma and is perceived through unique [sensory] cognitions—as being composed of both the existent and the non-existent, the entry into another's body (*parakāyapraveśana*), which consists of the previously mentioned universal form (*viśvarūpa*), is the attainment of oneness (*ekatvāpatti*). As for the entry into another's body while still remaining in the form of a body, that exists even in the case of mantra-sciences (*vidyā*); therefore, it is not relevant here, and it should be explained in this very way. The creation or emission of objects—such as the Great Principle (*mahat*), the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāra*), and so forth—at will, that is, by desire (*icchā*), is their production. The rest is clear. Thus, when yoga is accomplished through the nature of the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), one who abandons the body—which participates in the designations of the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) and the meditator (*dhyātṛ*) consisting of the higher and lower states—is fit, that is, capable, for immortality and non-return [to saṃsāra] by virtue of the supreme Brahman-nature. || 203–4 ||

Thus has the state of wandering mendicancy been described up to its ultimate attainment for those of pure essence who know reality. But for one who is incapable in this regard due to any defect of mind, speech, or body, he states this other variety of mendicancy: "Or else, practicing the Veda, having renounced ritual acts, dwelling with his son, eating what is unasked and being moderate in food, he shall attain supreme perfection. (3.205)

By practicing the Veda through the recitation and repetition of its words and meanings, having abandoned the performance of the *agnihotra* and other rites, and without distinguishing marks of his specific order, he should subsist solely on alms. Alternatively, if he is unable to do that, he may eat measured food—such as eight mouthfuls—without asking for it, and dwell in the house of a son or elsewhere. In this way, he shall attain Brahmanhood, which is characterized as the means to reaching the supreme perfection. || 205 ||

Although this instruction on liberation is given with reference to the life of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*), nevertheless, the specific stage of life (*āśrama*) is not a determining factor; for liberation is caused merely by the cessation of activity according to one's own will, and it is to be accomplished solely through knowledge. Since this is so, therefore: Even a householder is liberated if he possesses wealth acquired by righteous means, is devoted to the knowledge of reality, is fond of guests, performs ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), and speaks the truth. (3.206)

The word *śrāddha* is intended as an indicator for all the duties of a householder; the rest is clear. (206) Thus ends the section on the duties of ascetics (*yatidharma*). Now begins the section on the duties of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

Having thus declared the duties specific to each stage of life as well as those common to all, the author, now desiring to teach the occasional duties consisting of expiations for the purpose of destroying faults, first elaborates upon the fault caused by the transgression of prohibitions:
"Having reached the terrible and censured hells born of mortal sins (mahāpātaka), those who have committed such great sins are reborn here [in this world] upon the exhaustion of their karma. (3.207)

It should be explained as follows: those who die without having performed expiation after committing either a *mahāpātaka* (grave sin) or an *upapātaka* (minor sin), experience—due to that cause—the twenty-one most despicable hells related to the world of Yama, such as *Tāmisra* and others, which arise from those sins and are characterized by intense suffering. Once their experience of the fruits of those intense karmas is exhausted, they are born here in the manner to be described below for the purpose of experiencing the remainder of those karmas; thus they become *mahāpātakins*. If, however, it were explained as "only through the total exhaustion of karma," then the statement "but the *mahāpātakins* here... would be incoherent. Therefore, it must be explained as "from the exhaustion of karma" (*karmakṣayāt*). || 207 ||

In that regard, he will speak of the hells; however, he elaborates here on how they are born [there]: "The killer of a Brahmin goes into the wombs of dogs, pigs, deer, and camels; the drinker of spirituous liquor [goes] into those of donkeys, Pulkasas, and Śvasanas—of this there is no doubt. (3.208)
A thief of gold shall attain the state of worms, insects, and moths;
and one who violates the teacher’s bed shall gradually become a blade of grass, a shrub, or a creeper.

The dog and the others are well known. Here, the *sūkara* (pig) refers to the domestic pig because of its proximity to the dog. The word *mṛga* (wild animal) should also be understood as referring to jackals and the like, following the context. Since this presentation is for the sake of illustration, one need not strive excessively here to establish a distinction of scope with other Smṛtis. Furthermore, because the passage begins with "having reached the terrible hells born of mortal sins," this detailed exposition should be understood as concerning intentional major sins (*mahāpātaka*) and the like. This is because the specific connection between cause and effect is meaningful when it corresponds to the nature of the cause—namely, being produced by a terrible and censurable act. Otherwise, since that [distinction] would already be established by the word "hell" alone, the [additional detail] would be purposeless. Consequently, other Smṛtis should also be explained in this very way. And thus says the Vedic tradition: having begun with "Together with him, he then went forth," it concludes, "In this manner, these [beings] associate in that world; we, here, associate with them" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 11.6.1.3), thereby showing that the torment is indeed for those who act intentionally. Likewise, Vyāsa says:
"Sin committed intentionally is experienced in the hells;
those who have committed sins unintentionally shall encounter afflictions even in this very world. Thus it is said.

Therefore, even if there were statements in other Smṛtis regarding some degree of excessive torment even for an unintentional act, they must nevertheless be interpreted as being intended for censure (*nindā*) in order to ensure its absolute avoidance. The statement "the drinker of spirituous liquor [becomes] a donkey, a *pulkasa*, or a *veṇa*—of this there is no doubt" includes the phrase "no doubt" to preclude any suspicion that this might be a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Furthermore, the word "donkey" (*khara*) is intended to indicate any animal species similar to a donkey. A *pulkasa* is one born from a Kṣatriya woman by a Śūdra father; a *veṇa* is an actor. "The stealer of gold shall attain the state of worms, insects, and so forth"—here the prefix *sam-* is used to convey the sense of excessive suffering. "The violator of the Guru’s bed shall attain various kinds of stationary states such as grass and so on"—by using the word "gradually" (*kramaśaḥ*), he shows that through a single cause one undergoes a connection with affliction to be experienced over many births in various forms. The rest is clear. (208–9)
Having thus experienced birth in the animal realm in succession, they are thereafter born among the four castes. Furthermore, in that regard:

"The killer of a Brahmin shall suffer from consumption; the drinker of spirituous liquor shall have black teeth; the stealer of gold shall have deformed nails; and the violator of the Guru’s bed shall have diseased skin. (3.210)

Consumption (*kṣaya*) refers to pulmonary tuberculosis (*rājayakṣmā*). Those such as having black teeth (*śyāvadanta*) and so forth are clear. And skin diseases (*dauścarmya*) should be understood as applicable to women as well, according to the circumstances. Even for one who, though capable, does not perform expiation (*prāyaścitta*) despite having committed a sin unintentionally, these torments of hell are to be understood as occurring in accordance with his own karma. Furthermore, symptoms such as consumption and the like certainly manifest even for those who are incapable of performing expiation due to lack of ability. And thus it is said: "In this world, some [suffer] because of their current misconduct, and others likewise because of what was done in the past."
"Evil-minded men undergo a transformation of their physical form.

(MDh 11.48) Because of the expression "here by evil deeds," the meaning is that even in this life, due to evil deeds—whether committed in a previous birth for which no atonement was performed, or committed in this life for which atonement has not been undertaken—and because of the word "likewise" (*tathāśabdāt*), those of evil character who have somehow failed to perform atonement after the experience of hell and other such states, come to possess deformed bodies and undergo a transformation from their natural state, such as having white teeth and so forth, to having black teeth and the like. || 210 ||
Thus has it been stated regarding the four great sinners; as for association with them: "Whosoever drinks from the same vessel as any of these, he is born bearing their characteristic mark."

The meaning is that among those who have fallen [from their caste], whoever drinks with whomsoever, he is born with the very symptoms—whether individually or collectively, according to the nature of the association—of that person’s consumption disease (*kṣayaroga*) and so forth. Furthermore, because of the word *abhi* (towards/with), it should be understood that when the parents themselves are possessed of such diseases as consumption, the child is born with symptoms corresponding to them by virtue of being born into that lineage. However, if the reading is *yadi tu sa talliṅge ’bhijāyate*, then even if he himself does not possess those symptoms, it should be understood that whoever is born into a family possessing such symptoms has associated with those fallen ones in that manner. Consequently, it should also be applied to what follows that they must likewise perform penance (*prāyaścitta*).
To elaborate that deformities indeed occur even apart from the great sins (mahāpātaka), he first shows this regarding the matter of theft:
"The stealer of food shall be afflicted with consumption; the stealer of speech shall be mute. (3.211)
One who steals grain shall have an extra limb; a slanderer, a putrid nose; one who steals oil, a habit of drinking oil; and a backbiter, a foul-smelling mouth. (3.212)

Being afflicted by disease, however, refers to having a weak digestive fire (*mandāgni*). A "stealer of speech" is one who, by administering poison or the like, or through ignorance as a physician, or through improper treatment, steals away speech. Others maintain that "stealing speech" consists of reciting [the Veda] without permission and studying what has not been authorized; yet that is called "theft of Brahman" (*brahmasteya*), not the "stealing of speech. As Manu says: "But he who should obtain the Veda from one who is studying it without permission, being joined with the theft of Brahman, falls into hell" (MDh 2.116).

One who mixes other grains with grain for the purpose of selling it is a "grain-mixer. A "backbiter" (*piśuna*) is one who steals away the virtues of others. One with a "putrid nose" (*pūtināsika*) is one whose nose is rotten. A "stealer of oil" (*tailahṛt*) is a thief of mere oil. An "oil-drinker" (*tailapāyī*) is a specific kind of insect. One with a "putrid mouth" (*pūtivaktra*) is one whose mouth is rotten. A "slanderer" (*sūcaka*) is one who, upon another's acquisition of wealth or similar gain, brings forth verbal faults for the sake of destroying that [gain]. The rest is clear. 211–2.
Likewise: "Having abducted another's wife and having stolen the property of a Brahmin, one is born as a Brahma-rākṣasa in a waterless region in the forest. (3.213)

It should be explained that by seizing the wife of another who is superior—whether by birth or by virtue—who is to be enjoyed as a woman, or by stealing the property of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmasva*) or a kinsman, one becomes a *brahmarākṣasa*. A *brahmarākṣasa* is one whose body is subject to extreme torment, being burned internally and externally by the fire-like Veda (*brahman*). This state of being a *brahmarākṣasa* should be understood, by implication, to apply specifically to those who study the Vedas; therefore, even one endowed with the learning and recitation of the Śruti must not approach the wife of another who is superior. Thus says the sacred tradition (*Āmnāya*): "Therefore, one who knows this should not desire to joke even with the wife of a learned Śrotriya, for he who knows this perishes" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.12). Likewise: "He indeed dies devoid of sense organs, devoid of vigor, and with all his merit exhausted; what else could happen to him other than such a state of being a *brahmarākṣasa*? Therefore, it is well said that one is born as a *brahmarākṣasa* in the forest without water. 213.
Those who steal jewels are born into low castes; having stolen leaves or vegetables, one becomes a peacock, and having stolen fine fragrances, a muskrat. (3.214)
But in the *Mānava*:
"Having stolen gems, pearls, corals, and various other jewels out of greed, men are born among the goldsmiths" (MDh 12.61).

Thus, the status of being a goldsmith has been shown. Here, however, the phrase "in a low caste" is not contradictory because it serves as a definition for the final [category] in Manu’s statement; or else, it is intended to demonstrate the extreme degradation of the goldsmith caste. The rest is clear. || 214 ||
A mouse indicates the theft of grain; a camel, a vehicle; a monkey, fruit; a goat, livestock; a crow, milk; and a house-builder, household utensils. (3.215)

A vehicle refers to a cart and so forth; fruit refers to mangoes and so forth; livestock refers to horses and so forth; milk refers to cow's milk; a house-builder refers to a bricklayer or mason. The rest is clear. || 215 ||

A honey-thief becomes a gadfly; a thief of meat, a vulture; a thief of a cow, an iguana; likewise, a thief of fire, a heron; a thief of clothing, one afflicted with leprosy; a thief of liquids, a dog; and a thief of salt, a cricket.

*Madhu* refers to honey or wine; *pala* means meat. Here, by the word "cow" (*gām*), a female is to be understood, since the term "beast" (*paśu*) already denotes the entire class of cattle. The word "likewise" (*tathā*) here is intended to indicate the various species, such as the crane (*baka*), involved in the carrying of fire according to the different methods of consecrated (*saṃskṛta*) or domestic (*aupāsana*) fires. Similarly, in the subsequent passage, it is intended to indicate the distinction between red, white, and other colors of leprosy (*śvitra*) in accordance with the specific types of stains on clothing. A dog (*śvā*) is well known. Or [the reading may be] *arasam*, because the *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) is identical. Having stolen sapless food, such as stale food and the like, one attains the womb of a dog. The particle *tu* is for the sake of emphasis. This is also for the sake of showing respect: where even the theft of stale food results in becoming a dog, we do not know what will happen in the case of stealing more significant items, in order to demonstrate this. A *cīrī* is a particular kind of insect that is whirled about in the heat of the summer season. || 216 ||
Now he concludes:
"This has been stated by me for the purpose of illustration regarding the act of theft; for just as there are various kinds of objects, so too are there various classes of living beings. (3.217)

The phrase "in the case of theft" is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇārtha*). In all cases—in the act of killing, the act of eating forbidden food, and the act of approaching another's wife—one must elaborate upon the various forms of deformity, disease, poverty, separation from kinsmen, and so forth, as well as the afflictions of execution, imprisonment, and the like, occurring among animals and humans in accordance with one's own karma. He elaborates on this very point: just as the types of objects being stolen, the types of beings being killed, and the types of others' wives being approached are manifold, so too are the various species of living beings for the purpose of experiencing those [results]. Therefore, due to the engagement in prohibited acts, the non-performance of prescribed duties, and the failure to perform penance even when other causes such as marrying before an elder brother (*parivitti*) exist, one must elaborate upon the attainment of birth and the resulting afflictions in those various wombs that abound in the experience of suffering. (217)
This very point is clarified:
"Having thus practiced according to their karma, through the passage of time they are born as animals; then, fallen from their marks, they become impoverished and the lowest of men. (3.218)

Having experienced hells and rebirth as animals in accordance with the specific nature of their evil deeds, they are subsequently born—after the lapse of time—as the lowest of men, impoverished and devoid of the characteristics befitting virtuous persons; the intention is that no elevation is possible for them. Therefore, they must certainly perform penance even in this very life. Accordingly, Vasiṣṭha has stated: "One with deformed nails, having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, shall uplift himself" (VaDh 20.6). Thus, the intention is that penance must indeed be performed even by those who do not possess such physical marks, but are nonetheless impoverished and the lowest of men. Furthermore, since the possession of characteristics such as deformed nails is already included by the mention of "rebirth as an animal," it follows that after experiencing even that [animal state] over time, they are deprived of those marks like deformed nails and are born as the impoverished and lowest of men. Consequently, the intention is that penance must certainly be performed. (218)
Furthermore, those who, even after committing sins, properly perform the corresponding expiations—for them there is not even the slightest persistence of demerit.
Consequently, having become stainless, they are born into great families as enjoyers of wealth, endowed with auspicious marks, and possessed of riches and grain. (3.219)

The meaning of this verse is clear. Others, however, explain that they become free from stain precisely because of their enjoyment of the results of unwholesome karma; but since that interpretation serves little purpose and is contrary to the intended meaning, it should not be accepted. || 219 ||
Now he shows the occasion upon which penance must be performed:
"By the non-performance of what is prescribed, by the performance of what is censured, and by the lack of restraint over the senses, a man undergoes downfall. (3.220)

This is because of the non-performance of prescribed duties—both those based on Smṛti, such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and the *Aṣṭakā* rites, and those based on Śruti, such as the *Agnihotra*; and because of the indulgence in what is forbidden when, by implication, there was an occasion for censurable acts. For this very reason, although one might have said "of the forbidden," the term "censurable" (*nindita*) is used; otherwise, since even the performance of the *Ṣoḍaśī* sacrifice—which is forbidden for certain classes despite being prescribed by word—would result in a fall, [the specific term would be necessary]. Furthermore, "due to the non-restraint of the senses" means due to the failure to perform expiation (*prāyaścitta*). The mention of "man" (*nara*) is intended to show that this applies to all social classes (*sārvavarṇika*). As for the phrase "he incurs a fall" (*patanam ṛcchati*), "fall" is intended here specifically as becoming subject to expiation, and not as a loss of the status of the twice-born (*dvijāti*), for the latter pertains to mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*). Thus, in the *Mānava Dharmaśāstra*, it says, "the man becomes liable for expiation" (MDh 11.44), which refers precisely to the fitness for expiation. Now, one might object: "But the non-performance of expiation is itself simply the non-performance of what is prescribed. This is not so. Expiation is for the purpose of destroying a fault (*doṣa*), whereas the *Agnihotra* and other such rites are merely occasional (*naimittika*) obligations. Therefore, by its non-performance, the destruction of the fault simply does not occur; it does not, however, entail an additional fault. When the statement "and due to the non-restraint of the senses in this case" is present, it follows that not only is the destruction of the fault absent, but an additional cause for a fall is incurred. Consequently, this effort is made so that for such a person, the punishment and the expiation may be more severe. This is also stated in the *Mānava Dharmaśāstra*.

"By failing to perform prescribed duties, by practicing what is censured, and by becoming addicted to the objects of the senses, a man becomes liable to penance" (MDh 11.44). Thus, the failure to perform penance itself should be explained as addiction to the objects of the senses. However, if the phrase "becoming addicted to the objects of the senses" were stated with the intention of referring to objects that are neither prescribed nor prohibited—in order to prevent excessive indulgence—then:

There would be a contradiction with the statement, "One should not neglect dharma, artha, and kāma according to one's ability" (MDh 4.21), because the over-extension [of desire] has already been prevented by the verse, "Being devoted to desire is not praised" (MDh 2.2). Therefore, the previous explanation alone is superior. The rest is clear. || 220 ||

Because a person faces the risk of falling due to the non-performance of what is enjoined, the performance of what is censured, the failure to perform expiation, and the lack of restraint over the senses—which all entail the necessity of severe penance—therefore he must here perform expiation for the sake of purification. In this way, both his inner self and the world become gracious toward him. (3.221)

When a certain cause exists such that there is the risk of falling [from one's status] due to the failure to perform expiation (*prāyaścitta*), then that person possessing such a cause must necessarily perform expiation—either in secret according to the method of secret expiation to be described hereafter, or publicly according to the mode of public expiation—as appropriate to his standing, for the sake of self-purification and for the sake of establishing his reputation in worldly dealings. The word "here" (*iha*) signifies immediate succession; the meaning is: "right here," that is, at the time immediately following the occurrence of the cause. This being so, the inner self (*antarātman*) of this wrongdoer becomes pleased through the performance of secret expiation, and the world becomes pleased with him through the practice of public expiation; the meaning is that he becomes acceptable in the sphere of social interaction. (221)
For this reason as well, penance must necessarily be performed; for it is said:
"Sin committed through ignorance is removed by penances;
however, one who acts intentionally becomes fit for social intercourse here on earth only by virtue of a scriptural declaration. (3.222)

The meaning of the entire verse is that since sin—whether committed unintentionally or intentionally—is removed without remainder by means of specific expiations (prāyaścitta) consisting of both public and secret rites, therefore expiations must necessarily be performed.

Now, it may be argued that sin committed intentionally does not depart at all through penances. Even if, by the force of scriptural injunction, one becomes fit for social intercourse (*saṃvyavahāryatva*) here despite the sin not having departed, let it be so. For this very reason it was said: "But one who acts intentionally becomes fit for social intercourse in this world by virtue of the scriptural statement. The intention is that while fitness for social intercourse exists in this world, the sin itself does not depart. And thus Manu says: "This purification has been declared for having killed a twice-born man unintentionally."
"No expiation is prescribed for the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa" (MDh 11.89),
and likewise:
"When a sin has been committed unintentionally, an expiation is prescribed" (MDh 11.45).
Thus it was stated according to his own intention. Likewise, the presentation of the opinion of others was made by the second half of the verse:
"Some say that [the same applies] even when an act is done intentionally, because of the observation in the Śruti" (MDh 11.45).

The Blessed One’s intention is that some people, deluded by other Vedic *arthavāda* passages, claim there is expiation even for an act committed intentionally; however, that is not my view. Accordingly, similar statements are found in other Smṛtis such as the Vasiṣṭha-dharmaśāstra: “There is expiation for an offense committed unintentionally” (VaDh 20.1), and so forth. Therefore, this notion that sin is removed even by an intentional act through expiation is merely imagined by one's own intellect. How then is this verse [to be understood]?
"One should not engage in any business with those who have committed offenses until they have been purified" (MDh 11.189).

The meaning of this is also as follows: as long as those who have committed offenses do not perform penance, no transaction whatsoever should be carried out with them. For this very reason it has been said: "And one should never despise these people once they have performed purification" (MDh 11.189).

This is what is meant: although a sin committed intentionally does not depart through expiations (*prāyaścitta*), nevertheless, one should not despise these people even in the slightest when they have performed their expiation, particularly in matters of social interaction (*vyavahāra*). For otherwise, if it were simply stated that "one should not associate with those who have not been purified," it would follow by implication that one may indeed associate with those who have performed purification; in that case, the phrase "and these [who have] performed purification" would be entirely redundant. Therefore, in the case of intentional acts, there is merely the eligibility for social interaction, but no removal of the sin. Furthermore, he who, having seen a prohibition, proceeds to transgress it, does so only by accepting the experience of hell and other such states. Consequently, for such a person, an expiation—since it is not required for the purpose of destroying the sin—would serve only a transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Thus, this passage must be explained as meaning: "But [after penance], one is fit for social interaction despite the intentional act."

To this it is replied: First of all, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), being enjoined when a fault constitutes the occasion (*nimitta*), is understood to serve solely for the purpose of destroying that fault, since no other result can be logically established. In that context, even a specific qualification mentioned in connection with the occasion—such as in the case of "he whose both sacrificial offerings (*havis*) should meet with ruin" (cf. Śabara on PMS 6.4.31)—is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). Therefore, the instruction regarding expiation applies without distinction to both cases, such as the killing of a Brahmin and so forth. As for the statement: "No atonement is prescribed for the intentional killing of a Brahmin" (MDh 11.89).

Thus, that [statement] is for the purpose of censure or for the purpose of a penance ending in death (*maraṇāntika-prāyaścitta*), but not for the purpose of exempting one from penance, because that is already established by the first half [of the verse]; if it were so, there would be the consequence of its being purposeless (*ānarthakya*). For this very reason, even in the case of an intentional act, it was stated in the passage "but he may be dealt with socially" (*kāmato vyavahāryas tu*) for the sake of establishing a living penance.

Now, it might be argued: "In this context, it was said that social acceptability (*vyavahāryatva*) in this world arises from the scriptural statement, whereas sin committed unintentionally alone departs, and not the other."

This is not tenable, because it contradicts the Śruti. As it is said, beginning with: "Indra gave the Yatis to the hyenas; a vulgar voice cried out after him; he ran to Prajāpati; therefore, he gave him this Upahavya sacrifice," and continuing, "One should cause one who is being falsely accused to perform this sacrifice" (PB 18.9–10). Thus, by the force of the introductory context (*upakrama*), this is understood to apply only to intentional acts. Likewise, beginning with: "With this, indeed, Indra caused Daivāpa Śaunaka to perform the sacrifice for Janamejaya Pārīkṣita," and continuing, "Verily, he who performs the Aśvamedha destroys all evil deeds and all the sin of killing a Brahmin" (ŚB 13.5.4.1). Because of the use of the word "all," the Aśvamedha is understood to apply only to intentional acts. Therefore, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be performed for the removal of sin, not for the sake of establishing one's fitness for social intercourse. And so it is stated immediately thereafter: "The sacrificers belonging to the lineage of Pārīkṣita cast off both past and future evil karma through the Aśvamedhas, by means of meritorious action" (ŚB 13.5.4.3). This demonstrates the quality of removing sin. By saying "the meritorious [become] meritorious through meritorious action," it clearly shows the very eradication of the root of non-merit. Therefore, the interpretation of the Smṛti in accordance with the direct Śruti is the proper course. And so says Manu:
"Sin committed unintentionally is purified by the study of the Vedas," having said this, [the text continues]:
"But that which is committed intentionally through delusion is purified by various kinds of penances. (MDh 11.46)

In this context, "delusion" (*moha*) is intended to mean a disregard for the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* due to being conceited, and not delusion characterized by insanity and the like; for in the case of such a person who is insane, there would be no distinction between an act committed intentionally and one committed unintentionally. The intention is this: when someone—who behaves correctly regarding perceptible objects and understands the meaning of the scriptures—is nevertheless impelled by atheism or an excessive desire for worldly objects and, out of delusion, considers the scripture to be inconsistent, then the sin committed by him through that intentional delusion is removed by various kinds of extremely heavy expiations (*prāyaścitta*). Consequently, since it might follow that sins such as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) committed intentionally could only be removed by expiations ending in death, the Teacher has stated: "Even after committing a sin intentionally, by virtue of the explicit words of the *Śruti*, one becomes fit for social intercourse (*vyavahāryatva*) in this very life after washing away the sin through the Aśvamedha and other sacrifices. Furthermore, if through expiation there were merely fitness for social intercourse and not the destruction of the fault itself, then one who had performed the expiation once would not be unfit for social intercourse even if he committed the killing of a Brahmin again. On the other hand, if the expiation were for the purpose of destroying the fault, then because the fault would arise again even for one who has performed the expiation, it would follow that another expiation would be required to destroy that [new] fault. However, when the very fact of having performed the expiation is the cause for fitness for social intercourse, then since that state of having performed the expiation does not depart as long as one lives, why would he be unfit for social intercourse?

Now, it might be argued: even though expiation (prāyaścitta) removes sin, because it is occasional (naimittika), it would follow that it must be performed again whenever the occasion (nimitta) arises once more.

That is incorrect. This is not a contingent expiation (*naimittika-prāyaścitta*) prescribed for a specific occasion (*nimitta*), such as the injunction "one offers when [the ladle] is broken" (*bhinne juhoti*, Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.2.3), which applies to the occasion of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) and so forth. What then? It is for the sake of restoring social intercourse (*saṃvyavahāryatva*) even while one remains otherwise unfit for social intercourse (*asaṃvyavahāryatva*). In that regard, if the meaning of the statement were: "One should not drink from the same vessel with one who has committed a deed such as killing a Brahmin and has not performed expiation," then for one who has committed it once, the state of having performed expiation would exist until death; thus, there would be no state of unfitness for social intercourse. Alternatively, if the meaning were: "Whenever the killing of a Brahmin occurs, whenever the expiation is performed, then there is fitness for social intercourse"—in that case, the connection would be merely for the sake of time (*kālārtha-saṃyoga*). Consequently, if for some reason the expiation was not performed immediately after the act, then because the [prescribed] time had passed, it would provide no benefit whatsoever, just like the *sandhyopāsana* rite performed after sunrise when the time has already elapsed. Furthermore, if the contingent expiation were not for the purpose of destroying the fault (*doṣa-nirghāta*), then all the various expiations taught would have to be performed without distinction, since there would be no basis for option (*vikalpa*) or the differentiation of scope. For if all expiations serve the single purpose of destroying the fault, an option is logical due to their identical function, and the postulation of a differentiation of scope is also appropriate. However, if it were a contingent rite performed unintentionally (*akāmakṛta-naimittika*) without any other purpose, then in the absence of a single common effect, an option between them would be without authority. Even where an option is expressed by the word *vā* instead of *ca*, as for example: [text continues].

In such passages as, "Or, eating sacrificial food, he should follow the Sarasvatī upstream" (MDh 11.77), one might argue that even there, some single alternative would apply without restriction. However, this is not tenable here because it would result in the redundancy of the more arduous alternative; for its purpose is established as being specific to that case, serving to expiate the fault committed unintentionally. Now, it might be said: since penances are intended to restore the eligibility for the duties of the twice-born to one who has fallen and is thus disqualified, they indeed share a single purpose; therefore, the postulation of distinct scopes is entirely appropriate here as well.

That too is incorrect, precisely because it entails the same faults mentioned previously. Furthermore, even if [the expiation] were for the sake of eligibility (*adhikāra*), would the expiation effect the removal of the performer’s unfitness or the production of fitness? In that regard, unfitness is caused by such acts as the killing of a Brahmin. And that [unfitness] would exist either by virtue of possessing the defect produced by that act, or merely by the fact of being the agent. If it were merely the state of being the agent of the killing, then since that [agency] perishes immediately after the action, there would be no purpose in its removal. If, however, it persists even at a later time, then it could not be removed even by a thousand expiations. If, on the other hand, unfitness consists in the possession of a defect, then, since fitness can be produced through the power of removing that [defect], the expiation would serve solely the purpose of destroying the defect. If it were argued that the expiation produces another, distinct *apūrva* (transcendental result) in the form of fitness, rather than removing the unfitness consisting in the possession of a defect, then—just like the *Anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice—it would have to be performed only once; furthermore, it would follow that expiations are auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the ritual, and in this case too, one would have to postulate, without any evidence, that they assist the sacrifice and are for its sake. Moreover, if it were said that in the case of intentional (*kāmakṛta*) acts, the expiation serves only to establish eligibility, then death-penalty expiations (*maraṇāntika*) would apply only to unintentional acts, while living expiations would apply only to intentional ones, because eligibility is impossible for one who is dead, since it is only for the living that social reintegration (*saṃvyavahāryatva*) is required. In that case, statements such as those by Āpastamba—"In this world, his restoration is possible, but the stain is destroyed" (ĀpDh 1.24.25)—would become irrelevant. Likewise: [And so forth.]
"The established rule is that [the offense] is intentional, not to be described [further], and punishable by death.

(MDh 11.146) Thus, there is an instruction regarding the subject matter even in the case of ignorance. For example, the Vasiṣṭha-smṛti states: "In the case of drinking *surā* through ignorance, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is prescribed" (VaDh 20.19). Likewise:
"Having drunk *vāruṇī* through ignorance, one is purified by the purificatory rite alone" (MDh 11.146).
In this way, there would be inconsistency regarding all such types of Smṛti texts; furthermore, there would be no expiation for secret [sins].

Therefore, this verse of Yājñavalkya should be explained as follows: Just as sin arises even when a prohibited act is committed unintentionally because of the scriptural injunction regarding expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and that sin is removed by such expiations; in exactly the same way, even when a sin is committed intentionally, the expiation does not necessarily end with death. Rather, according to statements such as "he crosses over all evil" (VaDh 22.6), he becomes free from stain and fit for social interaction right here in this world. Enough of this digression. || 222 ||
He clarifies this very point with the following verse:
"Men who do not perform penance for their sins, who are devoted to evil deeds, and who feel no remorse, go to terrible and agonizing hells. (3.223)

For those who act out of desire, at the time of their engagement they bind themselves with an intense attachment to sins; being thus devoted to sin, if they should be without remorse, then, failing to perform expiations, they fall into painful and unbearable hells. Although the word "painful" (*kaṣṭa*) already establishes this, the addition of "terrible" (*dāruṇa*) is for the purpose of expressing excessive condemnation. However, those who might somehow commit a sin unintentionally necessarily become remorseful; nor is there any devotion to sin on their part. Even if they do not perform expiation, they will nevertheless undergo torment in this very world of humans—either in this birth or in another—but not in the *Tāmisra* and other hells associated with the realm of Yama; this has already been stated previously. Thus says a Vedic mantra: "May we not, acting crookedly, fall into hell. "Acting crookedly" (*jihmāyantaḥ*) means having engaged in deceit, that is to say, having acted out of deliberate desire. Therefore, in the case of what is done unintentionally, there is no falling into hell at all. And so says Vyāsa:
"Sin committed intentionally is experienced in the hells;
