those who commit sins unintentionally shall undergo afflictions even in this very world.
Therefore, since penance (*prāyaścitta*) is for the purpose of destroying faults, it is logical that by its non-performance one attains the most terrible hells. || 223 ||
He now shows those hells:
Tāmisra, Lohaśaṅku, Mahāniraya, Śalmali, Raurava, Kuḍmala, Pūtimṛttika, and Kālasūtraka. (3.224)
Saṃghāta, Lohitoda, Saviṣa, Saṃpratāpana,
the great Naraka Kākola, Saṃjīvana, and Nadīpatha.
Avīci, Andhatāmisra, and likewise Kumbhīpāka; Asipatravana and Tapana, making twenty-one in total.

Here, by means of two verses, sixteen hells are described, and by the third, five; thus, there are twenty-one in total. *Tāmisra* is that which is exceedingly full of darkness. *Lokaśaṅku* is that place where iron spikes are incessantly driven into all the limbs. *Mahāniraya* is where there is constant hurling with great speed and force. *Śalmali* is where thorny *śalmali* trees, made of copper and glowing like fire, are embraced. *Raurava* is where heated iron horns, having pierced the bones, rise up like the *ruru* deer. *Kuḍmala*—which means "unblossomed"—is so called because, just as an unblossomed lotus or the like remains in a closed state, so too there all the limbs are crushed and made into buds; this is the hell named *Kuḍmala*. There is another reading: *raurava-kaśmala*, meaning it is mostly hair and filth. *Pūtimṛttika* is self-evident. *Kālasūtraka* is where beings are held suspended in the air on black threads (*kālasūtra*) and those threads are constantly moved. *Saṃghāta* is where they are crowded together just as two very dirty people might join together to thresh rice and such. *Lohitatoda* is where there is blood in all water-related functions. *Saviṣa* is where venomous hooded serpents devour them incessantly. *Saṃpratāpana* is from being tormented intensely both inside and out. There is another reading: *ṛbīsa-saṃpratāpana*; therein, they are cooked while constantly situated within the womb-like interior of the belly. *Mahānaraka* is that in comparison to which other hells, such as *Kālasūtra* and others, are minor. *Kākola* is where they are pecked day and night by crows and owls with iron beaks. *Saṃjīvana* is where, after being revived again and again, they are killed in various ways. *Nadīpatha* refers to the hell whose path is the river named *Vaitaraṇī*, whose waters consist mostly of pus. *Avīci* is where they are buried face-down in a pit filled with embers and set ablaze by a forest fire. *Andhatāmisra* is where blind serpents, as if in *Tāmisra*, are crushed by carts. *Kumbhīpāka* is self-evident. *Asipatravana* is where they are dragged through a grove of palm trees whose leaves are as sharp as sword blades. *Tapana* is where the fierce sun alone scorches, and no other great elements exist there. (224–6)

Thus, these twenty-one hells are reached by the lowest of men who have failed to perform penance, being pursued by the terrible consequences of their great sins (mahāpātaka) as well as their minor offenses (upapātaka), in accordance with their own karma. (3.227)

The inclusion of the word "ghora" (terrible) is for the purpose of indicating intentional performance (*kāmakāra*). The intended meaning is that those who, being possessed of and joined with sins produced by great crimes (*mahāpātaka*) and minor crimes (*upapātaka*) committed intentionally, do not perform expiation (*prāyaścitta*) due to an excess of atheism (*nāstikya*), they alone go to these hells; however, this does not apply even to those whose sins were committed unintentionally. Apart from great crimes, minor crimes, and those [crimes] extended by analogy (*atideśika*) to them, there is no attainment of hell even when [the act] is performed intentionally; in that case, the result is merely rebirth as an animal (*tiryaktva*). As Manu said: "Whatever property of another a man may forcibly seize..."
"He necessarily goes to the state of an animal after having consumed an oblation that has not been offered. (MDh 12.68).
The meaning is "by force" or "through intentional action. || 227 ||
Who, then, are those who commit mortal sins? To this he says:

"The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, and likewise the violator of the Guru’s bed—these are the perpetrators of mortal sins, as is he who drinks with them for a year. (3.228)

He who kills a Brāhmaṇa, whether by his own hand or as an instigator, or causes him to be killed, is a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahā*). The word "intoxicant" (*madya*) should be understood here as referring specifically to that distilled from flour (*paiṣṭī*). A "thief" (*stena*) is one who steals the gold of a Brāhmaṇa. One who violates the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpagas*) is to be known as he who approaches the wife of his teacher or his father. With these persons—either individually or all together—one should "drink together," meaning one should engage in eating, drinking, and so forth, in their company. As for how long this should last, the author says: "for a year" (*samām*), which means for one full year. Such is the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*).

"The thief of gold, the drinker of spirituous liquor, the violator of the teacher's bed, and the slayer of a Brahmin—these four fall, as does the fifth who associates with them. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.9)

The word *hiraṇya* is used exclusively for gold (*suvarṇa*) except when accompanied by another qualifying term. This is established in the *Chāndogya*: "In all cases, one should understand *hiraṇya* to mean *jātarūpa* (gold). The Sūtra authors have stated this while adhering precisely to the method of the Śruti. Likewise, the Carakas, having introduced the topic with: "The Brāhmaṇa belongs to Agni; gold belongs to Agni; therefore, one should give gold to a Brāhmaṇa, just as gold is to be given to Agni [in the *āgnīdhra* ritual]," they continue: "Gold must not be stolen from Brāhmaṇas; a great evil indeed overtakes him who, having stolen it from Brāhmaṇas, keeps it for himself. Therefore, what is intended here is the theft of gold belonging to a Brāhmaṇa. Accordingly, Vasiṣṭha, having summarized these very same Śruti and Smṛti passages under the section on mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*), stated: "And the stealing of gold from a Brāhmaṇa" (VaDh 1.20). Regarding the phrase "and drinking liquor" (*surāṃ piban*), only the *paiṣṭī* (liquor made from flour) is intended. The word *surā* is primary (*mukhya*) only with respect to that; in the case of *gauḍī* (rum) and other varieties, its application is secondary (*gauṇa*) due to their common nature as intoxicants (*madya*). If it is argued that, according to the statement "Liquor is to be known as threefold" (MDh 11.94), all varieties are primary, it is not so. For it is not logical to assume multiple meanings in the absence of a restrictive factor. If one asks how the determination is made, it is because the usage of the word *surā* is seen in the Veda only for the *paiṣṭī* variety, specifically in the *surā-grahas* during the Vājapeya and Sautrāmaṇī sacrifices. Similarly, in the *Agnīṣomīya-brāhmaṇa* of the Carakas: "Now, that which was the *malya* (impurity), that was subsequently milked out; *malya* is indeed liquor (*surā*); that which is called untruth, evil, and darkness is liquor"—thus the word *surā* is used only for the *paiṣṭī*. And in the conclusion of that very passage, it is said: "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa shall not drink liquor. Hence, it is settled that the drinking of *paiṣṭī* alone is a mortal sin, and no other. Regarding the phrase "he should lie with the bed of his teacher" (*guros talpam āvaset*), the word *guru* refers to either the father or the preceptor (*ācārya*), or perhaps to the father alone.

"According to the statement of Manu: 'That Brahmin who performs the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony according to the rules, and who supports [the child] with food, is called the Guru' (MDh 2.142), it is appropriate that the status of the teacher (*ācārya*) toward the father is merely secondary (*gauṇa*), because of the metaphorical application of the term 'father. As it has been said:"

"In this regard, her mother is Sāvitrī, while the teacher is said to be her father. (MDh 2.170) In this manner, the distinction between words and their meanings should be applied elsewhere as well. Accordingly, Vasiṣṭha has extended the rule regarding violating the Guru's bed (*gurutalpa*) to others: "The same applies to the wives of the teacher’s son and pupil" (VaDh 20.15). As for that which was stated by Nārada:
"The mother, the mother’s sister, the mother-in-law, the maternal uncle’s wife, the father’s sister... [and so forth].
The wife of a paternal uncle, a female friend, a female disciple, a sister, her friend, and a daughter-in-law.
A daughter, a teacher’s wife, one of the same lineage, one who has sought refuge,
a queen, one who has gone forth, a nurse, a virtuous woman, and one of the highest caste.
Having approached any one of these women, he is called a violator of the Guru’s bed;
for him, no punishment other than the excision of the penis is ordained. (NSm 12.72–74)

Thus, because that [interpretation] contradicts both logic and the authority of Manu, it should be understood that the equality of punishment is intended for the sake of establishing parity in the penalty, not for the sake of restricting the literal wording. As for the passage here regarding "the father’s sister, the maternal uncle’s wife," and so forth, we shall discuss that in its proper place. Regarding the statement, "These four fall [from their caste]: the slayer of a Brahmin... (ChU 5.10.9), one must understand this to refer to a person who, apart from the case of an *ātatāyin* (one who attacks with intent to kill), kills a Brahmin independently on his own initiative, or causes another to kill him by bringing him under control through the giving of wealth and other means. Why is this so? Because of the scriptural injunction: "They say there is no sin for one who kills an *ātatāyin*, nor for one who deprives such a person of life" (VaDh 3.15). Likewise:
"He who kills an assailant born in a noble family and devoted to Vedic study does not thereby become a killer of an embryo; rather, it is fury that encounters fury. (VaDh 3.18).
Likewise:
"One should indeed kill an assailant who approaches, without hesitation—even if he be a teacher, a child, an elder, or a learned Brahmin. (MDh 8.350)

Because of the statement, "toward an assailant (*ātatāyin*) who approaches," the permission for battle is granted in this very verse. In the section concerning battle, there are permissions found throughout the *Smṛtis*, such as: "even one who has reached the end of the Vedas (*vedāntaga*) in battle" and "one may kill him who seeks to kill" (VaDh 3.17). However, in the case of one who kills having been bought with wealth or instigated by another, since the fruits of actions accrue to the master, there is no connection with the fruit produced by the killing of a Brahmin for that [agent], just as in the case of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). But is it not the case that because of the scriptural injunction, "A Brahmin must not be killed," the killing of a Brahmin certainly occurs even for one bought with wealth and so forth? This should be viewed as being like the *Śyena* sacrifice and others. Just as there is no fault for the officiating priests regarding the killing produced by the *Śyena* and other rites, so it is here as well. Just as in the case of the killing of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya*), the prohibition—"One should not harm any living beings"—does not apply to the officiating priests, so it is here too. Others, however, read this verse after having obtained it from some source.
"Whether out of passion, hatred, or negligence, whether by one's own hand or by another's, whoever should kill a Brāhmaṇa, every such person becomes a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa. Thus [it is said].

This, however, must be investigated because its basis is unknown. Even if such a case were possible, since it would be an extended application (*atideśika*), it would not constitute a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) for the time being. As it is said: "If one has been commissioned [to kill] in the slaying of a Brāhmaṇa, even after killing a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who are conscious [of the crime]," and so forth (cf. MDh 11.88). Likewise, those who follow worldly conduct recite: "And he whose property was seized unjustly," and so on. Regarding the statement, "They call him a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa," they say that even one who is not a slayer is called a slayer by the force of the scriptural declaration; the same would apply to one who kills for the sake of wealth and so forth. Therefore, the term "slayer of a Brāhmaṇa" here refers only to one who, acting of his own accord and uninstigated by another, either kills a Brāhmaṇa himself with a weapon or the like, or hires someone through payment and the like to kill him. Although the status of the four—such as the thief of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold—is established by the reading of the text, the repetition is for the purpose of excluding those who merely associate with such sinners. This very point was stated by the Teacher: "These are the perpetrators of mortal sins. In the passage, "The fifth who associates with them" (ChU 5.10.9), the status of being a mortal sinner applies only to associating with those four, and not even to one who is merely a social associate of them. The designation "the fifth" is mentioned for the sake of strengthening this very point. || 228 ||
Now follow those equal to the great sins (mahāpātaka):
excessive reviling of gurus, reviling the Vedas, killing a friend, and the destruction of what has been studied; for these are indeed equal to the killing of a Brahmin. (3.229)

And here, because of the plural number, all elders—including teachers and others—are to be understood. An "extreme insult" (*atyadhikṣepa*) is an excessive reproach toward them of the form: "You are guilty of a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*). In that case, the determination of the penance depends on the specific elder concerned and the specific nature of the insult. Now, one might object: even in the case of one who is not an elder, there is indeed an equivalence to a mortal sin, as stated [in Gautama Dharma Sūtra 21.17–18]: "In the case of falsely accusing a Brāhmaṇa, the fault is the same; twice so for one who is innocent. True; however, in that case, there is a different penance. As Vasiṣṭha says: "Having falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa of a crime causing loss of caste (*patanīya*) or one not causing loss of caste (*upapatanīya*), one should subsist on water for a month and repeat the *Śuddhavatī* verses" (VaDh 23.39). But here, the commencement [of this rule] is intended so that the very penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyā*) shall apply. However, in the case of an insult other than a mortal sin, the penance should be understood as being proportionate to that [offense]. Furthermore, "reviling the Vedas" (*vedanindā*) is the disregard for the Śrutis and Smṛtis—carried through to the point of non-performance—due to a mind corrupted by reliance on rationalistic treatises (*hetuśāstra*). Thus Manu says:

"Any twice-born man who, relying on the treatises of logic (*hetuśāstra*), would despise both of these [the Vedas and the Smṛtis], he—a nihilist (*nāstika*) and reviler of the Vedas—should be excluded by the virtuous. (MDh 2.11) The killing of a friend, however, refers to one who is not a Brāhmaṇa, because it is stated that such a person is equal to him [a Brāhmaṇa]. "Destruction of what has been studied" (*adhītanāśana*) means the abandonment of a Vedic branch (*śākhā*) studied from one's father or others, thinking, "This [branch] is not good"; others, however, say it refers specifically to the forgetting of what has been studied. That [latter view], however, is not very tenable due to the risk of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Manu, moreover, treats it as equal to the drinking of liquor (*surāpāna*).

Violating a Brahmin, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, killing a friend, eating forbidden food or what should not be eaten, and drinking liquor—these six are equal to the drinking of liquor. (MDh 11.56)

Thus it has been stated. Consequently, there is an option regarding the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). This same principle should be explained in other cases as well where multiple readings exist. Now, one might object: "Just like a contradiction with the Veda, a contradiction with Manu is also appropriate for the purpose of subverting other *smṛtis*. True, if there were indeed a contradiction. But here, since there is no difference in the fact that [the killing of a friend] is a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), and because the killing of a friend—which was already included among the acts equal to drinking liquor—is mentioned again within the enumeration of the extension (*atideśa*) of the rule concerning the killing of a Brahmin, there is no contradiction at all. We shall explain this even more clearly further below. (229)
Eating what is forbidden, dishonesty, speaking falsehood for the sake of self-exaltation, and tasting the mouth of a woman in her menses are equal to the drinking of liquor. (3.230)

The consumption of garlic and other prohibited items by one who knows the prohibition—due to an excess of atheism (*nāstikya*) and acting out of desire—is as Manu has stated: "Having intentionally eaten mushrooms, a village-pig, garlic, a village-cock, onions, or leeks, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste]. (MDh 5.19)

This is because of the specific mention [of these acts]. Even when there is no specific mention, these very acts are to be understood, precisely because of this statement of Manu. *Jaihmya* (crookedness), however, is said to be deceitfulness (*kauṭilya*). If someone, though capable of preventing it, neglects through deceit a Brāhmaṇa who is engaged in drinking liquor and the like, he alone is to be understood here as the offender. As Gautama says: "And in the case of injury to the weak, if one is capable of rescuing them... (GDh 21.19). There, the mention of "injury" (*hiṃsā*) should be regarded merely as an illustration; for in all cases, the extension of the penalty for a mortal sin applies to the neglect by one who is capable. And *jaihmya* is mentioned by Manu among the acts that cause loss of caste (MDh 11.67); we shall explain this further below. "And false speech regarding excellence"—this has been declared by Manu to be equal to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa (MDh 11.55). In this regard, the distinction is as follows: false speech in connection with the killing of a Brāhmaṇa is equal to that [act]; false speech in connection with the drinking of liquor is equal to that [act]. For example, if someone, out of partiality or the like, for the sake of exalting his own side, should say of an actual Brāhmaṇa-slayer, "This man is not such a person," or conversely [deny it of one who is], so it should be applied elsewhere as well. And here, the term *surāpī* (liquor-drinker) should be explained as referring to a menstruating woman (*rajasvalā*), not a woman in her courses (*udakyā*), because even approaching her involves only a minor fault, and because the tasting of the mouth is a subordinate part of the act of sexual union. This interpretation is appropriate because it conforms to the context. || 230 ||
The theft of a horse, a jewel, a human being, a woman, land, or a cow, as well as the misappropriation of a deposit, is indeed all equal to the theft of gold. (3.231)

In this context, the horse should be understood as either the primary means for accomplishing a sacrifice or the primary means for accomplishing battle. The cow, too, is indeed a constituent part of the sacrifice. The humans are those belonging to the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*). And the woman is one who has been taken in marriage by a Brāhmaṇa. The land, as well as a deposit (*nikṣepa*), must likewise have been dedicated to a Brāhmaṇa. The word "tathā" refers to silver and so forth. And thus says Manu:
"The misappropriation of a deposit, and of men, horses, and silver, as well as of land, clothing, and gems, is declared to be equal to the theft of gold. (MDh 11.57)

In the preceding [verse], it was made known that the mention of theft refers exclusively to gold; therefore, it should be explained that the deposit [referred to here] concerns something other than gold. || 231 ||

They consider sexual intercourse with the wives of friends, virgins, women of one's own uterine kin, women of the lowest castes, women of the same lineage, and the wives of sons to be equal to violating the Guru’s bed. (3.232)

The *antyaja* is the Śūdra; therefore, those born from him into the three preceding castes are *antya-jas*. Furthermore, by the phrase "in their own wombs," those related through the mother and father—such as paternal cousins (*pitṛṣvasrīya*) and others—are included. So too are the wives of sons who are of a different caste (*asavarṇā*), because daughters-in-law and sisters are mentioned later [in the verse]. The rest is clear. Moreover, in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra], regarding the rule "emission of semen in one's own wombs" (MDh 11.58), the inclusion of those belonging to the same *gotra* (lineage) is to be understood by the force of the two *ca*s (the word "and" used twice). || 232 ||
But he states them separately for the purpose of specifying an excessive penance:
"The father's sister, the maternal uncle's wife, the daughter-in-law, the mother's sister, as well as the mother's co-wife, a sister, and likewise the teacher's daughter... (3.233).

But he who approaches the wife of his teacher or his own daughter is a violator of the guru’s bed; his punishment is the cutting off of the penis and death, as is that of the woman if she was willing. (3.234)

In this context, the word *tu* is to be construed by extracting it from its position and applying it to the sense of the word *eva*: "one who approaches his teacher’s bed (*gurutalpaga*) alone. This is what is meant: while it is appropriate to speak of equality [in punishment] regarding the wives of friends and others, in the case of fathers’ sisters and the like, he is indeed a violator of the teacher’s bed (*gurutalpaga*). Just as when one asks, "Is this man equal to a king? regarding those who are highly honored, the answer is certainly, "He is a king himself. By speaking thus, it is shown that in the case of fathers’ sisters and others, there is neither a deficiency relative to the violation of the teacher’s bed nor an excess over it. Others, however, explain this as referring to the primary (*mukhya*) violation of the teacher’s bed itself. (That is incorrect? Indeed, that would be incorrect here because the mother is not mentioned; furthermore, in another Smṛti, after stating "the killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, and the violator of the teacher’s bed," it says, "one who has approached a woman related through the mother or father by birth" (GDh 21.1), and "some say he is equal to him in approaching a daughter-in-law or a cow, and in void excrement" (GDh 23.12–13). That would be inconsistent; therefore, the previous explanation alone is superior. Furthermore, the term "co-wife of the mother" (*mātuḥ sapatnī*) is intended to mean a woman of a different caste (*asavarṇā*), whereas in the case of others, the equality to the violation of the teacher’s bed is indeed primary. The rest is clear. (233–4)

Now the minor offenses (upapātaka) are stated: killing a cow, being a Vratya, theft, non-payment of debts, failing to maintain the sacred fires, selling forbidden goods, and marrying before one's elder brother. (3.235)
Receiving instruction for a fee, teaching for a fee, adultery, causing a younger brother to marry before the elder, usury, and the manufacture of salt. (3.236)
Killing a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; living by means of forbidden wealth; atheism; the abandonment of religious vows; and the sale of one's own sons. (3.237)
Stealing grain, silver, or cattle; officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice; abandoning one's father, mother, or friend; and the sale of a pond or a garden. (3.238)

Violating a maiden, officiating at the sacrifice for one who has married before his elder brother, giving a daughter in marriage to such a man, and crookedness—these constitute the destruction of Brahmanhood. (3.239)

Undertaking actions for one's own sake alone, consorting with women who drink liquor, abandoning sacred study, the sacrificial fire, and one's sons, as well as the abandonment of kinsmen—these are [the faults]. (3.240)
Cutting down trees for the sake of fuel, living by the slaughter of women or by medicinal herbs, the construction of murderous machines, and the sale of oneself—these are vices. (3.241)
Studying false scriptures, officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy of them, and selling one's wife—each of these is a minor offense (upapātaka). (3.242)

These eight verses are self-explanatory. The mention of each one individually is for the purpose of indicating that the penance becomes more severe when two or more such acts are committed. The designation *upapātaka* (minor sin) is likewise for this same purpose; for if they are committed repeatedly or habitually, they would indeed become *pātaka* (major sins). For this very reason, Gautama included the "habitual performance of censurable acts" among the major sins (GDh 21.1). Thus, by these eight verses, fifty-one minor sins have been stated. Other acts as well—such as being caught while the sun is rising (*sūryābhyudita*) or setting (*sūryābhinirmukta*)—should be understood as being included here by the force of the word "and so forth" (*tathā-ādi*). Alternatively, their inclusion here is for the sake of uniformity regarding the penances, and not to establish a restrictive definition of what constitutes a *upapātaka*. For instance, Śaṅkha enumerated only eighteen minor sins, as he said: "Henceforth, the following are the acts leading to degradation (*upapatanīya*): the defiler of a maiden, the seller of Soma, the husband of a *vṛṣalī*, the deserter of his wife from her youth, the drinker of *āsava* or liquor, the killer of a cow, the slayer of a Śūdra, the reviler of a Guru, an atheist, the ungrateful, the fraudulent dealer, the destroyer of livelihood, the false accuser, the stealer of gold, the associate with outcasts, the betrayer of friends, the killer of one who has sought refuge, and the one who acts with hostility—these are the eighteen minor sins. Similarly, Sumantu says: "The theft of a woman, silver, or a cow; sexual intercourse with a cow; causing abortion; falsehood regarding land; the killing of a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a cow; being a younger brother who marries before his elder (*parivitti*); being an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken the vow of celibacy); and living by forgery—these are the minor sins. In the text of Śātātapa, however, only eight minor sins are mentioned, beginning with "Now, the minor sins: the extinguisher of the sacred fires," and so on. In the Vāsiṣṭha Dharma Sūtra, however, starting with "One caught while the sun is rising, one caught while the sun is setting" (VaDh 1.18), the designation "sinners who are minor sinners" (*upapātakinām enasvin*) is used, because within that list, those whose status as minor sinners is beyond doubt, such as the *parivitti* and others, are enumerated. Therefore, this designation should be explained as applying only to those specifically mentioned, for the sake of uniformity regarding the penances. And in this context, adultery, theft, the killing of a woman, and so forth, should be understood as being greater than the *mahāpātaka* (major sins) and equal to them. (235–42)
Now he states the penances for killing a Brahmin and other such crimes as they have been described:
"Carrying a skull-topped staff as his banner, subsisting on alms while proclaiming his deed, and eating sparingly for twelve years, the killer of a Brahmin shall attain purification. (3.243)

He is described as such because his banner and emblem (*cihna*) is a skull (*kapāla*) fixed to his head. The mention of the "skull" is intended to exclude the case where the head is not severed. The rest is clear. And this penance applies to all castes (*sārvavarṇika*). However, in another *Smṛti*, there is a restriction based on capacity, as Śaṅkha says: "A killer of a Brāhmaṇa, permitted by the assembly (*pariṣad*), carrying a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), wearing the skin of a donkey, eating the remains of food fallen into an earthen vessel, proclaiming his own deed, should subsist on alms, eating only once a day, making his dwelling in empty houses, by rivers, in mountain caves, or at the roots of trees. In this manner, at the end of twelve years, he attains purification; or alternatively, by saving the life of a Brāhmaṇa from death, or by protecting twelve cows; or immediately, by bathing in the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice, he becomes pure. Having begun thus and set forth all the penances, and having further mentioned the gift of a thousand cows at the conclusion, it is stated again:
Performing the penance, remaining silent, he should touch water three times;
wearing a single garment or wet clothes, eating light food, and sleeping on the bare ground.

"The posture is the hero's seat (vīrāsana), silence, the muñja-grass girdle, the staff and water-pot, the practice of begging for alms, the fire-ritual, and [the consumption of] clarified butter daily with the Kūṣmāṇḍī mantras. Thus it is said.

For the performance of the fire-rite (*agnikārya*) with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras is not applicable to one who is not a member of the three [upper] castes (*traivarṇika*). Therefore, this [penance] belongs only to the *traivarṇika*. In some cases, the distinction arises from the explicit instruction itself; as Śātātapa says: "A Brāhmaṇa, having killed a Brāhmaṇa, having taken his skull... Here, the only distinction is the requirement regarding the skull. Thus, wherever the agent is obtained either through contextual implication (*sāmarthya*) or by direct statement, that [penance] has a restricted agent. However, where there is a statement without specification—as in this very case—it applies to all castes (*sārvavarṇika*). This should be applied similarly elsewhere. Nor should it be suspected that this twelve-year vow (*dvādaśavārṣika-vrata*) established in all the Smṛtis is one and the same; for it has been stated in the verse beginning "The speakers of the Dharmaśāstras... (YDh 1.4–5) that there is a difference in application (*prayoga-bheda*) for each Smṛti. For this very reason, if the twelve-year penance prescribed by Śaṅkha has been commenced, then purification occurs by releasing a Brāhmaṇa from death or by saving twelve cows during the interval; but otherwise, it must necessarily be completed. As for the ritual bath at the end of a horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedhāvabhṛtha*), even in the text of Śaṅkha, it should be explained as an alternative procedure (*kalpāntara*), because the Veda teaches it independently. For thus it is heard in the Śruti:

When the Unnetṛ priest leads the King [Soma] upward, then those who have committed sins approach him and confess: "In such a way I have killed a Brāhmaṇa; in such a way I have approached the wife of my teacher. To whatever extent the officiating priests and the King may speak to them, saying, "May you be purified by the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the Aśvamedha," they descend into the water. Just as a snake casts off its skin, so do they cast off all evil. One should not feel aversion toward them. He wins as much of the world as one wins by performing the Aśvamedha; he wins three times as much for one who, knowing this, allows those who have committed such sins to descend into the purificatory bath.

Thus says the *Jābāli-śruti*. This very same text was also recorded by Kātyāyana: "When the sacrificer has departed, those who have committed sins descend [into hell], unless they have performed the vows known as the *avabhṛtha* of the Aśvamedha. Therefore, it is not logical for this to serve as a means of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) prescribed in the Smṛtis. For a Śruti text cannot be postulated merely as a supplement to a Smṛti. If, however, this were intended for one who has already commenced the twelve-year penance, then it would have been enjoined in the Śruti itself by way of restating that [penance]. But no such Śruti exists. Furthermore, if there were a restatement of the twelve-year penance in the Śruti, then since it would not be obtained from any other source, that alone would have to be the thing enjoined. For when such a direct scriptural statement exists, it is not possible to postulate another basis for the Smṛti. In that case, the bath at the *avabhṛtha* of the Aśvamedha would be enjoined either as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) or for the sake of completion. However, the completion of an obligatory (*nitya*) act by means of an occasional (*anitya*) one is not appropriate. If, on the other hand, it were said to be an occasional completion, then if one should somehow fail to bathe, one would not be purified even after performing the twelve-year penance. Or, if it were said that the bath is an occasional auxiliary to that [penance], then even after bathing at the *avabhṛtha*, the remainder of the twelve-year penance would still have to be completed. Therefore, it is more reasonable to assume that the *avabhṛtha* of the Aśvamedha is independent. For this very reason, in the *Vasiṣṭha-dharma-sūtra*, it is stated elsewhere, bypassing the section on killing a learned Brāhmaṇa (*bhrūṇahatyā*): "Furthermore, for the slaying of a learned Brāhmaṇa, he should subsist on water for twelve nights, fast for twelve nights, or go to the *avabhṛtha* of an Aśvamedha" (VaDh 23.37). Because of its brevity, someone might suspect it is a supplement to something else. For this very reason, Śaṅkha also says: "Having bathed immediately at the *avabhṛtha* of an Aśvamedha, one becomes pure," and by the restriction "immediately" (*sadya eva*) and the absence of mention of the twelve-year penance, its independence is demonstrated. And this statement of Śaṅkha is to be understood as applying only to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas who have studied the Veda but do not maintain the sacred fires (*anagnika*), in the case of unintentionally killing a virtuous Brāhmaṇa; for if done intentionally, this very penance is augmented by the gift of a thousand cows. For a Śūdra as well, this applies only to an unintentional act, accompanied by the gift [of cows] but excluding the mantras. In the case of an intentional act, the Śūdra’s penance ends only in death. For those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*), even for an unintentional act, the penance ends only in death. Why is this? From the very words of Śaṅkha: having introduced the subject with "Beyond this are the causes of loss of caste (*patanīya*)," he states, "Their expiation has been ordained by the virtuous for acts done unintentionally. And this refers to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. For elsewhere, a rite involving fewer formalities is taught for a Brāhmaṇa, since [Śātātapa says]: "A Brāhmaṇa, having caused the death of a Brāhmaṇa, should take his skull-bone and wander to holy places (*tīrtha*), proclaiming his own sin; in the twelfth year he attains purity; or he sees an Aśvamedha, and by the mere sight of it, he attains purity. And because of the use of the specific term "Brāhmaṇa," this applies only to a Brāhmaṇa. Nor can it be said that this applies to a Brāhmaṇa even in the case of an intentional act, because of the expression "unintentionally" (*akāmakṛta*). Therefore, it is correct that this applies only to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. As for the Śūdra, this is not appropriate due to his lack of capacity. How is it known that this applies to those without sacred fires? Because no penance is prescribed for a man alone, and because rites accomplished by fire depend upon the wife, and she lacks a cause for loss of caste (*patana*). Only where both husband and wife fall does the penance related to the *vaitānika* fires apply. But when only one falls, eligibility belongs only to those rites accomplished by the body alone. And here there is no rite connected to the *aupāsana* or other domestic fires. As for the fire-rite with the *Kūśmāṇḍī* verses, that should be understood as the placing of fuel-sticks (*samid-ādhāna*), like the practice of a religious student (*brahmacārin*). And that is appropriate only in a common (*laukika*) fire. Furthermore, because of the instruction regarding the donkey-skin, if the animal sacrifice for a student who has broken his vow (*avakīrṇin*) should apply here, that too is appropriate only in a common fire. Thus, it is established that this applies only to one without sacred fires. Now, even if there were no use for the fire here, it does not follow that the penance is only for one without sacred fires. True. This would be so if there were no other penance involving fire here. But such a one is indeed heard in scripture. For example, the text of Manu: "Or he should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha" (MDh 11.74), etc. There, the Aśvamedha is only for the ruler of a kingdom, according to the Śruti: "Therefore, the ruler of a kingdom should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha. The *Svarjit* and other sacrifices belong to all three castes who have performed their first sacrifice. And there is no other penance for them, because since they are dependent [on the status of having sacrificed], an option between unequal injunctions is impossible. It is proper that there be another penance for those not entitled to those [sacrifices], because that [other penance] has no other scope, whereas the [Aśvamedha] is restricted to those who have performed their first sacrifice. Since it has no other scope, for one who has maintained the sacred fires but has not performed his first sacrifice, the *Agniṣṭoma* itself is the penance. Gautama, after mentioning the *avabhṛtha* of the Aśvamedha, says: "Even in another sacrifice, if it ends with the *Agniṣṭut*" (GDh 22.9–10). There is no sacrifice whatsoever that ends with the *Agniṣṭut*, because *Satras* and *Ahīnas* generally end with the *Atirātra*. Even where the *Atirātra* does not occur, there is certainly no ending with the *Agniṣṭut*. Therefore, this word *Agniṣṭut* should be understood as referring to the *Agniṣṭoma* stotra. And that which ends with it is the *Agniṣṭoma* itself. Since purification occurs by bathing at the *avabhṛtha* of even a sacrifice performed by another, the performance of the *Agniṣṭoma* is established by the maxim of the "stick and the lump of rice" (*daṇḍāpūpa-nyāya*) through one's own initiative. In the *Kaṭhaka* also, just as with the Aśvamedha, for the *Agniṣṭoma*: "He who performs the sacrifice ending in the *Agniṣṭoma* is released from the sin of killing a learned Brāhmaṇa"—this refers to the *Agniṣṭoma* of one who maintains the sacred fires and has not performed his first sacrifice. For the other, the *Svarjit* and others are to be seen. But for one who possesses only the *aupāsana* fire, another penance is stated by Śaṅkha himself. In that case, the penance applies

One who has fallen [from his status] should indeed uplift himself; he should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance for one year. Having shaved his head and become pure, he should descend into the water three times a day, wearing a single wet garment, observing silence like a piece of wood, and sit in the *vīrāsana* posture at night. During the day, he should remain standing, disciplined and intent on the fire-rituals, muttering the *Sāvitrī* mantra according to the [three] libations. Having undertaken the vow himself, wearing a girdle of *muñja* grass and dressed in *kuśa* grass, bark, or wooden planks, with *darbha* blades as a purifier in his hand, he should eat sacrificial food, *caru*, or blameless alms sufficient for his sustenance. He should also fast for twelve nights, satisfy the Brāhmaṇas, and provide daily fodder for cows. In this way he may be restored to social intercourse; otherwise, having fallen, he is not to be spoken to by the learned. Thus [it is said].

Although this was stated under the heading "One shall not sell things that ought not to be sold," following the declaration that "one falls immediately from caste by selling sesame, honey, molasses, clarified butter, oil, and so forth, up to indigo," nevertheless, it is not proper to regard this [text] as prescribing an expiation for that specific act, because of the Vedic scripture: "For one who has fallen must uplift himself. Nor does this [scripture] apply to the previous case, since that is already established by the context itself; furthermore, because the expiation is extremely grave, it is appropriate only for a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*). Therefore, since the context is set aside by the force of the scripture and its inherent meaning, it is established—following the uninterrupted tradition of the commentators—that this refers exclusively to the expiation for a mortal sin. And thus Sumantu says:

If, due to passion or hatred, an expiation cannot be obtained, one who is devoted to recitation, burnt offerings, study, and celibacy, subsisting on alms, carrying a staff and wearing a girdle, bathing at the three periods of the day, and sleeping on the ground, purifies even a great evil by his own effort. The teachers do not admit the fall of a Brāhmaṇa; for in the *Āṅgirasa*, it is said: "One who has incurred sin should be made to undergo penance. Thus it is stated.

And the mention of the Brāhmaṇa here is for the sake of illustration. Furthermore, in cases where purification through one's own undertaking is desired after a year, the assembly must certainly not grant a period longer than that. Thus it has been stated by this very author: "We shall declare the expiation for those who have committed the great sins (mahāpātaka), namely: killing a Brāhmaṇa, drinking liquor, violating the Guru’s bed, and stealing gold."

A killer of a Brāhmaṇa shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for one year, sleeping on the ground, proclaiming his own deed, subsisting on alms, and lying on the sandy banks of divine rivers; he shall frequent virtuous villages, hermitages, cow-pens, mountains, springs, and places of asceticism. When the year is complete, having given gold, gems, a cow, a bull, food, sesame seeds, land, and clarified butter to Brāhmaṇas, he becomes purified; or he is immediately purified by bathing at the concluding ceremony (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice. Thus it is said.

"Therefore, half and half [of the penance] is explained for the killing of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya"—by this, the previously mentioned practices such as devotion to recitation (*japa*), burnt offerings (*havana*), and Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) are to be combined. Furthermore, this term *kṛcchra* should be understood here as referring to the *taptakṛcchra*. This [penance] does not take place when the *aupāsana* fire is absent, because of the rule: "Smārta rites are to be performed in the marriage fire" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.96).

But surely this [penance] is also not appropriate for one who has fallen while being without a wife, because of the traditional law (smṛti): "No separation exists between husband and wife; for from the taking of the hand, there is unity in ritual acts and in the fruits of their property" (ĀpDh 2.14.16–18). Nor is there a falling away for the wife, since it has been stated: "One defiled by a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) must indeed be awaited until purification" (YDh 1.76).

This is true; for in the case of Vedic (vaitānika) rites, the performance of the ritual is impossible without the wife. However, the Smārta rites—those connected with the maintenance of the domestic fire (āvasathya)—belong to one who has established that fire alone, even when they pertain exclusively to the individual. This is the case, for example, with the expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) connected to the *brahmayajña*. Indeed, it cannot be said that there is an entitlement (*adhikāra*) for a husband accompanied by his wife in the *brahmayajña*; nor is there an entitlement to perform the *mahāvyāhṛti* oblations and so forth in the event of a transgression occurring therein. The same applies to the *upākarma* ceremony. And just as in that case, because the oblations are properly performed in the domestic fire (*aupāsana*), the engagement of even a single person in their performance—even in the event of [the wife's] absence—is entirely unimpeded. Enough of this digression.

Therefore, this is established: for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who does not maintain the sacred fires but has studied the Vedas, the twelve-year penance prescribed by Śaṅkha applies to the killing of a virtuous Brāhmaṇa. And for a Śūdra, Āpastamba has prescribed a twelve-year penance for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa in general. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate that the penance for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya is less than that for a Śūdra. Thus, this [penance] is said to apply to the killing of a virtuous Brāhmaṇa. However, in the case of a Kāka-kṛta (an act committed unintentionally or by mistake), it is accompanied by the gift of a thousand cows. Why is this? Precisely from the statement of Śaṅkha: "Having killed [a Brāhmaṇa] among the four castes, one should prescribe a vow for twelve years, six years, three years, and one year; at the end of these, one should give a thousand cows, half of that, half of that, and half of that again, according to the sequence of all [the castes]. And this penance for a Śūdra is to be understood as applying to one who possesses wealth, for it is not possible for those of higher castes to kill one of a lower caste in such a manner. For it has been stated: "In the case of mutual killing among all [castes], the Cāndrāyaṇa penance applies. Therefore, this penance belongs only to a wealthy Śūdra. But for one who is destitute, that which was spoken by Āpastamba applies, or that which was spoken for a Vaiśya applies in its entirety. Consequently, this [twelve-year penance] would apply to a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya when the act is intentional (*kāmakṛta*), precisely because of Śaṅkha’s statement: "That which is prescribed for a lower [caste] applies to an unintentional act, and that which is prescribed for a higher [caste] applies to an intentional act. Therefore, the direction is that in the case of an intentional act, it is accompanied by the gift of a thousand cows. This is the general principle.
But that which was stated by Āpastamba refers to the case of a Śūdra.

Having killed a Vedic student of the two higher castes, or one who has entered a *savana* sacrifice, one is accused (*abhiśasta*). This applies equally to killing any Brāhmaṇa whatsoever, as well as an embryo of unknown sex, and a woman who is pregnant with an Ātreya child. His penance is as follows: having built a hut in the forest, remaining silent, carrying a corpse’s head as his banner, and covering himself from below the navel to above the knees with a garment made of half-wool and half-hemp; his path is between two tracks. Upon seeing an Āryan, he should step aside. He should enter a village with a broken red bowl. Then, announcing his deed by saying, "Alms for the accused," he should go to seven houses. That is his livelihood. If he does not obtain anything, he should fast. He should also guard cows; the second purpose in the village is to attend to their going out and coming in. Having performed this for twelve years, he is purified and may associate with the virtuous. Alternatively, on the road to the sacrifice, one who desires to win over the cattle of a Brāhmaṇa is released after being thrice defeated or after winning them back. Or, by undergoing the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an Aśvamedha, he is released. This same rule applies to one who seizes wealth when there is a conflict between dharma and artha. Thus it is said. (ĀpDh 1.24.6–23)

And here, regarding the phrase "of the two preceding castes," the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya are mentioned in relation to the Śūdra; however, because of the statement "and only the Brāhmaṇa," it does not follow that the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya are the "preceding castes. Therefore, this [penance] should be understood as applying to the Śūdra. Furthermore, nothing such as *japa* or *homa* is heard of here, by which one might suspect that the subject matter concerns the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*). By this very principle, the distinctions based on caste and based on qualities in other cases should also be explained. Moreover, twelve years' penances are recited in the twelve *Smṛtis*; these are to be distinguished in the following way: among them, the [penances] of Manu and Yājñavalkya apply to all castes. And therein, for a Brāhmaṇa who intentionally kills a virtuous Brāhmaṇa, for a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya who unintentionally kills one devoid of virtues, and for a Śūdra who unintentionally kills even a mere Brāhmaṇa—in this manner, for a Vaiśya also [compared] to a Kṣatriya, and in all cases, a heavier penance is to be prescribed. (243)
For the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, there is this other expiation:
one should indeed offer oblations with these mantras in their proper order, beginning with the hair and ending with the marrow, saying "Svāhā to the hairs," and so forth. 3.244.

The words *hi* and *vai* are for the purpose of completing the meter (*pādapūraṇa*). The word *vā* is used to indicate an option regarding the substances, such as hair and so forth, in relation to clarified butter (*ājya*). *Tanuḥ* means the body. That [body] consists of everything beginning with hair and ending with hair, skin, blood, fat, flesh, sinew, bone, and marrow. One should offer oblations with these formulas recited in the *Yajurveda* pertaining to the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), which are repeated twice: "To the hairs, Svāhā! and so on. Alternatively, one may offer clarified butter with each of those sixteen formulas repeated twice. However, this second *vā* is used to indicate an option in relation to the full expiation (*pūrṇaprāyaścitta*); it does not refer to different performers. The meaning is that in the case of a single killing of a Brahmin, either the twelve-year penance or this [penance] should be performed by the eligible agents according to their respective qualifications. Consequently, by implication, this applies to one who has studied the Vedas and maintains the sacred fires (*agnimān*). Here, the status of the deities (*devatātva*) for the hair and other parts is established by the wording of the mantras themselves (*māntravarṇika*) through the use of the dative case. Therefore, eligibility belongs only to one who possesses knowledge of the internal (*adhyātma*), the divine (*adhidaiva*), and the sacrificial (*adhiyajña*) aspects of the hair, skin, and so forth. Furthermore, the arrangement of the options regarding the substances should be explained in consideration of specific levels of understanding. Moreover, there is no burning of the entire body here, as there is no scriptural statement to that effect. Since it is impossible to offer the hair and other parts in their entirety, they must necessarily be offered from a single limb, such as a finger. Thus, it should be explained that this is not a penance ending only in death (*maraṇāntika*). It is exactly the same in the *Vasiṣṭha-dharma-sūtra*: "A killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahan*), having kindled the fire, should offer oblations, beginning with 'I offer the hairs to Death; by the hairs I clothe Death first,' and ending with 'the marrow to Death'" (VaDh 20.25–26). Even there, it is merely an offering of oblations, since the casting away of the body is not taught. As for those who argue that the penance is minor because of its brevity, and because of another Smṛti text... [text continues].
Or he should throw himself three times head-first into a blazing fire. (MDh 11.73)

Because they observe the casting off of the body [in other cases], they describe the casting off of the body here as well; why then would they not perform the recitation until death during the study of the *Saṃhitā*, according to the rule: "Having recited the *Saṃhitā* three times, one should eat a restricted meal, and then again three times"? Thus, since all these penances for life (*jīvaprāyaścitta*) are minor, a [forced] interpretation would result in their being equated with those ending in death, as far as possible. If, however, some interpretation of the scope (*viṣaya*) is somehow applied to those [other penances], then the same is appropriate here too; it is not the case that the body should be cast into unconsecrated fire. Therefore, it is established that even in the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti*, it refers only to the *homa*. As for the repetition of the mention of fire—which was already obtained from the statement regarding the *homa*: "The killer of a learned Brahmin (*bhrūṇahan*), having kindled the fire, should offer oblations" (VaDh 20.25)—that too is not for the purpose of obtaining ordinary (*laukika*) fire, as that would entail the assumption of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Rather, it should be explained thus: lest some dull-witted person, due to the killing of a learned Brahmin, should fear the destruction of the consecrated fire. It is not that one should assume the abandonment of the consecrated fire already obtained by the text merely on the basis of a [separate] indicator (*jñāpaka*); this is the general direction. However, we shall explain the determination of the scope more clearly at the end of the section on penances (Prāyaścitta-prakaraṇa). || 244 ||
Likewise, this other optional [expiation] exists:
by saving a Brāhmaṇa, or by saving twelve cows, or likewise by bathing at the concluding purificatory rite (avabhṛtha) of a horse sacrifice, one may attain purification. (3.245)

In this context, the mention of the *brāhmaṇa* should be understood as referring to one who possesses [specific] qualities (*guṇavat*), and not merely to the caste (*jāti*) alone; for a compound has not been formed. Indeed, if it were a compound, the gender would not be manifested, and there would be the apprehension of the mere caste. [Objection: Even so, only "of a male" (*puṃsaḥ*) is obtained, and not "of one possessing qualities" (*guṇavataḥ*) as well. [Reply: True, that is so. However, if that were the case, because it would serve to exclude the female, it would result in a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*). Furthermore, since the singular number is intended to be significant just like the gender, a deficiency in merit (*vaiguṇya*) would follow if two Brāhmaṇas were saved. If, on the other hand, the gender is not the primary factor, then it must be for the purpose of obtaining qualities such as Vedic study associated with it; thus, there would be no fault. Therefore, it is correct to say "by saving a Brāhmaṇa who possesses qualities. And from the word *pari* (in *paritrāṇāt*), the meaning is "on all sides," even at the cost of sacrificing one's own life. In the phrase "or of a herd of twelve cows" (*gavāṃ dvādaśakasya vā*), the phrase "belonging to a Brāhmaṇa who possesses qualities" is also obtained by virtue of the governing context (*adhikāra*). The word *tathā* signifies "in the same manner. Just as one might attain purification through the passage beginning with "carrying a human skull," so too does one attain it through the saving of cows and Brāhmaṇas, even without depending on anything else. And so it was said by Manu:
"Having shaved his head, he should dwell at the edge of a village, or in a cow-pen, or in a hermitage,
or at the foot of a tree, devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins.
Having said this, it was further stated:
"By immediately sacrificing one's life for the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow, or by protecting a cow or a Brahmin, one is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin. (MDh 11.79)

From this it is known that this is a distinct expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and not an alternative for one who has already commenced the twelve-year penance. For if it were intended for that case, its purpose would already be fulfilled by the verse beginning with "devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins," and thus the commencement of another verse would be purposeless. Nor is it reasonable to claim that the commencement of the next verse is for the purpose of stating that one might become devoted to their welfare in this manner; for the word "or" (*vā*) would then be redundant, and furthermore, there is the repetition in the phrase "or a protector of cows and Brahmins. Therefore, this is intended by the Blessed One as an independent, alternative expiation. For this very reason, the Teacher has stated that this is optional (*vaikalpika*) in relation to the unambiguous ritual bath at the conclusion of a horse sacrifice (*aśvamedhāvabhṛthasnāna*).

"Or he may attain purification by bathing at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). As has already been demonstrated, just as the inclusion of the *aśvamedha-avabhṛtha* elsewhere is not possible, so too has it been explained that the statement by Śaṅkha—"having liberated [the Brahmins] from death in the interim"—refers specifically to the subject of the twelve-year penance and is not universal. (245)
Likewise, this other alternative is as follows:
having seen on the road a Brahmin or even a cow afflicted by a long and severe illness, the slayer of a Brahmin becomes pure by restoring them to health. (3.246)

*Āmaya* means disease. He is seized by that which is long-standing—having been rooted for a long time—and thus exceedingly difficult to cure, intense, and grave, such as *rājayakṣma* (consumption) or great leprosy (*mahākuṣṭha*). The use of the masculine gender in the word *brāhmaṇam* is intended solely to indicate qualities such as Vedic study and so forth, not to exclude women. The word *atha* is displaced and joined with the word *vā*: "or else even a cow possessing the aforementioned qualities. The particle *api* implies possibility in relation to a single number: the intention is that this applies even to one who belongs to the Brāhmaṇa caste though devoid of merit, and likewise to even a single person; how much more so then for those who are virtuous or numerous? The phrase "having seen on the road" is intended to preclude any ulterior motive. "Free from fear" (*nirātaṅkam*) means having made him secure by completely eliminating all diseases, and having removed all anxiety so that he is restored to health. From the word *vā*, it follows that he should serve until death, with his whole being, with all his possessions, and even at the risk of his own life. Although the subject under discussion is "the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure," the repetition "the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure" is for the purpose of establishing universal eligibility; this service is to be applied in all cases—whether unintentional or intentional—for the three twice-born castes, depending on the qualities of the Brāhmaṇa being served, the number of persons involved, and the capacity and virtues of the attendant. Even for a Śūdra, this protection is indeed a means of purification when done unintentionally, provided it concerns the immediate rescue. For example, if a house is ablaze and someone enters it, accepting his own death, to bring out a Brāhmaṇa or twelve cows who are unable to escape, he is purified by that rescue or by his own death. However, the present rule begins again with "service until freedom from illness or until death" to emphasize the duration of the service. [Verse 246]
Likewise, there is this other optional penance for the killing of a Brahmin:
having brought about the seizure of all the property of a Brahmin, or having robbed him or even caused him to be killed;
one who has been wounded by weapons on that account is purified even while living. (3.247)

The term "all his property" (*sarvasva*) is intended as an indication of a large amount, because it is difficult to recover stolen goods when they are numerous; however, "all one's property" may sometimes consist of only a single jar, which can be recovered with very little effort. In such a case, the mention of being "slain" would not be entirely appropriate. By the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "only slain" (*ghātita eva*), the text clarifies that "all one's property" refers to a situation where death itself follows as a matter of course upon the recovery of the stolen item. Consequently, even if one is wounded by weapons many times while exerting himself again and again to the best of his ability to recover the property, yet survives, he is purified even if the object is not recovered. This is the penance for one who is not a Kṣatriya and for whom the recovery of the property is possible. For a Kṣatriya, however, this cannot be prescribed, as [the duty to recover] is obligatory for him. Furthermore, for one for whom recovery is possible, the instruction "having brought it back" (*ānīya*) is not quite fitting. Therefore, it is established that this applies to a non-Kṣatriya for whom recovery is possible. And the mention of "taking up arms" is to demonstrate the invincibility of the adversary; thus, it should be understood that even if rendered motionless by non-lethal means such as stones, one is purified even without sustaining a wound. (247)
Likewise, there is this other pair of penances:
one who is self-restrained shall be purified by reciting the Vedic Saṃhitā three times in the forest, or by eating sparingly while traveling against the current of the Sarasvatī river. (3.248)

Having departed from the village and stayed in the forest, being extremely self-restrained and solely intent on contemplating its meaning, he [should recite] the Vedic *saṃhitā*—meaning both the *mantra* and the *brāhmaṇa*—three times. The mention of the *saṃhitā* is for the purpose of restricting the recitation to the *saṃhitā-pāṭha* alone, as one does not find pleasure in other [recited] forms. Since the *pada*, *krama*, and so forth are human compositions, they are excluded by their very nature; thus, the word "saṃhitā" is not intended to exclude them. Although the goal is achieved by merely saying "three," the expression "three times" (*triṣkṛtvaḥ*) is used to establish the application of the suffix *-kṛtvasuc* to denote repetition. By this, even cases such as "five times" or "six times" may be applied here, depending on the reduction of the qualities of the auxiliary [recitations]. This is also stated in the *Mānava-dharmaśāstra*:
"Or, with his diet restricted, he should recite the Saṃhitā of the Veda three times. (MDh 11.77)

Because of the connection with the word *triḥ* ("three times") applied to the Veda, one should understand that after reciting one Veda three times, one should then recite another Veda three times; this is to be construed in this manner precisely because of the use of the suffix *-kṛtvas*. Furthermore, by the particle *vai*, which indicates a well-known fact, this very point is illuminated: the meaning of the verse is to be understood as depending upon the tradition of other Smṛtis. And since this refers to those who are learned, the penance applies only to one who knows the meaning of the Vedas, and should be applied according to the specific details thereof. Others, however, explain that this refers specifically to a forest-dweller (*vanastha*), stating: "He who is disciplined in the forest, having recited the Vedic Saṃhitā three times, becomes pure. But that need not necessarily be accepted, because the term "forest" (*araṇya*) is not mentioned in the *Mānava* [Smṛti], and even though no distinction is stated there, the conclusion is established nonetheless. "Or he may become pure by eating moderately" (*śudhyeta vā mitāśītvā*): "eating moderately" means eating what is appropriate for his stage of life (*āśrama*), such as the rule, "The meal of a sage (*muni*) consists of eight morsels," and so forth; the meaning is that he should not eat to his heart's content even when exhausted on the road. "Mitāśī itvā" means "having gone while eating moderately. "Facing the current" means starting from Someśvara up to Plakṣa. In the *Mānava*, however, it is said: "Or subsisting on sacrificial food" (*haviṣyabhug vā*). And that refers specifically to alms-food (*bhaikṣa*) characterized as prescribed for ascetics (*yati*) and students (*brahmacārin*). For the other two stages of life, however, it should be understood as rice, barley, wild millet (*śyāmāka*), wild rice (*nīvāra*), and so forth, prepared in the domestic fire (*aupāsana*) or the fire of a hermit (*śrāmaṇaka*), in accordance with their own duties. Now, one might object: "There can be no fixed status of life-stages (*āśrama-vyavasthā*) for an outcaste (*patita*), precisely because he is an outcaste, according to the statement of Gautama: 'Falling away from the duties of the twice-born is degradation' (*dvijātikarmabhyo hāniḥ patanam*). This is true, provided it concerns the period prior to the commencement of the penance. Once the penance has commenced, however, one must act in accordance with one's caste and stage of life, without contradicting the requirements of the penance. If the loss of the status of life-stages were to result simply from being an outcaste, then injunctions such as the *agniṣṭut* sacrifice—which require the maintenance of the *āhavanīya* and other sacred fires—would become impossible for an outcaste. Therefore, even if degradation occurs, the status of a householder does not depart, and thus the fires are not lost. Consequently, even if one partner is degraded, the fires must be maintained by the other, just as in the case of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). After purification, the performance of rites resumes. If both partners are degraded, they must both maintain the fires without abandoning them. And the penance should be understood as consisting of recitation, oblations, and so forth, performed without abandoning the relationship with those fires. Thus, even the Sarasvatī-penance—characterized by the restriction of eating sacrificial food—should be explained in accordance with the stage of life and one's own duties. As for one who maintains no sacred fires, even a *snātaka* may subsist on alms, based on the statement of Hārīta: "Or, subsisting on alms, he should go against the current of the Sarasvatī. This is the general direction. 248.
This is another penance specifically for a Kṣatriya:
he shall attain purification if he is killed in battle while serving as a target.
Is this penance restricted to death alone? Indeed, the undertaking [of the vow] belongs only to one who has already resolved upon death.
But he who has thus engaged in it, though still living, is as if dead; afflicted by the blows, he is not purified. (3.249)

The mention of "battle" is intended to establish that this applies specifically to a Kṣatriya. One who has become a "target"—meaning one who does not protect himself, is devoid of armor and other equipment, and does not shield himself from the weapons of the enemy—is killed while facing the foe for the sake of the king, for the sake of cows, or for the sake of Brāhmaṇas, according to the rules of combat. And so says Vasiṣṭha: "In battle, he should cause himself to be slain while facing the foe for the sake of the king, for the sake of Brāhmaṇas, or for the sake of cows" (VaDh 20.27). Furthermore, the "king" here should be understood as one who is not his own master [i.e., a righteous ruler]. The use of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the phrase "he shall attain purity" is for the purpose of removing doubt. Thus Manu also says:

Or he may [volunteer] a hundred thousand of weapon-bearers, according to his own wish, provided they are learned [in weaponry], that is, experts in arms and skilled in battle—not at the will of the master or others. Without protecting himself, as if he were a mere target for arrows, he should face the enemy in battle. There should be no doubt in this matter; here too, the use of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is intended solely to exclude any hesitation.
Or he should cast himself three times head-first into a blazing fire. (MDh 11.73)

This [rule] also applies specifically to those other than Brāhmaṇas. Under the section on theft, Manu states: "But a Brāhmaṇa by austerity alone" (MDh 11.100); this means that a Brāhmaṇa should remove his sin through austerity alone, and not by means of penance ending in death. And although this was stated under the heading of theft, it should be understood as applying to all cases except where there is a specific statement to the contrary. Thus, Āpastamba, having begun with "One who has violated the Guru’s bed shall enter a glowing iron image and burn himself," concludes with the rule "He should perform [the penance] until his last breath" (ĀpDh 1.28.16–18), showing that this refers specifically to non-Brāhmaṇas, citing Hārīta: "Hārīta says this is false; for he who strikes either himself or another is indeed one who is already accursed. The Teacher (Manu), however, does not mention entering fire, because that is enjoined by direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*). For it is heard in the *Kāṭhaka*: "Emaciated by fasting, he should ascend the fire three times, head downwards. For this very reason, the Aśvamedha, Svarjit, and other such rites are not prescribed here. In the *Mānava* (Manu-smṛti), however, there is a presentation of both Vedic (*śrauta*) and Smārta penances combined, for the purpose of removing the suspicion that the Smārta penances might be sublated by the Vedic ones due to their having the same purpose. If that were so, it would be logical that the Smārta penances are indeed sublated, and thus the Blessed One’s effort would be in vain. True, if they had the same scope. Therefore, it has been explained according to a difference in scope. Otherwise, because of the word "or" (*vā*) and the connection to a single cause, there would be an arbitrary option (*yadṛcchā-vikalpa*). Where something applies without distinction, a restriction of scope (*viṣaya-vyavasthā*) occurs because other options would otherwise be rendered useless. As it has been shown: "He who sacrifices with the Aśvamedha, and he who knows it thus" (cf. Śabara on PMS 1.2.4). For no one would be able to sacrifice with the Aśvamedha without having studied [the Veda]. Precisely for this reason, it is shown in the *Śābara-bhāṣya*: "If one should find honey on an Arka tree, why should he go to the mountain? and "Those seeking honey should go to the mountain by that very path. Nor do smallness and greatness exist here [in the sense of relative difficulty]. For some person of a pure nature (*sāttvika*) who cannot endure hardship, even the twelve-year penance ending in death may be easy; but for another who can endure hardship but lacks purity, the other [shorter penance] is easier. Thus, in comparison to one of noble ambition, death and the giving away of all one's property are equal. And between a learned man and a fool, the same applies to the study of the Saṃhitā versus death, or the twelve-year penance and so forth. Nor did Manu begin his work assuming only one type of person who possesses the capacity for all thirteen [penances]. If that were the case, there would be a simple equal option. Therefore, the mutual explanation of Vedic and Smārta penances must be followed according to the force of the instruction itself by way of a restriction of scope, and not by making others useless. This is the general direction. || 249 ||
For a wealthy member of the three higher castes, there is this other expiation as an alternative to those previously mentioned:
"By giving sufficient wealth to a worthy recipient, one attains purification;
and for the sake of the purifier's own purification, the Vaiśvānara sacrifice is prescribed. (3.250)

Having given to a worthy recipient (*pātra*)—one endowed with learning, good conduct, and austerity—wealth such as cattle, land, sesame, gold, and so forth, in sufficient quantity, free from any intent to harm his own kin or any deceit, for the purpose of fulfilling his obligatory *śrauta* and *smārta* rites, one attains complete purification. The intention is that this alone is the most esteemed among all expiations (*prāyaścitta*). In the *Mānava* [Smṛti], however, the detailed exposition concerns the manner of giving and not the specific nature of the object to be given. As for the object to be given, it is simply this much: in some cases, one might surrender everything, saying, "All this is mine," thus offering it without remainder. But if, after considering the entirety of what is required for the lifelong performance of the recipient's duties, there remains more than the donor’s own property, then he should give only as much as is sufficient for the performance of the prescribed *śrauta* and *smārta* rites throughout his life. In some cases, having fulfilled the requirement with just that much wealth, he may even give his house along with its furnishings. Here, the choice lies with the donor; there is no difference regarding the quantity of the substance itself. And this should be understood to apply to a case of intentional killing of a virtuous Brāhmaṇa, because of the statement, "It must be given to a worthy recipient. For such a Brāhmaṇa cannot be won over by a small effort. How indeed would one who knows the Veda completely—in its text, its meaning, and its proper sequence according to logic—and who maintains the sacred fires and is devoted to his own duties, accept a gift? Or rather, how could one be freed from sin by giving such a small amount of wealth to such a worthy recipient? Therefore, a heavier expiation is appropriate. And that has been shown. Furthermore, for the sake of the purification of the one who does not give but accepts the gift, there is the *vaiśvānara* cake-offering on twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapāla-puroḍāśa*). Because of the word "and" (*ca*), it is established that this applies to the donor as well, provided he is an *āhitāgni* (one who maintains the sacred fires), possesses great wealth, or possesses only that much wealth. Even though this is a *śrauta* rite, the statement that it is "remembered" (*smṛtā*) as a *vaiśvānarī iṣṭi* is intended to dispel the suspicion that it is a "forgotten Smṛti" (*apasmṛti*) because it is not mentioned in the *Mānava*. The intention is that even if it is not mentioned there, it should be understood that this matter was indeed remembered by Manu himself. Its omission there is for the purpose of showing that there is no fixed rule for the donor. Thus, this general principle holds: even for one who does not maintain the sacred fires, this expiation of "all one's property to a knower of the Veda" certainly exists. This is the direction of the argument.

But is it not more reasonable that these [penances] are intended for the completion of the twelve-year vow already under discussion when one is unable [to fulfill it]? And so Manu, having begun with "A slayer of a Brāhmaṇa shall [perform penance] for twelve years," and having stated [the alternatives] from "Or he may be among weapon-bearers for a hundred thousand [times]" (MDh 11.74) up to "Or, with his diet restricted, he may mutter [the Veda]" (MDh 11.77), has again spoken [of them] specifically in connection with the twelve-year vow: "Or, having shaved his head, he may dwell at the edge of a village, or in a cow-pen, or in a hermitage, or at the foot of a tree, devoted to the welfare of cows and Brāhmaṇas. (MDh 11.78)
One who immediately gives up his life for the sake of a Brahmin or a cow,
or one who protects a cow or a Brahmin, is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
"Whether he has been defeated in battle, or having conquered all his property, or if he loses his life for the sake of a Brahmin—he is liberated. (MDh 11.78–80).
Having thus stated the completion of the twelve-year penance through such acts as the sacrifice of one's life for the sake of a Brahmin, [the author] concludes:
"Thus, one who is firm in his vows, constantly practicing celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and composed in mind, removes the sin of killing a Brahmin at the completion of twelve years. (MDh 11.81).
From both the introduction and the conclusion, it is understood that this is indeed a single expiation (*prāyaścitta*) along with its supplementary details. And likewise, further on:
"Having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown, one should observe this very same vow. (MDh 11.87)

This very [penance] is the subject under discussion as the twelve-year penance (*dvādaśavārṣika*); thus there would be consistency. Otherwise, it would not be known whose reference this phrase "this very [one]" (*etad eva*) is. Or, due to proximity, it might refer only to the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). However, that is impossible there, because the horse sacrifice occurs only occasionally (*kādācitkatvāt*), whereas the penance is required as a permanent obligation (*nityatvena*). Therefore, these [penances] such as "a hundred thousand [arrows] for those bearing weapons" (*lakṣaṃ śastrabhṛtām*, MDh 11.73) should be understood as being established by their respective scopes (*viṣayavyavasthayā*) within the context of the preceding [twelve-year penance], and not independently. Furthermore, a penance ending in death (*maraṇāntika*) is not appropriate, because it contradicts the purpose [of the rite]; for that [death] is intended for the sake of purification, and the purpose of purification belongs to one who is alive. Nor can there be an option between a living penance and the other [death-penance], because they are unequal (*vaiṣamyāt*). If one were to resolve upon a death-penance while another [living penance] is possible by one's own choice, the fault of self-destruction (*ātmaghāta*) would also follow. For this very reason, Āpastamba, having introduced [the topic] with "The violator of the Guru’s bed shall enter a glowing iron image and burn himself," states: "Hārīta says this is false," and "For he who strikes himself or another is indeed one who is already accursed" (ĀpDh 1.28.15–17). For this reason also, a death-penance is inappropriate. And where a double vow is prescribed for killing a Brahmin engaged in a Soma-sacrifice (*savanastha*) and so forth, there, since dying twice is impossible, that [double penance] would be logically untenable. Therefore, the assumption of a single penance is indeed more reasonable. Yet, this is not entirely logical. As for the claim that they are one based on considering the force of the opening and conclusion, that is improper because of the intervention of Vedic [rites] such as the horse sacrifice. Indeed, the injunctions regarding the horse sacrifice, the *svarjit*, and others cannot be construed as referring to the twelve-year period. For these must necessarily have a basis in direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*). But these [injunctions] are found in the Smṛti. Due to the impossibility of a sequential order there, the sacrificial rites (*kratu*) should be enjoined either by introducing the twelve-year penance for the murder of a Brahmin and stating, "He who is unable to complete this [penance] shall sacrifice with this horse sacrifice and so forth," or by introducing the sacrifices for the sake of results and stating, "Even if unable to perform the twelve-year penance, he shall sacrifice. Both ways are improper, because the qualification (*adhikāra*) belongs to both husband and wife, yet only the husband has commenced [the penance].
