Nor is it right to say that the wife should proceed because of the husband's inability, since the word "wife" (*patnī*) denotes the owner (*svāmin*); she has no qualification for the twelve-year penance itself, which is the primary act (*aṅgin*). In that case, whether the twelve-year penance applies to both falling together, or whether the sacrifices do not enter into it—since the twelve-year penance is enjoined independently, just as plowing and other acts are connected to the *āhavanīya* fire and other rituals, it is illogical to assume it is for the sake of the sacrifices. Therefore, the independence of the sacrifices must certainly be stated. Thus says the Veda: "He who sacrifices with the horse sacrifice destroys all the guilt of killing a Brahmin. One should cause him who is being falsely accused to sacrifice with the *agniṣṭut*. He who sacrifices with the *abhijit* is truly released from the guilt of killing an embryo" (cf. ŚB 13.5.4.1; GDh 19.10). There is no authority for bypassing these direct [Vedic texts] to assume unperceived intermediate sentences. Therefore, the injunctions regarding the horse sacrifice and others are independent of the previous context. Being separated by those [Vedic rites], the giving away of all one's property (*sarvasvadāna*) and so forth do not obtain a connection with the twelve-year period separated by them. In other Smṛtis, however, such as "The slayer of a Brahmin [should cast himself] into fire three times after being cut, or [go to] a battle against those bearing weapons for a hundred thousand [arrows], or carry a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvaṅga*) in his hand" (GDh 22.2–4), the twelve-year penance is indicated specifically for one unable to die, based on the consideration of the context. In the Vasiṣṭha-smṛti also, having introduced [the topic] with "The slayer of a Brahmin, having kindled a fire... and stated, "If he should kill himself facing the enemy for the sake of the King or for the sake of a Brahmin, he becomes pure after being struck three times," the twelve-year penance is then mentioned: "Having prescribed the vow for himself for twelve years, he shall dwell neither in a village nor in a forest, carrying a skull-topped staff in his hand" (VaDh 20.25–28). Here too, following the context, it is understood that the twelve-year penance applies only to one who was previously qualified [for the Vedic rites]. In other [texts], however, there is simply no instruction for the twelve-year penance. In the Vasiṣṭha-smṛti, the use of "it is known" (*vijñāyate*) and the fact that "being struck three times" is ordained by direct Vedic revelation makes it clear that it does not enter into the twelve-year period. Therefore, all [penances] are to be explained—and have been explained—as independent, according to their respective scopes. As for the concluding summary, it should be applied in relation to what was previously stated, but the previously stated is not dependent on that summary. For the summary refers to what has already been stated, not that something becomes stated because of the summary. Thus, the passage beginning with "Or, having shaved his head, he may dwell... (MDh 11.78) is a supplement to the entire previously mentioned set of penances. And in all cases, this collection of restrictive rules (*niyamakalāpa*) is entirely consistent. On the contrary, it is the twelve-year penance itself that is excluded from this [summary] due to its contradiction with the rule "having built a hut in the forest" (ĀpDh 1.24.11). Nor is an option (*vikalpa*) possible; if such an option were assumed, the exclusion of the twelve-year penance would be improper. As for the two subsequent verses, they teach other penances such as the sacrifice of one's life for the sake of cows or Brahmins, but they do not apply to the twelve-year penance already commenced, because there is no evidence for it, and because in the Vasiṣṭha-smṛti, the phrase "it is known" in the verse "or being struck three times" shows that it is based on direct Vedic revelation. As for the concluding summary "Thus, always firm in his vow... (MDh 11.81), this too is a supplement to everything. It should be construed as follows: "In this manner, by this penance, by me, through self-restraint, I am to be purified"—referring to the vow consisting of the twelve-year period, the state of being a warrior for a hundred thousand [arrows], entering the fire, performing sacrifices, and so forth. And thus the final summary becomes consistent: "When the twelve-year period or the vow is completed, he removes the guilt of killing a Brahmin. Thus the supreme summary is made coherent.
"Therefore, by adhering to any one of these methods and remaining well-restrained, a Brahmin may, through self-mastery, cast off the sin committed by killing a Brahmin.

(MDh 11.86) Otherwise, because they are singular, the expression "by adhering to any one of these" would be incoherent. Nor is it appropriate to say that he should adhere to any one of the methods for completing the twelve-year penance, such as the service of the fire and so forth; for if that were the case, since these would be subordinate, there could be no mention of them as primary. Furthermore, it has already been stated that it is impossible for those [methods] to have the purpose of completing that [twelve-year vow]. As for what follows immediately after:

"Having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown, one should observe this very same vow" (MDh 11.87). Here, because of immediate proximity, such rules as "having resorted to one of the [prescribed] methods" (MDh 11.86) and "one should observe the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa" (YDh 3.254) are to be applied, but not the twelve-year penance; for, due to the intervention [of other verses], the reference by the pronoun [in MDh 11.87] would be impossible. "A fourth part of the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa is prescribed for the killing of a Kṣatriya."
For a Vaiśya established in his proper conduct, an eighth part is to be known; for a Śūdra, however, a sixteenth part.
But having unintentionally caused the death of a Kṣatriya,
the best of the twice-born should give one thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh for the sake of his own purification.
Having said this, it was further stated:

"Or, being self-restrained, with matted hair, he shall perform for three years the vow of the slayer of a Brahmin, dwelling far away from a village and making his abode at the foot of a tree. (MDh 11.126–28)

And since that [penance] is already established by the mention of the fourth part itself, [the mention of the fourth part again] would be redundant. If, on the other hand, the giving of even the fourth part of one's entire property were to follow from the mention of the fourth part, then for one possessing great wealth, the instruction to give a thousand cows would be intended for an unintentional act, or else a three-year vow would have been prescribed. Otherwise, since a three-year vow would already be applicable even to an intentional act due to the preceding verse, the statement regarding the unintentional act would be inconsistent. Therefore, the explanation exactly as stated is the correct one. As for the argument that a penance ending in death is improper because it contradicts the purpose of the act, that too is incorrect; for the rule "and begging for alms for the sake of self-purification" (MDh 11.73) indicates that the penance is for the sake of purifying the *ātman*, not for the sake of purifying the body. It is the *ātman*—the very substance of the person—that is refined by the penance. And this is no different whether the penance ends in death or otherwise. As for the claim that an option between death and another penance is improper due to inequality, it has already been said that this is irrelevant, given the diversity of human intellects. As for the objection that if one chooses death when other penances are possible by one's own will, it results in the charge of suicide, that would lead to the same consequence in the case of the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice, where the choice is prescribed with a single animal among many; there too, the commission of sin would result from the killing of multiple living beings. Furthermore, if wine were optionally substituted by water or cow-urine of the color of fire, there would be a fault in its voluntary use. This same fault applies even if the intention is merely to complete the twelve-year penance. Moreover, the distinction of scope is exactly the same in both cases. The statement of Āpastamba, however—"until the last breath" (ĀpDh 1.24.24)—is intended either to exclude the penance ending in death for a Brāhmaṇa or to prescribe death as an alternative method. Otherwise, the instructions regarding penances ending in death would simply lack authority. We shall explain this more precisely in the section concerning violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*). As for the argument that a "twofold vow" implies the impossibility of dying twice, the implication here is that there is a repetition of the application of life-long penances based on capacity, rather than a connection solely to the twelve-year penance. Enough of this digression. (250)
Now he states the extended applications:

"Upon killing a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice, one should perform the vow prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa-slayer; likewise for a killer of an embryo according to its caste, and so too for a murderer of an Āryā. (3.251)

The mention of the *yāga* (sacrifice) is for the purpose of indicating that the fault occurs precisely during the performance [of the sacrifice]. Furthermore, this word *yāga* should be understood as referring specifically to the Soma-sacrifice, based on another Smṛti text: "And a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who has entered the *savana*" (VaDh 20.34). Thus, the Vedic tradition states: "Therefore they say, 'One should not kill one who has entered the *savana*; indeed, he who performs the *savana* becomes a sinner'" (ŚB 3.2.1.40). In the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma, this is supplementary to the announcement: "This Brāhmaṇa is consecrated. Consequently, some hold that the fault occurs after the announcement. However, it is more logical that it begins from the selection of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), because in the phrase "one who has entered the *savana*," the past sense is not intended; rather, the commencement of the ritual itself is intended. Otherwise, the fault would apply only to one whose sacrifice is already completed. As for the statement, "For by the announcement a Brāhmaṇa is born—he who is born from the sacrifice," that is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). In the Mānava [Smṛti], however, the phrase "and a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who have sacrificed" (MDh 11.87) should be construed with the intention of expressing mere agency, and not with the intention of expressing that the sacrifice has been completed. Alternatively, because of the scriptural mention of "one who has performed the *savana*" and Manu’s statement "who have sacrificed," the fault applies only to those who have offered the sacrifice. And here, because of the mention of the "performance" (*prayoga*), it should be explained that the fault applies even during the course of the performance. Regarding the "vow of a Brāhmaṇa-killer" (MDh 11.101), it should be applied according to the same jurisdictional rules as before, ending with the gift of sufficient wealth for the twelve-year penance and so forth. As for the killer of an embryo: whatever penance is prescribed for the killing of a person of a certain caste, that very same should be performed for the killing of an embryo of that caste. Likewise, having killed an *Ātreyī*, one should perform the penance prescribed for that caste. An *Ātreyī* is said to be a woman from the day of her first menstruation up to the sixteenth day. And this [penance] is to be understood as applying when her husband is present, prior to sexual intercourse, because the Vāsiṣṭha text cites the scriptural authority: "For in her, future offspring is produced" (VaDh 20.36). Others, however, connect the phrase "likewise the slayer of an *Ātreyī*" with "he should perform the vow of a Brāhmaṇa-killer" (MDh 11.101), and not with the subsequent rule "according to the caste"; and they describe the *Ātreyī* as a cow of Atri. That too is quite reasonable. Thus the Vedic tradition says, having stated, "From him Atri was born," "Therefore they call a woman of the Ātreyī class a sinner" (ŚB 1.4.5.13). By this, both [interpretations] are correctly explained. The rest is clear. || 251 ||
And this other [rule] is likewise an extension by analogy:
"Even if he has not killed, if he has come together for the purpose of killing, he should perform the vow;
but if it is a Brāhmaṇa engaged in a Soma-sacrifice, he should perform double the vow. (3.252)

When many people have gathered for the purpose of killing with the thought, "This Brahmin must certainly be killed by us," even he among them who did not actually strike the fatal blow must perform the penance prescribed by the aforementioned rule regarding the circumstances. This is to be understood as applying when the blow has been struck; however, when no blow has been struck: "When many have assembled for the purpose of killing a Brahmin or others, he through whose blow death occurs shall be guilty, and not the others likewise."

This is because of the instruction of Hārīta; and from the word *tathā* ("likewise"), it is understood that he likewise becomes fallen (*patita*), and not that he is merely defiled (*duṣṭa*). Regarding the rule "twofold for one present at a *savana*," this does not mean a repetition of the penance. What then? It means that the penance there is more severe. Consequently, one should look to such passages as Āpastamba states: "By this very procedure, he should perform [the penance] until the final breath" (ĀpDh 1.24.24). Or, there may be two penances according to the manner described by the words: "Having given away his entire property, or having performed the twelve-year penance, then [the penance] ending in death," and so forth. Otherwise, however, [the author] would have simply said, "one should prescribe the vow twice," rather than saying "twofold. Furthermore, regarding one present at a *savana*, this applies only to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and not to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*); yet even there, an excess of fault certainly exists, and the penance must be determined accordingly. Others, however, explain this verse differently:
One should observe the vow even if one does not kill, provided that one has approached with the intent to kill.

"Having intentionally performed an act that serves as a cause for killing" means having done so with full awareness. That specific act by which, through its intensity, a Brāhmaṇa proceeds toward his own death—such acts being the provocation of anger, the seizure of property, and so forth—even if it was not done with the conscious thought "let the Brāhmaṇa die," nevertheless, if upon such a voluntary act like the theft of property the Brāhmaṇa's life should perish without depending on any other intervening cause, then one should perform the vow associated with the killing of a Brāhmaṇa even though he has not actually killed him. This very point is also stated in the *Mānava* (Manusmṛti):
"Having given false testimony, likewise having reviled a guru, having misappropriated a deposit, and having committed the murder of a woman or a friend. (MDh 11.88)

In a case where, through false testimony given by a Brāhmaṇa—whether of his own accord or at the instigation of another—a loss of life occurs, even then, having spoken such a falsehood and thereby provoked or enraged a Guru by means of that very act, such as through a curse or the like, he must indeed perform the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyā-vrata*). This same rule should be understood to apply even when the Guru is not a Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, having stolen a deposit belonging to a Brāhmaṇa which causes his death; or having killed a woman belonging to a Brāhmaṇa who causes his death—even if she is not a Brāhmaṇa; or having killed a friend who is not a Brāhmaṇa but is in such a state [of causing death], the intention is that one must perform the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa in its entirety. Here, the word "tathā" (likewise) has the sense of "in this manner. The meaning is: "having produced some other cause of death for a Brāhmaṇa in this manner. And so Gautama says: "And also in the case of harming a weak person, if one is capable of rescuing him" (GDh 21.19); he states this for precisely this purpose. This should also be applied to the case of Kṣatriyas and others. And in the case of one engaged in a Soma-sacrifice (*savanastha*), this very penance is doubled; such is the general direction. 252.

Now he speaks concerning liquor: "Having drunk one of these—liquor, water, ghee, cow urine, or milk—that resembles fire in appearance, the drinker of liquor attains purification through death. (3.253)

The meaning of the verse is that having drunk liquor, water, cow-derived ghee, or cow-derived milk—[the latter] being like fire and capable of burning—one who drinks liquor is purified by death, being consumed by that very [substance]. Furthermore, in this context, the word *surā* refers exclusively to the liquor made from flour (*paiṣṭī*); this has already been stated in the passage: "The slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief... (YDh 3.228). And this penance applies to the intentional drinking of liquor by members of the three [lower] castes and by a Brāhmaṇī woman. However, for women of the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya castes, this penance does not apply.

"Having drunk *surā* through delusion, a twice-born man shall drink *surā* that is the color of fire" (MDh 11.90). Since this instruction regarding expiation applies only to the twice-born, and since women are not twice-born, how then does it apply to a Brāhmaṇī? [The answer is:
"That Brāhmaṇī who drinks *surā* does not go to the world of her husband" (YDh 3.256).

Thus [it is said], because of the force of the initial statement. And in Gautama’s Dharmasūtra: "In the case of a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk *surā*, they should pour hot *surā* into his mouth; when he is dead, he shall be purified" (GDh 23.1). Here, the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is made specifically for the sake of the woman [who has committed adultery]. Otherwise, he would have simply said "of the twice-born" (*dvijasya*). Nor is it reasonable to say that this is intended to exclude the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya, since Manu uses the term "twice-born. Nor is it for the purpose of a restrictive definition (*upasaṃhāra*), because in the verse containing the prohibition, all three castes are mentioned separately: "Surā is indeed the filth of foods, and sin is called filth."
Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink *surā*. (MDh 11.93)

Therefore, in Gautama’s rule regarding the Brāhmaṇa, the term "Brāhmaṇa" is intended to signify the connection with the Brāhmaṇa *caste* alone. It is not correct to interpret this as referring to a male Brāhmaṇa simply because of the masculine gender, for that would result in the redundancy of the specific mention [of the caste]. For this very reason, a separate prohibitory verse is introduced in the *Mānava* (Manu). Otherwise, since the penance would already be established by the instruction on penance itself—as in the case of killing a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyā*)—the separate mention would be purposeless. Consequently, although the term "wine-drinker" (*surāpa*) is used here without qualification, it should be explained in this way in accordance with other Smṛtis. Since the *gauḍī* (rice-liquor) and *mādhvī* (honey-liquor) are prohibited specifically in relation to the Brāhmaṇa, and since the penance is connected to the "twice-born" (*dvija*), this penance does not apply to them; furthermore, the instruction is given in connection with *surā* (grain-liquor), as in: "Having drunk *surā* through delusion, a twice-born man... (MDh 11.90). Moreover, the other two are not *surā*. Therefore, regarding the intentional drinking of *gauḍī* and *mādhvī*, the rule of Vasiṣṭha applies: "In the drinking of intoxicants, however, for *asurā* and *surā* when done unintentionally, there is a *kṛcchra* and an *atikṛcchra*, followed by consuming clarified butter and undergoing the purificatory rite again" (VaDh 20.19). Other statements concerning the drinking of *surā* should be applied accordingly. (253)
Thus, for repeated practice committed intentionally, the penance ending in death has been declared. Now, he states the penance for that same intentional act when it is not repeated:
"Clad in hair-cloth or with matted locks, he should perform the vow of the slayer of a Brahmin; or he should eat oil-cake or even grain-husks at night for a year. (3.254)

One should perform the vow for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa for one year; this is how the text should be construed. Nor should one fall into the error of thinking that two distinct penances are being taught, because [this text] forms a single syntactical unit with the Laws of Manu:
"To remove the guilt of drinking liquor, he may eat grains or oil-cake once at night, wearing clothes of hair, carrying a banner, and with matted locks" (MDh 11.92).
If a twice-born man, out of delusion, drinks liquor, he shall drink liquor that is red-hot like fire. (MDh 11.90)

Therefore, in this context as well, the Blessed One stated that [the penance] is for drinking only once, in order to exclude the drinking of *surā* liquor. Thus, it is established that this applies only to drinking done intentionally (*kāmakṛta*) once. In the *Śāṅkha-smṛti* as well, after stating with the intention of referring to repeated drinking done intentionally: "A drinker of *surā* shall drink water heated by fire; having his body consumed by that, he attains purification," it then says: "Alternatively, the drinker of *surā* dressed in bark garments and carrying a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), and the violator of the Guru’s bed, shall both perform the very same vow prescribed for killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyāvrata*); they attain purification in that much time. This refers specifically to the one-year penance (*sāṃvatsarika*) and not to the twelve-year penance (*dvādaśābdika*). In that case, the phrase "in that much time" would be entirely unnecessary. Therefore, the intention is that one should perform that very penance prescribed for killing a Brahmin, such as what was previously stated: "For a fallen person (*patita*) should rescue himself; he should perform the *taptakṛcchra* for one year" (cf. Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.243). In this way, consistency with Manu is achieved. Otherwise, due to contradiction with that, there would be a contradiction with a well-known meaning. As it has been said:
"Having carefully examined the Dharma spoken by the sages,
Śaṅkha and Likhita likewise extracted it correctly from the sacred tradition (āmnāya).
This very same point is also stated in the Sāṃvarta [Purāṇa]:
Or, for one year, he may subsist on grains while avoiding the essence of all foodstuffs. Thus it is said.

In this regard, there is a specific rule: "Clad in hair-cloth, with matted locks, eating once at night either barley or oil-cake. However, Āpastamba states: "Having drunk *surā*, having committed theft, or having violated the teacher’s bed—provided one has not committed the murder of a Brahmin—one becomes purified in three years by eating sparingly at every fourth mealtime and bathing three times a day" (ĀpDh 1.25.10). And this refers to cases where [the acts] have been committed cumulatively; otherwise, the phrase "provided one has not committed the murder of a Brahmin" would be unnecessary. Therefore, even if all three have been somehow committed unintentionally, one should follow the rule stated by Āpastamba. Even though, in the *Āṅgirasa* [Smṛti], the vow called *vajra* is described as follows:

"Those who are joined with great sins (mahāpātaka) are purified in three years"—this rule concerning the twelve-year penance should be understood as applying specifically to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, and only for learned Brāhmaṇas. Regarding the drinking of liquor, however:
"For the aforementioned period of time, Brāhmaṇas alone are the [qualified] agents."

What has been stated on that very point should be observed there: by saying "the Brāhmaṇas alone are the cause," he makes known that the restriction of time is dependent upon other Smṛtis. In this same manner, other penances for drinking liquor mentioned in other Smṛtis are also to be applied. || 254 ||

Having thus described the vow for killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyāvrata*)—which involves eating the food of a *kaṇa* beggar and so forth—for one year in cases of intentional practice, or until death in cases of unintentional practice, he now speaks to describe the case of unintentional [drinking]:
"But having drunk liquor unintentionally, or even semen, feces, or urine, the three castes deserve re-initiation; of this there is no doubt. (3.255)

Regarding the phrase "out of ignorance": this refers to the case where there is ignorance of the prohibition. This applies likewise to semen, feces, and urine. Consequently, the three castes—even those who have already undergone the purificatory rite of initiation (*upanayana*)—are required to undergo it again. Furthermore, since the expiation prescribed here is not minimal, it is made clear by the words "there is no doubt" that some other [expiation] must also be devised. However, for one who knows the prohibition and drinks [liquor] knowing it to be *surā*, even if it is not a habitual act, the rule of Vasiṣṭha (VaDh 20.19) applies. This should be applied similarly to urine and the rest as well. But regarding the drinking of liquor out of ignorance prior to initiation, purification is achieved through that very rite of initiation itself. Thus says Manu:
"Having drunk *vāruṇī* through ignorance, one becomes pure by means of the *saṃskāra* alone. (MDh 11.146).
Here, because the word "again" (*punaḥ*) is absent, the *saṃskāra* intended is the very first one. Accordingly, the word "again" is used elsewhere:
"Having consumed feces, urine, or that which has been touched by *surā*, through ignorance..."
"The three twice-born castes are eligible for re-consecration. (MDh 11.150)

Because of the mention of the "twice-born" (*dvijāti*) and the word "again" (*punaḥ*), this is understood to apply only to those for whom the initiation (*upanayana*) has already been performed. Consequently, the statement "he is purified by the purificatory rite alone" (*saṃskāreṇaiva śudhyati*) should be seen as referring to the first [initiation] rite. However, according to the text of Gautama—"A Brāhmaṇa [should avoid] liquor always" (GDh 2.20)—there is a fault even prior to initiation; yet there is no separate penance (*prāyaścitta*) for that case, because of the statement "he is purified by the purificatory rite alone. Therefore, some maintain that this half-verse also refers specifically to one who is uninitiated.
"Intentional, indescribable, and ending in death—this is the settled rule. (MDh 11.146)

This is its meaning: if one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*) should drink *aruṇī* or *paiṣṭī* liquor (*surā*) out of ignorance or unintentionally, then he becomes pure through the initiatory rite (*saṃskāra*) alone; however, having intentionally drunk an "indescribable" (*anirdeśya*) quantity, even for him the penance is that which ends with death—this is the settled rule. The intention is that no other penance need be considered here. The term "indescribable" (*anirdeśya*) is an adjective qualifying the drinking: it refers to drinking repeatedly and intentionally to such an extent that it cannot be described—namely, how many times or what the quantity was. Others also explain this without distinction, saying it applies only to one who is uninitiated; but since that is already established by the verse, "Having drunk *surā* out of delusion, a twice-born man... (MDh 11.90), it is of little use, and thus the previous explanation alone is correct. Furthermore, regarding the consumption of food touched by *surā*, because the instruction for the initiatory rite (*saṃskāra*) applies specifically to the initiated, the principle of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikā*) establishes that such a case would not primarily fall under this rule. Therefore, the determination of the subject matter is exactly as stated above; this is the general direction. || 255 ||

To demonstrate that this very same expiation for drinking liquor applies even to a Brāhmaṇī woman—being determined as appropriate according to whether she has been consecrated by marriage or not—the author introduces a deprecatory explanatory passage (arthavāda):
"A Brāhmaṇī who drinks liquor does not go to the world of her husband;
in this very world, she is reborn as a female dog, a vulture, or a sow. (3.256)

Even that *brāhmaṇī* who drinks *surā* does not go to the world of her husband, despite having earned it through her devotion to him. This word *surā* is used here as an indication for intoxicants (*madya*) in general, and not for the sake of denoting the primary substance *surā* (grain-liquor), because it occurs within an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). For if it were contained within an injunctive statement, then its primary meaning alone would have to be accepted. However, in an explanatory passage, the word *surā* is used to denote intoxicants in general for the purpose of censure. Now, one might object: since the Veda originates from a source beyond human intellect, its interpretation as an explanatory passage is appropriate; however, in the case of human-authored statements, being an explanatory passage implies a lack of deliberate intention. True, this would be so if the author intended the explanatory passage to serve merely as a rhetorical embellishment. But the authors of the *Smṛtis* do not employ explanatory passages with the sole aim of providing mere persuasion; rather, they use them specifically to convey particular practical injunctions. For this very reason, it has been explained that this verse is intended solely for the prescription of penance (*prāyaścitta*). Its presentation in the form of an explanatory passage is for the purpose of establishing the definition [of the offense]. And thus, from the statement "she does not go to the world of her husband," it is understood that the husband remains free from fault. As for the other *Smṛti* text:
Half of the body of that man whose wife drinks liquor falls [with her];
for one whose half-body has fallen, no expiation is prescribed. (VaDh 21.15)

Thus, this [penance] is to be understood as applying to one who, having heard the word "wife," does not abandon her, due to association with an outcast (*patita*). But here, it should be explained that she who drinks [liquor] after having been abandoned by her husband does not go to the world of her husband. For she, having experienced terrible hells, is born again in this very world in such animal wombs as a female dog, a vulture, or a village pig, and is produced repeatedly until the dissolution of the universe (*pralaya*), never being elevated; this is the intended meaning. In this way, for a Brāhmaṇa woman, whether intentionally or otherwise, in the case of drinking *surā* or drinking intoxicants (*madya*)—whether once or through repeated practice—the determination of penance is the same as for a Brāhmaṇa man. However, regarding the drinking of the primary *surā* by Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, Sumantu has stated: "The penance for a drinker of *surā* is six months of bathing in water from rivers whose mouths are in the ocean (*samudraukaḥ*), the pouring of ten thousand recitations of the *Sāvitrī* upon the head, and at the end, a *sāntapana*; he becomes pure through every *kṛcchra*. The meaning of this is as follows: he who has drunk *surā* excessively and intentionally is a "drinker of *surā*" (*surāpa*). For a compound occurs when there is a specific distinction (i.e., intentional drinking). Therefore, to establish that, it is said "intentionally" and "in repeated practice. The penance for that drinker of *surā* lasts six months. "Bathing in water from rivers whose mouths are in the ocean": *okaḥ* means dwelling; those rivers whose dwelling is the ocean are "ocean-mouthed" (*samudraukaḥ*), meaning they flow into the ocean. "Bathing in water from rivers whose mouths are in the ocean" (*vṛtasamudraukasaḥsnānam*): *vṛtāḥ* means surrounded by mats and the like. The meaning is: bathing in a river flowing to the ocean, in a place enclosed and protected by mats and so forth. At the end of the six months, there is the pouring of water on the head with ten thousand recitations of the *Gāyatrī*, and the *sāntapana*. This consists of fasting while drinking the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) on one day, and not drinking it on the other. This is not the *mahāsāntapana*; rather, one remains for six months performing either the *prājāpatya* or the *taptakṛcchra*. And although this is stated without qualification, it should nevertheless be understood as applying only to the wives of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. Why is that?
Women and those who are ill deserve only half of the penance. (ViDh 54.33)

Thus, from another Smṛti: "A year-long Kṛcchra penance is prescribed for the twice-born, and half of that for these [others]; therefore, because it is impossible for men, it applies to women of such a kind, as well as to children, the elderly, and the sick. And thus, the propriety of bathing within an enclosure (pariśrita) would be established through its connection with women and others. Here too, since the instruction regarding expiation for a Brāhmaṇī woman is the same as for a man, this is the general direction for the other two [castes]. However, in the case of intentional drinking once, there is a Kṛcchra and a Cāndrāyaṇa; if unintentional, there is only a Kṛcchra. As Manu said:

"One should perform this very same vow even in the case of women who have become outcastes; however, clothing and food should be given to them, and they should dwell near the house. (MDh 11.188) Since no other subsequent vow has been taught here, the vow prescribed specifically for women—even though it was separated by the verse concerning the abandonment and restoration of outcastes—is indicated by the phrase "one should perform this very same vow. And regarding that, it has been said:
"But if she should become defiled again after being enticed by one of equal status, the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances are declared to be her means of purification" (MDh 11.177).

Here, it is explained that the application of the words *ca* and *eva*—whether used separately or together—is understood through a systematic arrangement of the subject matter (*viṣayavyavasthayā*). Other penances for drinking liquor (*surāpāna*) should likewise be interpreted in this manner. Some, however, describe that there is no fault whatsoever in women drinking intoxicants (*madya*).
Wine, meat, and spirituous liquors are the food of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas;
that must not be eaten by a Brāhmaṇa who partakes of the sacrificial oblation for the gods. (MDh 11.95)

Thus, regarding this prohibition, because the connection with a male is heard [in the text], that [mention of the male] is intended solely to indicate the genus (*jāti*) and not for the purpose of indicating gender (*liṅga*), since a specific Brāhmaṇa individual cannot be the object of an injunction. Rather, by way of restating the drinking, a prohibition is enjoined for one characterized by the Brāhmaṇa genus; and those learned in the Nyāya maintain that an attribute of what is being characterized (the *lakṣyamāṇa*) is not intended to be significant. Others, however, considering even the word "Brāhmaṇa" to be merely indicative (*upalakṣaṇa*), describe the prohibition of drinking as applying to the Śūdra as well, because the explanatory statements (*nigada*) containing the reason apply without distinction.
"Or he may fall into impurity while intoxicated, or even recite a Vedic text [in such a state]. (MDh 11.96)

This [prohibition] indeed applies to a Śūdra as well. Moreover, for him alone there is a fault in consuming Vedic examples while in a healthy state; therefore, the reason [for the prohibition] becomes even more appropriate so that such an occasion does not arise when he is intoxicated. In this case too, the reason for it being an *upalakṣaṇa* (an indicative mark) must be stated. Why should the word *surā* not also be an *upalakṣaṇa* for food in general? For even from eating too much of that, this very reason occurs through dysentery and the like, as in: "Or, intoxicated, one might fall into impurity. Therefore, [your argument] is quite trivial. And in the following verse:
He whose Brahmanical nature, residing within his body, is once intoxicated by liquor, loses his status as a Brāhmaṇa and descends to the state of a Śūdra. (MDh 11.97)

Regarding what has been stated [in verse 255], it must be considered whether that does not apply to a Śūdra. However, the phrase "eating the oblation of the gods" (*devānām aśnatā haviḥ*) is untenable even for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, because they too are prohibited from consuming food consecrated by the *vaitānika* fires; how much more so, then, regarding the substance itself? If it were argued that, by virtue of their connection with *pākayajña* sacrifices, the phrase refers to the Śūdra eating the *pākayajñīya* oblation of the gods, then, since there would be no one to exclude (as both classes are equally excluded), the statement would be entirely redundant. Therefore, it is something quite arbitrary. Likewise, others explain the word *madya* as being based on its connection with intoxication (*mada*). Consequently, they claim that there is no fault even for a Brāhmaṇa if the intoxicating power has not yet arisen after the fermentation, or if it has subsequently subsided. Indeed, some people act in this manner in certain cases. But where such practice is not observed, the rule applies on the grounds that it was "contained in a vessel used for liquor" (MDh 11.147). That term, however, should be understood as referring specifically to that which produces intoxication—characterized by ingredients such as fermenting agents (*kiṇva*)—since it is not applied to things like *kodrava* rice, even though they are intoxicants. For common people use the word *madya* specifically through the process of fermentation. And since the world is the means for understanding the meaning of words, one should not overcomplicate the matter. Just as the established usage of cultured (*śiṣṭa*) people residing in Āryāvarta is followed, so too must the meaning of the Smṛti be followed, and not otherwise. The specific details regarding the category of mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*) have already been discussed; so, enough of this digression. (256)
Now, he speaks in order to declare the expiation for stealing gold, which follows in sequence:
"But one who steals the gold of a Brāhmaṇa shall present a mace to the king, proclaiming his own deed; whether slain by it or released, he is purified. (3.257)

He who steals gold belonging to a Brāhmaṇa shall go of his own accord to the presence of the king, carrying a club, for the sake of his own purification. Then, having declared his deed exactly as it happened, in its entirety and without guile, he should hand that club over to the king, saying: "May Your Majesty punish me with this. Thereupon, struck by the king with that club, he becomes purified. Or, if the king—considering that he is unfit for a penance ending in death, or out of compassion—does not strike him, nevertheless, being released or dismissed by the king, or freed from punishment, he shall indeed be pure; the intention is that he need not perform any other penance. Furthermore, by the use of the word *tu* ("but"), it is understood that this applies only to the mere act of stealing gold. The intention is that for one who has stolen and consumed it, and is unable to restore it, this is not at all a means of purification. However, the Śrauta penance does apply even to him. As Vasiṣṭha says: "In the case of stealing a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, having disheveled his hair, he should run toward the king, saying: 'I am a thief, sir; may you punish me! The king should give him a weapon made of Udumbara wood. He should kill himself with it; it is known from scripture that he becomes purified through death. Or, stripped of clothes and smeared with clarified butter, he should burn himself starting from the feet in a fire of dried cow-dung; it is known from scripture that he becomes purified through death" (VaDh 20.41–42). Here, because the phrase "it is known [from scripture]" (*vijñāyate*) introduces a Vedic text, it is logical to conceive the scope of the Smṛti rule as distinct from that. In that [Vedic] case, however, due to the absence of the word *tu*, it is understood that the theft extends until the gold is actually used. But in the rule "But he who steals a Brāhmaṇa’s gold... (*brāhmaṇasuvarṇahārī tu*), by the force of the word *tu*, it is understood that this [penance] applies only when the theft is committed by one capable of restoring it, since all castes have the duty to approach the king. Some say, however, that the king should carry out the execution only of non-Brāhmaṇas, while a Brāhmaṇa should be released from punishment. That is incorrect, because this [rule] was stated specifically with reference to a Brāhmaṇa. And so Manu says: [Manu 8.387–389].
A Brahmin who has committed the theft of gold, having approached the king, should proclaim his own deed and say: "May Your Majesty punish me."
"Then, taking up a club, the king himself shall strike him;
by execution the thief is purified, or a Brāhmaṇa by austerity alone. (MDh 11.99–100).

Nor can it be argued here that the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is for another purpose, because that would result in redundancy, since the mere term "thief" already includes him even without the mention of "Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that approaching the king is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa while the execution applies to others.
Then, taking up a mace, the king should strike him.

In this context, because of the expression "the Teacher," it is understood that the one under discussion is that very Brahmin. As for the interpretation that "a Brahmin [is purified] by penance alone"—whereby, by the force of the particle *eva*, they explain that for a Brahmin there is only penance, whereas for another there is either execution or penance—that too would be logically inconsistent, since no other person is under discussion here. However, the particle *eva* serves to exclude the possibility of alternative options, as penance and execution do not have the same purpose; thus, he is purified either by penance alone, or by execution through the process of appearing before the king. Consequently, if a Brahmin so desires, he should approach the king; whether killed by him or released, he is purified. Or, having gone before the king, he may perform penance. And that penance is what was stated by Saṃvarta.
"But having purified himself from the impurity born of stealing gold by means of independent penance,
the twice-born man, clothed in bark garments, shall perform the vow prescribed for a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa in the forest."

On account of the mark of dwelling in the forest (*araṇyavāsa*), this should indeed be the twelve-year penance; or rather, this is simply an extension (*atideśa*) of the vow for every instance of killing a Brahmin. Thus, the use of the plural in the concluding summary, “by these vows” (*etair vrataiḥ*, MDh 11.102), becomes appropriate; otherwise, there would have been only a dual. Furthermore, because of the mention of the twice-born (*dvija*), this applies only to one who has been initiated (*upanīta*); the intention is that for one who is uninitiated, there is no fault at all. As for those who explain that the mention of the Brahmin is merely indicative (*upalakṣaṇa*) because no other penance is taught for Kṣatriyas and others—they surely do not describe the words “Brahmin” and so forth in such injunctions as “A Brahmin must not be killed” or “Liquor must not be drunk” as being indicative of anyone who might be killed. What a marvel! Why do they not likewise explain the word “king” in the phrase “having approached the king” as being used figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*) to refer to teachers and others who merely provide instruction? Those who claim that killing a Brahmin is not fitting for a king and thus say that such [penances] apply only to Kṣatriyas and others, surely know dharma and adharma by themselves, independent of the operation of the Vedic injunctions; they are truly beyond remedy. Enough of this digression. || 257 ||

Now, he states another expiation for this very case: "Without having confessed it to the king, one should perform the penance for a liquor-drinker for the sake of purification; or one should give gold equal to one's own weight, or do what pleases a Brahmin. (3.258)
"One shall be purified by the vow for the drinker of spirituous liquor even without informing the king. Regarding this, [it is said]:
"Clad in hair-cloth or with matted locks, the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa should perform the vow;
he should eat oil-cake or grain-husks at night for a year" (YDh 3.254).

This should be understood as the penance for drinking liquor. Consequently, by that same logic, it would apply even to the theft of a small amount of gold when done intentionally. And "small" means less than a *suvarṇa*, because the word *suvarṇa* applies without distinction to both the substance and its measure. Nor is there any fault in accepting multiple meanings, since we observe [the term] used specifically for the measure pertaining to gold. Therefore, in this context, it must be taken as denoting the measure; the substance is understood by implication. Thus says Vyāsa: "In the theft of gold, even by a single *māṣaka*, there is a sin."
"But for one who steals a *niṣka* or even a quarter of it, we do not know what will happen.
And likewise: "One *suvarṇa*, one cow, or even a single finger's breadth of land..."
Having stolen from the foremost of the twice-born, one is certainly slain before long.

Thus, [the author] shows that there is less fault in cases prior to gold. Likewise: "In accordance with the magnitude of the gift and the excellence of the recipient, the fruit in giving and in taking away shall be middling, inferior, or superior. Thus it is said.

For this reason as well, the determination of penance is indeed appropriate with respect to the specific nature of the stolen object and the specific nature of the owner. Consequently, for thefts exceeding gold, the scope of penances for killing a Brahmin is determined based on the magnitude of the object. For a Brāhmaṇa who steals a hundred pieces of gold, he must go before the king; and there, if he is struck by the king with a club, that thief is released from that sin if he survives.

Thus, one would be purified according to the statement of Saṃvarta. However, if one does not go before the king, then one should give to a Brāhmaṇa gold equal to oneself—that is, weighed by oneself—or else one should give another object corresponding to that amount of gold, such as a village or the like, which brings satisfaction to the Brāhmaṇa. But for Kṣatriyas and others, in the case of stealing more than a hundred gold pieces, there shall be an option between the two penances prescribed by Vasiṣṭha. Āpastamba has also stated:
"Having committed theft, having drunk liquor, or having violated the teacher’s bed—but not having committed the killing of a Brāhmaṇa..."

"They should eat sparingly at the fourth meal-time and descend into water according to the ritual of the *savana*s. By alternating between standing and sitting, they destroy that evil in three years. (ĀpDh 1.25.10). This has already been explained as applying to the theft of gold less than a *suvarṇa* when unintentional, to sexual intercourse with the Guru’s wife when unintentional and occurring only once, and to the mere act of consuming *surā* unintentionally, provided all these occur simultaneously and somehow by chance. Furthermore, what was stated by Aṅgiras should also be applied together with the penances for killing a Brāhmaṇa, according to the specific circumstances of each case.
"Those joined with great sins (mahāpātaka) are purified in three years. Thus [it is said].

However, regarding a thief who possesses virtuous qualities, for stealing gold, Manu has prescribed the following for an intentional act: "A stealer of gold should offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter with the Sāvitrī mantra for one month; he becomes purified by performing the *sarvakṛcchra* penance. The same applies to other cases as well. If there were a penance for theft in another Smṛti, it should be applied according to this very method. Furthermore, in the case of stealing gold, it constitutes a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) only when the gold belongs to a virtuous Brāhmaṇa. For him alone is ownership over that property non-figurative (*anaupacārika*). For others, however, ownership is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), based solely on the fact of being the owner through mere worldly transaction, since the word "own" (*sva*) depends upon mere lordship (*prabhutvamātra*). Now, why is it that even those lacking virtues do not have ownership? Because the relationship of ownership is to be understood through the scriptures (*śāstra*). For if lordship were established by mere possession or mere lordship alone, then everyone would have it. And if that were the case, since such ownership could arise even through theft, the very act of seizing [another's property] would not constitute theft. Or, if ownership is indeed to be understood through scripture, why is it not accepted for one lacking virtues? Because the means of acquisition are restricted to receiving gifts and so forth, and these are impossible for one lacking virtues. As it has been said:
"However, one who is devoid of both learning and austerity must not accept gifts.
(YDh 1.200) The same applies to officiating at sacrifices and teaching. As Kātyāyana has said:
"One who is unlearned may be a sacrificer, or a teacher who is unstable."
Having punished both of them with the penalty for a thief, he should establish them on the road. (KSm 828)

In this way, other [texts] as well establish on numerous occasions that [the student] lacks the entitlement to accept gifts and so forth. Consequently, due to the absence of that [entitlement], there is simply an absence of ownership (*svatva*). However, livelihoods such as gathering ears of grain (*siloñcha*) and so on belong only to the *yāyāvara* (wandering) students. As for agriculture, trade, usury, and the like, these are explained as being merely incidental (*anvācaya*) to those who have already acquired property through gifts and other means, provided they are entitled [to them]. Likewise, property acquired by a father, grandfather, or others must be protected by the king until the student’s return home (*samāvartana*), in the event of the father’s or others’ absence; but thereafter, it belongs only to that virtuous one who has been admitted to the entitlement of performing ritual duties. If, however, he has some other virtuous heir, then that is indeed the property of a virtuous Brāhmaṇa. For this very reason, Nārada also stated the threefold nature of wealth:
"Property is of three kinds: white, variegated, and black.
That which is acquired by lawful means is 'white' and is righteous; the other is 'variegated' and is merely worldly. (cf. NSm 1.40). Also in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]:
"The wise know that the wealth of those who habitually perform sacrifices is the property of the gods; but the property of those who do not sacrifice is called the property of the asuras. (MDh 11.20)

That [wealth] does not first belong to the gods; for if that were so, there would be no sacrifice at all. Indeed, a sacrificer would not be able to relinquish what belongs to the gods. Therefore, in whatever manner it is relinquished with reference to the gods, in that same manner it becomes the property of the gods. Thus, it is shown by this very [text] that ownership over wealth is primary (*mukhya*) only for those whose nature is sacrifice, while for others it is secondary (*gauṇa*). Consequently, the wealth of non-sacrificers—which exists merely through possession, is conventional (*sāṃvyavahārika*), and serves only for the enjoyment of desires—is the property of the *asuras*; the intention is that they have no ownership over it. And thus says a Vedic verse (*mantravarṇa*): "What do the cows do for you among the Kīkaṭas?"—this makes it known that such [wealth] is indeed not to be withheld. Therefore, because ownership is merely figurative (*aupacārika*) in the case of Brahmins devoid of qualities, there is no connection with a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) in the theft of their [property]. However, even in that case, penance (*prāyaścitta*) must be determined in consideration of the relationship and utility of the possessor, the purpose of the theft, and the qualities of the thief. And that [penance], in the case of stealing a large amount or for the purpose of gambling and the like, is as stated by Śaṅkha: "A stealer of gold, one who transacts with outcasts, a betrayer of friends, a killer of one who has sought refuge, and one who lives by counterfeiting—these should perform the 'lying in water' (*jalaśayana*), the 'five heats' (*pañcatāpa*), and 'exposure to the open air' (*abhrāvakāśa*) during the summer, the rainy season, and the winter respectively. Since these have no fixed duration, they should be performed for a year, two years, or three years as appropriate. But if the thief is virtuous, the amount stolen is small, or if even a virtuous person uses it improperly through negligence, then the very [penance] stated by Śaṅkha immediately following the previous one applies: "Or they should drink cow-urine and barley-gruel for a month; thus they shall be purified. Other such [penances] should also be applied as appropriate to cases involving the gold of Brahmins lacking qualities. As for the punishment, however, it is that which is brought by the king's men by force, as stated in the section on punishments: [etc.]
A wise thief should go before the king with disheveled hair, confessing that evil deed: "I am a man of such deeds; punish me."
Taking up a club, or a staff made of khadira wood,
or a spear sharp at both ends, or even an iron mace.
"Whether through punishment or through release, the thief is freed from the theft;
but by failing to punish him, the king incurs the guilt of the thief. (MDh 8.314–6)

And this [penalty] is to be seen as applying only to one being led away by the king’s officers, and not to one who has come of his own accord for the sake of penance; for in that case, because of the rule "having taken up the mace from him," execution itself is certain. Here, however, depending on the nature of the offense, there may be either punishment—ranging from various verbal penalties up to execution—or release, perhaps in the case of one who is truly innocent but was brought before the court without due deliberation. For this very reason, it is said: "by punishment or by release. But how could there be any suspicion of release for one who has been approved by the assembly (*pariṣad*) after deliberation for the sake of penance? Consequently, even in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti*, the statement "whether killed or released, he is pure" (YDh 3.257) must be explained in accordance with the single consistent view of Saṃvarta as meaning: if one is killed by the king, and yet survives, then he becomes purified even without having received the [full] penalty, being thus released by the king. Likewise, in the section on royal punishments in the *Mānava-dharmaśāstra*, the fault of the king is stated: "by punishment or by release. This is what is meant: even by release, the thief is freed from the guilt; however, if the king should let him go without punishing him, then he incurs the sin of that [crime]. By whom? By the one worthy of punishment, the offender. And in that regard, there is no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa; rather, this [release] is precisely for the sake of penance. Here, even the penalty of death does not apply.

"Under no circumstances shall one kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is established in every kind of sin"—because of this prohibition, the meaning is that if a man who is indeed established in sin refuses to approach the king for the sake of penance, the king should not have him brought by force and killed. Since it is said, "There is no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa," the prohibition applies specifically to punishment; it does not apply to one who has come for the purpose of performing penance. This is the general direction. || 258 ||

Now he states the penances for violating the Guru’s bed: "He should lie upon a heated iron bed with an iron woman; having seized and cut off his testicles, he should cast away his body toward the southwest. (3.259)
One who has violated the Guru’s bed shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year,
or the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months while repeatedly reciting the Vedic Saṃhitā.

In this context, the term *gurutalpa* (violating the Guru’s bed) was not mentioned in the preceding verse because that section was dedicated solely to the enumeration of the mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*). Beginning with the words "the father’s sister, the maternal uncle’s wife," and ending with "having cut off his organ, he shall be executed, as shall the woman if she was willing" (YDh 3.233–4), the punishment is prescribed for the king; however, that is not what is being taught here, as it would contradict the current subject matter. Therefore, the meaning of that [previous] passage is that having cut off his organ along with the testicles, execution itself is his atonement and nothing else. Consequently, if one should approach these women intentionally or repeatedly, then this is the atonement; and the same applies to the woman if she was willing, or even if she was unwilling but approached such a man repeatedly, or even if she was unintentional. By the force of the word *ca* ("and"), this very atonement is indicated. For that reason, the term *gurutalpa* is used in the subsequent verse specifically to prescribe a different atonement. It was not repeated in the previous verse because it was already understood through its connection to the previously mentioned cutting of the organ. Thus, the present verse provides a specification of the methods for the previously taught excision of the organ and execution. This being so, if one should approach any of the father’s sisters and others unintentionally—either by force or by deception and repeatedly—then the following should be understood: "He shall lie upon a heated iron bed together with an iron woman. Since both are equally engaged in the act, the subsequent rule "and the woman if she was willing" (*sakāmāyāś ca yoṣitaḥ*) applies. Or rather, let both rules apply without distinction. In any case, these two types of atonement are to be known as applying to intentional repetition. The meaning is: on a red-hot iron plate, or in its midst, he should lie down, embracing her—who is like a woman glowing with fire—as if out of affection, thinking "this is she. The mention of the "woman" is illustrative; therefore, even a man may be embraced by a woman in this very manner. Alternatively, having had his testicles cut off, he should cast off his body in the southwest direction; the meaning is that he becomes pure through death. Having himself cut them off with a razor or other weapon and grasping the testicles with both hands, he should go toward the south-western direction by a straight path. If there is a well or similar obstacle in between, he should not avoid it. But if he is struck by something such as a tree in the way, he should remain right there until death. The mention of the "testicles" here is illustrative; thus, the organ is to be extracted along with the testicles. Accordingly, Vasiṣṭha says: "The violator of the Guru’s bed, having cut off his penis along with the testicles and holding them in his joined palms, shall go facing south. Wherever he is struck down, there he shall remain until death" (VaDh 20.13). Likewise: "Or, having shaved his head and smeared himself with clarified butter, he shall embrace a red-hot iron image of a woman (*sūrmi*); he becomes purified by death" (VaDh 20.14). *Niṣkālaka* means regardless of time, meaning desiring immediate death. Or, *niṣkālaka* refers to one from whom the "time" (blackness) inherent in the body—hair, beard, etc.—has been removed, since the word *kāla* is a synonym for black. The former interpretation is more appropriate. Here, *sūrmi* is an iron image, as indicated by the verb *pariṣvajet* ("shall embrace"). The rest is straightforward. The mention of the southern direction is either illustrative or optional. The rest is clear. The same is stated in the *Śāṅkha-smṛti*; the only difference is the cutting of the organ with a razor. As it says: "The violator of the Guru’s bed shall lie upon a heated iron bed, or having cut off his penis along with the testicles with a razor and holding them in his joined palms, shall walk toward the southwest without looking back; he becomes pure upon the fall of the body. Similarly: "In the case of approaching the maternal uncle’s wife, the father’s sister, the daughter-in-law, a sister, or a daughter—and by the word *ca* ('and'), the teacher’s wife is also included—and in the case of approaching the teacher’s daughter. From the plural *gamaneṣu* ("in the cases of approaching"), it is understood that this applies to repetition and to intentional acts. Furthermore, because the mother’s sister, daughter, and others are mentioned separately, it is known that the primary *gurutalpa* offense is elsewhere than with the mother; thus, in the case of the mother, this [atonement] applies only to unintentional, single instances. And the status of being "primary" (*mukhya*) belongs only to those wives of the father who are of the same caste as the father, because the father possesses a non-figurative (*anaupacārika*) status of "Guru. Accordingly, the extension of the rule to the teacher’s wife has been shown. In the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti*, the extension is explicit: "And likewise in the case of the teacher’s son, the student, and their wives" (VaDh 20.15). Therefore, the classification of the subject matter is well-stated. However, in the case of the mother, this [atonement] should apply only to a single instance of unintentional intercourse. As Saṃvarta says: [text follows].

"But for that lowest of men, that fool, who approaches his mother, his daughter, or his own sister, no atonement exists. This was stated with the intention of referring to atonement while one is still alive, because otherwise the atonement for violating the Guru's bed (*gurutalpa*) would result in being rendered meaningless. As it has been said by that same author:
"But one who has violated the bed of his guru shall sleep upon a heated iron bed,
or he shall embrace a glowing woman made of black iron.
And likewise Hārīta says:

"But that man who, having recognized her as his father's wife, or having recognized her as his own mother, approaches her, shall not attain purification unless he dies. Other Smṛti texts should also be explained in this manner; they are not cited here because they convey the same meaning. However, if there should be a single instance of approaching wives of one's father who are of the same caste, excluding one's own mother, due to ignorance—then...
"One who has violated the Guru’s bed shall perform the Prājāpatya penance or the Kṛcchra for a year" (YDh 3.260)—this is the rule.
"For a year" (samām) means for one year. The word "shall perform" (caret) is intended to include the carrying of a bedpost and so forth. As Manu says:
"Carrying a bedpost, clad in bark, with his beard unshorn, he shall dwell in a lonely forest..."
"One should perform the *prājāpatya* penance for one year with a concentrated mind" (MDh 11.105).
But regarding a single instance of unknowingly approaching women of a different caste:
"Or he should practice the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance and study the Vedic *saṃhitā* for three months" (MDh 11.106).

And this [penance] would apply only to the study of the Veda, by virtue of the context. However, one who is incapable of practicing the Veda should perform four *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, according to the rule: "three or even four. Because of the word "again," the intention is that if one approaches [the woman] again unintentionally, he should perform this very same penance repeatedly. Consequently, in the case of unintentional intercourse, there is a repetition of this very vow according to the number of instances. In the case of intentional intercourse, if it occurs once, the penance lasts for one year; and in the case of repeated practice, it ends only with death.
In any manner whatsoever, two hundred and forty mouthfuls of alms-food; (MDh 11.220)

This refers to the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance, and not to the *Yavamadhyā* and others, because of the force of the mention of "months" (*māsān*) and the presence of two *vā* particles. This determination of the subject matter is based on a synthesis with other *Smṛtis*. As long as the wife is under the husband’s protection, that is the occasion for the penances for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*). But when she has become unchaste (*vyabhicāriṇī*), then there should be only the penance for adultery (*pāradārya*). And that [penance] will indeed be stated later as either the *Cāndrāyaṇa* or the penance for killing a cow. Some hold that even if she is unchaste, if she has not been abandoned by the Guru, the offense of violating the Guru’s bed still exists. However, this would be the case only if the unchastity was unknown to the Guru, or if he had begun to have her perform the penance for that [unchastity]. But if the Guru himself accepts her as unworthy [of being his wife], then another penance generally prescribed must be determined according to the reason for not abandoning the Guru. Some, however, do not desire the penance for adultery at all in the case of women who have been abandoned, because the word "wife" (*dāra*) is based on the [sacramental] relationship. If that were so, there would be no adultery even in the case of widows. Nor is it logical that the status of "wife" is lost through unchastity and the like, because the word "wife" is based on the sacrament (*saṃskāra*), and that status does not cease even upon moral fall (*patana*). For this very reason, women who have fallen (*patitāḥ*) are not consecrated again even after they have performed penance; otherwise, since the sacrament would have ceased due to their fall, they would not be wives even after performing penance. Therefore, adultery certainly exists even in the case of unchaste women. However, a different penance for being a wanton woman (*svairiṇī*) certainly applies to them because it is specifically prescribed for that cause. As Śaṅkha says: "One who has had intercourse with a wanton *Śūdra* woman should bathe with his clothes on and give a water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa. With a *Vaiśya* woman, he should eat at every fourth meal-time and feed Brāhmaṇas. With a *Kṣatriya* woman, having fasted for three nights, he should give an *āḍhaka* of barley. With a Brāhmaṇa woman, having fasted for six days, he should give a vessel of clarified butter. It is the same for women who are merely promiscuous (*prakīrṇā*). It is otherwise for those who are not independent (*asvatantrā*). This should be understood to apply to unintentional intercourse with women who are not related to the Guru through non-uterine ties—such as female friends of the Guru and others—excluding those who are actually the Guru’s own relatives, and with women of lower castes than the man’s. But if it is intentional, the penance is simply that for a minor offense (*upapātaka*). And that is to be understood from Gautama’s rule: "Two years for another's wife, three for the wife of a *Śrotriya*" (GDh 22.29–30). But regarding unchaste women who have not been abandoned, if the act is unintentional, the rule of Vasiṣṭha applies: "If a Brāhmaṇa should unintentionally approach the wife of a Brāhmaṇa, a *Kṛcchra* penance is required if the husband has ceased his religious duties, and an *Atikṛcchra* if he has not ceased them" (VaDh 21.16). But if it is intentional, the *Cāndrāyaṇa* or the penance for killing a cow applies. In that regard, if she was not known to be unchaste and was not abandoned, then the *Cāndrāyaṇa* applies. But if he had begun to have her perform penance, then the penance for killing a cow applies, according to the statement: "In the case of a sin, heavy [penances] for heavy [sins], light for light" (GDh 19.19). However, regarding women who are not unchaste, if one unintentionally approaches highly qualified Brāhmaṇas and others of the same caste who are themselves qualified, the rule stated by Śaṅkha applies: "But in the case of women who are not promiscuous, it is otherwise: one who has had intercourse with a *Vaiśya* woman should perform the three daily ablutions for a year; with a *Kṣatriya* woman for two years; with a Brāhmaṇa woman for three years; and with a *Śūdra* woman, as in the case of a *Vaiśya*. And this applies to a *Śūdra* woman born of a Brāhmaṇa father—that is, a wife of superior caste. But if the intercourse is intentional and repeated, the penance for violating the Guru’s bed applies. As stated by Nārada in the section on punishments:
Mother, mother’s sister, mother-in-law, maternal uncle’s wife,
father’s sister, paternal uncle’s wife, the wife of a friend or pupil, sister, her female friend, and daughter-in-law.

"The daughter, the teacher's wife, a woman of the same lineage (*sagotrā*), one who has sought refuge, the king's queen, a female renunciant (*pravrajitā*), a nurse (*dhātrī*), a virtuous woman, and she who belongs to the highest caste— having approached any one of these, one is called a violator of the Guru’s bed. (NSm 12.72–74)

Because of the statement that [sexual intercourse] with a virtuous woman constitutes violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*), the penance pertaining to that offense would apply. Regarding women related to one's mother or father, the severity of the penance depends on the degree of proximity. Furthermore, paternal kinship begins from the eighth generation and maternal kinship from the sixth; these distinctions are to be understood according to the rules for marriage and the rules for ritual impurity (*āśauca*). Likewise, even among the female friends of those relatives, specific penances are to be determined based on their relative proximity or distance. However, in the case of the wives of one’s father other than one’s own mother, their brothers are considered *mātula*s (maternal uncles), and their sisters are *mātṛṣvasṛ*s (maternal aunts). Similarly, the co-wives of one’s sister are considered sisters, and their offspring are *bhāgineya*s (sisters' sons). Consequently, even in those cases, the penance should be slightly less than that prescribed for one’s own maternal uncle’s wife and others. Thus, Sumantu states: “All the wives of one’s father are mothers; their brothers are *mātula*s; their sisters are *mātṛṣvasṛ*s; likewise, the co-wives of one’s sister are sisters, and their offspring are *bhāgineya*s. Otherwise, having committed acts that cause social confusion (*saṃkara*), they become censurable and outcasts (*patita*”). This shows that the designation is indeed extended by analogy (*atideśika*). Therefore, the reduction in the penance is established. In this manner, a distinction must be made for other penances concerning these same subjects. However, for those specifically ordained, the determination of the scope is governed solely by the distinction between intentional acts (*kāmakāra*) and so forth. As stated in the Laws of Manu: [The text continues with the citation from Manu.]
"Having approached a daughter of his father's sister, a daughter of his own sister, a daughter of his mother's sister,
or a daughter of his mother's brother who is a close kinsman, one shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Thus [says] Saṃvarta.
Having approached the daughter of a guru, or his sister, or even his mother’s sister,
or her daughter as well, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
Having approached a maternal aunt, a mother-in-law, or the daughter of a maternal uncle out of delusion, one becomes pure by performing a Parāka penance.
In the case of approaching the wife of a paternal uncle, as well as approaching the wife of a brother, one must perform the penance for violating the Guru’s bed;
otherwise, there shall be no atonement.
And in the case of approaching a maiden, one should prescribe this very vow:
"Having approached the wife of a friend, a daughter-in-law, or the daughter of a mother’s sister, having fasted for a day and night, one should perform two *taptakṛcchra* penances. Thus it is said.

Likewise, Sumantu has stated in general terms: "In cases of approaching a woman who should not be approached, killing a woman, or contact with a *caṇḍāla*, one should perform three *kṛcchra* penances. He has also stated specifically: "In approaching one's mother, father’s sister, daughter-in-law, sister, sister’s daughter, or a *caṇḍālī* of the same lineage (*gotra*), one should perform three *taptakṛcchra*s and a *sāntapana*; in approaching an animal, a *prāṇāyāma* [is required]. Similarly, Gautama states: "In approaching the wife of a friend, a person of the same womb (*sayoni*), a person of the same *gotra*, a pupil, a daughter-in-law, or a cow, the penance is equal to that for violating the teacher’s bed (*talpasama*); some say it is an *avakīrṇin* penance" (GDh 23.12–13). An *avakara* is the penance prescribed for an *avakīrṇin*. In this way, penances of both specific and general types are recited in other *smṛtis* as well; however, they are not written here because their meaning is the same. All of this is to be applied appropriately according to the distinction between intentional acts and so forth. In all cases where no penance is specifically mentioned, the rule from Gautama—"The *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* and the *cāndrāyaṇa* constitute the universal penance" (GDh 19.20)—is to be applied either individually or collectively, since it is a statement regarding a universal penance. Furthermore, because the word "iti" implies "of such a kind," its repetition should be inferred according to the specific nature of the sin. This is the general direction.

The determination of penance for women is exactly the same: whatever [penance] applies to a Śūdra for approaching Brāhmaṇa women, that very same [penance] shall apply to a Brāhmaṇa woman for approaching a Śūdra; and so it is for Kṣatriya women and the others as well. The same applies even to approaching those related by blood. Thus Manu says:
"A husband should confine a woman who has become corrupted in a single room;
he should make her perform that same vow which is prescribed for a man regarding the wives of others. (MDh 11.176)

If, after having performed penance, she should engage [in misconduct] again, then one should cause her to perform that penance prescribed for a man who commits adultery with another's wife; furthermore, depending on the circumstances such as the frequency of the offense, she must perform a *kṛcchra* penance, which may be either alone or followed by a *cāndrāyaṇa*. As Manu says:
"If she, being solicited by a man of equal status, should become corrupt again, a *kṛcchra* and a *cāndrāyaṇa* are declared to be her means of purification" (MDh 11.177).

And regarding this, if the husband who is to protect her wishes to take her back, then he should have her confined within a single house as a penance; but if he does not take her back, there is no fault in abandoning her if she has become corrupted—this is understood from the mention of the "husband. Otherwise, since the matter would be established by the words alone—"he should confine her in one house"—the mention of the "husband" would be useless, as no one else could possibly exert such an effort. Furthermore, this is not an instruction for the king, because it has already been stated elsewhere in the section on punishments. Therefore, from the mention of the "husband," it is understood that if he wishes to maintain her, then he should cause this [penance] to be performed. The penances and other rules mentioned in the *Vāsiṣṭha-dharma-sūtra* are also, by implication, taught for the king himself: "If a Śūdra should violate a Brāhmaṇa woman, he should wrap the Śūdra in *vīraṇa* grass and cast him into the fire, and have the head of the Brāhmaṇa woman shaved," and so forth (*VaDh* 21.1). However, if the women themselves were to perform the penance, then [the following applies]: "In the case of a mental transgression against the husband, she should eat barley-gruel or milk-rice for three nights and sleep on the ground. After the three nights, while submerged in water, she should offer oblations with the *Sāvitrī* mantra recited eight hundred times for each head; it is declared that she becomes purified. In the case of verbal connection, having performed this same penance for a month, after the month, while submerged in water, she should offer oblations with the *Sāvitrī* recited eight hundred times for each of four heads; it is declared that she becomes purified. In the case of sexual intercourse, however, she should wear a cloth soaked in ghee for a year and sleep on the ground while eating from a bed of *kuśa* grass in a pit filled with cow dung. After a year, while submerged in water, she should offer oblations with the *Sāvitrī* recited eight thousand times for each head; it is declared that she becomes purified" (*VaDh* 21.6–8). And this [rule] regarding women of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) when they have approached men of the three higher castes should apply everywhere without distinction, precisely because no specific exception is taught; furthermore, a different penance is prescribed later for approaching a Śūdra.

Having stated, "Women of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes who have had intercourse with a Śūdra are purified by penance if they have not conceived, but not otherwise" (VaDh 21.12), the penance for those who have not conceived through intercourse with a Śūdra is then shown:
"They should undergo the penances in reverse order, beginning with the Kṛcchra and followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa. (VaDh 21.13)

And here, since the instruction regarding women of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) is given without distinction, it is understood that there was likewise no distinction in the preceding cases. When the determination of what ought to be done has been made and she is not deceived by another, her mind being firmly resolved of its own accord, the mental [transgression] occurs; the verbal is likewise so, and the physical union would be of this same nature. And in the context of a Śūdra, having committed this, it would be as stated: "they should undergo the penance for those who act in the reverse order of classes" (*pratiloma*), and this applies up until conception according to the number of approaches.
