But once conception has occurred, the penance is indeed that for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*); such is the general direction. However, if, through inadvertence, there should somehow be a transgression on the part of one who was deceived by a heart full of guile, then the penances spoken by Saṃvarta are to be accepted. As he said:
A Brahmin woman, having approached a Brahmin, should perform the Kṛcchra penance;
thus is purification declared, according to the words of Saṃvarta.
But if a Brāhmaṇī woman should have intercourse with a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya,
she becomes pure after ten nights by subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel.

"If, by some means, contact with a Śūdra should occur for a Brāhmaṇī woman, purification shall come through the Cāndrāyaṇa; that is her supreme purifier. Here, it should be explained that the Cāndrāyaṇa is a purifier superior to the Kṛcchra. The rest is clear. (260)

If a Brāhmaṇī woman should have sexual intercourse with a washerman, a hunter, an actor, or one who subsists by weaving bamboo or working in leather, she shall perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances.

[3.261] *Vyādha* means a hunter; *śailūṣa* means an actor. Here too, the expression "the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa" may be understood as "the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa," or "the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇas," or "the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇas. The rest is clear. [261]
If a Brāhmaṇa woman has sexual intercourse with a Śvapāka, a Pulkasa, a Mleccha, a Caṇḍāla, or likewise one who has fallen from his caste, she shall perform three Cāndrāyaṇa penances.

The *śvapāka*, the *marukuntika*, the *pulkasa*, the *meya*, the *mlecchas*, the *pulindas*, the *tārjikas*, and so forth—in this case as well, the word "likewise" (*tathā*) is intended to convey the same manner as described in the preceding verse. Consequently, these [penances] should be understood as preceded by the *kṛcchra* [vow]; and since the plural number is not intended to be significant in every instance regarding the act of approaching each one individually, [the penance applies even when approaching only one]. However, if she is somehow forcibly violated and enjoyed while she is afflicted with extreme suffering, then that which was stated by Hārīta should be observed:
"When she has been enjoyed after being forcibly violated, while he possesses a conscious mind..."
One is purified even by contact with Caṇḍālas or outcasts through the Prājāpatya penance.
But if she, thinking "this man is indeed my husband," should have been enjoyed with desire, then when that realization occurs:
"Women are an incomparable purifier; they are never defiled. For month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their misdeeds."

Thus, there is purposefulness for such statements as these. However, if later on she should somehow come to understand in a general sense merely that "I have been enjoyed by another man," then the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti* states:
"Whether she has been enjoyed by force, or has fallen into the hands of thieves, or has herself acted improperly, or has been led astray [by another]."
"A woman who has not been defiled by [a grave sin] is not to be abandoned; her abandonment is not ordained.
Having said this, it was further stated:
"She should wait for her fertile period; she becomes pure through the time of her menses. (VaDh 28.2–3)

This is its meaning: if she has contradicted her previous understanding of the situation by realizing for herself, "This is not my husband; he was seized by me through delusion with the idea that he was," or if she has been dissuaded from that notion by someone else saying, "This is not your husband," or if she has been forcibly enjoyed by someone of the same caste, or if, during a foreign invasion or similar upheaval, she has somehow fallen into the hands of thieves and been enjoyed by one of a lower caste—she is not to be abandoned. Why? Because she has been defiled in that very manner. For it is she who attains the state of being a *nārī* (a wife) that is considered defiled. However, when she is enjoyed by one of a lower order (*tiryagvidhi*) without attaining the status of a wife, her abandonment is not ordained even if she has been enjoyed repeatedly; rather, the intention is that she is to be accepted back. By the use of the word "is ordained" (*vidhīyate*), the abandonment based on the circumstances of the case is not prohibited at the husband's will; the intention is that taking her back by his own choice is also not blameworthy. But this is her penance: "She should wait for her menses (*puṣpakāla*)," and so forth. By the word *puṣpa*, the time of menstruation (*ṛtukāla*) is meant. She should remain eating barley-gruel, milk-rice, and so on, in a pit of cow-dung, sleeping on the ground, and wearing a garment of clarified butter, according to the previously mentioned rule, until the time of her menses. Then, having bathed at the end of three nights, she should remain following the same prescribed course of vows for sixteen nights. Thus she is purified by the time of her menses. This very point has been shown previously. There is an option between this and the *kṛcchra* penance mentioned by Hārīta in the words, "The penance for her has been stated among the secret penances. Even in the case of adultery with a woman of a higher caste (*pratiloma*), such a calculation of repeated practice should be applied; enough of this digression. This same procedure should also be applied to a man who approaches [another man's wife] thinking she is his own wife. For this very reason, Gautama said: "Some say that there is no falling [from caste] in the case of women, except for the violation of the Guru’s bed" (GDh 21.8). The intention is that in the case of violating the Guru’s bed, there is indeed a fall, even if done with the thought that she is one's own wife. And as for what was stated by Manu:

Regarding the rule, "Whatever [penance] is prescribed for a man regarding another's wife, he shall cause her also to perform that vow" (MDh 11.176), there the word "and" (ca) implies that whatever has been stated for women regarding another man applies likewise to the man; thus, the *kṛcchra* penance mentioned by Hārīta also certainly applies to the man in that same manner—this is the general direction. || 262 ||

Having thus set forth the penances for the four great sins (mahāpātaka), beginning with killing a Brahmin and ending with violating the Guru’s bed, he now states the penance for one who associates with those [sinners], by way of teaching a different matter at this opportune moment regarding penance:
"But he who drinks [with them] from the same vessel shall indeed become equal to them after a year.
He may marry a girl from among these [sinners] provided she is fasting and possesses nothing. (3.263)

In the enumeration of the *mahāpātakas*, it is stated [in Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.228]: "And he who drinks with these for a year," whereby their status as *mahāpātakin* is declared. This statement, however, regarding their equality, is for the purpose of prescribing expiation (*prāyaścitta*). The intention is this: among those sinners mentioned, beginning with the slayer of a Brahmin, he who "drinks with them"—that is, practices eating together and so forth—for a year, becomes equal to them after that year and is thus eligible for an expiation not different from theirs. Furthermore, the word "equal" (*sama*) here is intended to mean that his expiation shall be exactly the same as theirs—neither less nor more—in accordance with the previously established rules governing the specific cases. Therefore, on account of the word "equal," one should not suspect even a slight deficiency. And likewise, in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]:
Whatever man enters into association with one of these who has fallen, he must perform that very person’s vow for the sake of purification from that association. (MDh 11.181)

Thus, the equality of the expiation has been stated. The word *vatsarāt* (from a year) ends in the ablative case and should be construed by supplying the word *parataḥ* (beyond); the meaning is that beyond one year, he becomes liable for the expiation pertaining to that [offense]. However, we shall show a different expiation for the period prior to that. An exception to this rule is: "One should marry a maiden who is of unbroken virginity (*akṣatayoni*) with full certainty. But there is this specific qualification: "She should be fasting and possessing nothing. Some hold that the word "fasting" (*upavāsa*) here is intended to indicate expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in general. Yet it is more reasonable that the mere fast itself constitutes the expiation, since there is no reason for it to be an indication of something else. Furthermore, "possessing nothing" implies that not even a flower-garland belonging to her should be accepted. Thus says Hārīta: "But for the son of an outcast, one should bathe a maiden naked, have her fast for a day and night, and at dawn, having clothed her in a new white garment, she should declare three times aloud, 'I am not theirs, nor are they mine,' and then he should marry her at a sacred ford or in his own home. As for that which was stated by Manu:
"One falls by associating with an outcast for a year through officiating at sacrifices,
teaching, or marriage, but not through traveling, eating, or sitting together" (MDh 11.180).

By means of such things as vehicles, food, and seats obtained through officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) or teaching (*adhyāpana*), one does not become an outcast (*patita*) after a year. Rather, [one becomes an outcast] even before the end of a year. However, the intention is that by means of vehicles and the like used for worldly interaction, one becomes an outcast after a year. Furthermore, the singular treatment of *yājana* and *adhyāpana* is intended to show their inferiority compared to marriage (*yoni*). Thus, the construction of the words is: "associating with one who has become an outcast on account of officiating at sacrifices or teaching. From this, it is understood that in the case of officiating at sacrifices and teaching as well, there is indeed an outcasting. And where one intends, "I shall cause him to perform officiating at sacrifices and so forth," then even regarding vehicles, seats, and the like used for that purpose, the outcasting occurs even before a year; in such cases, it is established by implication that if one associates with them immediately, the outcasting is instantaneous—this is the intended meaning. Consequently, if a blood relationship (*yonisaṃbandha*) occurs through some other means, then there is outcasting. But if one marries a woman who is fasting and possesses nothing according to the aforementioned manner, there is no fault; thus the position is irreproachable. As for what Gautama stated—that one who does not abandon an outcast becomes an outcast himself (GDh 21.2)—that too applies only to those cases involving marriage and the like, since the rule begins elsewhere with: "and associating with them for a year" (GDh 21.3). Therefore, those who interact with an outcast through officiating at sacrifices and so forth are "those who do not abandon an outcast" (GDh 21.1). Those who, out of propriety, do not perform officiating at sacrifices and the like—even though they might have been expected to do so—thinking "this man is an outcast," are "those who abandon one who is not an outcast" (GDh 21.1). Those who, being considered trustworthy in their speech, are appointed to a council even when there is only doubt, yet support the state of outcasting with confident assertions, are "those who join in the sin" (GDh 21.2). And he who associates for a year with these primary outcasts is also an outcast through association, because of the statement: "and associating with them for a year" (GDh 21.3). However, there is no outcasting of others merely through contact with those who become outcasts by interacting for a year. As it is said: "And the fifth, by associating with them" (Āmnāya under 3.228); the mention of the "fifth" is for the purpose of excluding further [categories], such is the direction. In this regard, Vasiṣṭha states: "But in the case of association with outcasts, whether through the Brāhma [marriage] or the Yoni [blood relation], whatever goods were received from them, those must be abandoned; one should not live with them. Having gone toward the northern direction, fasting and studying the *Saṃhitā*, one becomes purified; so it is known" (VaDh 20.45–46). Because of the phrase "from them," there is no abandonment of those goods received for that very reason from his own relatives, friends, and so forth who are not outcasts. The mention of "goods" (*mātrā*) is for the purpose that there should be abandonment of even tobacco and other such items belonging to them. The term "received" (*upalabdha*) is for the purpose that there is no fault if they were not consciously perceived; and for the purpose that even if the original items are destroyed, one must abandon something else of equal value. "One should not live with them" is intended to exclude living in the same village or living nearby, since this is already established by the commencement of the penance itself. The rest is clear. Śaṅkha also says: "Those who associate with outcasts should practice lying in water, the five-fold heat (*pañcatāpa*), and staying in the open air during summer, the rainy season, and winter, respectively; or they should drink cow-urine and barley-gruel for a month; thus they are purified. Likewise, among the great sins (*mahāpātaka*), it is said: "And association with them is the fifth sin," yet no penance is mentioned there. Therefore, it is understood that what was stated generally—"For an outcast should rescue himself; he should perform the *taptakṛcchra* for a year"—which was explained in the section on killing a Brahmin, is intended here for the one who associates [with an outcast]. Similarly, Saṃvarta, having stated the penances for the four great sins, says:
"Whoever, deluded by sin, enters into contact with these [outcastes], shall perform the previously mentioned vow for six months or one year. Thus it is said.

Regarding this, some interpret the text as follows: "He who enters into association with these [sinners] for six months or one year shall perform the vow prescribed for those previously mentioned. However, if that were the case, since the duration of one year would already be established by the mention of the word *abda* (year), the phrase "or one" (*ekaṃ vā*) would be redundant. Therefore, this is an instruction regarding the time for penance (*prāyaścitta*), not the duration of the association itself. Accordingly, the meaning of the verse is this: he who enters into direct association (*abhimukhyena*) with these—beginning with the slayer of a Brahmin—in accordance with other Smṛtis such as "one falls [from caste] in a year" (MDh 11.180), shall perform for six months or one year that very same vow previously mentioned for them, such as the twelve-year penance and so forth. Furthermore, because of the particle *vā* ("or"), it is understood that two or three years may also be intended; likewise, six months or three months. Similarly, after Sumantu has stated the penance for stealing gold, he says: "One who has stolen gold should offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter with the Sāvitrī mantra for one month, and he becomes purified through every *kṛcchra* penance. Following that, he states: "If one should enter into association with any of these—whether through matrimonial, professional, or Vedic connections—one should prescribe this same penance for him as well. Due to the immediate proximity (*ānantarya*), it is understood that this refers specifically to the one connected to the theft, and not that the penance belongs solely to the person with whom the association occurred; thus, this interpretation is appropriate. In the *Śātātapa-smṛti*, however, it is stated: "One who associates with an outcast (*patita*) is purified by the *taptakṛcchra* penance. In other Smṛtis, the penances for associating with an outcast have the same purpose as those prescribed by Manu.
"Whichever among these a man comes into contact with by falling, he shall perform that very person's vow for the sake of purification from that association. (MDh 11.181)

In every respect, this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): regarding contact with an outcast (*patita*) performed intentionally, such as officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) or teaching (*adhyāpana*), the determination of the subject matter shall be according to the very rule stated in the verse, "Whoever [is associated] with whichever outcast. Even in that case, however, a penance ending in death (*maraṇāntika*) does not apply, because the text begins with the words, "For the purification from association with them. Otherwise, this final quarter-verse would be entirely meaningless. Therefore, in order to purify one's contact with an outcast and to establish contact with those who are not outcasts, one should perform that very life-long penance (*jīvaprāyaścitta*) which is prescribed for him. Even when the contact is with someone for whom a penance ending in death is appropriate, a heavier penance should be prescribed, but neither a penance ending in death nor a twelve-year penance; for there is the statement of Saṃvarta: "Six months or one year. Nor is a twelve-year penance appropriate for this person, because it is of the same nature as a penance ending in death. Furthermore, it is not fitting for one who is himself unworthy of that [twelve-year penance] to perform it even when in contact with someone worthy of it. Moreover, the kind of motive (*anubandha*) that exists for a killer is not possible in the case of one who associates with him. For a killer might intentionally kill a Brāhmaṇa endowed with learning, conduct, and austerity while he is engaged in a Soma sacrifice, or his own highly virtuous wife; but such a motive is not possible in the case of associating with him. Therefore, his penance must be determined solely in view of the cause of the association. And in determining that, there is no inclusion of another alternative (such as death) which would lead to the aforementioned calculation. Consequently, it is proper to determine the scope of the general rules taught alongside those specific rules prescribed in other Smṛtis for the purpose of association. Nor can a twelve-year penance or a penance ending in death be logically applied alongside those [specific rules]. Thus, those very penances previously cited—which are equal to going to the Sarasvatī, reciting the *Saṃhitā*, or eating cow-dung and oil-cake for a year—are to be understood as specifically prescribed for intentional association, for association with a most grievous motive, and for contact with those like the Sarasvatī. As for the mutual determination of the scope, it is already well known; so enough of this digression. The penances for contact with a Caṇḍāla are also to be explained by this same method. There too:

Having approached women of the Caṇḍāla or other lowest castes, or having eaten their food, or having accepted gifts from them, a Brahmin falls [from his caste] through ignorance; through knowledge, he becomes their equal. (MDh 11.175)

Because of this statement in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra] regarding the status of being an outcast (*patita*), all the penances prescribed for outcasts would apply. Furthermore, the statement, "But through knowledge he attains equality," means that there is an absence of penance only for one who acts intentionally in such a manner. And from this, it is understood that contact with such a person is more grievous than contact with other outcasts; however, the intention is not that there is an absolute absence of penance. Therefore, in this case, the twelve-year penance and the penance ending in death (*maraṇāntika*) certainly apply. Since the duration of the period of contact is not specified, the time previously mentioned should be understood to apply here as well.
"One falls [from caste] by associating with an outcast for a year" (MDh 11.180); and regarding the rules for touchability:
"A *divākīrti*, a woman in her courses, an outcast, and likewise a woman who has recently given birth... (MDh 5.85).

This is because they are recited within a single topical section (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore, for sexual intercourse with a woman out of desire after one year has passed, the penance ending in death applies; prior to that, the other penances mentioned in the section on mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*) should be applied according to the specific circumstances of the case. Likewise, in other *Smṛtis* regarding contact with a *caṇḍāla*, as stated in the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti*: "Having had intercourse with the wife of a teacher’s friend and so forth, one should perform a quarter of a *kṛcchra* for one year"; and having said this, it continues: "The same [penance] applies to eating the food of a *caṇḍāla* or an outcast" (*VaDh* 20.16–17). Here, by counting the *kṛcchras*, there are seven and a half *kṛcchras*. Thus, one should perform this after eating [such food] for seven nights. Why is this so?

"Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, there shall be a fast for three days; having eaten it intentionally, or having consumed semen, feces, or urine, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance"—
from this statement of Manu, and because the outcaste (patita) is mentioned among them.
"Of one who is accused, of a eunuch, of an unchaste woman, and of a hypocrite. (MDh 4.211)

If, however, one who is accused—even without an actual fall—is understood here as one accused of a *mahāpātaka* (grave sin), then by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpika*), since the state of being unfit for company (*abhogyatva*) is established even without explicitly mentioning the distinction of those guilty of *mahāpātaka*s, the penance for eating [their food] once intentionally is a *kṛcchra*. Consequently, because this refers to a repeated occurrence, the rule of Vasiṣṭha, "one should perform a quarter of a year-long *kṛcchra*" (VaDh 10.16), is settled as referring to a period of seven days. As for eating the food of a *caṇḍāla*, although it is listed without distinction from eating the food of a fallen person (*patita*), it is nevertheless more serious due to common worldly usage and the indicative evidence of Manu. Therefore, for unintentionally eating the food of a *caṇḍāla*, the penance is a *kṛcchra*; but for intentional eating even once, there is indeed a fall [from caste], according to the statement of Manu: "Through knowledge, he attains equality [with them]" (MDh 11.175). However, through ignorance, a fall occurs after one year. Prior to a year, the application of the subject matter is like that of contact with a fallen person. But where a *caṇḍāla* or similar person stays in someone's house without being known, and others deal with him through that person rather than directly with the *caṇḍāla* himself—for them, before a year and after six months, that which was stated by Saṃvarta applies: [The text continues with the citation: "Those who eat the food of such people, those who accept gifts from them, and those who associate with them—even if they do not know [the status], they become equal to them within a year. For those who do not know, the penance is a *parāka* for
"A Brahmin who has intermingled with Caṇḍālas, or even with Śvapākas or Pulkasas, becomes pure in one month by subsisting on cow's urine and barley-gruel. Thus it is said.

In this context, only contact through mixing (*saṃkara*) is mentioned, not direct contact. Thus Kāśyapa says: "In the case of contact with *caṇḍālas*, *śvapākas*, *pulkasas*, and others, when there is an intervening separation, one should drink cow’s urine and barley-gruel (*yāvaka*) for six months, increasing the duration by five days each month until the revolution of the sun. The revolution of the sun occurs in six months; therefore, 'prior to six months' is the meaning of this [rule]. Because of the mention of the *vipra* (twice-born), this applies only to a Brāhmaṇa; for the others, however, it is three *kṛcchras*. And that should be a *prājāpatya*. As Sumantu says: 'In the case of approaching women who should not be approached, the killing of a woman, or contact with *caṇḍālas*, one should perform three *kṛcchras*. But regarding one who stays in the house of another [through direct contact], that which was stated by Parāśara applies:"
But if a Caṇḍāla should dwell in someone's house unrecognized,
O Brahmins, they show favor to him once he has presented himself with full knowledge of his status.
Reciting the Dharmas that have issued from the mouths of the sages, those who recite the Dharma and are experts in the treatises on Dharma should rescue him as he is falling.
Combined with curd, milk, and ghee, one should consume the *kṛcchra* penance of barley-gruel mixed with cow's urine,
while bathing at the three junctions of the day along with one's attendants.
First, one should eat with curd for three days, then subsequently with ghee;
then one should eat with milk for three days, and again likewise with each of them individually for three days.
One should remain for as many days as it takes and act in this manner;
one should not eat anything corrupted by impure intent, even if it is naturally saturated with cow's milk products.
Three palas of curd, one pala of milk, and one pala of clarified butter;
or, in case of inability, by fasting or by subsisting on fruits and roots.
In mines, there shall be complete purification of metallic objects;
the purification of garments is by means of water; and one should discard those made of clay.
One should place safflower, jaggery, cotton, salt, oil, and clarified butter at the door; one should place grains and kindle a fire within the house.
"Purified and accompanied by his servants, he should provide a feast for Brāhmaṇas;
he should present twenty cows and one bull to the Brāhmaṇas. In this way, he attains purification according to the doctrine of Parāśara. (PSm 6.34–41)

The term *kṛcchra* is a qualification of the cow-urine and barley-gruel (*yāvaka*). Consequently, it should be performed with cow-urine alone in such a way that it becomes difficult to consume; it is to be eaten mixed with curds and other substances in the quantities previously specified. The duration for the dependents and the householder is determined according to the degree of their contact. This expiation applies if the offense is recognized before twelve nights have passed; however, beyond that time, this very penance must be practiced for a number of days corresponding to the elapsed period. The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), however, remains the same. But after one year, the case would be equivalent to that of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*); after three years, it results in a penance ending only in death. As for others who have associated with such a person, once a year has passed, the application of the rule is to be understood as being like that of contact with an outcast (*patita*); enough of this digression. Regarding the drinking of water taken by a Caṇḍāla, however, the penance is the minor *Sāntapana*.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass,
along with a fast for one night, would purify even a dog-eater.
According to this statement:
"If one eats food from which a Caṇḍāla has not been excluded, and especially if one has touched it,
one should perform a Kṛcchra penance if the fact was unknown, and a Cāndrāyaṇa if it was known."
Thus, the statement of Atri is indeed clear in its meaning:
"If one should drink even a little water taken up by a Caṇḍāla,
he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night, bathing, and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)."
If one should unintentionally drink even a little [water] that has been touched by a Caṇḍāla,
one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance for the sake of one's own purification.
But he who, out of desire, should eat the food of those who dwell at the ends [of society],
shall perform either the Cāndrāyaṇa penance or the Taptakṛcchra.

These are the verses of Āṅgirasa. In that regard, he who unknowingly drinks water from a well or similar source belonging to a Caṇḍāla that has been directly touched by him incurs the Mahāsāntapana penance. He who does so unintentionally from a well or other source maintained by such a person incurs the Kṣullakasāntapana. However, he who knowingly prepares and eats food belonging to such a person himself incurs the Cāndrāyaṇa. Furthermore, he who intentionally eats cooked food from those of the *pratiloma* castes who are worthy of ritual sipping (*ācamana*) incurs the Taptakṛcchra; but for doing so unintentionally, he incurs the Prājāpatya.
But having unintentionally eaten the food of those of inverse castes, such as Sūtas and others,
one should perform the Prājāpatya penance, eating only what is collected for three nights.
This is because of the statement of Atri. Furthermore, in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]:
"Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one should fast for three days" (MDh 4.222).

This should be understood as referring specifically to having eaten cooked food brought from his house; however, regarding eating at his house, the rule stated by Yājñavalkya—namely, a four-day fast—is the general direction.

Others, however, explain passages such as "having eaten the food of any one of these" as being merely *arthavāda* (explanatory or commendatory statements). They argue that only that which is recited within the specific context (*prakaraṇa*) of penance serves the purpose of a penance; whereas in a non-contextual passage, it is more appropriate to regard it simply as an *arthavāda*. If that were the case, then the statement in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*, in the middle book (*madhyamakāṇḍa*), within the section on penances in the *Pauroḍāśika* book—namely, "He touches what has spilled: *bhūpataye svāhā*" (ŚB 1.3.3.17)—would also have to be considered an *arthavāda*. Furthermore, it has already been stated that it is not logical for *arthavādas* in the *Smṛti* to terminate in their own mere meaning. Moreover, there would be no similarity to an *arthavāda* here at all. Therefore, the intention [of the opponent] is likely nothing more than this: "There is a type of sentence called an *arthavāda*, and I am aware of it"—an argument that should be disregarded. (263)

Thus, the expiation for all five great sins has been declared. Now, he states the expiation for the killing of those who are superior by birth and those who are inferior by birth: "Having killed all those who are inferior by birth, even a Śūdra, though lacking [Vedic] entitlement, becomes pure through this very penance; he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa. (3.264)

A Brāhmaṇa, having killed those inferior to himself—such as a Kṣatriya and others; a Kṣatriya, those such as a Vaiśya; a Vaiśya, those such as a Rathakāra (carpenter); and a Śūdra, those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*)—should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Now, it might be argued that a Śūdra has no entitlement at all to recitation (*japa*), eating (*grāsa*), or consecration (*anumantraṇa*). This is true. However, even though he lacks such entitlement, "the Śūdra is purified by this [Cāndrāyaṇa] over time. The intention is that by eating for a month morsels (*grāsa*) the size of a peacock's egg, increasing by one each day and so on, he becomes pure even without mantras. Others, however, explain that since other penances will be prescribed for the killing of a Kṣatriya and so forth, this penance applies only to the killing of those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*). If that were the case, the word "all" (*sarva*) in the phrase "all those who are inferior" would be redundant. For Śaṅkha says without qualification: "In the case of the mutual killing of those who are inferior to one another, the Cāndrāyaṇa [penance applies]. Even though it is stated without distinction, for a Brāhmaṇa, the Cāndrāyaṇa applies specifically to the killing of a Kṣatriya; but for the killing of a Vaiśya, another lesser penance must be devised. Because of the expression "mutual killing of those who are inferior," a specific arrangement should be devised according to the particular mode of the Cāndrāyaṇa. As for the specific penances prescribed for Kṣatriyas and others, they are to be understood as applying when the killer is indeed inferior but the victim is superior. We shall state the specific details regarding that very point later. (264)

But if, even when a person of lower caste such as a Kṣatriya has gone to another country or has been killed, someone—though knowing perfectly well that "this man was a Kṣatriya"—should out of malice falsely accuse him, saying, "This man was a Brāhmaṇa, and he was killed by him," would there be fault for him, or would there be an expiation, or not? Likewise, regarding one who, though the killing of a Brāhmaṇa or some other sin has occurred in the world, proclaims it as having happened when it was actually unknown—who is he? To this, [the author] says:
"The fault of one who makes a false accusation is twice as great as that of one who speaks of what actually occurred."
And by speaking falsely, one takes upon oneself the sin of one who has been falsely accused. (3.265)

First, for one who makes a false accusation, the fault is twofold; that is to say, it is double. But for one who makes known a fact that is true yet previously unknown by accusing someone, his fault is equal to that of the person being accused. Why, then, is there a doubling of the fault for the false accuser? Because, by means of the accusation, he becomes an associate in the sin and is thus taught to be equally fallen. Furthermore: whatever sin belongs to that person falsely accused, the accuser takes that upon himself by speaking falsely of a faultless man as being guilty. Therefore, since the accused has no fault at all, it is logical that both the imputed fault and the resulting state of being an accuser are the faults of the accuser alone. The doubling of the fault is established by the very manner already mentioned. Moreover, whatever other sin he may have committed, he too takes that upon himself through the false accusation; consequently, the intention is that the accused is released even from previously committed sins. And this is appropriate, because the experience of suffering is the cause for the destruction of sin. As for the prescription of penance for the accused, we shall explain that later. (265)

Having thus explained in detail the penances for the great sins (*mahāpātaka*), the occasion for the penances for minor sins (*upapātaka*) now arises according to the order of enumeration. Among these, he first speaks regarding the killing of a cow:

"Drinking the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the killer of a cow shall remain self-restrained for one month; sleeping in a cow-pen and following the cows, he becomes purified by the gift of a cow. (3.266)

And in this case, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) are for the purpose of food. Therefore, all five—cow urine and the others—should be mixed together in equal proportions and consumed once every day. Regarding self-restraint (*saṃyama*) here, one should abide by the procedure prescribed for the *Cāndrāyaṇa* vow, or follow other rules mentioned in another Smṛti, such as wearing a cow-hide or bathing with cow urine. Because of the mention of "self-restraint," it must be stated here as follows: "The killer of a cow, eating *pañcagavya* for a month, should sleep at night in a cow-pen itself in the presence of a cow, and during the day he should follow after the cows; the meaning is that he should follow them as an attendant so that they may move about freely and comfortably according to their own will. Then, at the end, having made a gift of a cow, he becomes pure. And because the gender of the victim is not specified, the gift of a bull and a milch-cow should be applied according to the specific gender. (266)
Likewise, this other [penance] pertains specifically to the killing of a cow:
one should perform either the *kṛcchra* or the *atikṛcchra* with a concentrated mind;
or, having fasted for three nights, one should give eleven cows along with a bull. (3.267)

In this context, by the use of the particle *eva* (only) in the phrase “*kṛcchraṃ caiva*” and the word *api* (also), it is understood that even each one [of these] is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Therefore, these expiations are threefold: the *kṛcchra*, the *atikṛcchra*, and both together. Furthermore, the term *samāhitaḥ* (concentrated/composed) serves, as before, to include the duties mentioned in other Smṛtis. Likewise, there is this other rule: “Having fasted for three nights, he should give ten cows and an eleventh bull. Thus, these five expiations for killing a cow, mentioned in the two verses, are to be applied according to the specific circumstances of the case. Some explain that there are only three, because the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* constitute a single expiation when combined. This being so, all three are optional alternatives (*vikalpa*) due to their equal status. Others, however, maintain that there is only one expiation: “Drinking the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for a month, he should perform both the *kṛcchra* and the *atikṛcchra*. And because of the word *api*, they construe it as: “Or else, independent of the former, he should perform the *kṛcchra* and the *atikṛcchra*,” in accordance with other Smṛtis. Thus Hārīta, after stating the three-month penance of Manu, says:
"Or, having remained for a month on the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should perform two kṛcchra penances.
Although this is stated without specific distinction, it should be understood that the second [penance] is the *atikṛcchra*, in accordance with this very [rule]. || 267 ||
This very rule he extends by way of option along with other penances even for other minor offenses (upapātaka):
"The purification for a minor offense may likewise be accomplished by a Cāndrāyaṇa, or by drinking milk for a month, or again by a Parāka. (3.268)

For every minor offense (*upapātaka*) enumerated among those such as officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice (*ayājyayājana*) or adultery (*pāradārya*), purification shall be achieved by the penances for cow-slaughter mentioned in the two preceding verses; or else by the *Cāndrāyaṇa* fast; or else by subsisting on milk for a month; or else by the *Parāka* penance—the *Parāka* being a twelve-night fast. Furthermore, due to the word "again" (*punar*), these may be applied individually or collectively, and through repetition. A systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) should also be devised in accordance with other *Smṛtis*. In this regard, various types of penances for cow-slaughter are recited in other *Smṛtis*, as are those for other minor offenses. Moreover, many specific penances are recited for many different cases; it is indeed proper to determine their application according to the context (*prasaṅga*). As stated, for example, in the *Mānava*:
By these vows, those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin) may remove their impurities;
likewise, those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) [may do so] by means of these various kinds of vows.
Having said this, he further stated:
"A cow-killer who has committed a minor offense (upapātaka) shall drink barley-gruel for one month;
having shaved his head, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with the hide of that very cow."
For two months, with his senses restrained, he should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent salt, at every fourth mealtime, and perform his bath using cow urine.
He should follow those cows during the day, and while standing, he should inhale the dust rising from them;
having served and paid homage to them, he should remain in the *vīrāsana* posture at night.
While they stand, he should stand; while they walk, he should follow;
likewise, while they sit, he should sit, self-restrained and free from envy.
One should liberate with all one's strength those who are afflicted by illness, those beset by fears such as thieves and tigers, those who have fallen, and those stuck in the mud.
Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently,
one should not seek protection for oneself without first having done so for the cow to the best of one's ability.
Whether it be one's own or another's cow, one should not speak of her while she is eating in a field, a house, or a threshing floor, nor of a calf while it is drinking.
But he who, being a cow-killer, follows cows according to this rule,
removes the sin committed by the killing of a cow within three months.
Some, however, read "in three years.
One who has well-performed his vow should give cows with a bull as the eleventh;
if these are unavailable, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas.

"Twice-born men who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) should perform this very same vow for the sake of purification, with the exception of the *avakīrṇin* [the student who has broken his vow of chastity], or else they may perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. Thus it is said in the *Mānava Dharmaśāstra* (11.107–117).
The same has been stated by Āṅgirasa as well.
A cow-killer who has committed a minor offense (upapātaka) shall subsist on barley-gruel;
his food must be unseasoned with alkaline salt, dry, and he shall eat only at the sixth meal-time.
Having shaved his head, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with a cow-hide;
for two months, even his bathing is prescribed to be performed with cow-urine.
One should perform all acts of purification for drinking with water alone;
one should carry a staff and a girdle without mantras, just as prescribed for a vow.
He should always follow after the cows and constantly drink their dust;
he should recite the Gomatī-vidyā, the syllable Om, and the Veda itself.
But everything else is no different from that prescribed by Manu. However, this is the distinction:
"The cow-killer who follows cows according to this rule indeed removes the sin committed by killing a cow within two months. Thus it is said.

Likewise: "In the absence of a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should adopt the appearance and characteristics of that [animal]. But Saṃvarta says: "A cow-killer should take up residence in a cow-pen in the vicinity of a cow;
there he should lie down for half a month, sleeping on the bare ground."
A self-controlled man, seeking liberation from that sin, should eat these in succession: powdered grain, barley-gruel, alms-food, milk, and curd.
He is purified within half a month, being devoid of nails and hair;
he should perform the three daily ablutions, self-restrained and free from envy.
He should daily recite the Gāyatrī and all the purificatory mantras;
then, when half a month has passed, he should feed the Brahmins.
"When the Brahmins have finished eating, the twice-born man should give cows according to his capacity. Thus it is said.

Likewise, Kaśyapa has stated specifically regarding the killing of a cow: “Expiation applies when the act is committed unintentionally; some say it also applies when done intentionally. For milch cows and the like, the expiation consists in giving a milch cow as a gift. Furthermore, regarding the fear of disease, or when [the cow] dies due to the application of bells, ornaments, and decorations, or through the administration of drinks, oils, medicinal herbs, and treatments, Kaśyapa says: “Having informed the Brāhmaṇas and shaved his head including the top-knot (*śikhā*), he should perform the *Prājāpatya* penance. At its conclusion, he should give a cow or a sesame-cow (*tiladhenu*). Now, for another caste [the Kṣatriya]: “Clad in that hide, he should live in a cow-pen for one month. Bathing three times a day, subsisting constantly on the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), or eating only at every sixth meal-time, or subsisting on milk, he should follow the cows when they move and not sit down when they stand still. He should not walk too fast, nor should he lead them over uneven ground, nor into shallow water or onto sparse pasture. At the end, he should perform a libation to the Brāhmaṇas and give a cow or a sesame-cow,” so says Kaśyapa. Similarly, in the *Śāṅkha-smṛti*: “The cow-killer, subsisting on the five products of the cow, should remain for twenty-five nights. Having shaved his head including the top-knot and being clad in a cow-hide, he should follow the cows. He should live in a cow-pen and make a gift of a cow. In the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti*, however, after stating the nature of the two penances—“If he should kill a cow, he should remain for six months clad in her wet hide, performing either the *Kṛcchra* or the *Taptakṛcchra* penance”—and having described their procedure, it is said: “He should give a bull and a female calf. Paiṭhīnasi also says: “The cow-killer shall be purified by eating for a month a gruel boiled with a handful of rice while doing what is pleasing to the cows. Sumantu, however, states: “For the cow-killer, there is sleeping in a cow-pen for twelve nights, subsisting on the five products of the cow, and following the cows. Likewise, Yama also [says].
Or from being tied to a tree or a stone, from being yoked with an excessive yoke or driven too hard,
or from being cast down into a river, a wilderness, a chasm, or a precipice.
In this manner, wherever a cow dies, purification is prescribed;
having performed a tonsure including the top-knot, remaining silent, and wearing only a loincloth.

"Eating barley-gruel with cow's urine for one month, he shall go among the cows as their equal. Likewise, another [rule] in this very same context: "A killer of a cow who has committed a minor offense (upapātaka) shall eat barley-gruel" (cf. MDh 11.108).
Thus, this is not distinct from that of Āṅgirasa in terms of both text and meaning; however, this is the distinction:
one should perform the daily recitation of ten thousand repetitions of the Gāyatrī, and one should also recite the Gomatī-vidyā.
And so forth. Likewise:
"One who has well-observed his vows should give a thousand cows or even a hundred;
if these are not available, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas" (cf. MDh 11.116).

And in the Gautama Dharma Sūtra, an extension [of the rule] is made: "And for killing a cow, as in the case of a Vaiśya" (GDh 22.18). Regarding the killing of a Vaiśya, it is stated: "One should observe the standard three-year period of celibacy and give away cows with a bull as the eleventh" (GDh 22.15). However, Bṛhaspati says: "By twelve days [of penance], the killer of a cow is liberated from that sin;
during that time, he should subsist on milk, or perhaps consume milk and curds."
Likewise, there is this other [method]:
one should recite the Gāyatrī ten thousand times while subsisting on barley-gruel;
having shaved the head bald, remaining silent, and wearing only a loincloth.
He should dwell among the cows in the cow-pen and go out with them during the day;
at the conclusion of the vow, he should give a cow and gold to the twice-born.

Likewise, there is another [text] on that very point: "One should subsist on the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for twelve nights, or on barley-gruel (*yāvaka*) for six nights, and dwell in a cow-pen; or it may be according to one's capacity regarding place, time, and physical strength. Having removed his beard and nails and having prostrated before the Brahmins, he should, when permitted by them, give a cow or a bull at the end; having fed the Brahmins, he becomes purified—so says Bṛhaspati. But in the Śātātapa [Smṛti]: "One should perform three *kṛcchra* penances, such as the *prājāpatya*, and recite the *gomatī* mantra. However, in the Pārāśara [Smṛti]:
"Death may occur through the ropes used for tethering cows unintentionally.
One should confess an unintentionally committed sin to the Brāhmaṇas," thus beginning [the section] (PSm 8.1).
Having shaved his head, including the top-knot, he should bathe at the three junctions of the day;

he should dwell among cows at night and move along with them. (PSm 8.31). Having thus described the manner of following the cows, the *Prājāpatya* penance (*kṛcchra*) is prescribed: "Then, at the conclusion of the performance, there shall be a feeding of Brāhmaṇas and the gift of a cow together with a bull. Similar penances for the killing of a cow are found in other Smṛtis as well. And regarding this, by the Self-born One (Manu):
But those who are born spontaneously [as celestial beings] are thus [born] through these various kinds of vows. (MDh 11.107)

Having said this, he stated: "The cow-killer associated with a minor offense (*upapātaka*)," and so forth (MDh 11.108). By this, it is known that there is indeed the status of being a cow-killer even apart from a minor offense; otherwise, the qualification would be entirely meaningless. And that [cow-killing] is of two kinds: some is distinct from the association with a minor offense and falls within the category of a major offense (*pātaka*), while some is less than a minor offense. In that regard, what is recited in the *Aṅgirasasmṛti*, beginning with "the cow-killer associated with a minor offense," is presented as an alternative to the [rule] of Manu. However, that which is more severe than Manu’s and not associated [with a specific offense], such as the rule of Gautama, and likewise that which is found in the *Yāmyasmṛti*:
One who has well observed his vows may give a thousand or even a hundred cows.

Thus, since the opening statement there is of the form "the cow-killer associated with a minor offense (*upapātaka*)," and because this is not distinct from the [rule] of Manu, it should be explained as an optional alternative. However, the other [penance] consisting of a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*sahasradakṣiṇā*) is to be understood as an option according to Gautama, because it is appropriate for a major sin (*pātaka*). The gift of a hundred [cows] is also to be applied to that same subject matter in consideration of the attendant circumstances (*anubandha*) and so forth. As for those [penances] which are lesser, found in the works of Śaṅkha, Yājñavalkya, Pracetas, and others, they are to be regarded as applying to cases prior to the [category of] minor offenses, because they are not taught as being associated with a minor offense and because of their smallness. Among these, the scope concerns the killing of cows intended for Vedic sacrifices (*kratvartha*), which exceeds [the requirements] of Manu’s rule. In other cases, however, the "association with a minor offense" refers to the killing of one who was already intent upon slaughter. But as for that which occurs when one is intent on something else, even if it is recited among the minor offenses, it is still lesser, due to the force of the qualification "the cow-killer associated with a minor offense. Nor is it proper here to establish the scope by considering the [specific] possession [of the cow], because that is irrelevant to the act of killing. As for the greater severity of punishment mentioned for stealing a cow belonging to a Brāhmaṇa:
In the case of cows belonging to Brahmins, for breaking a fence,
and likewise for the theft of livestock, a fine of half a pāda shall be imposed.

Thus, that [rule] is appropriate precisely in the section concerning theft (*steya*), for there the specific determination of the punishment is made solely with reference to the identity of the owner and the nature of the substance stolen. Here, however, even if one's own cow is killed, the penance would be exactly that much or perhaps more. Therefore, in this case, the question "Whose cow is this? is not relevant. Consequently, in the killing of a cow belonging to an inferior person or one belonging to a superior person, the determination of the case depends solely on the attendant circumstances (*anubandha*) residing in the killer. From the scriptural statement, however, one understands an excess of fault in the case of injury intended for a ritual purpose (*kratvartha-hiṃsā*), as Śaṅkha says:

"The sacrificial animals belong to the Maruts, as do the divine Maruts and the quarters; therefore, one should perform the vow for killing a Vaiśya upon the slaughter of these. Although only "animals" (*paśu*) are mentioned here, nevertheless, based on the statement from Gautama, "And [the penance for killing] a cow is like that for a Vaiśya" (GDh 22.18), it should be understood that this refers specifically to cows. Furthermore, this same method should be applied to other major expiations (*prāyaścitta*), as stated in the *Svāyambhuva*:
"Having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay, a frog, as well as a dog, an iguana, an owl, and a crow, one shall perform the vow for killing a Śūdra. (MDh 11.131)

This penance for killing a Śūdra would apply specifically to the killing of those [animals] used for ritual purposes (*kratvartha*). This is likewise stated in other *smṛtis*. For example, in Gautama: "And in the case of harming frogs, mongooses, crows, chameleons, small mice, and horses" (GDh 22.19). Here too, by the word "and" (*ca*), the very vow prescribed for killing a Śūdra is taught. A *bimba* is a chameleon; a *daharamūṣikā* is a muskrat (*cucchundarī*). However, this is more severe than the rule of Manu. For it is also said in the *Mānava*: "A killer of a Śūdra shall perform this entire vow for six months."
"Or else, one should give ten white cows and a bull to a Brahmin. (MDh 11.130)

In Gautama’s [Dharma Sūtra], however, it is stated: “Upon killing a Śūdra, one shall observe the standard vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for one year and give eleven cows with a bull as the eleventh” (GDh 22.16). Here too, the rule of Manu applies to the killing of a Śūdra intended for a sacrificial purpose (*kratvartha*), while Gautama’s rule concerns cases other than those involving a Brāhmaṇa. In this manner, elsewhere as well, the scope of penances for injury should be determined by considering whether the act is for a sacrificial purpose or for a human purpose, and by considering the attendant circumstances (*anubandha*) pertaining to the killer. Some, however, explain that this refers to the killing of frogs and others when combined together. But that is incorrect, because of the plural number in the phrase “and in cases of injuries” (GDh 22.19) and because it contradicts logical reasoning. Therefore, it should be explained solely as referring to the sacrificial context. Within that context, if one unintentionally kills a cow used as a means for the *Agnihotra* and other rites, the rule of Vasiṣṭha applies; but if intentional, the rule of Gautama applies. Regarding animals such as the *somakrayaṇī* cow used as an accessory to the *Soma* sacrifice, if killed unintentionally, Gautama’s rule applies, but if intentional, the gift of a thousand cows according to Yama applies. Other cases of this kind should be explained similarly. As for killing for a human purpose, if intentional, the rule of Manu applies; if unintentional, the rule of Yājñavalkya applies even in the case of killing an *ātatāyin* (one who poses an immediate threat). For there is indeed the possibility of killing for one engaged in hunting and the like, who does not know it is a cow in the dark and so forth, even though unintentionally. Now, one might argue: “It is not right that there be any fault in killing an *ātatāyin*. True; however, since the activity of animals is not preceded by conscious intent, it is not proper to treat them as equal to humans. Thus Sumantu says: “There is no penance for killing an *ātatāyin*, except in the case of cows and Brāhmaṇas. Therefore, even in their case, there is certainly a penance; yet, because the killing occurs only unintentionally due to the intent being merely self-preservation, a small penance is appropriate. As for those cases which are specifically recited, such as:
"In the case of cattle, death may occur unintentionally while they are tied with a tethering rope" (Pārāśara Smṛti 8.1);

thus it is stated in the Pārāśara [Smṛti], and these [rules] are established by the Śruti itself. Furthermore, in this matter, there is no status as a minor offense (upapātaka). Therefore, that which is stated in general terms—"Having incurred the necessity of penance, whether by fate or by what was done previously..."—[applies here].

"A twice-born man shall not associate with the virtuous as long as the penance has not been performed" (MDh 11.47). This rule applies specifically to the cases of *pātaka* (grave sins) and *upapātaka* (minor sins); therefore, it would not apply to such a killing of a cow where [the act] does not constitute an *upapātaka*. It applies only where there is the status of an *upapātaka*, and not in cases such as tethering for the purpose of restraint, because that would lead to the collapse of social and economic activity. Therefore, if the death occurs through tethering for the sake of concealment or through yoking for the sake of agriculture and so forth, then the penance prescribed by Parāśara should be understood to apply. As for the statement: "One shall not incur sin by tethering or binding [an animal] for the purpose of yoking it at evening" (PSm 9.1).
Thus, it is only the confining and binding that are faultless, but not the killing caused by them. Accordingly, it is stated elsewhere:
"One may provide medicine, oil, or food for a cow or a Brahmin;
even if death occurs because of that, there is only merit, not sin."

Thus, it is understood that in other cases there is indeed a fault. Others, however, read this verse at the very time of the world's dissolution (*saṃvarta*): "Whether in the house or in the forest, for those who have been restrained [from sin], there is no transgression in death caused by wild beasts and the like, or even by lightning, snakes, or fire."
Thus it is said; however, that must be further examined. As for what Saṃvarta himself stated:
"If someone should be killed by many through some stroke of fate, they shall each perform a quarter of the penance for the killing individually."

Thus, what is heard even in the section concerning the killing of a cow (*govadha-prakaraṇa*) should be understood to apply to the injury of Brāhmaṇas and others as well, because of the instruction given without qualification by the word "anyone" (*kaścit*). And this is its scope: if, in the case of injuring a weak [cow], many people capable of rescuing it are present—either individually or collectively—and if, through some stroke of fate, no rescue is performed out of mutual indifference, then the meaning is that each person is purified by one-fourth (*pāda*) of whatever penance would otherwise accrue to a single individual. Furthermore, that which was stated by Parāśara should apply to all castes (*varṇa*) without distinction, precisely because of the lack of specific qualification. However, that which was stated by Saṃvarta—"I shall declare the expiation even for the killer of a cow"—should be understood to refer to a member of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) when he is somehow unable to prevent a cow from reaching death other than by killing her; here, the word "even" (*api*) indicates the absence of intentional killing. Therefore, the instruction regarding *japa* (recitation) should be seen as applying to such a case of direct killing. The rule of Āṅgirasa, however, is an alternative to that of Manu. That too, due to the instruction regarding *japa*, should be understood to apply only to the three higher castes in the case of intentional killing. The rule of Kāśyapa is easily understood because it is enjoined specifically in connection with milch cows and so forth. "Milch cows and so forth" (*dogdhry-ādayaḥ*) refers to those beginning with milch cows. In that context, it applies to the death of a cow restrained for milking, or to the blowing [of air] for that same purpose; or to the blowing of a cow whose calf has died, etc., which is well known among cattle-breeders. Likewise, it should be understood to include the blowing of bells, ornaments, and so on as part of the process of sale, as well as the administration of oil or medicine intended solely for the purpose of sale or for the sake of rapid nourishment. This also applies to all castes. The second rule, however, stated by Kāśyapa, should be seen as having the same scope as that of Saṃvarta, but applying specifically to a Śūdra. Regarding the consumption of *pañcagavya* (the five products of the cow), the meal consists of that every day; but if one subsists on milk alone, then food is taken only at every sixth meal-time. The rest is the same. The statement of Śaṅkha should also be applied to this very subject according to one's capacity. The rule of Paiṭhīnasi, however, should be understood to apply to women and others in this same situation who are unable to follow the cow in death (*anugamana*). But the rule ordained by Sumantu applies to women and others when a cow, while causing trouble in a house, field, or threshing floor, is struck and somehow falls into a pit or similar place. And in this very situation, the rule of Yama applies to those who are capable: *(Note: The provided text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the content available.)*
Having begun with [the offenses] such as "binding by the feet or the neck" or "driving too fast with an excessive yoke," that which is prescribed is as follows:
"Eating barley-gruel with cow's urine for one month, he should walk together with cows."
This is how it should be understood. As for that which is stated in the same [text]:

"One who has killed a cow, being joined with a minor offense (upapātaka), shall eat barley-gruel (yāvaka)," and so forth—that is equivalent to the rule of Aṅgiras. Furthermore, as for that which is stated in the same [text]:

"One who has observed his vows well should give a thousand or even a hundred cows"—this [statement] has already been explained as referring to the slaughter of a cow for the sake of a sacrifice (*kratvartha*), being an optional alternative (*vaikalpika*) according to Gautama. However, the rule concerning Bṛhaspati, namely "the killer of a cow [is purified] by twelve days," is an optional alternative for the three *varṇas* alone, according to Parāśara. As for the recitation of a hundred thousand [mantras], it is for Brahmins alone:
"A Brahmin may indeed attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt in this matter" (MDh 2.87).

Because of this statement. As for the rule in that same [text], "For twelve nights, one should subsist on *pañcagavya*," that is an optional alternative (*vaikalpika*) according to Saumantava. As for the rule in that same [text], "For six nights, one should subsist on *yāvaka*," that is to be applied to that very same subject matter with regard to children, the elderly, and so forth. However, what was stated by Śātātapa is to be applied as an optional alternative to what was stated by Saṃvarta, depending on the specific nature of the offense (*anubandha*). In this way, there is also a determination of the respective scopes among those rules stated by the Lord of Yogins (*Yogīśvara*). And in every case within the section on penance (*prāyaścitta-prakaraṇa*),...
Having fully ascertained the connection— taking into account the caste, capacity, and qualities, as well as the act performed intentionally and its frequency— one should prescribe the expiation.
This is the very summary rule. Likewise:
"But for the removal of sins for which no expiation has been stated, one should prescribe an expiation after considering both the capacity [of the offender] and the nature of the sin" (MDh 11.209).
Likewise: "Whatever expiation for sins those three who know the Vedas may prescribe, that shall serve for their purification; for the word of the learned is purifying. (MDh 11.85)

This same principle should be applied everywhere. Regarding the group of minor offenses (*upapātaka*) such as officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice (*ayājyayājana*), one must determine the scope of application by correlating them with specific prescriptions alongside the extension (*atideśa*) of the penance for killing a cow. First, there is a specific rule in the *Svāyaṃbhuvamanu-smṛti*:

"Twice-born men who have committed minor offenses (*upapātakin*) shall perform this very vow for the sake of purification, except for the student who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*); or else, they may perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. (MDh 11.117)

By the use of the words *atha* and *api*, there is an inclusion of those [penances] mentioned in other Smṛtis. In that regard, the Cāndrāyaṇa is an optional alternative to the penance for killing a cow; because of the mention of the "twice-born," it pertains specifically to that subject. Furthermore, as stated by Yogīndra:
"In this manner, or else by the Cāndrāyaṇa, there shall be purification from minor offenses" (YDh 3.268).
Here, the word "in this manner" (*evam*) is an extension (*atideśa*) of the penances for killing a cow prescribed in the preceding verse. And as for the Cāndrāyaṇa—
In any manner whatsoever, two hundred and forty morsels of food [should be offered]. (YDh 3.322)

This is how it should be understood. Therefore, this [penance] is to be seen as applicable to all castes (*sārvavarṇika*) in the case of all minor offenses (*upapātaka*). And with respect to one's capacity, the phrase "or even for a month with milk" is also to be taken as an option. In the passage "or again by the *parāka* penance," because of the words *api* ("even") and *punaḥ* ("again"), it should be construed as "again" (*punar api*), following the verse: "dependent on caste, capacity, and quality. Thus, the arrangement is according to the specific circumstances (*anubandha*), whether individually or collectively, such as "by the Cāndrāyaṇa or even with milk. Furthermore, where a specific rule has been prescribed for a particular minor offense, that too should apply according to the determination of the subject matter; however, the general rule is not to be disregarded simply because of the existence of a specific rule, for that would result in the redundancy of its inclusion among the minor offenses. For example, regarding the state of being a *vrātya* due to the passing of the time for initiation (*upanayana*), before sixteen years have passed, Pāraskara states: "In the case of the lapse of time, [the rite is performed] as prescribed" (PārG 2.5.41). Regarding the term "as prescribed" (*niyatavat*), they explain that if the specific details are unknown, there is an oblation with the three Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*), a fourth oblation with all [four], and the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). This is the expiation for the lapse of the initial time for initiation. However, for one who is currently being initiated...
A Brāhmaṇa who has committed the Triṣṭubh [mantra] to memory should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
if he is unable, he should do so by quarters, after which he becomes worthy of the sacramental rites.

From this statement of Hārīta, it is understood that initiation (*upanayana*) is to be performed only for one who has already completed the penance. However, after the sixteenth year, the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra] states:

"Those twice-born men for whom the *Sāvitrī* has not been recited according to the rule—having made them perform three *kṛcchra* penances, one should initiate them according to the rule" (MDh 11.191).

This [period] applies until the twenty-second year for a Brāhmaṇa who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*), according to the statement of Śaṅkha: "In the case of the transgression of each subsequent time-limit, one falls from each preceding status. According to Gautama, this same period applies to all [classes], because it is stated: "For a Vaiśya, two years more" (GDh 1.14), and because of the statement: "Beyond this, they become those whose *Sāvitrī* has fallen" (VaDh 11.74). And after that, there is the rule of Vasiṣṭha: "One should perform the Uddālaka-vow: one should subsist on *yāvaka* for two months, on milk for one month, on *āmikṣā* for half a month, on clarified butter for eight nights, on unasked food for six nights, subsist on water for three nights, and fast for a day and night; or one should go to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice" (VaDh 11.76–78). However, if one has not been initiated for forty-eight years starting from the original time for initiation, then for him there is the Vrātyastoma sacrifice, because of the instruction regarding the Vrātyastoma: "He who should pass the time for the vow without being consecrated should sacrifice with the first [of these]. But as for those who, having been initiated, have done something else without studying the Veda, yet have not abandoned the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and other duties; or those who, having studied, have become lax in the performance of the twilight worship and other rites—they too, having diligently performed three *kṛcchra* penances, should study the Veda and be diligent in their conduct. As Manu says:

"But for those twice-born who, engaged in forbidden acts and abandoned by the Veda, desire to perform penance, one should prescribe this [penance] as well" (MDh 11.192). Thus, the Uddālaka-vow is an optional alternative to the cow-slaughter penance, while the Cāndrāyaṇa is an alternative to three Kṛcchras. Other Smṛti texts should be explained in the same manner. This same method applies even to theft and other such offenses; we shall explain it in detail in the commentary on the text. Now, the subject at hand is being discussed. || 268 ||

Since the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya is listed among the minor sins (*upapātaka*), a general expiation has already been stated [in verse 3.268]: "The purification for a minor sin may be accomplished by this [penance] or by the *Cāndrāyaṇa*," and so forth. Now, however, he speaks in order to state the specific expiation for those very same acts:
"For the killing of a Kṣatriya, a man should give a thousand cows with one bull as the eleventh, or else he should perform the vow for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa for three years. (YDh 3.269)
A killer of a Vaiśya shall perform this penance for one year, or give one hundred cows;
a killer of a Śūdra shall likewise do so for six months, or give ten milch-cows.

Those cows of which there is one bull in addition to a thousand are "one-thousand-and-a-bull" (*ṛṣabhaikasahasrāḥ*). The rest is clear. Furthermore, the word "man" (*pumān*) is used for the sake of specifying that this penance applies only to the killing of a Śūdra by a Kṣatriya or others, and likewise when it is unintentional. As Manu says: "But having unintentionally killed a Kṣatriya, the best of the twice-born should give a thousand cows with one bull in addition for the sake of his own purification. (MDh 11.127)

This [penance] applies to the killing of one who is established in his religious duties (*vṛttastha*), as indicated by the rule: "Having killed a Vaiśya established in his duties" (MDh 11.129). Now, an objection may be raised: "But this refers only to a Brāhmaṇa, because of the expression 'the best of the twice-born' (*dvijottama*). This is not a case of grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) meaning "the best among the twice-born"; rather, it should be understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound: "one for whom the twice-born is the highest. Why is this so? Because for the killing of an inferior person, a *cāndrāyaṇa* penance is prescribed. Furthermore, the term "best of the twice-born" is employed in both of these two verses: "The best of the twice-born (*dvijottama*) shall perform this very penance for a year."
"Having killed a Vaiśya who is established in his duty, one should give one hundred cows. (MDh 11.129).
Regarding the third [caste], however:
"A killer of a Śūdra should perform this entire vow for six months. (MDh 11.130).

In this regard, this [penance] does not apply at all, because it is useless. However, in the previous case, the statement was intended for a Śūdra whose superior was a twice-born man (dvija)—whether a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya—if that inferior were to kill the superior, then he should perform that [penance]; such was the purpose of that statement. But here, since the killing is committed by one of the same caste, it would be logical that no such statement be made, as that very rule already applies. Otherwise, since it was stated at the outset that what is established by the general qualification applies to subsequent cases as well, it should not have been stated again; or else, it should have been stated in every instance. Therefore, due to the repeated mention in the *Yogīśvara-smṛti* and following the logic already explained here, it is correct to conclude that this refers specifically to a Śūdra. Consequently, its inclusion among the minor offenses (*upapātaka*) also becomes meaningful in view of the superior caste; otherwise, its mention among the minor offenses on equal footing would seem unintentional or accidental. And thus, the statement of Śaṅkha—"For the mutual killing of all [castes], there is the Cāndrāyaṇa"—would also be consistent. If, however, one must necessarily justify this as applying only to a Brāhmaṇa based on the mention of the "best of the twice-born," then it should be explained according to the statement regarding those "established in their conduct" (*vṛttastha*), namely as referring to those engaged in the performance of rituals, and specifically to the context of *iṣṭi*s, animal sacrifices, and so forth—excluding the Soma sacrifice—by virtue of the connection with the *savana*s and the extension (*atideśa*) of the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa. Outside of ritual contexts, however, the penance is simply that for a minor offense (*upapātaka*). Even in that case, if unintentional, it is the Cāndrāyaṇa; if intentional, it is the penance for killing a cow. And depending on the circumstances (*anubandha*) and other factors, there may be fulfillment through recitations (*japa*) and so forth. But this [Cāndrāyaṇa] applies to the killing of those of lower status when unintentional. If intentional, however: *(The text continues with the specific penances for intentional acts.)*
"A fourth part of the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa is prescribed for the murder of a Kṣatriya;
an eighth part for a Vaiśya who is established in his duty, and it should be known as a sixteenth part for a Śūdra. (MDh 11.126).
However, regarding one who is not established in his duty, Saṃvarta has stated:
Having killed a Kṣatriya through delusion, one is purified by three Kṛcchras in succession:
namely, the Prājāpatya, the Atikṛcchra, and the Taptakṛcchra.
"A man who has killed a Vaiśya should perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances;
but having killed a Śūdra, he should perform the Kṛcchra as well as the Sāntapana. Thus it is said.

Regarding, however, the unintentional killing of a person of lower status or of the same caste belonging to a sacrifice other than the *soma* sacrifice, the rule of Gautama applies: "For killing a *rājanya*, one shall observe the standard vow of celibacy for six years and give a thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh; for killing a *vaiśya*, for three years and give a hundred cows with a bull as the eleventh; but for killing a *śūdra*, for one year and give eleven cows with a bull as the eleventh" (GDh 22.14–16). For intentional killing, however, the rule of Vasiṣṭha applies: "Having killed a *rājanya* in this manner, one shall perform [the penance] for eight years; for a *vaiśya*, six; for a *śūdra*, three" (VaDh 20.31–33). But for the killing of a *śūdra* engaged in a *savana* sacrifice, the penance for Brahmin-killing (*brahmahatyā*) prescribed by Āpastamba applies (ĀpDh 1.24.6–23). In all cases, a specific adjustment should be determined after considering the superiority or inferiority of the castes. And it has been said: "[The penance] depends on the caste, capacity, and qualities. The statement of Śaṅkha, which conveys the same meaning as that of Gautama, should also be applied according to the circumstances (*anubandha*): "Having killed [someone] among the four castes, one should perform the penance for twelve years, six, three, or one; at the end of that, one should give a thousand cows, half of that, half of that, and half of that again. Some, however, believe that Gautama’s rule relates specifically to a Brāhmaṇa. They detach the word "of a Brāhmaṇa" from the preceding sūtra—"In the case of an unknown fetus, [the penance is] for a Brāhmaṇa" (GDh 22.13)—and connect it with the subsequent sūtra, interpreting it as: "For a Brāhmaṇa killing a *rājanya*, the penance lasts six years. Consequently, following this very logic, the mention of the "best of the twice-born" in the *Mānava* [Smṛti] would be clearly justified as intending a Brāhmaṇa. But this is not very reasonable; for on the contrary, an undesirable consequence would follow, since it would imply that even when the killing of a Brāhmaṇa is committed by a *rājanya*, the six-year vow would apply. Furthermore, the term "of a Brāhmaṇa" cannot be a qualifier of the agent, because of the grammatical rule: "When both [agent and object] are possible, [the genitive is used] for the object" (Pāṇini 2.3.66). Thus, it would undesirably follow that the Brāhmaṇa becomes the object [of the action]. For this very reason, Asahāya and others have explained [Gautama’s rule] simply as: "In the case of an unknown fetus, [the penance is] for a Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, the determination of the subject matter is exactly as stated above. And thus says the Vedic tradition: "Therefore, even if a king attains the highest state... and so on, concluding: "Killing destroys him; he returns to his own womb and becomes more sinful, just as one who has harmed a superior" (BāU 1.4.11). This shows, by way of an established example, that the killing of a superior by an inferior is inherently defective. Likewise, regarding verbal abuse, there is the rule of Svāyambhuva:

"A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred [paṇas]; a Vaiśya, one hundred and fifty or two hundred; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment. By this [verse], he states that for those of lower status, the excess of guilt increases according to their superiority [of caste]. Likewise:
"A Brahmin shall be fined fifty [paṇas] for defaming a Kṣatriya;
for a Vaiśya, forty-five; and for a Śūdra, the fine is twelve. (MDh 8.268). Thus, there is a reduction according to the degree of inferiority. Likewise:

"By addressing a twice-born man with harsh speech, a once-born man shall suffer the cutting off of his tongue, for he is of low origin. By this statement, which provides a reason, [the author] declares that the injury of a superior by those who are inferior is a grave offense. In the same manner, other statements regarding assault and so forth are to be followed accordingly. (MDh 8.270) 270.
Now, since the killing of a woman is listed among the minor offenses (*upapātaka*), and thus the penance prescribed for those would apply, he states an exception in certain cases:

"For the killing of women who are ill-behaved Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, one should give, respectively, a leather water-bag, a bow, a goat, or a sheep for the sake of purification. (3.271)
