Having killed a woman of ill-conduct who is related to a Brāhmaṇa or others, one should give, in order, a leather bag (*dṛti*) and so forth. A *dṛti* is a water-skin used for drawing up water; a *basta* is a young goat. The rest is clear. Furthermore, the killing of a woman of ill-conduct is ordained specifically for the king. As Manu says in the section on punishments (*saṃgrahaṇa*):

"But a woman of the family who, arrogant because of her kin or her virtues, should transgress against her husband—the king shall have her devoured by dogs in a public place frequented by many" (MDh 8.371).

In Gautama’s section on penance (*prāyaścitta*), it is stated: “The king should have a woman who has had intercourse with a man of lower caste devoured by dogs in public; he should have the man executed” (GDh 23.14–15). Therefore, this penance belongs to the king alone and not to anyone else. [Objection: But surely penance is inappropriate for a king because he is engaged in the performance of his prescribed duties. [Reply: This is correct, just as in the case of witnesses giving false testimony:
“They should offer oblations of cooked rice (*caru*) to Sarasvatī, whose deity is Speech” (MDh 8.105).

In this regard, from the very prescription of this expiation, it is known that the killing of a woman is absolutely forbidden. Thus also says the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "Indeed, they do not kill a woman. For this very reason, in the *Svāyaṃbhuvamanu*:

"One should not drink [from the same lineage] with those who kill children, those who are ungrateful, those who have killed one seeking refuge, and those who have killed women—even if these are purified according to the law" (MDh 11.191).

And for this reason, there is an absolute absence of expiation in the case of a woman's killing committed intentionally. However, if it occurs unintentionally—whether by some chance or through fate—then expiations are to be applied with due regard to her status as a woman, the purpose of the ritual (*kratvartha*), and the attendant circumstances (*anubandha*) pertaining to the killer. Some, however, maintain that in the case of a husband killing a wife whose conduct was unstable, there is the gift of a cow (*dhenu*) and so forth; others, on the other hand, hold this to be universal. That point, moreover, requires further deliberation. (271)

Having thus described the giving of a cow and so forth for killing a woman who is unchaste, he now speaks regarding one who is chaste: "Having killed a woman who is not corrupt, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra;
likewise for a thousand vertebrate animals, and for a cartload of those without bones. (3.272)

Having somehow unintentionally killed a woman who is neither corrupt nor unchaste, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra. And the instruction to perform this penance is to be explained as being intended to exclude the rule that "one should give ten cows" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.270). This [penance] applies specifically to the case of a woman of low birth:
"But having killed a woman of inferior caste who is known [to be such], and who is not corrupt, even if she is the mother of a superior man, one should perform this [six-month penance]."

This is because of the statement of Bṛhaspati. And by the word "this" (*etac-chabdena*) in that context, the one-year vow for killing a Śūdra mentioned in the preceding verse is referred to. Regarding the other [castes], however, there is the rule of Vasiṣṭha: "Having killed a non-Ātreyī Kṣatriya woman in the case of injuring a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya woman in the case of injuring a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra woman in the case of injuring a Śūdra, [one shall observe the penance] for one year" (VaDh 20.37–40). The rule of Gautama as well is to be understood as referring to the killing of a Śūdra woman who is specifically a non-Ātreyī and is possessed of extreme virtues: "And likewise in the case of a non-Ātreyī" (GDh 22.17), in accordance with the rule of Vasiṣṭha. As for the Mānava rule, "and having committed the murder of a woman or a friend" (MDh 11.88), that is [to be understood] from the statement of Aṅgiras.
Having killed the blameless wife of a foremost twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires, one should perform the penance for killing a Brahmin; the same applies to the killer of an Ātreyī woman.

This refers specifically to that [case]. However, what was stated by Śātātapa is an optional alternative to the rule of Yājñavalkya. The statement of Śaṅkha, "The killer of a woman shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for six months," has the same scope as that of Gautama. The rule, "In the case of killing women, one should prescribe the vow for killing a Śūdra," is to be applied with regard to the excellence of the woman's qualities. But when she has attempted [the act] and the adultery is not completed, the penances for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) are to be applied according to the specific circumstances. Other Smṛti texts are also to be explained by this same method; for example, Sumantu has prescribed three *kṛcchras* for killing a woman, and likewise in the *Aṅgirasasmṛti*:

"For the wives of those who have not maintained the sacred fires, as well as for the women of the Vaiśya and Kṣatriya castes, and likewise for Śūdras, one should always perform the vow of the cow-slayer. Thus it is stated in the Saṃvarta [Smṛti].

"Whoever causes the death of a woman shall perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance. In this manner, other [penances] as well should be applied by considering the variations of mental, verbal, and physical transgressions. Thus, according to the first half of the verse: "Having killed a woman who is not corrupt, one shall perform the vow for killing a Śūdra."
Having said this with the second half [of the verse]:
"A thousand of those with bones, and likewise a cartload of those without bones."

Thus, this very penance for killing a Śūdra has been declared. For those bony creatures for whom no specific penance has been stated, having killed a thousand of them, one must perform the six-month penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra. As for boneless creatures such as ants and the like, the quantity shall be as much as can be carried by two middle-sized oxen on a cart. This is because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "For boneless creatures, [the penance is] for the load of oxen" (GDh 22.21), where by "load of oxen" (*anaḍudbhāra*) is understood specifically the load carried by oxen, according to the statement of Manu: "And when the load of boneless creatures is full" (MDh 11.140). And this should be understood to apply to those harmless creatures that die without any specific cause being assigned.
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure finds no happiness anywhere, whether he is alive or even dead. (MDh 5.45)

This is because of the statement of Manu. As for those creatures whose nature is inherently harmful, such as lice, mosquitoes, leeches, and the like—if their death should occur while they are being removed according to one's capacity, there is no fault whatsoever. However, if the act is intentional (*kāmatas*), there is indeed a fault even regarding lice and similar creatures. Likewise, in the case of those creatures that possess bones, for which specific penances have been prescribed, and those who constantly cause harassment such as snakes and rats—their killing for the purpose of removing them by means such as trapping them with cats and so forth—is entirely without fault. Furthermore, there is no fault when they are killed through sweeping, smearing, or the processing of grain, or when they enter into firewood and the like, or into water-jars and such vessels; for in these cases, the activity is undertaken for the sake of accomplishing a task or as a necessary part of maintaining the body. But for those whose activity is based solely on the desire for enjoyment, there is indeed a fault even in those instances. This very point was demonstrated by the Self-Existent One (*Svayambhū*) in the verse: "The householder has five slaughter-houses" (MDh 3.68). Here, the mention of "a thousand" and the mention of "many" are intended to indicate a large quantity and are not restrictive rules, because no other penance is taught for fewer or more than that number, and because there is no reason to assume a collective enumeration of the creatures being killed. Such is the general direction. || 272 ||
Having thus spoken in general terms, he now states the specific rules for certain cases:
"Having killed a cat, an iguana, a mongoose, a frog, a dog, or a bird, one should drink milk for three days or perform a quarter-kṛcchra penance. (3.273)

In the *Svāyaṃbhuvamanu*, however, there is a specific instruction regarding the crow, the owl, and the blue jay (*kākolūkacāṣāṇām*) alone (MDh 11.131). That too must be explained as being intended to indicate birds in general by way of referring to those used for sacrificial purposes; or else, it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). Thus, it has been explained that [the penance] applies only to killing for the sake of ritual performance. But here, it should be explained that even when the act is not for the sake of a sacrifice (*akratvartha*), one must observe a three-night fast on milk or perform a quarter-*kṛcchra* penance. And in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra] as well: "Having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay, or a frog, as well as a dog, an iguana, an owl, and a crow, one should perform the vow prescribed for the killing of a Śūdra" (MDh 11.131).
Having said this, it was immediately stated:
"One should drink milk for three nights, or travel a distance of one *yojana*, or bathe in a flowing river, or mutter the hymn addressed to the waters (*ab-daivata-sūkta*). (MDh 11.132)

Nor is it appropriate for these [penances] to be treated as optional alternatives to the vow for killing a Śūdra; therefore, the determination of the scope [of the penances] is exactly as stated. Furthermore, in this context, bathing applies to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas when traveling on a journey, whereas the recitation of mantras (*japa*) applies only to Brāhmaṇas, according to the statement: "A Brāhmaṇa may attain perfection through recitation alone" (MDh 2.87). However, the *pādakṛcchra* consisting of drinking milk applies to the Śūdra. Thus Vyāsa says: "When no specific vow has been prescribed, one should employ a Śūdra in austerity (*tapas*), a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya in purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), and a Brāhmaṇa in the act of recitation."
Likewise:

"Even in the killing of living beings for the sake of sacrifice, or in the slaughter of small creatures, they declare the performance of such acts to be terrible; for from sacrifice comes the stability of the world."
In this manner, other Smṛti texts are also to be explained. As Aṅgiras says:
"In the case of an elephant, a tiger, a horse, a rhinoceros, a black antelope, a wolf, a lion, a dog, a boar, and even among birds such as the peacock..."
"The Lord Aṅgiras has declared that those who kill a blue jay, a peacock, a swift bird, a *ṭiṭṭibha*, or a wagtail are to be treated like a Śūdra.
Some, however, read it as "as with a cow, so [with these]. Even a jackal is called a peacock.

The peacock is designated as *mayūra* and the jackal as *gomāyu*, according to the statement in the *Nāmaratnamālā*: "It is called *mayūra* [and] *sṛgāla*. By this it is said, "among birds, even the peacock"; the word "even" (*api*) implies that the jackal is also included. The hawk is *śīghra*. The rest is clear. However, those [animals] which are much smaller than these should be understood as referring to the unintentional killing of creatures not intended for sacrifice, as stated by Pārāśara:
"A swan, a crane, a curlew, a ruddy goose, and a cock..."
Having killed a ram or a peacock, one is purified by eating only at night.
Likewise: "A blue jay, a vulture, a pigeon, a śārikā bird, or a partridge—
one is purified from these by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma) during both twilights while remaining within the water" (PSm 6.4).
Likewise:
"For killing a vulture, a hawk, a jackal, a pigeon, or an owl, one should remain eating uncooked food for a day; in the case of a lizard, one should subsist on air. (PSm 6.5)

"Having killed a mongoose, a frog, a snake, a python, or a water-snake, one should feed a Brahmin *kṛsara* (rice and peas), and an iron staff is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)" (PSm 6.9). Likewise, various other [penances] cited in other *smṛtis* should also be applied according to this same method. For example, in the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti*: "Having killed a dog, a cat, a mongoose, a rat, or a small mouse, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights and give some gift" (VaDh 21.24). This is to be applied specifically to intentional killing for the sake of a sacrifice, or otherwise to cases involving a more serious consequence. || 273 ||
Thus far, the expiation for killing cats and other such animals has been stated. Now, he speaks regarding the killing of others that are used for sacrificial purposes:
"For an elephant, five dark-colored bulls; for a parrot, a two-year-old calf; for a donkey, a goat, or a sheep, a bull should be given; and for a crane, a three-year-old [bull]. (3.274)

Because there is no difference in meaning with the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra], and because in that context the injury intended for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha-hiṃsā*) is primarily the subject, the phrase "having struck down a Vaiśya established in his conduct" (MDh 11.129)—where the term "established in conduct" (*vṛttastha*) signifies one established in sacrifice—this too must be explained as referring specifically to that [sacrificial] context. The rest is clear. || 274 ||
Having killed a hawk, a monkey, a carnivorous beast, or a water-fowl, and having killed a vulture, one should give a cow; among non-carnivorous animals, a calf.

"Kravya" means flesh. Those who eat that are "kravyādas" (carnivores). Some of them, such as herons and others, live in water; some, such as vultures and others, live on land. "Śikhaṇḍin" refers to the peacock. The rest is clear. || 275 ||
For killing snakes, an iron rod [is the fine]; for a eunuch, a māṣaka of tin; for a boar, a jar of ghee; for a camel, a guñjā seed; and for a horse, a piece of fine cloth. (3.276)

The plural number in "among serpents" (*urageṣu*) is intended to include the *ḍuṇḍubha* and other such creatures. A *paṇḍaka* is a eunuch; a *kola* is a boar; a *guñjā* is a *kṛṣṇala* (a small weight of gold); a *haya* is a horse; and *aṃśuka* is a garment. In every case within this section on penance (*prāyaścitta*), because of the specific scriptural statement, there is no distinction based on the act of appropriation itself—this has already been explained under the topic of cow-slaughter (*govadha*). Some, however, maintain that because of the context of serpents, the term *paṇḍaka* refers to a *gonasa* (a kind of snake); for they also record in that regard: "a load of straw" (MDh 11.133). || 276 ||
But one who is unable to give a drona of sesame seeds for each of the tittiri birds, elephants, and so forth, shall perform a kṛcchra penance for the purification of each individual. (3.277)

In the case of all types of partridges, such as the *kapiñjala*, *kṛkara*, *lāvaka*, and so forth, one *droṇa* of sesame must be given for the killing of each individual bird. Starting from the rule "for a [killing of] an elephant, five dark bulls," and continuing down to the killing of a partridge, if one is unable to perform the prescribed gift for each, one should perform a *prājāpatya* penance for each instance. Some, however, believe that based on this very indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), giving is the primary alternative in every section concerning injury. That, however, is incorrect, because a *kṛcchra* penance is seen to be prescribed without distinction for the sake of three *māṣas* of gold and for the sake of five bulls. Nor can that refer to the items taken together, because the employment of the distributive repetition "of each" (*ekaikasya*) would otherwise be redundant. Therefore, since the scripture is not to be subject to arbitrary doubt, it is established that the emphasis is on giving in the cases of elephants and the like, whereas in other cases, it is simply austerity (*tapas*). Thus Manu says:

"Even those who have committed the great sins (mahāpātakin), as well as others who have performed forbidden acts, are released from that defilement by means of well-performed austerity alone. (MDh 11.239).
The word "alone" (eva) clarifies that austerity is the primary and foremost remedy for all sins. Likewise:

"Being unable to perform the purification for killing snakes and other such creatures by means of giving gifts, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance individually for the sake of purification. (MDh 11.139).

Here too, when one is unable to give gifts for the sake of snakes and so forth, austerity (*tapas*) must be performed; however, in other cases, when one is unable to perform austerity, giving is prescribed. Furthermore, throughout this section on expiations (*prāyaścitta*), whenever giving is enjoined, it should be understood as not being merely figurative. || 277 ||
However, this is stated everywhere for the purpose of providing atonement for what has not been mentioned:
something should be given in the case of killing a creature with bones; but for a boneless creature, there should be a breath-control exercise (prāṇāyāma).
For cutting down trees, shrubs, creepers, or climbing plants, one hundred Ṛg-verses should be recited.

Since the term "something" (kiṃcit) is used without qualification, it should be understood as referring to the gift of mere alms, which is extremely lowly; however, a higher degree may be assumed depending on the attendant circumstances. The rest is clear. || 278 ||

Thus far, penances have been declared for those cases where sin accrues through being the actual agent or the instigator. Now, he speaks in order to explain how sin arises and what the penance is even when an action is performed by another, provided one has become an accessory such as the object of the act (*karman*) and so forth:
"Having been bitten by a harlot, a donkey, a camel, a dog, or a crow, one becomes pure by performing breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) in water and consuming clarified butter. (3.279)

A *puṃścalī* is a harlot; others say it refers to a woman who has lost her virtue. Monkeys and the like are well known. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is understood that this same penance applies even for being scratched by nails and so forth. And by the restrictive particle "only" (*eva*), it is understood that this applies whether the acts are performed individually or collectively. Regarding the plural number in "breath-suppressions" (*prāṇāyāmān*), it should be explained without distinction as ranging from three up to a hundred, depending on the part of the body [scratched]. Thus says Śaṅkha: "One bitten by a man, a crow, a donkey, a monkey, a horse, or a harlot becomes pure by going to a river flowing to the ocean, performing a hundred breath-suppressions, and consuming clarified butter. In this context, for those cases where no specific penance has been prescribed, the determination of the subject matter depends precisely upon the part of the body involved. Furthermore, in all instances where a penance accompanied by mantras is traditionally taught, it should be understood that for women and Śūdras, that very same penance is to be performed without mantras. (279)
If one kills a living being produced from fruit, flower, food, or sap, one should subsist on ghee;
if one cuts medicinal herbs in vain, one should follow cows for a day and subsist on milk. (3.280)

In fruits such as the jujube (*badara*) and the fig (*udumbara*), there are beings such as worms and gnats; likewise in flowers, in raw or cooked food, in fermented liquids such as *kāñjika*, and in other similar things. One who subsists on ghee alone for a single night is "one who eats ghee" (*ghṛtāśī*). Similarly, for the useless cutting of rice and other medicinal herbs, one observing the milk-vow (*kṣīravrata*) should follow cows for one day. 280.
If semen should be discharged while one is asleep or awake, one should not perform purification;

rather, having consecrated the discharged semen with the two verses beginning "That which is my semen today," one should touch the space between the breasts or the space between the eyebrows with that [semen] using the ring finger. (3.281)

The word *vā* (or) serves to indicate an option between touching and the recitation of the mantra. Having recited the two mantras taught in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*, "Whatever semen of mine today has fallen upon the earth" and "May my virility return to me" (*BĀU* 6.4.5), he should wipe [the semen] away with that [finger]—using the ring finger and the middle finger—between the breasts and the eyebrows; no other purification need be performed. The lack of explicit mention in this verse is due to metrical constraints. As for the instruction regarding purification found in another *Smṛti*, that should be understood as applying to one who is not authorized for or ignorant of the mantras. (281)
Having seen one's own reflection in water, one should mutter "Maya tejaḥ";
likewise, when one has seen something impure, or acted with fickleness, or even spoken a falsehood, one should mutter the Gāyatrī.
The Yajus mantra, "mayi tejaḥ" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.6), as recorded in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, should be recited using the Brāhmaṇa accent alone. The rest is clear. || 282 ||
Since the *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of chastity) is also mentioned among those guilty of minor offenses (*upapātakin*), the author states another penance for him:
"A student (*brahmacārī*) who, having gone to a woman, becomes an *avakīrṇin*, is purified by sacrificing an ass as an animal dedicated to Nirṛti. (3.283)

A student (*brahmacārī*), whether one who is still under training (*upakurvāṇa*) or one who is lifelong (*naiṣṭhika*), is called an *avakīrṇin* upon having sexual intercourse with a woman. He becomes purified by performing a sacrifice to Nirṛti with a donkey, as prescribed in another Smṛti, and by wearing its hide while observing the vow. The statement, "having sacrificed a donkey as the victim," is to be explained as intending the completion of the entire ritual procedure. (283)
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) who,
being free from illness, neglects the begging for alms and the fire-ritual for seven nights,
shall offer two oblations of clarified butter (ājya), reciting the mantra "kāmāvakīrṇa" (RV 10.165.4).

Thereafter, he should perform the worship with the mantra, "Sprinkle me" (*saṃ mā siñca*). Having offered two oblations of clarified butter according to the rules for *pākayajña* with these two [mantras]: "I am besmeared by lust" (*kāmāvakīrṇo 'smi*) and "I am afflicted by lust" (*kāmabhidrugdho 'smi*), he becomes purified after worshipping the Sun with this verse recited in the *Taittirīyaka*: "May the Maruts sprinkle me" (*saṃ mā siñcantu marutaḥ*). However, if within seven nights he does not attend to the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*) or has not laid the sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*), [he must perform the following].
By reciting the Gāyatrī during the latter part of the day, one destroys sin.
Such passages as these are to be understood as stated in other Smṛtis. However, this expiation applies without distinction to students, forest-dwellers, and wandering mendicants alike. (284–5b)
In the case of eating honey or meat, one must perform the Kṛcchra penance as well as the remaining vows.
As Manu has said:
"But he who, while observing a vow, should somehow eat honey or meat,
having performed the ordinary *kṛcchra* penance, shall complete the remainder of his vow" (MDh 11.158).
The remainder of the vow, however, must be completed after the time for the penance has elapsed; the standard *kṛcchra* is indeed the *prājāpatya*. The rest is clear. (285cd)
And if the teacher should send the student on some business of his own, and death should occur while he is away on that journey,
then the teacher must perform three *kṛcchra* penances if the one sent has died.
This rule should also be understood to apply to any other servant who expects wages and the like.

But a disciple who, being capable, commits a transgression of the teacher's command or undertakes some other harmful act, becomes pure by propitiating him after having acted in opposition to the guru. (3.286)
And from another Smṛti text: "having bathed with one's clothes on. Here, the mention of the "guru" (teacher) is to be explained as an elliptical indication for anyone worthy of respect. || 286 ||

In that case, one might fear that just as there is a fault in the death resulting from sending someone on a mission, there would likewise be a fault in the death resulting from giving medicine and so forth; to dispel this doubt, he says:
"But when assistance is being rendered through the giving of medicine, food, and the like, or by means of medical treatments and other such measures, there is no sin if the Brahmin dies."
In the case of the maturation [of karma], such as for bulls and the like, and in the performance of medicinal treatments and fire-rituals. || 3.287 ||

The various medical procedures, such as cutting, burning, and so forth, which are performed in many ways by physicians and doctors upon a patient whose limbs have been bound down, are called "medical treatments" (*bhiṣagyoga*). When assistance is rendered with purity of intention, there is no fault for the physician, the attendant, or those who cause the treatment to be performed, nor for those who provide abundant food that is oily and so forth out of affection, even if the Brāhmaṇa dies. Likewise, there is no fault when a transformation occurs due to medicine or the application of fire to a bull and the like, or if death results from that cause. The mention of the Brāhmaṇa and the cow is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). (Verse 287)

Even regarding death, which arises from the administration of medicine, food, and so forth, if one should falsely accuse another out of malice or pride in one's own learning, imputing guilt by saying, "This man is a killer of a Brahmin" or "He is a killer of a cow," and thus charge another with a great or minor sin, he shall subsist on water for a month, reciting [mantras] with his senses restrained. (3.288)

The inclusion of the word *pari* (in *parigrahaṇa*) is for the purpose of making it known that there is no fault for one who, out of a desire for purity, might report himself as being guilty of a fault before an assembly. Furthermore, even though the recitation (*japa*) is not specified, it refers specifically to the *Śuddhavatī* verses. As Vasiṣṭha says: "Having falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa of a sin causing loss of caste (*pātaka*) or a sin not causing loss of caste (*upapātaka*), one should subsist on water for a month and repeat the *Śuddhavatī* verses" (VaDh 23.39). Although no distinction is stated here, because of the difference in the cause (*nimitta*), the rule as previously stated applies to an accusation of a major sin causing loss of caste. However, in the case of a minor sin causing loss of caste (*upapātaka*), it should be explained that one should remain with controlled senses while reciting. The rest is clear. || 288 ||

It has been stated regarding the accuser; now, as for him who is accused: "An accused person who is falsely charged shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance dedicated to Agni, or he may offer a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) to Vāyu, or even an animal sacrifice to Vāyu. (3.289)

The fact that the *puroḍāśa* and animal sacrifices pertain specifically to one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) is to be explained by the correspondence with their respective occasions. However, for others, it is a *kṛcchra* penance. And this [penance] is an occasional rite (*naimittika*) for one who has been falsely accused, just as in the case of burning a house and so forth; it is not, however, for the purpose of expiating a fault, because there is no evidence for such a fault. As for the postulation of an inference of a fault from a previous birth, that is no different even in the case of the *agnihotra* and other rites, since they too involve the assumption of a body. As for the rule of Vasiṣṭha: "By this, one who is falsely accused is explained" (VaDh 23.37), that should be explained as referring to a case where someone, having unjustly seized another's property, gives up his own life on account of that person; for in that case, there is no mention of the qualifying term "falsely accused. But this present case, because it is specified as "one falsely accused [shall perform] a *kṛcchra*," the settled rule is exactly as stated above. || 289 ||
One who approaches his brother's wife without being authorized should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
having approached a woman in her courses, he becomes pure by consuming clarified butter at the end of three nights. (3.290)

One who is other than the appointed [husband] is "unappointed. And there is no one else of that description. Therefore, at any time other than the period of the *ṛtu*—which is characterized by the time of the menstrual cycle—he alone is to be understood as unappointed. Furthermore, even for a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya woman may indeed be his brother's wife. However, in the case of another [wife], namely the wife of a uterine brother, the penance for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*) applies. Regarding a woman in her courses (*udakyā*), having approached her on the fourth day at the end of three nights, he must consume clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*). Others, however, explain it thus: "In the case of approaching a woman in her courses, one who has fasted for three nights becomes purified by consuming clarified butter at the end of those three nights. But that is incorrect, because Manu has prescribed the *sāntapana* penance for approaching a menstruating woman (MDh 11.173), and here too, approaching her—characterized specifically by tasting her mouth while she is in her courses—is taught to be equal to drinking liquor. Therefore, the explanation exactly as stated above is superior. || 290 ||

Now he states the penance for accepting gifts from a Śūdra or from another evildoer: "Dwelling in a cow-pen as a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), subsisting on milk for one month and intent upon the recitation of the Gāyatrī, one is released from the sin of accepting what should not be accepted. (3.291)

"Acceptance of what is improper" (*asatpratigraha*) refers to the acceptance of gifts from those who are unworthy, such as *śūdras* and the like, or from those whose gifts should not be accepted, such as those accused of crimes (*abhiśasta*). "Devotion to the recitation of the *gāyatrī*" means reciting it three thousand times every day. The rest is clear. Thus, the *Mānava-dharmaśāstra* states:

"But having recited the *sāvitrī* three thousand times with a concentrated mind, and drinking only milk for a month in a cow-pen, one is released from the sin of accepting improper gifts. (MDh 11.194)
And daily, there shall be three thousand recitations and the observance of a milk-vow. || 291 ||

Now he states the penance for one who performs sacrifices for Vratyas and for one who practices malevolent magic: "One who performs sacrifices for Vratyas, as well as one practicing malevolent magic, shall perform three Kṛcchra penances; likewise, one who has forgotten the Veda shall subsist on barley for a year after abandoning one who has sought refuge. (3.292)

The word "is purified" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. By the force of the word "api" (also), this also applies to one who officiates as a priest for a malevolent rite (*abhicāra*). "Eating barley-food" means subsisting on barley. The rest is clear. || 292 ||

One who has traveled in a vehicle drawn by donkeys or camels, or one who has bathed naked, or slept during the day, or approached a woman during the day, should perform breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) after bathing.

A "vehicle drawn by donkeys" (*kharayāna*) is a vehicle yoked with donkeys; likewise, a "vehicle drawn by camels" (*uṣṭrayāna*) is one yoked with camels. There are three breath-restraints. The determination of their repetition depends on the gravity of the offense, its recurrence, and so forth. The rest is clear. (3.293)
Having addressed the guru with "thou," having uttered "hum" [in defiance], and having defeated a Brahmin in debate; ||| 3.294 ||

Having struck or bound one quickly, or having addressed a venerable person such as a teacher, father, or the like with disrespectful words such as "you," or having reviled a Brāhmaṇa who is not his dependent with a "hum" or similar sound, or having defeated him in a worldly dispute, or having struck or bound him out of excessive anger merely to cause humiliation by pulling at his clothes and so forth—one should immediately appease him and eat only at night, or fast for a day. However, depending on the circumstances such as the consequences of the act, there may be a practice of fasting. || 294 ||

But if, out of anger and with the very intent to kill, one should raise a staff or the like against a Brāhmaṇa, then: "For raising a staff against a Brāhmaṇa, the penance is a Kṛcchra; for striking him down, an Atikṛcchra" (3.295).

If blood is emitted, the penance is Kṛcchrātikṛcchra; if the blood is internal, it is Kṛcchra. This refers to what will be stated later: "Kṛcchrātikṛcchra consists of subsisting on milk for twenty-one days" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.323). Alternatively, Kṛcchrātikṛcchra is an Atikṛcchra accompanied by a Kṛcchra. The rest is clear. || 295 ||
In every section concerning expiation, it is indeed with reference to the qualified person [that the rule applies]:
"Having carefully considered the place, the time, the age, the capacity, and the sin—expiation should be prescribed where no specific atonement has been stated. (3.296)

The intention is that the determination of the scope of penances—whether they be heavy or light—is made entirely in consideration of the capacity and other factors of the person concerned, and not by any other means. Furthermore, where the presence of a fault is known through deprecatory explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) or by its contrariety to worldly norms, yet no specific penance has been prescribed, then a penance such as *japa* (recitation) and so forth, taught in other Smṛtis, is to be determined in accordance with the capacity of the person concerned. The rest is clear. || 296 ||

Thus has been explained the method for understanding the expiations for both those sins for which an expiation has been stated and those for which one has not been stated. However, if someone, out of atheism (*nāstikya*), should not perform the expiation, he must be censured and repeatedly excluded. For such a wicked person who has fallen due to excessive atheism, the severance of water-rites (*udakaccheda*) should be performed in this manner:
"His own kinsmen should pour out a jar full of water [in his name];
they should exclude him from all rites. (MDh 3.297)

Having brought a jar filled with water from the house of a female slave belonging to that very family, and having gone outside the village toward the southern direction, the sapindas and samānodakas, in the presence of all kinsmen, elders, disciples, and officiating priests, should overturn it with their feet and, without looking back, return home; they shall then spend one night [in mourning]. Furthermore, in all matters—whether pertaining to visible or invisible consequences—they should exclude him [from their community]. Thus Manu says: "The sapindas and kinsmen should perform the ritual pouring of water for the outcast outside [the village], on an inauspicious day in the evening, in the presence of disciples, officiating priests, and elders. (MDh 11.182)
And so forth. || 297 ||

Or, if he has been cast out but later performs penance out of remorse, then when he has returned after having fulfilled his vow, they should pour out a new jar [of water] for him; they should not despise him, nor should they drink with him in any way. (3.298)
The meaning of this verse is clear. And so Manu says:
"When he has returned having completed his vow, they should bathe and cast a new jar full of water into a sacred body of water along with him. (MDh 11.186)
And so forth. || 298 ||
This very same procedure that has been declared for those who have fallen from their caste—beginning with the overturning of the water-pot—is proclaimed for women who have likewise fallen;
they should be given a dwelling near the house, as well as food, clothing, and protection. (3.299)

For women who have fallen [from their status] and do not perform penance, this very procedure for the removal of the water-pot (*ghaṭāpavarjana*) has been proclaimed and ordained in detail by Manu and others. However, there is this distinction: when they engage in the performance of penance, then a dwelling (*āvasatha*) should be provided for them near their own home, food and sustenance should be given in accordance with the requirements of the penance, and clothing along with protection should be provided. And so says the *Svāyambhuva*:
"This same rule should be applied even to women who have fallen."
"However, clothing and food should be given to them, and they should dwell near the house. (MDh 11.188).
This repetition of what was previously stated is for the purpose of indicating that in the case of those sins causing loss of caste through specific acts, there is only abandonment. 299.
Approaching a low-caste man, causing an abortion, and harming one's husband—these also certainly constitute acts that cause women to fall. (3.300)

The word "api" (also/even) should be construed as "even for women. One should not act with a soft heart by wondering, "How can these women be abandoned? For the intended meaning is that these [faults] are certainly and definitively grounds for abandonment even for women, being causes for their specific downfall. || 300 ||

Just as there is an absolute abandonment of women who approach those of low status and so forth, so too one should not associate with these: those who harm those who have come for refuge, children, or women—even if they are virtuous and have completed their vows—along with the ungrateful. (3.301)

And this statement is not intended as a condemnation, because the purpose of the instruction is that those who kill those who have sought refuge and so forth are indeed unfit for social intercourse even after they have performed their penance; however, from the instruction regarding penance, it should be understood that they are indeed free from fault in a future birth. || 301 ||

Not only those who kill one who has sought refuge and the like are excluded from social intercourse, but others as well. To demonstrate that even those for whom the "breaking of the jar" (*ghaṭāpavarjana*) has been performed become fit for social intercourse once they have completed their penance—even when water is poured into a new jar, it is only when it has been honored by cows that it may be used—[the author] says:

"When the jar has been discarded, he who stands in the midst of his kinsmen should first offer fodder to the cows. [Only then] may there be joint activity with one who has been honored by the cows. (3.302)
The word "kāryā" (should be done) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Gosatkāra" means the feeding of grass to cows. The rest is clear. || 302 ||
Having thus set forth the penances for those whose sins are publicly known, he now speaks in order to introduce the secret penances:
"One whose fault is well-known should perform the vow approved by an assembly;
but one whose fault is not well-known should practice a secret vow. (3.303)
And so Manu says:
"By these vows, the twice-born whose sins have been made manifest are purified;
but those whose sins are unmanifested are purified by mantras and purificatory fire-oblations. (MDh 11.226)

Even members of the twice-born classes who have manifested their sin must be purified after having approached the assembly for the purpose of penance. However, the intention is that those twice-born whose sins have not been manifested, and who know the true meaning of the Śruti and Smṛti, should purify themselves by their own accord—without even reporting to the assembly—through the recitation of mantras such as the Aghamarṣaṇa and others to be described, as well as through oblations (homa) such as the Śākala, which are prescribed for the sake of purification. Regarding those who are ignorant and of non-twice-born status, even if their sins have not been manifested, the subsequent verse from the *Mānava* [Smṛti] begins as follows:

"By confession, by remorse, by austerity, and by Vedic study, as well as by giving gifts in times of distress, the doer of evil is released from that evil. (MDh 11.227) A secret vow must be performed even without being known by those nearby, under the pretext of a religious duty (*dharma*) or similar means. As for another Smṛti text:
If one, out of delusion, should perform an expiation under the pretext of dharma, there shall be no purification for him by that act; rather, he becomes even more burdened with sin.

Thus, this should be understood as referring to cases where the sin has been disclosed. Nor should the following objection be raised here: "Why is the penance small for those whose transgressions have not been disclosed? For the scripture is not to be subjected to such critical inquiry (*amīmāṃsyatva*), and because, by virtue of his learning, he lacks any connection with that sin. Accordingly, the author will indeed state later: "One who is patient but devoted to a semblance of the Veda" (YDh 3.313), and so forth. Furthermore, since the undertaking [of penance] has the purification of the self as its primary goal, a smallness of penance is entirely appropriate. The manner of secrecy is established from common worldly usage: even if a learned man commits a sin openly in the presence of the unlearned, he himself knows it, while the others do not know that "this man has committed a sin"; thus, even though it was done openly, it remains secret. In the same way, secrecy should be applied based on the lack of public knowledge due to factors such as place and time. (303)
Having thus stated the scope of secret penances, he now teaches them:
"A killer of a Brahmin, having fasted for three nights and recited the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn while submerged in water, becomes purified after giving a milch cow. (3.304)

The construction [of the verse] is as follows: "Having fasted for three nights, submerged within the water, having muttered the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn, and having given a milch cow to a Brahmin, one becomes purified. Others, however, describe two distinct penances: "One who has fasted for three nights, having muttered the *Aghamarṣaṇa* while submerged in water, shall be purified; and having given a milch cow, he shall be purified. This being the case, the former [penance] would apply to all four stages of life (*āśrama*), whereas the latter would apply only to those entitled to giving gifts; thus, the great scope of the scripture would be further enhanced. And so, the Self-existent One (Brahmā) has stated that for one who has fasted for three nights, the *Aghamarṣaṇa* is to be muttered even without the gift [of a cow].
"One who is self-controlled should fast for three days, bathing in water three times a day;
by reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, he is released from all sins. (MDh 11.259).
Therefore, even the conceptualization of the Veda is entirely appropriate. 304.

Regarding the killing of a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires, however, he states another penance as an alternative to the previous one: "Or, subsisting on air for a day while sleeping in water, he should offer forty oblations of clarified butter with the mantra 'To the body-hairs, svāhā'. (3.305)

"Subsisting on air during the day" is intended to prohibit the drinking of water; other [passages] should likewise be explained in this manner. "Having slept in water" means that he should remain standing in water throughout the night. Then, according to the procedure for *pākayajña* sacrifices, he should offer forty oblations of clarified butter into the *aupāsana* fire with the *śukriya* formulas beginning with "Svāhā to the body hairs" (VS 39.10). || 305 ||
But for one who has drunk liquor or stolen gold,
having fasted for three nights and offered clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras, he becomes pure.
However, a drinker of liquor or a thief of gold becomes pure by standing in water and reciting the Rudra-hymns.

One who has drunk *surā* shall become pure by fasting for three nights and, as before, offering clarified butter (*ghṛta*) while reciting the *Kūṣmāṇḍī* verses beginning with "yad devā devaheḍanam" (TB 2.4.4.8), which are recorded in the Taittirīya [Saṃhitā]. However, one who has stolen gold shall likewise fast for three nights; standing in water reaching up to his navel and muttering the Rudra-hymn (VS 16.1), he shall be pure—thus the text is to be construed. And so says Bhāradvāja: "Standing in water reaching his navel, meditating on Rudra with a concentrated mind, one who has stolen gold becomes purified after fasting for three nights and having muttered [the mantra]. (306)

Having fasted for three nights as before, one who has violated the Guru’s bed is purified by the recitation of the *Sahasraśīrṣā* and other [hymns]. At the conclusion of the rite, a milch cow must be given separately for each of these [offenses]. (3.307)

Having recited this sixteen-verse hymn beginning with “The Puruṣa has a thousand heads” (RV 10.90), one who has violated the teacher’s bed is purified. Furthermore, for those authorized to perform the rites of the *Puruṣasūkta*—beginning with “Hail to the body hairs! (VS 30.10) and ending with the recitation of the *Puruṣasūkta*—a milch cow should be given to a Brāhmaṇa at the conclusion of both the fire-oblation (*homakarma*) and the recitation (*japakarma*), separately for each specific sin. Even for those not authorized to perform the oblations and so forth, a cow must be given after fasting for three nights. In all cases within the section on secret sins (*rahasyaprakaraṇa*), the determination of the scope [of the penance] should not be conceived based on whether the act was intentional or otherwise; rather, the determination is made by personal inclination or by capacity, as is the case with those possessing the sacred fires regarding injunctions for oblations. However, for public expiations, the determination of the scope has already been shown. But in the case of secret sins, for one whose stains have been burnt away by the fire of knowledge, self-satisfaction alone is the cause of purification. And thus it was stated by the Self-existent One (*Svayambhū*) specifically regarding secret sins:
"In whatever action he has performed that causes unease in his mind, he should perform penance for that until it becomes a source of satisfaction. (MDh 11.233).

Thus, it is stated that self-satisfaction alone is the determining factor in assessing the gravity or lightness of an offense. In other matters, however, one should determine what is heavy or light by considering the assembly and the injunctions of the scriptures; self-satisfaction is not the determining factor there. || 307 ||

Thus has it been stated regarding the four great sins (mahāpātaka). Now, concerning association with those [guilty of them], and indeed regarding all classes of minor offenses (upapātaka) for which no specific penance has been prescribed: "One should perform one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) for the removal of all sins. (3.308)

Although the phrase "for the removal of all sins" (*sarvapāpāpanuttaye*) is stated without qualification, it should be interpreted according to the context as meaning "for the removal of that sin which arises from association with those who have committed great crimes (*mahāpātakin*). This same expiation applies not only to all sins born of association, but also to those arising from minor offenses (*upapātaka*). It should further be understood that this very same rule applies even to those cases where no other specific expiation has been prescribed. (308)
A twice-born man who has consumed semen, feces, or urine after having observed the fast should drink purifying Soma-water consecrated with the syllable *oṃ*. (3.309)

Having fasted for a day and night, on the following day, having pressed the Soma with the syllable *Oṃ*, one should then drink that purifying Soma-liquid known as *Oṃkāra* using water from a sacred ford (*tīrtha*). This is how the construction should be understood. The rest is clear. The mention of "twice-born" (*dvija*) is for the sake of the Brāhmaṇa, because for the other two [castes] there is a prohibition against drinking Soma; or else, it is intended to indicate that those who are not twice-born lack the qualification for secret penances (*rahasya-prāyaścitta*). (Verse 309)

However, that which is committed by an agent even without his own conscious intent does not give rise to any fault for those who perform the scriptural obligatory duties prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti; in order to elaborate upon this point, he says:
"Whatever sin is committed through ignorance, whether at night or even by day, all of that perishes by performing the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) at the three periods of the day. (3.310)
The verse has been explained. || 310 ||
The recitation of the Śukriya Āraṇyaka and the Gāyatrī mantra a thousand times is declared to be the remover of all sins, as is the Rudraikādaśinī.

For all secret sins, including the great crimes (mahāpātaka) and others, for which no specific penance has been prescribed, as well as those for which a penance has been enjoined, the recitation of the *Śukriya* or the *Āraṇyaka* performed even once constitutes the expiation. However, for the *Gāyatrī*, it must be recited one thousand times; for the *Rudrādhyāya*, eleven times; and for the *Brāhmaṇa* of the *Āraṇyaka*, the *Śukriya* mantras [are to be recited]. 311.
And in all secret matters, even when an expiation has been performed;
wherever a twice-born man considers himself defiled, in each such case there should be an oblation with sesame seeds or the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra. (3.312)
The word "kārya" (should be done) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The mention of the "dvija" (twice-born) has the meaning already stated. || 312 ||

Whether secret or manifest, those [transgressions] that remain unrecognized do not touch one who is devoted to the study of the Vedas, who is patient, and who is intent on the performance of the five great sacrifices— even those arising from mortal sins. (3.313)
The meaning of this verse is clear. || 313 ||

And he who is thus devoted to the study of the Vedas, whether in secret or in public, should somehow— provided it was not done intentionally— subsist on air during the day while standing, spend the night in water looking at the sun,
and by reciting the Gāyatrī a thousand times, he shall be purified from [all sins] except for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. (3.314)

As for the greater severity of penance prescribed for the learned, that should be understood to apply to cases of intentional and public transgression. The mention of subsisting on air is intended to prohibit the drinking of water; this is to be construed with the phrase "having passed the night standing. The rest is clear. || 314 ||
For those authorized in the *Rahasya* and other [tantras], all expiations are to be recited as follows:
"Celibacy, compassion, patience, meditation, truthfulness, sincerity, non-violence, non-stealing, absence of malice, and self-restraint—these are remembered as the *yamas*. (3.315)
These restraints (yamās) are to be understood as applicable even to those authorized for the public expiations, since there is no contradiction. || 315 ||
As before:
bathing, silence, fasting, sacrifice, study of the Vedas, restraint of the generative organ, service to the teacher, purity, freedom from anger, and generosity are the observances (niyamas). (3.316)

Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the avoidance of sexual intercourse in accordance with the scriptures; its distinction is the restraint of the genitals and the absence of desire for women. Generosity (*pradātṛtā*) is the excellence of the habit of giving. The rest is clear. || 316 ||

Now, in order to explain the nature of those austerities such as the *sāntapana*—which are taught in various places for the purpose of expiating sins and for the attainment of worldly prosperity—he says:
"Having drunk the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)—namely, cow's milk, curd, urine, dung, and ghee—one should fast on the following day while performing the *sāntapana-kṛcchra*. (3.317)

The mention of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) here is for the purpose of indicating that they should be accompanied by water infused with *kuśa* grass, even though this was not explicitly stated [in other texts]. The phrase "cow's milk" (*gokṣīra*) is intended to mean milk that has been recently yielded. Furthermore, this consumption is for the sake of a meal, not for the sake of an unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭa*). The term "hardship" (*kṛcchra*) is used for the purpose of applying the rules pertaining to the *kṛcchra* penance. Thus says Hārīta: "Having consumed at one time cow's milk that is warm from the udder, as well as curd, dung, urine, and clarified butter, all purified by mantras, one should fast on the following day; that is the *sāṃtapana*. (317)
With these very substances—milk and the rest—each separately constituting a *sāntapana* substance, one observes a six-day fast; this seven-day rite is known as the *mahāsāntapana*. (3.318)

For six days, one should eat a single meal at one time, using each of the *sāntapana* substances—beginning with milk and ending with water boiled with *kuśa* grass—separately. It should be understood that "water boiled with *kuśa*" refers to water in which *kuśa* grass has been decocted throughout; the rest is clear. || 318 ||
The *parṇakṛcchra* is declared to consist of [subsisting on] the leaves of the *parṇa*, *udumbara*, lotus, and *bilva* trees, along with *kuśa* water, each practiced individually for one day.

*Parṇa* is the *palāśa* tree; *rājīva* is the lotus. The rest is clear. The meaning is that one should subsist for five nights on water boiled with the leaves of the *palāśa* and other such trees. Although no specific application for the *parṇakṛcchra* is mentioned anywhere, it should nevertheless be understood [as appropriate] in the absence of an explicit instruction, depending on the gravity of the offense. Its status as a means to spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*), however, will indeed be stated later. || 319 ||
One should drink hot milk, hot ghee, and hot water, each for one day respectively, followed by a fast for one night; this is declared to be the *taptakṛcchra* penance. (3.320)

In another Smṛti, however, it is stated: "Milk, ghee, water, or air, [consumed] daily while heated, constitutes a *kṛcchra* penance" (GDh 23.2). Regarding this, commentators describe even the drinking of heated air. That, however, requires further consideration. Here, on the other hand, because of the mention of fasting (*upavāsa*), the inclusion of air is intended for the purpose of understanding that [the penance] consists of fasting; it should be explained that it is not to be connected with the phrase "while heated. || 320 ||
Eating once a day, eating only at night, likewise eating only what is unasked for, and fasting for one day— this is proclaimed as the *pādakṛcchra* penance.

And this term *pādakṛcchra* is employed for one-third of a *prājāpatya*; this same principle should be followed in the case of the *parṇakṛcchra* and other such penances as well. The rest is clear. || 321 ||
In whatever manner it may be performed, this threefold rite is called the Prājāpatya;
this very same rite becomes an Atikṛcchra for one who eats only as much food as fills his hand.

The phrase "in any manner whatsoever" is intended to show that the sequence beginning with eating a single meal (*ekabhakta*) is not intended here. This [principle] should also be understood as applying to the *parṇakṛcchra* and other such penances. Among these very rites constituting the *prājāpatya*, when the performer eats only as much food as fills the palm at the times of eating, this should be understood as being designated an *atikṛcchra*. "Pāṇipūrānna" means that amount of food by which the hand is filled; he who eats that is a "pāṇipūrānnabhojī. And because the context concerns eating, it should be understood as whatever quantity is taken once for the purpose of a meal. Thus Manu says: "He should eat each morsel one by one" (MDh 11.213). || 322 ||
The *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* consists of subsisting on milk for twenty-one days;
the *parāka* is proclaimed to consist of fasting for twelve days. (3.323)

Subsisting on milk for twenty-one nights constitutes the *kṛchrātikṛcchra*. Not eating for twelve nights is the *parāka*. And in these cases, there is no division into quarters and so forth. || 323 ||
Taking one of each— oil-cake, water from boiled rice, buttermilk, water, and barley-meal— day by day, along with a fast, this is called the Saumya Kṛcchra.

*Piṇyāka* is oil-cake. *Ācāma* is the water used for rinsing boiled rice, that is to say, the scum (*maṇḍa*). *Takram* is churned buttermilk. *Ambusaktavaḥ* are barley-meal mixed with water. By consuming each of these one per day, and fasting on the fifth day—this is the penance named *Saumya*. It is called *Saumya* because the *ṛṣi* (seer) here is Soma. In the same way, in the case of the *Prājāpatya* and other penances, it should be understood that the name is derived from the *ṛṣi* who is its source. || 324 ||
Regarding these [substances] beginning with oil-cake:
through the three-night repetition of each one in succession, this is to be known as the "Tulāpuruṣa" penance, which lasts for fifteen days. (3.325)

The designation "tulāpuruṣa" (the man on the scale) signifies that a person joined with sins such as the great transgressions (*mahāpātaka*), when weighed by this austerity, remains as righteousness alone due to his superiority over his sins; the rest is clear. || 325 ||
One performing the Cāndrāyaṇa vow should take rice-balls the size of a peacock’s egg, increasing them according to the lunar days during the bright fortnight;
during the dark fortnight, one should decrease the rice-balls by one each day.

Regarding the phrase "by the increase of lunar days" (*tithivṛddhyā*): starting from the first day (*pratipat*) at the beginning of the bright fortnight, one should practice—that is, eat—increasing the number of mouthfuls (*grāsa*) until the full moon. Then, having eaten fifteen mouthfuls even on the first day of the dark fortnight, one should decrease the number by one mouthful each day starting from the second day. This is the *yavamadhya* (barley-shaped) *cāndrāyaṇa*. The rest is clear. || 326 ||
Alternatively, one may consume two hundred and forty morsels of food in a single month; this is another form of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (3.327)

"In whatever manner" (*yathākathaṃcit*) is intended to include the methods of the *cāndrāyaṇa* mentioned in other *smṛtis*, such as "having a middle like an ant" (*pipīlikāmadhyatayā*), "with eight morsels," or "in the manner of the child's *cāndrāyaṇa*" (*śiśucāndrāyaṇaprakāreṇa*). The phrase "two hundred and forty" is for the purpose of obtaining fifteen morsels even on the first day of the *yavamadhya* [type of *cāndrāyaṇa*], as stated in the verse: "Now another *cāndrāyaṇa*. By supplying the word "or" (*vā*), the meaning is that this is either that [method] or indeed another instruction regarding the method of *cāndrāyaṇa*. || 327 ||

Of these penances that have been described, such as the Sāntapana and others, one should perform each one individually; likewise, one who bathes at the three periods of the day should perform the Kṛcchra and the Cāndrāyaṇa, recite purifying prayers, and consecrate the morsel of food with the Gāyatrī mantra. (3.328)
The verse has been stated [as follows]. || 328 ||
Purification for unspecified sins is achieved through the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
he who performs this for the sake of dharma attains the same world as the Moon. (3.329)

Those [offenses] which are not specified by the assembly are "unspecified" (*anādiṣṭa*), meaning they are secret. Alternatively, those for which no other expiation has been prescribed are "unspecified. However, he who, being entirely faultless, performs the *cāndrāyaṇa* for the sake of merit (*dharma*), attains the same world as the Moon (*salokatā*). The meaning is that he obtains the enjoyment of heaven within the lunar orb. || 329 ||

But he who performs [an act] without aiming for a reward, for the sake of his own self-cultivation—though practicing with difficulty and desiring only dharma—he enjoys great prosperity and attains the fruit of the sacrifice according to its gravity; of this there is no doubt. (3.330)

In this context, the word *kṛcchra* includes the *cāndrāyaṇa* as well. The meaning is that one who performs *kṛcchra* or *cāndrāyaṇa*, desiring dharma and seeking only the fulfillment of what is enjoined, does not desire the fruit [of the ritual]. "Great prosperity" refers to the enjoyment of Indra via the path of the gods (*devayāna*). Regarding the phrase "as with the light": the meaning is that he obtains that same fruit which results from a minor rite through a minor penance such as *sāntapana*, or from a weightier rite through a weightier penance such as *parāka* or *cāndrāyaṇa*. || 330 ||

Having heard these duties spoken by Yājñavalkya—beginning with "In that land where the deer is black" (YDh 1.2) and ending with "He obtains the fruit of the sacrifice according to his teacher, of this there is no doubt" (YDh 3.330)—those high-souled sages spoke thus to the Lord of Yogins, who possesses immeasurable splendor:
3.331. Having heard these duties spoken by Yājñavalkya, those high-souled sages spoke thus to the Lord of Yogins, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
Those who, free from sloth, shall uphold this treatise on Dharma will attain fame in this world and thereafter go to the third heaven.
Moreover: "One who desires knowledge shall obtain knowledge; one who desires wealth shall obtain riches;
likewise, one who desires long life shall obtain long life, and one who desires prosperity shall obtain great prosperity. (3.333)
Likewise: "For whoever shall cause even these three verses to be heard at a *śrāddha* ceremony, there shall be for the ancestors therein an infinite satisfaction; of this there is no doubt. (3.334)
Moreover: "By the retention of this scripture, a Brāhmaṇa attains the state of being a worthy recipient, a Kṣatriya becomes victorious, and a Vaiśya becomes possessed of grain and wealth. (3.335)
The remainder is "both in terms of the text and in terms of the meaning. || 335 ||
And this is another matter:

that twice-born man who, being self-restrained, causes this to be heard by Brahmins on the sacred festival days (parvan), his reward shall be the fruit of the horse-sacrifice; may you grant your approval of this.
The meaning of this verse is clear. || 336 ||
Having heard this which had been requested by the sages, Yājñavalkya, with a joyful soul, said "So be it," after bowing to the Self-existent One (Brahmā). (3.337)

The proposal made by the sages, saying "Let this and that be so," when the instruction on Dharma was given to them, is for the purpose of making known their satisfaction; and for the sake of establishing the unquestionable authority (*prāmāṇya*) of this treatise on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*). It is also Yājñavalkya’s response, with a pleased mind, saying "Let it be so indeed," so that [the sages might think]: "This treatise on Dharma spoken by me has been correctly grasped by these [sages]. It is for the purpose of establishing the fruitfulness of the instruction, namely: "From this treatise on Dharma, the supreme good (*naiḥśreyasa*) shall come to those belonging to the castes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*). It is also for the purpose of establishing the authoritative status of the word of Brāhmaṇas as Dharma, such that: "And whatever the Brāhmaṇas, established according to the law of the assembly (*pariṣad*), should say—'Let it be thus'—that shall be exactly so. Furthermore, it is for the purpose of maintaining the tradition of right conduct (*sadācāra*), namely: "In the presence of a teacher, disciples must not independently determine the Dharma without the teacher's consent. Regarding the phrase "having paid homage to the Self-existent One" (*namaskṛtvā svayaṃbhuve*): the meaning is "having paid homage to Manu. And this is for the purpose of maintaining the tradition of right conduct. For the intention is that regarding a matter derived from sacred tradition (*āgamika*), nothing should be said independently without first honoring the teacher. Moreover, the fact that this entire subject matter is based on the *Smṛti* of Manu is also clarified by that very homage. Consequently, just as in the case of contradiction with the Veda, other *Smṛtis* lack authority when they contradict Manu. The determination of doubtful points even in the text of Manu is to be made in accordance with other *Smṛtis*, because the very same meaning found in a *Smṛti* of Manu is also present in other *Smṛtis*. Therefore, it is well said: "Having paid homage to the Self-existent One. (Verse 337)

Victorious is that Knower of Brahman, the solitary swan (ekahaṃsa), who, having obtained from Vivasvat the most difficult-to-attain secret white Yajus formulas, made manifest both heaven and liberation.

Whatever has been poorly stated here due to an error of judgment, or whatever has not been stated at all, all that should be correctly discerned by compassionate and unselfish scholars through the power of their own intelligence, with an undisturbed mind.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Bālakrīḍā*, a commentary on the *Dharmaśāstra* composed by Viśvarūpa, written by the supreme lord and master of yogins.
And this treatise is completed.
May there be auspiciousness!
